ANATOMY
1.	
Which muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve?
(A)	Dorsal interossei 
(B)	 Abductor digiti minimi 
(C)	4th lumbrical 
(D)	All of the above 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(D) All of the above
The ulnar nerve is the primary motor nerve of the hand, responsible for fine motor control. It innervates all the intrinsic muscles of the hand except for the three thenar muscles (Abductor Pollicis Brevis, Flexor Pollicis Brevis, Opponens Pollicis) and the lateral two lumbricals (1st and 2nd), which are supplied by the median nerve. Let's analyze the options:
(A)	
The Dorsal interossei (DAB) are responsible for finger abduction and are all supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
(B)	
The Abductor digiti minimi is a key muscle of the hypothenar eminence, which is entirely supplied by the ulnar nerve.
(C)	
The 4th lumbrical (along with the 3rd) is one of the two medial lumbricals, which are supplied by the ulnar nerve, in contrast to the 1st and 2nd lumbricals (supplied by the median nerve).
Since the ulnar nerve supplies all three of these structures, the correct answer is (D) All of the above.
2.	
What is the function of the muscle that attaches 
to the indicated area?
(A)	Protraction 
(B)	 Retraction 
(C)	Depression 
(D)	Elevation 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(C) Depression 
The image indicates the gluteus medius muscle, which arises from the outer surface of the ilium and inserts into the greater trochanter of the femur. The gluteus medius is one of the principal muscles of the hip and plays a crucial role in maintaining pelvic stability during locomotion.
The primary function of the gluteus medius is abduction of the thigh at the hip joint. In addition, it is responsible for stabilizing the pelvis during walking or standing on one leg. When one foot is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius on the opposite side contracts to prevent the pelvis from tilting downward. This action is essential for maintaining balance and proper gait. Weakness of this muscle results in a positive Trendelenburg sign.
The muscle does not primarily produce protraction or retraction, which are movements associated with the scapula. It also does not cause elevation in this context. While it contributes to hip abduction and medial rotation, among the given options, the closest related movement affecting pelvic mechanics is depression, referring to stabilization and prevention of pelvic drop.
Therefore, the correct answer is : (C) Depression
3.	
Which nerve is not related to olfaction? 
(A)	Hypoglossal 	
(B)	 Trigeminal 
(C)	Glossopharyngeal 	(D)	Vagus 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Hypoglossal
Olfaction (the sense of smell) is a complex sensation. While the olfactory nerve (CN I) is the primary nerve for detecting odorants, other nerves contribute to the overall perception.
The trigeminal nerve (CN V) (B) is related because it provides general sensation from the nasal mucosa, detecting chemical irritants or qualities like the "cooling" of menthol or the "burn" of ammonia (chemosensation).
The glossopharyngeal (CN IX) (C) and vagus (CN X) (D) nerves are related because they mediate taste from the posterior tongue and pharynx. The perception of "flavor" is a combined sensory experience that intimately links retronasal olfaction with taste.
In contrast, the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) (A) is a purely motor nerve. It supplies the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue (except palatoglossus), controlling tongue movement. It has no sensory function related to smell, taste, or flavor perception.
4.	
What is the nerve supply to the piriform fossa? 
(A)	Internal laryngeal nerve 
(B)	 Recurrent laryngeal nerve 
(C)	External laryngeal nerve 
(D)	Glossopharyngeal nerve 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Internal laryngeal nerve
The piriform fossa (or recess) is a depression in the laryngopharynx located on either side of the laryngeal inlet. The sensory innervation of the larynx is divided by the vocal cords.
The mucosa above the vocal cords, which includes the piriform fossa, is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve (A). This nerve is a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, which arises from the vagus (CN X). This innervation is critical as it provides the sensory (afferent) limb of the cough reflex for this area.
(B)	
The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the mucosa below the vocal cords.
(C)	
The external laryngeal nerve is a motor nerve that supplies the cricothyroid muscle.
(D)	
The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies sensation to the oropharynx (e.g., tonsils, posterior tongue), which is superior to the piriform fossa.
5.	
A 35-year-old man comes to the emergency 
department complaining that food is stuck in 
his throat. Examination reveals a bone lodged in 
the left piriform recess. Which function is most 
likely to be affected?
(A)	Cough reflex 	
(B)	 Gag reflex 
(C)	Mastication 	
(D)	Salivation 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Cough reflex
This clinical scenario is a direct application of the anatomy from the previous question. The piriform recess is innervated by the internal laryngeal nerve. This nerve provides the sensory afferent limb for the cough reflex (A) for any foreign material at or above the laryngeal inlet. A foreign body, such as a fishbone, lodged in this recess can mechanically or by local inflammation/edema, "anesthetize" the nerve endings. This impairs the protective reflex, which normally detects the foreign body and triggers a cough to expel it. This impairment significantly increases the risk of aspiration. The gag reflex (B) is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) in the oropharynx, a different location. Mastication (C) (CN V) and salivation (D) (CN VII, CN IX) are unrelated to this specific location.
6.	
What is the action of the muscle marked in the 
image? 
(A)	Internal rotation 	 (B)	 Hip abduction 
(C)	Knee extension 	
(D)	Knee flexion 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) Hip abduction
The image displays the posterior view of the hip, with arrows pointing to the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles. These muscles originate from the ilium and insert on the greater trochanter of the femur. Their primary and most powerful action is hip abduction (B), which is the movement of the thigh away from the body's midline. These muscles are the main abductors of the hip. They also play a crucial role in pelvic stability. When standing on one leg, the gluteus medius and minimus on the standing side contract isometrically to prevent the pelvis from dropping on the opposite (swinging) side, a function tested by the Trendelenburg test. While the anterior fibers of these muscles can assist in internal rotation (A), their main function is abduction. Knee extension (C) and knee flexion (D) are actions at the knee joint, controlled by the quadriceps and hamstrings, respectively.

(A) Back of neck
The innervation of the dura mater is divided by the tentorium cerebelli.
1.	
Supratentorial dura (above the tentorium) : Innervated by the trigeminal nerve (CN V). Pain is referred to the face, vertex (C) , and forehead (D).

8.	
Which of the following is not a boundary of the 
hepatocystic triangle?
(A)	Common hepatic duct 
(B)	 Cystic duct 
(C)	Right lobe of liver 
(D)	Cystic artery 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(D) Cystic artery
The hepatocystic triangle, also known as the Triangle of Calot, is a critical anatomical space for surgeons, especially during a cholecystectomy (gallbladder removal). Its boundaries are:
1.	
Medially: The common hepatic duct (A) 
2.	
Laterally: The cystic duct (B) 
3.	
Superiorly: The inferior (visceral) surface of the liver (C) 
The cystic artery (D) is a vital structure, but it is a content of the triangle, not a boundary. The triangle is significant because it typically contains the cystic artery, the cystic lymph node (of Lund), and autonomic nerves. The surgeon must carefully identify all three boundaries of the triangle to safely locate and ligate the cystic duct and cystic artery within it, avoiding damage to the common hepatic duct.
9.	
Which muscles are supplied by the superficial 
peroneal nerve? 
(A)	Peroneus longus & Brevis 
(B)	 Extensor hallucis longus 
(C)	Peroneus tertius 
(D)	Both A & C 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Peroneus longus & Brevis
The common peroneal (fibular) nerve divides into two main branches: the superficial and deep peroneal nerves.
1.	
The superficial peroneal nerve (also called the superficial fibular nerve) supplies the muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg. These muscles are the Peroneus longus and Peroneus brevis (A). Their primary function is eversion of the foot, and they also assist in plantarflexion.
2.	
The deep peroneal nerve (deep fibular nerve) supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg. These muscles are responsible for dorsiflexion of the foot and extension of the toes. They include the tibialis anterior, Extensor hallucis longus (B), extensor digitorum longus, and Peroneus tertius (C).
Therefore, only the peroneus longus and brevis are supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve.
10.	 A teenager comes to the emergency department 
with wrist pain after falling off his skateboard 
and has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. 
Which bone is most likely fractured? 
(A)	Scaphoid 
(B)	 Trapezoid 
(C)	Capitate 
(D)	Trapezium 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Scaphoid
This is a classic clinical presentation. A fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) is the most common mechanism for a scaphoid fracture (A). The anatomical snuffbox is a triangular depression on the dorsal, radial side of the wrist. Its floor is formed by the scaphoid bone, and tenderness upon palpation in this specific area ("snuff-box tenderness") is the hallmark clinical sign of a scaphoid fracture. The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. It is critical to diagnose and treat properly because it has a tenuous, retrograde blood supply, which puts it at high risk for avascular necrosis and non-union (failure to heal) if the fracture is missed. The trapezium (D) also lies in the snuffbox floor but is fractured far less often. The trapezoid (B) and capitate (C) are not associated with snuffbox tenderness.
11.	 What is the diagnosis suggested by the eye 
movement abnormality shown in the image?
(A)	Internuclear ophthalmoplegia 
(B)	 3rd nerve palsy 
(C)	6th nerve palsy 
(D)	Horizontal gaze palsy 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Internuclear ophthalmoplegia
The image depicts a classic Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO) (A), specifically a left INO. The diagram shows that on attempted right gaze:
1.	
The left eye (which should be adducting) fails to move medially past the midline.
2.	
The right eye (which is abducting) moves fully and exhibits nystagmus.
This specific combination—failure of adduction on the affected side with nystagmus in the abducting contralateral eye—is pathognomonic for an INO. It is caused by a lesion in the Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF) on the same side as the adducting deficit (in this case, the left MLF). The MLF is the pathway that coordinates the 6th nerve nucleus (for abduction) with the contralateral 3rd nerve nucleus (for adduction). A 6th nerve palsy (C) would cause a failure of abduction. A 3rd nerve palsy (B) would involve ptosis and a "down and out" eye.
12.	 Primary muscle repair in cleft lip surgery 
involves reconstruction of which muscle?
(A)	Orbicularis oris 
(B)	 Orbicularis oculi 
(C)	Levator palpebrae superioris 
(D)	Masseter 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Orbicularis oris
A cleft lip is a congenital defect resulting from the failure of fusion of the facial prominences during embryonic development. This defect creates a gap in the upper lip. The key muscle that is disrupted is the Orbicularis oris (A). This is the circular muscle that surrounds the mouth and acts as the oral sphincter, responsible for closing and puckering the lips. In a cleft lip, the muscle fibers do not form a continuous ring; instead, they are interrupted and run abnormally, inserting onto the margins of the cleft. A primary goal of surgical cleft lip repair (cheiloplasty) is to dissect these abnormal muscle fibers, re-orient them into their correct horizontal position, and suture them together. This "primary muscle repair" is essential to restore normal lip function (like suckling), symmetry, and cosmetic appearance. The orbicularis oculi (B) , levator palpebrae superioris (C) , and masseter (D) are muscles of the eye and jaw, respectively, and are not involved.

1.	 Seminal vesicles

4.	 Vas deferens

In the given male pelvic anatomy diagram, label D represents the seminal vesicles. These are paired, elongated, sac-like glands located posterior to the urinary bladder and superior to the prostate. They appear as folded or coiled structures and contribute fructose-rich fluid to semen.

15.	 By what mechanism does the marked structure 
exert its effects on nearby cells?
(A)	Nerve mediated 
(B)	 Vein mediated 
(C)	Paracrine 
(D)	Epithelium to mesothelium 
transformation 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(C) Paracrine
The image shows a histology slide of the pancreas. The "marked structure" is the Islet of Langerhans, a pale-staining cluster of endocrine cells, surrounded by the darker-staining exocrine acinar tissue. The Islets contain multiple cell types (e.g., alpha, beta, delta cells) that secrete different hormones (e.g., glucagon, insulin, somatostatin). These cells are in close proximity and regulate each other's function. This form of local, cell-to-cell signaling, where a hormone released from one cell acts on an adjacent cell, is the definition of paracrine signaling (C). For example, insulin secreted by beta cells inhibits glucagon release from neighboring alpha cells, and somatostatin from delta cells inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion. This local paracrine network is essential for fine-tuning the endocrine output of the pancreas.
PHYSIOLOGY
16.	 Which of the following is seen in high altitude? 
(A)	Metabolic acidosis 
(B)	 Metabolic alkalosis 
(C)	Respiratory acidosis 
(D)	Respiratory alkalosis 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(D) Respiratory alkalosis
An high altitude, the atmospheric pressure is lower, leading to a decreased partial pressure of inspired oxygen (PO2). This causes hypoxemia (low oxygen in the blood), which is sensed by the peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies). These chemoreceptors stimulate the respiratory center in the brainstem to increase the rate and depth of breathing (hyperventilation). This is a compensatory mechanism to increase oxygen intake. However, this hyperventilation also causes an excessive "blowing off" of carbon dioxide (CO2). Since CO2 is a volatile acid in the blood (forming carbonic acid), its excessive loss leads to a decrease in arterial PCO2. A primary decrease in PCO2 raises the blood pH, resulting in respiratory alkalosis (D). This is the primary, acute acid-base disturbance seen at high altitude.
17.	 IGF-1 and IGF-2 are structurally most similar to 
which molecule?
(A)	Insulin 
(B)	 Preproinsulin 
(C)	Proinsulin 
(D)	C-peptide 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Insulin
Insulin-like growth factors IGF-1 and IGF-2 are structurally most similar to insulin. They are single-chain polypeptides with significant amino acid sequence homology to proinsulin, but in their active circulating form, they closely resemble insulin in overall three-dimensional structure.
Both IGFs contain A and B domains analogous to insulin’s A and B chains, along with additional C and D domains. Although they are synthesized as larger precursor molecules, their functional structure shows strong similarity to insulin, including conserved disulfide bonds that stabilize the molecule.
Functionally, IGFs also share similarities with insulin. While insulin primarily regulates glucose metabolism, IGF-1 and IGF-2 mainly promote growth, cell proliferation, and differentiation. However, because of their structural resemblance, IGFs can weakly bind to insulin receptors at high concentrations.
They are not most similar to preproinsulin, proinsulin, or C-peptide. Preproinsulin and proinsulin are precursor forms in insulin synthesis, and C-peptide is simply a connecting peptide removed during insulin maturation. Therefore, the best answer is Insulin.
18.	 During which situation does the surface tension 
of the fluid lining the alveoli increase?
(A)	Expiration 
(B)	 Inspiration 
(C)	Standing 
(D)	Supine 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) Inspiration
The fluid lining the alveoli is coated with pulmonary surfactant, a substance that reduces surface tension. This reduction is not static; it changes with the breathing cycle.
During expiration (A), the alveoli decrease in size. This compresses the surfactant molecules on the surface, increasing their concentration and dramatically decreasing surface tension, which prevents the alveoli from collapsing.
During inspiration (B), the alveoli expand, and their surface area increases. This spreads the surfactant molecules farther apart, decreasing their concentration at the air-liquid interface. With this "dilution" of surfactant, its tension-reducing effect is lessened, and the surface tension of the fluid lining increases (or, more accurately, returns towards its higher baseline).
Posture (C, D) affects ventilation-perfusion matching but not the direct physics of alveolar surface tension in this manner.
19.	 Which of the following are features of Bezold 
Jarisch reflex? 
1.	 Hypopnea 
2.	 Tachycardia 
3.	 Bradycardia 
4.	 Hypotension 
(A)	1,2,3 
(B)	 1,3,4 
(C)	1,3 
(D)	All of the above 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) All of the above
The Bezold-Jarisch reflex is a cardio-inhibitory reflex, meaning it slows down and unloads the heart. It is a protective reflex originating from chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors in the ventricular walls, often triggered by noxious stimuli, certain drugs, or situations like an "empty" ventricle in severe hypovolemia. The reflex arc involves vagal afferents and efferents. The classic triad of responses is:
1.	
Hypotension (4), caused by peripheral vasodilation (inhibition of sympathetic tone).
2.	
Bradycardia (3), caused by a surge in parasympathetic (vagal) output to the heart.
3.	
Apnea or Hypopnea (1)	
(a decrease in respiratory rate or depth).
Tachycardia (2) (a fast heart rate) is the opposite of this reflex. Therefore, the correct features are 1, 3, and 4. This corresponds to option (B).
20.	 In a normal awake person resting with eyes 
closed, which EEG waves diminish when the 
eyes are opened?
(A)	Beta waves 
(B)	 Theta waves 
(C)	Alpha waves 
(D)	Delta waves 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(C) Alpha waves
Alpha waves (C) (8-13 Hz) are the dominant EEG rhythm in a normal adult who is awake and at rest with their eyes closed. This state is often called "eyes-closed-relaxed." These waves are most prominent in the occipital (visual) cortex. The most characteristic feature of this alpha rhythm is its immediate attenuation (reduction or blocking) as soon as the person opens their eyes or engages in a mental task. This "alpha block" signifies the brain shifting from a relaxed, idling state to an active, processing state, which is characterized by higher-frequency, lower-amplitude Beta waves (A). Theta waves (B) and Delta waves (D) are associated with drowsiness and deep sleep, respectively.
21.	 Given a latent period of 10 ms, a contraction 
period of 40 ms, and a relaxation period of 40 
ms, how would you calculate the tetanizing 
frequency?
(A)	20 Hz 
(B)	 30 Hz 
(C)	40 Hz 
(D)	25 Hz 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(D) 25 Hz
Tetanizing frequency is the minimum stimulation frequency required to cause individual muscle twitches to fuse into a smooth, sustained contraction (tetanus). This fusion occurs when a new stimulus arrives before the muscle has finished relaxing from the previous one. To achieve complete, fused tetanus, the next stimulus must arrive before the relaxation phase can even begin. This means the time interval (T) between stimuli must be equal to or less than the contraction period.
Given Contraction Period (T) = 40 ms 
To convert milliseconds (ms) to seconds (s): T = 40 / 1000 = 0.04 seconds
Frequency (f) is the inverse of the time period (f = 1 / T).
f = 1 / 0.04 s = 25 Hz
Therefore, a stimulation frequency of 25 Hz (or higher) will send a new impulse every 40 ms, initiating a new contraction just as the previous one peaks, leading to fused tetanus. The latent period and relaxation period are not needed for this specific calculation.
22.	 Which of the following is an example of feed 
forward mechanism? 
(A)	HR increases from supine to standing 
(B)	 Vasoconstriction in response to cooling 
(C)	Increase in cardiac output in response to 
anemia 
(D)	Temperature regulation 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) HR increases from supine to standing
A feed-forward mechanism is an anticipatory control system. It initiates a response before a change (or "error") in the system is actually detected, in anticipation of that change.
(A)	
HR increases from supine to standing: This is the best example. As a person initiates the action of standing, the central nervous system sends signals (central command) that increase heart rate (HR) before the blood pressure has a chance to drop from the effects of gravity. This anticipatory rise helps prevent orthostatic hypotension.
(B)	
Vasoconstriction in response to cooling: This is a classic negative feedback loop. The stimulus (cold) is detected, and the body responds (vasoconstriction) to correct the error (heat loss).
(C)	
Increase in cardiac output in response to anemia: This is a negative feedback compensation. The body detects the error (low oxygen delivery) and responds (increasing cardiac output) to compensate.
(D)	
Temperature regulation: This is a prime example of a system controlled by negative feedback.

23.	 A patient comes to the OPD with fever. Which 
area is most likely affected?
(A)	Insular cortex 
(B)	 Pre-optic nucleus 
(C)	Periventricular hypothalamus 
(D)	Dorsomedial hypothalamus 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) Pre-optic nucleus
Fever is a regulated rise in the body's thermoregulatory set-point, which is controlled by the hypothalamus. The specific "thermostat" of the body is located in the Pre-optic nucleus (also called the pre-optic area) of the anterior hypothalamus (B). During an infection, inflammatory cytokines (pyrogens) stimulate the production of Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) in this region. PGE2 then acts on neurons within the pre-optic nucleus to "raise" the set-point. The rest of the body then perceives the normal temperature as being "too cold" relative to this new, higher set-point. This triggers heat-generating mechanisms (e.g., shivering, peripheral vasoconstriction) that cause the body temperature to rise until it matches the new febrile set-point.
24.	 Which of the following is not a mechanism by 
which ADH acts? 
(A)	Increases water permeability in collecting 
ducts 
(B)	 Increases absorption of urea in medullary 
collecting duct 
(C)	Increases absorption of NaCl in thin 
ascending limb 
(D)	Increases absorption of urea in descending 
limb of loop of Henle 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(C) Increases absorption of NaCl in thin ascending limb
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also called vasopressin, primarily acts on the late distal tubule and collecting duct of the nephron. Its main function is to conserve water and concentrate urine.
ADH increases water permeability in the collecting ducts (Option A) by inserting aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane of principal cells via V2 receptor activation and cAMP signaling. This allows more water to be reabsorbed into the bloodstream.
ADH also increases urea permeability in the inner medullary collecting duct (Option B). This enhances urea recycling into the medullary interstitium, helping maintain the hyperosmotic medullary gradient necessary for water reabsorption.
However, ADH does not increase NaCl absorption in the thin ascending limb (Option C). The thin ascending limb has limited active transport capacity and is relatively impermeable to water; ADH does not significantly act here. Sodium reabsorption in the ascending limb is primarily a function of the thick ascending limb via the NKCC2 cotransporter.
Option (D) is incorrect physiologically, but the best answer among the given choices is (C).
25.	 Tight junctions are mainly found in which 
region of the cell?
(A)	Apical
(B)	 Apicolateral
(C)	Basolateral
(D)	Basal
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Apical
Tight junctions (zonula occludens) are located at the apical region of epithelial cells. They form the most apical part of the junctional complex and encircle the cell like a belt. Because they are positioned at the top of the lateral membrane, just beneath the apical surface, they are commonly described in exams as being present in the apical region.
Their main function is to seal adjacent epithelial cells together, preventing paracellular movement of substances. This helps maintain selective permeability and preserves cell polarity by separating the apical and basolateral membrane domains.
Structurally, tight junctions are composed of proteins such as claudins and occludin, which create a barrier to diffusion between cells. Since they are the uppermost component of the junctional complex, the best exam-oriented answer is Apical.

26.	 Two specimens from two different patients 
are received. Which technique can be used 
to confirm that they come from different 
individuals (in the context of Mycobacterium 
tuberculosis)? 
(A)	RFLP 
(B)	 Mutation analysis 
(C)	Pyrosequencing 
(D)	RAPD 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) RFLP
The question asks for a technique to determine if two Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) isolates are from different individuals, which is the fundamental task of molecular epidemiology—tracking an outbreak. This requires a "fingerprinting" method to compare the strains.
Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (RFLP) (A) is the classic, gold-standard method for M.tb genotyping. It uses restriction enzymes to cut the bacterial DNA, and the resulting fragments are separated by size. The pattern, often based on the IS6110 insertion sequence, creates a unique "fingerprint." If the RFLP patterns from the two patients are different, it confirms they are infected with different strains and are not part of the same immediate transmission chain.
Mutation analysis (B) and Pyrosequencing (C) are techniques used to look for specific, known mutations (e.g., for drug resistance), not to generate a comprehensive genomic fingerprint. RAPD (D) is another, older fingerprinting method, but RFLP is the traditional standard for M.tb.

28.	 A 90-kg obese man is consuming a carbohydrate-
rich diet. Which enzyme or intermediate is likely 
to be increased in his body? 
1.	 Malonyl CoA 
2.	 Acetyl CoA Carboxylase 
3.	 PDH 
4.	 Citrate Lyase 
(A)	1,2,3 	
(B)	 2,3,4 
(C)	1,3,4 	
(D)	1,2,3,4 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(D) 1,2,3,4
This scenario describes a high-energy, high-carbohydrate state, which strongly promotes de novo lipogenesis (fat synthesis). All four listed components are key players in this pathway.
1.	
A carbohydrate-rich diet leads to high glucose, high insulin, and high glycolysis, producing pyruvate. Pyruvate enters the mitochondria and is converted to acetyl-CoA by Pyruvate Dehydrogenase (PDH) (3), which is activated (dephosphorylated) by insulin.
2.	
This acetyl-CoA combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate. When energy needs are met, excess citrate is shuttled from the mitochondria to the cytoplasm.
3.	
In the cytoplasm, Citrate Lyase (4) cleaves citrate back into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. This is the source of cytoplasmic acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis.
4.	
The rate-limiting, committed step of lipogenesis is catalyzed by Acetyl-CoA Carboxylase (ACC) (2), which carboxylates acetyl-CoA to form Malonyl-CoA (1). ACC is allosterically activated by citrate and also activated by insulin-mediated dephosphorylation.
Therefore, in this fed state, the entire pathway is active, and all four enzymes and intermediates will be elevated.
29.	 Which of the following does not inhibit 
cytochrome c oxidase in the electron transport 
chain?
(A)	Carbon monoxide (CO) 
(B)	 Nitric oxide (NO) 
(C)	Cyanide (CN) 
(D)	Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) Nitric oxide (NO)
Cytochrome C oxidase (Complex IV) is the final enzyme in the electron transport chain, transferring electrons to molecular oxygen. It contains heme iron and copper centers that are targets for several classic poisons. Cyanide (CN) (C) and Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S) (D) are potent inhibitors that bind to the ferric (Fe3+) state of the heme a3 iron, preventing electron transfer and halting aerobic respiration. Carbon Monoxide (CO) (A) also inhibits Complex IV, but it binds to the ferrous (Fe2+) state of the heme iron, competing with oxygen for the same binding site. This is the same mechanism by which it binds to hemoglobin.
In contrast, Nitric Oxide (NO) (B) is primarily a physiological regulator of Complex IV, not a classic toxic blocker. While very high, non-physiological concentrations of NO can inhibit the enzyme, its normal role is as a reversible, signaling molecule that modulates respiration rates based on cellular needs. Therefore, in the context of classic ETC "blockers" or poisons, NO is the exception.
30.	 At what pH does glycine exist predominantly in 
its zwitterionic form, as indicated on its titration 
curve?
BK
page  9  	
INICET Examination Paper
(A)	6 
(B)	 4.4 
(C)	2 
(D)	9 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) 6
The titration curve shown is for the amino acid glycine. A zwitterion is the molecular form that has both a positive (NH3
+) and a negative (COO-) charge, resulting in a net charge of zero. This form predominates at a specific pH known as the isoelectric point (pI). The pI is the pH at which the molecule is electrically neutral. On a titration curve for an amino acid with non-ionizable side chains, the pI is found exactly halfway between the two pKa values.
From the graph:
1.	
The first pKa (pK1), for the carboxyl group, is 2.34.
2.	
The second pKa (pK2), for the amino group, is 9.86.
3.	
The isoelectric point (pI) is calculated as the average of these two values:
pI = (pK1 + pK2) / 2 = (2.34 + 9.86) / 2 = 12.20 / 2 = 6.10
The question asks for the pH of the zwitterion, which is the pI. The closest answer to the calculated pI of 6.10 is 6 (A). The other options represent pH values near the pKa values or far from the isoelectric point.
31.	 Which of these tissues is unable to take up 
glucose in states of insulin resistance, absence 
of insulin, or diabetes mellitus?
(A)	Skeletal muscle 
(B)	 Red blood cells 
(C)	Brain 
(D)	Kidney 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Skeletal muscle
Glucose uptake into cells is mediated by glucose transporters (GLUTs). The most important distinction is between insulin-dependent and insulin-independent transporters. Skeletal muscle (A) and adipose tissue are the primary users of the GLUT4 transporter. GLUT4 is an insulin-dependent transporter, meaning it is stored in intracellular vesicles and only translocates to the cell membrane to facilitate glucose uptake in response to insulin signaling. Therefore, in a state of insulin absence (like Type 1 Diabetes) or insulin resistance (like Type 2 Diabetes), glucose uptake into skeletal muscle is severely impaired.
In contrast, the Brain (C) uses GLUT1 (at the blood-brain barrier) and GLUT3 (on neurons), both of which are insulin-independent to ensure a constant, vital supply of glucose. Red blood cells (B) exclusively use insulin-independent GLUT1. The Kidney (D) uses insulin-independent GLUT1 and GLUT2 (as well as SGLT) for glucose reabsorption from the filtrate.

32.	 Least common finding in diabetic kidney is 
(A)	Podocyte loss 
(B)	 Armani Ebstein 
(C)	Mesangial widening 
(D)	GBM thickening 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) Armani Ebstein
Diabetic nephropathy is characterized by several progressive structural changes. GBM (Glomerular Basement Membrane) thickening (D) is one of the earliest and most consistent findings. Mesangial widening (C), due to the accumulation of extracellular matrix, is also a very early and common feature, which eventually progresses to the classic nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions). Podocyte loss (A) and effacement of their foot processes are now understood to be critical and common events that directly contribute to the development of albuminuria.
The Armani-Ebstein lesion (B) refers to the presence of glycogen-filled vacuoles within the epithelial cells of the renal proximal convoluted tubules (pars recta). While this finding is virtually pathognomonic for diabetes mellitus, it is a rare finding in modern practice. It was historically seen in patients with extremely poor glycemic control and massive glycosuria, often in the setting of diabetic ketoacidosis, before effective insulin therapy was widely available. Therefore, among the choices, the Armani-Ebstein lesion is the least common finding in a modern context.
33.	 Alleles of gene pool belong to 
(A)	Individual 
(B)	 Family 
(C)	Population 
(D)	Cell 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(C) Population
The term "gene pool" is a core concept in population genetics. It is defined as the complete set of all genes and their different alleles (genetic variations) that are present within a specific population (C). A population is a group of individuals of the same species that live in the same area and are capable of interbreeding. The gene pool represents the entire genetic diversity available to that population, which serves as the raw material for natural selection and evolution. An individual (A) carries only a small subset of the total gene pool (a maximum of two alleles for any given gene). A family (B) represents a closely related subset of the gene pool, but not its entirety. A single cell (D) contains the genetic information of only one individual. Thus, the concept of a "gene pool" is only meaningful at the level of a population.
34.	 In which type of thyroid carcinoma are multiple 
lytic skull lesions typically seen?
(A)	Papillary carcinoma thyroid 
(B)	 Follicular carcinoma 
(C)	Hurthle cell carcinoma 
(D)	Thyroid lymphoma 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) Follicular carcinoma
The metastatic patterns of thyroid cancers differ significantly. Follicular carcinoma (B) is classically known for its tendency to spread via hematogenous (bloodstream) dissemination, in contrast to papillary carcinoma, which spreads via lymphatics. Common sites for distant metastases from follicular carcinoma are the bone and lungs. Bone metastases are often osteolytic (bone-destroying) and can present as multiple lytic lesions on imaging. The skull, ribs, and vertebrae are common sites. Therefore, multiple lytic lesions in the skull are a classic presentation of metastatic follicular thyroid carcinoma.
Papillary carcinoma (A) is the most common type and primarily spreads to cervical lymph nodes. Hurthle cell carcinoma (C), a variant of follicular carcinoma, also has a high propensity for vascular invasion and distant bone metastases, but follicular carcinoma is the classic answer. Thyroid lymphoma (D) is a hematological malignancy and does not typically present with lytic bone lesions as its primary feature.
35.	 You would test for BRCA1 (and usually BRCA2) 
mutations, with BRCA1 being the primary gene 
associated with a strong family history of both 
breast and ovarian cancers.
(A)	BRCA1/2 
(B)	 P53 
(C)	PTEN 
(D)	CDH1 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) BRCA1/2
A strong family history of both breast and ovarian cancer is the classic hallmark of Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer (HBOC) syndrome. This syndrome is most commonly caused by an inherited germline mutation in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes (A). Mutations in these genes confer a significantly increased lifetime risk for developing breast cancer (often early-onset, triple-negative, or bilateral) and epithelial ovarian cancer, as well as other cancers like pancreatic and prostate cancer (especially BRCA2).
While the other genes are also tumor suppressors, they are associated with different syndromes. P53 (B) mutations cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, which involves a wide array of cancers (sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, adrenocortical carcinoma). PTEN (C) mutations cause Cowden syndrome, linked to breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancers. CDH1 (D) mutations cause hereditary diffuse gastric cancer and lobular breast cancer. For the specific combination of breast and ovarian cancer, BRCA1/2 testing is the most appropriate first step.
36.	 BRCA testing is done by 
(A)	RT-PCR 
(B)	 Whole exome sequencing 
(C)	qPCR 
(D)	Southern blot 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) Whole exome sequencing
Testing for hereditary cancer syndromes like those caused by BRCA1/2 mutations involves identifying any of a vast number of possible pathogenic variants (mutations) that can occur anywhere along the entire coding sequence of these large genes. The most comprehensive and standard modern method for this is Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS). Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) (B) is a broad NGS technique that sequences all coding regions (exons) of the genome, which would include the BRCA genes. In clinical practice, a more "targeted" NGS panel that focuses on BRCA1/2 and other relevant cancer-susceptibility genes is often used.
RT-PCR (A) and qPCR (C) are methods used to detect and quantify RNA (gene expression), not to identify unknown DNA mutations. Southern blot (D) is an older technique used to detect large-scale DNA rearrangements or deletions. While large deletions can occur in BRCA, they are typically tested for using MLPA (Multiplex Ligation-dependent Probe Amplification), and the primary method for finding the more common point mutations and small insertions/deletions is sequencing.

38.	 Caspase-1 
mediated 
cell 
death 
with 
inflammation is known as 
(A)	Pyroptosis 
(B)	 Necroptosis 
(C)	Ferroptosis 
(D)	Necrosis 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Pyroptosis
Pyroptosis (A) is a lytic, highly inflammatory form of programmed cell death. It is defined by its dependence on the activation of Caspase-1. Pyroptosis is typically triggered by intracellular pathogens or danger signals, which are sensed by cytosolic inflammasomes (e.g., NLRP3). The inflammasome complex then cleaves pro-Caspase-1 into its active form. Active Caspase-1 has two key functions:
1.	
It cleaves the pore-forming protein Gasdermin D, which inserts into the cell membrane and causes cell lysis (oncosis) and the release of intracellular contents.
2.	
It cleaves pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 into their active, mature forms, which are then released from the lysing cell, driving a potent inflammatory response.
Necroptosis (B) is also programmed and inflammatory but is caspase-independent (mediated by RIPK1/RIPK3/MLKL). Ferroptosis (C) is iron-dependent cell death via lipid peroxidation. Necrosis (D) is an un-programmed, pathological form of cell death.
39.	 Most common inherited bleeding disorder is 
(A)	Von Willebrand disease 
(B)	 Factor V deficiency 
(C)	Hemophilia A 
(D)	Hemophilia B 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Von Willebrand disease
Von Willebrand disease (vWD) (A) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, with an estimated prevalence of up to 1% of the general population, although the number of clinically symptomatic individuals is lower. It is caused by a quantitative or qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor (vWF), a protein crucial for platelet adhesion (primary hemostasis) and for stabilizing Factor VIII in circulation. It typically presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (e.g., easy bruising, nosebleeds, menorrhagia).
Hemophilia A (C), a deficiency of Factor VIII, is the second most common inherited coagulation disorder, but it is much rarer than vWD, affecting approximately 1 in 5,000-10,000 males. Hemophilia B (D), a Factor IX deficiency, is even less common. Factor V deficiency (B) is an extremely rare bleeding disorder. Therefore, vWD is by far the most prevalent inherited bleeding disorder.
40.	 In which condition is erythropoietin considered 
beneficial for treatment?
(A)	Anemia in chronic kidney disease 
(B)	 Anemia in myelodysplastic syndrome 
(C)	Nutritional anemia 
(D)	Aplastic anemia 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Anemia in chronic kidney disease
Erythropoietin (EPO) is a hormone produced primarily by the peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney in response to tissue hypoxia. It stimulates the bone marrow to produce red blood cells (erythropoiesis). In Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) (A), the progressive damage to the kidneys leads to a failure of these cells to produce adequate EPO. This results in the classic "anemia of chronic disease" or "anemia of CKD," which is a normocytic, normochromic anemia. This is a state of true EPO deficiency. Therefore, treatment with synthetic EPO (recombinant human erythropoietin or other erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, ESAs) is a cornerstone of management, as it directly replaces the missing hormone.
In Nutritional anemia (C), the problem is a lack of substrates (e.g., iron, B12), and EPO levels are appropriately high. In Aplastic anemia (D), the bone marrow stem cells have failed; EPO levels are extremely high, but the marrow cannot respond. In MDS (B), the anemia is complex, and while some patients may respond to EPO, the most direct and classic indication is CKD.
41.	 A 32-year-old woman presents with easy bruising 
and petechiae, a platelet count of 18,000/mm³, 
normal hemoglobin and leukocyte counts, and 
a recent mild upper respiratory infection. Her 
peripheral smear is normal. What is the most 
appropriate next step in management?
(A)	Oral corticosteroids 
(B)	 Platelet transfusion 
(C)	Bone marrow biopsy 
(D)	Splenectomy 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Oral corticosteroids 
This patient has isolated thrombocytopenia (platelet count 18,000/mm³) with normal hemoglobin and leukocyte counts, a normal peripheral smear, and a recent viral infection. This presentation is classic for immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), an autoimmune condition in which antibodies (usually IgG) target platelets, leading to their destruction in the spleen.
In adults with symptomatic ITP or platelet count below 30,000/mm³, the first-line treatment is corticosteroids (such as oral prednisone or dexamethasone). Steroids reduce antibody production and decrease splenic clearance of platelets.
Platelet transfusion is reserved for severe or life-threatening bleeding, as transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed. Bone marrow biopsy is not routinely required when the clinical picture clearly suggests ITP. Splenectomy is considered a second-line therapy for chronic or steroid-refractory cases.
Therefore, the most appropriate next step is oral corticosteroids.

42.	 A deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase is 
associated with which pattern of bilirubin 
levels?
(A)	Direct bilirubin increased, indirect bilirubin 
decreased, and urine urobilinogen/urobilin 
increased 
(B)	 Direct bilirubin normal, indirect bilirubin 
increased, and urobilinogen normal 
(C)	Raised direct bilirubin, normal indirect 
bilirubin, and absent urine bilirubin 
(D)	Indirect bilirubin increased, direct bilirubin 
normal, and raised urine urobilinogen 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(D) Indirect bilirubin increased, direct bilirubin normal, and raised urine urobilinogen 
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is an inherited enzymatic defect that makes red blood cells highly susceptible to oxidative stress. G6PD normally generates NADPH through the pentose phosphate pathway, which helps maintain glutathione in its reduced form. Reduced glutathione protects red blood cells from oxidative damage. When G6PD is deficient, oxidative stress (from infections, certain drugs, or fava beans) leads to hemolysis.
During hemolysis, hemoglobin is released and broken down into heme, which is converted into biliverdin and then into unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin. Because this bilirubin is produced in excess, its level in blood rises. The liver itself is structurally normal and capable of conjugation, so direct (conjugated) bilirubin remains normal. However, increased amounts of unconjugated bilirubin reach the liver and then the intestine after conjugation.
In the intestine, bilirubin is converted into urobilinogen. Since more bilirubin is being processed due to hemolysis, more urobilinogen is formed and reabsorbed into the bloodstream, leading to increased urinary urobilinogen levels.
Thus, G6PD deficiency produces indirect hyperbilirubinemia with normal direct bilirubin and raised urine urobilinogen, corresponding to option (D).
43.	 Neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis is caused

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025

Idiopathic Granulomatous Mastitis (IGM) is a rare, chronic inflammatory breast condition. While often labeled "idiopathic," a specific subgroup known as Cystic Neutrophilic Granulomatous Mastitis has been strongly and specifically associated with infection by the lipophilic, gram-positive rod Corynebacterium kroppenstedtii (A). This organism is fastidious and difficult to culture, which is why the association was only recently established. It is thought to colonize and infect the breast ducts, triggering a robust inflammatory response characterized by granulomas (collections of histiocytes) and a prominent neutrophilic infiltrate, often leading to abscesses and sinus tracts.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis (C) causes tuberculous mastitis, which features classic caseating granulomas, but not typically a neutrophilic component. 44.	 Which of the following malignancies is

(A)	Stomach 
(B)	 Pancreas 
(C)	Meningioma 
(D)	Multiple myeloma 
AAns

Obesity is a major modifiable risk factor for many cancers, acting through mechanisms like chronic inflammation, insulin resistance, and hormonal (adipokine/estrogen) dysregulation. 45.	 Histopathological features of granulosa cell 
tumor include all except: 
(A)	Call-Exner bodies 
(B)	 Inhibin A 
(C)	CA-125 positivity 
(D)	Coffee bean nuclei

Granulosa cell tumor (GCT) is the most common malignant sex cord-stromal tumor of the ovary. It has a set of classic histopathological and immunohistochemical features.

Call-Exner bodies (A) are a pathognomonic finding, representing small, rosette-like structures where granulosa cells arrange around a central eosinophilic, PAS-positive space.
2.

46.	 Which stain is not used to identify organisms in 
a renal transplant biopsy?
(A)	Gomori methenamine silver 
(B)	 PAS (Periodic acid-Schiff) stain 
(C)	Masson Fontana 
(D)	Congo red 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(D) Congo red
In a renal transplant (immunocompromised) patient, a biopsy is often stained to rule out opportunistic infections.
Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) (A) is the classic stain for fungi, highlighting fungal walls in black. It is used to identify Pneumocystis, Candida, or Aspergillus.
PAS (Periodic Acid-Schiff) (B), while a standard stain for basement membranes, also stains fungal walls (magenta) and can help identify them.

This stain is used to diagnose amyloidosis, a protein deposition disease, and is not used to identify infectious organisms.
47.	 Why does not every Helicobacter pylori infection 
lead to ulcers? 
(A)	Disease associated with host factors and 
environmental influences 
(B)	 Increased risk of peptic ulcer disease when 
H. pylori is present with NSAIDs 
(C)	H. pylori infects the antrum even in 
asymptomatic individuals 
(D)	Majority of H. pylori infections are 
asymptomatic 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(D) Majority of H. pylori infections are asymptomatic
Helicobacter pylori is a spiral-shaped, gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the gastric mucosa, particularly the antrum. Although it is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease and is associated with gastritis, gastric carcinoma, and MALT lymphoma, most infected individuals never develop clinically significant disease.
The reason not every infection leads to ulcers is that the majority of infections remain asymptomatic. Many people harbor the organism for years without developing mucosal damage severe enough to produce ulceration. Ulcer formation depends on multiple interacting factors such as bacterial virulence (e.g., CagA, VacA strains), host immune response, gastric acid secretion levels, genetic susceptibility, and environmental influences like smoking or NSAID use.
In many individuals, the infection causes only mild chronic gastritis without disrupting the protective mucosal barrier to the extent required for ulcer formation. Therefore, while H. pylori infection is common worldwide, only a small proportion of infected individuals develop peptic ulcers.
Hence, most H. pylori infections do not lead to ulcers because they are asymptomatic and non-ulcerative in the majority of cases.
48.	 In which of the following situations does 
transplant rejection not occur?
(A)	Bare lymphocyte syndrome 
(B)	 Chronic granulomatous disease 
(C)	Severe 
Combined 
Immunodeficiency 
(SCID) 
(D)	DiGeorge syndrome 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(C) Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)Transplant rejection is an immune response mediated by the recipient's T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes, which recognize the donor graft as foreign. This requires a functional adaptive immune system.
Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) (C) is a group of genetic disorders characterized by a profound failure of both T-cell and B-cell development and function. Patients with "classic" SCID have no adaptive immune system and are therefore incapable of mounting an immune response. They cannot recognize or attack a foreign graft, so transplant rejection does not occur. (Instead, they are at high risk of Graft-versus-Host Disease from any T-cells within the transplant).
Bare lymphocyte syndrome (A) is a type of SCID, so it is also correct, but SCID is the broader and more definitive answer. DiGeorge syndrome (D) involves T-cell deficiency but is often partial, so rejection is still possible. Chronic granulomatous disease (B) is a defect in phagocyte (innate) immunity, but T-cell (adaptive) immunity is intact and fully capable of rejection.
49.	 Identify the structure labeled in the histology 
image shown.
(A)	Terminal bronchiole 
(B)	 Respiratory bronchiole 
(C)	Alveolar duct 
(D)	Bronchus 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Terminal bronchiole 
A terminal bronchiole is the last part of the conducting portion of the respiratory system. It is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium (often ciliated) and may contain Clara (club) cells. Importantly, its walls do not contain alveoli, which distinguishes it from respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts.
In the given histology image, the labeled structure appears as a small airway with a relatively continuous wall and a well-defined lumen. There are no outpouchings of alveoli opening directly into its wall. This rules out:
1.	
Respiratory bronchiole – would show alveoli budding from its walls.
2.	
Alveolar duct – would have almost entirely alveolar walls with very little continuous bronchiolar epithelium.
3.	
Bronchus – would contain cartilage plates and submucosal glands, which are absent here.
Since the structure lacks cartilage, lacks glands, and does not show alveoli arising from its wall, it corresponds to a terminal bronchiole, the final purely conducting airway before the respiratory portion begins.
50.	 What explains increased oxygen consumption 
by cancer cells? 
(A)	Cancer 
cells 
need 
increased 
lactate 
production 
Click Here to Buy book on Amazon
page  11  	
INICET Examination Paper
(B)	 Cancer cells have increased mitochondrial 
function 
(C)	Cancer cells rely on anaerobic glycolysis 
even in presence of oxygen (Warburg effect) 
(D)	Cancer cells undergo increased oxidative 
phosphorylation 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(C) Cancer cells rely on anaerobic glycolysis even in presence of oxygen (Warburg effect)
The phenomenon known as the Warburg effect, described by Otto Warburg, explains the altered metabolism of cancer cells. Normally, in the presence of oxygen, healthy cells generate energy primarily through oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria, which is efficient and produces large amounts of ATP. However, cancer cells preferentially use glycolysis to generate energy, even when adequate oxygen is available. This process is termed “aerobic glycolysis.”
Although glycolysis produces far less ATP per glucose molecule compared to oxidative phosphorylation, cancer cells compensate by markedly increasing glucose uptake and glycolytic rate. The metabolic intermediates produced during glycolysis are diverted into biosynthetic pathways that support rapid cell proliferation, such as nucleotide, lipid, and amino acid synthesis.
Thus, the key explanation is not increased mitochondrial activity or oxidative phosphorylation, but rather the paradoxical reliance on glycolysis despite oxygen availability. This metabolic reprogramming supports tumor growth and is the basis for FDG-PET imaging in oncology.
51.	 Identify the antibody shown in the diagram that 
contains a joining chain and is primarily located 
in mucosal surfaces.
(A)	IgG 
(B)	 IgM 
(C)	IgE 
(D)	IgA 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(D) IgA
The diagram shows a classic dimeric antibody structure, which consists of two monomer units linked by a "Joining chain" (J-chain). It also shows a "Secretory protein" (also called the secretory component) wrapped around the dimer. This specific structure is secretory IgA (sIgA).
IgA (D) is the predominant immunoglobulin found in mucosal secretions, such as saliva, tears, breast milk, and respiratory and gastrointestinal fluids. The dimeric structure and the secretory component (which is added by epithelial cells during transport) protect the antibody from degradation by proteases in these harsh environments, allowing it to perform "immune exclusion" by neutralizing pathogens at the mucosal surface.
IgG (A) and IgE (C) are monomers. IgM (B) is a pentamer (five units) in serum, also held together by a J-chain, but it is not the primary secretory antibody in this dimeric form.
52.	 What technique is illustrated in the graph that 
depicts antigen-antibody interaction and the 
kinetics of the immune response?
(A)	Competitive ELISA for antibody affinity 
(B)	 Competitive 
ELISA 
for 
antibody 
concentration 
(C)	Surface plasmon resonance for affinity 
(D)	Surface 
plasmon 
resonance 
for 
concentration 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(C) Surface plasmon resonance for affinity
Although no graph is shown, the question's text provides the key clues. The technique must be one that demonstrates "response kinetics" for an "antibody-antigen interaction."
This implies a real-time measurement of the binding process. ELISA (A, B) is an endpoint assay; it measures the total amount of binding that has occurred after a set time and washing steps, but it does not show the "kinetics" (the rate of binding and unbinding).
Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR) (C, D) is the gold-standard technique for measuring real-time biomolecular interactions. In SPR, one molecule (e.g., antigen) is fixed to a sensor chip, and the other (e.g., antibody) is flowed over it. The binding and dissociation events are monitored in real-time, producing a "response" curve. From this kinetic data, one can calculate the association rate (kon) and dissociation rate (koff), which are then used to determine the affinity ($K_D$) of the interaction. Therefore, SPR is the technique used to measure interaction kinetics for determining affinity.
53.	 In which disease is an HLA-mismatched 
transplant not considered problematic?
(A)	Bare lymphocyte syndrome 
(B)	 Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome 
(C)	Job's syndrome 
(D)	Chediak-Higashi syndrome 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Bare lymphocyte syndrome
An HLA-mismatched transplant normally fails due to Graft Rejection (recipient T-cells attack the graft) or Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD) (donor T-cells attack the recipient). This question asks in which condition this "problem" doesn't occur.
Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome (BLS) (A) is a form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID). In BLS Type II (the most common form), there is a genetic defect that prevents the expression of MHC Class II molecules. Without MHC II, the patient's antigen-presenting cells cannot activate CD4+ "helper" T-cells. This results in a profound T-cell immunodeficiency, meaning the patient cannot mount an immune response to reject the graft. Furthermore, because the recipient's own tissues also lack MHC II, the donor T-cells in the graft have a reduced ability to recognize the host, significantly mitigating the risk of GVHD. This unique situation makes BLS one of the few conditions where an HLA-mismatched transplant can be successful.
The other conditions (B, C, D) are all immunodeficiencies, but T-cell function is sufficiently intact to cause either rejection or severe GVHD.
54.	 What is the role of Pro calcitonin in pneumonia? 
(A)	Guiding initiation of antibiotic 
(B)	 Early antibiotic discontinuation 
(C)	Requirement of further investigation 
(D)	No role 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) Early antibiotic discontinuation
Procalcitonin (PCT) is a biomarker that is highly specific for systemic bacterial infections. Its levels rise significantly in response to bacterial endotoxins but typically remain low in viral infections or non-infectious inflammatory states. This makes it very useful in managing respiratory infections like pneumonia.
While a very low PCT level can guide initiation (A) (by suggesting a viral cause where antibiotics may be withheld), its most robust, evidence-based, and widely adopted role is in guiding antibiotic discontinuation (B). In a patient being treated for bacterial pneumonia, PCT levels will fall as the infection is controlled. Serial monitoring of PCT allows clinicians to identify when the infection has resolved, even if the patient has other reasons for inflammation (e.g., post-operative state). Following a PCT-guided algorithm (e.g., stopping antibiotics when PCT drops by >80% from its peak) has been shown to safely reduce the total duration of antibiotic therapy, which helps minimize side effects and antibiotic resistance.

56.	 What is the recommended treatment for

(C)	Tetracycline

Neisseria gonorrhoeae has a remarkable ability to develop antibiotic resistance. It is now resistant to many older therapies, including penicillins (like Amoxicillin (B)) and Tetracyclines (C). The current standard of care and recommended treatment, especially for penicillin-resistant strains and for complicated gonorrhoea (e.g., pelvic inflammatory disease, disseminated gonococcal infection), is a third-generation cephalosporin. 57.	 All of the following is/are adverse effects of

Topical corticosteroids are widely used for their anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects, but they carry a risk of significant local adverse effects, especially with prolonged use or high potency. (D)	Both inhibit norepinephrine reuptake
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(C) Both have anti-muscarinic actions
This question involves a drug-drug interaction, specifically a pharmacodynamic additive effect.
1.	
Imipramine is a Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA). While its primary therapeutic effect is inhibiting the reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin, it is also known for its "dirty" receptor profile, which includes potent blockade of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors.
2.	
Diphenhydramine is a first-generation antihistamine (H1 blocker). A primary property of first-generation antihistamines is their strong anti-muscarinic (anticholinergic) activity.
When both drugs are administered together (C), their individual anti-muscarinic effects will add up, leading to a high risk of anticholinergic toxicity. 60.	 Which of the following is a clinical cure for 
malaria?
(A)	Primaquine
(B)	 Chloroquine
(C)	Artesunate
(D)	Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(D) Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine
A clinical cure in malaria means elimination of the asexual erythrocytic (blood) stages of the parasite, thereby resolving symptoms such as fever and anemia. It does not necessarily eliminate dormant liver forms (hypnozoites), so relapse may still occur in Plasmodium vivax or Plasmodium ovale infections.
Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine is a combination antifolate therapy that acts synergistically by inhibiting folate synthesis in the malaria parasite. Sulfadoxine inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, while pyrimethamine inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. This dual blockade prevents DNA synthesis in the parasite’s blood stages, leading to clearance of parasitemia and resolution of clinical symptoms.
In contrast:
1.	
Primaquine provides a radical cure by eliminating hepatic hypnozoites.
2.	
Chloroquine and Artesunate are also blood schizonticides but are not specifically referred to as clinical cure agents in this context.
Therefore, sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine achieves a clinical cure by clearing the blood-stage parasites responsible for symptoms.

This question assesses the pharmacology of GABA-A modulators.

(B)	
Alcohol also enhances GABA-A transmission. When combined with either benzodiazepines or barbiturates, it results in a synergistic and potentially fatal CNS depression.

62.	 Which of the following anti-epileptics is not 
given during pregnancy?
(A)	Lamotrigine
(B)	 Valproate
(C)	Levetiracetam
(D)	Carbamazepine
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) Valproate
Valproate (Valproic Acid) (B) is the anti-epileptic drug that is most strongly contraindicated in pregnancy, especially during the first trimester. It is a known human teratogen with a high risk (up to 10%) of causing major congenital malformations, most notably neural tube defects (such as spina bifida). It is also associated with a "fetal valproate syndrome" and significant long-term neurodevelopmental problems, including reduced cognitive function (lower IQ) and an increased risk of autism spectrum disorders in the offspring. Because of these severe risks, its use in women of childbearing potential is highly restricted. In contrast, Lamotrigine (A) and Levetiracetam (C) are considered among the safest anti-epileptics in pregnancy and are often the first-line choices. Carbamazepine (D) also carries some teratogenic risk (e.g., neural tube defects, though less than valproate), but valproate is by far the most dangerous and avoided.
63.	 Mechanism of action of Fenoldopam drug is:
(A)	D1 agonist
(B)	 Alpha-1 antagonist
(C)	Beta-2 agonist
(D)	D2 antagonist
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) D1 agonist
Fenoldopam is a parenteral (IV) antihypertensive drug used in the treatment of hypertensive emergencies and for short-term blood pressure control. Its primary mechanism of action is as a selective postsynaptic Dopamine-1 (D1) receptor agonist (A). Activation of D1 receptors, which are highly expressed in renal, mesenteric, coronary, and cerebral vasculature, leads to stimulation of adenylyl cyclase and an increase in intracellular cAMP. This causes potent arteriolar vasodilation and a rapid decrease in systemic blood pressure. A unique and beneficial effect of its D1 agonism is that it specifically increases renal blood flow, glomerular filtration, and natriuresis (sodium excretion). This makes it a favorable choice in patients with hypertensive emergencies and concomitant renal insufficiency. It does not act as an alpha-1 antagonist (B), beta-2 agonist (C), or D2 antagonist (D).

Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (India), different schedules classify drugs based on their regulation, prescription control, and special precautions.

Schedule H – Insulin (A-1)
Insulin is a prescription-only medicine. Schedule H drugs cannot be sold without a valid prescription from a registered medical practitioner.

67.	 A patient taking carbamazepine is also given 
erythromycin and subsequently develops ataxia 
and dizziness. What is the underlying cause of 
these symptoms?
(A)	Toxicity of erythromycin
(B)	 Toxicity of carbamazepine
(C)	Erythromycin speeds up carbamazepine 
metabolism
(D)	Causes recurrent seizure episodes
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) Toxicity of carbamazepine
This is a classic and clinically significant drug-drug interaction.
Carbamazepine is an antiepileptic drug with a narrow therapeutic index. Its adverse effects, which occur at high concentrations, include dizziness, diplopia, and ataxia (unsteady gait).
Carbamazepine is metabolized primarily by the cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) enzyme in the liver.

The patient's symptoms of ataxia and dizziness are the direct result of this carbamazepine toxicity (B). The symptoms are not due to erythromycin toxicity (A) or seizures (D).

68.	 One of the following statements regarding 
venom is incorrect:

(B)	 Common krait - Neurotoxic
(C)	Elapidae - Myotoxic
(D)	Viperidae - Hemotoxic
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(C) Elapidae - Myotoxic
This question evaluates knowledge of snake venom properties.
Common cobra (A) and Common krait (B) both belong to the Elapidae family. The venom of these snakes is predominantly neurotoxic. It contains toxins that block postsynaptic (cobra) or presynaptic (krait) acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, leading to progressive descending paralysis and respiratory failure.
Viperidae (D) (vipers) typically have venom that is predominantly hemotoxic (also called vasculotoxic). This venom damages blood vessels, disrupts the coagulation cascade, and causes hemolysis, leading to local swelling, pain, necrosis, and systemic bleeding.
The statement Elapidae - Myotoxic (C) is the incorrect generalization. While some elapids (like sea snakes or certain Australian species) have myotoxic components, the primary and defining feature of the Elapidae family as a whole, especially the Indian cobras and kraits, is potent neurotoxicity. Therefore, labeling the entire family as "myotoxic" is incorrect.
69.	 The triad of abrasions, bruises and punctate 
lacerations are typically seen in:
(A)	Fall from height
(B)	 Bomb blast injuries
BK
page  13  	
INICET Examination Paper
(C)	Road traffic accidents
(D)	Firearm injuries
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) Bomb blast injuries
In blast injuries, the body is exposed to multiple mechanisms of trauma occurring simultaneously. An explosion generates a high-pressure shock wave followed by flying debris and environmental impact. Because of this, victims commonly show a characteristic triad of abrasions, bruises, and punctate lacerations.
Abrasions occur due to friction against rough surfaces or debris. Bruises (contusions) result from blunt force trauma caused by the blast wave or impact with surrounding objects. Punctate lacerations are small, penetrating wounds caused by shrapnel, splinters, metallic fragments, glass pieces, or other projectiles propelled by the explosion. These multiple small penetrating wounds are especially typical of bomb blasts.
In contrast, fall from height usually produces fractures and localized blunt injuries, road traffic accidents cause patterned blunt injuries, and firearm injuries generally produce entry and exit wounds rather than multiple punctate lacerations.
Thus, the combination of abrasions, bruises, and punctate lacerations is classically associated with bomb blast injuries.
70.	 Which of the following findings is not seen in 
a worker exposed to mercury in a thermometer 
manufacturing company?
(A)	Tremors and Mad Hatter's disease
(B)	 Basophilic stippling
(C)	Mees' lines
(D)	Peripheral neuropathy
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(C) Mees' lines
Chronic exposure to mercury, especially in thermometer manufacturing, leads to a condition historically known as erethism or “Mad Hatter’s disease.” This includes behavioral changes (irritability, shyness, excitability), memory problems, and fine tremors that may progress to coarse tremors. Peripheral neuropathy can also occur due to toxic effects on the nervous system.
Basophilic stippling may be seen in heavy metal poisoning, including mercury, though it is more classically associated with lead poisoning. Neurological manifestations remain the hallmark of chronic mercury exposure.
Mees’ lines, however, are transverse white lines seen on the nails and are classically associated with arsenic poisoning rather than mercury toxicity. Therefore, they are not a typical finding in workers exposed to mercury in thermometer manufacturing.
Thus, among the options given, Mees’ lines are not characteristic of mercury exposure, making option (C) the correct answer.

(C) 18 years
According to India's Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, 1971, and its subsequent amendments, the concept of consent is tied to the age of majority. A "minor" is defined as a person who has not attained the age of 18 years.
For a woman who is 18 years of age or older (i.e., an adult), only her own written consent is required for an MTP. She has the full legal right to make this decision independently.
For a "minor" (a girl under the age of 18), she cannot give valid legal consent on her own. The law requires the written consent of her guardian to be obtained.
Therefore, the minimum age at which a girl can give her own valid consent, without requiring the consent of a guardian, is the age of majority, which is 18 years (C).

The MTP Act, as amended in 2021, specifies the requirements for medical opinions based on gestational age:

2.

75.	 A patient has burns on the face, both upper limbs, 
and the front of the chest. What percentage of 
total body surface area is involved?
(A)	27 to 30
(B)	 30 to 37
(C)	38 to 42
(D)	25 to 48
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) 27 to 30
The percentage of total body surface area (TBSA) involved in burns is commonly estimated using the Rule of Nines in adults. This method divides the body into regions, each representing 9% or multiples of 9% of the total surface area. It provides a rapid and practical way to assess burn severity and guide fluid resuscitation.
According to the Rule of Nines, the entire head and neck together account for 9% of TBSA. Each upper limb contributes 9%, so both upper limbs together account for 18%. The anterior chest accounts for 9% (the anterior trunk is 18%, divided into chest 9% and abdomen 9%).
In this patient, burns involve the face, both upper limbs, and the front of the chest. If the face alone is considered, it approximates about 4.5% (anterior half of the head). Adding both upper limbs (18%) and anterior chest (9%) gives approximately 31.5%. However, in exam-based calculations, rounding and approximations are commonly applied, often considering the head as 9% or simplifying the calculation.
Thus, the closest and most appropriate answer is 27–30% TBSA involvement.

Emasculation (A)
Permanent privation (loss) of sight, hearing, or a "member" or joint.
Loss of a member (D) (e.g., an arm or leg) or destruction/permanent impairing of the powers of any member or joint.
Fracture or dislocation of a bone (B) or tooth.

The statement Severe body pain for 5 days (C) does not meet this legal definition. The law specifies a duration of 15 days of severe pain or inability to work. Therefore, pain for only 5 days would be classified as "simple hurt," not "grievous hurt."

78.	 Which X-ray is used to confirm that a person is

(A)	Appearance of inner end of clavicle, knee

(B)	 Fusion of ischial tuberosity and lower end 
of humerus
(C)	Medial end of clavicle and sternum
(D)	Medial end of clavicle and skull
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Appearance of inner end of clavicle, knee joint, and wrist joint
Age estimation in medicolegal practice is commonly done using X-ray examination of ossification centers and epiphyseal fusion. Around the age of 18 years, most long bone epiphyses such as those at the wrist (distal radius and ulna) and knee joint (lower end of femur and upper end of tibia) have fused or are in the final stages of fusion. These findings help in determining whether an individual has attained majority.
The medial (inner) end of the clavicle is particularly important because it is the last epiphysis in the body to fuse. Its appearance and partial fusion begin around 18 years and complete fusion usually occurs by 21–22 years. Therefore, radiological examination of the medial clavicle, along with wrist and knee joints, provides supportive evidence that a person is at least 18 years old.
Other options mention structures that either fuse earlier or are not standard primary markers for confirming attainment of 18 years in routine medicolegal assessment.
Hence, option (A) is correct.

81.	 Cyanide and carbon monoxide poisoning inhibit 
which enzyme as their primary mechanism of 
action?
(A)	NADH dehydrogenase
(B)	 Succinate dehydrogenase
(C)	Cytochrome C oxidoreductase
(D)	Cytochrome C oxidase
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(D) Cytochrome C oxidase
Cyanide (CN) and Carbon Monoxide (CO) are classic inhibitors of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC). Both substances act by binding to and inhibiting Cytochrome C oxidase (Complex IV) (D), the final enzyme complex in the chain. This enzyme is responsible for transferring electrons from cytochrome c to molecular oxygen (the final electron acceptor) to form water. Cyanide binds to the ferric (Fe3+) state of the heme iron in Complex IV, while carbon monoxide binds to the ferrous (Fe2+) state. In both cases, this binding prevents electron transfer to oxygen, effectively halting aerobic respiration and leading to rapid cytotoxic hypoxia and cell death. NADH dehydrogenase (A) is Complex I. Succinate dehydrogenase (B) is Complex II. Cytochrome C oxidoreductase (C) is Complex III.

83.	 Choose the correct statement(s):
1.	 Weil-Felix test is done for typhus fever
2.	 Widal test is done in the first week of fever
3.	 Standard agglutination test is done for 
brucellosis
4.	 Microscopic agglutination test is done for 
leptospirosis
(A)	1, 2, 3 are correct
(B)	 1, 3, 4 are correct
(C)	1, 2, 3, 4 are correct
(D)	1, 4 are correct
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) 1, 3, 4 are correct
Let's evaluate each statement:
1.	
Weil-Felix test is done for typhus fever. (Correct). This is a classic heterophile agglutination test used to diagnose rickettsial infections, including typhus fever. It uses Proteus antigens (OX-19, OX-2, OX-K) that cross-react with antibodies produced against Rickettsia.
2.	
Widal test is done in the first week of fever. (Incorrect). The Widal test is a serological test for typhoid fever (enteric fever). It detects antibodies (anti-O and anti-H) against Salmonella Typhi. These antibodies take time to develop, and the test is typically not positive in the first week of illness; it becomes reliable only from the second week onwards.
3.	
Standard agglutination test is done for brucellosis. (Correct). The Standard Agglutination Test (SAT), or tube agglutination test, is a primary serological method for diagnosing brucellosis, detecting antibodies against Brucella antigens.
4.	
Microscopic agglutination test is done for leptospirosis. (Correct). The Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT) is the gold standard serological test for diagnosing leptospirosis. It involves testing patient serum against a panel of live Leptospira serovars and observing for agglutination under a dark-field microscope.
Therefore, statements 1, 3, and 4 are correct, making (B) the right answer.

85.	 Which

The Kanagawa phenomenon refers to the production of a heat-stable hemolysin (Thermostable Direct Hemolysin, TDH) by pathogenic strains of Vibrio parahaemolyticus (C). 88.	 Which parasite among the following is capable 
of causing autoinfection?
(A)	Strongyloides stercoralis
(B)	 Ancylostoma duodenale
(C)	Ascaris lumbricoides
(D)	Hymenolepis nana
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(A) Strongyloides stercoralis
Autoinfection is a cycle where an infection is re-established or amplified without the parasite leaving the host or coming from an external source.
1.	
Strongyloides stercoralis (A) is the classic example of a nematode (roundworm) that causes autoinfection. Its rhabditiform larvae can mature into infective filariform larvae within the host's intestine. These larvae can then penetrate the colonic mucosa or perianal skin, re-entering the circulation and migrating back to the lungs to restart the life cycle. This "internal autoinfection" can lead to a massive, disseminated "hyperinfection" in immuno compromised patients.
2.	
Hymenolepis nana (D) (dwarf tapeworm) is a cestode (tapeworm) that also causes autoinfection. However, Strongyloides is the more clinically significant and classic answer, especially regarding internal autoinfection. Ascaris (C) and Ancylostoma (B) require an external soil maturation phase. Given the options, Strongyloides is the best answer.
89.	 All of the following are dimorphic fungi except:
(A)	Coccidioides
(B)	 Talaromyces
(C)	Histoplasma
(D)	Cryptococcus
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(D) Cryptococcus
Dimorphic fungi are fungi that exist in two different morphological forms depending on the temperature. They grow as a mold (filamentous form) in the environment (at 25-30°C) and as a yeast (unicellular form) in host tissues (at 37°C). The mnemonic "Cold is mold, Heat is yeast" applies.
1.	
Coccidioides immitis (A) is dimorphic, though it's an exception to the rule. It's a mold in the soil and forms a unique spherule (not yeast) in the lungs.
2.	
Talaromyces marneffei (B) (formerly Penicillium marneffei) is a true dimorphic fungus.
3.	
Histoplasma capsulatum (C) is a classic dimorphic fungus (mold in soil, yeast in macrophages).
4.	
Cryptococcus neoformans (D) is the exception. It is monomorphic. It exists only as an encapsulated yeast form, both in the environment and in the host. It does not have a mold form associated with infection.
90.	 Identify the organism that demonstrates the 
satellite phenomenon shown in the image.
(A)	Streptococcus pneumoniae
(B)	 Hemophilus influenzae
(C)	Corynebacterium diphtheriae
(D)	Klebsiella pneumoniae
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025
(B) Hemophilus influenzae
The image shows a satellitism test. The plate is a blood agar plate that has been "seeded" with the unknown organism. A single streak of another bacterium (the vertical line) has been made down the center. The image shows that the unknown organism is only growing in tiny colonies immediately adjacent to the central streak, a phenomenon called satellitism.
This is the classic test for Hemophilus influenzae (B). H. influenzae is a fastidious organism that requires two growth factors: X factor (hemin) and V factor (NAD). Standard blood agar provides X factor (from lysed RBCs) but not enough V factor. The central streak is typically made with Staphylococcus aureus, which secretes V factor (NAD) as a metabolic byproduct. Therefore, H. influenzae can only grow where it can "leech" the V factor from the Staphylococcus, resulting in satellite colonies.
