Early diagnosis through β-hCG measurement and transvaginal ultrasound is critical to prevent rupture. This condition remains a leading cause of first-trimester maternal mortality, making timely recognition and surgical intervention lifesaving.
165.	 What is the correct dose of steroid for fetal lung 
maturity?
(A)	Betamethasone 12 mg – 4 doses every 12 
hours
(B)	 Betamethasone 6 mg – 2 doses every 12 
hours
(C)	Dexamethasone 6 mg – 4 doses every 12

(D)	Dexamethasone 12 mg – 2 doses every 24

AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(C) Dexamethasone 6 mg – 4 doses every 12 hours
Antenatal corticosteroid therapy promotes fetal lung maturation and reduces the risk of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in preterm births. Dexamethasone 6 mg intramuscularly every 12 hours for 4 doses (total 24 mg) or Betamethasone 12 mg every 24 hours for 2 doses are the recommended regimens. The therapy is advised between 24–34 weeks of gestation in women at risk of preterm labor within the next 7 days. This therapy is a cornerstone of modern perinatal care, significantly improving neonatal survival rates.
166.	 In a hypertensive patient with postpartum 
hemorrhage, 
which 
medication 
is

(B)	 Methylergometrine
(C)	Misoprostol
(D)	PGF-2 alpha
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(B) Methylergometrine
Methylergometrine (Methergine) is a potent uterotonic agent that induces sustained uterine contractions by acting on smooth muscle serotonin and alpha-adrenergic receptors. However, it also causes significant vasoconstriction, which can lead to severe hypertension, cerebrovascular accidents, or myocardial ischemia in patients with pre-existing hypertension, pre-eclampsia, or eclampsia. Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone are given only if gestation is <34 weeks to enhance fetal lung maturity — not indicated here. After stabilization, delivery is induced or cesarean section performed based on obstetric indications. Postpartum monitoring continues for 48 hours due to persistent risk of eclampsia. Early recognition and multidisciplinary care reduce maternal and perinatal mortality significantly.

(A) Imperforate hymen
An imperforate hymen is a congenital anomaly resulting from failure of the inferior end of the vaginal plate to canalize. It presents at puberty with cyclical abdominal pain, primary amenorrhea, and urinary retention due to accumulation of menstrual blood behind the intact hymen (hematocolpos or hematometra). 173.	 Under normal physiological conditions, which 
is the most potent form of natural estrogen?
(A)	Estradiol
(B)	 Estriol
(C)	Conjugated estrogen
(D)	Estrone
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(A) Estradiol
Among the three naturally occurring estrogens — estradiol (E₂), estrone (E₁), and estriol (E₃) — estradiol is the most potent and biologically active form. It is primarily secreted by the granulosa cells of ovarian follicles during the reproductive years under the influence of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Estrone is produced in peripheral tissues, especially adipose tissue, from androstenedione and predominates after menopause, while estriol is mainly synthesized in the placenta during pregnancy and is the least potent. Estradiol binds strongly to estrogen receptors in target tissues like the uterus, breast, bone, and brain, promoting proliferation and maintenance of secondary sexual characteristics, endometrial growth, and bone density. Its plasma concentration fluctuates throughout the menstrual cycle, peaking before ovulation. Measurement of estradiol levels is useful in assessing ovarian function and fertility. Its potency is due to its high receptor affinity and longer biological half-life compared to other natural estrogens.

(A) Mullerian agenesis
Mullerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome) is a congenital absence of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina due to failure of Müllerian duct development. Affected individuals present with primary amenorrhea and normal development of secondary sexual characteristics (breasts, pubic hair) because the ovaries and hypothalamic–pituitary axis function normally, producing normal estrogen levels. 177.	 Annular lesions are seen in all of the following

(D)	Pityriasis rosea

Annular lesions are ring-shaped skin lesions with central clearing and a well-defined active edge. They are characteristic of several dermatoses, including tinea corporis, pityriasis rosea, and porokeratosis. Correct morphological recognition aids diagnosis since many conditions can appear similar. Understanding lesion morphology is vital in dermatological diagnosis, guiding further investigations and specific therapy.

179.	 Which form of vitiligo becomes stable and non-

(A)	Mixed
(B)	 Segmental
(C)	Acrofacial
(D)	Focal
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(B) Segmental
Segmental vitiligo is characterized by depigmented macules confined to a unilateral, dermatomal distribution. It usually appears early in life, progresses rapidly for a short period, and then stabilizes, making it non-progressive and localized. Unlike non-segmental vitiligo, which is autoimmune and symmetrical, segmental vitiligo is believed to result from neural or somatic mosaicism affecting melanocyte function. 180.	 A mother had painful vesicular genital lesions

Neonatal herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) infection results from perinatal transmission during vaginal delivery in mothers with active genital herpes. The presence of multinucleated giant cells on a Tzanck smear or biopsy indicates a herpes infection. HSV-2 is the predominant cause of genital herpes and is more commonly transmitted to neonates than HSV-1. 181.	 Drug resistance is most seen with which sexually 
transmitted infection (STI)?
(A)	Chancroid
(B)	 Donovanosis
(C)	Syphilis
(D)	Gonorrhea
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(D) Gonorrhea
Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the causative organism of gonorrhea, has shown remarkable antimicrobial resistance development over decades. Initially sensitive to sulfonamides, penicillin, and tetracyclines, resistance has progressively evolved due to β-lactamase production, altered penicillin-binding proteins, and efflux pumps. Fluoroquinolone resistance emerged globally, followed by decreased susceptibility to macrolides and third-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone, cefixime). Multidrug-resistant strains now pose a major public health concern, leading WHO to classify gonorrhea as a “priority pathogen.” Treatment failures with oral regimens have made dual therapy — ceftriaxone (500 mg IM single dose) plus azithromycin (1 g PO single dose) — the standard recommendation. Resistance surveillance and molecular typing (NG-MAST, NG-STAR) are critical to track resistant strains. Other STIs such as chancroid (caused by Haemophilus ducreyi) and donovanosis (Klebsiella granulomatis) show far less resistance. Continuous antibiotic stewardship and new drug development are essential to prevent gonorrhea from becoming untreatable.

183.	 Which of the following is the induction 
anesthesia of choice in the pediatric age group?
(A)	Sevoflurane
(B)	 Desflurane
(C)	Halothane
(D)	Isoflurane
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(A) Sevoflurane
Sevoflurane is the preferred inhalational induction agent for pediatric anesthesia due to its non-pungent odor, rapid onset, and smooth induction characteristics. It has a low blood-gas partition coefficient (0.65), leading to quick equilibration between alveolar and brain concentrations, ensuring rapid induction and recovery. Thus, sevoflurane has largely replaced halothane in pediatric anesthesia practice.

185.	 A patient undergoing surgery under general

Sugammadex is a novel selective relaxant binding agent that rapidly reverses neuromuscular blockade induced by rocuronium and vecuronium, even after full-dose administration. 188.	 Which of the following is true about CT 
(Computed Tomography)?
(A)	Water has HU of zero
(B)	 Unfiltered X-ray beam is used
(C)	CT head dose is 20 mSv
(D)	First investigation for gallstones
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(A) Water has HU of zero
In CT imaging, tissue density is quantified in Hounsfield Units (HU), where water is assigned a reference value of 0 HU and air is –1000 HU. Dense structures like bone may have +1000 HU, while fat and soft tissue fall between –100 and +100 HU. CT scanners use filtered X-ray beams that rotate around the patient, producing cross-sectional images reconstructed by computer algorithms. CT is, however, excellent for detecting calcifications, fractures, vascular lesions, and neoplasms. Understanding HU values helps differentiate between tissues (e.g., distinguishing cystic from solid lesions). Thus, recognizing that water has a zero HU forms a fundamental concept in radiologic interpretation.
189.	 Which type of contrast can be given to patients 
with chronic kidney disease (CKD)?
(A)	Ionic iodinated contrast
(B)	 Non-ionic iodinated contrast
(C)	Ultrasound contrast
(D)	Gadolinium
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(C) Ultrasound contrast
Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at risk of contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) when exposed to iodinated (CT) or gadolinium-based (MRI) contrast agents. Hence, ultrasound contrast, composed of microbubbles of inert gases (e.g., sulfur hexafluoride), is safest as it is not nephrotoxic and is excreted via the lungs. Non-ionic iodinated contrast, though safer than ionic types, still poses nephrotoxic risk. Gadolinium is contraindicated in advanced CKD due to the risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF). Ultrasound contrast enhances visualization of blood flow, liver lesions, and vascular structures without renal compromise. For patients with impaired renal function, non-contrast MRI or ultrasound contrast imaging are preferred diagnostic modalities. Pre-hydration and avoidance of nephrotoxic drugs further minimize CIN risk if iodinated contrast use becomes unavoidable. Hence, ultrasound contrast is the safest and most appropriate choice for CKD patients requiring imaging studies.

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(C) Aberrant right subclavian artery (ARSA)
An Aberrant Right Subclavian Artery (ARSA) is the most common aortic arch anomaly, occurring in about 1% of the population. Normally, the right subclavian artery arises from the brachiocephalic trunk, but in ARSA, it originates distally from the aortic arch, beyond the left subclavian artery. The vessel passes posterior to the esophagus and trachea to reach the right upper limb. This retroesophageal course can compress the esophagus, leading to a characteristic symptom called “dysphagia lusoria.” On contrast-enhanced CT or MRI, ARSA appears as a vascular structure crossing behind the esophagus at the level of the thoracic inlet. Clinically, most patients remain asymptomatic, and the anomaly is usually discovered incidentally. However, it is crucial to recognize before procedures such as esophageal surgery or catheterization to prevent iatrogenic injury. Rarely, aneurysmal dilatation at the origin, known as Kommerell’s diverticulum, can cause dysphagia or respiratory distress. Mnemonic: “A Right artery goes Around” — reminding that the aberrant right subclavian artery loops behind the esophagus.
192.	 A 45-year-old patient presents with fever, pain, 
and shortness of breath. Based on the X-ray, 
which statement about this condition is false?
(A)	Loud S1
(B)	 Pericardiocentesis
(C)	Collapse of right atrium or 
ventricle
(D)	Pulsus paradoxus
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(A) Loud S1
The X-ray image shows a “water-bottle” or “flask-shaped” cardiac silhouette, characteristic of pericardial effusion. Pericardial effusion involves the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac, which compresses the cardiac chambers and may lead to cardiac tamponade. In tamponade, diastolic filling is impaired, causing reduced stroke volume and hypotension. The typical findings include muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension, and pulsus paradoxus (a >10 mmHg fall in systolic BP during inspiration). Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis by showing diastolic collapse of the right atrium or ventricle. Pericardiocentesis is the emergency therapeutic procedure that removes the excess fluid. The statement “Loud S1” is false, because in pericardial effusion, heart sounds are actually distant and muffled due to fluid insulation, while a loud S1 is seen in mitral stenosis. Mnemonic: “Beck’s triad — Hypotension, Muffled heart sounds, JVD” helps recall the features of tamponade. Recognizing the “water-bottle heart” on X-ray is essential for early intervention and prevention of hemodynamic collapse.
193.	 Identify the given image.
(A)	Extradural Hemorrhage
(B)	 Subdural Hemorrhage
(C)	Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
(D)	Intraventricular Hemorrhage
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(A) Extradural Hemorrhage
The given image is a non-contrast CT scan of the head showing a hyperdense (bright) collection adjacent to the inner table of the skull. The hemorrhage appears biconvex (lentiform) in shape and is limited by cranial sutures. This characteristic appearance is typical of an extradural (epidural) hemorrhage.
Extradural hemorrhage usually occurs due to rupture of the middle meningeal artery, most commonly following temporal bone trauma. Because the blood collects between the skull and the dura mater, it forms a lens-shaped collection that does not cross suture lines, as the dura is tightly adherent at sutures. Clinically, it may present with a history of head injury, brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, and subsequent neurological deterioration due to raised intracranial pressure.
In contrast, a subdural hemorrhage appears crescent-shaped and can cross sutures. Subarachnoid hemorrhage is seen within sulci and cisterns, while intraventricular hemorrhage is located within the ventricular system.
Therefore, based on the characteristic biconvex hyper dense lesion seen on CT, the correct diagnosis is (A) Extradural Hemorrhage.

194.	 Which of the following is NOT characteristic of

Rapid cycling bipolar disorder is defined by the occurrence of four or more mood episodes (mania, hypomania, or depression) within a 12-month period. It reflects a more severe and treatment-resistant subtype of bipolar disorder. The exact mechanism is not fully understood, but biological, endocrine, and medication-related factors play a role. It is most commonly seen in women and is strongly associated with hypothyroidism, especially in patients on lithium therapy, which may impair thyroid function. Antidepressant use can precipitate or worsen rapid cycling by triggering mood switches. Hence, option D (“occurs commonly in men”) is incorrect because women are affected more frequently. Clinically, these patients show poor response to lithium and may require valproate or lamotrigine as mood stabilizers. Mnemonic: “4 F’s” — Four episodes, Female, Fluctuating thyroid, From antidepressants — helps recall key associations. Early identification is crucial because rapid cycling often predicts chronicity, higher suicide risk, and poor functional outcome without appropriate mood stabilizer therapy.
195.	 Which of the following is not part of the

According to DSM-5 diagnostic criteria, Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is defined by two essential domains: (1) deficits in social communication and social interaction, and (2) restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities. These symptoms must be present from early developmental periods and must cause clinically significant impairment. While cognitive dysfunction may be seen in some individuals with ASD, it is not a defining diagnostic criterion. 196.	 Which of the following is not a component of 
Beck’s Cognitive Theory of Depression?
(A)	Cognitive distortions
(B)	 Automated thoughts
(C)	Introjection
(D)	Dysfunctional belief
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(C) Introjection
Aaron Beck’s Cognitive Theory of Depression postulates that depression results from distorted negative thinking rather than unconscious conflict. The theory focuses on three major cognitive components:
1.	
Automatic thoughts : spontaneous negative thoughts about oneself, the world, and the future.
2.	
Cognitive distortions : systematic errors in thinking such as overgeneralization, catastrophizing, and black-and-white thinking.
3.	
Dysfunctional core beliefs : deep-seated negative schemas developed from early experiences.
These collectively form the “Negative Cognitive Triad”. Introjection, however, belongs to Freud’s psychodynamic theory, referring to internalization of others’ beliefs or values, and thus is not part of Beck’s model. The cognitive theory is the foundation for Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), a structured, evidence-based psychotherapeutic approach widely used for depression and anxiety disorders. Mnemonic: “A.C.D.” — Automatic thoughts, Cognitive distortions, Dysfunctional beliefs — captures Beck’s components. CBT targets these distorted thought patterns, helping patients replace maladaptive cognitions with realistic and adaptive ones, ultimately reducing depressive symptoms and preventing relapse.
197.	 Which of the following sleep stages is 
represented in the EEG image shown?
(A)	NREM 1
(B)	 NREM 2
(C)	NREM 3
(D)	REM
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(D) REM
The EEG image shows low-amplitude, high-frequency activity, resembling an awake or alert pattern. This pattern is characteristic of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep.
REM sleep is also known as paradoxical sleep because the EEG activity during this stage resembles that of wakefulness. It is characterized by desynchronized brain waves, rapid eye movements, and muscle atonia. Dreams are most vivid and frequent during this stage. On EEG, REM sleep displays low-voltage, mixed-frequency waves similar to beta activity seen in the awake state.
In contrast, NREM stage 1 shows theta waves, NREM stage 2 is marked by sleep spindles and K-complexes, and NREM stage 3 (deep sleep) shows high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves.
Since the tracing in the image demonstrates desynchronized, low-amplitude, fast activity without sleep spindles or delta waves, the sleep stage represented is REM sleep.
Therefore, the correct answer is : (D) REM
198.	 The mhGAP program includes all of the

The Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) was launched by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2008 to scale up services for mental, neurological, and substance use disorders, especially in low- and middle-income countries where mental health resources are limited. The program focuses on priority conditions that contribute most to the global disease burden: depression, psychosis, epilepsy, suicide prevention, dementia, substance use, and developmental disorders. 199.	 Cannabidiol is not used to treat which of the 
following conditions?
(A)	Dravet syndrome
(B)	 Tuberous sclerosis complex
(C)	Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
(D)	Rett syndrome
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(D) Rett syndrome
Cannabidiol (CBD), the non-psychoactive component of Cannabis sativa, has gained FDA approval for the treatment of rare, severe childhood epilepsies, including Dravet syndrome, Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, and Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC). Its mechanism involves modulation of endocannabinoid receptors, calcium channels, and adenosine signaling, leading to decreased neuronal excitability and seizure control. CBD is marketed as Epidiolex® in oral solution form.
Rett syndrome, however, is a neurodevelopmental disorder primarily affecting females, caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene on the X chromosome. It is characterized by early developmental regression, hand-wringing stereotypies, loss of speech, and autonomic dysfunction. Although seizures occur in Rett syndrome, CBD is not an approved therapy for it, and its efficacy remains under investigation. Current management focuses on supportive care, physiotherapy, and antiepileptic drugs. Mnemonic: “Let’s Treat Dravet, Lennox, Tuberous — not Rett” helps recall approved indications. Recognizing FDA-approved uses of CBD is essential for avoiding off-label prescribing and understanding its role in modern epilepsy pharmacotherapy.
200.	 Supportive therapy is not typically provided for 
which type of patient?
(A)	A patient who is severely ill, non-
cooperative, and unable to participate in 
therapy
(B)	 A person who is motivated and has good 
control over emotions
(C)	A person with cognitive and functional 
abilities intact
(D)	A patient who is severely ill and has lost ego 
integrity
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
(A) A patient who is severely ill, non-cooperative, and unable to participate in therapy
Supportive psychotherapy is primarily indicated for patients who are severely ill, have impaired ego strength, poor insight, or reduced capacity to tolerate insight-oriented therapy. Its main goal is to maintain current functioning, provide reassurance, strengthen coping mechanisms, and prevent further psychological deterioration. It is commonly used in patients with chronic psychiatric illness, severe stress, or loss of ego integrity.
However, supportive therapy requires at least a minimum level of cooperation and participation from the patient. If a patient is severely ill, non-cooperative, and unable to participate in therapy, meaningful therapeutic engagement is not possible. In such cases, immediate medical stabilization, pharmacotherapy, or even inpatient management may be required before psychotherapy can be initiated.
A motivated person with good emotional control and intact cognitive and functional abilities is usually better suited for insight-oriented or cognitive therapies rather than purely supportive therapy. Meanwhile, severely ill patients with compromised ego strength are classic candidates for supportive therapy.
Therefore, supportive therapy is not typically provided for (A) a patient who is severely ill, non-cooperative, and unable to participate in therapy.

are 
Aldosterone 
(a),

(b),

Which statement about cardiac muscle depolarization is incorrect?
(A)	
Large refractory period
(B)	
Tetany
(C)	
All or none law
(D)	
Length-Tension relationship
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
15.	 (B) Tetany
Cardiac muscle possesses several unique 
physiological properties. It adheres to the all 
or none law (Option C), meaning a stimulus 
above threshold causes the entire muscle fiber 
to contract maximally. It also exhibits a length-
tension relationship (Option D), known as the 
Frank-Starling mechanism, where increased 
initial fiber length (preload) results in a more 
forceful contraction. A critical feature of the 
cardiac action potential is its long plateau 
phase due to calcium influx, which results in 
a large refractory period (Option A). This long 
refractory period is essential as it prevents the 
summation of individual muscle twitches. 
Consequently, cardiac muscle cannot undergo 
a sustained contraction, or tetany (Option B). 
Tetanus is a characteristic of skeletal muscle but 
is physiologically impossible in cardiac muscle, 
ensuring the heart functions as a pump with 
distinct relaxation (filling) phases.
A decrease in GFR associated with which of the following?
(A)	
Increased renal blood flow (RBF)
(B)	
Increased glomerular hydrostatic pressure
(C)	
Decreased Bowman's oncotic pressure
(D)	
Increased glomerular oncotic pressure
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
16.	 (D) Increased glomerular oncotic pressure
The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is 
determined by the balance of hydrostatic 
and oncotic pressures across the glomerular 
capillary wall (Starling forces). GFR is favored 
by glomerular hydrostatic pressure, and opposed 
by Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure and 
glomerular oncotic pressure. A decrease in 
GFR would be caused by factors that either 
reduce the forces favoring filtration or increase 
the forces opposing it. Increased RBF (A) and 
increased glomerular hydrostatic pressure (B) 
would both increase GFR. Decreased Bowman's 
oncotic pressure (C) is typically negligible and a 
decrease would slightly increase GFR. However, 
an increased glomerular oncotic pressure (D) 
directly opposes filtration. This occurs, for 
example, in dehydration or conditions with 
high plasma protein concentration, increasing 
the oncotic "pull" that holds fluid within the 
capillaries and thereby decreasing the GFR.

Select the correct sequence of events in the CAMP signaling pathway:
(A)	
CAMP PKA → Adenyl cyclase
(B)	
Adenyl cyclase → CAMP → РКА
(C)	
CAMP Adenyl cyclase → РКА
(D)	
Adenyl cyclase → PKA CAMP
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
20.	 (B) Adenyl cyclase → CAMP → РКА
The cyclic AMP (cAMP) signaling pathway is 
a common second messenger system initiated 
by the binding of a ligand (like epinephrine) 
to a G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR). This 
binding activates the G protein, which in turn 
activates the membrane-bound enzyme adenylyl 
cyclase. Adenylyl cyclase then catalyzes the 
conversion of ATP into cyclic AMP (cAMP). The 
increase in intracellular cAMP concentration 
activates Protein Kinase A (PKA). Activated 
PKA then phosphorylates various downstream 
target proteins, leading to a cellular response. 
Therefore, the correct sequence of events is the 
activation of adenylyl cyclase, which produces 
cAMP, which in turn activates PKA. This 
corresponds to option B.

Given the Lineweaver–Burk plots for Inhibitor A and Inhibitor B, what type of enzyme inhibition does each inhibitor represent?
(A)	
Competitive and Non-competitive
(B)	
Uncompetitive and Non-competitive
(C)	
Non-competitive and Uncompetitive
(D)	
Non-competitive and Competitive
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
22.	 (A) Competitive and Non-competitive
In a Lineweaver–Burk plot (double reciprocal 
plot of 1/V versus 1/[S]), different types of 
enzyme inhibition show characteristic patterns.
For Inhibitor A, the lines with and without 
inhibitor intersect at the Y-axis. This indicates 
that Vmax remains unchanged, while Km 
increases. Since competitive inhibitors compete 
with the substrate for the active site, increasing 
substrate concentration can overcome the 
inhibition. Therefore, Vmax is unaffected, but 
Km increases due to reduced apparent affinity. 
This pattern represents competitive inhibition.
For Inhibitor B, the lines intersect on the X-axis. 
This shows that Km remains unchanged, but 
Vmax decreases. Non-competitive inhibitors 
bind to an allosteric site rather than the active 
site, and their effect cannot be reversed by 
increasing substrate concentration. Because 
enzyme activity is reduced regardless of 
substrate concentration, Vmax decreases while 
Km remains constant. This pattern represents 
non-competitive inhibition.
Thus, Inhibitor A is competitive and Inhibitor B 
is non-competitive, making option (A) correct.
Congenital lactic acidosis results from a defect in which enzyme?
(A)	
Transketolase
(B)	
Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase
(C)	
Isocitrate dehydrogenase
(D)	
Pyruvate dehydrogenase
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
23.	 (D) Pyruvate dehydrogenase
Lactic acidosis occurs when lactate production 
exceeds its clearance. A major cause of 
congenital lactic acidosis is a deficiency in the 
pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex. This 
crucial mitochondrial enzyme complex converts 
pyruvate, the end product of glycolysis, into 
acetyl-CoA for entry into the Krebs cycle. When 
NODIA
page  108  	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024 Answer
the PDH complex is deficient, pyruvate cannot 
be efficiently metabolized aerobically. Instead, 
it is shunted into the anaerobic pathway and 
converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, 
leading to a significant accumulation of lactic 
acid in the blood. Branched-chain ketoacid 
dehydrogenase deficiency (B) causes Maple 
Syrup Urine Disease. Transketolase (A) is a 
pentose phosphate pathway enzyme. Isocitrate 
dehydrogenase (C) is a Krebs cycle enzyme 
whose deficiency would impair the cycle but 
not be the primary cause of congenital lactic 
acidosis.
Which of the following is not produced during the breakdown of heme?
(A)	
Ferrous ion
(B)	
Aminolevulinic acid
(C)	
Biliverdin
(D)	
Carbon monoxide
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
24.	 (B) Aminolevulinic acid
Heme catabolism is the breakdown pathway for 
heme, primarily from senescent red blood cells. 
The first and rate-limiting step is catalyzed by 
the enzyme heme oxygenase. This enzyme opens 
the porphyrin ring to produce three products: 
biliverdin (C), a linear tetrapyrrole; ferrous 
iron (Fe2+) (A), which is recycled; and carbon 
monoxide (CO) (D), a signaling molecule that is 
eventually exhaled. Biliverdin is then converted 
to bilirubin. In contrast, aminolevulinic acid 
(ALA) is a key intermediate in the synthesis 
of heme, not a product of its breakdown. The 
synthesis of heme begins with the condensation 
of glycine and succinyl-CoA to form ALA, 
catalyzed by ALA synthase. Therefore, ALA is a 
precursor to heme, not a catabolic product.
Which gene defect causes familial hypercholesterolemia?
(A)	
Apo E
(B)	
Apo CII
(C)	
LDL receptor
(D)	
Apo B48
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
25.	 (C) LDL receptor
Familial 
hypercholesterolemia 
(FH) 
is 
an autosomal dominant genetic disorder 
characterized by very high levels of low-
density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol in the 
blood, leading to premature atherosclerotic 
cardiovascular disease. The most common cause 
of FH, accounting for over 90% of cases, is a

on the surface of cells, primarily hepatocytes,

also cause a similar phenotype, but LDL receptor 
defects are the primary cause. Defects in Apo E 
(A), Apo CII (B), and Apo B48 (D) are associated

21-Beta hydroxylase deficiency
(B)	
11-Beta hydroxylase deficiency
(C)

(D)

26.	 (B) 11-Beta hydroxylase deficiency
This

puberty 
(virilization),

and

of 
11-Beta 
hydroxylase 
deficiency, 
a 
form

hyperplasia 
(CAH). The enzyme deficiency blocks the

Interpret the following arterial blood gas (ABG) values: pH=7.5, pCO2=50 mm Hg, HCO3-=30 mEq/L
(A)	
Metabolic acidosis
(B)	
Metabolic alkalosis
(C)	
Respiratory acidosis
(D)	
Respiratory alkalosis
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
27.	 (B) Metabolic alkalosis
To interpret an ABG, we follow a systematic 
approach. First, check the pH. A pH of 7.5 is 
above the normal range (7.35-7.45), indicating 
alkalosis. Second, determine if the primary cause 
is respiratory or metabolic. The pCO2 is 50 mm 
Hg, which is higher than the normal range (35-
45 mm Hg). An elevated pCO2 causes acidosis, 
which is opposite to the patient's alkalotic 
state, so the primary problem is not respiratory. 
The HCO3- is 30 mEq/L, which is higher than 
the normal range (22-26 mEq/L). An elevated 
HCO3- causes alkalosis. Therefore, the primary 
disorder is metabolic alkalosis. The elevated 
pCO2 represents a respiratory compensation, 
where the body hypoventilates to retain CO2 (an 
acid) to counteract the metabolic alkalosis.
Which of the following is not involved in post-transcriptional modification?
(A)	
Methylation
(B)	
Endonuclease cleavage
(C)	
5' capping
(D)	
Glycosylation
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
28.	 (D) Glycosylation
Post-transcriptional 
modification 
refers 
to 
the processes that a primary RNA transcript 
(pre-mRNA) undergoes to become a mature 
messenger RNA (mRNA) before it can be 
BK
BK 
INICET Examination Paper
translated into a protein. Key modifications 
include the addition of a 5' cap (a modified 
guanine nucleotide) (C), splicing to remove 
introns which involves endonuclease cleavage 
(B), and the addition of a poly-A tail to the 3' end. 
RNA molecules themselves can also undergo

contrast, glycosylation (D) is a post-translational

a post-transcriptional modification.

29.	 (B) Zinc (Zn)
Zinc (Zn) is an essential trace mineral that 
functions as a cofactor for hundreds of enzymes 
and is crucial for numerous physiological 
processes, including immune function, wound 
healing, and protein synthesis. A key role

Zinc deficiency is classically associated with

Which type of mutation leads to restoration of the wild-type phenotype when the mutant gene is suppressed?
(A)	
Frameshift mutation of coding gene
(B)	
Addition of another normal gene
(C)	
Deletion of mutant gene
(D)	
Mutation of tRNA
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
30.	 (D) Mutation of tRNA
This question describes a suppressor mutation, 
where a second mutation at a different site 
reverses the effect of the first mutation, restoring 
the wild-type phenotype. One classic example of 
this is a nonsense suppressor, which involves 
a mutation of a tRNA gene. For instance, if a 
primary mutation changes a codon for an amino 
acid into a premature stop codon (a nonsense 
mutation), it causes truncated protein synthesis. 
A second mutation in the anticodon of a tRNA 
molecule can allow that tRNA to recognize the 
stop codon and insert an amino acid instead, 
allowing translation to continue and producing 
a full-length (and often functional) protein. 
A frameshift mutation (A) is not typically 
reversed this way. Adding a normal gene (B) is 
complementation, not suppression. Deleting the 
mutant gene (C) would not restore the function.
Which diagnostic tool is preferred for metabolic disease screening in children?

(B)	
Complete blood count
(C)	
Urinalysis
(D)

31.	 (A) Tandem mass spectrometry
Newborn screening for inborn errors of

of tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS). This 
powerful analytical technique allows for the 
rapid, simultaneous, and quantitative detection 
of dozens of different metabolites (like amino

enables screening for a wide array of metabolic

amino 
acidopathies 
(e.g., PKU), organic acidemias, and fatty acid

urinalysis (C) and complete blood count (B) 
are common tests, they are not comprehensive 
screening tools for metabolic diseases. Genetic 
testing (D) is typically used as a confirmatory 
test after an abnormal screening result from 
MS/MS, rather than as the initial screening tool

Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) can identify all of the following except which one?
(A)	
Translocation
(B)	
Amplification
(C)	
Deletion
(D)	
Point mutation
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
32.	 (D) Point mutation
Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) is a 
cytogenetic technique that uses fluorescently 
labeled DNA probes to visualize specific 
DNA sequences on chromosomes. It is highly 
effective for detecting large-scale chromosomal 
abnormalities. It can identify translocations (A), 
where a piece of one chromosome breaks off and 
attaches to another (e.g., using fusion or break-
apart probes). It can detect gene amplification 
(B), seen as multiple copies of a fluorescent 
signal for a specific gene. It can also identify 
deletions (C) of chromosomal regions, indicated 
by the absence of a fluorescent signal where 
one is expected. However, FISH is not sensitive 
enough to detect very small-scale changes like 
point mutations (D), which involve a change in a 
single DNA base pair. Detecting point mutations 
requires DNA sequencing or allele-specific PCR 
techniques.

The metabolism of folate and vitamin B12 are

KIT proto-oncogene (D), a receptor tyrosine 
kinase. A smaller subset has mutations in a 
related receptor, PDGFRA. Wild-type GISTs 
(those without KIT or PDGFRA mutations) 
can have mutations in other genes, including 
the succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) complex 
genes (B). PDGFRB (A) mutations are rare but 
have been described in GIST. In contrast, NRG1 
(Neuregulin 1) fusions are oncogenic drivers 
found in other solid tumors, particularly lung 
adenocarcinoma, but they are not characteristic 
markers or drivers of GISTs.
All of the following are growth-promoting proto-oncogenes except?
(A)	
FGF
(B)	
PDGF
(C)	
TGF alpha
(D)	
TGF beta
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
40.	 (D) TGF beta
Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that, when 
mutated or overexpressed, can contribute 
to cancer formation. Many code for growth 
factors or their receptors. Fibroblast Growth 
Factor (FGF, A), Platelet-Derived Growth 
Factor (PDGF, B), and Transforming Growth 
Factor-alpha (TGF-alpha, C) are all potent 
growth factors whose genes function as proto-
oncogenes; their overexpression can drive cell 
proliferation. In contrast, Transforming Growth 
Factor-beta (TGF-beta) has a complex, context-
dependent role but is primarily considered a 
tumor suppressor. It inhibits the proliferation of 
many cell types, including epithelial cells, and 
promotes apoptosis. Loss-of-function mutations 
in the TGF-beta signaling pathway are common 
in many cancers, allowing cells to escape its 
growth-inhibitory effects. Therefore, TGF-beta 
is not a growth-promoting proto-oncogene.
In a trauma patient with an unknown blood type who is unstable and needs an immediate transfusion, which blood type should be given?
(A)	
A+
(B)	
AB+
(C)	
O+
(D)	
O-
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
41.	 (D) O-
In an emergency trauma situation where a patient 
is hemodynamically unstable and requires 
immediate blood transfusion before blood 
typing and cross-matching can be completed, 
the universal donor blood type is used. This is 
O-negative (O-) blood. Group O red blood cells 
lack both A and B antigens, so they will not 
be attacked by the recipient's anti-A or anti-B 
antibodies. The Rh-negative designation means 
they also lack the RhD antigen, preventing an 
immune reaction in an Rh-negative recipient. 
While O-positive (C) blood can be given to Rh-
positive recipients, it can cause sensitization 
in Rh-negative recipients, especially females of 
childbearing age. A+ (A) and AB+ (B) blood 
types have A and/or B antigens and cannot 
be given universally. Therefore, O-negative is 
the safest universal red blood cell product for 
emergency transfusion.

Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD)

Which of the following is/are associated with an anaphylactic reaction?
(A)	
Persistent abdominal cramps
(B)	
Hypertension
(C)	
Urticaria & Swollen lips
(D)	
Both A & C
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
44.	 (D) Both A & C
Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening, 
systemic Type I hypersensitivity reaction. 
It is caused by the widespread release of 
inflammatory mediators (like histamine) from 
mast cells and basophils. These mediators 
cause vasodilation and increased vascular 
permeability, leading to characteristic signs. 
Skin and mucosal involvement, such as 
urticaria (hives) and angioedema (swollen lips), 
is very common (C). Gastrointestinal symptoms 
like persistent abdominal cramps, nausea, and 
vomiting can also occur due to smooth muscle 
contraction and mucosal edema (A). A key 
cardiovascular sign is hypotension (low blood 
pressure) due to vasodilation and fluid leakage 
from the capillaries, not hypertension (B). 
Therefore, both persistent abdominal cramps 
and urticaria/swollen lips are associated with 
anaphylaxis.
In Sahli’s colorimetric method for estimating hemoglobin, which component is not used?

Sahli's method is a visual colorimetric method 
for estimating hemoglobin concentration. The

What is the inheritance pattern shown in the given pedigree?

Which neurotransmitter is released by the SA node when blood pressure rises?
(A)	
Acetylcholine
(B)	
Dopamine
(C)	
Epinephrine
(D)	
Norepinephrine
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
47.	 (A) Acetylcholine
This question describes the baroreceptor reflex. 
When blood pressure increases, baroreceptors 
in the aortic arch and carotid sinus increase 
their firing rate. These signals travel to the 
cardiovascular control center in the medulla 
oblongata. The medulla responds by increasing 
NODIA
BK 
INICET Examination Paper
parasympathetic (vagal) outflow to the heart 
and decreasing sympathetic outflow. The 
parasympathetic nerve fibers, part of the vagus 
nerve, innervate the sinoatrial (SA) node and 
atrioventricular (AV) node. At the SA node, 
these nerve endings release the neurotransmitter 
acetylcholine (ACh). ACh binds to muscarinic 
(M2) receptors on the pacemaker cells, 
which 
increases 
potassium 
permeability, 
hyperpolarizes the cell, and decreases the rate 
of spontaneous depolarization, thereby slowing 
the heart rate to help lower blood pressure. 
Epinephrine (C) and norepinephrine (D) are 
sympathetic neurotransmitters that would 
increase heart rate.
A 30-year-old woman who recently lost her newborn is experiencing breast engorgement from milk production, putting her at risk for milk stasis and a possible breast abscess. Which medication can be used to prevent this?

Mifepristone
(B)	
Cabergoline
(C)	
Chlorpromazine
(D)	
Metoclopramide
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
48.	 (B) Cabergoline
Lactation (breast milk production) is primarily 
stimulated by the hormone prolactin, which 
is released from the anterior pituitary gland. 
Prolactin secretion itself is tonically inhibited 
by dopamine from the hypothalamus. To 
suppress lactation, a dopamine agonist can 
be administered. Cabergoline is a potent, 
long-acting D2 dopamine receptor agonist 
that effectively suppresses prolactin secretion 
from the pituitary gland, thereby inhibiting 
milk production and relieving symptoms 
of engorgement. It is the drug of choice for 
the suppression of postpartum lactation. 
Metoclopramide (D) is a dopamine antagonist 
and can actually increase prolactin levels, 
causing galactorrhea. Chlorpromazine (C) is 
also a dopamine antagonist. Mifepristone (A) 
is a progesterone and glucocorticoid receptor 
antagonist used for medical termination of 
pregnancy.
Which antidiabetic medication is linked to a higher risk of urinary tract infections?
(A)	
Dapagliflozin
(B)	
Sitagliptin
(C)	
Pioglitazone
(D)	
Metformin
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
49.	 (A) Dapagliflozin
Dapagliflozin belongs to the class of drugs known 
as sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) 
inhibitors. These drugs work by blocking 
the reabsorption of glucose in the proximal 
convoluted tubules of the kidney, thereby 
promoting the excretion of glucose in the urine 
(glucosuria). While this mechanism effectively 
lowers blood glucose levels, the resulting high 
concentration of sugar in the urine creates a 
favorable environment for bacterial growth. This 
significantly increases the risk of genitourinary 
infections, including urinary tract infections 
(UTIs) and genital mycotic infections (yeast 
infections). Sitagliptin (B), a DPP-4 inhibitor, 
pioglitazone (C), a thiazolidinedione, and 
metformin (D) do not work by this mechanism 
and are not associated with a similar increased 
risk of UTIs.

Enterococcal endocarditis requires bactericidal

caution. Piperacillin (D) is a penicillin derivative

Identify the source of the trauma indicated in the image of the skull.
(A)	
Bullet
(B)	
ROD
(C)	
Axe
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
54.	 (A) Bullet
The image displays a circular defect in a skull, 
which is characteristic of a gunshot entry 
wound. The key forensic feature is the presence 
of internal beveling. This means the hole on 
the inner table of the skull is larger and more 
cone-shaped than the hole on the outer table. 
This funnel-like effect is created as the kinetic 
energy of the bullet dissipates upon passing 
through the bone, chipping away a larger piece 
of the inner lamina. This finding is considered 
pathognomonic for a bullet's entry point. 
Trauma from a rod (B) or an axe (C) would 
typically cause depressed, linear, or comminuted 
fractures with different characteristics. A scissor 
(D) would create a puncture wound that would 
not produce this specific beveling pattern in the

Which of the following substances are antidotes for cyanide poisoning?
1.	
Amyl nitrite
2.	
Sodium nitrate
3.	
Sodium thiosulphate
4.	
Benzyl thiocyanate
(A)	
1,2,3
(B)	
1,2,3,4
(C)	
1,2
(D)	
1,3,4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
55.	 (A) 1,2,3
The standard treatment for cyanide poisoning 
involves a multi-step approach using a specific 
kit of antidotes. The strategy is to convert 
hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which has a 
higher affinity for cyanide than cytochrome 
oxidase does. This is achieved by administering 
nitrites, such as inhaled amyl nitrite (1) 
followed by intravenous sodium nitrite (2). This 
sequesters the cyanide as cyanmethemoglobin. 
The second step is to enhance the body's 
natural detoxification pathway by providing a 
sulfur donor. Intravenous sodium thiosulfate 
(3) is administered, which allows the enzyme 
rhodanese to convert the cyanide from 
cyanmethemoglobin into the much less toxic 
thiocyanate, which is then excreted in the 
urine. Benzyl thiocyanate (4) is not part of this 
standard antidote regimen.

Which of the following is not associated with Korsakoff psychosis?
(A)	
Confabulation
(B)	
Polyneuropathy
(C)	
Amnesia
(D)	
Psychosis
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
57.	 (B) Polyneuropathy
Korsakoff psychosis is a chronic neuropsychiatric 
syndrome caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) 
deficiency, most commonly seen in chronic 
alcohol use. It primarily affects memory and 
cognition.
The core features of Korsakoff psychosis include:
1.	 Amnesia – especially severe anterograde 
amnesia, meaning inability to form new 
memories.
2.	 Confabulation – patients fabricate stories 
to fill gaps in memory, without intent to 
deceive.
3.	 Disorientation and cognitive impairment – 
sometimes loosely referred to as “psychosis” 
in exam contexts due to behavioral 
disturbances.
Polyneuropathy, however, is not a defining 
feature of Korsakoff psychosis. Although chronic 
alcoholics may develop peripheral neuropathy 
due to nutritional deficiencies, this is a separate 
complication and not part of the core clinical 
features of Korsakoff syndrome itself.

The World Medical Association’s 1970 Declaration of Oslo refers to which statement?
(A)	
Therapeutic abortion
(B)	
Torture, degradation, or cruel treatment of prisoners
(C)	
Ethical aspects for medical research
(D)

58.	 (A) Therapeutic abortion
The World Medical Association (WMA) issues 
various declarations and statements on medical 
ethics. The Declaration of Oslo, first adopted in 
1970 and subsequently amended, specifically 
addresses the issue of therapeutic abortion. It 
provides guidance to physicians regarding their 
ethical duties and personal convictions when 
faced with a request for the termination of a 
pregnancy. It affirms the physician's right to

on ethical aspects of medical research (C) is 
the Declaration of Helsinki. The WMA has 
also issued declarations on hunger (D), but the 
Declaration of Oslo is specific to therapeutic 
abortion.
What is the proper sequence of examinations during a fetal autopsy to distinguish a live birth from a stillbirth?
(A)	
Abdomen > Head > Thorax
(B)	
Thorax > Head > Abdomen
(C)	
Head Abdomen > Thorax
(D)	
Head > Thorax > Abdomen
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
59.	 (D) Head > Thorax > Abdomen
In a medicolegal autopsy to determine live 
birth versus stillbirth, a specific sequence of 
dissection is followed to preserve key evidence. 
The head is examined first to look for signs of 
birth trauma, such as caput succedaneum or 
cephalhematoma, which indicate the fetus 
was alive during delivery. Next, the thorax is 
opened to perform the hydrostatic test on the 
lungs. This test determines if the lungs float 
in water, which is a crucial sign that the infant 
breathed after birth. The abdominal organs are 
examined last. Opening the abdomen first (A, B, 
C) could introduce air artifacts into the thoracic 
cavity or damage the diaphragm, potentially 
compromising the results of the hydrostatic test, 
which is the most critical piece of evidence for 
establishing live birth. Therefore, the correct 
sequence is Head > Thorax > Abdomen.
A 40-year-old woman ingested a white rodenticide powder and now has a potassium level of 2.5 mEq/L, an irregular pulse, muscle paralysis, and an ECG showing multiple ventricular ectopics. What poison is most likely responsible?
(A)	
Aluminum phosphide
(B)	
Zinc phosphide
(C)	
Warfarin toxicity
(D)	
Barium carbonate
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
60.	 (D) Barium carbonate
The clinical presentation is highly suggestive 
of barium poisoning. Barium carbonate is a 
component of some rodenticides. Barium ions 
are potent toxins that block potassium channels, 
leading to a rapid and severe influx of potassium 
into cells from the extracellular fluid. This causes 
profound hypokalemia, as seen in the patient 
(K+ of 2.5 mEq/L). The severe hypokalemia is 
responsible for the characteristic symptoms of 
barium poisoning, including muscle weakness 
progressing to paralysis and significant cardiac 
arrhythmias, such as ventricular ectopics, due to 
altered membrane excitability. Phosphide-based 
rodenticides (A, B) cause a different toxicity 
profile related to phosphine gas production. 
Warfarin toxicity (C) causes coagulopathy and 
bleeding, not acute hypokalemia and paralysis.

by

diphtheriae. However, the reason is false. 
Diphtheria is primarily a toxin-mediated disease. 
The bacterium itself typically remains localized 
in the pharynx and does not cause a significant 
Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024 Answer
bacteremia (widespread presence of bacteria 
in the blood). The systemic complications,

FISH can detect all except
(A)	
Amplification
(B)	
Deletion
(C)	
Translocation
(D)	
Point mutation
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
62.	 (D) Point mutation
Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) is a 
cytogenetic technique that uses fluorescently 
labeled DNA probes to visualize specific 
DNA sequences on chromosomes. It is highly 
effective for detecting large-scale chromosomal 
abnormalities. It can identify gene amplification 
(A), seen as multiple copies of a fluorescent 
signal for a specific gene. It can also identify 
deletions (B) of chromosomal regions, indicated 
by the absence of a fluorescent signal where 
one is expected. It can identify translocations 
(C), where a piece of one chromosome breaks 
off and attaches to another (e.g., using fusion 
or break-apart probes). However, FISH is not 
sensitive enough to detect very small-scale 
changes like point mutations (D), which involve 
a change in a single DNA base pair. Detecting 
point mutations requires DNA sequencing or 
allele-specific PCR techniques.

64.	 (A) Fresh frozen plasma
Hemophilia B, also known as Christmas disease, 
is an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder 
caused by a deficiency of coagulation Factor IX. 
The mainstay of treatment is replacement of the 
deficient factor. While recombinant or purified 
Factor IX concentrates are the ideal treatment, 
Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) can be used as it 
contains all the coagulation factors, including 
Factor IX. Cryoprecipitate (B) is rich in Factor 
VIII, fibrinogen, and von Willebrand factor, 
making it the treatment for Hemophilia A, 
but it contains very little Factor IX. Factor VIII 
concentrate (C) is specifically for Hemophilia A. 
Cryo-poor plasma (D) is the plasma remaining 
after cryoprecipitate has been removed, so 
it is deficient in the very factors found in 
cryoprecipitate and is not used for hemophilia.
Which disorder is characterized by recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms?
(A)	
X-linked hypogammaglobulinemia
(B)	
Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)
(C)	
Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)
(D)	
Chediak-Higashi syndrome
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
65.	 (B) Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)
Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) is a 
primary immunodeficiency caused by defects 
in the NADPH oxidase enzyme complex in 
phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages). This 
defect impairs the phagocyte's ability to produce 
reactive oxygen species (the "respiratory burst") 
needed to kill ingested microorganisms. As a 
result, patients with CGD are highly susceptible 
to recurrent, severe infections. A key feature is 
that they can handle catalase-negative organisms 
(which produce their own hydrogen peroxide 
that the phagocyte can use), but they cannot kill 
catalase-positive organisms (e.g., Staphylococcus 
aureus, Serratia, Aspergillus) because these 
organisms break down any hydrogen peroxide. 
X-linked hypogammaglobulinemia (A) affects 
antibody production. SCID (C) affects both 
B and T cells. Chediak-Higashi (D) involves 
defective phagolysosome fusion.

Which of the following organisms shows parthenogenesis?

(B)

Parthenogenesis is a form of reproduction in 
which an ovum can develop into a new individual 
without fertilization by a male gamete. Among 
the given intestinal nematodes, Strongyloides 
stercoralis is unique in its ability to undergo 
a free-living cycle as well as a parasitic cycle 
that involves parthenogenesis. In the parasitic 
cycle within the human host, only females are 
present in the small intestine. These parasitic

What is the best investigation for malaria speciation identification?
(A)	
Thick smear
(B)	
Thin smear with acridine orange
(C)	
Thin smear with Giemsa
(D)	
Quantitative Buffy Coat (QBC)
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
69.	 (C) Thin smear with Giemsa
The gold standard for the diagnosis of malaria 
involves microscopic examination of blood 
smears. Two types of smears are prepared. 
The thick smear is used for screening and 
detection, as it concentrates a larger volume 
of blood, making it easier to find parasites, 
especially in low-density infections. However, 
the red blood cells are lysed, distorting parasite 
morphology. The thin smear is used for species 
identification and quantification of parasitemia. 
In a thin smear, the red blood cells remain 
intact, allowing for clear visualization of the 
parasite's morphology (e.g., ring size, presence 
of 
Schüffner's 
dots, 
gametocyte 
shape), 
which is essential for distinguishing between 
Plasmodium species like P. falciparum and P. 
vivax. Giemsa stain is the preferred stain for 
both smears. QBC (D) and fluorescent stains (B) 
are sensitive screening tools but are inferior to 
the Giemsa-stained thin smear for speciation.

Assertion: Plasmodium falciparum doesn't show the schizont stage in the peripheral blood. 
Reason: This is due to cytoadherence to the cerebral endothelial cells.
(A)	
Assertion is true, reason is true, and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
(B)	
Assertion is true, reason is true, and reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
(C)	
Assertion is true, reason is false.
(D)	
Assertion is false, reason is true.
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
72.	 (A) Assertion is true, reason is true, and reason 
is the correct explanation of the assertion.
The assertion is true. In a typical Plasmodium 
falciparum infection, only early ring-stage 
trophozoites and gametocytes are seen in the 
peripheral blood smear. The more mature stages, 
including late trophozoites and schizonts, are 
sequestered in the microvasculature of deep 
organs and are not typically seen in circulation. 
The reason is also true and correctly explains the 
assertion. P. falciparum-infected red blood cells 
express a protein (PfEMP1) on their surface that 
mediates cytoadherence to endothelial receptors 
(like ICAM-1) in capillaries of organs like the 
brain, placenta, and lungs. This sequestration of 
mature forms in the deep vasculature is a key 
pathogenic mechanism of falciparum malaria, 
leading to microcirculatory obstruction and 
complications like cerebral malaria. It is also 
the reason why these stages are absent from 
peripheral blood smears.

In ABO blood grouping, which of the following statements is FALSE?
(A)

(B)	
ABO antibodies are natural and present since birth
(C)	
ABO antigens are carbohydrate antigens
(D)	
Antibodies are present only if the antigen is absent
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
76.	 (B) ABO antibodies are natural and present 
since birth
Let's evaluate the statements about the ABO 
blood group system.
A.	 The naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B 
antibodies 
("isohemagglutinins") 
are 
predominantly of the IgM class. This is 
true.
C.	 The A and B antigens are oligosaccharide 
chains attached to proteins or lipids 
on the red blood cell surface. They are 
carbohydrate antigens. This is true.
D.	 This describes Landsteiner's law : if an ABO 
antigen is present on an individual's red 
blood cells, the corresponding antibody will 
be absent from their plasma, and vice versa. 
This is true.

present since birth is false.

Which of the following does NOT have a polysaccharide capsule?

(D)

78.	 (C) Hepatitis B virus (HBV)
A polysaccharide capsule is a major virulence 
factor for many pathogenic bacteria, as it 
helps them evade phagocytosis. Haemophilus 
influenzae type b (Hib) (A), Streptococcus 
pneumoniae (Pneumococcus) (B), and Neisseria 
meningitidis (D) are all classic examples of 
encapsulated bacteria. Their polysaccharide 
capsules are the targets for the conjugate 
vaccines developed to protect against the invasive 
diseases they cause (meningitis, pneumonia, 
epiglottitis). In contrast, Hepatitis B virus (HBV) 
(C) is a virus, not a bacterium. Viruses have a 
protein capsid and, in the case of HBV, a lipid 
envelope containing surface antigens (HBsAg). 
They do not possess a polysaccharide capsule.

be autoclaved, autoclavable plastics (like

the pipettes are autoclavable plastic, this is the 
best option for achieving sterility.

Patients who need urgent, life-saving treatment are placed under which triage color category?
(A)	
Red
(B)	
Yellow
(C)	
Green
(D)	
Black
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
81.	 (A) Red
Triage is the process of prioritizing patients 
based on the severity of their condition, 
especially in mass casualty incidents or busy 
emergency departments. A color-coded system 
is commonly used.
1.	 Red (Priority 1) : Indicates patients with 
immediate, life-threatening injuries (e.g., 
airway obstruction, severe bleeding, shock) 
who have a high chance of survival if they 
receive immediate medical intervention.
2.	 Yellow (Priority 2) : For patients with 
serious injuries that are not immediately 
life-threatening but require urgent care 
(e.g., major fractures, open wounds).
3.	 Green (Priority 3) : The "walking wounded"; 
patients with minor injuries who can wait 
for treatment (e.g., minor cuts, sprains).
4.	 Black (Priority 0) : For patients who are 
deceased or have injuries so severe that they 
are unlikely to survive even with medical 
care.
Therefore, patients requiring immediate life-
threatening care are tagged as Red.
What is the most reliable indicator of some dehydration?
(A)	
Sunken eyes
(B)	
Lethargy
(C)	
Thirst
(D)	
Delayed skin pinch
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
82.	 (C) Thirst
In the assessment of dehydration, especially 
according to WHO/IMNCI guidelines, thirst is 
considered the most reliable and early indicator 
of some dehydration. It reflects the body’s 
physiological response to fluid deficit. When 
plasma osmolality rises or intravascular volume 
falls, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus 
stimulate the thirst center, prompting the child 
or patient to drink eagerly.
Other signs like sunken eyes and delayed 
skin pinch can help in assessment but are less 
reliable individually. Sunken eyes may normally 
be present in malnourished children, and 
skin turgor can vary with age and nutritional 
status. Lethargy is usually a sign of more severe 
dehydration rather than some dehydration.
Therefore, among the given options, thirst is the 
most consistent and reliable clinical indicator of 
some dehydration.

Choose the correct option regarding graft survival.
(A)	
CD4 and CD8 both play a role in graft rejection
(B)	
CD8 only plays a role in graft rejection
(C)	
CD4 only plays a role in graft rejection
(D)	
None of the above
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
86.	 (A) CD4 and CD8 both play a role in graft 
rejection
Allograft rejection is a complex cell-mediated 
immune response orchestrated primarily by 
T lymphocytes that recognize foreign MHC 
molecules on the donor graft. Both major subsets 
of T cells are critically involved. CD4+ helper T 
cells play a central role by recognizing foreign 
MHC class II molecules on antigen-presenting 
cells from the graft. Once activated, they 
orchestrate the rejection process by producing 
cytokines that activate macrophages and help 
activate other immune cells. CD8+ cytotoxic 
T lymphocytes (CTLs) recognize foreign MHC 
class I molecules expressed on all nucleated 
cells of the graft. Upon activation, these CTLs 
directly kill the graft cells, leading to tissue 
destruction. Therefore, both CD4+ and CD8+ T 
cells play distinct but essential and cooperative 
roles in the process of graft rejection.
On the fifth day of dengue hemorrhagic fever, which diagnostic test is most appropriate?
(A)	
IgM ELISA
(B)	
NS1 Antigen
(C)	
RT-PCR
(D)	
Viral culture
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
87.	 (A) IgM ELISA
The choice of diagnostic test for dengue infection 
is highly dependent on the timing of the illness. 
In the early febrile phase (days 1-5), the virus is 
circulating, making tests that detect the virus 
or its components, like the NS1 antigen test (B) 
or RT-PCR (C), most useful. However, as the 
illness progresses beyond day 5, the viral load 
and NS1 antigen levels decline rapidly and may 
become undetectable. Concurrently, the host 
immune response begins, with the production 
of antibodies. IgM antibodies are the first to 
appear, typically becoming detectable around 
day 4-5 of the illness and remaining elevated for 
several months. Therefore, on Day 5, while NS1 
may still be positive, the most reliable diagnostic 
test to confirm a recent infection is an IgM 
ELISA.

Which of the following sign is not associated with otitis media with effusion?
(A)	
Mostly bilateral
(B)

(C)	
Mostly resolves on its own
(D)	
None

91.	 (B) AD curve on tympanometry with conductive 
hearing loss
Otitis Media with Effusion (OME), or "glue 
ear," is characterized by the presence of non-
purulent fluid in the middle ear space. It is 
often bilateral (A) and, in many cases, is self-
limiting and resolves on its own (C) within three 
months. The fluid in the middle ear dampens 
the movement of the tympanic membrane and 
ossicles, leading to conductive hearing loss. The

which is the opposite of what is seen in OME. 
Therefore, an AD curve is not associated with 
otitis media with effusion.
A 42-year-old obese man presents with disrupted sleep and daytime sleepiness. Which of the following statements is incorrect?

Apnea with awakening
(B)

The

are 
classic 
for

Which structure passes between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictor muscles?
(A)	
Glossopharyngeal nerve
(B)	
Stylopharyngeus muscle
(C)	
Pharyngeal branch of vagus nerve
(D)	
Superior laryngeal artery
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
93.	 (B) Stylopharyngeus muscle
The stylopharyngeus muscle arises from the 
styloid process of the temporal bone and 
descends between the superior and middle 
pharyngeal constrictor muscles to enter the 
pharyngeal wall. It then spreads out within the 
pharynx and helps elevate the pharynx during 
swallowing and speech.
Importantly, the glossopharyngeal nerve 
(CN IX) accompanies the stylopharyngeus 
muscle and also passes between the superior 
and middle constrictors to supply it. However,

The pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve 
contributes to the pharyngeal plexus on the 
outer surface of the pharynx, and the superior 
laryngeal artery does not pass between these 
two constrictor muscles.
Therefore, the correct answer is Stylopharyngeus 
muscle.

Which of the following is not an action of the superior oblique muscle?
(A)	
Depression
(B)	
Intorsion
(C)	
Abduction
(D)	
Adduction
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
95.	 (D) Adduction
The superior oblique muscle, innervated by the 
trochlear nerve (CN IV), has three actions on 
the eyeball. Its primary action is intorsion (B), 
which is rotational movement of the top of the 
cornea toward the nose. Its secondary action is 
depression (A), moving the eye downward, which 
is most prominent when the eye is adducted. Its 
tertiary action is abduction (C), moving the eye 
outward, away from the nose. The muscle that 
performs adduction (moving the eye inward) is 
primarily the medial rectus, with contributions 
from the superior and inferior recti muscles. 
The superior oblique abducts the eye, it does not 
adduct it. Therefore, adduction is not an action 
of the superior oblique muscle.
A 40-year-old man reports experiencing flashes of light. What is the most likely underlying cause?
(A)	
Retinal detachment
(B)	
CRAO (Central Retinal Artery Occlusion)
(C)	
SAH (Subarachnoid Hemorrhage)
(D)	
CRVO (Central Retinal Vein Occlusion)
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
96.	 (A) Retinal detachment
The symptom of photopsia, described as seeing 
flashes of light, is a classic sign of vitreoretinal 
traction. This occurs when the vitreous gel inside 
the eye pulls on the light-sensitive retina. This 
mechanical stimulation of the photoreceptors 
is perceived as flashes of light. Vitreoretinal 
traction is the primary mechanism leading to 
a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), which 
can in turn cause a retinal tear and progress to a 
full retinal detachment. While other conditions 
can cause visual disturbances, sudden, painless 
flashes of light, especially when accompanied 
by new floaters, are highly suggestive of a PVD 
or retinal tear/detachment and constitute an 
ophthalmic emergency. CRAO (B) and CRVO 
(D) typically cause sudden, painless loss of 
vision, not flashes. SAH (C) can cause headache 
and visual changes but not typically isolated 
photopsia.
An 80-year-old patient presents with eye pain, redness, and decreased vision. IOP is 16 mmHg in the right eye and 50 mmHg in the left. The left eye shows a deep anterior chamber flare, a white cataractous lens, and an enlarged lens. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	
Phacolytic glaucoma
(B)	
Phacomorphic glaucoma
(C)	
Fuchs' heterochromic uveitis
(D)	
Malignant glaucoma
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
97.	 (A) Phacolytic glaucoma
The patient has a mature, white (hyper-mature) 
cataractous lens. Phacolytic glaucoma is a type 
of secondary open-angle glaucoma caused by 
leakage of high-molecular-weight lens proteins 
through the capsule of a hyper-mature cataract. 
These proteins are ingested by macrophages in 
the anterior chamber, which then obstruct the 
trabecular meshwork, leading to a significant rise 
in intraocular pressure (IOP), corneal edema, 
and inflammation (flare). The key features are 
a hyper-mature cataract, deep anterior chamber 
with flare, and very high IOP, which match 
the description. Phacomorphic glaucoma (B) 
is caused by an intumescent (swollen) cataract 
physically pushing the iris forward, causing 
angle closure, which would result in a shallow, 
not deep, anterior chamber.

A patient reports losing vision in the superior quadrant for the past week and has untreated rheumatic heart disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	
CRAO
(B)	
CRVO
(C)	
BRAO
(D)	
BRVO

99.	 (C) BRAO
The patient's history of rheumatic heart disease 
(RHD) places them at risk for cardiac valve 
vegetations and atrial fibrillation, both of 
which are sources of emboli. Sudden, painless 
vision loss affecting a specific quadrant of the 
visual field is characteristic of an occlusion of a 
branch of the retinal artery or vein. An arterial 
occlusion typically causes a more profound 
and sudden visual field defect than a venous 
occlusion. A Branch Retinal Artery Occlusion 
(BRAO) occurs when an embolus lodges in one

field defect that corresponds to the affected 
retinal quadrant. A Central Retinal Artery 
Occlusion (CRAO) (A) would cause vision loss 
in the entire eye, not just a quadrant. Venous 
occlusions (B, D) typically cause a less dense 
visual field defect.
What is the most common cause of proptosis in the middle age group?

Ocular hemangioma
(B)

(C)

(D)

100.	 (B) Thyroid disorder
Proptosis, or exophthalmos, is the forward 
protrusion of the eyeball. In adults and the 
middle-aged population, the most common 
cause of both unilateral and bilateral proptosis 
is Thyroid Eye Disease (TED), also known 
as 
Graves' 
ophthalmopathy. 
This 
is 
an 
autoimmune condition associated with Graves' 
disease (hyperthyroidism). The autoimmune

can cause proptosis, thyroid eye disease is by far 
the most frequent etiology in this age group.
What is the appropriate next step in managing a construction worker who got lime (chuna) particles in their eye?

(C)

101.	 (A) Irrigation with normal saline
A chemical injury to the eye, particularly an 
alkali burn from lime (calcium hydroxide), is an 
ophthalmological emergency. The single most 
important and immediate action is copious

examination can proceed. Scraping (D) is not an 
initial management step.
Which of the following statements is false regarding the condition shown in the image?

102.	 (B) Night blindness is seen in late stages
The image shows bone-spicule pigmentation in 
the peripheral retina, which is a pathognomonic 
sign of Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP). RP is a group 
of inherited disorders (D) causing progressive 
retinal degeneration. It is primarily a rod-cone 
dystrophy, meaning the rod photoreceptors are 
affected first and more severely, followed by

loss of peripheral vision (tunnel vision) follows.

a late-stage symptom is false.

The ECG shows a rapid, wide-complex

Which drug is known to increase the risk of urinary tract infections?
(A)	
Dapagliflozin
(B)	
Pioglitazone
(C)	
Sitagliptin
(D)	
Metformin
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
107.	 (A) Dapagliflozin
Dapagliflozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 
2 (SGLT2) inhibitor. This class of drugs lowers 
blood glucose by blocking its reabsorption in 
the proximal renal tubules, leading to increased 
glucose excretion in the urine (glucosuria). This 
high concentration of sugar in the urinary tract 
creates a favorable environment for the growth 
of bacteria and yeast. Consequently, a well-
known side effect of SGLT2 inhibitors is an 
increased incidence of genitourinary infections, 
including both bacterial urinary tract infections 
and genital mycotic (yeast) infections. The 
other listed antidiabetic agents—pioglitazone 
(B), sitagliptin (C), and metformin (D)—do not 
share this mechanism and are not associated 
with a similarly elevated risk of UTIs.

A male patient presents with purple striae, thin skin, a non-healing wound, and a pendulous abdomen. What is the most likely underlying cause?
(A)	
Insulin resistance
(B)	
Hypercortisolism
(C)

109.	 (B) Hypercortisolism
This constellation of signs is pathognomonic 
for Cushing's syndrome, a condition caused by 
prolonged exposure to excess corticosteroids 
(hypercortisolism). Cortisol has catabolic effects 
on protein, which leads to the breakdown of 
collagen and subcutaneous tissue. This results 
in thin, fragile skin, easy bruising, poor wound 
healing, and the development of wide (>1 cm),

hump"), and a pendulous abdomen. While 
insulin resistance (A) and hypercholesterolemia 
(D) can be associated with Cushing's syndrome, 
hypercortisolism is the underlying endocrine 
cause. Hypothyroidism (C) presents with 
different symptoms, such as weight gain, fatigue, 
and dry, coarse skin.
Which of the following is NOT a complication of hypokalemia?
(A)	
Ventricular Tachycardia
(B)	
Cerebral Edema
(C)	
Diabetes Insipidus
(D)

110.	 (B) Cerebral Edema
Hypokalemia (low serum potassium) has 
significant effects on excitable tissues. Severe 
hypokalemia can cause ECG changes (U 
waves, ST depression) and predispose to 
cardiac arrhythmias, including ventricular 
tachycardia (A) and fibrillation. It can lead

a complication of hypokalemia. It is classically 
associated with the overly rapid correction of 
hypernatremia or as a complication of diabetic 
ketoacidosis treatment.
Which diabetes medication is preferred for a 65-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), given its proven cardiovascular benefits?

For patients with type 2 diabetes and comorbid

cardiovascular outcomes, and glipizide (D) can

sputum induction to facilitate sample collection 
for CBNAAT (Cartridge-Based Nucleic Acid

Reason (R) : Acetylcysteine acts as a mucolytic 
agent that helps to liquefy and clear respiratory 
secretions.
This is also true. Acetylcysteine breaks

Thus, both the assertion and reason are true,

A 55-year-old man comes to the emergency department with chest pain. His ECG shows ST-segment depression in leads V2 and V3, and his troponin levels are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	
STEMI
(B)	
NSTEMI
(C)	
Posterior wall MI
(D)	
Unstable angina
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
114.	 (B) NSTEMI
This patient presents with chest pain, ST-
segment depression in leads V2 and V3, and 
elevated troponin levels.
Elevated troponin indicates myocardial necrosis, 
meaning there is actual myocardial infarction 
rather than just ischemia. Therefore, unstable 
angina (which has normal troponin levels) is 
excluded.
In STEMI, there is persistent ST-segment 
elevation in the involved leads due to complete 
coronary artery occlusion. This patient instead 
shows ST-segment depression, not elevation.
ST-segment depression with positive cardiac 
biomarkers is characteristic of Non-ST Elevation 
Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI). NSTEMI 
usually results from partial coronary artery 
occlusion, causing subendocardial infarction.
Although isolated ST depression in V2–V3 
can sometimes suggest posterior wall MI (which 
is technically a STEMI equivalent), the question 
does not mention posterior leads (V7–V9) or ST 
elevation patterns. Based on the given findings 
alone—ST depression plus elevated troponin—
the most appropriate diagnosis is NSTEMI.
Least common cause for bilateral pedal edema
(A)	
CLD
(B)	
CKD
(C)	
HF With reduced ejection fraction
(D)

115.	 (D) Chronic vascular insufficiency
Bilateral pedal edema is caused by systemic 
conditions that lead to generalized fluid 
retention 
or 
decreased 
plasma 
oncotic 
pressure. Chronic liver disease (CLD, A) with 
cirrhosis causes hypoalbuminemia and portal 
hypertension, leading to ascites and peripheral 
edema. Chronic kidney disease (CKD, B), 
particularly with nephrotic syndrome, causes 
massive protein loss and sodium retention, 
resulting in generalized edema. Heart failure 
(HF, C) leads to increased hydrostatic pressure 
in the venous system due to impaired cardiac 
output, causing dependent edema. In contrast, 
chronic venous insufficiency is a common cause 
of pedal edema, but it is often asymmetrical, 
being more severe in one leg than the other. 
While it can be bilateral, it is a local vascular 
issue rather than a primary systemic cause, 
making it a less common cause of perfectly

This patient presents with altered sensorium

While femoral hernias are much more common

Which of the following is not a marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST)?
(A)	
SDH (Succinate Dehydrogenase)
(B)	
C-kit
(C)	
PDGF (Platelet-Derived Growth Factor)
(D)

121.	 (D) Nestin
Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GISTs) are 
mesenchymal neoplasms defined by specific 
molecular markers. The vast majority (~95%) 
are positive for the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT 
(CD117) (B). A subset of KIT-negative GISTs 
have mutations in the related receptor PDGFRA 
(C). A small percentage of GISTs lacking KIT

neural stem cells and progenitor cells. While it 
can be expressed in some other tumors, it is not 
a characteristic or diagnostic marker for GISTs.

All of the following statements regarding Wilms tumor are true, EXCEPT:
(A)	
Presents as an abdominal mass
(B)	
Most commonly seen <5 years of age

Majority of patients recover due to chemotherapy and radiotherapy

123.	 (D) Lung metastasis is rare and occurs late
Wilms tumor, or nephroblastoma, is the most 
common renal malignancy in children. It 
typically presents as a large, asymptomatic 
abdominal mass (A) discovered by a parent, 
usually in children under the age of 5 (B). 
The prognosis for Wilms tumor is generally 
excellent, with high cure rates achieved through 
a multimodal approach that includes surgery, 
chemotherapy, and often radiotherapy (C). 
However, Wilms tumor is known to metastasize, 
and the lung is the most common site of 
distant spread. Contrary to the statement, lung 
metastases are not rare; they are present at 
diagnosis in approximately 10-15% of patients 
and are a significant factor in staging and 
treatment planning. Therefore, the statement 
that lung metastasis is rare and occurs late is 
false.

The instrument shown in the image is a

stomach. PEG is indicated in patients who

A 45-year-old woman has recurrent right flank pain, hematuria, and a history of UTIs. Her urine is alkaline (pH 8.0), and the image shows urine crystals. What is the most likely underlying cause of her condition?
(A)	
Triple phosphate stone
(B)	
Calcium oxalate stone
(C)	
Uric acid stone
(D)	
Cystine stone
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
125.	 (A) Triple phosphate stone
The image displays crystals with a characteristic 
"coffin-lid" shape. This morphology is diagnostic 
for magnesium ammonium phosphate, also 
known as struvite or triple phosphate crystals. 
These crystals form exclusively in alkaline urine, 
as noted in the patient's urinalysis (pH 8.0). The 
formation of struvite stones is almost always 
associated with urinary tract infections (UTIs) 
caused by urease-producing organisms, such 
as Proteus, Klebsiella, or Pseudomonas. These 
bacteria split urea into ammonia and carbon 
dioxide, raising the urine pH and promoting the 
precipitation of these crystals. This leads to the 
formation of infection stones, which can grow 
rapidly to form large staghorn calculi, causing 
the patient's symptoms of flank pain and 
hematuria.

The TNM staging system for breast cancer

a hyperdense, biconvex (lens-shaped) collection

A 45-year-old patient reports several months of food regurgitation and weight loss, and a barium swallow has been performed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	
Achalasia cardia
(B)	
Esophageal carcinoma
(C)	
Zenker's diverticulum

128.	 (A) Achalasia cardia
The image from the barium swallow shows a 
massively dilated, tapering esophagus that ends 
in a narrowed gastroesophageal junction. This 
"bird's beak" appearance is the pathognomonic 
radiological sign for achalasia cardia. Achalasia 
is a primary esophageal motility disorder 
characterized by the failure of the lower

A 55-year-old man develops weakness of the left lower lip after recent parotid gland surgery. Based on the surgery and symptoms, where is the most likely location of the lesion?
(A)	
Main trunk of facial nerve
(B)	
Temporal branch of facial nerve
(C)	
Cervical branch of facial nerve
(D)	
Parotid duct
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
129.	 (C) Cervical branch of facial nerve
After parotid gland surgery, injury to branches 
of the facial nerve is a well-known complication 
because the facial nerve divides within 
the substance of the parotid gland into its 
terminal branches. These include the temporal, 
zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and 
cervical branches.
In this case, the patient develops weakness 
of the left lower lip, indicating involvement of 
muscles responsible for depressing the lower 
lip, particularly the depressor anguli oris and 
depressor labii inferioris. These muscles are 
supplied by the lower division of the facial 
nerve. The cervical branch of the facial nerve 
supplies the platysma muscle and contributes 
to movements of the lower lip region. Damage 
to this branch during parotid surgery can result 
in drooping or weakness of the lower lip on the 
affected side.
If the main trunk of the facial nerve were 
injured, there would be complete ipsilateral 
facial paralysis. Injury to the temporal branch 
would affect forehead movement and eye 
closure, while damage to the parotid duct would 
not cause facial muscle weakness.
Therefore, based on the localized weakness 
of the lower lip following parotid surgery, the 
most likely site of lesion is the cervical branch 
of the facial nerve.
