He is in acute distress with a heart rate of 120 bpm, blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, and a respiratory rate of 28/min. Breath sounds are reduced on the right side, and a chest X-ray is provided. The patient's presentation with hemodynamic

(hypotension,

and 
respiratory distress following chest trauma 
is highly concerning. The physical finding of 
decreased breath sounds and the X-ray finding 
of a large pneumothorax with contralateral

Which of the following is least likely to cause hoarseness of voice after thyroid surgery?

(B)	
Exploring bearh's triangle
(C)	
Tubercle of zuckerkandi dissection
(D)

133.	 (A) Dissecting/Retracting strap muscle
Hoarseness of voice after thyroidectomy is 
primarily caused by injury to the laryngeal 
nerves. The external branch of the superior 
laryngeal nerve is at risk during ligation of the 
superior thyroid vessels (D) at the upper pole 
of the gland. The recurrent laryngeal nerve 
(RLN) is at high risk during dissection near the 
tubercle of Zuckerkandl (C) and when exploring

The Mount Fuji sign on CT is seen in which of the following conditions?
(A)	
Pneumocephalus
(B)	
Pneumoperitoneum
(C)	
Pneumomediastinum
(D)	
Pneumothorax
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
134.	 (A) Pneumocephalus
The Mount Fuji sign is a specific radiological 
sign seen on a non-contrast CT scan of the 
head in patients with tension pneumocephalus. 
Pneumocephalus is the presence of air or 
gas within the cranial cavity. In tension 
pneumocephalus, the trapped intracranial 
air exerts mass effect. The Mount Fuji sign 
describes the appearance of bilateral subdural 
air collections that compress both frontal 
lobes, causing them to separate and collapse, 
resembling the silhouette of Mount Fuji in Japan. 
This is a neurosurgical emergency that requires 
prompt intervention to decompress the trapped 
air. This sign is specific to the intracranial space 
and is not seen in pneumoperitoneum (B), 
pneumomediastinum (C), or pneumothorax 
(D).
A 20-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with severe hematemesis. Ultrasound reveals a distended portal vein and a hyperechoic liver. Pantoprazole has been started. What should be the next step in management?
(A)	
Initiate a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics
(B)	
Order a liver biopsy to assess for fibrosis
(C)	
Administer IV fluids and electrolytes
(D)	
Perform an endoscopy to look for varices
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
135.	 (C) Administer IV fluids and electrolytes
A 20-year-old chronic alcoholic presenting with 
severe hematemesis and ultrasound findings 
of a distended portal vein with a hyperechoic 
liver strongly suggests portal hypertension 
secondary to alcoholic liver disease, most likely 
complicated by esophageal variceal bleeding. 
Hematemesis in this setting is a medical 
emergency and requires immediate stabilization 
before definitive diagnostic or therapeutic 
procedures are undertaken.
The first priority in any patient with massive 
upper gastrointestinal bleeding is hemodynamic 
stabilization. This includes securing airway if 
necessary, establishing large-bore intravenous 
access, and administering intravenous fluids and 
correction of electrolytes to restore circulating 
blood volume. Blood transfusion may also be 
required depending on hemoglobin levels and 
hemodynamic status. Stabilization helps prevent 
hypovolemic shock and organ hypo perfusion.
Although endoscopy is essential to identify 
and treat varices (e.g., band ligation), it should 
be performed only after the patient is adequately 
stabilized. 
Broad-spectrum 
antibiotics 
are 
recommended in variceal bleeding but are 
not the immediate first step. Liver biopsy is 
contraindicated in an unstable bleeding patient.

A child presents with short stature, a bone age younger than his chronological age, and parents of normal height. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	
Constitutional short stature
(B)	
Familial short stature
(C)	
Cretinism
(D)	
Malnutrition
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
136.	 (A) Constitutional short stature
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is a 
common cause of short stature in children. It is 
a variation of normal growth, not a disease. The 
key features are a delayed bone age compared 
to the chronological age, a growth velocity that 
is normal for the bone age, and often a family 
history of a similar "late bloomer" growth pattern. 
The child's eventual adult height is typically 
normal, consistent with the normal height of 
the parents. In familial short stature (B), the 
bone age is consistent with the chronological 
age, and the child's height is appropriate for 
their genetic potential (i.e., short parents). 
Cretinism (congenital hypothyroidism) (C) 
and malnutrition (D) are pathological causes of 
short stature that would have other associated 
clinical signs.

Which nutrient deficiency can cause a collagen defect?
(A)	
Vitamin A
(B)	
Vitamin B complex
(C)	
Vitamin C + copper
(D)	
Vitamin D
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
138.	 (C) Vitamin C + copper
Collagen synthesis is a complex process requiring 
several essential cofactors. Vitamin C (ascorbic 
acid) is a critical cofactor for the enzymes 
prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase. These 
enzymes are responsible for the hydroxylation 
of proline and lysine residues in procollagen 
chains, a step that is essential for the formation 
of stable triple-helix collagen molecules. A 
deficiency of vitamin C leads to scurvy, a disease 
characterized by impaired collagen synthesis, 
resulting in poor wound healing and fragile 
capillaries. Copper is also essential for collagen 
integrity; it is a cofactor for the enzyme lysyl 
oxidase, which catalyzes the cross-linking of 
collagen and elastin fibers, providing them with 
tensile strength. Deficiencies in vitamins A, B, 
and D affect other systems.
Which statement correctly describes the condition shown in the image?
(A)	
Kwashiorkor due to insufficient protein intake
(B)

(C)	
Marasmus due to insufficient calorie intake
(D)

139.	 (A) Kwashiorkor due to insufficient protein 
intake
The image shows a child with marked abdominal 
distension (ascites) and peripheral edema, classic 
signs of kwashiorkor. Kwashiorkor is a form of 
severe acute malnutrition that is thought to be 
primarily caused by insufficient protein intake 
in the context of an adequate or near-adequate 
calorie intake (often from a carbohydrate-rich 
diet). The profound hypoalbuminemia resulting 
from protein deficiency leads to a decrease in 
plasma oncotic pressure, causing fluid to shift 
into the interstitial space, resulting in edema

protein, resulting in extreme wasting and loss

edema of kwashiorkor.

What is the fluid of choice for treating shock in a child with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and hypoglycemia?
(A)	
Ringer lactate
(B)	
10% dextrose
(C)	
Normal saline
(D)	
Ringer lactate + 5% dextrose
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
142.	 (D) Ringer lactate + 5% dextrose
Children with Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) 
are at high risk of both hypoglycemia and 
electrolyte imbalances, and they handle fluid 
poorly. Standard resuscitation fluids like plain 
normal saline or Ringer lactate can lead to fluid 
overload and heart failure. The WHO protocol 
for managing septic shock in a SAM child 
recommends a specific fluid called ReSoMal

unavailable, a half-strength Darrow's solution

and glucose. Ringer lactate with 5% dextrose is a 
suitable alternative. Giving 10% dextrose alone 
(B) would not correct the shock, while giving 
plain Ringer lactate (A) or normal saline (C) 
would not address the critical hypoglycemia.
Which of the following statements about the ABCDE approach in Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) is incorrect?
(A)	
A-Airway
(B)	
B-Breathing
(C)	
C Circulation
(D)	
D-Dehydration
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
143.	 (D) D-Dehydration
The ABCDE approach is a systematic framework 
used for the rapid assessment and management 
of critically ill or injured children in PALS. The 
mnemonic stands for:
A :	 Airway - Assess and manage airway patency.
B :	 Breathing - Assess respiratory rate, effort, 
and oxygenation.
C :	 Circulation - Assess heart rate, blood 
pressure, perfusion, and establish IV access.
D :	 Disability - Assess neurological status 
using a scale like AVPU (Alert, Voice, Pain, 
Unresponsive) and check blood glucose.
E :	 Exposure - Undress the child to perform 
a full examination and check for signs 
of trauma or injury, while preventing 
hypothermia.
Dehydration is a clinical condition that would 
be assessed under 'C' for circulation and 'E' for 
exposure (skin turgor), but it does not represent 
one of the primary headings of the ABCDE 
assessment itself.
An infant with a doll-like face is diagnosed with Von Gierke disease. Which enzyme deficiency is responsible for this condition?
(A)	
Phosphorylase
(B)	
Glucose-6-phosphatase
(C)	
Debranching enzyme
(D)	
Fructose-6-phosphatase
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
144.	 (B) Glucose-6-phosphatase
Von Gierke disease is Glycogen Storage Disease 
Type Ia, the most common form of GSD. It is 
caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucose-6-
phosphatase. This enzyme is crucial for the final 
step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, 
as it is required to release free glucose from 
glucose-6-phosphate into the bloodstream. 
Its deficiency leads to a severe inability to 
maintain blood glucose levels during fasting, 
resulting in profound hypoglycemia, lactic 
acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia. 
The accumulation of glycogen in the liver and 
kidneys causes massive hepatomegaly and 
renomegaly. The characteristic "doll-like" facies 
with chubby cheeks is a classic clinical sign. 
Phosphorylase deficiency (A) causes McArdle's 
disease (muscle) or Hers disease (liver). 
Debranching enzyme deficiency (C) causes 
Cori's disease.
A post-term neonate is defined as a neonate that is born:
(A)

(B)

(C)	
Beyond 40 weeks
(D)

145.	 (D) Beyond 42 weeks
Gestational age is categorized to define the 
maturity of a newborn. A full-term pregnancy 
is defined as lasting from 37 weeks and 0 days 
to 41 weeks and 6 days. A neonate is considered 
preterm if born before 37 completed weeks of

According to neonatal resuscitation guidelines, what initial oxygen concentration should be administered to a term newborn with apnea and bradycardia?
(A)	
21%
(B)	
30%
(C)	
50%
(D)	
100%
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
147.	 (A) 21%
Current neonatal resuscitation guidelines have 
moved away from the routine use of 100% oxygen 
due to concerns about hyperoxia and oxidative 
stress. For term neonates (≥35 weeks gestation) 
who require positive pressure ventilation (PPV) 
at birth for apnea or bradycardia, resuscitation 
should be initiated with 21% oxygen, which is 
the concentration found in room air. The infant's 
oxygen saturation is then monitored with a pre-
ductal pulse oximeter, and the concentration of 
supplemental oxygen is titrated up or down as 
needed to meet target saturation levels for the 
specific age in minutes. The use of 100% oxygen 
is reserved for specific situations, such as when 
chest compressions are initiated, or if the infant 
fails to improve with lower concentrations.

A 5-year-old child ingests 10 iron tablets and presents with nausea and abdominal pain. What is the antidote for iron poisoning?

(B)	
British Anti-Lewisite
(C)	
EDTA
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
150.	 (D) Deferoxamine
Iron is highly toxic in overdose, causing severe 
gastrointestinal irritation, metabolic acidosis, 
and shock. When a patient has signs of systemic 
iron toxicity or a significantly elevated serum iron 
level, chelation therapy is indicated. The specific 
chelating agent and antidote for iron poisoning 
is deferoxamine. Deferoxamine is a hexadentate 
chelator that binds with high affinity to ferric 
iron (Fe3+), forming ferrioxamine, a stable,

poisoning. British Anti-Lewisite (BAL) (B) is 
used for arsenic, mercury, and lead poisoning. 
EDTA (C) is primarily used for lead poisoning.

A 6-year-old child presents with hematuria, RBC casts, a recent upper respiratory infection, and edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
(B)	
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)
(C)	
Minimal change disease (MCD)
(D)	
Membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN)
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
152.	 (B) 
Post-streptococcal 
glomerulonephritis 
(PSGN)
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) 
is an immune complex–mediated renal disorder 
occurring 1–3 weeks after infection with 
nephritogenic strains of group A β-hemolytic 
Streptococcus. It is most common in children aged 
5–12 years. The disease results from deposition 
of immune complexes in the glomeruli, leading 
to complement activation and inflammation. 
Clinical presentation includes periorbital and 
pedal edema, cola-colored urine (hematuria), 
oliguria, and mild hypertension. Laboratory 
findings show RBC casts in urine, elevated 
antistreptolysin-O (ASO) titers, and reduced 
complement (C3) levels. On light microscopy, 
glomeruli appear enlarged and hypercellular, 
while electron microscopy reveals subepithelial 
“hump-shaped” deposits. Treatment is mainly 
supportive, focusing on fluid balance and 
hypertension control. Antibiotics are used to 
eradicate any residual streptococcal infection. 
Prognosis in children is excellent, with complete 
recovery in the majority of cases, though adults 
may have persistent renal dysfunction or chronic 
glomerulonephritis.
An 8-year-old child has high fever, restlessness, neck stiffness, and low glucose on lab tests. What is the most likely diagnosis?

153.	 (A) Bacterial meningitis
Bacterial meningitis is an acute purulent

space, most commonly caused by Streptococcus 
pneumoniae, 
Neisseria 
meningitidis, 
or 
Haemophilus influenzae in children. The

inflammatory 
complications. Early antibiotic therapy and

What is the preferred treatment for a 26-year-old man with a fracture of the proximal one-third of the femoral shaft?
(A)	
Interlocking Nail
(B)	
Hip Spica
(C)	
Above Knee Slab
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
156.	 (A) Interlocking Nail
In adult patients, fractures of the femoral 
shaft — particularly in the proximal or middle 
third — are best managed surgically using 
closed intramedullary interlocking nailing. 
This method provides stable fixation, allows 
early mobilization, and maintains proper limb 
alignment. Interlocking nails are inserted 
through the greater trochanter or piriform fossa 
into the medullary canal and locked proximally 
and distally with screws to control rotation and 
length. Conservative methods such as traction 
or hip spica are reserved for pediatric cases or 
medically unfit adults. The procedure promotes 
early weight-bearing, reducing complications 
like joint stiffness, muscle atrophy, and 
thromboembolism. Union typically occurs 
within 4–6 months. Complications may include 
infection, nail breakage, or malalignment, but 
overall success rates exceed 95%. Interlocking 
nailing is considered the gold standard for 
femoral shaft fractures due to its biomechanical 
stability and high union rate.
Which of the following is an osteoporotic fracture?
(A)	
Vertebrae
(B)	
Subtrochanteric Fracture
(C)	
Glenoid Fracture
(D)

157.	 (A) Vertebrae
Osteoporotic fractures occur due to decreased 
bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration, 
rendering bones fragile and susceptible to 
fractures even with minimal trauma. The most 
common sites include the vertebral bodies, distal 
radius (Colles’ fracture), and proximal femur 
(neck of femur fracture). Vertebral compression 
fractures are classic for osteoporosis, typically 
occurring in the thoracolumbar region. Patients 
present with acute back pain, loss of height, 
and kyphotic deformity (“dowager’s hump”). 
The pathogenesis involves accelerated bone 
resorption relative to formation, often due to 
postmenopausal estrogen deficiency, aging, 
or corticosteroid use. Diagnosis is confirmed 
through dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry 
(DEXA) showing a T-score ≤ –2.5. Management 
includes pain relief, bracing, physiotherapy, 
and antiresorptive agents like bisphosphonates 
or denosumab. Calcium and vitamin D 
supplementation 
and 
lifestyle 
measures 
are preventive strategies. In severe cases, 
vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty may be performed 
to stabilize the spine and relieve pain.
Which of the following is the Zone of Calcification in the image given below?
(A)	
1
(B)	
2
(C)	
3
(D)	
4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
158.	 (D) 4
The image depicts the histological zones of 
the epiphyseal (growth) plate of a long bone. 
The growth plate is organized into distinct 
zones from epiphysis to metaphysis: zone of 
resting cartilage, zone of proliferation, zone of 
hypertrophy, and zone of calcification (followed 
by ossification).
Zone 1 represents the resting (reserve) 
cartilage, 
composed 
of 
small, 
scattered 
chondrocytes. Zone 2 is the proliferative 
zone, where chondrocytes are arranged in 
longitudinal columns due to rapid mitotic 
activity. Zone 3 corresponds to the hypertrophic 
zone, characterized by enlarged chondrocytes 
with expanded lacunae.
The zone of calcification lies just beneath 
the hypertrophic zone. In this region, the 
cartilage matrix becomes calcified, and the 
chondrocytes 
undergo 
degeneration 
and 
apoptosis. The lacunae appear empty, and 
the matrix stains more deeply due to mineral 
deposition. This prepares the scaffold for 
invasion by blood vessels and osteogenic cells 
during endochondral ossification.
In the image, this calcified region is labeled 
as Zone 4, which is located adjacent to the 
metaphyseal side where new bone formation 
begins.
Therefore, the correct answer is : (D) 4
Which of the following is a complication of intermittent administration of Teriparatide?
(A)	
Osteonecrosis of Jaw
(B)	
Net Bone Loss
(C)	
Osteosarcoma
(D)	
Subtrochanteric Fracture of Femur
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
BK
BK 
INICET Examination Paper
159.	 (C) Osteosarcoma
Teriparatide is a recombinant parathyroid 
hormone (PTH 1–34) analog used for treating 
severe 
osteoporosis. 
When 
administered 
intermittently in low doses, it stimulates 
osteoblast activity and enhances bone formation. 
However, prolonged or excessive exposure can 
lead to uncontrolled bone turnover, predisposing 
to osteosarcoma, as observed in animal studies. 
For this reason, therapy duration is limited to 
a maximum of two years. Patients with Paget’s 
disease, unexplained elevations of alkaline 
phosphatase, or a history of skeletal malignancy 
are contraindicated for its use. Common side 
effects include hypercalcemia, dizziness, and 
leg cramps. Unlike bisphosphonates, which 
inhibit bone resorption, Teriparatide promotes 
bone formation, thereby increasing bone 
mineral density, particularly in vertebral and 
femoral regions. After cessation, patients are 
usually transitioned to antiresorptive therapy to 
maintain gains. Regular monitoring of calcium 
levels and renal function ensures safety. While 
the osteosarcoma risk in humans is extremely 
low, caution is warranted in long-term users or

All of the following regarding Ankylosing Spondylitis are true except:
(A)	
Occurs before the age of 20, never after 40
(B)

(C)

160.	 (A) Occurs before the age of 20, never after 40
Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic 
inflammatory seronegative spondyloarthropathy 
that primarily affects the axial skeleton, 
especially the sacroiliac joints and spine. 
It typically presents in young adults, most 
commonly between 20 and 40 years of age. 
Although onset is uncommon after 40 years, it 
is not impossible. Therefore, the statement that 
it “occurs before the age of 20, never after 40” is 
incorrect.
AS is more common in males than females, 
with a male-to-female ratio of approximately 
2–3:1. A strong genetic association exists with 
HLA-B27, which is positive in more than 90% 
of patients in many populations. The disease 
is characterized by inflammation leading to 
new bone formation and eventual ankylosis of 
the spine. Peripheral joint involvement, when 
present, is typically non-erosive and affects large 
joints such as the hips and shoulders.
Thus, among the given options, the false 
statement is that ankylosing spondylitis occurs 
before the age of 20 and never after 40. The 
correct answer is (A).
What is the typical dose of Antara?
(A)	
150 mg
(B)	
200 mg

250 mg

Antara is a brand preparation of fenofibrate, a 
fibric acid derivative used in the management of 
hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia. 
It works by activating peroxisome proliferator-
activated receptor alpha (PPAR-α), which 
increases lipolysis and enhances the clearance

The typical recommended dose of Antara

Higher doses such as 200 mg, 250 mg, or 300 
mg are not standard dosing regimens for Antara.

In the context of multiple pregnancies, which of the following is not possible?
(A)	
MCMA (Monochorionic Monoamniotic)
(B)	
MCDA (Monochorionic Diamniotic)
(C)	
MADC (Monoamniotic Dichorionic)
(D)	
DCDA (Dichorionic Diamniotic)
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
162.	 (C) MADC (Monoamniotic Dichorionic)
In twin pregnancies, the terms “chorionicity” 
and “amnionicity” refer to the number of 
placentas and amniotic sacs, respectively. These 
configurations depend on the timing of zygotic 
division. Monoamniotic Dichorionic (MADC) 
twins are embryologically impossible because a 
dichorionic pregnancy always has two separate 
placentas, which must have formed before 
the amniotic sac development. Dichorionicity 
occurs when division happens within the first 
3 days after fertilization, leading to DCDA 
twins — the most common type, including 
all dizygotic and some monozygotic twins. If 
division occurs between days 4–8, MCDA twins 
form; after day 8, MCMA twins arise, sharing 
both amnion and chorion. Very late division 
(after day 13) can lead to conjoined twins. 
Determination of chorionicity and amnionicity 
via ultrasound (lambda or T-signs) is crucial for 
risk stratification, as monochorionic twins have 
higher risks of complications like twin-to-twin 
transfusion syndrome. Thus, MADC cannot 
occur as it violates embryologic timing and 
membrane formation principles.

A ruptured ectopic pregnancy is a life-threatening

A woman at 40 weeks gestation has been in the second stage of labor for 2 hours, with 4 contractions every 10 minutes. The fetal head is at +3 station and caput is present. What is the most appropriate management?

(B)

(C)

(D)

171.	 (A) Outlet forceps
Outlet forceps are indicated when the fetal head 
is visible at the perineum, the scalp is visible 
without separating the labia, and the head has 
reached the pelvic floor (+3 station or lower). In 
this case, the woman has been in the second stage 
of labor for 2 hours with good contractions and 
the fetal head at +3 station — fulfilling criteria 
for outlet forceps delivery. The aim is to expedite

morbidity. Ventouse (vacuum extraction) is

needed. Properly performed, it safely shortens

A 14-year-old girl presents with acute urinary retention and cyclical abdominal pain. Examination shows a tense blue swelling in the vaginal area and a suprapubic bulge on rectal exam. What is the most likely cause of her condition?
(A)	
Imperforate hymen
(B)	
Transverse vaginal septum
(C)	
Longitudinal vaginal septum
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
172.	 (A) Imperforate hymen
An imperforate hymen is a congenital anomaly 
resulting from failure of the inferior end of 
the vaginal plate to canalize. It presents at 
puberty with cyclical abdominal pain, primary 
amenorrhea, and urinary retention due to 
accumulation of menstrual blood behind the 
intact hymen (hematocolpos or hematometra). 
The bluish bulge seen at the introitus represents 
distension of the hymenal membrane by retained 
blood. On rectal or abdominal examination, a 
midline pelvic mass may be palpable. Diagnosis 
is clinical and can be confirmed by pelvic 
ultrasonography showing a fluid-filled vagina 
and uterus. Treatment is surgical — cruciate 
or annular hymenotomy, allowing drainage 
of retained blood and relief of symptoms. 
Failure to recognize this condition can lead to 
complications like endometriosis, infection, 
or infertility due to retrograde menstruation. 
Transverse vaginal septum presents similarly 
but with a higher-level obstruction; however, 
it lacks the typical bluish hymenal bulge. Early 
diagnosis ensures prompt relief and preservation 
of reproductive function.
Under normal physiological conditions, which is the most potent form of natural estrogen?
(A)	
Estradiol
(B)	
Estriol
(C)

(D)

173.	 (A) Estradiol
Among the three naturally occurring estrogens 
— estradiol (E₂), estrone (E₁), and estriol (E₃) 
— estradiol is the most potent and biologically 
active form. It is primarily secreted by the 
granulosa cells of ovarian follicles during the 
reproductive years under the influence of 
follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Estrone is 
produced in peripheral tissues, especially adipose 
tissue, from androstenedione and predominates 
after menopause, while estriol is mainly 
synthesized in the placenta during pregnancy 
and is the least potent. Estradiol binds strongly 
to estrogen receptors in target tissues like the 
uterus, breast, bone, and brain, promoting 
proliferation and maintenance of secondary 
sexual characteristics, endometrial growth, and 
bone density. Its plasma concentration fluctuates 
throughout the menstrual cycle, peaking before 
ovulation. Measurement of estradiol levels is 
useful in assessing ovarian function and fertility. 
Its potency is due to its high receptor affinity 
and longer biological half-life compared to other 
natural estrogens.

A 28-year-old primigravida at 32 weeks comes for a routine prenatal checkup. During the ultrasound, several measurements are taken to assess fetal growth. Which of the following is not used as a criterion for diagnosing intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)?
(A)	
Fetal weight less than the 3rd percentile (-3 SD)
(B)	
Uterine artery pulsatility index (PI) greater than 95th percentile
(C)	
Umbilical artery absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF)
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
176.	 (B) Uterine artery pulsatility index (PI) greater 
than 95th percentile
IUGR is diagnosed when the fetus fails to achieve 
its genetically predetermined growth potential. 
Diagnostic ultrasound parameters include fetal 
weight and abdominal circumference below 
the 10th percentile (or 3rd percentile for severe 
IUGR), and Doppler studies such as absent or 
reversed end-diastolic flow (AEDF/REDF) in

marker suggesting uteroplacental insufficiency.

findings provides a comprehensive assessment 
of fetal health. Management involves close 
monitoring, optimizing maternal nutrition, and 
timely delivery if fetal compromise develops. 
Early detection and differentiation between 
symmetrical and asymmetrical IUGR are crucial, 
as the latter (due to placental insufficiency) is 
more common and amenable to intervention. 
Accurate 
diagnosis 
minimizes 
perinatal 
morbidity and mortality through appropriate 
timing of delivery and neonatal care.

Which form of vitiligo becomes stable and non-progressive?

Segmental

is 
characterized 
by

(D)

181.	 (D) Gonorrhea
Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the causative organism of 
gonorrhea, has shown remarkable antimicrobial 
resistance development over decades. Initially 
sensitive to sulfonamides, penicillin, and 
tetracyclines, 
resistance 
has 
progressively 
evolved 
due 
to 
β-lactamase 
production, 
altered penicillin-binding proteins, and efflux 
pumps. Fluoroquinolone resistance emerged 
globally, followed by decreased susceptibility to 
macrolides and third-generation cephalosporins

Multidrug-resistant

critical to track resistant strains. Other STIs such 
as chancroid (caused by Haemophilus ducreyi)

show far less resistance. Continuous antibiotic 
stewardship and new drug development are 
essential to prevent gonorrhea from becoming 
untreatable.

183.	 (A) Sevoflurane
Sevoflurane is the preferred inhalational 
induction agent for pediatric anesthesia due to 
its non-pungent odor, rapid onset, and smooth 
induction characteristics. It has a low blood-
gas partition coefficient (0.65), leading to 
quick equilibration between alveolar and brain 
concentrations, ensuring rapid induction and

complications include emergence delirium 
and fluoride ion production with prolonged 
exposure, though clinically insignificant. Thus, 
sevoflurane has largely replaced halothane in 
pediatric anesthesia practice.

The American Heart Association (AHA)

for

Which of the following is true about CT (Computed Tomography)?
(A)	
Water has HU of zero
(B)	
Unfiltered X-ray beam is used
(C)	
CT head dose is 20 mSv
(D)	
First investigation for gallstones
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
188.	 (A) Water has HU of zero
In CT imaging, tissue density is quantified in 
Hounsfield Units (HU), where water is assigned 
a reference value of 0 HU and air is –1000 HU. 
Dense structures like bone may have +1000 HU, 
while fat and soft tissue fall between –100 and 
+100 HU. CT scanners use filtered X-ray beams 
that rotate around the patient, producing cross-
sectional images reconstructed by computer 
algorithms. The radiation dose for a CT head 
is typically 1–2 mSv, not 20 mSv. CT is not the 
first investigation for gallstones — ultrasound is 
preferred due to better detection of radiolucent 
stones and absence of radiation. CT is, however, 
excellent for detecting calcifications, fractures, 
vascular lesions, and neoplasms. Understanding 
HU values helps differentiate between tissues 
(e.g., distinguishing cystic from solid lesions). 
Thus, recognizing that water has a zero HU 
forms a fundamental concept in radiologic 
interpretation.
Which type of contrast can be given to patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD)?
(A)	
Ionic iodinated contrast
(B)	
Non-ionic iodinated contrast
(C)	
Ultrasound contrast
(D)	
Gadolinium
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
189.	 (C) Ultrasound contrast
Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are 
at risk of contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) 
when exposed to iodinated (CT) or gadolinium-
based (MRI) contrast agents. Hence, ultrasound 
contrast, composed of microbubbles of inert 
gases (e.g., sulfur hexafluoride), is safest as it is 
not nephrotoxic and is excreted via the lungs. 
Non-ionic iodinated contrast, though safer 
than ionic types, still poses nephrotoxic risk. 
Gadolinium is contraindicated in advanced 
CKD due to the risk of nephrogenic systemic 
fibrosis (NSF). Ultrasound contrast enhances 
visualization of blood flow, liver lesions, and 
vascular structures without renal compromise. 
For patients with impaired renal function, non-
contrast MRI or ultrasound contrast imaging 
are 
preferred 
diagnostic 
modalities. 
Pre-
hydration and avoidance of nephrotoxic drugs 
further minimize CIN risk if iodinated contrast 
use becomes unavoidable. Hence, ultrasound 
contrast is the safest and most appropriate choice 
for CKD patients requiring imaging studies.

Identify the anatomic variation seen in this CT scan.
(A)	
Tracheal diverticulum
(B)	
Double esophagus
(C)	
Aberrant right subclavian artery (ARSA)
(D)	
Right aortic arch
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
191.	 (C) Aberrant right subclavian artery (ARSA)
An Aberrant Right Subclavian Artery (ARSA) 
is the most common aortic arch anomaly, 
occurring in about 1% of the population. 
Normally, the right subclavian artery arises 
from the brachiocephalic trunk, but in ARSA, it 
originates distally from the aortic arch, beyond 
the left subclavian artery. The vessel passes 
posterior to the esophagus and trachea to reach 
the right upper limb. This retroesophageal 
course can compress the esophagus, leading 
to a characteristic symptom called “dysphagia 
lusoria.” On contrast-enhanced CT or MRI, 
ARSA appears as a vascular structure crossing 
behind the esophagus at the level of the 
thoracic inlet. Clinically, most patients remain 
asymptomatic, and the anomaly is usually 
discovered incidentally. However, it is crucial to 
recognize before procedures such as esophageal 
surgery or catheterization to prevent iatrogenic 
injury. Rarely, aneurysmal dilatation at the 
origin, known as Kommerell’s diverticulum, 
can cause dysphagia or respiratory distress. 
Mnemonic: “A Right artery goes Around” — 
reminding that the aberrant right subclavian 
artery loops behind the esophagus.
A 45-year-old patient presents with fever, pain, and shortness of breath. Based on the X-ray, which statement about this condition is false?
(A)	
Loud S1
(B)	
Pericardiocentesis
(C)	
Collapse of right atrium or ventricle
(D)	
Pulsus paradoxus
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
192.	 (A) Loud S1
The X-ray image shows a “water-bottle” or 
“flask-shaped” cardiac silhouette, characteristic 
of pericardial effusion. Pericardial effusion 
involves the accumulation of fluid in the 
pericardial sac, which compresses the cardiac 
chambers and may lead to cardiac tamponade. 
In tamponade, diastolic filling is impaired, 
causing reduced stroke volume and hypotension. 
The typical findings include muffled heart 
sounds, jugular venous distension, and pulsus 
paradoxus (a >10 mmHg fall in systolic BP 
during inspiration). Echocardiography confirms 
the diagnosis by showing diastolic collapse of 
the right atrium or ventricle. Pericardiocentesis 
is the emergency therapeutic procedure that 
removes the excess fluid. The statement “Loud 
S1” is false, because in pericardial effusion, 
heart sounds are actually distant and muffled 
due to fluid insulation, while a loud S1 is seen 
in mitral stenosis. Mnemonic: “Beck’s triad — 
Hypotension, Muffled heart sounds, JVD” helps 
recall the features of tamponade. Recognizing 
the “water-bottle heart” on X-ray is essential 
for early intervention and prevention of 
hemodynamic collapse.

Which of the following is not a component of Beck’s Cognitive Theory of Depression?
(A)	
Cognitive distortions
(B)	
Automated thoughts
(C)	
Introjection
(D)	
Dysfunctional belief
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
196.	 (C) Introjection
Aaron Beck’s Cognitive Theory of Depression 
postulates that depression results from distorted 
negative thinking rather than unconscious 
conflict. The theory focuses on three major 
cognitive components:
1.	 Automatic thoughts : spontaneous negative 
thoughts about oneself, the world, and the 
future.
2.	 Cognitive distortions : systematic errors 
in thinking such as overgeneralization, 
catastrophizing, 
and 
black-and-white 
thinking.
3.	 Dysfunctional core beliefs : deep-seated 
negative schemas developed from early 
experiences.
These collectively form the “Negative Cognitive 
Triad”. 
Introjection, 
however, 
belongs 
to 
Freud’s psychodynamic theory, referring to 
internalization of others’ beliefs or values, and 
thus is not part of Beck’s model. The cognitive 
theory is the foundation for Cognitive Behavioral 
Therapy (CBT), a structured, evidence-based 
psychotherapeutic approach widely used for 
depression and anxiety disorders. Mnemonic: 
“A.C.D.” — Automatic thoughts, Cognitive 
distortions, Dysfunctional beliefs — captures 
Beck’s components. CBT targets these distorted 
thought patterns, helping patients replace 
maladaptive cognitions with realistic and 
adaptive ones, ultimately reducing depressive 
symptoms and preventing relapse.

REM sleep is also known as paradoxical

Supportive therapy is not typically provided for which type of patient?
(A)	
A patient who is severely ill, non-cooperative, and unable to participate in therapy
(B)	
A person who is motivated and has good control over emotions
(C)	
A person with cognitive and functional abilities intact

A patient who is severely ill and has lost ego integrity
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024
200.	 (A) A patient who is severely ill, non-cooperative, 
and unable to participate in therapy
Supportive psychotherapy is primarily indicated 
for patients who are severely ill, have impaired 
ego strength, poor insight, or reduced capacity 
to tolerate insight-oriented therapy. Its main 
goal is to maintain current functioning, provide 
reassurance, strengthen coping mechanisms, 
and prevent further psychological deterioration. 
It is commonly used in patients with chronic 
psychiatric illness, severe stress, or loss of ego 
integrity.
However, supportive therapy requires at least 
a minimum level of cooperation and participation 
from the patient. If a patient is severely ill, 
non-cooperative, and unable to participate in 
therapy, meaningful therapeutic engagement 
is not possible. In such cases, immediate 
medical stabilization, pharmacotherapy, or even 
inpatient management may be required before 
psychotherapy can be initiated.
A motivated person with good emotional 
control and intact cognitive and functional 
abilities is usually better suited for insight-
oriented or cognitive therapies rather than 
purely supportive therapy. Meanwhile, severely 
ill patients with compromised ego strength are 
classic candidates for supportive therapy.
Therefore, supportive therapy is not typically 
provided for (A) a patient who is severely ill, 
non-cooperative, and unable to participate in 
therapy.

ANATOMY
1.	
What deficit results from an injury to the 
posterior interosseous nerve?
(A)	Wrist drop
(B)	 Loss of finger extension
(C)	Inability to extend the wrist
(D)	Inability to adduct the fingers/thumb
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(B) Loss of finger extension
The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) is the deep, purely motor branch of the radial nerve. It innervates the muscles in the extensor compartment of the forearm. A crucial anatomical point is that the radial nerve gives off branches to the main wrist extensors (extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis) before the PIN is formed. Therefore, in an isolated PIN palsy, wrist extension is largely preserved, and a complete wrist drop (A) does not occur. However, the PIN supplies the extensor digitorum communis, extensor indicis, extensor digiti minimi, and extensor pollicis longus. Consequently, injury to this nerve results in a characteristic "finger drop," which is an inability to extend the fingers and thumb at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints. Adduction of the fingers (D) is a function of the ulnar nerve.
2.	
Which cranial nerve is not contained within the

(A)	III
(B)	 IV
(C)	II
(D)	VI
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(C) II
The superior orbital fissure is a crucial opening in the sphenoid bone that connects the middle cranial fossa with the orbit. It transmits several important neurovascular structures. The contents include the oculomotor nerve (CN III), the trochlear nerve (CN IV), the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1), and the abducens nerve (CN VI). This anatomical separation is a frequently tested point in neuroanatomy, distinguishing the pathways for vision from those controlling eye movement and sensation.

The image displays an early embryo, likely around the third week of gestation, during the process of gastrulation. (A) Lacosamide
Voltage-gated sodium channels can exist in resting, open, and inactivated states. The inactivated state can be fast or slow.
Lacosamide (A) is a newer antiepileptic drug with a distinct mechanism of action. Unlike traditional sodium channel blockers, Lacosamide selectively enhances the slow inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels. This action stabilizes the channel in a non-conducting state for a longer duration, which preferentially affects neurons that are persistently depolarized or firing repetitively, as seen in a seizure focus. 58.	 Which of the following statements regarding 
Thiopentone is false?
(A)	It is lipid soluble
(B)	 It is maximally excreted by the kidney, so it 
has a short duration of action
(C)	It is redistributed to adipose tissue and 
muscles
(D)	It reaches maximum concentration in the 
brain after IV infusion
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(B) It is maximally excreted by the kidney, so it has a short duration of action
This question concerns the pharmacokinetics of the intravenous anesthetic Thiopentone.
(A)	
It is lipid soluble : True. Thiopentone is highly lipid-soluble, which allows it to rapidly cross the blood-brain barrier and induce anesthesia within seconds.
(C)	
It is redistributed to adipose tissue and muscles : True. The termination of its clinical effect after a single bolus dose is due to rapid redistribution from the vessel-rich central compartment (like the brain) to less perfused tissues, initially muscle and later adipose tissue.
(D)	
It reaches maximum concentration in the brain after IV infusion : True. Due to its high lipophilicity and the brain's high blood flow, it achieves a peak concentration in the brain very quickly (within one minute) after intravenous injection.
(B) It is maximally excreted by the kidney, so it has a short duration of action : This statement is false. The short duration of action is due to redistribution, not elimination. The actual elimination of Thiopentone from the body is a slow process involving hepatic metabolism followed by renal excretion of its inactive metabolites. Its elimination half-life is long (10-12 hours).

65.	 Which drug is preferred for treating diastolic 
hypertension?
(A)	ACE inhibitors
(B)	 Beta-blockers
(C)	Calcium channel blockers
(D)	Diuretics
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) ACE inhibitors
Diastolic hypertension refers to a condition in which the diastolic blood pressure (the lower reading) is persistently elevated, usually above 90 mmHg. It is commonly seen in younger individuals and is primarily related to increased peripheral vascular resistance. The main goal of treatment is to reduce systemic vascular resistance and prevent long-term complications such as stroke, myocardial infarction, and renal damage.
ACE inhibitors (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme inhibitors) are preferred because they block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor. By reducing angiotensin II levels, these drugs cause vasodilation, decrease peripheral resistance, and lower diastolic blood pressure effectively. They also reduce aldosterone secretion, which decreases sodium and water retention, further helping in blood pressure control.
In addition, ACE inhibitors provide protective effects on the heart and kidneys. They are especially beneficial in patients with diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or heart failure. Compared to some other antihypertensive drugs, they have a favorable side-effect profile and improve long-term cardiovascular outcomes, making them a preferred choice in diastolic hypertension management.

Pretomanid is a nitroimidazooxazine antimicrobial agent that was specifically developed for treating tuberculosis (TB). 13.	 Which of the following types of transport does 
not require ATP?
A.	 Paracellular transport
B.	 Simple diffusion
C.	 Facilitated diffusion
D.	 Na+/K+ ATPase
E.	 Symport/Antiport
(A)	A, B, C
(B)	 A, B, C, D
(C)	A, C, D
(D)	B, D
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) A, B, C
Cellular transport can be active or passive. Active transport requires energy, typically from ATP hydrolysis, to move substances against their concentration gradient. Na+/K+ ATPase (D) is the quintessential example of primary active transport. Symport/Antiport (E) are forms of secondary active transport, which use the energy stored in an electrochemical gradient (created by primary active transport) rather than direct ATP hydrolysis. In contrast, passive transport does not require metabolic energy. Simple diffusion (B) is the movement of substances directly across the membrane down their concentration gradient. Facilitated diffusion (C) uses a channel or carrier protein to move substances down their gradient. Paracellular transport (A) is the movement of substances through the tight junctions between cells, also driven by electrochemical gradients. Thus, paracellular transport, simple diffusion, and facilitated diffusion are all passive processes that do not directly consume ATP.
14.	 What factors contribute to the latent period in a 
single muscle twitch?
1	
Excitation-contraction coupling
2	
Time interval from the point of stimulus to 
the onset of contraction
3	
Neuromuscular 
junction 
(NMJ) 
transmission
4	
Transfer 
of 
calcium 
back 
into 
the 
sarcoplasmic reticulum via SERCA
(A)	1,2,3
(B)	 2,3,4
(C)	1,3,4
(D)	2,3,4
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) 1,2,3
The latent period is defined as the time interval from the point of stimulus to the onset of muscle contraction (2). It is a brief delay during which a series of electrochemical and mechanical events occur before tension develops. These events include the transmission of the action potential across the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) (3), including the release of acetylcholine and generation of an end-plate potential. Following this, the process of excitation-contraction coupling (1) takes place. This involves the propagation of the muscle action potential along the sarcolemma and into the T-tubules, triggering the release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and their binding to troponin, which initiates the cross-bridge cycle. The transfer of calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum (4) is the process that causes muscle relaxation and occurs after the contraction phase, not during the latent period.
15.	 Which of the following helps to decrease the 
Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)?
(A)	Decreasing filtration constant
(B)	 Decreasing oncotic pressure of glomerulus
(C)	Increasing hydrostatic pressure of the 
glomerulus
(D)	Increasing hydrostatic pressure of Bowman's 
capsule
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(D) Increasing hydrostatic pressure of Bowman's capsule
The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is determined by the balance of Starling forces across the glomerular capillaries. Filtration is favored by the glomerular hydrostatic pressure and opposed by the glomerular oncotic pressure and the hydrostatic pressure in Bowman's capsule. Therefore, to decrease GFR, one must either decrease the forces favoring filtration or increase the forces opposing it. Increasing glomerular hydrostatic pressure (C) or decreasing glomerular oncotic pressure (B) would both increase GFR. Decreasing the filtration constant (A) would decrease GFR, but this is a physiological property, not a dynamic pressure. Increasing the hydrostatic pressure of Bowman's capsule (D) directly opposes the hydrostatic pressure in the glomerulus, reducing the net filtration pressure and thereby decreasing GFR. This can occur clinically in cases of urinary tract obstruction, such as from a kidney stone or enlarged prostate.
16.	 Static 2-point discrimination is primarily 
assessed by which of the following receptors?
(A)	Merkel's discs
(B)	 Meissner's corpuscles
(C)	Pacinian corpuscles
(D)	All of the above
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) Merkel's discs
Two-point discrimination is the ability to perceive two simultaneous points of contact on the skin as distinct. This sensory modality requires mechanoreceptors with small, well-defined receptive fields and high spatial resolution. Merkel's discs are slow-adapting mechanoreceptors that are densely packed in areas like the fingertips and lips. They are specialized for detecting fine touch, pressure, and texture, and their small receptive fields make them the primary receptors responsible for static two-point discrimination. Meissner's corpuscles (B) are rapidly adapting receptors with slightly larger receptive fields, involved in detecting light touch and flutter. Pacinian corpuscles (C) are also rapidly adapting but have very large receptive fields and are responsible for sensing deep pressure and high-frequency vibration, making them unsuitable for fine spatial discrimination.
17.	 Which of the following statements accurately 
describes physiological dead space?
(A)	Inadequately ventilated alveoli
(B)	 Inadequately perfused alveoli
(C)	Less than anatomical dead space
(D)	Can be measured by spirometry
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(B) Inadequately perfused alveoli
Dead space refers to the volume of inspired air that does not participate in gas exchange. Anatomical dead space is the volume of the conducting airways. Physiological dead space is the sum of the anatomical dead space and the alveolar dead space. Alveolar dead space is composed of alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused with blood, or are inadequately perfused relative to their ventilation (high V/Q ratio). In a healthy individual, alveolar dead space is negligible, so physiological dead space equals anatomical dead space. However, in lung diseases (e.g., pulmonary embolism), perfusion can be impaired, increasing alveolar dead space and making physiological dead space greater than anatomical dead space (making C incorrect). Physiological dead space is measured using Bohr's equation with expired CO2, not by simple spirometry (D).
18.	 Peripheral chemoreceptors exhibit their greatest 
sensitivity in which of the following conditions?
(A)	Hypoxia
(B)	 Hypercapnia
(C)	Alkalosis
(D)	Acidosis
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) Hypoxia
The body has two sets of chemoreceptors that regulate breathing. Central chemoreceptors in the medulla are highly sensitive to changes in PaCO2 (hypercapnia) and pH in the cerebrospinal fluid. Peripheral chemoreceptors, located in the carotid and aortic bodies, are sensitive to changes in PaCO2, pH, and PaO2 in the arterial blood. However, their most critical and unique function is the detection of hypoxia (low PaO2). The central chemoreceptors do not respond directly to hypoxia. The peripheral chemoreceptors' firing rate increases significantly when arterial PaO2 drops below about 60 mmHg, providing the primary drive to breathe in response to hypoxia. While they do respond to hypercapnia (B) and acidosis (D), the central chemoreceptors provide the dominant response to these stimuli under normal conditions.

6.	
A patient reports that food gets trapped between 
the cheek and the teeth. Weakness of which 
muscle is associated with this complaint?
(A)	Buccinator
(B)	 Orbicularis Oris
(C)	Zygomaticus Major
(D)	Risorius
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) Buccinator
The buccinator is a thin, quadrilateral muscle that forms the principal muscular component of the cheek. Its primary function during mastication is to press the cheek firmly against the molar teeth. This action keeps food on the occlusal (chewing) surfaces of the teeth and prevents it from accumulating in the oral vestibule, which is the space between the teeth/gums and the cheek. Weakness or paralysis of the buccinator muscle, typically due to an injury of the facial nerve (CN VII), results in the inability to perform this function effectively. Consequently, food tends to pocket or get stuck in the oral vestibule during chewing, matching the patient's complaint precisely. The orbicularis oris (B) closes the lips, while the zygomaticus major (D) and risorius (D) are involved in smiling.
7.	
The first migration of epiblast cells leads to the 
formation of which germ layer?
(A)	Ectoderm
(B)	 Endoderm
(C)	Mesoderm
(D)	Notochord
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(B) Endoderm
During the third week of embryonic development, a process called gastrulation transforms the bilaminar embryonic disc into a trilaminar disc. This process begins at the primitive streak, where cells of the superficial layer, the epiblast, proliferate and migrate inwards. The very first wave of epiblast cells to invaginate through the primitive streak pushes aside and completely replaces the cells of the underlying hypoblast layer. This newly formed deep layer is the definitive embryonic endoderm. Shortly after, a second wave of migrating epiblast cells positions itself between the epiblast and the new endoderm, forming the middle layer, the mesoderm. The remaining cells of the epiblast that do not migrate constitute the ectoderm. Therefore, the endoderm is the first of the three primary germ layers to be formed from migrating epiblast cells.

9.	
While receiving the second dose of the COVID 
vaccine, a patient developed a flabby, flattened, 
and uneven shoulder. A nurse observed a loss of 
the normal shoulder contour. Which anatomical 
structure is likely to have been damaged, and 
could this injury have been avoided?
(A)	Rotator cuff
(B)	 Posterior circumflex artery
(C)	Lateral cutaneous nerve of arm
(D)	Axillary nerve
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(D) Axillary nerve
The rounded contour of the shoulder is primarily formed by the deltoid muscle. The symptoms described—a flabby, flat, and asymmetrical shoulder—are indicative of deltoid muscle atrophy or paralysis. The deltoid muscle is responsible for arm abduction and is innervated by the axillary nerve. This nerve courses around the surgical neck of the humerus, approximately 5-7 cm below the acromion. Intramuscular injections, such as vaccines, should be administered into the thickest part of the deltoid muscle, well above the course of the axillary nerve. An injection given too low on the arm can directly injure the axillary nerve, leading to deltoid paralysis, atrophy, and the observed loss of shoulder contour. This is a known iatrogenic injury that is preventable by using the correct injection landmarking technique.
10.	 Which arteries originate from the anterior 
division of the internal iliac artery?
1

(A)	1,2,3,5	
(B)	 2,3,4,6
(C)	2,3,4,5,6	
(D)	1,4,5,6
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(C) 2,3,4,5,6
The internal iliac artery divides into a posterior and an anterior division. The posterior division supplies the pelvic wall and gluteal region. Its branches are the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal artery (1). The anterior division supplies the pelvic viscera, perineum, and medial thigh. Its branches are numerous and include the umbilical artery (which gives off the superior vesical artery (3)), obturator artery, inferior vesical artery (5) in males, uterine artery (which gives off the vaginal artery (6) in females), middle rectal artery (4), internal pudendal artery, and the inferior gluteal artery (2). Therefore, all the listed arteries except the superior gluteal artery are branches of the anterior division.

(D) Menkes disease
Lysyl oxidase is a crucial enzyme responsible for the cross-linking of collagen and elastin fibers, which provides connective tissues with their tensile strength and elasticity. This enzyme requires copper as an essential cofactor. Menkes disease is a rare, X-linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the ATP7A gene, which codes for a copper-transporting ATPase. This defect leads to a systemic copper deficiency because copper cannot be properly absorbed and distributed to various tissues. The resulting deficiency of copper-dependent enzymes like lysyl oxidase leads to defective connective tissue, causing the characteristic clinical features of Menkes disease, such as sparse, kinky hair, growth failure, neurodegeneration, and arterial tortuosity. Scurvy (A) is due to vitamin C deficiency. Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (C) is a group of genetic disorders of collagen synthesis itself.

32.	 Sickle cell anemia is caused by which of the 
following changes?
(A)	Val → Glu
(B)	 Lys → Glu
(C)	Glu → Lys
(D)	Glu → Val
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(D) Glu → Val
Sickle cell anemia is a genetic disorder caused by a specific point mutation in the gene encoding the beta-globin chain of hemoglobin. This mutation occurs at the sixth codon of the beta-globin gene. The normal DNA codon (GAG) codes for the amino acid glutamic acid (Glu), which is hydrophilic and negatively charged. In sickle cell disease, a single nucleotide substitution (A to T) changes the codon to GTG. This altered codon codes for the amino acid valine (Val), which is hydrophobic and uncharged. This seemingly minor change from glutamic acid to valine at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain dramatically alters the properties of the hemoglobin molecule (creating HbS), causing it to polymerize under deoxygenated conditions and leading to the sickling of red blood cells.
33.	 Which protein plays a role in the process of 
epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT)?
(A)	SNAIL & TWIST
(B)	 TF1 & TF2
(C)	MMP9
(D)	Cathepsin
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) SNAIL & TWIST
Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a fundamental biological process where epithelial cells lose their cell-cell adhesion and polarity, and acquire a migratory, mesenchymal phenotype. This process is crucial in embryonic development and wound healing, and it is co-opted by cancer cells to promote invasion and metastasis. The EMT is driven by a network of key transcription factors that repress epithelial genes (like E-cadherin) and activate mesenchymal genes. Among the most important and well-studied of these master regulators are the zinc-finger transcription factor SNAIL and the basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor TWIST. Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) like MMP9 (C) and cathepsins (D) are proteases that are often upregulated during EMT and help degrade the extracellular matrix, facilitating invasion, but they are downstream effectors, not the primary transcription factors driving the transition.
34.	 Which is the most essential fatty acid?
(A)	Linoleic acid
(B)	 Linolenic acid
(C)	Arachidonic acid
(D)	Oleic acid
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) Linoleic acid
Essential fatty acids are polyunsaturated fatty acids that humans must obtain from their diet because the body cannot synthesize them. There are two primary essential fatty acids: linoleic acid (LA), an omega-6 fatty acid, and alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), an omega-3 fatty acid. From these two precursors, the body can synthesize other important long-chain fatty acids. Arachidonic acid (C) can be synthesized from linoleic acid, making it conditionally essential. Oleic acid (D) is a monounsaturated omega-9 fatty acid that the body can synthesize and is therefore non-essential. Between the two essential fatty acids, linoleic acid is often considered the most essential because its deficiency is more readily produced and has more prominent clinical signs, and the quantitative requirement for it is higher than for alpha-linolenic acid.

35.	 Which anticoagulant is most suitable for 
collecting blood samples for HbA1c testing?
(A)	EDTA
(B)	 Fluoride
(C)	Citrate
(D)	Heparin
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) EDTA
Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) is a measure of long-term glycemic control, reflecting the average blood glucose level over the preceding 2-3 months. For this test, a whole blood sample is required, and it is crucial to prevent the blood from clotting after collection. The anticoagulant of choice for HbA1c estimation, as well as for most hematological tests like a complete blood count, is EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid), which is found in lavender-top tubes. EDTA works by chelating calcium ions, which are essential for the coagulation cascade, thereby preventing clotting and preserving the integrity of the red blood cells that contain the hemoglobin. A fluoride tube (B) is used for glucose estimation as it inhibits glycolysis, but it is not ideal for HbA1c. Citrate (C) is used for coagulation studies, and heparin (D) is used for plasma chemistry.
36.	 Which of the following is true regarding serum 
calcium estimation?
(A)	Clenching the fist is advised
(B)	 Tight tourniquet is to be applied
(C)	Prolonged immobilization causes increased 
free and total calcium
(D)	Citrate and oxalate tubes are to be used
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(C) Prolonged immobilization causes increased free and total calcium
Several pre-analytical factors can affect the accuracy of serum calcium measurements. Fist clenching (A) and prolonged or tight tourniquet application (B) can cause a localized increase in lactate and a decrease in pH, which displaces calcium from albumin, and can cause hemoconcentration, falsely elevating the total calcium level. Citrate and oxalate tubes (D) are not used because these anticoagulants chelate calcium, making it unmeasurable. Statement (C) is true; prolonged immobilization or bed rest leads to increased bone resorption without a compensatory increase in bone formation. This imbalance results in the release of calcium from the bones into the bloodstream, causing a true physiological increase in both total and ionized (free) serum calcium levels (disuse hypercalcemia).
37.	 Umbilical cord bleeding with normal BT, PT, and 
APTT, along with a positive urea clot solubility 
test, suggests a deficiency of which coagulation 
factor?
(A)	Factor XIII
(B)	 Factor IX
(C)	Factor XII
(D)	Factor VIII
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) Factor XIII
This is a classic presentation for congenital Factor XIII deficiency. Factor XIII, also known as fibrin-stabilizing factor, is responsible for cross-linking fibrin strands to form a strong, stable clot. Its deficiency results in a fragile clot that is easily broken down, leading to a characteristic pattern of delayed bleeding. Bleeding from the umbilical stump in the neonatal period is a hallmark sign. Because the initial formation of the fibrin clot is normal, the standard coagulation screening tests—PT, APTT, and Bleeding Time—are all normal. The diagnosis is confirmed by a specific assay, the urea clot solubility test. A normal, cross-linked clot is insoluble in 5M urea, whereas the weak, un-cross-linked clot found in Factor XIII deficiency will readily dissolve, yielding a positive test result.

76.	 What is the drug of choice (DOC) for Fasciola 
hepatica?
(A)	Albendazole
(B)	 Praziquantel
(C)	Triclabendazole
(D)	Mebendazole
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(C) Triclabendazole
Fasciola hepatica, the sheep liver fluke, causes the disease fascioliasis.
Triclabendazole (C) is the undisputed drug of choice for treating human fascioliasis. It is a benzimidazole anthelmintic that is highly effective against both the adult and immature migrating stages of the fluke. This is a notable exception in the treatment of trematodes.
Praziquantel (B) is the drug of choice for most other fluke (trematode) infections (e.g., Schistosomiasis, Clonorchiasis) and tapeworm (cestode) infections. However, it has very poor efficacy against Fasciola species and is not used.
Albendazole (A) and Mebendazole (D) are broad-spectrum benzimidazoles primarily used for nematode (roundworm) infections. They are not effective for fascioliasis.
77.	 Which 
of

is

(C)	All pathogenic species are urease positive
(D)	CD4 > 500
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(B) Associated with bird droppings
Cryptococcus is an encapsulated yeast, most commonly Cryptococcus neoformans, which is strongly associated with pigeon droppings and soil contaminated with bird excreta. The organism survives and multiplies in nitrogen-rich environments such as dried bird droppings. Humans acquire infection by inhalation of aerosolized yeast cells or spores from the environment.
Although Cryptococcus infection is frequently seen in AIDS patients, especially when CD4 counts fall below 100 cells/µL, option (A) is not the most specific identifying feature because the organism can also infect other immuno compromised individuals and occasionally immunocompetent hosts.

Therefore, the most accurate and characteristic statement about Cryptococcus is its association with bird droppings.
78.	 All of the following drugs are used in the 
management of uncomplicated Plasmodium 
falciparum malaria, except:
(A)	Artemether
(B)	 Primaquine
(C)	Chloroquine
(D)	Sulphadoxine/pyrimethamine
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(B) Primaquine
Uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria is primarily treated with artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT). Drugs such as artemether (usually combined with lumefantrine) are first-line treatments because they rapidly reduce parasite load and are highly effective against resistant strains. Sulphadoxine–pyrimethamine has also been used in combination regimens, although resistance limits its use in many regions.
Chloroquine was previously used for P. falciparum, but widespread resistance has made it ineffective in most endemic areas; however, it may still be used in specific regions where sensitivity is documented.
Primaquine, on the other hand, is not used for treating uncomplicated P. falciparum blood-stage infection. Its primary role is in eliminating hypnozoites (dormant liver forms) of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale to prevent relapse. In P. falciparum, primaquine may be given as a single low dose to reduce gametocyte carriage and transmission, but it is not used as a standard treatment for uncomplicated infection.
Therefore, primaquine is the correct exception.

79.	 Which of the following is not included in the 
criteria for Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM)?
(A)	Low weight for height
(B)	 Mid-upper arm circumference
(C)	Low height for age
(D)	Pedal edema
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(C) Low height for age
The World Health Organization (WHO) defines Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) in children (6-59 months) by the presence of at least one of the following three criteria:
1	
Low weight for height (A) : A weight-for-height Z-score of less than -3 standard deviations below the WHO growth standard median. This indicates severe wasting.
2	
Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) (B) : A MUAC measurement of less than 11.5 cm.
3	
Pedal edema (D) : The presence of bilateral pitting nutritional edema.
Low height for age (C), defined as a height-for-age Z-score of less than -2, is the definition of stunting. Stunting is an indicator of chronic malnutrition, reflecting a long-term failure to grow. While a child with SAM may also be stunted, stunting itself is not a diagnostic criterion for the acute condition of SAM.

81.	 Screening family members of hypertension and 
diabetes in a village is best classified as:

(B)	 Multiphasic screening
(C)	Mass screening
(D)	Anonymous screening
AAns

(A) Selective screening
This scenario describes a specific type of screening strategy.
Selective screening (A), also known as high-risk screening, involves targeting specific subgroups of the population who are identified as having a higher risk of developing a particular disease. Family members of individuals with chronic, heritable conditions like hypertension and diabetes constitute a well-defined high-risk group due to shared genetic predispositions and environmental factors. Screening this group is a classic example of a selective approach.
(C)	
Mass screening would involve screening everyone in the village, regardless of their family history or risk factors.
(B)	
Multiphasic screening refers to the application of multiple tests at the same time (e.g., checking BP, blood sugar, and cholesterol), but the defining feature here is the population being targeted, not the number of tests.
(D)	
Anonymous screening is done for surveillance purposes where results are delinked from personal identifiers.
82.	 Which of the following is NOT a component of

(D)	6 interventions

The Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, launched by the Government of India, is built upon a comprehensive 6x6x6 framework to combat anemia. This framework includes:
Six Beneficiary Groups (A): Children (6-59 months), Children (5-9 years), Adolescents (10-19 years), Pregnant women, Lactating women, and Women of Reproductive Age (15-49 years).

83.	 What is the best level of evidence in research?
(A)	Case-control study
(B)	 Cohort study
(C)	Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT)
(D)	Meta-analysis
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(D) Meta-analysis
The hierarchy of evidence is a model used to rank the relative strength of results obtained from different types of research studies.
At the pinnacle of this hierarchy are Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (D). A systematic review critically appraises all relevant studies on a specific topic, and a meta-analysis uses statistical methods to combine the results of several of these studies (ideally, multiple high-quality RCTs). This synthesis provides a more powerful and precise estimate of an intervention's effect than any single study alone.
A single Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) (C) is the next highest level and is considered the gold standard for a primary experimental study.
Below RCTs are observational studies, with Cohort studies (B) generally providing stronger evidence than Case-control studies (A).
Expert opinion and case reports are at the bottom of the pyramid.
84.	 What is the correct sequence of steps in a 
randomized controlled trial (RCT)?
(A)	Randomization, Exclusion and Inclusion, 
Blinding, Analysis
(B)	 Exclusion and Inclusion, Randomization, 
Blinding, Analysis
(C)	Blinding, 
Randomization, 
Analysis, 
Exclusion and Inclusion
(D)	Analysis, Blinding, Exclusion and Inclusion, 
Randomization
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(B) Exclusion and Inclusion, Randomization, Blinding, Analysis
A randomized controlled trial follows a logical and standardized sequence to ensure its validity and minimize bias. The correct order is:
1	
Exclusion and Inclusion : The process begins by defining the target population and screening potential participants against a set of predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. This ensures that a suitable and relatively homogenous group of subjects is enrolled in the study.
2	
Randomization : Once eligible participants have provided informed consent and been enrolled, they are randomly assigned to one of the study arms (e.g., the intervention group or the control group). This is the core step that minimizes selection bias.
3	
Blinding : During the intervention phase of the trial, blinding (masking) of participants, investigators, and/or outcome assessors to the treatment allocation is implemented whenever feasible to prevent performance and detection bias.
4	
Analysis : After the follow-up period is complete, the collected data is analyzed to compare the outcomes between the groups and draw conclusions about the intervention's effectiveness.
85.	 Which of the following is a key feature of a 
randomized controlled trial (RCT)?
(A)	Participants are randomly assigned to 
groups to reduce bias.
(B)	 The study design always uses a placebo in 
the control group.
(C)	Results are always applicable to the general 
population.
(D)	All of the Above
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) Participants are randomly assigned to groups to reduce bias.
The defining, core feature of an RCT is the random allocation of participants to study groups.
(A)	
The process of randomization is the cornerstone of the RCT design. It aims to ensure that both known and unknown confounding variables are distributed evenly between the intervention and control groups. This minimizes selection bias and allows for a more valid comparison, strengthening the inference of causality.
(B)	
This is incorrect. While a placebo is a common type of control, the control group in an RCT can also receive the current standard of care (an active comparator), usual care, or no intervention at all.
(C)	
This is incorrect. RCTs often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, which can limit the study sample's diversity. This can affect the generalizability (or external validity) of the results to the broader, more heterogeneous general population.
(D)	
Incorrect, as B and C are false.
86.	 The analysis that uses ICER (Incremental Cost-
Effectiveness Ratio) as a model is:
(A)	Cost-effective analysis
(B)	 Cost analysis
(C)	Cost-benefit analysis
(D)	Cost evaluation
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) Cost-effective analysis
Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER) is the principal measure used in cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA). ICER compares two interventions by calculating the additional cost required to gain one additional unit of health outcome. It is expressed as:
ICER = (Cost of Intervention A − Cost of Intervention B) ÷ (Effect of A − Effect of B)
The outcome is measured in natural health units such as life-years gained, cases prevented, or quality-adjusted life years (QALYs).
In contrast, cost analysis only compares expenses without considering outcomes. Cost-benefit analysis converts both costs and benefits into monetary terms. Cost evaluation is a broader, less specific term and does not specifically rely on ICER.
Therefore, ICER is specifically associated with cost-effectiveness analysis, making option (A) correct.

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) syndromes are inherited disorders causing tumors in multiple endocrine glands. MEN 2B is an aggressive subtype caused by a specific mutation in the RET proto-oncogene. Its three core components are:

48.	 Which finding is commonly associated with 
glomerular hematuria?
(A)	Dysuria
(B)	 Crystals
(C)	Brown urine
(D)	Edema
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(C) Brown urine
Hematuria originating from the glomerulus has distinct features compared to bleeding from the lower urinary tract. When red blood cells (RBCs) pass through the damaged glomerular basement membrane, they are often misshapen (dysmorphic RBCs) and can form RBC casts. As this blood travels down the nephron, the hemoglobin is exposed to the acidic environment of the tubular fluid, which converts it to methemoglobin. This gives the urine a characteristic smoky, brown, or "cola-colored" appearance. In contrast, bleeding from the lower tract (e.g., bladder, prostate) results in bright red urine. Dysuria (A) points to lower tract inflammation. Crystals (B) are related to stone disease. Edema (D) is a feature of nephrotic or nephritic syndrome but is not a direct characteristic of the urine itself.
49.	 Which of the following is not a germ cell tumor?
(A)	Granulosa cell tumor
(B)	 Dysgerminoma
(C)	Yolk sac tumor
(D)	Teratoma
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(A) Granulosa cell tumor
Ovarian tumors are classified based on their cell of origin. Germ cell tumors arise from the primordial germ cells of the ovary. This category includes dysgerminoma (B) (the ovarian equivalent of seminoma), yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus tumor) (C), choriocarcinoma, and teratoma (D). In contrast, the granulosa cell tumor (A) is the most common malignant tumor in the sex cord-stromal category. These tumors arise from the supporting cells of the ovary—the granulosa, theca, Sertoli, or Leydig cells—which are responsible for hormone production. Therefore, a granulosa cell tumor is of stromal origin, not germ cell origin.

Carney complex is a rare autosomal dominant multiple neoplasia syndrome most commonly caused by mutations in the PRKAR1A gene.
It classically includes:
1.	
Cardiac and extracardiac myxomas (especially atrial myxoma)
2.	
Spotty skin pigmentation (lentigines / lentiginosis)

Endocrine overactivity (e.g., Cushing syndrome due to primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease)

Now evaluating the options:

Atrial myxoma : Classic feature of Carney complex

This question tests the association between specific microscopic inclusion bodies and their corresponding diseases.

Lewy Bodies are eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic neuronal inclusions that are the pathological hallmark of Parkinsonism (A) and dementia with Lewy bodies. They are found primarily in the neurons of the substantia nigra.

52.	 When collecting a blood sample for serum 
calcium estimation, which practice must be 
avoided to prevent incorrect or misleading 
calcium results?
a.	 Collection in a sodium citrate vial
b.	 Forearm exercise and fist clenching
c.	 Prolonged immobilization of the patient
d.	 Rapid removal of the tourniquet
(A)	a, b, d
(B)	 a, b, c
(C)	b, c, d
(D)	a, b, c, d
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(B) a, b, c
Several pre-analytical factors can significantly alter serum calcium levels, leading to erroneous results.
(a)	
Collection in a sodium citrate vial : This must be avoided. Anticoagulants like citrate and EDTA chelate (bind) calcium ions, which will falsely decrease the measured calcium level in the sample. Serum samples should be collected in plain red-top or serum separator tubes.
(b)	
Forearm exercise and fist clenching : This action during phlebotomy can cause localized lactic acidosis. The resulting decrease in pH causes more calcium to dissociate from its protein carrier, albumin, thereby falsely increasing the ionized (free) calcium concentration.
(c)	
Prolonged immobilization : While a physiological state rather than a collection error, prolonged bed rest or immobilization leads to bone resorption, which genuinely increases total serum calcium levels. If a baseline calcium is desired, this confounding factor must be considered.
(d)	
Rapid removal of the tourniquet : This is a correct procedure. It is prolonged tourniquet application (>1 minute) that should be avoided, as it causes hemoconcentration and protein leakage, falsely elevating the concentration of total calcium (since about 45% of calcium is protein-bound).
Thus, factors a, b, and c must be avoided or accounted for to prevent erroneous reporting.
PHARMACOLOGY
53.	 Which drug attaches to the CD4 receptor and 
exhibits activity at both CXCR4 and CCR5?
(A)	Maraviroc
(B)	 Ibalizumab
(C)	Dolutegravir
(D)	Tenofovir
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(B) Ibalizumab
This question concerns the mechanism of action of different antiretroviral drugs. The HIV virus requires binding to the primary CD4 receptor and a coreceptor (either CCR5 or CXCR4) to enter a T-helper cell.
Ibalizumab (B) is a humanized monoclonal antibody. It is a post-attachment inhibitor that binds to domain 2 of the CD4 receptor on the host T-cell. This binding induces a conformational change that prevents the HIV-1 gp120 protein from interacting with the CCR5 or CXCR4 coreceptors, thereby blocking viral entry into the cell. Because it acts on the CD4 receptor itself after the virus has attached, it is effective against HIV strains that use either the CCR5 or CXCR4 coreceptor for entry (dual-tropic activity).
Maraviroc (A) is a CCR5 antagonist; it blocks only the CCR5 coreceptor and is ineffective against viruses that use the CXCR4 coreceptor.
Dolutegravir (C) is an integrase inhibitor, acting inside the cell to prevent viral DNA integration.
Tenofovir (D) is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor, also acting inside the cell.
54.	 Which topical antifungal agent is approved for 
treating toenail onychomycosis?
(A)	Caspofungin
(B)	 Tavaborole
(C)	Itraconazole
(D)	Griseofulvin
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2024
(B) Tavaborole
The treatment of onychomycosis (fungal infection of the nail) can be either oral or topical. The question specifically asks for a topical agent approved for toenails.
Tavaborole (B) is an oxaborole antifungal agent that is available as a topical solution (brand name Kerydin). It is specifically approved by the FDA for the topical treatment of onychomycosis of the toenails caused by the dermatophytes Trichophyton rubrum or Trichophyton mentagrophytes. It works by inhibiting fungal leucyl-tRNA synthetase, an enzyme essential for fungal protein synthesis. Other approved topical agents include efinaconazole and ciclopirox.
Caspofungin (A) is an echinocandin antifungal administered only intravenously for serious systemic fungal infections.
Itraconazole (C) and Griseofulvin (D) are both oral antifungal agents that can be used for onychomycosis. They are not used topically for this indication. Itraconazole and terbinafine are the most commonly used oral agents today.
55.	 Which of the following is correctly matched as 
an antidote with the given drug toxicity?
(A)	Benzodiazepines : Flumazenil
(B)	 Atropine : L-carnitine
(C)	Barbiturates : Fomepizole
(D)	Arsenic : Desferrioxamine
AAns
