AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
A number of diseases, known as proteinopathies or protein misfolding diseases, are caused by the accumulation of abnormally folded proteins that aggregate and cause cellular damage. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is the classic example of a human prion disease, which falls into this category. It is caused by the conversion of the normal cellular prion protein (PrPC) into an abnormal, misfolded, and infectious isoform (PrPSc). This misfolded protein is resistant to degradation and acts as a template to convert more normal PrPC into the abnormal form, leading to its exponential accumulation as insoluble aggregates in the brain. This process results in spongiform encephalopathy and a rapidly progressive, fatal neurodegenerative disease. In contrast, sickle cell anemia is caused by a mutation leading to hemoglobin polymerization, and megaloblastic anemia is due to impaired DNA synthesis, not protein misfolding.
24.	 In gonadal sex reversal syndrome with an XX 
karyotype, what is the most common underlying 
cause?
(A)	Point mutation 
(B)	 Deletion 
(C)	Translocation 
(D)	Non-sense mutation 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Translocation
46,XX testicular disorder of sex development (also known as XX male syndrome) is a condition where an individual has a female karyotype (46,XX) but develops a male phenotype, including testes. The primary determinant of male development is the SRY (Sex-determining Region Y) gene, which is normally located on the Y chromosome. The most common cause of 46,XX male syndrome, accounting for about 80% of cases, is an unequal crossing-over event during paternal meiosis. This results in the translocation of the SRY gene from the Y chromosome onto the X chromosome. The resulting X chromosome now carries the SRY gene. When an embryo inherits this SRY-positive X chromosome along with a normal X chromosome from the mother, it will have a 46,XX karyotype but will develop as a male due to the presence of the SRY gene, which initiates testis development.
25.	 Inheritance of pattern:
(A)	Autosomal Dominant 
(B)	 Autosomal Recessive 
(C)	X linked Recessive 
(D)	X linked Dominant 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Autosomal Dominant
The provided pedigree chart demonstrates several key features that are characteristic of an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. First, the trait appears in every generation, indicating vertical transmission from parent to child without skipping generations. Affected individuals are present in generations I, II, and III. Second, affected individuals transmit the trait to approximately half of their children, which is consistent with dominant inheritance (e.g., couple 1-2 have two affected and one unaffected child). Third, both males and females are affected, and critically, there is evidence of male-to-male transmission (affected father in individual 1 passes the trait to his affected son, individual 5). Male-to-male transmission definitively rules out X-linked inheritance. Autosomal recessive inheritance is unlikely as the trait does not skip generations and affected individuals have unaffected offspring.
26.	 Which of the following genes functions as an 
inhibitor of apoptosis?
(A)	BAK 
(B)	 MCL-1 
(C)	BID 
(D)	NOXA 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) MCL-1
The intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis is tightly regulated by the BCL-2 family of proteins, which includes both pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic members. The pro-apoptotic members include the "effectors" like BAX and BAK , which form pores in the mitochondrial membrane, and the "BH3-only" sensors like BID  and NOXA, which activate the effectors or inhibit the anti-apoptotic members. The anti-apoptotic (pro-survival) members act as inhibitors of apoptosis by binding to and sequestering the pro-apoptotic proteins. This group includes BCL-2, BCL-XL, and MCL-1 (Myeloid Cell Leukemia-1). Therefore, MCL-1 is a key inhibitor of apoptosis, and its overexpression is a common mechanism for cancer cells to evade cell death. BAK, BID, and NOXA are all pro-apoptotic proteins that promote cell death.
27.	 How can IDA be interpreted?
a.	 Low serum ferritin
b.	 Low transferrin saturation
c.	 Low serum iron
d.	 Increased TIBC
(A)	abcd 
(B)	 ab
(C)	cd
(D)	acd
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) abcd
Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA) has a characteristic pattern on iron studies that reflects the body's depleted iron stores and its attempt to compensate. Serum ferritin is a measure of stored iron, and a low level is the most specific and earliest indicator of iron deficiency (a). Serum iron measures the amount of iron circulating in the blood bound to transferrin, and it is also low in IDA (c). The Total Iron-Binding Capacity (TIBC) is an indirect measure of transferrin, the protein that transports iron. In an effort to acquire more iron, the liver increases the production of transferrin, leading to an increased TIBC (d). Finally, the transferrin saturation, calculated as (serum iron / TIBC) x 100, is low because there is very little iron available to saturate the increased amount of transferrin (b). All four of these findings together form the classic biochemical profile of iron deficiency anemia.
28.	 What does the absence of CD40 indicate in an 
individual?
(A)	B cell absent 
(B)	 T cell absent 
(C)	IgM increase 
(D)	IgG increase 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) IgM increase
The interaction between the CD40 receptor, expressed on B cells and other antigen-presenting cells, and its ligand, CD40L (CD154), expressed on activated T helper cells, is a critical step in humoral immunity. This interaction is essential for inducing immunoglobulin class switching in B cells, allowing them to switch from producing IgM to producing other isotypes like IgG, IgA, and IgE. It is also required for the formation of germinal centers and the development of memory B cells. In an individual with a genetic defect leading to the absence of functional CD40 (or CD40L), class switching cannot occur. As a result, B cells can only produce IgM antibodies. This leads to a specific type of immunodeficiency known as Hyper-IgM Syndrome, which is characterized by normal or, more typically, increased levels of serum IgM and a profound deficiency of IgG, IgA, and E.
29.	 To prevent contamination, blood should be 
drawn into vacutainers in the following order:
(A)	Red, Light blue, Violet, Grey 
(B)	 Blue, Violet, Red, Grey 
(C)	Blue, Red, Violet, Grey 
(D)	Grey, Blue, Red, Violet 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Blue, Red, Violet, Grey
When drawing multiple tubes of blood from a single venipuncture, a specific "order of draw" must be followed to prevent cross-contamination of additives between tubes, which could interfere with test results. The standardized order is based on the type of additive in the tube stopper. While the exact order can have minor variations, the generally accepted sequence is: First, blood culture bottles (if needed). Second, coagulation tubes, which have a light blue top and contain sodium citrate. Third, serum tubes, which can be a red top (no additive, allows clotting) or a serum separator tube (SST). Fourth, tubes with heparin (green top). Fifth, tubes with EDTA, which have a lavender or violet top. Finally, tubes with a glycolysis inhibitor, which have a grey top (containing sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate). Therefore, the correct sequence among the given options is Blue, Red, Violet, Grey.

33.	 Which of the following methods is not used to 
detect abnormal gene sequences?
(A)	RFLP analysis 
(B)	 Flow cytometry 
(C)	FISH 
(D)	Pyrosequencing 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Flow cytometry
The detection of abnormal gene sequences involves various molecular biology techniques. Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (RFLP) analysis  is a classic technique that can detect sequence variations that alter restriction enzyme cutting sites. Pyrosequencing  is a method of DNA sequencing that can identify the exact nucleotide sequence of a gene. Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH)  uses fluorescent probes to detect the presence, absence, or location of specific DNA sequences on chromosomes, and is used for detecting larger scale abnormalities like deletions or translocations. In contrast, flow cytometry  is a technique used to analyze the physical and chemical characteristics of cells. It is primarily used to measure cell surface protein expression (immunophenotyping), cell size, and granularity, and for cell sorting. It analyzes proteins on the cell surface, not the underlying gene sequence.
34.	 What does IDA stand for and how is it interpreted 
in the medical field?
(A)	Low serum ferritin 
(B)	 Low transferrin saturation 
(C)	Increased TIBC 
(D)	All of the above 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(D) All of the above
IDA stands for Iron Deficiency Anemia. Its diagnosis is confirmed by a characteristic pattern on a panel of blood tests known as iron studies. This pattern reflects both the depletion of the body's iron stores and its compensatory physiological responses. Low serum ferritin  is the most specific indicator, as ferritin is the primary iron storage protein, and its levels directly correlate with total body iron stores. The body responds to the deficiency by increasing the liver's production of transferrin, the protein that transports iron. This is measured as an increased Total Iron-Binding Capacity (TIBC). Since there is very little iron to be transported, the transferrin saturation, which reflects the percentage of transferrin that is actually carrying iron, is consequently low. Therefore, the combination of low ferritin, low serum iron, increased TIBC, and low transferrin saturation is the classic profile for interpreting a diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia.
35.	 In Cystic Fibrosis, which membrane channel is 
primarily impacted?
(A)	Sodium 
(B)	 Chloride 
(C)	Calcium 
(D)	Potassium 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Chloride
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene. The protein encoded by this gene functions as an ATP-gated ion channel located in the apical membrane of epithelial cells in various organs, including the lungs, pancreas, intestines, and sweat glands. The primary function of the CFTR protein is to transport chloride ions across the cell membrane. Defective CFTR protein results in impaired chloride transport, which in turn leads to abnormal transport of sodium and water across the epithelial surface. This disruption of ion and water flux is the fundamental defect that causes the production of abnormally thick, viscous mucus in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts and abnormally salty sweat, which are the hallmarks of the disease.
36.	 Which of the following statements about 
amyloidosis is correct?
(A)	Beta pleated sheets 
(B)	 Secondary amyloidosis is AL 
(C)	Amyloidosis is called so because of 
deposition of complex carbohydrates 
(D)	All of the above 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Beta pleated sheets
Amyloidosis is a group of diseases characterized by the extracellular deposition of abnormal, insoluble fibrillar proteins in various tissues and organs. While the precursor proteins that form amyloid deposits are diverse (e.g., immunoglobulin light chains in AL amyloidosis, serum amyloid A in AA amyloidosis), all amyloid fibrils share a common and defining ultrastructural feature. This is their characteristic cross-beta-pleated sheet conformation. This specific protein fold makes the fibrils extremely stable and resistant to proteolysis, leading to their progressive accumulation and subsequent tissue damage. The term "amyloid" was originally a misnomer, as it was thought to be a starch-like carbohydrate deposit, but it is in fact proteinaceous (C is false). Secondary (AA) amyloidosis is caused by deposition of serum amyloid A protein, not immunoglobulin light chains (AL), which cause primary amyloidosis (B is false).

37.	 A diabetic woman’s HbA1c decreased from 7.6 
to 6.7 after receiving a medication that raised 
GIP and GLP-1 levels and lowered glucagon 
secretion. Which drug was most likely given?
(A)	Pramlintide 
(B)	 Voglibose 
(C)	Sitagliptin 
(D)	Liraglutide 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Sitagliptin
The physiological effects described—increased levels of the incretin hormones GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide) and GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1), and a subsequent decrease in glucagon levels—are characteristic of the mechanism of action of dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors. Sitagliptin is a member of this class of oral antidiabetic drugs. The DPP-4 enzyme is responsible for the rapid degradation of endogenous incretin hormones. 38.	 Which monoclonal antibody, recently approved,

Rett syndrome is a rare, severe neurodevelopmental disorder primarily affecting females. In March 2023, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved trofinetide (brand name Daybue) for the treatment of Rett syndrome in adult and pediatric patients two years of age and older. 39.	 Which of the following statements about the 
clinical therapeutic index is correct?
(A)	Therapeutic index is LD50/ED50 
(B)	 Dose in which efficacy and toxicity can be 
balanced in an individual 
(C)	Indicative of therapeutic index in a 
population vs individual 
(D)	All of the Above 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Therapeutic index is LD50/ED50
The therapeutic index (TI) is a quantitative measure of the relative safety of a drug. It is a ratio that compares the dose of a drug that produces a toxic effect to the dose that produces a therapeutic or desired effect. The classical definition of the therapeutic index, derived from preclinical animal studies, is the ratio of the LD50 (the dose that is lethal to 50% of the population) to the ED50 (the dose that is therapeutically effective in 50% of the population). A higher therapeutic index indicates a wider margin of safety, meaning a much larger dose is needed to cause toxicity than is needed for the desired effect. Conversely, a drug with a low or narrow therapeutic index requires careful monitoring as the effective and toxic doses are close together. The other options describe concepts related to therapeutic drug monitoring or risk-benefit analysis rather than the formal definition of the TI.
40.	 For vancomycin dosage, which nomogram scale

(C)	Hallstead scale 
(D)	Rumack Matthew nomogram 
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023

Dosing vancomycin, an antibiotic used for serious Gram-positive infections, requires careful consideration of a patient's renal function to achieve therapeutic trough concentrations while avoiding nephrotoxicity. Several nomograms have been developed to guide initial dosing based on creatinine clearance (CrCl). The Matzke nomogram is a well-known and widely used tool for this purpose. It provides recommendations for vancomycin maintenance doses and dosing intervals based on the patient's calculated CrCl. By using this nomogram, clinicians can more accurately select an initial regimen that is likely to achieve the target therapeutic range. The Rumack-Matthew nomogram (D) is used specifically for assessing the risk of hepatotoxicity after an acute paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose. The other scales mentioned are not standard tools for vancomycin dosing.

43.	 Which of the following statements is false 
regarding a girl found deceased in a lake, 
indicating a case of ante-mortem drowning?
(A)	Water in the stomach 
(B)	 Froth on nose and mouth 
(C)	No Mud and vegetation in respiratory tract 
(D)	Cadaveric spasm in hand muscle 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) No Mud and vegetation in respiratory tract
Ante-mortem drowning means the person was alive when they entered the water and died as a result of submersion. The autopsy findings reflect the active process of breathing in water. A classic external sign is the presence of fine, lacy, and persistent froth at the mouth and nose, which is formed by the mixing of air, water, and mucus during agonal respirations. Internally, as the victim gasps for air underwater, they will inhale and swallow water, leading to the presence of water in the stomach and duodenum. If the drowning occurs in natural water, it is also common to find foreign material from the water body, such as mud, sand, and vegetation, deep within the respiratory tract, extending to the terminal bronchioles. Cadaveric spasm  may be present, with the victim's hands tightly clutching weeds or debris. Therefore, the absence of mud and vegetation in the airways would be inconsistent with typical ante-mortem drowning.

When collecting a blood sample for the medicolegal estimation of blood alcohol concentration, it is absolutely critical to avoid any potential contamination of the sample with external alcohol. Therefore, the venipuncture site must not be cleaned with any alcohol-containing swab, such as an alcohol-based spirit. The correct procedure is to clean the skin with a non-alcoholic antiseptic solution or simply with soap and water. 45.	 Which substance is responsible for producing a 
bitter taste that helps discourage the ingestion of 
toxic compounds?
(A)	Amino acids 
(B)	 Hydrogen ions 
(C)	Alkaloids 
(D)	Aldehyde 
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Alkaloids
The sense of taste has evolved to help organisms identify nutritious foods and avoid harmful toxins. The five basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, umami, and bitter. The perception of a bitter taste is thought to serve as a primary warning system against ingesting potentially poisonous substances. Many toxic compounds found in nature, particularly in plants, are alkaloids. These are naturally occurring nitrogen-containing compounds that often have potent physiological effects and are frequently toxic. Examples include caffeine, nicotine, strychnine, and quinine. The human gustatory system has a large family of bitter taste receptors (T2Rs) that can detect a vast array of these structurally diverse and potentially harmful alkaloid compounds, triggering an aversive response. 46.	 A patient presents with peripheral neuropathy 
and a condition known as “black foot disease.”

(B)	 Lead

This combination of symptoms is highly characteristic of chronic arsenic poisoning. Chronic exposure to arsenic, often through contaminated drinking water, leads to a multisystem disease. 47.	 What is the type of hypoxia caused by carbon 
monoxide poisoning?
(A)	Anemic hypoxia 
(B)	 Hypoxic hypoxia
(C)	Stagnant hypoxia
(D)	Histotoxic hypoxia
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Anemic hypoxia
Hypoxia is classified into four main types based on its underlying cause. Anemic hypoxia is defined as a condition where the partial pressure of oxygen in the arterial blood (PaO2) is normal, but the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood is reduced. This is precisely the mechanism of carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. CO has an affinity for hemoglobin that is over 200 times greater than that of oxygen. When inhaled, CO avidly binds to hemoglobin to form carboxyhemoglobin (COHb), which is incapable of transporting oxygen. This effectively reduces the amount of functional hemoglobin available to carry oxygen to the tissues, thus decreasing the blood's total oxygen content, despite a normal PaO2. This is functionally equivalent to having a severe anemia. Histotoxic hypoxia (D) is caused by cyanide, which prevents cells from using oxygen.

49.	 A man frequently encounters cat feces during his 
activities. Which stage of the organism present 
in the feces is capable of causing infection?
(A)	Tachyzoite 
(B)	 Gametocyte 
(C)	Oocyst 
(D)	Bradyzoite 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Oocyst
This question describes the transmission of Toxoplasma gondii, the parasite that causes toxoplasmosis. Cats are the definitive hosts for this parasite, meaning they are the only host in which the parasite's sexual life cycle can occur. This sexual cycle takes place in the intestinal epithelium of the cat and results in the formation of oocysts, which are then shed in the cat's feces. These oocysts are not immediately infectious but must undergo a process of sporulation in the environment, which takes 1-5 days. Once sporulated, these oocysts become highly infectious to intermediate hosts, including humans, who can acquire the infection by ingesting contaminated soil, water, or food. Tachyzoites are the rapidly dividing forms found in acute infection, and bradyzoites are the dormant forms found in tissue cysts in chronically infected hosts.

1.	
What is the correct order of structures in the 
auditory pathway?
(A)	Eight nerve cochlear nuclei superior olivary

AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Eight nerve cochlear nuclei superior olivary nucleus lateral lemniscus inferior colliculus → medial geniculate body → auditory cortex
The central auditory pathway is a complex, polysynaptic route that transmits sound information from the inner ear to the cerebral cortex for conscious perception. The pathway begins with the spiral ganglion neurons, whose axons form the cochlear division of the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII). These fibers make their first synapse in the cochlear nuclei located in the brainstem. From here, auditory information ascends bilaterally, with a major synapse in the superior olivary nucleus, which is crucial for sound localization. The pathway continues upward through a major ascending tract known as the lateral lemniscus. The next significant relay station is the inferior colliculus in the midbrain, another key auditory processing center. Subsequently, fibers project to the medial geniculate body of the thalamus, the final subcortical relay nucleus. Finally, thalamocortical radiations carry the processed auditory information to the primary auditory cortex located in the temporal lobe.
2.	
Which nerve provides innervation to the gluteus 
maximus muscle?
(A)	Femoral nerve 
(B)	 Sciatic nerve 
(C)	Inferior Gluteal Nerve 
(D)	Superior gluteal nerve 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Inferior Gluteal Nerve
The gluteus maximus is the largest and most superficial of the three gluteal muscles, and it serves as the primary extensor of the hip joint. Its motor innervation is provided solely by the inferior gluteal nerve. This nerve arises from the posterior divisions of the ventral rami of the L5, S1, and S2 spinal nerves within the lumbosacral plexus. It exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, inferior to the piriformis muscle, and travels a short course to innervate the overlying gluteus maximus muscle. It's important to differentiate this from the innervation of the other gluteal muscles; the gluteus medius and minimus, which are responsible for hip abduction and stabilization, are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve. The femoral nerve  supplies the anterior thigh muscles, while the sciatic nerve  innervates the posterior thigh and the leg and foot, passing deep to the gluteus maximus without supplying it.

5.	
Arrange the neural columns in medial-to-lateral 
order
1.	 Special somatic afferent
2.	 Special visceral efferent
3.	 General somatic efferent
4.	 General somatic afferent
(A)	GSE, SVE, GSA, SSA 
(B)	 SVE, GSA, SSA, GSE 
(C)	GSA, SSA, GSE, SVE 
(D)	SVE, GSE, GSA, SSA 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) GSE, SVE, GSA, SSA
During the development of the brainstem, the cranial nerve nuclei are organized into longitudinal functional columns arranged in a specific medial-to-lateral sequence. The sulcus limitans divides the plate into a medial motor (basal) plate and a lateral sensory (alar) plate. The motor columns are thus medial to the sensory columns. Within the motor plate, the most medial column is the General Somatic Efferent (GSE), innervating skeletal muscles derived from somites. Lateral to it is the Special Visceral Efferent (SVE) column, supplying muscles from the pharyngeal arches. In the sensory plate, the General Somatic Afferent (GSA) column  is medial to the Special Somatic Afferent (SSA) column, which is the most lateral of all the columns. Therefore, the correct medial-to-lateral arrangement of the specified columns is GSE, SVE, GSA, and SSA.

59.	 In biostatistics, the formula given below stands 
for?
(σ) = √[Σ(x - μ)² / N]
(A)	Standard Deviation
(B)	 Sample Variance
(C)	Sample Mean
(D)	Median
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Standard Deviation
The formula provided, σ = √[Σ(x - μ)² / N], is the precise mathematical definition of the population standard deviation. The Greek letter sigma (σ) is the standard symbol for this parameter. The formula calculates the square root of the average of the squared deviations of each data point (x) from the population mean (μ). The sum of the squared deviations is divided by N, the total size of the population. This differs slightly from the sample standard deviation, which uses the sample mean (x̄) and divides by (n-1) to provide an unbiased estimate. The standard deviation is a fundamental and widely used measure of the dispersion or variability of a set of data. It quantifies the average amount by which individual data points in a distribution differ from the mean of that distribution, expressed in the original units of the data.

60.	 A male farmer from a tropical region in South 
India presents to the ENT outpatient department 
with a reddish mass protruding from his nostril. 
Histopathological examination of the lesion has 
been performed. Based on these findings, which 
diagnosis is most likely?
(A)	Rhinosporidiosis
(B)	 Nasal polyp
(C)	Rhinophyma
(D)	Rhinoscleroma
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Rhinosporidiosis
The clinical scenario of a farmer from a tropical region like South India presenting with a reddish, polypoid, and friable nasal mass is highly suggestive of rhinosporidiosis. This is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by the aquatic protistan parasite Rhinosporidium seeberi. The infection is typically acquired through contact with contaminated water in ponds or rivers, which aligns with the patient's occupation as a farmer. The characteristic lesion is a polypoidal, strawberry-like mass in the nose or nasopharynx that bleeds easily on touch. The histopathological examination would be confirmatory, revealing the pathognomonic feature of thick-walled, spherical sporangia of varying sizes, filled with numerous endospores, embedded within a fibromyxomatous stroma containing a dense chronic inflammatory infiltrate. 61.	 A 14-year-old girl visits an ENT specialist 
because she can hear sounds and understand 
speech sounds but cannot comprehend their 
meaning. Her Pure Tone Audiometry and 
Auditory Brainstem Response tests are normal. 
What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	Malingering
(B)	 Auditory cortex lesion
(C)	Mixed transcortical aphasia
(D)	Wernicke's aphasia
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(D) Wernicke's aphasia
This 14-year-old girl can hear sounds normally and her Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA) and Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) are normal. This confirms that the peripheral auditory system and brainstem auditory pathways are intact. Therefore, the problem is not related to hearing loss or auditory nerve dysfunction.
However, she is unable to comprehend the meaning of speech despite being able to hear it clearly. This indicates a disorder of language processing rather than sound perception. The area of the brain responsible for understanding spoken language is Wernicke’s area, located in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere (usually the left).
In Wernicke’s aphasia, also called receptive aphasia, patients have fluent speech but impaired comprehension. They hear words but cannot interpret their meaning. Speech may be fluent yet nonsensical.
An auditory cortex lesion would impair sound perception itself. Mixed transcortical aphasia affects both expression and comprehension. Malingering is unlikely given objective normal auditory testing.
Thus, the most likely diagnosis is Wernicke’s aphasia.
62.	 In the provided image, which nerve is subjected 
to blockage?
(A)	Anterior ethmoidal nerve
(B)	 Nasociliary nerve
(C)	Supratrochlear nerve
(D)	Long ciliary nerve
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Nasociliary nerve
The image shows a local anesthetic injection being administered at the medial aspect of the upper nose, near the bridge and medial canthus region. This area corresponds to the sensory distribution of the nasociliary nerve, which is a branch of the ophthalmic division (V₁) of the trigeminal nerve.
The nasociliary nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure and runs medially within the orbit. It gives off several branches, including the anterior ethmoidal nerve, long ciliary nerves, and infratrochlear nerve. These branches supply sensation to the cornea, medial eyelids, dorsum and tip of the nose, and parts of the nasal cavity.
Blocking the nasociliary nerve provides anesthesia for procedures involving the nasal bridge, medial canthus, or anterior nasal cavity.

Thus, the nerve subjected to blockade in the image is the nasociliary nerve.
63.	 What is the accurate order of the auditory 
pathway?
(A)	Cochlea Spiral Ganglion Cochlear Nerve → 
Superior Olivary N
(B)	 Spiral Ganglion Cochlea Cochlear Nerve → 
Superior Olivary N
(C)	Spiral Ganglion Cochlear Nerve → Cochlea 
→ Superior Olivary N
(D)	Cochlea Spiral Ganglion Cochlear Nerve → 
Inferior Olivary N
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Cochlea Spiral Ganglion Cochlear Nerve → Superior Olivary N
This question asks for the correct initial sequence of the peripheral auditory pathway. Sound vibrations are first transduced into neural signals by the hair cells within the cochlea of the inner ear. These hair cells synapse with the first-order neurons of the auditory pathway. The cell bodies of these first-order neurons are located in the spiral ganglion, which is also situated within the cochlea. The axons of these spiral ganglion neurons then bundle together to form the cochlear nerve, which is the auditory division of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII). This nerve then travels from the cochlea to the brainstem, where its fibers make their first central synapse in the cochlear nuclei. From there, the pathway continues to the superior olivary nucleus. Therefore, the correct sequence from the site of transduction to the first central relay stations is Cochlea → Spiral Ganglion → Cochlear Nerve → Superior Olivary Nucleus.
64.	 What is the recommended treatment for an ICU

AAns

The appropriate treatment for a patient with severe influenza infection, particularly one requiring ICU admission, is an antiviral medication that specifically targets the influenza virus. The primary class of drugs recommended for this purpose is the neuraminidase inhibitors. The most commonly used agent in this class is oseltamivir, which is administered orally. For critically ill patients who cannot take oral medications, an intravenous formulation of a neuraminidase inhibitor, such as peramivir, may be used. Amantadine (A) is an older antiviral that is no longer recommended due to widespread resistance in circulating influenza strains. The other options are incorrect: Cephalosporin (B) is a beta-lactam antibiotic for bacterial infections, ganciclovir (B) is an antiviral for cytomegalovirus, and clarithromycin (C) is a macrolide antibiotic. 65.	 Based on the blanching of vascularity seen after 
administering phenylephrine, as shown in the 
image, what is the likely diagnosis?
NODIA
page  227  	
INICET Examination Paper
(A)	Nodular phlycten
(B)	 Nodular scleritis
(C)	Nodular episcleritis
(D)	Conjunctivitis
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Nodular episcleritis
The phenylephrine blanching test is a simple yet crucial diagnostic maneuver used to differentiate between episcleritis and scleritis, two conditions that cause a red eye with a localized nodule. Episcleritis is an inflammation of the episclera, a thin vascular layer that lies between the conjunctiva and the sclera. Scleritis is a more severe inflammation of the deeper scleral tissue itself. Phenylephrine is a topical vasoconstrictor. When applied to the eye, it effectively constricts the blood vessels in the superficial episcleral plexus. Therefore, in a case of nodular episcleritis, the administration of phenylephrine will cause the inflamed vessels to constrict, leading to a visible blanching or whitening of the red nodule. In contrast, in nodular scleritis, the inflammation involves the deep scleral and episcleral vessels, which are not significantly affected by topical phenylephrine. The redness in scleritis will persist despite the instillation of the drops.
66.	 Which lens is utilized in direct gonioscopy?
(A)	Goldmann
(B)	 Koeppe
(C)	Zeiss
(D)	Sussman
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Koeppe
Gonioscopy is the clinical technique used to visualize the iridocorneal angle, the anatomical angle between the iris and the cornea where the aqueous humor drains from the eye. It is essential for diagnosing and managing glaucoma. Gonioscopy can be either direct or indirect. Direct gonioscopy provides an upright, direct view of the angle. This technique requires the patient to be in a supine position and uses a large diagnostic contact lens that is placed directly on the cornea. The classic and prototypical lens used for direct gonioscopy is the Koeppe lens. In contrast, indirect gonioscopy is performed with the patient seated at the slit lamp and uses smaller lenses that contain mirrors or prisms, such as the Goldmann single-mirror or three-mirror lens and the Zeiss or Sussman four-mirror lenses, to provide an inverted, mirror-image view of the opposite angle.

68.	 What is the correct sequence of staining used in 
patients with dry eye disease?
i	
= Fluorescein stain
ii	
= Lissamine green
iii	 = Rose Bengal stain
(A)	i, iii, ii
(B)	 i, ii, iii
(C)	ii, i, iii
(D)	iii, ii, i
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) i, ii, iii
Vital staining of the ocular surface is a key component of the diagnosis and assessment of dry eye disease. When multiple stains are used during the same examination, they should be applied in a specific order to prevent one stain from masking the results of another. The recommended sequence is based on the staining characteristics and potential for interference. The standard order is to first instill fluorescein stain (i), which is used to assess tear film breakup time and to highlight corneal epithelial defects. After this, lissamine green (ii) is applied. Lissamine green stains devitalized, membrane-damaged epithelial cells of the conjunctiva and cornea with minimal irritation. Finally, Rose Bengal stain (iii) can be used. It also stains devitalized cells but is more irritating to the eye than lissamine green. Because Rose Bengal can mask the fluorescence of fluorescein, it should always be applied last.
69.	 What is the earliest perimetric sign of glaucoma?
(A)	Tunnel vision defect
(B)	 Complete vision loss
(C)	Isopter contraction + baring of blind spot
(D)	Complete field loss
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Isopter contraction + baring of blind spot
Glaucoma is a progressive optic neuropathy characterized by the gradual loss of retinal ganglion cells and their axons, which results in characteristic patterns of visual field loss. The earliest visual field defects detected by automated perimetry are often subtle and found in the paracentral region. These early changes include an increase in the size of the physiological baring of the blind spot, which is an exclusion of the blind spot from the central visual field isopter. Other early signs include isolated paracentral scotomas and nasal steps. Isopter contraction, particularly in the nasal field, is also an early sign of generalized depression of the visual field. Tunnel vision (A) represents a very advanced stage of the disease where only a small island of central vision remains. Complete vision loss (B, D) is the end stage. Therefore, the combination of isopter contraction and baring of the blind spot represents the earliest detectable changes.

70.	 A 27-year-old woman has an enlarged thyroid

AAns

(C) Superior vena cava syndrome
A significantly enlarged thyroid gland, or goiter, can cause compressive symptoms by impinging on adjacent structures in the neck. Compression of the trachea can cause dyspnea and stridor. Posterior extension can compress the esophagus, leading to dysphagia (B). While this is possible with a very large retrosternal goiter, it is a rare complication. In contrast, dysphagia and hoarseness are relatively common compressive symptoms. Therefore, among the options listed, SVC syndrome is the least expected and most unusual complication of a cervical goiter.
71.	 Which ion channels are mainly impaired due to 
the defect seen in cystic fibrosis?
(A)	Cl-
(B)	 Ca2+
(C)	Na+
(D)	K+
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Cl-
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the gene that encodes the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein. The CFTR protein is an ATP-gated ion channel located in the apical membrane of epithelial cells in many different organs. The primary function of this channel is the transport of chloride ions (Cl-) out of the epithelial cells into the lumen. In patients with cystic fibrosis, the CFTR channel is either absent or dysfunctional, leading to defective chloride secretion. This primary defect in chloride transport disrupts the normal balance of ions and water across the epithelial surface, leading to the production of abnormally thick, dehydrated, and viscous mucus in the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and reproductive tracts. The diagnostic sweat test for CF is based on this defect, as impaired chloride reabsorption in sweat ducts leads to abnormally high salt concentrations in the sweat.

74.	 Which of the following tests is not performed 
for Turner mosaic screening?
(A)	ANA	
(B)	 Audiometry
(C)	Echo	
(D)	GTT
AAns

Turner syndrome (45,X0) and its mosaic variants are associated with a number of specific health issues that require routine screening and surveillance. Congenital heart defects, particularly bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta, are common, making a baseline echocardiogram (Echo) essential. Sensorineural hearing loss is also a frequent finding, so regular audiometry is recommended. Cardiac auscultation is performed systematically over specific areas of the precordium where the sounds from each heart valve are best heard. The chest X-ray shows bilateral consolidation, and the nasopharyngeal swab confirms Rhinovirus, which is a viral pathogen. Viral pneumonias usually do not require antibiotics; however, mild empirical coverage is often initiated to prevent secondary bacterial infection, which can complicate viral illness.
Ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin, provides effective coverage against common community-acquired bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. It is well-tolerated, requires once-daily dosing, and adequately covers the possible bacterial superinfection without promoting unnecessary broad-spectrum resistance.
Other regimens like Ceftazidime + Azithromycin or Piptaz + Ciprofloxacin are too broad and are reserved for severe or hospital-acquired pneumonia. Similarly, Ceftriaxone + Levofloxacin is excessive in this mild case. Therefore, Ceftriaxone alone is the most rational, evidence-based choice for a stable patient with Rhinovirus-associated pneumonia.
78.	 For a pneumonia patient on mechanical

(B)	 Increase tidal volume

The patient's arterial blood gas (ABG) shows a mixed acidosis (pH 7.3, high pCO2, low bicarbonate), but the most critical parameter to address immediately is the oxygenation status. 79.	 What is the ECG depicted in the following 
image?
(A)	Torsades de pointes
(B)	 Pericarditis
(C)	Viral myocarditis
(D)	Cardiac tamponade
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Torsades de pointes
The ECG strip displays a life-threatening cardiac arrhythmia known as Torsades de pointes (TdP). This is a specific form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that is characterized by a distinctive morphology on the ECG. The QRS complexes are wide and have a continuously changing axis and amplitude, appearing to twist or spiral around the isoelectric baseline. This "twisting of the points" gives the arrhythmia its name. TdP occurs in the setting of a prolonged QT interval, which can be congenital or acquired (e.g., due to electrolyte abnormalities or medications). The arrhythmia is typically rapid and hemodynamically unstable, often degenerating into ventricular fibrillation and causing syncope or sudden cardiac death if not promptly recognized and treated. The other conditions listed have entirely different ECG manifestations (e.g., diffuse ST elevation in pericarditis, electrical alternans in cardiac tamponade).

130.	 Based on the observation that a surgeon could 
retract the hernial sac but not its contents 
during examination, what type of hernia does 
the image likely depict?
(A)	Incarcerated hernia
(B)	 Reduction en masse
(C)	Sliding hernia
(D)	Maydl's
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Reduction en masse
The image and the description portray a specific and dangerous complication known as reduction en masse. This occurs when an incarcerated or strangulated hernia is forcibly reduced without first ensuring that the contents of the sac are freed from the constricting neck of the hernia. The entire hernial sac, along with its trapped contents, is pushed as a single unit back through the fascial defect into the preperitoneal or intra-abdominal space. This creates a misleading appearance of a successful reduction because the external lump disappears. However, the bowel loop within the sac remains incarcerated and strangulated by the tight hernia neck, leading to persistent ischemia and eventual gangrene if not recognized and surgically corrected. The surgeon's ability to retract the sac without its contents being reducible is a key feature of this phenomenon.

93.	 A 58-year-old man arrives with sudden dizziness, 
nausea, and difficulty swallowing. Examination 
reveals ipsilateral facial numbness with loss of 
pain and temperature, contralateral loss of pain 
and temperature in the body, right-sided ptosis 
and miosis, along with hoarseness, ataxia, and

(A)	Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
(B)	 Superior cerebellar artery
(C)	Basilar artery
(D)	Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
This is a classic presentation of the lateral medullary syndrome, also known as Wallenberg syndrome. This stroke syndrome is caused by an infarction of the lateral portion of the medulla oblongata. The most common vascular occlusion leading to this syndrome is of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), which is a branch of the vertebral artery. The specific combination of signs and symptoms is due to the damage to the various tracts and nuclei located in this area: crossed sensory loss (spinothalamic tract), ipsilateral ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle), vertigo and nystagmus (vestibular nuclei), dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), and an ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis due to descending sympathetic fibers). 94.	 A “slapped cheek” appearance is classically 
associated with Parvovirus B19 infection 
(Erythema infectiosum / Fifth disease).
(A)	Pure Red Cell Aplasia
(B)	 Molluscum contagiosum
(C)	Herpes zoster
(D)	Kaposi sarcoma
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Pure Red Cell Aplasia
The "slapped cheek" appearance, a bright red rash on both cheeks, is the characteristic initial sign of Erythema Infectiosum, also known as Fifth Disease. This common childhood illness is caused by infection with Parvovirus B19. While typically a benign, self-limiting illness in healthy children, Parvovirus B19 has a specific tropism for erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow. Therefore, while the rash is the link, the underlying hematological complication associated with the causative agent of the "slapped cheek" rash is red cell aplasia.
95.	 Which of the following tests is not necessary for 
diagnosing Turner mosaic syndrome?
(A)	Echocardiogram (Echo)
(B)	 Antinuclear antibody (ANA) test
(C)	Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
(D)	Audiometry
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Antinuclear antibody (ANA) test
Turner syndrome (45,X0) and its mosaic variants are associated with a number of specific health issues that require routine screening and surveillance. Congenital heart defects, particularly bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta, are common, making a baseline echo cardiogram (Echo) essential. Sensorineural hearing loss is also a frequent finding, so regular audiometry is recommended. Individuals with Turner syndrome also have an increased risk of developing glucose intolerance and type 2 diabetes, so screening with a glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is part of standard care. Other screenings include thyroid function tests and renal ultrasound. However, an antinuclear antibody (ANA) test is used to screen for systemic autoimmune diseases like lupus. While autoimmune disorders (like autoimmune thyroiditis) are more common in Turner syndrome, a screening ANA test is not part of the standard initial workup for every patient.
96.	 Which medication should be given to a patient 
who presents with dizziness, cool clammy skin, 
pinpoint pupils, cyanosis of the lips and nails,

on coughing?
(A)	Naloxone
(B)	 Atropine
(C)	Phentolamine
(D)	Physostigmine
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Naloxone
This clinical picture is a classic presentation of a severe opioid overdose. The key signs are central nervous system depression (dizziness), constricted (miotic) pupils, and profound respiratory depression, which can lead to cyanosis. A particularly ominous sign of severe opioid overdose is the development of non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, which manifests as pink, frothy sputum. This is a medical emergency that requires immediate intervention to reverse the effects of the opioid. The specific and life-saving antidote for opioid overdose is naloxone. Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist that competitively binds to opioid receptors, rapidly displacing the opioid agonist (like heroin or fentanyl) and reversing its effects, particularly the life-threatening respiratory depression. Atropine (B) is for cholinergic crisis, and phentolamine (C) is an alpha-blocker.
97.	 For individuals with which of the following 
disorders 
is 
administering 
vaccines 
not 
contraindicated?
(A)	Complement fixation disorders
(B)	 Digeorge syndrome
(C)	Wiskott Aldrich syndrome
(D)	Ataxia telangiectasia
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Complement fixation disorders
The safety of vaccination, particularly with live attenuated vaccines, depends on the nature of the primary immunodeficiency. Live vaccines (e.g., MMR, varicella) are generally contraindicated in individuals with significant T-cell immunodeficiencies because the weakened pathogen can cause severe or disseminated disease. DiGeorge syndrome (B), Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (C), and ataxia-telangiectasia (D) are all complex primary immunodeficiencies that involve substantial defects in T-cell number or function. Therefore, live vaccines are contraindicated in these patients. In contrast, patients with isolated complement deficiencies have a defect in a component of the innate immune system but typically have intact B-cell and T-cell function. They are therefore able to mount a safe and effective immune response to both live and inactivated vaccines. In fact, due to their high risk of invasive infections with encapsulated bacteria, vaccination is strongly recommended.

(A) Acute laryngotracheobronchitis
The patient is a young child presenting with stridor following an upper respiratory infection (URI). The radiograph shown is an anteroposterior (AP) view of the neck. It displays the classic radiological finding of subglottic narrowing, which creates an appearance resembling a church steeple. This is known as the "steeple sign." 142.	 A 2-month-old pediatric patient has had a 
persistent swelling on the head since birth. 
What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	Cephalhematoma
(B)	 Caput succedaneum
(C)	Soft tissue swelling
(D)	None of the above
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Cephalhematoma
The key differentiating feature in this clinical scenario is the persistence of the head swelling for two months after birth. A caput succedaneum is a diffuse, edematous swelling of the scalp that is present at birth. It is caused by pressure on the presenting part of the scalp during delivery, crosses suture lines, and characteristically resolves within the first few days of life. In contrast, a cephalhematoma is a subperiosteal collection of blood caused by the rupture of blood vessels between the skull and the periosteum. It is sharply demarcated, does not cross suture lines, and, crucially, resolves much more slowly. A cephalhematoma can take several weeks to months to completely resolve and may undergo calcification. Therefore, a head swelling that is still present at 2 months of age is almost certainly a cephalhematoma, not a caput succedaneum.

144.	 A 40-year-old female patient experiencing 
vulvovaginal itching is currently prescribed an 
antidiabetic medication. Which of the following 
medications could likely be associated with her 
symptoms?
(A)	Metformin	
(B)	 Canagliflozin
(C)	Linagliptin	
(D)	Liraglutide
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Canagliflozin
Vulvovaginal itching is a hallmark symptom of vulvovaginal candidiasis (a yeast infection). Canagliflozin is an oral antidiabetic drug that belongs to the class of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors. The mechanism of action of SGLT2 inhibitors is to block the reabsorption of glucose in the kidneys, thereby promoting the excretion of large amounts of glucose in the urine (glucosuria). This high concentration of sugar in the genitourinary tract creates a favorable environment for the proliferation of yeast, particularly Candida albicans. Consequently, a common and well-recognized side effect of all SGLT2 inhibitors, including canagliflozin, is a significantly increased risk of developing genital mycotic infections in both men and women. Metformin (A), linagliptin (C), and liraglutide (D) work through different mechanisms and are not associated with this specific side effect.
145.	 On which of the following is the SRY gene 
located?
(A)	Y chromosome short arm
(B)	 Y chromosome long arm
(C)	X chromosome short arm
(D)	X chromosome long arm
Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

(A)	Allen test
(B)	 Adson test
(C)	Barbeau test
(D)	Homans test
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Allen test
The image depicts the procedure for performing the Allen test. This is a clinical test used to assess the patency of the ulnar and radial arteries and the integrity of the palmar arches of the hand. The procedure involves the patient clenching their fist tightly while the examiner manually occludes both the radial and ulnar arteries at the wrist. The patient then opens their hand, which will appear pale or blanched. The examiner releases the pressure on one of the arteries (typically the ulnar artery first) and observes the time it takes for color to return to the hand. Normal reperfusion should occur within 5-7 seconds. The test is then repeated, releasing the other artery. This test is crucial for ensuring adequate collateral circulation from the ulnar artery before procedures that might compromise the radial artery, such as arterial blood gas sampling or radial artery cannulation.
109.	 In HER2-positive breast cancer that is resistant to 
trastuzumab, which of the following treatment 
options is considered appropriate?
(A)	Lapatinib
(B)	 Sorafenib
(C)	Vemurafenib
(D)	Erlotinib
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Lapatinib
HER2-positive breast cancer is characterized by the overexpression of the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2. The primary targeted therapy for this subtype is trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody that binds to the extracellular domain of the HER2 receptor. However, some tumors may develop resistance to trastuzumab. In such cases, other HER2-targeted agents are used. Lapatinib is a small-molecule dual tyrosine kinase inhibitor that targets both the HER2 receptor and the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). By inhibiting the intracellular tyrosine kinase domain, it blocks downstream signaling pathways and can be effective even when resistance to the extracellularly-acting trastuzumab has developed. It is often used in combination with chemotherapy or other agents for patients with advanced HER2-positive breast cancer that has progressed on a trastuzumab-containing regimen. The other drugs listed target different pathways: sorafenib and vemurafenib are used for other cancers, and erlotinib is an EGFR inhibitor.
110.	 Osimertinib is used to treat non-small cell lung 
cancer (NSCLC) associated with which genetic 
mutation?
(A)	L858R mutation
(B)	 T890M mutation
(C)	T790M mutation
(D)	M790T mutation
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) T790M mutation
Osimertinib is a third-generation, irreversible epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI). It is a highly effective targeted therapy for patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) whose tumors harbor specific EGFR mutations. While it is also active against the common sensitizing mutations like exon 19 deletions and the L858R mutation (A), its key indication and the reason for its development was its potent activity against the T790M resistance mutation. The T790M mutation is the most common mechanism of acquired resistance that develops in patients who are initially treated with first- or second-generation EGFR TKIs (like erlotinib or gefitinib). Osimertinib was specifically designed to overcome this resistance mechanism, and it is now also a standard first-line treatment for EGFR-mutated NSCLC, as it is effective against both the initial sensitizing mutations and can prevent the emergence of the T790M resistance clone.
111.	 In a patient with a pelvic fracture who is actively

(C)	Perform Internal definite fixation

AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(D) Use Pelvic Binders
An unstable pelvic fracture in a hemodynamically unstable trauma patient is a life-threatening emergency. The primary source of bleeding is typically from the large venous plexuses and cancellous bone surfaces within the pelvis. The immediate and most critical first step in management is to stabilize the pelvis mechanically to reduce the pelvic volume and tamponade the bleeding. This is most rapidly and effectively achieved by the application of a pelvic binder or a circumferential pelvic sheet. This simple, non-invasive maneuver can significantly reduce pelvic hemorrhage and help stabilize the patient's hemodynamics while further resuscitation and investigation are underway. While fluid resuscitation (A) is also essential and happens concurrently, the mechanical stabilization is the key intervention for hemorrhage control. 112.	 A patient presents with abnormal sensations

(D)	Axillary nerve
AAns 


(A) Ulnar nerve
This constellation of symptoms points directly to a lesion of the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve provides sensory innervation to the medial one-and-a-half digits of the hand, which includes the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger. Paresthesias or numbness in this specific distribution is a classic hallmark of ulnar neuropathy. The ulnar nerve also provides motor innervation to most of the intrinsic muscles of the hand, including the interossei, the hypothenar muscles, and the adductor pollicis. Weakness of these muscles leads to a weak grip, difficulty with fine motor tasks, and a lack of finger coordination, such as the inability to abduct and adduct the fingers. 113.	 In the scenario where a surgeon reduces the

(D) Reduction en masse
Reduction en masse is a rare but serious complication of attempting to reduce an incarcerated or strangulated hernia. It occurs when the entire hernia sac, along with its constricted neck and strangulated contents, is forcibly pushed from its subcutaneous position back through the fascial defect into the abdominal cavity. This maneuver gives the false impression of a successful reduction because the external bulge disappears. However, the contents of the hernia (typically a loop of bowel) remain trapped and strangulated within the hernial sac inside the abdomen. The image depicts this exact scenario, where the entire sac and its contents have been displaced internally without relief of the constriction.
114.	 Which of the following are not considered

(C)	Jejunum
(D)	Superior mesenteric artery
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Fundus of gallbladder
The third part of the duodenum, also known as the horizontal part, runs transversely from right to left, anterior to the inferior vena cava and the aorta. It has several important anterior relations. It is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric artery and vein as they descend from behind the pancreas. The root of the mesentery of the small intestine also originates from this area and crosses anteriorly. Coils of the jejunum also lie anterior to the third part of the duodenum. In contrast, the fundus of the gallbladder is located in the right upper quadrant, in a fossa on the visceral surface of the liver. Its primary duodenal relation is with the superior (first) part of the duodenum, which it lies posterior to. It is not an anterior relation of the much lower, third part of the duodenum.
115.	 After surgical repair of a left-sided varicocele, a

The testis has a complex venous drainage system. The primary route is through the pampiniform plexus, which coalesces to form the testicular (internal spermatic) vein. A varicocele is a dilation of these pampiniform plexus veins. Surgical correction, or varicocelectomy, involves ligating these incompetent testicular veins. 101.	 A 25-year-old woman with a one-month history 
of fever presents with headache and ataxia. 
Brain imaging reveals dilated ventricles and 
prominent basal exudates. What CSF finding is 
most likely?
(A)	Lymphocytosis, Low Glucose, High protein
(B)	 Lymphocytosis, Low Glucose, Normal 
protein
(C)	Lymphocytosis, Low Glucose, Normal 
protein
(D)	Neutrophilia, Low glucose, Low Protein
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Lymphocytosis, Low Glucose, High protein
The clinical presentation of a subacute illness lasting a month, coupled with neurological signs and imaging that reveals hydrocephalus (dilated ventricles) and prominent inflammation at the base of the brain (basal exudates), is highly characteristic of tuberculous (TB) meningitis. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis in TB meningitis has a classic profile that distinguishes it from other forms of meningitis. It typically shows a moderate pleocytosis (increased white blood cell count) with a marked predominance of lymphocytes. A key feature is a significantly low glucose level (hypoglycorrhachia), often less than 40% of the serum glucose, due to impaired transport into the CSF and consumption by the inflammatory process. Finally, due to the intense inflammation and breakdown of the blood-brain barrier, there is a markedly high protein concentration, often exceeding 100-200 mg/dL. This specific triad of CSF findings is the hallmark of tuberculous meningitis.
102.	 A 42-year-old patient reports chronic fatigue, 
feeling warm, and being unable to gain weight 
despite a good appetite. Which laboratory result 
would most likely be expected?
(A)	Decreased TSH with elevated T3 or T4 levels
(B)	 Elevated TSH with normal T3 or T4 levels
(C)	Elevated TSH with euthyroid levels of T3 
and T4
(D)	Increased T3 levels with decreased T4 levels
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Decreased TSH with elevated T3 or T4 levels
The patient's constellation of symptoms—persistent fatigue, heat intolerance ("warm body"), and weight loss despite a good or increased appetite—strongly suggests a hypermetabolic state consistent with hyperthyroidism. This condition is caused by an excess of circulating thyroid hormones (T3 and T4). The endocrine regulation of the thyroid gland is governed by a negative feedback loop. The pituitary gland secretes Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH), which prompts the thyroid to produce T3 and T4. In primary hyperthyroidism (the most common cause, such as Graves' disease), the thyroid gland itself autonomously overproduces these hormones. The resulting high levels of T3 and T4 in the blood then feed back to the pituitary gland, suppressing its production and release of TSH. Therefore, the classic and expected laboratory profile for primary hyperthyroidism is a low or suppressed TSH level in the presence of elevated free T4 and/or T3 levels.
103.	 A 
hypertensive 
patient 
is 
on 
multiple 
medications, and the ECG shown reflects a 
specific pattern. Which medications are likely 
responsible for this ECG finding?
(A)	Spironolactone
(B)	 Thiazides
(C)	Prazosin
(D)	Metoprolol
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Spironolactone
The ECG shows tall, narrow-based, and symmetrically peaked T-waves, often referred to as "tented" T-waves. This is the earliest and most characteristic electrocardiographic sign of hyperkalemia (elevated serum potassium levels). This finding reflects altered ventricular repolarization due to the high extracellular potassium concentration. The question requires identifying which of the listed antihypertensive medications is known to cause hyperkalemia. Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic that functions as an aldosterone antagonist. By blocking the action of aldosterone in the renal collecting ducts, it prevents sodium reabsorption and, crucially, inhibits potassium secretion. This leads to the retention of potassium in the body, which can result in hyperkalemia. This side effect is a well-known risk, particularly in patients with renal impairment or those concurrently taking other medications that can also increase potassium levels, such as ACE inhibitors or ARBs. Thiazide diuretics, in contrast, typically cause hypokalemia.
104.	 A 10-year-old boy is admitted with severe 
dehydration, nausea, vomiting, urine sugar 3+, 
RBS 550 mg/dL, ABG showing pH of 7.1, and 
HCO3= 7 mmol/L. What is the appropriate line 
of management as per ISPAD (International 
Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes) 
guidelines?
(A)	10 ml per kg of IV fluids & 0.1 unit/kg/hr 
bolus
(B)	 10 ml per kg of IV fluids & after 1 hour of 
fluid 0.1 unit/kg/hr of insulin
(C)	20 ml per kg of IV fluids & 0.1 unit/kg/hr of 
insulin bolus
(D)	20 ml per kg of IV fluids & after 1 hour of 
fluid 0.1 unit/kg/hr of insulin bolus
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) 10 ml per kg of IV fluids & after 1 hour of fluid 0.1 unit/kg/hr of insulin
The patient's presentation with hyperglycemia, ketonuria, and metabolic acidosis is diagnostic of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Management according to ISPAD guidelines is systematic and cautious. The first priority is to correct dehydration and restore circulatory volume. The initial fluid bolus for a child in DKA who is not in profound shock is 10 ml/kg of isotonic saline (0.9% NaCl) given over the first hour. Importantly, insulin therapy should not be started immediately. It should be initiated only after the initial fluid resuscitation has begun, typically about one hour after starting IV fluids. This delay helps to prevent a rapid fall in glucose and osmolarity, which could increase the risk of cerebral edema. Once started, insulin is given as a continuous low-dose intravenous infusion, typically at a rate of 0.05-0.1 unit/kg/hour, without an initial bolus. Therefore, the correct approach is an initial 10 ml/kg fluid bolus, followed by the start of an insulin infusion one hour later.

105.	 Which of the following statements about CPR 
is incorrect?
(A)	Ventilation 22-25/min
(B)	 Depth of chest compression up to 5-6 cm
(C)	Allow adequate chest recoil
(D)	Chest compression rate 100-120/min
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Ventilation 22-25/min
High-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is crucial for improving outcomes from cardiac arrest. The current guidelines emphasize several key components. The recommended rate of chest compressions for an adult is between 100 and 120 per minute. The depth of compressions should be at least 2 inches (5 cm) but not more than 2.4 inches (6 cm). It is also vital to allow for complete chest recoil between each compression, as this is necessary for the heart to fill with blood. When an advanced airway (such as an endotracheal tube) is in place, ventilations are given asynchronously with compressions at a rate of 1 breath every 6 seconds, which translates to 10 breaths per minute. A ventilation rate of 22-25 breaths per minute is excessive and can lead to hyperventilation, which increases intrathoracic pressure, decreases venous return and cardiac output, and worsens outcomes.

The patient presents with flank pain and hematuria, which are classic symptoms of kidney stones. 107.	 What was the primary aim of the Keynote-189 
trial involving pembrolizumab?
(A)	Pembrolizumab with chemo given for

(C)	Only Pembrolizumab for NSCLC
(D)	Only nivolumab for NSCLC

The KEYNOTE-189 clinical trial was a landmark phase 3 study that fundamentally changed the first-line treatment paradigm for a specific subset of patients with advanced lung cancer. The primary objective of this trial was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of adding the immune checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab (an anti-PD-1 antibody) to a standard platinum-based chemotherapy regimen (pemetrexed plus either cisplatin or carboplatin). 125.	 Which of the following statements accurately

A thymoma is a tumor that arises from the epithelial cells of the thymus gland, and it is indeed the most common primary neoplasm of the thymus and the anterior mediastinum in adults. 127.	 Which of the subsequent conditions is linked

Perineural invasion (PNI), the process of tumor cells invading in, around, and along nerves, is a well-known feature of certain malignancies and is associated with a poorer prognosis. 128.	 What is the minimum platelet count necessary 
for surgical procedures?

The decision to proceed with surgery in a patient with thrombocytopenia depends on the type of procedure and the risk of bleeding. While there is some variation in practice, a generally accepted and safe threshold for the minimum platelet count required for most major, non-neuraxial surgical procedures is 50,000/µL. (C) Diastolic murmur
Aortic regurgitation (or aortic insufficiency) is a condition where the aortic valve fails to close completely at the end of systole. This incompetence allows blood to leak backward from the aorta into the left ventricle during diastole. This retrograde flow of blood across the incompetent valve is what generates the characteristic heart murmur. Therefore, the murmur of aortic regurgitation is a diastolic murmur. It is typically described as a high-pitched, blowing, decrescendo murmur that is best heard at the left sternal border with the patient sitting up and leaning forward in full expiration. The murmur begins immediately after the second heart sound (S2). In contrast, an ejection systolic murmur (B) is caused by the forward flow of blood through a narrowed (stenotic) aortic or pulmonary valve during systole.
81.	 Which of the following is not a cause of high-
output cardiac failure?
(A)	Cor pulmonale
(B)	 Beri beri
(C)	Anemia
(D)	Systemic AV shunt
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Cor pulmonale
High-output cardiac failure is a form of heart failure where the cardiac output is normal or even elevated, but it is insufficient to meet the body's heightened metabolic demands. This condition is caused by a significant decrease in systemic vascular resistance. Classic causes include severe chronic anemia (C), where reduced blood viscosity and tissue hypoxia cause widespread vasodilation; beriberi (thiamine deficiency) (B), which causes peripheral vasodilation; and large systemic arteriovenous (AV) shunts or fistulas (D), which bypass the systemic resistance arterioles. In contrast, cor pulmonale is defined as right-sided heart failure resulting from chronic pulmonary hypertension. The primary problem is an increased afterload on the right ventricle due to high resistance in the pulmonary circulation. This leads to low-output right heart failure, not high-output failure.
82.	 Which statement best describes Subclinical 
acute myocarditis?
(A)	Low LVEF on 2D ECHO
(B)	 Palpitations
(C)	Elevated pro-BNP, Trop T
(D)	Regional wall abnormalities on 2D ECHO
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Elevated pro-BNP, Trop T
Subclinical myocarditis refers to inflammation of the heart muscle that is not severe enough to cause overt clinical symptoms of heart failure, such as dyspnea or overt signs like a significantly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) on echo cardiography. However, there is still underlying myocardial injury and stress occurring. This subclinical inflammation and myocyte damage can be detected by measuring sensitive and specific cardiac biomarkers in the blood. The release of troponin T (Trop T) or troponin I into the circulation is a direct indicator of cardiomyocyte necrosis or injury. An elevated pro-BNP (or BNP) level is a marker of ventricular wall stress and strain. The presence of elevated levels of these biomarkers in a patient without overt heart failure symptoms or significant systolic dysfunction would be the best indicator of a subclinical myocarditis. Palpitations are a symptom, and low LVEF or wall motion abnormalities would indicate clinical, not subclinical, disease.
83.	 Which artery is involved in Lateral Medullary 
Syndrome?
(A)	Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
(B)	 Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
(C)	Superior cerebellar artery
(D)	Inferior cerebellar artery
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Lateral medullary syndrome, also known as Wallenberg syndrome, is a specific type of stroke that produces a classic and well-defined constellation of neurological deficits. This syndrome is caused by an infarction of the lateral portion of the medulla oblongata. The most common vascular cause for this stroke is an occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), which is a branch of the vertebral artery. Occasionally, the syndrome can be caused by an occlusion of the vertebral artery itself before the origin of the PICA. The infarction damages several key structures in the lateral medulla, including the vestibular nuclei, inferior cerebellar peduncle, nucleus ambiguus, and the spinothalamic tract, leading to the characteristic symptoms of vertigo, ataxia, dysphagia, and crossed sensory loss. Occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) causes a lateral pontine syndrome.

One of its most common and well-known side effects, which can occur even at therapeutic serum concentrations, is a fine postural tremor, particularly of the hands. This is a frequent finding and does not necessarily indicate toxicity. Statement (A) is false; lithium is a known teratogen, classically associated with an increased risk of Ebstein's anomaly, a congenital heart defect, when taken during the first trimester of pregnancy. Statement (B) is false; lithium is rapidly and almost completely absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract. Statement (D) is also false; lithium has no efficacy in the treatment of absence seizures and can, in some cases, even exacerbate seizures. The drug of choice for absence seizures is ethosuximide or valproic acid.
85.	 For which of the following conditions are 
vaccines 
not 
contraindicated 
in 
affected 
individuals?
(A)	DiGeorge syndrome
(B)	 Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
(C)	Complement deficiency
(D)	Ataxia telangiectasia
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Complement deficiency
The safety of vaccination depends on the specific type of primary immunodeficiency. Live attenuated vaccines (such as MMR and varicella) are generally contraindicated in patients with severe T-cell immunodeficiencies, as the weakened pathogen can cause disseminated disease. DiGeorge syndrome (A), Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (B), and ataxia-telangiectasia (D) are all complex immunodeficiencies that involve significant defects in T-cell function. Therefore, live vaccines are contraindicated in these patients. In contrast, patients with isolated complement deficiencies have a defect in the complement system, which is part of the innate immune system, but they typically have intact T-cell and B-cell function. They can therefore mount an appropriate and safe immune response to both live and inactivated vaccines. In fact, vaccination, particularly against encapsulated bacteria like Neisseria meningitidis, is strongly recommended in these patients.

88.	 A 62-year-old patient experiences calf pain 
while walking that subsides with rest. Which of 
the following features is not typically associated 
with intermittent claudication?
(A)	Muscle cramping during physical activity
(B)	 Pain starting on taking the first step
(C)	Atheroma as the most frequent underlying 
cause
(D)	Level of occlusion cannot be decided based 
on symptoms
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Pain starting on taking the first step
Intermittent claudication is the classic symptom of peripheral artery disease (PAD). It is characterized by a reproducible cramping pain or ache in a muscle group (e.g., the calf) that is induced by a consistent level of exercise or physical activity and is relieved promptly by rest. This is caused by ischemia resulting from an inadequate blood supply to meet the increased metabolic demands of the exercising muscle. The most frequent underlying cause of the arterial narrowing is atherosclerosis (C). The location of the pain can give a clue to the level of the arterial occlusion, but it is not always precise (D). A key feature of claudication is that the pain begins after a certain amount of exertion and is not present at the beginning of the activity. Pain that starts on taking the first step is not characteristic of claudication; it is more suggestive of a musculoskeletal or orthopedic issue, such as plantar fasciitis or osteoarthritis.
89.	 Which of the following is not recognized as a 
complication of massive blood transfusion?
(A)	Hypocalcemia
(B)	 Hypokalemia
(C)	Hypothermia
(D)	Hypernatremia
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(D) Hypernatremia
Massive blood transfusion (the replacement of a patient's entire blood volume within 24 hours) is associated with several well-known metabolic and physiological complications. The citrate anticoagulant used in stored blood chelates calcium, which can lead to clinically significant hypocalcemia (A), especially when large volumes are infused rapidly. Stored red blood cells leak potassium, and the transfused blood is typically cooler than body temperature, which can lead to hypothermia (C). Interestingly, while stored blood contains a high concentration of potassium, massive transfusions are more often associated with hypokalemia (B) initially, due to factors like dilution, alkalosis from citrate metabolism, and sympathetic drive. In contrast, hypernatremia (high sodium) is not a recognized complication. The sodium concentration in packed red blood cells and the anticoagulant solutions is similar to that of normal plasma, so transfusion does not typically cause an increase in serum sodium levels.
90.	 Which marker is indicative of alcohol-related 
illness?
(A)	SGPT
(B)	 SGOT
(C)	GGT
(D)	ANP
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) GGT
While several liver enzymes can be elevated in alcohol-related liver disease, Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT) is considered a particularly sensitive, though not entirely specific, marker of chronic alcohol consumption and alcohol-related liver injury. Alcohol is a potent inducer of the microsomal GGT enzyme in the liver. Therefore, chronic heavy drinking often leads to a significant and disproportionate elevation of serum GGT levels, even in the early stages of liver disease before other enzymes are substantially affected. While SGOT (AST) and SGPT (ALT) are also elevated in alcoholic hepatitis (B, A), typically with an AST:ALT ratio > 2, GGT is a more sensitive indicator of alcohol ingestion itself. The management of acute diverticulitis depends on its severity. Uncomplicated diverticulitis is typically managed conservatively with antibiotics. However, the development of complications is an indication for more aggressive management, including potential surgery. The finding of a pericolic abscess on a CT scan represents a complicated diverticulitis (Hinchey stage I or II). 137.	 What are the appropriate treatment options for 
a child exhibiting symptoms of a six-day fever, 
strawberry tongue, conjunctival congestion, and 
skin peeling?
(A)	Aspirin + clopidogrel
(B)	 Warfarin
(C)	IVIG
(D)	LMWH
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) IVIG
The patient's constellation of symptoms—prolonged fever (>5 days), strawberry tongue (oral mucosal changes), conjunctival congestion, and skin peeling (desquamation of the extremities)—are classic diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki disease is an acute, self-limited vasculitis of childhood that primarily affects the medium-sized arteries. Its most serious complication is the development of coronary artery aneurysms, which can lead to myocardial infarction and sudden death. The standard and essential treatment for acute Kawasaki disease is the administration of a high dose of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), typically 2 g/kg as a single infusion over 10-12 hours. IVIG has been shown to dramatically reduce the incidence of coronary artery aneurysms from about 25% to less than 5%. High-dose aspirin is also a standard part of the acute treatment, but IVIG is the cornerstone immunomodulatory therapy.

139.	 During a temple visit, a child with his

(B)	 Adrenaline
(C)	Methylprednisolone
(D)	Anti snake venom
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Prazosin
This unusual and dramatic clinical presentation is the classic toxidrome of a scorpion sting, particularly from the Indian red scorpion (Mesobuthus tamulus). The venom of this scorpion contains potent neurotoxins that cause a massive and uncontrolled release of catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) from the adrenal glands and sympathetic nerve endings, leading to a "sympathetic storm." The image shows the characteristic "slapped cheek" rash of Erythema Infectiosum, also known as Fifth Disease. This common childhood exanthem is caused by infection with Parvovirus B19.
