116.	 Which test would be suitable for assessing 
incompetence of the superficial femoral vein 
(SFJ) in a patient who has dull aching pain and 
twisted veins in both lower limbs?
(A)	Fegan's test
(B)	 Homan's test
(C)	Modified Perthes test
(D)	Brodie Trendelenburg test
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(D) Brodie Trendelenburg test
The patient's symptoms are suggestive of varicose veins due to chronic venous insufficiency. The Brodie-Trendelenburg test is a classic clinical maneuver used to assess the competence of the valves in the superficial venous system, specifically at the saphenofemoral junction (SFJ), and in the perforating veins. The test involves elevating the patient's leg to empty the superficial veins, then applying a tourniquet at the upper thigh to occlude the great saphenous vein. The patient then stands up. If the varicose veins fill slowly from below, it indicates competent perforator valves. Rapid filling from below suggests incompetent perforators. The tourniquet is then released. A sudden, rapid downward filling of the veins from above indicates incompetence of the valve at the saphenofemoral junction. Homan's test (B) is for deep vein thrombosis.

120.	 A 45-year-old woman with early-stage breast 
cancer is considering her surgical options 
with her surgeon. Which of the following does

(B)	 Post-operative radiotherapy

AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(D) Axillary dissection
Breast conservation surgery (BCS), also called lumpectomy or wide local excision, is performed in early-stage breast cancer to remove the tumor along with a margin of normal surrounding tissue while preserving most of the breast. The primary goal is to achieve oncological safety with good cosmetic outcome.
A key component of BCS is wide local excision, making option (A) correct. After surgery, post-operative radiotherapy is routinely given to the remaining breast tissue to reduce the risk of local recurrence; therefore, option (B) is also a standard part of treatment.

122.	 Which of the subsequent options is not 
considered a perianal approach for rectal

(B)	 Frykman and Goldberg's
(C)	Thiersch
(D)	Delorme
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Frykman and Goldberg's
The surgical management of a full-thickness rectal prolapse can be performed via either an abdominal approach or a perineal (perianal) approach. The choice of procedure depends on the patient's age, comorbidities, and the surgeon's preference. The perineal approaches are performed through an incision around the anus. These include the Altemeier procedure (a perineal rectosigmoidectomy), the Delorme procedure (a mucosal sleeve resection with placation of the muscle wall), and the Thiersch procedure (the placement of a circumferential suture to narrow the anal orifice, now rarely used). 123.	 A 28 year old female reported to OPD with C/O 
swelling in mouth On Clinical examination

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Y chromosome short arm
The SRY gene, which stands for the Sex-determining Region Y, is the master gene responsible for initiating male development in mammals. It acts as a transcription factor that triggers a cascade of downstream gene expression leading to the development of the undifferentiated embryonic gonads into testes. In the absence of a functional SRY gene, the gonads will default to developing into ovaries. This critical gene is located on the short arm (p arm) of the Y chromosome. 146.	 In puberty, what is the primary reason for the 
occurrence of menorrhagia?
(A)	Endometriosis
(B)	 Anovulation
(C)	Malignancy
(D)	Primary amenorrhea
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Anovulation
Menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding) and irregular bleeding are very common in the first few years after menarche. The primary underlying reason for this is the immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis. In early puberty, the positive feedback mechanisms required to trigger the mid-cycle luteinizing hormone (LH) surge are not yet fully established. This frequently results in anovulatory cycles, where a follicle develops and produces estrogen, but ovulation does not occur, and a corpus luteum is not formed. In the absence of the progesterone that would normally be produced by the corpus luteum, the endometrium is exposed to prolonged, unopposed estrogen. This leads to excessive endometrial proliferation, which eventually outgrows its blood supply and breaks down irregularly and heavily. This anovulatory bleeding is the most common cause of abnormal uterine bleeding in adolescents.

Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) can grow rapidly during pregnancy due to the influence of high estrogen levels. 150.	 What are clue cells?
(A)	Vaginal epithelial cells lined by bacteria
(B)	 Cervical epithelial cells lined by bacteria
(C)	Uterine endothelial cells lined by bacteria
(D)	Abdominal cells lined by bacteria
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Vaginal epithelial cells lined by bacteria
Clue cells are the single most reliable microscopic finding for the diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis (BV). They are defined as vaginal squamous epithelial cells that are so densely coated with adherent coccobacilli (primarily Gardnerella vaginalis and other BV-associated anaerobes) that the borders of the epithelial cells become obscured and indistinct. This dense bacterial coating gives the cells a characteristic stippled or granular appearance when viewed under a microscope on a saline wet mount of the vaginal discharge. The presence of clue cells in more than 20% of the epithelial cells on the slide is one of the four Amsel criteria for diagnosing BV and is considered the most specific sign. These cells are exfoliated from the vaginal mucosa, not the cervix, uterus, or abdomen.
151.	 For a patient presenting with a retroverted 
uterus, dysmenorrhea, and dyspareunia, what 
is the recommended next step in investigation?
(A)	Ultrasound (USG)
(B)	 Diagnostic Laparoscopy
(C)	Laparotomy
(D)	HSG (Hysterosalpingography)
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Diagnostic Laparoscopy
A retroverted uterus alone is often a normal anatomical variant and may not cause symptoms. However, when it is associated with dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation) and dyspareunia (pain during intercourse), it strongly suggests an underlying pelvic pathology, most commonly endometriosis or pelvic adhesions.
Endometriosis occurs when endometrial tissue is present outside the uterus, often involving the ovaries, uterosacral ligaments, and pouch of Douglas. It can cause a fixed retroverted uterus due to adhesions between pelvic structures. The symptoms of progressive dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, and chronic pelvic pain are classic for this condition.
While ultrasound may detect ovarian endometriomas, it often misses small peritoneal implants or subtle adhesions. Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is primarily used to evaluate tubal patency in infertility cases and does not help diagnose endometriosis. Laparotomy is not indicated as an initial investigation.
Diagnostic laparoscopy is considered the gold standard because it allows direct visualization of endometriotic lesions and adhesions, and biopsy can be taken for confirmation. It also provides the opportunity for simultaneous therapeutic intervention.
Therefore, diagnostic laparoscopy is the recommended next step.
152.	 A 15-year-old girl presents with primary 
amenorrhea, development of pubic hair, 
prepubertal breasts, a blind-ending vagina, 
clitoromegaly, normal testosterone levels, and a 
46 XY karyotype. What condition explains these 
clinical findings?
(A)	17-Hydroxylase deficiency
(B)	 Swyer syndrome
(C)	5-alpha reductase deficiency
(D)	Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome 
(AIS)
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) 5-alpha reductase deficiency
The patient has a 46,XY karyotype but has developed along female lines, indicating a disorder of sex development. The key to the diagnosis is the specific pattern of androgen effects. Normal testosterone levels indicate functional testes. The development of pubic hair and clitoromegaly at puberty demonstrates that the body is responsive to testosterone. However, the external genitalia were female-appearing at birth (blind-ending vagina), and breast development has not occurred. This specific dissociation between the effects of testosterone and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is the hallmark of 5-alpha reductase deficiency. In this condition, the enzyme that converts testosterone to the more potent DHT is absent. Since DHT is required for the masculinization of the external genitalia in utero, these individuals are born with female or ambiguous genitalia. At puberty, the surge in testosterone drives virilization (pubic hair, clitoromegaly, voice deepening) but does not lead to breast development.

(D) d-4
This question matches pelvic organ prolapse conditions with their surgical repairs. A hysterectomy can be part of the surgical management for severe uterine prolapse (a-1). Sacrospinous fixation is a common procedure used to suspend the vaginal vault after a hysterectomy to correct vault prolapse (b-2). 154.	 What is the underlying reason for the absence of 
fructose in seminal fluid?
(A)	Congenital absence of seminal vesicle
(B)	 Ejaculatory duct obstruction
(C)	Both of the above
(D)	None of the above
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Both of the above
Fructose is the primary source of energy for sperm motility and is produced almost exclusively by the seminal vesicles. The seminal vesicles secrete their fructose-rich fluid into the ejaculatory ducts. Therefore, the absence of fructose in a semen analysis (azoospermia with low volume and acidic pH) points to a problem with either the production or the transport of seminal vesicle fluid. This can be caused by two main conditions. First, a congenital bilateral absence of the seminal vesicles (often associated with congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, a condition linked to the cystic fibrosis gene) would mean that fructose is not produced. Second, a bilateral ejaculatory duct obstruction would prevent the fluid from the seminal vesicles and the sperm from the vas deferens from entering the urethra and being ejaculated. In either case, the resulting ejaculate would be low in volume and fructose-negative.
155.	 Which of the following outcomes is associated 
with Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT)?
(A)	Decreased risk of breast cancer
(B)	 Decreased risk of endometrial cancer
(C)	Increased risk of vertebral fracture
(D)	Decreased risk of colon cancer
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(D) Decreased risk of colon cancer
The risks and benefits of menopausal hormone replacement therapy (HRT) have been extensively studied. It is well-established that combined estrogen-progestin therapy is associated with a small but significant increased risk of breast cancer (A is false). Unopposed estrogen therapy in a woman with a uterus dramatically increases the risk of endometrial cancer (B is false). One of the primary benefits and indications for HRT is the prevention of osteoporosis; it significantly decreases the risk of osteoporotic fractures, including vertebral fractures (C is false). An interesting and consistent finding from large randomized trials, such as the Women's Health Initiative, was an unexpected benefit: women randomized to HRT (both combined and estrogen-only) had a statistically significant decreased risk of developing colorectal (colon) cancer compared to those on placebo. The exact mechanism for this protective effect is not fully understood but is a well-documented association.

(A)	Agranulocytosis
(B)	 Renal bleed

(A) Agranulocytosis
Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic medication that is uniquely effective for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, but its use is restricted due to the risk of several rare yet potentially fatal adverse effects. The most well-known and feared of these is agranulocytosis, a severe form of neutropenia where the absolute neutrophil count drops to dangerously low levels. This catastrophic loss of neutrophils renders the patient profoundly immuno compromised and at high risk for life-threatening infections. Because of this risk, patients prescribed clozapine must be enrolled in a mandatory registry and undergo regular, rigorous monitoring of their white blood cell and absolute neutrophil counts, typically weekly for the first several months, then bi-weekly, and eventually monthly. While other serious side effects like seizures (D), myocarditis, and metabolic syndrome can occur, it is the risk of agranulocytosis that necessitates the most stringent monitoring protocol associated with this drug.
199.	 Which uncommon adverse effect in patients 
with schizophrenia taking clozapine requires 
routine blood monitoring?
(A)	Seizures
(B)	 Cerebral bleed
(C)	Agranulocytosis
(D)	Myocarditis
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Agranulocytosis
Clozapine is a highly effective second-generation antipsychotic reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia due to its unique side effect profile, which includes several rare but serious conditions requiring diligent monitoring. The most critical of these, and the one that mandates a strict protocol of regular blood monitoring, is the risk of agranulocytosis. This is a potentially fatal condition characterized by a severe reduction in the number of neutrophils, a type of white blood cell, which dramatically increases the patient's susceptibility to severe infections. To mitigate this risk, patients on clozapine must have their blood counts checked frequently throughout their treatment course. Other serious adverse effects include a dose-dependent risk of seizures (A), myocarditis (D), and significant metabolic effects like weight gain and diabetes. However, it is the specific, idiosyncratic risk of agranulocytosis that necessitates the mandatory, regular hematological monitoring that is synonymous with clozapine therapy.

(A) Hepatitis A.
Perinatal transmission refers to infection passed from mother to infant during pregnancy, at the time of delivery, or shortly after birth. The likelihood of vertical transmission varies among infectious agents.
1.	
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is one of the most common congenital infections. It is frequently transmitted transplacentally, especially during primary maternal infection, with a transmission rate of around 30–40%.
2.	
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) can also be transmitted perinatally, particularly during vaginal delivery if the mother has an active genital lesion. In primary maternal infection near term, the transmission risk may reach 30–50%.
3.	
Rubella is transmitted transplacentally when maternal infection occurs during pregnancy, especially in the first trimester, with a very high fetal transmission rate.
In contrast, Hepatitis A is primarily transmitted through the fecal–oral route. Vertical or perinatal transmission of Hepatitis A is extremely rare. Although maternal infection may occur during pregnancy, it seldom leads to congenital infection.
Therefore, among the given options, Hepatitis A has the lowest possibility of perinatal transmission.

167.	 What condition is the banana sign observed in?
(A)	Spina bifida	
(B)	 NCC
(C)	Omphalocele	
(D)	Anencephaly
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Spina bifida
The "banana sign" is a specific and important ultrasonographic marker that is highly associated with open spina bifida. This sign refers to the abnormal shape of the fetal cerebellum, which appears flattened and curved like a banana. The abnormal shape is a direct consequence of the Arnold-Chiari II malformation, a condition in which the cerebellum and brainstem are pulled downward and herniate through the foramen magnum. This herniation is caused by the tethering effect of the open spinal cord defect further down the back. The presence of the banana sign on a second-trimester prenatal ultrasound is a strong indicator of an underlying open neural tube defect and should prompt a detailed examination of the fetal spine to identify the spina bifida lesion. Neurocysticercosis (NCC) and omphalocele are unrelated conditions. Anencephaly involves absence of the cranial vault.
168.	 What is the identification of the images 
depicted?
(A)	Langer's lines
(B)	 Blaschko lines
(C)	Hinderer's line
(D)	Dermatomes
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Langer's lines
The image shows characteristic linear patterns over the face and body that correspond to the natural orientation of collagen fibers within the dermis. These are known as Langer’s lines, also called skin tension lines. They represent the direction of maximum skin tension and are clinically important in surgical practice.
Incisions made parallel to Langer’s lines tend to heal better and produce less noticeable scars because they follow the natural alignment of collagen fibers. In contrast, incisions made perpendicular to these lines are more likely to gape and result in wider scars.
Blaschko’s lines represent embryologic cell migration patterns and are typically invisible unless highlighted by certain skin disorders. Dermatomes represent areas of skin supplied by specific spinal nerves, and Hinderer’s lines are used in cosmetic facial surgery.
The patterns shown in the image are continuous, curved, and symmetrical over the body and face, consistent with the classic depiction of Langer’s lines. Therefore, the structure identified in the image is Langer’s lines.
169.	 What is the most probable diagnosis for a male 
patient who has a persistent, itchy rash on his 
side that hasn’t responded to over-the-counter 
treatments such as Lotrimin and hydrocortisone, 
and who also has similar lesions on one palm 
and one sole, with no involvement of the oral 
mucosa?
(A)	Urticaria
(B)	 Viral exanthem
(C)	Tinea corporis
(D)	Erythema multiforme
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(D) Erythema multiforme
This patient has a persistent itchy rash on the side that did not respond to antifungal (Lotrimin) or steroid (hydrocortisone) creams, along with lesions on one palm and one sole. The involvement of acral surfaces (palms and soles) strongly suggests erythema multiforme (EM).
Erythema multiforme is an acute, immune-mediated condition often triggered by infections (commonly herpes simplex virus) or medications. It typically presents with target or iris lesions, especially on the extremities, including palms and soles. Lesions are often symmetric and may spread to the trunk.
Importantly, absence of oral mucosal involvement suggests erythema multiforme minor, rather than Stevens-Johnson syndrome or EM major.
Other options are less likely:
1.	
Urticaria presents with transient wheals that resolve within 24 hours.
2.	
Viral exanthem usually presents with widespread symmetric rash and systemic symptoms.
3.	
Tinea corporis causes annular, scaly lesions but does not typically involve palms and soles simultaneously in this pattern.
Given acral involvement and lack of response to antifungal therapy, the most probable diagnosis is erythema multiforme.

A Wood's lamp exam uses ultraviolet A (UVA) light to detect fluorescence in certain skin conditions.
1.	
Erythrasma, a superficial bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum, characteristically fluoresces a striking coral-red color due to the production of porphyrins by the bacteria (1 -> b).
2.

4.

171.	 What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient 
receiving nivolumab (anti-PD1 therapy) who 
develops pruritus, eczema, and urticarial lesions, 
with biopsy showing a subepidermal blister 
and direct immunofluorescence demonstrating 
linear C3 and IgG deposition along the basement 
membrane?
(A)	Dermatitis herpetiformis
(B)	 Pemphigus vulgaris
(C)	Pemphigus foliaceous
(D)	Bullous pemphigoid
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(D) Bullous pemphigoid
Immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as the anti-PD-1 antibody nivolumab, can cause a variety of immune-related adverse events, including autoimmune skin diseases. The clinical and laboratory findings in this patient are classic for bullous pemphigoid. This is an autoimmune blistering disease characterized by autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins (BP180 and BP230) in the basement membrane zone. Histopathology reveals a subepidermal blister with an eosinophilic infiltrate. The pathognomonic finding is on direct immunofluorescence (DIF), which shows linear deposition of IgG and/or C3 along the dermal-epidermal junction. In contrast, pemphigus vulgaris (B) is characterized by intraepidermal, suprabasal blisters and shows a "chicken-wire" pattern of intercellular IgG deposition on DIF. Dermatitis herpetiformis (A) shows granular IgA deposition in the dermal papillae.
172.	 Which of the following is not associated with 
non-scarring alopecia?
(A)	Alopecia areata
(B)	 Androgenetic alopecia
(C)	Frontal fibrosing alopecia
(D)	Telogen effluvium
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Frontal fibrosing alopecia
Alopecias are broadly classified into non-scarring and scarring (cicatricial) types. In non-scarring alopecias, the hair follicle is preserved, and hair regrowth is possible. This category includes alopecia areata (an autoimmune condition), androgenetic alopecia (male and female pattern baldness), and telogen effluvium (diffuse shedding after a stressor). In contrast, scarring alopecias involve inflammation and fibrosis that destroy the hair follicle, leading to permanent hair loss. Frontal fibrosing alopecia is a classic example of a primary cicatricial alopecia. It is considered a clinical variant of lichen planopilaris and is characterized by a progressive, band-like recession of the frontal and temporal hairline, with associated loss of eyebrows, and evidence of perifollicular inflammation and fibrosis on histology.

(A) PTH adenoma
The abdominal X-ray shows multiple, dense, branching calcifications within the collecting systems of both kidneys. This appearance is known as nephrocalcinosis, and the branching pattern is suggestive of staghorn calculi. The patient's symptoms of dysuria and back pain are consistent with kidney stones (nephrolithiasis). The most common cause of non-malignancy-related hypercalcemia is primary hyperparathyroidism, which is most often (in ~85% of cases) caused by a benign parathyroid adenoma (PTH adenoma). The excess parathyroid hormone secreted by the adenoma leads to increased bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption, causing the high calcium levels that precipitate in the kidneys. Wilms' tumor and renal cell carcinoma are renal malignancies.
186.	 In a 35-year-old patient with six weeks of 
dysentery and right upper abdominal pain, an 
ultrasound shows a hypoechoic, hyperdense 
liver lesion. What condition does this finding 
most likely represent?
(A)	Amoebic liver abscess
(B)	 Pyogenic liver abscess
(C)	Hydatid cyst
(D)	Hemangioma
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Amoebic liver abscess
The patient's clinical history is the key to this diagnosis. A history of dysentery (bloody diarrhea) followed by the development of right upper quadrant pain, fever, and a liver lesion strongly suggests an extraintestinal complication of an amoebic infection. The causative organism is Entamoeba histolytica. After invading the colonic mucosa, the amoebic trophozoites can enter the portal circulation and travel to the liver, where they cause liquefactive necrosis of the hepatocytes, leading to the formation of an amoebic liver abscess. The ultrasound appearance of a typical amoebic abscess is a round or oval, hypoechoic lesion located in the right lobe of the liver, often near the capsule, without a significant surrounding rim. The contents are often described as resembling "anchovy paste." A pyogenic abscess (B) is also possible but is less likely to be preceded by dysentery.
187.	 A 52-year-old woman comes for her routine

She is worried about these findings. What BI-

(A)	BI-RADS 1; findings are benign
(B)	 BI-RADS 2; findings are benign
(C)	BI-RADS 2; findings are highly suggestive of 
malignancy
(D)	BI-RADS 3; another mammogram is needed 
to comment on malignancy potential
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) BI-RADS 2; findings are benign
The Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) is a standardized system for reporting mammogram findings. BI-RADS 1 means the mammogram is completely negative. BI-RADS 2 is used for cases where there are definite benign findings. This category includes things like calcified fibroadenomas, secretory calcifications, or, as in this case, scattered punctate calcifications that are morphologically benign and have shown stability over time (unchanged from a prior mammogram). The key message for the patient is that the findings are benign and that she should continue with routine annual screening. BI-RADS 3 indicates a probably benign finding that requires short-interval follow-up. BI-RADS 4 and 5 indicate suspicion of a malignancy. Since the calcifications are stable and benign-appearing, BI-RADS 2 is the appropriate assessment.

(C) Bipartite patella- Do radiograph of the other knee
The radiograph shows what appears to be a bone fragment at the superolateral aspect of the patella. While this could be mistaken for a fracture, several features suggest it is a bipartite patella. A bipartite patella is a common and normal anatomical variant where one of the ossification centers of the patella fails to fuse with the main body of the bone during development. The key differentiating features from an acute fracture are that the edges of the fragments are smooth and well-corticated, not sharp and irregular. It is most commonly located in the superolateral quadrant. Since a bipartite patella is bilateral in about 40-50% of cases, the most appropriate next step in management to confirm the diagnosis and differentiate it from a fracture is to obtain a radiograph of the contralateral (other) knee. If the same finding is present bilaterally, it confirms the diagnosis of a congenital variant.

181.	 A 40-year-old man comes to the emergency 
department with pain and swelling in his 
right shoulder after a fall. An X-ray indicates 
a possible tear of a shoulder ligament. Which 
ligament is most likely injured?
(A)	Coracoclavicular ligament
(B)	 Acromioclavicular ligament
(C)	Both A & B
(D)	Glenohumeral ligament
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Both A & B
The radiograph shows a significant injury to the acromioclavicular (AC) joint, often referred to as a "separated shoulder." The image demonstrates a marked superior displacement of the distal end of the clavicle relative to the acromion process of the scapula. This degree of separation (classified as a Type III AC joint injury or higher) indicates a complete tear of not only the acromioclavicular (AC) ligament, which provides horizontal stability to the joint, but also the coracoclavicular (CC) ligaments (the conoid and trapezoid ligaments), which are the primary providers of vertical stability. 183.	 What is the association between a filling defect 
and the condition observed in the MRCP image?

(C)	Cholecystitis
(D)	Stones
AAns

The image provided is from a Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP), a non-invasive imaging technique that visualizes the biliary and pancreatic ducts. The image clearly shows the common bile duct (CBD), which appears dilated. Within the distal portion of this dilated CBD, there is a distinct, dark, ovoid signal void, which represents a filling defect. 184.	 In the USG image, what is the observed 
anatomical variation of the gallbladder?
(A)	Phrygian sign
(B)	 Murphy sign
(C)	Claw sign
(D)	Omega sign
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Phrygian sign
The ultrasound image of the gallbladder shows a common and benign congenital anatomical variation. The fundus of the gallbladder is seen folded over the body of the gallbladder, creating a septum or indentation. This specific folded appearance is known as a Phrygian cap. The name is derived from its resemblance to the soft, conical hats with the top bent over that were worn by the ancient inhabitants of Phrygia in Anatolia. A Phrygian cap is a normal variant found in a small percentage of the population and has no clinical significance; it does not predispose to gallstones or other gallbladder diseases. The Murphy sign (B) is a clinical sign of cholecystitis. The claw sign (C) is a radiological sign used to determine the origin of a mass.

(B) Pityriasis Rosea
The image shows multiple, oval, erythematous plaques with a fine scale, arranged with their long axes along the lines of skin cleavage, creating a "Christmas tree" pattern on the back. This eruption is characteristic of pityriasis rosea. Pityriasis rosea is a common, acute, self-limiting skin condition. 177.	 What is the most appropriate immediate response 
when a patient’s blood pressure suddenly falls to 
40 mmHg during squint surgery?
(A)	Give atropine
(B)	 Increase level of anesthesia
(C)	Ask the surgeon to stop the surgery
(D)	Give adrenaline
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Ask the surgeon to stop the surgery
During squint (strabismus) surgery, traction on the extraocular muscles—especially the medial rectus—can trigger the oculocardiac reflex (OCR). This is a trigemino-vagal reflex in which stimulation of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve leads to increased vagal tone via the vagus nerve. The result can be bradycardia, hypotension, arrhythmias, or even asystole.
If the patient’s blood pressure suddenly falls to 40 mmHg intraoperatively, the most immediate and crucial step is to stop the surgical stimulus. Removing the traction on the extraocular muscle often reverses the reflex rapidly.
After stopping the stimulus:
1.	
Ensure adequate oxygenation.
2.	
Deepen anesthesia if required.
3.	
Administer atropine if bradycardia persists.
Adrenaline is not the first-line response unless there is cardiac arrest or severe unresponsive hypotension.
Therefore, the most appropriate immediate action when sudden hypotension occurs during squint surgery is to ask the surgeon to stop the surgery.
178.	 Murphy's eye is seen in -
(A)	Macintosh laryngoscope
(B)	 Endotracheal tube
(C)	LMA
(D)	Flexible laryngoscope
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Endotracheal tube
The Murphy's eye is a specific design feature found on most modern endotracheal tubes (ETTs). It is a small, oval-shaped hole located on the side of the ETT, opposite the beveled tip. The primary purpose of the Murphy's eye is to serve as a safety feature. If the main distal opening of the ETT becomes occluded, for example, by pressing against the tracheal wall or by a mucus plug, the Murphy's eye provides an alternative, patent opening through which gas can still flow, thereby preventing a complete airway obstruction and allowing for continued ventilation of the patient. This feature is unique to endotracheal tubes and is not found on other airway devices like a laryngeal mask airway (LMA) or on instruments like laryngoscopes.
179.	 A patient under general anesthesia suddenly 
develops tachycardia, sweating, high blood 
pressure, and rapid breathing. What is the most 
appropriate immediate action to take in this 
situation?
(A)	IV beta-blocker
(B)	 Abandon the surgery
(C)	Deepen the plane of Anaesthesia
(D)	Nothing is required
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Deepen the plane of Anaesthesia
The sudden onset of tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, and tachypnea in a patient under general anesthesia is a classic presentation of a sympathetic nervous system response to a painful surgical stimulus. This indicates that the current level of anesthesia is insufficient to block the patient's autonomic reflexes to the surgical procedure. The patient is "light," meaning the plane of anesthesia is too shallow. The best and most immediate step for the anesthesiologist to take is to deepen the plane of anesthesia. This can be achieved by increasing the concentration of the volatile anesthetic agent being administered or by giving a bolus of an intravenous anesthetic agent like propofol or an opioid like fentanyl. This will rapidly suppress the sympathetic response, control the hemodynamic changes, and ensure the patient remains adequately anesthetized for the remainder of the procedure.

190.	 Active pulmonary TB can be diagnosed on CT

AAns

While several CT findings can be seen in pulmonary tuberculosis, the "tree-in-bud" appearance is highly suggestive of active, endobronchial spread of the infection. 191.	 What could be the potential reason behind 
irreversible dementia?
(A)	NPH
(B)	 Hypothyroid
(C)	Lewy body
(D)	Vitamin B12 deficiency
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Lewy body
Dementia is a syndrome of cognitive decline that can be caused by a wide range of conditions. It is crucial to identify potentially reversible causes of dementia, as prompt treatment can restore cognitive function. These reversible causes include Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH), severe hypothyroidism, and vitamin B12 deficiency. In these conditions, treating the underlying cause (e.g., with a shunt, thyroid hormone replacement, or B12 injections) can lead to significant cognitive improvement. In contrast, neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by the progressive death of neurons and are currently considered irreversible. Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is the second most common neurodegenerative dementia after Alzheimer's disease. It is caused by the abnormal accumulation of Lewy body protein aggregates in the brain, leading to progressive and irreversible cognitive decline, parkinsonism, and visual hallucinations.
192.	 Why are routine blood tests required for a 
35-year-old man with schizophrenia who is 
being treated with clozapine?
(A)	Cerebral bleed
(B)	 Myocarditis
(C)	Agranulocytosis
(D)	Seizures
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Agranulocytosis
Clozapine is a highly effective atypical antipsychotic medication, often used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. However, its use is carefully regulated due to the risk of several serious adverse effects. The most critical and well-known of these is agranulocytosis, a rare but potentially fatal condition characterized by a severe decrease in the number of white blood cells, specifically neutrophils. This profound neutropenia leaves the patient extremely vulnerable to life-threatening infections. Because of this risk, any patient prescribed clozapine must be enrolled in a mandatory monitoring program that requires regular blood tests (typically a complete blood count with differential) to check their neutrophil count. The frequency of this monitoring is highest at the beginning of treatment and continues for the entire duration of therapy. While myocarditis and seizures are also serious risks, it is the danger of agranulocytosis that necessitates the stringent blood monitoring protocol.
193.	 A 35-year-old man with a mood disorder, who 
was recently started on a new psychiatric 
medication, arrives at the surgical emergency 
department with a painful erection lasting 
7 hours. Which medication is most likely 
responsible for this condition?
(A)	Trazodone
(B)	 Tianeptine
(C)	Venlafaxine
(D)	Mirtazapine
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Trazodone
The patient is presenting with priapism, a prolonged and painful erection that is a urological emergency. Priapism is a well-known, albeit rare, side effect of several psychotropic medications, most notably the antidepressant trazodone. Trazodone has a complex pharmacology, but its association with priapism is thought to be primarily due to its potent alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blocking activity. This alpha-blockade can lead to an imbalance of blood flow in the corpus cavernosum, with increased inflow and decreased outflow, resulting in a persistent erection. While other antidepressants and antipsychotics have been occasionally linked to priapism, the association is strongest and most classically described with trazodone. Therefore, in a patient with a mood disorder who develops priapism after starting a new medication, trazodone should be the first drug suspected.
194.	 In which of the following conditions is La belle

(A)	Conversion disorder
(B)	 Cotard syndrome
(C)	Schizophrenia
(D)	Depression
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Conversion disorder
La belle indifférence, a French term meaning "beautiful indifference," is a classic psychiatric sign that describes a paradoxical lack of concern or an inappropriate nonchalance shown by a patient towards what appears to be a severe and dramatic medical symptom. For example, a patient might describe being suddenly paralyzed or blind with a calm and detached demeanor that is incongruent with the seriousness of the disability. This sign was originally described by Freud and is most classically associated with conversion disorder (also known as functional neurological symptom disorder). In this condition, psychological distress is thought to be "converted" into a neurological symptom. While it is a classic sign, it is important to note that it is not present in all patients with conversion disorder and is not specific to the condition.

196.	 A patient tells their psychiatrist, “My brain is 
gone. There’s no reason to eat. I’m already dead.” 
How would you classify the type of delusion this 
patient is experiencing?
(A)	Delusion of misidentification
(B)	 Nihilistic delusion
(C)	Bizarre delusion
(D)	Hypochondriacal delusion
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) Nihilistic delusion
The patient's statements are a classic example of nihilistic delusions, which are a core feature of Cotard's syndrome (also known as the delusion of negation). A nihilistic delusion is a false and fixed belief centered on themes of non-existence, death, or the futility of everything. The patient may believe that they are already dead, that parts of their body (like their brain) are missing or have ceased to function, or that the world itself has ended. The statements "my brain is gone" and "I am already deceased" directly reflect this profound sense of negation and non-existence. A hypochondriacal delusion (D) is a belief of having a serious illness, but not of being dead or non-existent.

158.	 Which of the following is not a cause of non-
immune hydrops?
(A)	Parvovirus
(B)	 ABO incompatibility
(C)	Cardiovascular causes
(D)	Thalassemia
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(B) ABO incompatibility
Hydrops fetalis is the excessive accumulation of fluid in the fetal extravascular compartments. It is broadly divided into immune and non-immune causes. Immune hydrops is caused by alloimmune hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, most classically due to Rh(D) incompatibility, although other red cell antibodies can be responsible. ABO incompatibility is a cause of hemolytic disease, but it very rarely, if ever, leads to the severe anemia required to cause hydrops fetalis. In contrast, non-immune hydrops fetalis (NIHF) accounts for about 90% of cases and has a wide range of causes. The most common etiologies include cardiovascular abnormalities (e.g., structural heart defects, arrhythmias), chromosomal anomalies, and severe fetal anemia from non-immune causes. These causes of anemia include infections like Parvovirus B19 (A), which causes aplastic crisis, and alpha-thalassemia major (D), which leads to a complete inability to produce functional hemoglobin.
159.	 Which of the following statements is incorrect?
(A)	Zygote is Bipotential at 8 weeks
(B)	 DHT is necessary for the development of 
external genitals
(C)	MIS inhibits the formation of Mullerian 
duct
(D)	WD forms male internal genitalia
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Zygote is Bipotential at 8 weeks
Sexual differentiation is a sequential process. Initially, the embryo, including the gonads, is bipotential, meaning it has the potential to develop into either a male or a female. This bipotential state exists up to around the 6th or 7th week of gestation. The presence of the SRY gene on the Y chromosome then directs the bipotential gonad to differentiate into a testis. The developing testis produces two key hormones: testosterone and Müllerian-inhibiting substance (MIS). MIS, also known as anti-Müllerian hormone, causes the regression of the Müllerian ducts (the precursors of the female internal genitalia). Testosterone supports the development of the Wolffian ducts (WD) into the male internal genitalia (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles). Testosterone is also converted to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which is essential for the development of the male external genitalia. The zygote itself is genetically determined at fertilization, and by 8 weeks, differentiation is already underway.
160.	 What is the outcome of the absence or mutation 
of the SRY gene?
(A)	Agenesis of testis
(B)	 Undescended testis
(C)	Hydrocele testis
(D)	None of the above
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(A) Agenesis of testis
The SRY (Sex-determining Region Y) gene, located on the Y chromosome, is the master switch that initiates male development. In a 46,XY embryo, the SRY gene product acts as a transcription factor that directs the bipotential, undifferentiated gonads to develop into testes. If the SRY gene is absent (e.g., due to a deletion from the Y chromosome) or has a loss-of-function mutation, the signal for testicular development is never initiated. In the absence of this SRY signal, the undifferentiated gonads will follow their default developmental pathway and differentiate into ovaries, and the embryo will develop along female lines despite having a 46,XY karyotype. This condition is known as 46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis, or Swyer syndrome. Therefore, the direct outcome of an absent or non-functional SRY gene is the failure of the testes to form, which can be described as agenesis of the testis.
161.	 Which medication should be given to reverse 
respiratory distress in a woman who received 
morphine sulfate for labor pain?
(A)	Epinephrine	
(B)	 Atropine
(C)	Pralidoxime	
(D)	Naloxone
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(D) Naloxone
Morphine is a potent opioid analgesic commonly used for pain management. The most serious and life-threatening adverse effect of opioid administration is respiratory depression, which can progress to apnea and respiratory arrest. The patient's development of respiratory distress after receiving morphine is a clear sign of opioid-induced toxicity. The specific and life-saving antidote for opioid overdose is naloxone. Naloxone is a pure, competitive opioid receptor antagonist. It has a high affinity for mu-opioid receptors and works by rapidly displacing the opioid agonist (morphine, in this case) from these receptors in the central nervous system. This action promptly reverses the effects of the opioid, most critically the respiratory depression. Epinephrine (A) is used for anaphylaxis, atropine (B) for bradycardia or cholinergic poisoning, and pralidoxime (C) for organophosphate poisoning.

The clinical triad of dyspareunia (painful intercourse), dysmenorrhea (painful periods), and adnexal tenderness is highly suggestive of underlying pelvic pathology, particularly conditions like endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), or ovarian cysts. 163.	 What condition is associated with the sign seen

The ultrasound image displays the fetal cerebellum and posterior fossa, showing the characteristic "banana sign." This sign describes the abnormal, crescent or banana-like shape of the cerebellum, which is effaced and pulled inferiorly. 164.	 Which of the following is not a potential

Massive blood transfusion (usually defined as replacement of one blood volume within 24 hours or ≥10 units of packed RBCs) can lead to several metabolic and physiological complications.
Common complications include:
1.	
Hypothermia (A) → Stored blood is refrigerated, and rapid transfusion can lower body temperature.

165.	 Which one of the following is not transmitted 
during the perinatal period?
(A)	CMV	
(B)	 Rubella
(C)	Meningitis	
(D)	Hepatitis B
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
(C) Meningitis
Perinatal transmission refers to infections that are passed from mother to child during pregnancy (transplacental), during labor and delivery, or shortly after birth. Several infectious agents are well known to be transmitted in this period.
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is one of the most common congenital infections. It is transmitted transplacentally and can also be acquired during delivery or through breast milk. Rubella virus is transmitted transplacentally when a mother acquires primary infection during pregnancy, especially in the first trimester, leading to congenital rubella syndrome. Hepatitis B virus is commonly transmitted during childbirth from an infected mother to her newborn, particularly if the mother is HBsAg positive.
In contrast, meningitis is not a specific infectious agent but a clinical condition characterized by inflammation of the meninges. While certain organisms causing neonatal meningitis (such as Group B Streptococcus) may be transmitted during birth, meningitis itself is not transmitted as a disease entity.
Therefore, among the options given, meningitis is not transmitted during the perinatal period.

(A) Eight nerve cochlear nuclei superior olivary 
nucleus lateral lemniscus inferior colliculus → 
medial geniculate body → auditory cortex
The central auditory pathway is a complex, 
polysynaptic 
route 
that 
transmits 
sound 
information from the inner ear to the cerebral 
cortex for conscious perception. The pathway 
begins with the spiral ganglion neurons, 
whose axons form the cochlear division of the 
vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII). 
These fibers make their first synapse in the 
cochlear nuclei located in the brainstem. From 
here, auditory information ascends bilaterally, 
with a major synapse in the superior olivary 
nucleus, which is crucial for sound localization. 
The pathway continues upward through a major 
ascending tract known as the lateral lemniscus. 
The next significant relay station is the inferior 
colliculus in the midbrain, another key auditory 
processing center. Subsequently, fibers project 
to the medial geniculate body of the thalamus, 
the final subcortical relay nucleus. Finally, 
thalamocortical radiations carry the processed 
auditory information to the primary auditory 
cortex located in the temporal lobe.
Which nerve provides innervation to the gluteus maximus muscle?
(A)	
Femoral nerve 
(B)	
Sciatic nerve 
(C)	
Inferior Gluteal Nerve 
(D)	
Superior gluteal nerve

2.	
(C) Inferior Gluteal Nerve
The gluteus maximus is the largest and most 
superficial of the three gluteal muscles, and 
it serves as the primary extensor of the hip 
joint. Its motor innervation is provided solely 
by the inferior gluteal nerve. This nerve arises 
from the posterior divisions of the ventral rami 
of the L5, S1, and S2 spinal nerves within the 
lumbosacral plexus. It exits the pelvis through 
the greater sciatic foramen, inferior to the 
piriformis muscle, and travels a short course 
to innervate the overlying gluteus maximus 
muscle. It's important to differentiate this from 
the innervation of the other gluteal muscles; 
the gluteus medius and minimus, which are 
responsible for hip abduction and stabilization, 
are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve. 
The femoral nerve  supplies the anterior thigh 
muscles, while the sciatic nerve  innervates the 
posterior thigh and the leg and foot, passing 
deep to the gluteus maximus without supplying 
it.

The muscle highlighted in the image is the 
trapezius, a large, diamond-shaped superficial 
muscle of the back and neck. The trapezius has 
three distinct sets of fibers—upper, middle, and 
lower—each with a different primary action 
on the scapula. While the upper fibers elevate 
the scapula and the lower fibers depress it, the 
horizontally oriented middle fibers are primarily 
responsible for scapular retraction. This action, 
also known as scapular adduction, involves 
pulling the scapulae medially, towards the 
vertebral column, as in the motion of "squaring 
the shoulders." This function is essential for 
stabilizing the scapula during movements of 
the arm and for maintaining proper posture. 
The other actions listed, such as adduction, 
extension, and medial rotation of the shoulder, 
are movements of the glenohumeral joint itself 
and are primarily executed by muscles that 
insert on the humerus, like the latissimus dorsi 
and pectoralis major, not the trapezius.

Arrange the neural columns in medial-to-lateral order
1.	
Special somatic afferent
2.

3.	
General somatic efferent
4.	
General somatic afferent
(A)	
GSE, SVE, GSA, SSA 
(B)	
SVE, GSA, SSA, GSE 
(C)	
GSA, SSA, GSE, SVE 
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
5.	
(A) GSE, SVE, GSA, SSA
During the development of the brainstem, 
the cranial nerve nuclei are organized into 
longitudinal functional columns arranged in a 
specific medial-to-lateral sequence. The sulcus 
limitans divides the plate into a medial motor 
(basal) plate and a lateral sensory (alar) plate. 
The motor columns are thus medial to the 
sensory columns. Within the motor plate, the 
most medial column is the General Somatic 
Efferent (GSE), innervating skeletal muscles 
derived from somites. Lateral to it is the Special 
Visceral Efferent (SVE) column, supplying 
muscles from the pharyngeal arches. In the 
sensory plate, the General Somatic Afferent 
(GSA) column  is medial to the Special Somatic 
Afferent (SSA) column, which is the most 
lateral of all the columns. Therefore, the correct 
medial-to-lateral arrangement of the specified 
columns is GSE, SVE, GSA, and SSA.
What is the main factor responsible for causing acceleration in the fetal heart rate?
(A)	
Carotid baroreceptor 
(B)	
Aortic baroreceptor 
(C)	
Autonomic function of brainstem 
(D)	
Chemoreceptors 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
6.	
(C) Autonomic function of brainstem
Fetal heart rate (FHR) accelerations are transient 
increases in the heart rate of at least 15 beats per 
minute above the baseline, lasting for at least 15 
seconds. These accelerations are a key indicator 
of fetal well-being on cardiotocography. They 
are primarily mediated by the fetal autonomic 
nervous system, specifically through sympathetic 
nervous system stimulation in response to 
fetal movement. When the fetus moves, the 
sympathetic nervous system is activated, 
leading to the release of catecholamines that 
increase the heart rate. The presence of these 
accelerations indicates that the fetus has an 
intact and responsive central nervous system, 
particularly the autonomic control centers 
within the brainstem. Baroreceptors (A, B) 
are primarily involved in responding to blood 
pressure changes, typically causing a decrease in 
heart rate when pressure rises. Chemoreceptors 
(D) respond to changes in oxygen and carbon 
dioxide levels.
All vessels demonstrate the Windkessel effect except:
(A)	
Abdominal aorta 
(B)	
Aorta 
(C)	
Renal artery 
(D)	
Radial artery 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
7.	
(D) Radial artery
The Windkessel effect describes the phenomenon 
where the pulsatile flow of blood ejected from 
the heart is converted into a more continuous, 
smoother flow in the distal vasculature. This is 
achieved by the elastic recoil of large arteries. 
During systole, the walls of large elastic arteries 
like the aorta  and its major branches (e.g., 
abdominal aorta, subclavian artery) stretch 
to accommodate the stroke volume, storing 
potential energy. During diastole, these elastic 
walls recoil, pushing the stored blood forward 
and maintaining diastolic pressure and flow. 
As arteries travel further from the heart, their 
composition 
changes 
from 
predominantly 
elastic to more muscular. The radial artery, a 
muscular artery in the forearm, has significantly 
less elastin in its walls compared to the 
aorta. Therefore, it exhibits a much-reduced 
Windkessel effect and demonstrates a more 
pulsatile pressure waveform. The renal artery 
is still a large branch off the aorta and retains 
significant elastic properties.
Arrange the following sarcomere components from the most peripheral region to the most central region.
1.	
Z line
2.	
M line
3.	
A band
4.	
H zone
(A)	
1,3,4,2 
(B)	
4,2,3,1 
(C)	
2,3,4,1 
(D)	
3,1,4,2 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
8.	
(A) 1,3,4,2
The sarcomere is the fundamental contractile 
unit of striated muscle, extending between 
two adjacent Z lines. When arranging its 
components from the outermost boundary 
towards the absolute center, the correct 
sequence is based on their defined anatomical 
positions. The outermost boundary of a single 
sarcomere is the Z line (1), which anchors the 
thin (actin) filaments. Moving inward from the 
Z line, one encounters the A band. The A band 
(3) represents the entire length of the thick 
(myosin) filaments. Within the central region of 
the A band, there is a lighter area where the thin 
filaments do not overlap the thick filaments; 
this is known as the H zone (4). Finally, at the 
very center of the H zone, and thus the absolute 
center of the sarcomere, is the M line (2), which 
serves to anchor the thick filaments. Therefore, 
the correct sequence from the outer boundary 
to the innermost point is Z line → A band → H 
zone → M line.
What accounts for the initial rise in blood pressure at the radial artery during the Valsalva maneuver?
(A)	
Increase in Left ventricular volume

(B)	
Increase in Left ventricular pressure 
(C)	
Increase in aortic pressure 
(D)	
Decrease in aortic pressure 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
9.	
(C) Increase in aortic pressure
The Valsalva maneuver involves a forced 
expiration against a closed glottis, which causes a 
sequence of hemodynamic changes divided into 
four phases. The question asks about Phase I, 
the initial moment of the maneuver. During this 
phase, the forceful straining action significantly 
increases intrathoracic pressure. This increased 
pressure mechanically compresses the aorta 
and other large vessels within the chest. This 
direct compression effectively squeezes the 
blood that is already present within the aorta, 
causing a transient, purely mechanical increase 
in the mean aortic pressure. This pressure spike 
is transmitted down the arterial tree and is 
recorded as the initial increase in blood pressure 
at the radial artery. This phase is very brief and 
is immediately followed by Phase II, where the 
high intrathoracic pressure impedes venous 
return, leading to a fall in cardiac output and 
blood pressure. The other options are incorrect 
for this initial phase.
Assertion (A) : The resting membrane potential (RMP) is affected by negatively charged proteins and phosphate ions within the cell
Reason (R) : The Nernst equation determines an ion’s diffusion potential according to the concentration gradient across the cell membrane. 
(A)	
Both the assertion and reason are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation for the assertion. 
(B)	
Both the assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation for the assertion. 
(C)	
The assertion is true, but the reason is false. 
(D)	
The assertion is false, but the reason is true. 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
10.	 (B) Both the assertion and reason are true, and 
the reason is the correct explanation for the 
assertion. 
The resting membrane potential (RMP) is 
primarily determined by the distribution of ions 
across the cell membrane, especially potassium 
(K⁺). Inside the cell, there are large negatively 
charged proteins and organic phosphate ions 
that are impermeable to the cell membrane. 
These fixed intracellular anions contribute to 
the overall negative charge within the cell and 
influence the distribution of diffusible ions such 
as K⁺ and Na⁺. Because K⁺ tends to diffuse out 
of the cell down its concentration gradient, the 
impermeable negative proteins help retain some 
positive ions inside, thereby contributing to the 
negative resting membrane potential.
The 
Nernst 
equation 
calculates 
the 
equilibrium (diffusion) potential for a specific 
ion based on its concentration gradient across 
the membrane. Since RMP largely depends on 
the equilibrium potential of potassium, and 
the intracellular negatively charged proteins 
influence the potassium concentration gradient, 
the Nernst equation helps explain how these 
gradients generate membrane potential.
Thus, both statements are correct, and the 
reason appropriately explains the assertion.
Which factors are responsible for the latent period observed in a single muscle twitch?
1.	
Excitation-contraction coupling
2.	
Time interval from the point of stimulus to the onset of contraction
3.	
Neuromuscular junction (NMJ) transmission
4.	
Transfer of calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum via SERCA
(A)	
1,2,3 
(B)	
1, 2, 3, 4 
(C)	
1,3,4 
(D)	
2,3,4 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
11.	 (A) 1,2,3
The latent period of a muscle twitch is defined 
as the time interval from the application of a 
stimulus to the beginning of the actual muscle 
contraction. It is a brief delay during which 
a series of critical electrochemical events 
must occur before tension can be generated. 
These events include the transmission of the 
action potential across the neuromuscular 
junction (NMJ), which involves the release 
of acetylcholine, binding to receptors, and 
depolarization of the sarcolemma. Following 
this, the process of excitation-contraction 
coupling  takes place. This involves the 
propagation of the muscle action potential along 
the T-tubules, triggering the release of calcium 
from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and the 
binding of calcium to troponin to initiate cross-
bridge cycling. The reuptake of calcium into the 
sarcoplasmic reticulum by the SERCA pump (4) 
is the process that causes muscle relaxation and 
occurs after the contraction phase, not during 
the latent period.
What is the correct sequence of band arrangement within a sarcomere?
(A)	
I-Z-M-A-H
(B)	
Z-H-M-A-I
(C)	
Z-I-A-H-M 
(D)	
Z-H-I-A-M
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
12.	 (C) Z-I-A-H-M
This question asks for the correct spatial 
arrangement of the bands and lines within a 
sarcomere, the fundamental contractile unit 
of a muscle fiber. A sarcomere is defined as 
the segment between two successive Z lines. 
Moving from one Z line towards the center of 
the sarcomere, the first region encountered is 
the I band, which is a light band containing only 
thin (actin) filaments. The Z line itself bisects 
the I band. Next is the A band, a dark band 
that represents the entire length of the thick 
(myosin) filaments. Within the center of the A 
band, there is a paler region where the thin and 
thick filaments do not overlap; this is the H zone. 
Finally, at the very center of the H zone and 
the sarcomere is the M line, which anchors the 
thick filaments. Therefore, the correct sequence 
of structures from the edge to the center is Z-I-
A-H-M.
Which option results in the greatest thermogenic effect?

(D)	
All have same effect

13.	 (B) Protein

INICET Examination Paper
The thermic effect of food (TEF), also known as 
specific dynamic action, refers to the increase in 
metabolic rate (energy expenditure) that occurs 
after ingesting food. This energy is required for 
the digestion, absorption, processing, and storage 
of the nutrients. The magnitude of the TEF varies 
significantly depending on the macronutrient 
composition of the meal. Protein has the highest 
thermic effect of all macronutrients. The body 
expends approximately 20-30% of the energy 
content of the ingested protein to process it. 
This is substantially higher than the TEF for 
carbohydrates , which is around 5-10%, and for 
fats, which have the lowest TEF at only 0-3%. 
This high energy cost for protein metabolism 
is due to the complex processes of deamination 
and the synthesis of urea, among other metabolic 
pathways involved in handling amino acids.
What is the cause of Pompe disease?
(A)	
Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase 
(B)	
B-Hexosaminidase-A 
(C)	
B-Galactocerebrosidase 
(D)	
B-Glucocerebrosidase 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
14.	 (A) Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase
Pompe disease, also known as Glycogen Storage 
Disease Type II, is an autosomal recessive 
lysosomal storage disorder. It is caused by a 
deficiency of the enzyme lysosomal acid alpha-
glucosidase, also known as acid maltase. In a 
healthy individual, this enzyme is responsible 
for breaking down glycogen into glucose within 
the lysosomes. When the enzyme is deficient, 
glycogen accumulates progressively within the 
lysosomes of various tissues, leading to cellular 
damage and organ dysfunction. The most 
severely affected tissues are cardiac and skeletal 
muscle, resulting in profound muscle weakness 
(hypotonia), respiratory insufficiency, and, in 
the classic infantile form, a massive hypertrophic 
cardiomyopathy that typically leads to death 
within the first year of life. The other enzymes 
listed are deficient in different lysosomal storage 
diseases : B-Hexosaminidase-A in Tay-Sachs 
disease , B-Galactocerebrosidase in Krabbe 
disease , and B-Glucocerebrosidase in Gaucher 
disease.
Which vitamin deficiency is linked to xanthurenic aciduria?
(A)	
Vitamin B6 
(B)	
Vitamin B12 
(C)	
Vitamin B5 
(D)	
Vitamin B7 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
15.	 (A) Vitamin B6
Xanthurenic aciduria refers to the excessive 
excretion of xanthurenic acid in the urine. 
This is a characteristic biochemical finding in 
vitamin B6 deficiency. Vitamin B6, in its active 
form pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), is an essential 
cofactor for numerous enzymes involved in 
amino acid metabolism. One such enzyme is 
kynureninase, which is part of the metabolic 
pathway that converts tryptophan to niacin. 
When there is a deficiency of vitamin B6, the 
activity of kynureninase is impaired. This 
creates a metabolic block, causing the upstream 
intermediate, 
3-hydroxykynurenine, 
to 
be 
shunted into an alternative pathway where it is 
converted to xanthurenic acid. This abnormal 
metabolite then accumulates and is excreted 
in the urine. Therefore, measuring urinary 
xanthurenic acid after a tryptophan load is a 
functional test used to assess vitamin B6 status.
What is the cause of Barth syndrome?

(B)

(C)

(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
16.	 (A) Cardiolipin
Barth syndrome is a rare, X-linked genetic 
disorder 
characterized 
by 
a 
triad 
of 
cardiomyopathy (often dilated), neutropenia, 
and skeletal myopathy with growth retardation. 
The underlying cause is a mutation in the TAZ 
gene, which encodes for an enzyme called 
tafazzin. Tafazzin is essential for the remodeling 
of cardiolipin, a unique phospholipid found 
almost exclusively in the inner mitochondrial 
membrane. This remodeling process is critical 
for maintaining the proper structure and 
function of cardiolipin. Defective tafazzin 
leads to abnormal cardiolipin composition, 
which in turn impairs the structure of the inner 
mitochondrial membrane and the function 
of the electron transport chain, leading to 
deficient energy production. This mitochondrial 
dysfunction is responsible for the diverse clinical 
manifestations of the syndrome, particularly 
affecting energy-demanding tissues like the 
heart and skeletal muscle. The other lipids listed 
are involved in different cellular structures and 
metabolic pathways.

17.	 (B) 40
To calculate the Anion Gap (AG), we use the 
formula:
Anion Gap = (Na⁺ + K⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)
Now substitute the given values:
	
Na⁺	= 145 mEq/L
	
K⁺	= 4 mEq/L
	
Cl⁻	= 90 mEq/L
	
HCO₃⁻	= 15 mEq/L
NODIA
page  250  	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023 Answer
Step 1: Add sodium and potassium
	
145 + 4	= 149
Step 2: Add chloride and bicarbonate
	
90 + 15	= 105
Step 3: Subtract
	
149 − 105	= 44
So, the calculated anion gap is 44 mEq/L.
However, in many clinical settings potassium is 
often omitted from the formula:
	
AG	= Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)
	
145	− (90 + 15)
	
145	− 105 = 40
Since most MCQs use the formula without 
potassium, the correct answer is : (B) 40 This 
indicates a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, 
which can be seen in conditions like diabetic 
ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, or renal failure.
The liver is capable of producing ketone bodies but cannot utilize them because it lacks which enzyme?
(A)	
Thiophorase 
(B)	
Alkaline phosphatase 
(C)	
Alanine transaminase 
(D)	
Thiolase 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
18.	 (A) Thiophorase
During periods of fasting, starvation, or 
uncontrolled 
diabetes, 
the 
liver 
engages 
in 
ketogenesis, 
producing 
ketone 
bodies 
(acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate) from 
fatty acid oxidation. These ketone bodies are 
then exported into the bloodstream to be used 
as an energy source by extrahepatic tissues like 
the brain, heart, and skeletal muscle. For these 
peripheral tissues to utilize ketone bodies, they 
must first convert acetoacetate back into acetyl-
CoA for entry into the TCA cycle. This activation 
step is catalyzed by the mitochondrial enzyme 
succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid-CoA transferase, more 
commonly known as thiophorase. The liver is 
the site of ketone body synthesis but notably 
lacks this thiophorase enzyme. This enzymatic 
deficiency prevents the liver from utilizing the 
ketones it produces, ensuring that they are 
available for export to other tissues that critically 
need them for energy.

19.	 (A) Rothera's test
The image shows a laboratory test tube with a 
distinct purple or permanganate-colored ring 
formed at the junction of two liquid layers. 
This specific result is the positive outcome for 
Rothera's test, a qualitative chemical test used to 
detect the presence of ketone bodies (specifically 
acetoacetate and acetone) in a sample, typically 
urine. The test reagent is a mixture of sodium 
nitroprusside, ammonium sulfate, and sodium 
carbonate. In an alkaline medium, the sodium 
nitroprusside reacts with the ketone bodies 
to produce the characteristic purple-colored 
complex. This test is clinically significant for 
diagnosing ketosis and ketoacidosis, particularly 
in patients with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus. 
Benedict's test and Fehling's test are used to 
detect reducing sugars and would produce a 
color change from blue to green, yellow, orange, 
or brick-red. The Biuret test detects peptide 
bonds and produces a violet color.

20.	 (A) Lysosomal acid alpha glucosidase
Pompe disease is also known as Glycogen 
Storage Disease Type II. It is an autosomal 
recessive metabolic disorder that results from a 
deficiency of the enzyme lysosomal acid alpha-
glucosidase, also commonly called acid maltase. 
This enzyme's function is to break down glycogen 
into glucose within the acidic environment of 
the lysosomes. A deficiency of this enzyme leads 
to the massive accumulation of glycogen within 
the lysosomes of virtually all cells in the body. 
This lysosomal engorgement disrupts normal 
cellular function and leads to organ damage. The 
most severely affected tissues are cardiac and 
skeletal muscle, which rely heavily on glycogen 
metabolism. The classic infantile form presents 
with severe muscle weakness (hypotonia), 
respiratory distress, and a massive hypertrophic 
cardiomyopathy. The other enzymes listed are 
deficient in different glycogen storage diseases: 
Glucose-6-phosphatase in Von Gierke disease 
and muscle phosphorylase in McArdle disease.

The image displays the result of an indirect 
immunofluorescence (IIF) test for antinuclear 
antibodies (ANA) using HEp-2 cells as a 
substrate. The pattern of fluorescence is 
characterized by discrete, speckled staining

32.	 (D) Hairy cell
The image provided is a peripheral blood 
smear showing a lymphocyte with distinct 
morphological features. The cell has a round to 
indented nucleus, moderately abundant pale-
blue cytoplasm, and, most characteristically, 
fine, irregular, hair-like cytoplasmic projections 
that extend around its entire circumference. 
This unique appearance is the pathognomonic 
feature of a hairy cell, the neoplastic cell found 
in Hairy Cell Leukemia (HCL). HCL is a rare, 
indolent B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder. 
The presence of these cells on a peripheral smear, 
along with pancytopenia and splenomegaly, 
is highly suggestive of the diagnosis, which is 
then typically confirmed by flow cytometry and 
bone marrow biopsy showing a characteristic 
"fried-egg" appearance. Gaucher cells (A)

Which of the following methods is not used to detect abnormal gene sequences?
(A)	
RFLP analysis 
(B)	
Flow cytometry 
(C)	
FISH 
(D)	
Pyrosequencing 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
33.	 (B) Flow cytometry
The detection of abnormal gene sequences 
involves various molecular biology techniques. 
Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism 
(RFLP) analysis  is a classic technique that can 
detect sequence variations that alter restriction 
enzyme cutting sites. Porcelainizing  is a method 
of DNA sequencing that can identify the exact 
nucleotide sequence of a gene. Fluorescence 
In Situ Hybridization (FISH)  uses fluorescent 
probes to detect the presence, absence, or location 
of specific DNA sequences on chromosomes, and 
is used for detecting larger scale abnormalities 
like deletions or translocations. In contrast, flow 
cytometry  is a technique used to analyze the 
physical and chemical characteristics of cells. It 
is primarily used to measure cell surface protein 
expression (immunophenotyping), cell size, 
and granularity, and for cell sorting. It analyzes 
proteins on the cell surface, not the underlying 
gene sequence.
What does IDA stand for and how is it interpreted in the medical field?
(A)	
Low serum ferritin 
(B)	
Low transferrin saturation 
(C)	
Increased TIBC 
(D)	
All of the above 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
34.	 (D) All of the above
IDA stands for Iron Deficiency Anemia. Its 
diagnosis is confirmed by a characteristic 
pattern on a panel of blood tests known as iron 
studies. This pattern reflects both the depletion 
of the body's iron stores and its compensatory 
physiological responses. Low serum ferritin 
is the most specific indicator, as ferritin is the 
primary iron storage protein, and its levels 
directly correlate with total body iron stores. The 
body responds to the deficiency by increasing 
the liver's production of transferrin, the protein 
that transports iron. This is measured as an 
increased Total Iron-Binding Capacity (TIBC). 
Since there is very little iron to be transported, 
the transferrin saturation, which reflects 
the percentage of transferrin that is actually 
carrying iron, is consequently low. Therefore, 
the combination of low ferritin, low serum iron, 
increased TIBC, and low transferrin saturation 
is the classic profile for interpreting a diagnosis 
of iron deficiency anemia.

How can IDA be interpreted?

27.	 (A) abcd
Iron 
Deficiency 
Anemia 
(IDA) 
has 
a 
characteristic pattern on iron studies that 
reflects the body's depleted iron stores and 
its attempt to compensate. Serum ferritin is 
a measure of stored iron, and a low level is 
the most specific and earliest indicator of 
iron deficiency (a). Serum iron measures the 
amount of iron circulating in the blood bound 
to transferrin, and it is also low in IDA (c). 
The Total Iron-Binding Capacity (TIBC) is an 
indirect measure of transferrin, the protein that 
transports iron. In an effort to acquire more iron, 
the liver increases the production of transferrin, 
leading to an increased TIBC (d). Finally, the 
transferrin saturation, calculated as (serum iron 
/ TIBC) x 100, is low because there is very little 
iron available to saturate the increased amount 
of transferrin (b). All four of these findings 
together form the classic biochemical profile of 
iron deficiency anemia.
What does the absence of CD40 indicate in an individual?
(A)	
B cell absent 
(B)	
T cell absent 
(C)	
IgM increase 
(D)	
IgG increase 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
28.	 (C) IgM increase
The interaction between the CD40 receptor, 
expressed on B cells and other antigen-
presenting cells, and its ligand, CD40L (CD154), 
expressed on activated T helper cells, is a critical 
step in humoral immunity. This interaction is 
essential for inducing immunoglobulin class 
switching in B cells, allowing them to switch 
from producing IgM to producing other isotypes 
like IgG, IgA, and IgE. It is also required for 
the formation of germinal centers and the 
development of memory B cells. In an individual 
with a genetic defect leading to the absence of 
functional CD40 (or CD40L), class switching 
cannot occur. As a result, B cells can only 
produce IgM antibodies. This leads to a specific 
type of immunodeficiency known as Hyper-IgM 
Syndrome, which is characterized by normal or, 
more typically, increased levels of serum IgM 
and a profound deficiency of IgG, IgA, and E.
To prevent contamination, blood should be drawn into vacutainers in the following order:
(A)	
Red, Light blue, Violet, Grey 
(B)	
Blue, Violet, Red, Grey 
(C)	
Blue, Red, Violet, Grey 
(D)	
Grey, Blue, Red, Violet 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
29.	 (C) Blue, Red, Violet, Grey
When drawing multiple tubes of blood from a 
single venipuncture, a specific "order of draw" 
must be followed to prevent cross-contamination 
of additives between tubes, which could interfere 
with test results. The standardized order is based 
on the type of additive in the tube stopper. While 
the exact order can have minor variations, the 
generally accepted sequence is: First, blood 
culture bottles (if needed). Second, coagulation 
tubes, which have a light blue top and contain 
sodium citrate. Third, serum tubes, which can 
be a red top (no additive, allows clotting) or a 
serum separator tube (SST). Fourth, tubes with 
heparin (green top). Fifth, tubes with EDTA, 
which have a lavender or violet top. Finally, tubes 
with a glycolysis inhibitor, which have a grey 
top (containing sodium fluoride and potassium 
oxalate). Therefore, the correct sequence among 
the given options is Blue, Red, Violet, Grey.

What immunologic defect is seen in B cells when CD40 is absent?

22.	 (B) Decreased IgG and increase in IgM
The interaction between the CD40 ligand 
(CD40L or CD154) on activated helper T cells 
and the CD40 receptor on B cells is absolutely 
essential for B cell activation, proliferation, 
and differentiation. Specifically, this T-cell

What occurs when misfolded proteins accumulate abnormally?
(A)	
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease 
(B)	
Nephritic syndrome 
(C)	
Sickle cell anemia 
(D)	
Megaloblastic anemia 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
23.	 (A) Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
A number of diseases, known as proteinopathies 
or protein misfolding diseases, are caused by the 
accumulation of abnormally folded proteins 
that aggregate and cause cellular damage. 
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is the classic 
example of a human prion disease, which falls 
into this category. It is caused by the conversion 
of the normal cellular prion protein (PrPC) into 
an abnormal, misfolded, and infectious isoform 
(PrPSc). This misfolded protein is resistant to 
degradation and acts as a template to convert 
more normal PrPC into the abnormal form, 
leading to its exponential accumulation as 
insoluble aggregates in the brain. This process 
results in spongiform encephalopathy and a 
rapidly progressive, fatal neurodegenerative 
disease. In contrast, sickle cell anemia is 
caused by a mutation leading to hemoglobin 
polymerization, and megaloblastic anemia is 
due to impaired DNA synthesis, not protein 
misfolding.
In gonadal sex reversal syndrome with an XX karyotype, what is the most common underlying cause?
(A)	
Point mutation 
(B)	
Deletion 
(C)	
Translocation 
(D)	
Non-sense mutation 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
24.	 (C) Translocation
46,XX testicular disorder of sex development 
(also known as XX male syndrome) is a condition 
where an individual has a female karyotype 
(46,XX) but develops a male phenotype, 
including testes. The primary determinant of 
male development is the SRY (Sex-determining 
Region Y) gene, which is normally located on 
the Y chromosome. The most common cause 
of 46,XX male syndrome, accounting for about 
80% of cases, is an unequal crossing-over 
event during paternal meiosis. This results 
in the translocation of the SRY gene from 
the Y chromosome onto the X chromosome. 
The resulting X chromosome now carries the 
SRY gene. When an embryo inherits this SRY-
positive X chromosome along with a normal 
X chromosome from the mother, it will have a 
46,XX karyotype but will develop as a male due 
to the presence of the SRY gene, which initiates 
testis development.
Inheritance of pattern:
(A)

(B)

(D)

25.	 (A) Autosomal Dominant
The provided pedigree chart demonstrates 
several key features that are characteristic of 
an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. 
First, the trait appears in every generation, 
indicating vertical transmission from parent to 
child without skipping generations. Affected 
individuals are present in generations I, II, and 
III. Second, affected individuals transmit the 
trait to approximately half of their children, 
which is consistent with dominant inheritance 
(e.g., couple 1-2 have two affected and one 
unaffected child). Third, both males and females 
are affected, and critically, there is evidence 
of male-to-male transmission (affected father 
in individual 1 passes the trait to his affected 
son, individual 5). Male-to-male transmission 
definitively rules out X-linked inheritance. 
Autosomal recessive inheritance is unlikely as 
the trait does not skip generations and affected 
individuals have unaffected offspring.

36.	 (A) Beta pleated sheets
Amyloidosis is a group of diseases characterized 
by the extracellular deposition of abnormal, 
insoluble fibrillar proteins in various tissues 
and organs. While the precursor proteins 
that form amyloid deposits are diverse (e.g., 
immunoglobulin light chains in AL amyloidosis, 
serum amyloid A in AA amyloidosis), all 
amyloid fibrils share a common and defining 
ultrastructural feature. This is their characteristic 
cross-beta-pleated sheet conformation. This 
specific protein fold makes the fibrils extremely 
stable and resistant to proteolysis, leading to 
their progressive accumulation and subsequent 
tissue damage. The term "amyloid" was 
originally a misnomer, as it was thought to be 
a starch-like carbohydrate deposit, but it is in 
fact proteinaceous (C is false). Secondary (AA) 
amyloidosis is caused by deposition of serum 
amyloid A protein, not immunoglobulin light 
chains (AL), which cause primary amyloidosis 
(B is false).

The physiological effects described—increased 
levels of the incretin hormones GIP (glucose-
dependent insulinotropic polypeptide) and GLP-

decrease in glucagon levels—are characteristic 
of the mechanism of action of dipeptidyl

member of this class of oral antidiabetic drugs. 
The DPP-4 enzyme is responsible for the rapid

the circulating half-life and concentration of

the patient's reduction in HbA1c. Liraglutide

the action of GLP-1 but does not increase GIP 
levels.

Which of the following statements about the clinical therapeutic index is correct?
(A)

(B)

(C)	
Indicative of therapeutic index in a population vs individual
