EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
39.	 (A) Therapeutic index is LD50/ED50
The therapeutic index (TI) is a quantitative 
measure of the relative safety of a drug. It is 
a ratio that compares the dose of a drug that 
produces a toxic effect to the dose that produces 
a therapeutic or desired effect. The classical 
definition of the therapeutic index, derived from 
preclinical animal studies, is the ratio of the LD50 
(the dose that is lethal to 50% of the population) 
to the ED50 (the dose that is therapeutically 
effective in 50% of the population). A higher 
therapeutic index indicates a wider margin of 
safety, meaning a much larger dose is needed 
to cause toxicity than is needed for the desired 
effect. Conversely, a drug with a low or narrow 
therapeutic index requires careful monitoring as 
the effective and toxic doses are close together. 
The other options describe concepts related to 
therapeutic drug monitoring or risk-benefit 
analysis rather than the formal definition of the 
TI.

Which of the following statements is false regarding a girl found deceased in a lake, indicating a case of ante-mortem drowning?

(C)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
43.	 (C) No Mud and vegetation in respiratory tract
Ante-mortem drowning means the person was 
alive when they entered the water and died as 
a result of submersion. The autopsy findings 
reflect the active process of breathing in water. 
A classic external sign is the presence of fine, 
lacy, and persistent froth at the mouth and nose, 
which is formed by the mixing of air, water, and 
mucus during agonal respirations. Internally, 
as the victim gasps for air underwater, they 
will inhale and swallow water, leading to 
the presence of water in the stomach and 
duodenum. If the drowning occurs in natural 
water, it is also common to find foreign material 
from the water body, such as mud, sand, and 
vegetation, deep within the respiratory tract, 
extending to the terminal bronchioles. Cadaveric 
spasm  may be present, with the victim's hands 
tightly clutching weeds or debris. Therefore, the 
absence of mud and vegetation in the airways 
would be inconsistent with typical ante-mortem 
drowning.

What is the type of hypoxia caused by carbon monoxide poisoning?
(A)	
Anemic hypoxia 
(B)	
Hypoxic hypoxia
(C)	
Stagnant hypoxia
(D)	
Histotoxic hypoxia
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
47.	 (A) Anemic hypoxia
Hypoxia is classified into four main types based 
on its underlying cause. Anemic hypoxia is 
defined as a condition where the partial pressure 
of oxygen in the arterial blood (PaO2) is normal, 
but the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood 
is reduced. This is precisely the mechanism of 
carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. CO has an 
affinity for hemoglobin that is over 200 times 
greater than that of oxygen. When inhaled, 
CO avidly binds to hemoglobin to form 
carboxyhemoglobin (COHb), which is incapable 
of transporting oxygen. This effectively reduces 
the amount of functional hemoglobin available 
to carry oxygen to the tissues, thus decreasing 
the blood's total oxygen content, despite a 
normal PaO2. This is functionally equivalent to 
having a severe anemia. Histotoxic hypoxia (D) 
is caused by cyanide, which prevents cells from 
using oxygen.

(B)	
No motility at 22°c and motile at 37°C
(C)	
Motile at both 37°C and 22°C
(D)	
Non-motile at both 37°C and 22°C
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
51.	 (A) Motile at 22°C and non-motile at 37°C
Listeria 
monocytogenes, 
a 
Gram-positive 
bacillus, is a significant cause of meningitis, 
particularly in neonates, the elderly, and 
immunocompromised individuals. A key and 
distinctive laboratory feature used to identify 
this organism is its temperature-dependent 
motility. When Listeria is cultured in broth at 
room temperature (approximately 22-25°C), it 
exhibits a characteristic end-over-end "tumbling 
motility," which is observable on a wet mount 
preparation. This movement is facilitated by the 
expression of peritrichous flagella. However, 
the expression of these flagellar genes is 
regulated by temperature. When the organism is 
incubated at human body temperature (37°C), 
the production of flagella is downregulated, 
and the bacterium becomes non-motile. This 
unique characteristic of being motile at room 
temperature but non-motile at 37°C is a crucial 
diagnostic test in the clinical microbiology 
laboratory, helping to differentiate Listeria 
monocytogenes from other morphologically 
similar but often non-pathogenic Gram-positive 
bacilli, such as Corynebacterium species.
What determines the DNA sequence?
(A)	
Flow cytometry
(B)	
FISH
(C)	
RFLP
(D)	
PCR
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
52.	 (D) PCR
The question, "What determines the DNA 
sequence?", is ambiguously phrased. However, 
interpreting it as asking which of the listed 
techniques is most fundamental to the process 
of analyzing or identifying a DNA sequence, 
the best answer is Polymerase Chain Reaction 
(PCR). PCR is a foundational molecular biology 
method used to amplify a specific segment 
of DNA exponentially, generating millions 
of copies from a minute starting sample. 
This amplification step is essential and often 
precedes direct DNA sequencing methods (like 
Sanger or next-generation sequencing), which 
are the ultimate techniques that "determine" 
the exact order of nucleotides. In contrast, Flow 
cytometry (A) analyzes cell characteristics, not 
DNA sequences. FISH (B) visualizes the location 
of a known DNA sequence on a chromosome. 
RFLP (C) is a method that detects variations 
in DNA sequences by analyzing differences in 
restriction enzyme cutting sites, but it doesn't 
determine the full sequence itself. Therefore, 
PCR is the most critical enabling technology 
among the choices for any process that involves 
determining a DNA sequence.

Which type of amyloidosis is typically seen in patients on dialysis?
(A)	
A-beta
(B)	
ß2-microglobulin
(C)	
aTTR
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
56.	 (B) ß2-microglobulin
Dialysis-related amyloidosis (DRA) is a serious 
long-term complication that occurs in patients 
with end-stage renal disease who have been 
on chronic hemodialysis for many years. This 
specific type of amyloidosis is caused by the 
deposition of amyloid fibrils derived from β2-
microglobulin. β2-microglobulin is a small 
protein that is a component of the MHC class 
I molecule and is normally filtered by the 
glomeruli and catabolized in the renal tubules. 
In patients with kidney failure, this protein 
cannot be adequately cleared from the blood, 
and conventional dialysis membranes are 
also inefficient at removing it. Over time, the 
chronically elevated levels of β2-microglobulin 
lead to its aggregation into amyloid fibrils, 
which deposit predominantly in osteoarticular 
structures, causing conditions like carpal tunnel 
syndrome and destructive spondyloarthropathy. 
The other amyloid types listed are associated 
with different diseases: AL with multiple 
myeloma, Aβ with Alzheimer's disease, and 
ATTR with familial or senile amyloidosis.

What is the correct order for cardiac auscultation from superior to inferior?

sounds from each heart valve are best heard.

valves in a superior-to-inferior direction is

What is the accurate order of the auditory pathway?
(A)	
Cochlea Spiral Ganglion Cochlear Nerve → Superior Olivary N
(B)	
Spiral Ganglion Cochlea Cochlear Nerve → Superior Olivary N
(C)	
Spiral Ganglion Cochlear Nerve → Cochlea → Superior Olivary N
(D)	
Cochlea Spiral Ganglion Cochlear Nerve → Inferior Olivary N
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
63.	 (A) Cochlea Spiral Ganglion Cochlear Nerve → 
Superior Olivary N
This question asks for the correct initial 
sequence of the peripheral auditory pathway. 
Sound vibrations are first transduced into neural 
signals by the hair cells within the cochlea of 
the inner ear. These hair cells synapse with the 
first-order neurons of the auditory pathway. 
The cell bodies of these first-order neurons are 
located in the spiral ganglion, which is also 
situated within the cochlea. The axons of these 
spiral ganglion neurons then bundle together to 
form the cochlear nerve, which is the auditory 
division of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN 
VIII). This nerve then travels from the cochlea 
to the brainstem, where its fibers make their first 
central synapse in the cochlear nuclei. From 
there, the pathway continues to the superior 
olivary nucleus. Therefore, the correct sequence 
from the site of transduction to the first central 
relay stations is Cochlea → Spiral Ganglion → 
Cochlear Nerve → Superior Olivary Nucleus.

In biostatistics, the formula given below stands for?
(σ) = √[Σ(x - μ)² / N]
(A)	
Standard Deviation
(B)	
Sample Variance
(C)	
Sample Mean
(D)	
Median
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
59.	 (A) Standard Deviation
The formula provided, σ = √[Σ(x - μ)² / N], 
is the precise mathematical definition of the 
population standard deviation. The Greek 
letter sigma (σ) is the standard symbol for this 
parameter. The formula calculates the square 
root of the average of the squared deviations of 
each data point (x) from the population mean 
(μ). The sum of the squared deviations is divided 
by N, the total size of the population. This differs 
slightly from the sample standard deviation, 
which uses the sample mean (x̄) and divides 
by (n-1) to provide an unbiased estimate. The 
standard deviation is a fundamental and widely 
used measure of the dispersion or variability of 
a set of data. It quantifies the average amount 
by which individual data points in a distribution 
differ from the mean of that distribution, 
expressed in the original units of the data.

70.	 (C) Superior vena cava syndrome
A significantly enlarged thyroid gland, or goiter, 
can cause compressive symptoms by impinging 
on adjacent structures in the neck. Compression 
of the trachea can cause dyspnea and stridor. 
Posterior extension can compress the esophagus, 
leading to dysphagia (B). The recurrent laryngeal 
nerve runs in the tracheoesophageal groove, 
and compression or invasion by the goiter can 
lead to vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness of 
the voice (A). However, for a goiter to cause 
Superior Vena Cava (SVC) syndrome, it must 
extend substernally deep into the superior 
mediastinum to compress the SVC. While this is 
possible with a very large retrosternal goiter, it is 
a rare complication. In contrast, dysphagia and

Which ion channels are mainly impaired due to the defect seen in cystic fibrosis?
(A)	
Cl-
(B)	
Ca2+
(C)	
Na+
(D)	
K+
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
71.	 (A) Cl-
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive 
genetic disorder caused by mutations in the gene 
that encodes the cystic fibrosis transmembrane 
conductance regulator (CFTR) protein. The 
CFTR protein is an ATP-gated ion channel 
located in the apical membrane of epithelial 
cells in many different organs. The primary 
function of this channel is the transport of 
chloride ions (Cl-) out of the epithelial cells into 
the lumen. In patients with cystic fibrosis, the 
CFTR channel is either absent or dysfunctional, 
leading to defective chloride secretion. This 
primary defect in chloride transport disrupts 
the normal balance of ions and water across 
the epithelial surface, leading to the production 
of abnormally thick, dehydrated, and viscous 
mucus in the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and 
reproductive tracts. The diagnostic sweat test for 
CF is based on this defect, as impaired chloride 
reabsorption in sweat ducts leads to abnormally 
high salt concentrations in the sweat.

Nadas’ criteria are used for the clinical diagnosis 
of congenital heart disease (CHD) and are 
divided into major and minor criteria.

1.	 Cyanosis
2.	 Congestive cardiac failure
3.	 Grade ≥3 systolic murmur

6.	 Significant cardiomegaly
Minor criteria include:
7.	 Grade 1 or 2 systolic murmur
8.	 Abnormal ECG
9.	 Abnormal chest X-ray
10.	Blood pressure abnormalities

under minor grouping for suspicion, which

in some exam keys.

For a pneumonia patient on mechanical ventilation with the following parameters: 50 kg body weight, respiratory rate (RR) of 14 breaths per minute, bicarbonate level of 18 mEq/L, pH of 7.3, pCO2 of 48 mmHg, pO2 of 110 mmHg, PEEP of 12 cm H2O, tidal volume (TV) of 420 mL, SpO2 of 100%, and FiO2 of 90%, what adjustment should be made to their ventilator settings?

Increase PEEP
(B)	
Increase tidal volume
(C)	
Decrease RR

The patient's arterial blood gas (ABG) shows 
a mixed acidosis (pH 7.3, high pCO2, low 
bicarbonate), but the most critical parameter to 
address immediately is the oxygenation status. 
The patient's PaO2 is 110 mmHg and the SpO2 
is 100% while on a very high level of inspired 
oxygen (FiO2 of 90%). A PaO2 above 100 mmHg 
indicates hyperoxia, which can be toxic to the 
lungs, causing oxidative stress and absorption 
atelectasis. The primary goal of oxygen therapy

a PaO2 of 60-80 mmHg or an SpO2 of 92-96%) 
using the lowest possible FiO2. Since this patient

appropriate and urgent ventilator adjustment

monitoring the SpO2. Increasing PEEP or tidal 
volume is not indicated for hyperoxia, and 
decreasing the respiratory rate would worsen 
the existing respiratory acidosis.
What is the ECG depicted in the following image?

79.	 (A) Torsades de pointes
The ECG strip displays a life-threatening cardiac 
arrhythmia known as Torsades de pointes 
(TdP). This is a specific form of polymorphic 
ventricular tachycardia that is characterized by 
a distinctive morphology on the ECG. The QRS 
complexes are wide and have a continuously 
changing axis and amplitude, appearing to twist 
or spiral around the isoelectric baseline. This 
"twisting of the points" gives the arrhythmia its 
name. TdP occurs in the setting of a prolonged 
QT interval, which can be congenital or 
acquired (e.g., due to electrolyte abnormalities 
or medications). The arrhythmia is typically 
rapid and hemodynamically unstable, often 
degenerating into ventricular fibrillation and 
causing syncope or sudden cardiac death if 
not promptly recognized and treated. The 
other conditions listed have entirely different 
ECG manifestations (e.g., diffuse ST elevation 
in pericarditis, electrical alternans in cardiac 
tamponade).
How would you describe the characteristic murmur of aortic regurgitation?
(A)	
Ventricular contraction
(B)	
Ejection systolic murmur
(C)	
Diastolic murmur
(D)	
Systolic murmur
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
80.	 (C) Diastolic murmur
Aortic regurgitation (or aortic insufficiency) 
is a condition where the aortic valve fails to 
close completely at the end of systole. This 
incompetence allows blood to leak backward 
from the aorta into the left ventricle during 
diastole. This retrograde flow of blood across 
the incompetent valve is what generates the 
characteristic heart murmur. Therefore, the 
murmur of aortic regurgitation is a diastolic 
murmur. It is typically described as a high-
pitched, blowing, decrescendo murmur that 
is best heard at the left sternal border with the 
patient sitting up and leaning forward in full 
expiration. The murmur begins immediately 
after the second heart sound (S2). In contrast, 
an ejection systolic murmur (B) is caused by 
the forward flow of blood through a narrowed 
(stenotic) aortic or pulmonary valve during 
systole.

(B)

(C)

(D)

81.	 (A) Cor pulmonale
High-output cardiac failure is a form of heart 
failure where the cardiac output is normal or 
even elevated, but it is insufficient to meet the 
body's heightened metabolic demands. This 
condition is caused by a significant decrease 
in systemic vascular resistance. Classic causes 
include severe chronic anemia (C), where 
reduced blood viscosity and tissue hypoxia cause 
widespread vasodilation; beriberi (thiamine 
deficiency) 
(B), 
which 
causes 
peripheral 
vasodilation; and large systemic arteriovenous 
(AV) shunts or fistulas (D), which bypass the 
systemic resistance arterioles. In contrast, cor 
pulmonale is defined as right-sided heart failure 
resulting from chronic pulmonary hypertension. 
The primary problem is an increased afterload 
on the right ventricle due to high resistance in 
the pulmonary circulation. This leads to low-
output right heart failure, not high-output 
failure.

Gonioscopy is the clinical technique used to 
visualize the iridocorneal angle, the anatomical 
angle between the iris and the cornea where the 
aqueous humor drains from the eye. It is essential 
for 
diagnosing 
and 
managing 
glaucoma. 
Gonioscopy can be either direct or indirect.

What is the correct sequence of staining used in patients with dry eye disease?
i = Fluorescein stain
ii = Lissamine green
iii = Rose Bengal stain
(A)	
i, iii, ii
(B)	
i, ii, iii
(C)	
ii, i, iii
(D)	
iii, ii, i
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
68.	 (B) i, ii, iii
Vital staining of the ocular surface is a key 
component of the diagnosis and assessment 
of dry eye disease. When multiple stains are 
used during the same examination, they should 
be applied in a specific order to prevent one 
stain from masking the results of another. The 
recommended sequence is based on the staining 
characteristics and potential for interference. 
The standard order is to first instill fluorescein 
stain (i), which is used to assess tear film 
breakup time and to highlight corneal epithelial 
defects. After this, lissamine green (ii) is applied. 
Lissamine green stains devitalized, membrane-
damaged epithelial cells of the conjunctiva and 
cornea with minimal irritation. Finally, Rose 
Bengal stain (iii) can be used. It also stains 
devitalized cells but is more irritating to the eye 
than lissamine green. Because Rose Bengal can 
mask the fluorescence of fluorescein, it should 
always be applied last.

A 62-year-old patient experiences calf pain while walking that subsides with rest. Which of the following features is not typically associated with intermittent claudication?
(A)	
Muscle cramping during physical activity
(B)	
Pain starting on taking the first step
(C)	
Atheroma as the most frequent underlying cause
(D)	
Level of occlusion cannot be decided based on symptoms
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
88.	 (B) Pain starting on taking the first step
Intermittent 
claudication 
is 
the 
classic 
symptom of peripheral artery disease (PAD). 
It is characterized by a reproducible cramping 
pain or ache in a muscle group (e.g., the calf) 
that is induced by a consistent level of exercise 
or physical activity and is relieved promptly 
by rest. This is caused by ischemia resulting 
from an inadequate blood supply to meet the 
increased metabolic demands of the exercising 
muscle. The most frequent underlying cause of 
the arterial narrowing is atherosclerosis (C). The 
location of the pain can give a clue to the level of 
the arterial occlusion, but it is not always precise 
(D). A key feature of claudication is that the 
pain begins after a certain amount of exertion 
and is not present at the beginning of the 
activity. Pain that starts on taking the first step 
is not characteristic of claudication; it is more 
suggestive of a musculoskeletal or orthopedic 
issue, such as plantar fasciitis or osteoarthritis.
Which of the following is not recognized as a complication of massive blood transfusion?
(A)	
Hypocalcemia
(B)	
Hypokalemia
(C)	
Hypothermia
(D)	
Hypernatremia
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
89.	 (D) Hypernatremia
Massive blood transfusion (the replacement of a 
patient's entire blood volume within 24 hours) 
is associated with several well-known metabolic 
and physiological complications. The citrate 
anticoagulant used in stored blood chelates 
calcium, which can lead to clinically significant 
hypocalcemia (A), especially when large 
volumes are infused rapidly. Stored red blood 
cells leak potassium, and the transfused blood is 
typically cooler than body temperature, which 
can lead to hypothermia (C). Interestingly, while 
stored blood contains a high concentration of 
potassium, massive transfusions are more often 
associated with hypokalemia (B) initially, due 
to factors like dilution, alkalosis from citrate 
metabolism, and sympathetic drive. In contrast, 
hypernatremia (high sodium) is not a recognized 
complication. The sodium concentration in 
packed red blood cells and the anticoagulant 
solutions is similar to that of normal plasma, so 
transfusion does not typically cause an increase 
in serum sodium levels.

For which of the following conditions are vaccines not contraindicated in affected individuals?

(B)

85.	 (C) Complement deficiency
The safety of vaccination depends on the 
specific type of primary immunodeficiency. Live 
attenuated vaccines (such as MMR and varicella) 
are generally contraindicated in patients with 
severe T-cell immunodeficiencies, as the 
weakened pathogen can cause disseminated 
disease. DiGeorge syndrome (A), Wiskott-

This clinical picture is a classic presentation

A 10-year-old boy is admitted with severe dehydration, nausea, vomiting, urine sugar 3+, RBS 550 mg/dL, ABG showing pH of 7.1, and HCO3= 7 mmol/L. What is the appropriate line of management as per ISPAD (International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes) guidelines?
(A)	
10 ml per kg of IV fluids & 0.1 unit/kg/hr bolus
(B)	
10 ml per kg of IV fluids & after 1 hour of fluid 0.1 unit/kg/hr of insulin
(C)	
20 ml per kg of IV fluids & 0.1 unit/kg/hr of insulin bolus
(D)	
20 ml per kg of IV fluids & after 1 hour of fluid 0.1 unit/kg/hr of insulin bolus
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
104.	 (B) 10 ml per kg of IV fluids & after 1 hour of 
fluid 0.1 unit/kg/hr of insulin
The patient's presentation with hyperglycemia, 
ketonuria, and metabolic acidosis is diagnostic 
of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Management 
according to ISPAD guidelines is systematic 
and cautious. The first priority is to correct 
dehydration and restore circulatory volume. 
The initial fluid bolus for a child in DKA who 
is not in profound shock is 10 ml/kg of isotonic 
saline (0.9% NaCl) given over the first hour. 
Importantly, insulin therapy should not be 
started immediately. It should be initiated only 
after the initial fluid resuscitation has begun, 
typically about one hour after starting IV fluids. 
This delay helps to prevent a rapid fall in glucose 
and osmolarity, which could increase the risk of 
cerebral edema. Once started, insulin is given 
as a continuous low-dose intravenous infusion, 
typically at a rate of 0.05-0.1 unit/kg/hour, 
without an initial bolus. Therefore, the correct 
approach is an initial 10 ml/kg fluid bolus, 
followed by the start of an insulin infusion one 
hour later.
Which of the following statements about CPR is incorrect?
(A)	
Ventilation 22-25/min
(B)	
Depth of chest compression up to 5-6 cm
(C)	
Allow adequate chest recoil
(D)	
Chest compression rate 100-120/min
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
105.	 (A) Ventilation 22-25/min
High-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation 
(CPR) is crucial for improving outcomes from 
cardiac arrest. The current guidelines emphasize 
several key components. The recommended rate 
of chest compressions for an adult is between 100 
and 120 per minute. The depth of compressions 
should be at least 2 inches (5 cm) but not 
more than 2.4 inches (6 cm). It is also vital to 
allow for complete chest recoil between each 
compression, as this is necessary for the heart to 
fill with blood. When an advanced airway (such 
as an endotracheal tube) is in place, ventilations 
are given asynchronously with compressions 
at a rate of 1 breath every 6 seconds, which 
translates to 10 breaths per minute. A ventilation 
rate of 22-25 breaths per minute is excessive and 
can lead to hyperventilation, which increases 
intrathoracic pressure, decreases venous return 
and cardiac output, and worsens outcomes.

What is the test depicted in the provided image called?
(A)	
Allen test
(B)	
Adson test
(C)	
Barbeau test
(D)	
Homans test
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
108.	 (A) Allen test
The image depicts the procedure for performing 
the Allen test. This is a clinical test used to 
assess the patency of the ulnar and radial 
arteries and the integrity of the palmar arches 
of the hand. The procedure involves the patient 
clenching their fist tightly while the examiner 
manually occludes both the radial and ulnar 
arteries at the wrist. The patient then opens 
their hand, which will appear pale or blanched. 
The examiner releases the pressure on one of 
the arteries (typically the ulnar artery first) and 
observes the time it takes for color to return to 
the hand. Normal re perfusion should occur 
within 5-7 seconds. The test is then repeated, 
releasing the other artery. This test is crucial for 
ensuring adequate collateral circulation from 
the ulnar artery before procedures that might 
compromise the radial artery, such as arterial 
blood gas sampling or radial artery cannulation.
In HER2-positive breast cancer that is resistant to trastuzumab, which of the following treatment options is considered appropriate?
(A)	
Lapatinib
(B)	
Sorafenib
(C)	
Vemurafenib
(D)	
Erlotinib
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
109.	 (A) Lapatinib
HER2-positive breast cancer is characterized 
by the overexpression of the human epidermal 
growth factor receptor 2. The primary targeted 
therapy for this subtype is trastuzumab, 
a monoclonal antibody that binds to the 
extracellular domain of the HER2 receptor. 
However, some tumors may develop resistance 
to trastuzumab. In such cases, other HER2-
targeted agents are used. Lapatinib is a small-
molecule dual tyrosine kinase inhibitor that 
targets both the HER2 receptor and the epidermal 
growth factor receptor (EGFR). By inhibiting 
the intracellular tyrosine kinase domain, it 
blocks downstream signaling pathways and 
can be effective even when resistance to 
the extracellularly-acting trastuzumab has 
developed. It is often used in combination with 
chemotherapy or other agents for patients with 
advanced HER2-positive breast cancer that 
has progressed on a trastuzumab-containing 
regimen. The other drugs listed target different 
pathways: sorafenib and vemurafenib are used 
for other cancers, and erlotinib is an EGFR 
inhibitor.
Osimertinib is used to treat non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) associated with which genetic mutation?
(A)	
L858R mutation
(B)	
T890M mutation
(C)	
T790M mutation
(D)	
M790T mutation
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
110.	 (C) T790M mutation
Osimertinib is a third-generation, irreversible 
epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) 
tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI). It is a highly 
effective targeted therapy for patients with 
non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) whose 
tumors harbor specific EGFR mutations. While 
it is also active against the common sensitizing 
mutations like exon 19 deletions and the 
L858R mutation (A), its key indication and 
the reason for its development was its potent 
activity against the T790M resistance mutation. 
The T790M mutation is the most common 
mechanism of acquired resistance that develops 
in patients who are initially treated with first- or 
second-generation EGFR TKIs (like erlotinib or 
gefitinib). Osimertinib was specifically designed 
to overcome this resistance mechanism, and it 
is now also a standard first-line treatment for 
EGFR-mutated NSCLC, as it is effective against 
both the initial sensitizing mutations and can 
prevent the emergence of the T790M resistance 
clone.

A patient presents with abnormal sensations in the little finger and part of the ring finger, weakness on the palmar side of the hand, and impaired finger coordination. Which nerve is most likely injured?
(A)	
Ulnar nerve
(B)	
Radial nerve
(C)	
Median nerve
(D)	
Axillary nerve
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
112.	 (A) Ulnar nerve
This constellation of symptoms points directly 
to a lesion of the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve 
provides sensory innervation to the medial one-
and-a-half digits of the hand, which includes 
the little finger and the medial half of the 
ring finger. Paresthesias or numbness in this 
specific distribution is a classic hallmark of 
ulnar neuropathy. The ulnar nerve also provides 
motor innervation to most of the intrinsic 
muscles of the hand, including the interossei, 
the hypothenar muscles, and the adductor 
pollicis. Weakness of these muscles leads to a 
weak grip, difficulty with fine motor tasks, and a 
lack of finger coordination, such as the inability 
to abduct and adduct the fingers. The radial 
nerve (B) is responsible for wrist and finger 
extension, while the median nerve (C) provides 
sensation to the other digits and innervates the 
thenar muscles.
In the scenario where a surgeon reduces the hernia sac into the abdominal cavity without manually repositioning its contents, as shown in the image, which type of hernia is illustrated?
(A)	
Strangulated hernia
(B)	
Maydl's hernia
(C)	
Sliding hernia
(D)	
Reduction en masse
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
113.	 (D) Reduction en masse
Reduction en masse is a rare but serious 
complication of attempting to reduce an 
incarcerated or strangulated hernia. It occurs 
when the entire hernia sac, along with its 
constricted neck and strangulated contents, 
is forcibly pushed from its subcutaneous 
position back through the fascial defect into the 
abdominal cavity. This maneuver gives the false 
impression of a successful reduction because 
the external bulge disappears. However, the 
contents of the hernia (typically a loop of bowel) 
remain trapped and strangulated within the 
hernial sac inside the abdomen. The constriction 
at the neck of the sac persists, and the blood 
supply to the bowel remains compromised. 
This leads to ongoing ischemia and eventual 
gangrene and perforation if not recognized and 
surgically corrected immediately. The image 
depicts this exact scenario, where the entire sac 
and its contents have been displaced internally 
without relief of the constriction.
Which of the following are not considered anterior relations of the third part of the duodenum?
(A)	
Root of mesentery
(B)	
Fundus of gallbladder
(C)	
Jejunum
(D)	
Superior mesenteric artery
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
114.	 (B) Fundus of gallbladder
The third part of the duodenum, also known 
as the horizontal part, runs transversely from 
right to left, anterior to the inferior vena cava 
and the aorta. It has several important anterior 
relations. It is crossed anteriorly by the superior 
mesenteric artery and vein as they descend from 
behind the pancreas. The root of the mesentery of 
the small intestine also originates from this area 
and crosses anteriorly. Coils of the jejunum also 
lie anterior to the third part of the duodenum. 
In contrast, the fundus of the gallbladder is 
located in the right upper quadrant, in a fossa 
on the visceral surface of the liver. Its primary 
duodenal relation is with the superior (first) 
part of the duodenum, which it lies posterior to. 
It is not an anterior relation of the much lower, 
third part of the duodenum.
After surgical repair of a left-sided varicocele, a 30-year-old man asks how venous drainage will mainly occur. What should the surgeon identify as the primary drainage route?
(A)	
Penile veins
(B)	
Cremasteric veins
(C)	
Ectopic drainage in the iliac fossa
(D)	
At the usual location
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
115.	 (B) Cremasteric veins
The testis has a complex venous drainage system. 
The primary route is through the pampiniform 
plexus, which coalesces to form the testicular 
(internal spermatic) vein. A varicocele is a 
dilation of these pampiniform plexus veins. 
Surgical correction, or varicocelectomy, involves 
ligating these incompetent testicular veins. 
Following this ligation, the venous drainage of 
the testis must rely on its collateral pathways. 
The main collateral routes are the cremasteric 
(external spermatic) veins, which drain into the 
inferior epigastric vein, and the deferential veins 
(veins of the vas deferens), which drain into the 
pelvic venous plexus. Of these, the cremasteric 
venous system is considered the predominant 
collateral pathway that takes over testicular 
drainage after the main testicular vein has been 
surgically ligated. Therefore, this becomes the 
primary route for venous outflow post-surgery.

After lap cholecystectomy what should be the urine output of the patient if the renal function of the patient is normal?
(A)	
0.1 CC/hr
(B)	
0.5 ml/min
(C)	
0.5-1.5 ml/kg/min
(D)	
1 ml/kg/min
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
126.	 (B) 0.5 mL/min.
After 
laparoscopic 
cholecystectomy, 
urine 
output is an important indicator of adequate 
renal perfusion and overall hemodynamic 
stability. In adults with normal renal function, 
the standard benchmark for adequate urine 
output is at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour. This value is 
widely used in postoperative monitoring and 
critical care settings to assess kidney function 
and tissue perfusion.
For example, in a 60 kg adult, the minimum

corresponds to approximately 0.5 mL per 
minute, which matches option (B).
(C)	Option, 0.5–1.5 mL/kg/min, is incorrect 
because that would represent an excessively 
high urine output. For a 60 kg person, it 
would equal 30–90 mL per minute, or 1800–
5400 mL per hour, which is physiologically 
unrealistic.
(A)	Option is too low and inadequate to indicate 
normal renal function, and option (D) 
overestimates the normal expected output.
Thus, the correct postoperative urine output 
in a patient with normal renal function is best 
represented by 0.5 mL/min.
Which of the subsequent conditions is linked with perineural invasion?
(A)	
Adenoid cystic carcinoma
(B)	
Pleomorphic adenoma
(C)	
Mucoepidermoid tumor
(D)	
Pancreatic cancer
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
127.	 (A) Adenoid cystic carcinoma
Perineural invasion (PNI), the process of tumor 
cells invading in, around, and along nerves, is a 
well-known feature of certain malignancies and 
is associated with a poorer prognosis. Among 
salivary gland tumors, adenoid cystic carcinoma 
is notorious for its marked propensity for 
perineural invasion. This is a key histological 
feature of the tumor and is responsible for its 
tendency to spread extensively along nerve 
pathways, often far beyond the primary tumor 
site, leading to a high rate of local recurrence 
and late distant metastases. While perineural 
invasion can also be seen in pancreatic cancer 
and high-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma, it 
is a defining and almost universal characteristic 
of adenoid cystic carcinoma. Pleomorphic 
adenoma is a benign tumor and does not exhibit 
PNI.

128.	 (A) 50,000(10^9/L)
The decision to proceed with surgery in a 
patient with thrombocytopenia depends on 
the type of procedure and the risk of bleeding. 
While there is some variation in practice, a 
generally accepted and safe threshold for the 
minimum platelet count required for most 
major, non-neuraxial surgical procedures is 
50,000/µL. A count at or above this level is 
usually considered sufficient to ensure adequate 
primary hemostasis and prevent excessive 
intraoperative or postoperative bleeding. For 
procedures with a very low bleeding risk, a 
lower count might be acceptable. Conversely, 
for high-risk procedures, such as neurosurgery 
or epidural catheter placement, a much higher 
platelet count, often approaching 100,000/
µL, is typically required. Platelet counts below 
20,000/µL (B) are associated with a high risk of 
spontaneous bleeding, and surgery would be 
contraindicated without a pre-operative platelet 
transfusion.

121.	 (D) Duct ectasia
While smoking is a known risk factor for 
breast cancer, it has a stronger and more direct 
association with certain benign breast conditions. 
Mammary duct ectasia is an inflammatory 
condition characterized by the dilation of the 
large milk ducts located beneath the nipple.

Which of the subsequent options is not considered a perianal approach for rectal prolapse?

The surgical management of a full-thickness 
rectal prolapse can be performed via either an 
abdominal approach or a perineal (perianal) 
approach. The choice of procedure depends 
on the patient's age, comorbidities, and the 
surgeon's preference. The perineal approaches 
are performed through an incision around the 
anus. These include the Altemeier procedure

suture to narrow the anal orifice, now rarely 
used). In contrast, the Frykman-Goldberg 
procedure is an abdominal approach. It is a type 
of rectopexy that involves mobilizing the rectum 
and fixing it to the sacrum, often combined with 
a sigmoid resection, and is performed via an 
abdominal incision or laparoscopically.
A 28 year old female reported to OPD with C/O swelling in mouth On Clinical examination swelling in the floor of the mouth can be seen which was non tender and soft in consistency, based on the provided image What can be the correct diagnosis?

123.	 (B) Ranula
The image shows a translucent, bluish, dome-
shaped swelling located in the floor of the 
mouth, to one side of the midline. This is the 
classic clinical appearance of a ranula. A ranula 
is a type of mucocele, or mucus extravasation 
cyst, that arises specifically from a sublingual 
salivary gland. It occurs when the duct of the 
gland is obstructed or traumatized, leading 
to the leakage and pooling of saliva in the 
surrounding soft tissues, forming a pseudocyst. 
The term "ranula" comes from the Latin word 
for frog ("rana"), as the swelling can resemble a 
frog's belly. A "plunging" ranula occurs when the 
swelling extends through the mylohyoid muscle 
into the neck. A mucocele (D) is a more general 
term for a mucous cyst, which can occur from 
any minor salivary gland, often on the lower lip.

The surgical instrument shown in the image is a

is that its jaws are angled at 90 degrees to the

A 25-year-old woman with a one-month history of fever presents with headache and ataxia. Brain imaging reveals dilated ventricles and prominent basal exudates. What CSF finding is most likely?
(A)	
Lymphocytosis, Low Glucose, High protein
(B)	
Lymphocytosis, Low Glucose, Normal protein
(C)	
Lymphocytosis, Low Glucose, Normal protein
(D)	
Neutrophilia, Low glucose, Low Protein
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
101.	 (A) Lymphocytosis, Low Glucose, High protein
The clinical presentation of a subacute illness 
lasting a month, coupled with neurological signs 
and imaging that reveals hydrocephalus (dilated 
ventricles) and prominent inflammation at the 
base of the brain (basal exudates), is highly 
characteristic of tuberculous (TB) meningitis. 
The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis in TB 
meningitis has a classic profile that distinguishes 
it from other forms of meningitis. It typically 
shows a moderate pleocytosis (increased white 
blood cell count) with a marked predominance 
of lymphocytes. A key feature is a significantly 
low glucose level (hypoglycorrhachia), often less 
than 40% of the serum glucose, due to impaired 
transport into the CSF and consumption by 
the inflammatory process. Finally, due to the 
intense inflammation and breakdown of the 
blood-brain barrier, there is a markedly high 
protein concentration, often exceeding 100-200 
mg/dL. This specific triad of CSF findings is the 
hallmark of tuberculous meningitis.
A 42-year-old patient reports chronic fatigue, feeling warm, and being unable to gain weight despite a good appetite. Which laboratory result would most likely be expected?
(A)	
Decreased TSH with elevated T3 or T4 levels
(B)	
Elevated TSH with normal T3 or T4 levels
(C)	
Elevated TSH with euthyroid levels of T3 and T4
(D)	
Increased T3 levels with decreased T4 levels
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
102.	 (A) Decreased TSH with elevated T3 or T4 levels
The patient's constellation of symptoms—
persistent fatigue, heat intolerance ("warm 
body"), and weight loss despite a good or increased 
appetite—strongly suggests a hypermetabolic 
state consistent with hyperthyroidism. This 
condition is caused by an excess of circulating 
thyroid hormones (T3 and T4). The endocrine 
regulation of the thyroid gland is governed by 
a negative feedback loop. The pituitary gland 
secretes Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH), 
which prompts the thyroid to produce T3 and T4. 
In primary hyperthyroidism (the most common 
cause, such as Graves' disease), the thyroid 
gland itself autonomously overproduces these 
hormones. The resulting high levels of T3 and 
T4 in the blood then feed back to the pituitary 
gland, suppressing its production and release 
of TSH. Therefore, the classic and expected 
laboratory profile for primary hyperthyroidism 
is a low or suppressed TSH level in the presence 
of elevated free T4 and/or T3 levels.

Based on the observation that a surgeon could retract the hernial sac but not its contents during examination, what type of hernia does the image likely depict?
(A)	
Incarcerated hernia
(B)	
Reduction en masse
(C)	
Sliding hernia
(D)	
Maydl's
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
130.	 (B) Reduction en masse
The image and the description portray a specific 
and dangerous complication known as reduction 
en masse. This occurs when an incarcerated or 
strangulated hernia is forcibly reduced without 
first ensuring that the contents of the sac are 
freed from the constricting neck of the hernia. 
The entire hernial sac, along with its trapped 
contents, is pushed as a single unit back through 
the fascial defect into the preperitoneal or intra-
abdominal space. This creates a misleading 
appearance of a successful reduction because the 
external lump disappears. However, the bowel 
loop within the sac remains incarcerated and 
strangulated by the tight hernia neck, leading 
to persistent ischemia and eventual gangrene 
if not recognized and surgically corrected. The 
surgeon's ability to retract the sac without its 
contents being reducible is a key feature of this 
phenomenon.
For a 52-year-old female patient with HER-2 positive breast cancer showing resistance to trastuzumab, which treatment option is being considered next by the oncologist?
(A)	
Lapatinib
(B)	
Sorafenib
(C)	
Vemurafenib
(D)	
Erlotinib
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
131.	 (A) Lapatinib
Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody that 
targets the extracellular domain of the HER2 
receptor and is a cornerstone of therapy for 
HER2-positive breast cancer. However, acquired 
resistance to trastuzumab can develop. In this 
setting, alternative HER2-targeted agents are 
employed. Lapatinib is an oral small-molecule 
tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that targets 
the intracellular kinase domain of both the 
HER2 receptor and the epidermal growth 
factor receptor (EGFR). By blocking the 
intracellular signaling cascade, lapatinib can 
overcome resistance to the extracellularly acting 
trastuzumab. It is often used in combination 
with chemotherapy for patients with advanced 
or metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer 
that has progressed on a trastuzumab-based 
regimen. The other drugs listed are TKIs that 
target different pathways: sorafenib is a multi-
kinase inhibitor, vemurafenib targets BRAF, 
and erlotinib targets EGFR.

A 45-year-old male presents with a diagnosis of acute diverticulitis, which was managed with nothing by mouth (NPO), IV cephalosporin, and metronidazole. While the patient reports decreased left lower quadrant pain, it persists. He no longer has diarrhea, and a CT scan is recommended. (A)

(B)	
Family history
(C)	
Low-grade leukocytosis
(D)	
Abscess on CT
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
135.	 (D) Abscess on CT
The management of acute diverticulitis depends 
on its severity. Uncomplicated diverticulitis 
is typically managed conservatively with 
antibiotics. However, the development of 
complications is an indication for more 
aggressive management, including potential 
surgery. The finding of a pericolic abscess on a 
CT scan represents a complicated diverticulitis 
(Hinchey stage I or II). While small abscesses 
(<4 cm) can sometimes be managed with 
antibiotics alone, larger abscesses often require 
percutaneous drainage. The presence of a 
complicated episode, such as one involving 
an abscess, significantly increases the risk of 
recurrence and future complications. Therefore, 
after the acute episode has resolved, the presence 
of an abscess is a strong relative indication for 
recommending an elective sigmoid colectomy 
to prevent further episodes. A second episode 
of uncomplicated diverticulitis is also an 
indication, but an abscess is a more compelling 
reason after the first episode.

What are the appropriate treatment options for a child exhibiting symptoms of a six-day fever, strawberry tongue, conjunctival congestion, and skin peeling?
(A)	
Aspirin + clopidogrel
(B)	
Warfarin
(C)

(D)

The patient's constellation of symptoms—
prolonged 
fever 
(>5 
days), 
strawberry 
tongue (oral mucosal changes), conjunctival 
congestion, and skin peeling (desquamation of 
the extremities)—are classic diagnostic criteria 
for Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki disease is an 
acute, self-limited vasculitis of childhood that 
primarily affects the medium-sized arteries. Its 
most serious complication is the development 
of coronary artery aneurysms, which can lead

What is the most appropriate immediate response when a patient’s blood pressure suddenly falls to 40 mmHg during squint surgery?
(A)	
Give atropine
(B)	
Increase level of anesthesia
(C)	
Ask the surgeon to stop the surgery
(D)	
Give adrenaline
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
177.	 (C) Ask the surgeon to stop the surgery
During squint (strabismus) surgery, traction on 
the extraocular muscles—especially the medial 
rectus—can trigger the oculocardiac reflex 
(OCR). This is a trigemino-vagal reflex in which 
stimulation of the ophthalmic division of the 
trigeminal nerve leads to increased vagal tone via 
the vagus nerve. The result can be bradycardia, 
hypotension, arrhythmias, or even asystole.
If the patient’s blood pressure suddenly 
falls to 40 mmHg intraoperatively, the most 
immediate and crucial step is to stop the 
surgical stimulus. Removing the traction on 
the extraocular muscle often reverses the reflex 
rapidly.
After stopping the stimulus:
1.	 Ensure adequate oxygenation.
2.	 Deepen anesthesia if required.
3.	 Administer atropine if bradycardia persists.
Adrenaline is not the first-line response unless 
there is cardiac arrest or severe unresponsive 
hypotension.
Therefore, the most appropriate immediate 
action when sudden hypotension occurs during 
squint surgery is to ask the surgeon to stop the 
surgery.

(B)

(C)

(D)

178.	 (B) Endotracheal tube
The Murphy's eye is a specific design feature 
found on most modern endotracheal tubes 
(ETTs). It is a small, oval-shaped hole located 
on the side of the ETT, opposite the beveled 
tip. The primary purpose of the Murphy's eye 
is to serve as a safety feature. If the main distal 
opening of the ETT becomes occluded, for 
example, by pressing against the tracheal wall 
or by a mucus plug, the Murphy's eye provides 
an alternative, patent opening through which 
gas can still flow, thereby preventing a complete 
airway obstruction and allowing for continued 
ventilation of the patient. This feature is unique 
to endotracheal tubes and is not found on other 
airway devices like a laryngeal mask airway 
(LMA) or on instruments like laryngoscopes.
A patient under general anesthesia suddenly develops tachycardia, sweating, high blood pressure, and rapid breathing. What is the most appropriate immediate action to take in this situation?

IV beta-blocker
(B)	
Abandon the surgery
(C)	
Deepen the plane of Anaesthesia
(D)

The sudden onset of tachycardia, hypertension, 
sweating, and tachypnea in a patient under 
general anesthesia is a classic presentation of 
a sympathetic nervous system response to a 
painful surgical stimulus. This indicates that 
the current level of anesthesia is insufficient 
to block the patient's autonomic reflexes to 
the surgical procedure. The patient is "light," 
meaning the plane of anesthesia is too shallow. 
The best and most immediate step for the 
anesthesiologist to take is to deepen the plane of 
anesthesia. This can be achieved by increasing 
the concentration of the volatile anesthetic 
agent being administered or by giving a bolus 
of an intravenous anesthetic agent like propofol 
or an opioid like fentanyl. This will rapidly 
suppress the sympathetic response, control 
the hemodynamic changes, and ensure the 
patient remains adequately anesthetized for the 
remainder of the procedure.

148.	 (C) Rubella
Perinatal (vertical) transmission rates vary 
among infections:
1.	 CMV is the most common congenital viral 
infection. Primary maternal infection has 
a transmission rate of about 30–40%, and 
even higher in later pregnancy.
2.	 HIV has a transmission rate of 15–45% 
without treatment, but this can be reduced

4.	 Transmission mainly occurs during primary

dramatically 
reduced 
the 
incidence

in vaccinated populations.

occurrence of perinatal transmission is lower 
compared to CMV and untreated HIV.
Therefore, among the given options, 
the condition with the lowest occurrence of 
perinatal transmission is Rubella.

What are clue cells?
(A)	
Vaginal epithelial cells lined by bacteria
(B)	
Cervical epithelial cells lined by bacteria
(C)	
Uterine endothelial cells lined by bacteria
(D)	
Abdominal cells lined by bacteria
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
150.	 (A) Vaginal epithelial cells lined by bacteria
Clue cells are the single most reliable microscopic 
finding for the diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis 
(BV). They are defined as vaginal squamous 
epithelial cells that are so densely coated with 
adherent coccobacilli (primarily Gardnerella 
vaginalis and other BV-associated anaerobes) 
that the borders of the epithelial cells become 
obscured and indistinct. This dense bacterial 
coating gives the cells a characteristic stippled 
or granular appearance when viewed under a 
microscope on a saline wet mount of the vaginal 
discharge. The presence of clue cells in more 
than 20% of the epithelial cells on the slide is 
one of the four Amsel criteria for diagnosing BV 
and is considered the most specific sign. These 
cells are exfoliated from the vaginal mucosa, not 
the cervix, uterus, or abdomen.

A 15-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea, development of pubic hair, prepubertal breasts, a blind-ending vagina, clitoromegaly, normal testosterone levels, and a 46 XY karyotype. What condition explains these clinical findings?

152.	 (C) 5-alpha reductase deficiency
The patient has a 46,XY karyotype but has 
developed along female lines, indicating a 
disorder of sex development. The key to the 
diagnosis is the specific pattern of androgen 
effects. Normal testosterone levels indicate 
functional testes. The development of pubic hair 
and clitoromegaly at puberty demonstrates that 
the body is responsive to testosterone. However, 
the external genitalia were female-appearing 
at birth (blind-ending vagina), and breast 
development has not occurred. This specific 
dissociation between the effects of testosterone 
and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is the hallmark 
of 5-alpha reductase deficiency. In this 
condition, the enzyme that converts testosterone 
to the more potent DHT is absent. Since DHT is 
required for the masculinization of the external 
genitalia in utero, these individuals are born 
with female or ambiguous genitalia. At puberty, 
the surge in testosterone drives virilization 
(pubic hair, clitoromegaly, voice deepening) but 
does not lead to breast development.

What is the underlying reason for the absence of fructose in seminal fluid?
(A)	
Congenital absence of seminal vesicle
(B)	
Ejaculatory duct obstruction
(C)	
Both of the above
(D)	
None of the above
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
154.	 (C) Both of the above
Fructose is the primary source of energy 
for sperm motility and is produced almost 
exclusively by the seminal vesicles. The seminal 
vesicles secrete their fructose-rich fluid into 
the ejaculatory ducts. Therefore, the absence of 
fructose in a semen analysis (azoospermia with 
low volume and acidic pH) points to a problem 
with either the production or the transport of 
seminal vesicle fluid. This can be caused by two 
main conditions. First, a congenital bilateral 
absence of the seminal vesicles (often associated 
with congenital bilateral absence of the vas 
deferens, a condition linked to the cystic fibrosis 
gene) would mean that fructose is not produced. 
Second, a bilateral ejaculatory duct obstruction 
would prevent the fluid from the seminal 
vesicles and the sperm from the vas deferens 
from entering the urethra and being ejaculated. 
In either case, the resulting ejaculate would be 
low in volume and fructose-negative.

Which of the following is not a cause of non-immune hydrops?

158.	 (B) ABO incompatibility
Hydrops fetalis is the excessive accumulation of 
fluid in the fetal extravascular compartments. 
It is broadly divided into immune and non-
immune causes. Immune hydrops is caused 
by alloimmune hemolytic disease of the fetus 
and newborn, most classically due to Rh(D) 
incompatibility, although other red cell antibodies 
can be responsible. ABO incompatibility is a 
cause of hemolytic disease, but it very rarely, 
if ever, leads to the severe anemia required to 
cause hydrops fetalis. In contrast, non-immune 
hydrops fetalis (NIHF) accounts for about 90% 
of cases and has a wide range of causes. The 
most common etiologies include cardiovascular 
abnormalities (e.g., structural heart defects, 
arrhythmias), chromosomal anomalies, and 
severe fetal anemia from non-immune causes. 
These causes of anemia include infections like 
Parvovirus B19 (A), which causes aplastic crisis, 
and alpha-thalassemia major (D), which leads 
to a complete inability to produce functional 
hemoglobin.
Which of the following statements is incorrect?
(A)

(B)

(C)

(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
159.	 (A) Zygote is Bipotential at 8 weeks
Sexual differentiation is a sequential process. 
Initially, the embryo, including the gonads, 
is bipotential, meaning it has the potential to 
develop into either a male or a female. This 
bipotential state exists up to around the 6th 
or 7th week of gestation. The presence of the 
SRY gene on the Y chromosome then directs 
the bipotential gonad to differentiate into a 
testis. The developing testis produces two 
key hormones: testosterone and Müllerian-
inhibiting substance (MIS). MIS, also known as 
Click Here to Buy book on Amazon
BK 
INICET Examination Paper
anti-Müllerian hormone, causes the regression 
of the Müllerian ducts (the precursors of the 
female internal genitalia). Testosterone supports 
the development of the Wolffian ducts (WD) 
into the male internal genitalia (epididymis, vas 
deferens, seminal vesicles). Testosterone is also 
converted to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which 
is essential for the development of the male 
external genitalia. The zygote itself is genetically 
determined at fertilization, and by 8 weeks, 
differentiation is already underway.
What is the outcome of the absence or mutation of the SRY gene?
(A)	
Agenesis of testis
(B)	
Undescended testis
(C)	
Hydrocele testis
(D)	
None of the above
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
160.	 (A) Agenesis of testis
The SRY (Sex-determining Region Y) gene, 
located on the Y chromosome, is the master 
switch that initiates male development. In a 
46,XY embryo, the SRY gene product acts as a 
transcription factor that directs the bipotential, 
undifferentiated gonads to develop into testes. If 
the SRY gene is absent (e.g., due to a deletion 
from the Y chromosome) or has a loss-of-
function mutation, the signal for testicular 
development is never initiated. In the absence 
of this SRY signal, the undifferentiated gonads 
will follow their default developmental pathway 
and differentiate into ovaries, and the embryo 
will develop along female lines despite having 
a 46,XY karyotype. This condition is known as 
46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis, or Swyer 
syndrome. Therefore, the direct outcome of an 
absent or non-functional SRY gene is the failure 
of the testes to form, which can be described as 
agenesis of the testis.

Morphine is a potent opioid analgesic commonly

and life-threatening adverse effect of opioid 
administration is respiratory depression, which 
can progress to apnea and respiratory arrest. 
The patient's development of respiratory 
distress after receiving morphine is a clear 
sign of opioid-induced toxicity. The specific 
and life-saving antidote for opioid overdose 
is naloxone. Naloxone is a pure, competitive 
opioid receptor antagonist. It has a high affinity 
for mu-opioid receptors and works by rapidly 
displacing the opioid agonist (morphine, in 
this case) from these receptors in the central 
nervous system. This action promptly reverses 
the effects of the opioid, most critically the 
respiratory depression. Epinephrine (A) is used 
for anaphylaxis, atropine (B) for bradycardia or 
cholinergic poisoning, and pralidoxime (C) for 
organophosphate poisoning.

Massive blood transfusion (usually defined

Which one of the following is not transmitted during the perinatal period?
(A)	
CMV
(B)	
Rubella
(C)	
Meningitis
(D)	
Hepatitis B
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
165.	 (C) Meningitis
Perinatal transmission refers to infections 
that are passed from mother to child during 
pregnancy (transplacental), during labor and 
delivery, or shortly after birth. Several infectious 
agents are well known to be transmitted in this 
period.
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is one of the most 
common congenital infections. It is transmitted 
transplacentally and can also be acquired during 
delivery or through breast milk. Rubella virus 
is transmitted transplacentally when a mother 
acquires primary infection during pregnancy, 
especially in the first trimester, leading to 
congenital rubella syndrome. Hepatitis B virus 
is commonly transmitted during childbirth from 
an infected mother to her newborn, particularly 
if the mother is HBsAg positive.
In contrast, meningitis is not a specific 
infectious agent but a clinical condition 
characterized by inflammation of the meninges. 
While certain organisms causing neonatal 
meningitis (such as Group B Streptococcus) may 
be transmitted during birth, meningitis itself is 
not transmitted as a disease entity.
Therefore, among the options given, 
meningitis is not transmitted during the 
perinatal period.
What is the lowest possibility of perinatal transmission?

(B)	
HSV
(C)

(D)

166.	 (A) Hepatitis A.
Perinatal transmission refers to infection passed 
from mother to infant during pregnancy, at 
the time of delivery, or shortly after birth. The 
likelihood of vertical transmission varies among 
infectious agents.
1.	 Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is one of the 
most common congenital infections. It is 
frequently transmitted transplacentally, 
especially 
during 
primary 
maternal 
infection, with a transmission rate of 
around 30–40%.
2.	 Herpes simplex virus (HSV) can also be 
transmitted perinatally, particularly during 
vaginal delivery if the mother has an 
active genital lesion. In primary maternal 
infection near term, the transmission risk 
may reach 30–50%.
3.	 Rubella is transmitted transplacentally 
when maternal infection occurs during 
pregnancy, especially in the first trimester, 
with a very high fetal transmission rate.
In contrast, Hepatitis A is primarily transmitted 
through the fecal–oral route. Vertical or perinatal 
transmission of Hepatitis A is extremely 
rare. Although maternal infection may occur 
during pregnancy, it seldom leads to congenital 
infection.
Therefore, among the given options, Hepatitis 
A has the lowest possibility of perinatal 
transmission.

168.	 (A) Langer's lines
The image shows characteristic linear patterns 
over the face and body that correspond to the 
natural orientation of collagen fibers within 
the dermis. These are known as Langer’s lines, 
also called skin tension lines. They represent 
the direction of maximum skin tension and are 
clinically important in surgical practice.
Incisions made parallel to Langer’s lines 
tend to heal better and produce less noticeable 
scars because they follow the natural alignment 
of collagen fibers. In contrast, incisions made 
perpendicular to these lines are more likely to 
gape and result in wider scars.
Blaschko’s lines represent embryologic cell 
migration patterns and are typically invisible 
unless highlighted by certain skin disorders. 
Dermatomes represent areas of skin supplied by 
specific spinal nerves, and Hinderer’s lines are 
used in cosmetic facial surgery.
The patterns shown in the image are 
continuous, curved, and symmetrical over 
the body and face, consistent with the classic 
depiction of Langer’s lines. Therefore, the 
structure identified in the image is Langer’s 
lines.

Which of the following is not associated with non-scarring alopecia?

172.	 (C) Frontal fibrosing alopecia
Alopecias are broadly classified into non-
scarring and scarring (cicatricial) types. In non-
scarring alopecias, the hair follicle is preserved, 
and hair regrowth is possible. This category 
includes alopecia areata (an autoimmune 
condition), androgenetic alopecia (male and 
female pattern baldness), and telogen effluvium 
(diffuse shedding after a stressor). In contrast, 
scarring alopecias involve inflammation and 
fibrosis that destroy the hair follicle, leading to 
permanent hair loss. Frontal fibrosing alopecia 
is a classic example of a primary cicatricial 
alopecia. It is considered a clinical variant of 
lichen planopilaris and is characterized by a 
progressive, band-like recession of the frontal 
and temporal hairline, with associated loss 
of eyebrows, and evidence of perifollicular 
inflammation and fibrosis on histology.

Statement 1 A 59-year-old patient presents with flaccid bullae. Histopathology shows a suprabasal acantholytic split. 
Statement 2 The row of tombstones appearance is diagnostic of Pemphigus vulgaris. Which of the following statements is correct?
(A)	
Statement 1 is incorrect
(B)	
Statements 1 & 2 are correct, 2 is not explaining 1
(C)	
Statement 1 and 2 is incorrect
(D)	
Statements 1 and 2 are correct and 2 is the correct explanation for 1
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
174.	 (D) Statements 1 and 2 are correct and 2 is the 
correct explanation for 1
Both statements describe classic features of 
pemphigus vulgaris, a severe autoimmune 
blistering disease. Statement 1 is correct: 
Pemphigus 
vulgaris 
is 
characterized 
by 
autoantibodies against desmoglein 3, leading 
to the loss of adhesion between keratinocytes 
(acantholysis). This process occurs just above 
the basal cell layer, resulting in a fragile, 
suprabasal split on histopathology, which 
clinically manifests as easily ruptured, flaccid 
bullae and erosions. Statement 2 is also correct 
and directly explains the histological finding 
in Statement 1. The "row of tombstones" 
appearance is the specific histopathological 
term for this suprabasal split. It describes the 
intact basal keratinocytes that remain attached 
to the basement membrane, resembling a row of 
tombstones, while the overlying epidermis has 
lifted off due to acantholysis. Therefore, both 
statements are correct, and the second statement 
provides the specific name for the histological 
finding described in the first.

A 40-year-old female patient experiencing vulvovaginal itching is currently prescribed an antidiabetic medication. Which of the following medications could likely be associated with her symptoms?

Vulvovaginal itching is a hallmark symptom 
of vulvovaginal candidiasis (a yeast infection). 
Canagliflozin is an oral antidiabetic drug 
that belongs to the class of sodium-glucose 
cotransporter 
2 
(SGLT2) 
inhibitors. 
The 
mechanism of action of SGLT2 inhibitors is 
to block the reabsorption of glucose in the 
kidneys, thereby promoting the excretion 
of large amounts of glucose in the urine

in the genitourinary tract creates a favorable 
environment for the proliferation of yeast, 
particularly Candida albicans. Consequently, a 
common and well-recognized side effect of all 
SGLT2 inhibitors, including canagliflozin, is a 
significantly increased risk of developing genital 
mycotic infections in both men and women. 
Metformin (A), linagliptin (C), and liraglutide 
(D) work through different mechanisms and are 
not associated with this specific side effect.
On which of the following is the SRY gene located?
(A)	
Y chromosome short arm
(B)	
Y chromosome long arm
(C)	
X chromosome short arm
(D)	
X chromosome long arm
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
145.	 (A) Y chromosome short arm
The SRY gene, which stands for the Sex-
determining Region Y, is the master gene 
responsible for initiating male development 
in mammals. It acts as a transcription factor 
that triggers a cascade of downstream gene 
expression leading to the development of the 
undifferentiated embryonic gonads into testes. 
In the absence of a functional SRY gene, the 
gonads will default to developing into ovaries. 
This critical gene is located on the short arm (p 
arm) of the Y chromosome. Its presence on the Y 
chromosome is the fundamental genetic reason 
why the inheritance of a Y chromosome typically 
leads to a male phenotype. The long arm (q arm) 
of the Y chromosome contains other genes, 
including those involved in spermatogenesis, 
but the SRY gene is specifically on the short arm.
In puberty, what is the primary reason for the occurrence of menorrhagia?
(A)	
Endometriosis
(B)	
Anovulation
(C)	
Malignancy
(D)	
Primary amenorrhea
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2023
146.	 (B) Anovulation
Menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding) and 
irregular bleeding are very common in the 
first few years after menarche. The primary 
underlying reason for this is the immaturity 
of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) 
axis. In early puberty, the positive feedback 
mechanisms required to trigger the mid-cycle 
luteinizing hormone (LH) surge are not yet 
fully established. This frequently results in 
anovulatory cycles, where a follicle develops 
and produces estrogen, but ovulation does 
not occur, and a corpus luteum is not formed. 
In the absence of the progesterone that would 
normally be produced by the corpus luteum, 
the endometrium is exposed to prolonged, 
unopposed estrogen. This leads to excessive 
endometrial proliferation, which eventually 
outgrows its blood supply and breaks down 
irregularly and heavily. This anovulatory 
bleeding is the most common cause of abnormal 
uterine bleeding in adolescents.

Which of the following drains directly into the

AAns

(C) Left renal vein
The venous drainage pattern on the left and right sides of the body is asymmetrical. The left renal vein is a large vein that travels from the left kidney to drain directly into the inferior vena cava (IVC). It is notable for receiving blood from several other veins on the left side, including the left gonadal (testicular or ovarian) vein and the left adrenal (suprarenal) vein. 12.	 Which portion of the inguinal canal is 
constituted by fibers from the internal oblique 
and transversus abdominis muscles?
(A)	Anterior Wall 
(B)	 Roof 
(C)	Floor 
(D)	Both A & C 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Roof
The inguinal canal is an oblique passage in the lower anterior abdominal wall with four boundaries: a roof, a floor, and anterior and posterior walls. The roof (superior wall) of the inguinal canal is formed by the arching inferior fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. These muscle fibers arch over the spermatic cord (in males) or the round ligament (in females) and then descend to form the conjoint tendon, which reinforces the posterior wall medially. The anterior wall is primarily formed by the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle. The floor is formed by the inguinal ligament. Therefore, the arching fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles are correctly identified as forming the roof of the inguinal canal.

PHYSIOLOGY
14.	 What contributes to the zero phase of the action 
potential in the SA node? 
(A)	Calcium (Ca) only 
(B)	 Sodium (Na) 
(C)	Potassium (K) 
(D)	Calcium (Ca) and Sodium (Na)
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Calcium (Ca) only
The action potential of the sinoatrial (SA) node, the heart's natural pacemaker, differs significantly from that of ventricular myocytes. The upstroke, or phase 0, of the SA node action potential is primarily mediated by the influx of calcium ions (Ca²⁺) through L-type calcium channels. This is a slower process compared to the rapid sodium influx that characterizes phase 0 in ventricular and atrial muscle cells, which is why SA nodal action potentials have a less steep upstroke. While sodium influx through the "funny" current (If) is crucial for the pacemaker potential (phase 4) that brings the cell to threshold, the depolarization phase itself (phase 0) is calcium-dependent. Potassium efflux is responsible for repolarization (phase 3). 
15.	 With respect to glucose entry into cells, which 
organ or tissue does not rely on insulin for 
glucose uptake? 
(A)	RBC 
(B)	 Pancreas 
(C)	Adipose tissue 
(D)	Hepatocytes 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Adipose tissue
Most tissues in the body require insulin for glucose uptake, but some have insulin-independent mechanisms. This question asks to identify the tissue that is insulin-dependent. Adipose tissue and skeletal muscle primarily use the GLUT4 transporter, which is insulin-sensitive. In the presence of insulin, GLUT4 translocates from intracellular vesicles to the cell membrane to facilitate glucose entry. In contrast, red blood cells (RBCs) use GLUT1, the brain uses GLUT1 and GLUT3, the pancreas (beta-cells) uses GLUT2, and hepatocytes (liver cells) use GLUT2. All of these transporters (GLUT1, GLUT2, GLUT3) are insulin-independent, meaning they can take up glucose from the blood without the need for insulin signaling. Therefore, adipose tissue is the exception as its glucose uptake is critically dependent on insulin.
16.	 What is the main mechanism through which 
parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases blood 
calcium levels?
(A)	Increased renal reabsorption of calcium 
(B)	 Stimulation of osteoclast activity 
(C)	Stimulates Vitamin D synthesis 
(D)	All are true 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) All are true
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is the principal regulator of calcium homeostasis in the body, and it employs multiple mechanisms to increase serum calcium levels. Firstly, PTH acts directly on bone to stimulate osteoclast activity, which leads to the resorption of bone matrix and the release of calcium and phosphate into the bloodstream. Secondly, PTH acts on the kidneys to increase the reabsorption of calcium in the distal convoluted tubules, thereby reducing urinary calcium excretion. Thirdly, PTH stimulates the renal enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which is responsible for converting inactive 25-hydroxyvitamin D into its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). Calcitriol then acts on the intestines to significantly increase the absorption of dietary calcium. Since all three of these mechanisms are primary actions of PTH that contribute to elevating blood calcium, all the statements are true. 
17.	 The diagram illustrates neuronal physiology. 
What processes occur at labels 3 to 4 in the 
diagram?
(A)	Na+ entering the cell 
(B)	 Na+ exiting the cell 
(C)	K+ exiting the cell 
(D)	K entering the cell 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) K+ exiting the cell
The diagram illustrates a typical action potential in a neuron. The phase from label 3 to label 4 represents repolarization, the process by which the membrane potential returns to its negative resting state after the peak of depolarization. This phase is initiated by the inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels and the opening of voltage-gated potassium channels. The opening of these potassium channels allows positively charged potassium ions (K+) to diffuse out of the cell, down their steep electrochemical gradient. This efflux of positive charge from the neuron's interior is what causes the membrane potential to become negative again. The initial depolarization phase (before label 3) is caused by the rapid influx of Na+ ions entering the cell. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is responsible for maintaining the long-term ion gradients but is not the primary driver of the rapid repolarization phase. 
18.	 Which component of the nerve fiber provides 
the motor innervation to the muscle spindle?
(A)	Alpha 
(B)	 Beta 
(C)	Gamma 
(D)	Delta 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Gamma
Muscle spindles are proprioceptive sensory organs within skeletal muscles that detect changes in muscle length and the rate of change in length. While they are primarily sensory, their intrafusal muscle fibers (specialized fibers within the spindle capsule) receive motor innervation to regulate their sensitivity. This motor supply is provided by gamma motor neurons. The axons of gamma motor neurons terminate on the polar ends of the intrafusal fibers, causing them to contract. This contraction stretches the central, non-contractile sensory region of the spindle, thereby increasing its sensitivity to stretch of the main muscle. In contrast, alpha motor neurons (A) innervate the extrafusal muscle fibers, which are the main force-generating fibers of the muscle. This co-activation of alpha and gamma motor neurons allows the spindle to remain sensitive to stretch across a wide range of muscle lengths. 
19.	 Which of the following statements most 
accurately explains the mechanism of coughing? 
1	
Forceful expiration against an open glottis 
2	
Expiration against an open glottis 
3	
Deep inspiration against a closed glottis 
4	
Removing harmful substances. 
(A)	1,4 
(B)	 1,2,3 
(C)	2,4 
(D)	2,3 
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) 1,4
A cough is a protective reflex that helps clear the airways of irritants, mucus, and foreign particles. The process begins with a deep inspiration, followed by the closure of the glottis. Next, a powerful contraction of the expiratory muscles (abdominal and internal intercostal) builds up high intrathoracic pressure. The final step is the abrupt opening of the glottis, resulting in a forceful expiration that carries material out of the respiratory tract. Statement 2 is incorrect because the expiration is forceful, not passive, and it occurs after the glottis opens, not against an already open glottis. Statement 3 is incorrect as the inspiration phase occurs with an open glottis to allow air entry.

30.	 A 26-year-old woman presents with a bleeding

The key information in this scenario is the autosomal dominant inheritance pattern of the bleeding disorder, affecting both males (father) and females (patient and her sister). 32.	 Which stain produces the characteristic brown 
coloration observed in HER2/neu-positive 
breast carcinoma cells?
(A)	FITC 
(B)	 Phycoerythrin 
(C)	Cyanate dye 
(D)	Diaminobenzidine (DAB) 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) Diaminobenzidine (DAB)
The image shows the result of an immunohistochemistry (IHC) stain, a technique used to detect the presence of specific proteins in tissue sections. For HER2/neu testing in breast cancer, a primary antibody against the HER2 protein is applied to the tissue. This is followed by a secondary antibody linked to an enzyme, most commonly horseradish peroxidase (HRP). To visualize the location of the HRP-linked antibody, a chromogen substrate is added. The most widely used chromogen in this system is 3,3'-Diaminobenzidine (DAB). The HRP enzyme catalyzes the oxidation of DAB, which results in the formation of a permanent, insoluble, dark brown precipitate at the site of the target protein (the HER2 receptor on the cell membrane). FITC and phycoerythrin are fluorescent dyes used in immunofluorescence, not IHC with a light microscope. 
33.	 A patient was evaluated for hepatic cirrhosis and

•

What is the most likely conclusion?

(C)	Post-vaccination status 
(D)	Remote infection with complete recovery 
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) Remote infection with complete recovery
Interpreting hepatitis B serology requires understanding each marker. HBsAg is the surface antigen, indicating current infection. Anti-HBs is the antibody to the surface antigen, indicating immunity from vaccination or recovery. Anti-HBc is the core antibody; IgM indicates acute infection, while total (mostly IgG) indicates past or current infection. In this case, HBsAg is negative, ruling out active chronic infection. Total Anti-HBc is reactive, indicating the patient has been exposed to the virus at some point. However, the patient is Anti-HBs negative. This pattern (HBsAg negative, Anti-HBc positive, Anti-HBs negative) is most consistent with a remote infection where the level of protective Anti-HBs antibodies has waned over time to undetectable levels. It is less likely to be the window period, as IgM Anti-HBc would be positive. It is not a chronic carrier state because HBsAg is negative. It is not a post-vaccination status, as vaccination only produces Anti-HBs, not Anti-HBc. 
34.	 Which of the following statements about sickle 
cell anemia is correct? 
(A)	Low mechanical fragility, high osmotic 
fragility 
(B)	 High mechanical fragility, high osmotic 
fragility 
(C)	Low mechanical fragility, low osmotic 
fragility 
(D)	High mechanical fragility, Low osmotic 
fragility 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) High mechanical fragility, Low osmotic fragility
Sickle cell anemia is characterized by the presence of hemoglobin S, which polymerizes under low oxygen conditions, causing red blood cells (RBCs) to deform into a rigid, sickle shape. This rigidity makes the cells highly susceptible to damage as they pass through narrow capillaries, leading to a high mechanical fragility and subsequent hemolysis. Osmotic fragility, on the other hand, tests the RBC's ability to withstand hypotonic solutions. Sickled cells are dehydrated and have a decreased surface-area-to-volume ratio. This makes them relatively more resistant to swelling and lysis in hypotonic solutions compared to normal biconcave discs. Therefore, they exhibit low osmotic fragility. This combination of high mechanical fragility (leading to in vivo hemolysis) and low osmotic fragility (an in vitro finding) is a characteristic feature of sickle cell anemia.

10.	 In which region do the fibers of the internal

Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic medication
