(D)	Glucose 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Calcium
Glycogen phosphorylase is the key enzyme in glycogenolysis, catalyzing the breakdown of glycogen into glucose-1-phosphate. Its activity is tightly regulated by both allosteric mechanisms and covalent modification (phosphorylation). In muscle tissue, calcium ions (Ca²⁺) act as a crucial allosteric activator. During muscle contraction, Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This Ca²⁺ binds to calmodulin, which is a subunit of the enzyme phosphorylase kinase. The Ca²⁺ calmodulin complex activates phosphorylase kinase, which in turn phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase, synchronizing glycogen breakdown with the muscle's immediate energy needs. In contrast, ATP and glucose-6-phosphate are allosteric inhibitors of glycogen phosphorylase, signaling a state of high energy. Glucose is also an inhibitor, particularly in the liver. 
21.	 Hybridoma technology uses which of the 
following? 
(A)	HMP shunt 
(B)	 TCA cycle 
(C)	Purine Salvage pathway 
(D)	Glycolysis 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Purine Salvage pathway
Hybridoma technology is a method for producing large numbers of identical antibodies (monoclonal antibodies). It involves fusing antibody-producing B cells with immortal myeloma (cancerous plasma) cells. A crucial step in this process is the selection of fused hybridoma cells from the unfused myeloma cells. This is accomplished using the HAT medium (Hypoxanthine-Aminopterin-Thymidine). Aminopterin blocks the de novo purine synthesis pathway. This forces the cells to rely on the purine salvage pathway to synthesize nucleotides and survive. The myeloma cells used are specifically chosen because they are deficient in an enzyme of the salvage pathway, hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). Therefore, unfused myeloma cells cannot survive in the HAT medium. However, when fused with a B cell, the resulting hybridoma inherits a functional salvage pathway from the B cell and can thus survive and proliferate, allowing for the selection of the desired antibody-producing hybrid cells. 
22.	 Which of the following is not involved in the 
repair of DNA double-strand breaks? 
(A)	ATP 	
(B)	 RAD 51 
(C)	ATM 	
(D)	Ku 70 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) ATP
DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are highly cytotoxic lesions that are primarily repaired by two major pathways: non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR). The proteins listed are key players in these pathways. ATM (Ataxia-Telangiectasia Mutated) is a sensor kinase that detects DSBs and initiates the signaling cascade for repair. Ku70 (along with Ku80) is a critical component of the NHEJ pathway; it binds directly to the broken DNA ends and recruits other repair factors. RAD51 is a central protein in the HR pathway, where it forms a filament on the single-stranded DNA and mediates the search for and invasion of a homologous template sequence. While ATP is required as an energy source for the enzymatic activities of many DNA repair proteins (e.g., kinases, ligases, helicases), it is not a structural or signaling component of the repair machinery itself in the same way as ATM, Ku70, and RAD51. Therefore, it does not directly "contribute" to the repair in a mechanistic sense but rather fuels the process.
23.	 The active site of an enzyme is mostly 
complementary to: 
(A)	Allosteric activator 
(B)	 Substrate 
(C)	Product 
(D)	Transition state 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Substrate
Although enzymes bind substrates, the active site is most complementary to the transition state, not the substrate itself.
According to modern enzyme theory (transition state theory), enzymes catalyze reactions by stabilizing the transition state — the high-energy, unstable intermediate formed during conversion of substrate to product. The active site is shaped and chemically arranged to bind this transition state more tightly than either the substrate or the product.
If the active site were perfectly complementary to the substrate, the enzyme would bind the substrate too tightly and would not efficiently convert it into product. Instead, by preferentially stabilizing the transition state, the enzyme lowers the activation energy and speeds up the reaction.
Allosteric activators bind at a different regulatory site, not the active site.
The product binds less strongly because it must be released after the reaction.
Therefore, the active site is most complementary to the transition state, making option (D) correct.
24.	 Regarding the entry of glucose, which body organ 
or tissue demonstrates insulin-independent 
glucose uptake, except for: 
(A)	RBC 
(B)	 Pancreas 
(C)	Adipose tissue 
(D)	Brain 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Adipose tissue
Most tissues in the body require insulin for glucose uptake, but some have insulin-independent mechanisms. This question asks to identify the tissue that is insulin-dependent. Adipose tissue and skeletal muscle primarily use the GLUT4 transporter, which is insulin-sensitive. In the presence of insulin, GLUT4 translocates from intracellular vesicles to the cell membrane to facilitate glucose entry. In contrast, red blood cells (RBCs) use GLUT1, the brain uses GLUT1 and GLUT3, and the pancreas (beta-cells) uses GLUT2. All of these transporters (GLUT1, GLUT2, GLUT3) are insulin-independent, meaning they can take up glucose from the blood without the need for insulin signaling. Therefore, adipose tissue is the exception as its glucose uptake is critically dependent on insulin. 
25.	 2,3-BPG binds to which part of hemoglobin? 
(A)	Central part of hemoglobin 
(B)	 Outer part of hemoglobin 
(C)	Heme part of hemoglobin 
(D)	Globin part of hemoglobin 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Central part of hemoglobin
2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) binds in the central cavity of deoxyhemoglobin, between the two β-chains of the hemoglobin tetramer. This central pocket is present in the T (tense) state of hemoglobin.
2,3-BPG is negatively charged and interacts with positively charged amino acid residues (such as lysine and histidine) located in the central region of the globin chains. By binding in this cavity, 2,3-BPG stabilizes the T-state of hemoglobin, thereby reducing its affinity for oxygen and promoting oxygen release to tissues.
It does not bind to the heme portion directly. Instead, it binds to the globin chains within the central cavity, not on the outer surface.
Thus, the binding site of 2,3-BPG is the central part of hemoglobin, making option (A) correct.

Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is characterized histologically by extensive crescent formation in the glomeruli. 28.	 Following class switching, a specific antibody 
class is generated, yet IgM and IgD continue to 
be co-expressed. Which mechanism accounts 
for this?
(A)	Allelic exclusion 
(B)	 Alternate RNA splicing 
(C)	Somatic hypermutation 
(D)	Affinity maturation 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Alternate RNA splicing
Naive mature B cells, before encountering an antigen, co-express both IgM and IgD on their surface. This is not a result of class switching, which is a later, irreversible DNA recombination event that changes the constant region of the heavy chain. Instead, the co-expression of IgM and IgD is achieved through alternate RNA splicing. A single long primary RNA transcript is synthesized, which contains the variable region (VDJ) along with the constant regions for both the mu (μ for IgM) and delta (δ for IgD) heavy chains. This primary transcript is then processed in two different ways. Depending on which polyadenylation sites are used and how the RNA is spliced, either the Cμ or the Cδ segment is joined to the VDJ segment, resulting in mature mRNAs that code for either IgM or IgD heavy chains, respectively. Allelic exclusion, somatic hypermutation, and affinity maturation are other important processes in B cell development but are not responsible for this specific co-expression. 
29.	 A patient shows reduced serum transferrin 
saturation. What is the most probable underlying 
condition?
(A)	Iron Deficiency Anemia 
(B)	 Hemochromatosis 
(C)	Sideroblastic anemia 
(D)	Pernicious anemia 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Iron Deficiency Anemia
Transferrin saturation is a key laboratory parameter used to assess iron status. It is calculated as (Serum Iron / Total Iron-Binding Capacity) × 100%. In Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA), the body's iron stores are depleted. This leads to a low serum iron level. Simultaneously, the liver increases the production of transferrin (the protein that transports iron), leading to a high Total Iron-Binding Capacity (TIBC). The combination of low serum iron and high TIBC results in a significantly low transferrin saturation percentage, often below 15%. In contrast, conditions of iron overload like hemochromatosis would show a high transferrin saturation. Sideroblastic anemia can have normal or high saturation because iron is available but cannot be properly incorporated into heme. Pernicious anemia is a type of vitamin B12 deficiency anemia and does not directly affect iron saturation levels in this manner.

37.	 Following an orchidectomy, the specimen 
reveals the presence of Reinke’s crystals. What 
is the most probable diagnosis? 
(A)	Seminoma 
(B)	 Leydig Cell Tumor 
(C)	Metastasis 
(D)	Yolk Sac Tumor 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Leydig Cell Tumor
Reinke's crystals are distinctive, eosinophilic, rod-shaped or rhomboid cytoplasmic inclusions. Their presence is a pathognomonic histological feature of a Leydig cell tumor. Leydig cells are the testosterone-producing cells of the testes, and tumors arising from them are a type of sex cord-stromal tumor. These tumors can be hormonally active, leading to symptoms of androgen excess like precocious puberty in children or gynecomastia in adults. 38.	 Decreased % transferrin saturation is seen in? 
(A)	Hemochromatosis 
(B)	 Iron deficiency anemia 
(C)	Megaloblastic anemia 
(D)	Hemosiderosis 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Iron deficiency anemia
Transferrin saturation is a key laboratory parameter used to assess iron status. It is calculated as (Serum Iron / Total Iron-Binding Capacity) × 100%. In Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA), the body's iron stores are depleted. This leads to a low serum iron level. Simultaneously, the liver increases the production of transferrin (the protein that transports iron), leading to a high Total Iron-Binding Capacity (TIBC). The combination of low serum iron and high TIBC results in a significantly low transferrin saturation percentage, often below 15%. In contrast, conditions of iron overload like hemochromatosis and hemosiderosis would show a high transferrin saturation. Megaloblastic anemia is a type of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anemia and does not directly affect iron saturation levels in this manner.

39.	 Which 
recently 
approved 
anti-diabetic 
medication is indicated for patients who have 
heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and 
decreased urine output? 
(A)	Linagliptin 
(B)	 Empagliflozin 
(C)	Pioglitazone 
(D)	Degludec 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Empagliflozin
Empagliflozin is a sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor. Initially developed for treating type 2 diabetes, large cardiovascular outcome trials (like the EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial) have demonstrated significant benefits for patients with heart failure, including those with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). SGLT2 inhibitors have been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalization for heart failure, independent of their glucose-lowering effects. Their mechanism includes promoting osmotic diuresis (hence beneficial for fluid overload in heart failure) and other favorable hemodynamic and metabolic effects. Linagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor, Pioglitazone is a thiazolidinedione (which can worsen heart failure), and Degludec is a long-acting insulin analog; none of these have the specific approved indication and proven benefit for HFrEF that SGLT2 inhibitors like empagliflozin have. 
40.	 Which antigen is present in the HPV vaccine? 
(A)	E1+E2 
(B)	 E6+E7 
(C)	L1 
(D)	L2 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) L1
The currently available prophylactic HPV vaccines (Gardasil, Cervarix) are based on virus-like particles (VLPs) that are produced by recombinant DNA technology. These VLPs are composed of the L1 major capsid protein of the human papillomavirus. The L1 proteins have the ability to self-assemble into particles that mimic the structure of the native HPV virion but are non-infectious because they contain no viral DNA. This structure is highly immunogenic, inducing a strong and durable neutralizing antibody response that prevents the virus from infecting host cells. The E6 and E7 proteins are the viral oncogenes responsible for carcinogenesis but are not used in the prophylactic vaccine. The L2 protein is a minor capsid protein and is a target for next-generation vaccines but is not the primary antigen in current vaccines. 
41.	 Which drug exerts its effect by inhibiting ATP-
binding cassette (ABC) transporters? 
(A)	Nifedipine 
(B)	 Diltiazem 
(C)	Tacrolimus 
(D)	Verapamil 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) Verapamil
ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters are a family of transmembrane proteins that transport various substrates across cell membranes. One of the most well-known is P-glycoprotein (P-gp), encoded by the ABCB1 gene, which functions as an efflux pump that can extrude drugs from cells, contributing to multidrug resistance in cancer. Certain drugs can inhibit the function of these transporters. Verapamil, a calcium channel blocker, is a well-known inhibitor of P-glycoprotein. By blocking the efflux pump, verapamil can increase the intracellular concentration of other drugs that are P-gp substrates, which has been studied as a strategy to overcome chemotherapy resistance. While nifedipine and diltiazem are also calcium channel blockers, verapamil is the most classic and potent inhibitor of P-gp among the options. Tacrolimus is an immunosuppressant and is a substrate, not an inhibitor, of P-gp. 
42.	 A patient presents with exertional and nocturnal 
breathlessness, fatigue, cardiomegaly, pedal 
edema, a gallop rhythm on examination, and 
bilateral lung rales. Based on these findings, 
which medication is best suited to slow the 
progression of the disease? 
(A)	Furosemide 
(B)	 Digoxin 
(C)	Captopril 
(D)	Carvedilol 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Captopril
The patient's symptoms are classic for congestive heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. While furosemide (a diuretic) is essential for relieving symptoms of fluid overload (edema, dyspnea), it does not halt the progression of the disease. Similarly, digoxin can improve symptoms and reduce hospitalizations but does not have a proven mortality benefit. The cornerstones of therapy that have been proven to halt disease progression and reduce mortality in HFrEF are drugs that modulate the neurohormonal system, primarily the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and the sympathetic nervous system. Captopril, an ACE inhibitor, blocks the RAAS, leading to reduced vasoconstriction, decreased aldosterone levels, and prevention of adverse cardiac remodeling. Beta-blockers like carvedilol also improve survival but are typically initiated after the patient is stable on an ACE inhibitor. 
43.	 Which of the following is the disadvantage of 
oxcarbazepine over carbamazepine? 
(A)	Hepatotoxicity 
(B)	 Stevens-Johnson syndrome 
(C)	Thrombocytopenia 
(D)	Dilutional hyponatremia 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) Dilutional hyponatremia
Oxcarbazepine is a structural analog of carbamazepine, another antiepileptic drug. While oxcarbazepine is generally better tolerated, with a lower incidence of severe side effects like hepatotoxicity and skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), it has one notable disadvantage. Oxcarbazepine is associated with a significantly higher incidence of dilutional hyponatremia (low blood sodium levels) compared to carbamazepine. This is thought to be due to an increased sensitivity of the renal tubules to antidiuretic hormone (ADH), leading to water retention and dilution of serum sodium. This side effect is particularly important to monitor in elderly patients or those on other medications that can affect sodium balance, such as diuretics. Thrombocytopenia is a potential side effect of both drugs, but not a specific disadvantage of oxcarbazepine. 
44.	 All of the following drugs are used in thyroid 
storm except? 
(A)	Propranolol 
(B)	 Lugol's lodine 
(C)	Propylthiouracil 
(D)	Aspirin 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) Aspirin
Thyroid storm is a life-threatening hypermetabolic state caused by excessive release of thyroid hormones. Management involves a multi-pronged approach. Beta-blockers like propranolol are used to control the adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor). Thionamides like propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole are used to block the synthesis of new thyroid hormones. Iodine solutions, such as Lugol's iodine or potassium iodide, are given at least one hour after the thionamide to block the release of pre-formed hormone from the thyroid gland (Wolff-Chaikoff effect). Corticosteroids are also used to reduce peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and treat potential adrenal insufficiency. Aspirin, however, is contraindicated. Aspirin can displace thyroid hormone from its binding proteins, which can paradoxically increase the levels of free, active thyroid hormone in the circulation and worsen the storm. Acetaminophen is the preferred antipyretic.
45.	 A patient presents with purpura and is found 
to have isolated thrombocytopenia. Which 
tyrosine kinase inhibitor is used to treat isolated 
thrombocytopenia? 
(A)	Oprelvekin 
(B)	 Fostamatinib 
(C)	Eltrombopag 
(D)	Romiplostim 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Fostamatinib
The question asks for a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for isolated thrombocytopenia, such as Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP). Fostamatinib is an oral spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) inhibitor. In ITP, antibody-coated platelets are destroyed by macrophages in the spleen. This process is mediated by Fcγ receptors on the macrophages, and Syk is a critical signaling molecule downstream of these receptors. By inhibiting Syk, fostamatinib blocks this pathway of platelet destruction, leading to an increase in platelet count. In contrast, eltrombopag and romiplostim are thrombopoietin (TPO) receptor agonists; they work by stimulating platelet production in the bone marrow, not by inhibiting a tyrosine kinase. Oprelvekin is a recombinant form of IL-11 that also stimulates platelet production but is not a TKI.

INICET Examination Paper
(B)	 EIEC (Enteroinvasive E. coli)
(C)	Salmonella
(D)	None of the above
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Listeria
Listeria monocytogenes is a facultative intracellular bacterium renowned for its unique mode of motility within host cells. After being phagocytosed, it escapes the phagosome and replicates in the cytoplasm. It then utilizes the host cell's actin cytoskeleton for movement. A Listeria protein, ActA, recruits and polymerizes host actin filaments at one pole of the bacterium, forming a "comet tail." The continuous assembly of this actin tail propels the bacterium through the cytoplasm. This force is powerful enough to push the bacterium into neighboring cells, forming a protrusion that is then engulfed by the adjacent cell. This process of moving from cell to cell without exiting into the extracellular space is a form of transcellular spread. While some other pathogens like Shigella and EIEC also use actin-based motility, Listeria is the classic and most studied example of this phenomenon. Salmonella typically remains within vacuoles.
PSM
80.	 A longitudinal, observational, and analytical 
study is also known as?
(A)	Case Control Study
(B)	 Cohort Study
(C)	Ecological Study
(D)	Randomized Control Trial
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Cohort Study
A cohort study is a type of epidemiological study that fits the description perfectly. It is longitudinal because it follows a group of individuals (the cohort) over a period of time. It is observational because the investigator does not intervene or assign exposures but instead observes the outcomes that naturally occur. It is analytical because it is designed to test hypotheses about the relationship between exposures and outcomes by comparing the incidence of the outcome in the exposed group to the incidence in the unexposed group. A case-control study is typically retrospective and starts with the outcome. An ecological study analyzes data at the population level, not the individual level. A randomized controlled trial is an experimental (interventional) study, not an observational one.
81.	 Which type of graph is used to represent 
healthcare and disease-related data in a 
population? What are qualitative studies 
addressing health-related problems called?
(A)	Bar diagram
(B)	 Histogram
(C)	Multiple regression model
(D)	Ishikawa diagram/Fishbone diagram
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) Ishikawa diagram/Fishbone diagram
The question asks for a tool used in qualitative studies to analyze health problems. An Ishikawa diagram, also known as a fishbone diagram or cause-and-effect diagram, is a visualization tool used to explore and categorize the potential causes of a specific problem or effect. In healthcare, it is frequently used in quality improvement and root cause analysis to systematically brainstorm and display the various factors contributing to an adverse event or a health system issue. The "head" of the fish represents the problem (effect), and the "bones" represent different categories of potential causes (e.g., personnel, equipment, procedures, environment). Bar diagrams and histograms are quantitative tools for displaying frequency distributions. A multiple regression model is a statistical technique for quantitative analysis of relationships between variables.
82.	 The socially acquired learned behavior is known 
as?
(A)	Custom	
(B)	 Culture
(C)	Socialization	
(D)	Mores
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Culture
Culture is the broad and encompassing term for the set of shared attitudes, values, goals, and practices that characterizes an institution or organization, and the knowledge and beliefs that are acquired by a person as a member of a society. It represents the entire complex of socially acquired and learned behaviors, beliefs, arts, morals, laws, and customs. Customs (A) are specific, traditional ways of behaving that are part of a culture. Socialization (C) is the process by which individuals learn and internalize the values, beliefs, and norms of a given society and learn to function as members of that society. Mores (D) are customs and norms that are considered to have a moral significance and are strictly observed. While all the terms are related, "culture" is the most comprehensive term for the entire system of socially acquired behavior.

BK	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A)	Suicidal gun-shot wound
(B)	 Electrocution
(C)	Drowning
(D)	Traumatic asphyxia
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Electrocution
Cadaveric spasm, also known as instantaneous rigor, is a rare form of muscular stiffening that occurs at the moment of death, persists into the period of rigor mortis, and is often associated with violent deaths under conditions of extreme physical or emotional stress. It is thought to result from an exhaustion of ATP at the moment of death, causing the muscles to lock in their state of contraction. It is classically seen in cases of suicidal gun-shot wounds where the weapon is found firmly grasped in the deceased's hand, and in drowning cases where the victim is found clutching weeds or gravel from the riverbed. It can also occur in deaths from traumatic asphyxia. However, electrocution typically causes violent tetanic muscle contractions during the shock, followed by post-mortem flaccidity before the onset of regular rigor mortis. It is not classically associated with the instantaneous, localized stiffening of cadaveric spasm.
57.	 A patient presents with altered sensorium, 
hypotension, and constricted pinpoint pupils. 
Which of the following is most likely responsible 
for the poisoning?
(A)	Opioids
(B)	 Datura
(C)	Cocaine
(D)	Amphetamine
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Opioids
The clinical triad of central nervous system depression (altered sensorium), respiratory depression (which can lead to hypotension), and pupillary constriction (miosis or "pinpoint pupils") is the classic toxidrome for opioid poisoning. Opioids like morphine, heroin, and fentanyl stimulate the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, leading to parasympathetic activation and profound pupillary constriction. In contrast, poisoning with anticholinergic substances like Datura (B) causes mydriasis (dilated pupils), tachycardia, and dry skin. Sympathomimetic agents like cocaine (C) and amphetamine (D) also cause mydriasis, along with hypertension, tachycardia, and psychomotor agitation. Therefore, the presence of constricted pinpoint pupils is a key diagnostic feature that strongly points towards opioid toxicity as the cause of the patient's presentation.
58.	 Which of the following injuries is not commonly 
associated with a patient presenting after a road 
traffic accident (RTA)?
(A)	Contusion
(B)	 Abrasions
(C)	Laceration
(D)	Chop wound
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) Chop wound
Road traffic accidents (RTAs) can cause a wide variety of blunt and sharp force injuries. Abrasions (grazes or scrapes), contusions (bruises), and lacerations (tears or splits in the skin) are extremely common due to the impact with the vehicle, the road surface, or other objects. These are all typical blunt force injuries. A chop wound, however, is a distinct type of injury caused by a heavy weapon with a sharp cutting edge, such as an axe, hatchet, or machete. It combines features of both sharp force (incised wound) and blunt force (crushing of underlying bone and tissue). This type of injury is characteristic of a deliberate assault and would be highly unusual to sustain in a typical road traffic accident. Therefore, a chop wound is the injury least likely to be associated with an RTA.
59.	 All of the following are used in the identification 
of a dead body except:
(A)	Teeth
(B)	 Blood
(C)	Nail
(D)	Muscle
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) Muscle
Forensic identification of a deceased individual relies on unique and durable characteristics. Teeth (A) are extremely valuable for identification through dental records (forensic odontology) due to their durability and unique fillings, restorations, and morphology. Blood (B) is fundamental for DNA profiling, which provides a definitive genetic identity. Nails (C) can also be a source of DNA, and their physical characteristics (e.g., length, polish) can sometimes provide circumstantial clues. In contrast, muscle tissue (D) is not a primary tool for identification. While it can be a source of DNA, it decomposes relatively quickly compared to teeth and bones. It lacks the unique, individualizing characteristics found in dental records or fingerprints. Other tissues like bone or hair are far more useful and durable for DNA analysis in decomposed remains. Therefore, muscle is the least useful of the options listed for routine identification purposes.

61.	 Which of the following diseases is not 
transmitted by the vector shown in the image?

tsutsugamushi

(C)	Babesia

The image shows a hard tick, which is a vector for numerous diseases. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever is a viral disease transmitted by ticks of the Hyalomma genus. 62.	 Which of the following substances is not used 
as a chelating agent for treating heavy metal 
poisoning?
(A)	Deferiprone
(B)	 EDTA
(C)	Penicillamine
(D)	Oximes
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) Oximes
Chelating agents are molecules that can form multiple bonds with a single metal ion, sequestering it and facilitating its excretion from the body. They are the mainstay of treatment for heavy metal poisoning. Deferiprone is an oral iron chelator used in iron overload conditions like thalassemia. EDTA (Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) is a broad-spectrum chelator used for lead poisoning. Penicillamine is used for copper poisoning (Wilson's disease) as well as lead and mercury poisoning. In contrast, oximes, such as pralidoxime (2-PAM), are not chelating agents. They are cholinesterase reactivators used specifically for treating organophosphate pesticide poisoning. They work by cleaving the bond between the organophosphate and the acetylcholinesterase enzyme, thereby restoring the enzyme's function. They do not act by binding to metals.
63.	 An autopsy on a man with a history of drowning 
revealed no water in the lungs, and the case was 
classified as dry drowning. What is the most 
probable cause of death?
(A)	Asphyxia
(B)	 Vagal inhibition
(C)	Laryngospasm
(D)	Ventricular fibrillation
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Laryngospasm
Drowning is typically categorized as "wet" or "dry." In wet drowning, which is the majority of cases, water enters the lungs. In dry drowning, which accounts for about 10-15% of cases, very little or no water is aspirated into the lungs. The cause of death in these cases is asphyxia resulting from an intense, reflex laryngospasm. When a small amount of water first enters the larynx, it triggers a powerful and sustained spasm of the vocal cords, which effectively seals the airway. This prevents further water from entering the lungs but also prevents air from entering, leading to asphyxiation. While vagal inhibition can cause sudden cardiac arrest upon sudden contact with cold water, and ventricular fibrillation can occur, the specific finding of no water in the lungs with a history of immersion points directly to laryngospasm as the immediate mechanism of fatal airway obstruction.

46.	 Which of the following antimicrobial drug–
mechanism pairs is incorrectly matched? 
(A)	Linezolid: Binds to 30S ribosome and 
inhibits protein synthesis 
(B)	 Rifampicin: Inhibits DNA dependent RNA 
polymerase 
(C)	Aztreonam: Inhibit cell wall synthesis 
(D)	Daptomycin: 
Cause 
depolarization 
of 
membranes 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Linezolid: Binds to 30S ribosome and inhibits protein synthesis
Linezolid is an oxazolidinone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis. However, its mechanism is unique. It binds to the 23S ribosomal RNA of the 50S subunit, preventing the formation of a functional 70S initiation complex. The statement that it binds to the 30S ribosome is incorrect; aminoglycosides and tetracyclines bind to the 30S subunit. The other options are correctly matched. Rifampicin is a rifamycin that inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, blocking transcription. Aztreonam is a monobactam, a class of beta-lactam antibiotics, that inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins. Daptomycin is a cyclic lipopeptide that inserts into the bacterial cell membrane, causing rapid depolarization and subsequent cell death. 
47.	 Which drug shows intrinsic resistance? 
(A)	Fluconazole - Candida glabrata and Candida 
krusei 
(B)	 Itraconazole - Sporothrix 
(C)	Voriconazole - Aspergillus fumigatus 
(D)	Amphotericin B - Candida glabrata 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Fluconazole - Candida glabrata and Candida krusei
Intrinsic resistance refers to a naturally occurring resistance of a microorganism to a particular antimicrobial agent. Among the options, Candida krusei is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole, a commonly used azole antifungal. Candida glabrata often exhibits dose-dependent resistance or acquired resistance, but it is well-known for being less susceptible to fluconazole than Candida albicans. This makes the pairing in option A the best example of intrinsic or near-intrinsic resistance. In contrast, itraconazole is a drug of choice for sporotrichosis. Voriconazole is the primary treatment for invasive aspergillosis caused by Aspergillus fumigatus. While resistance can develop, it is not considered intrinsic. Amphotericin B has a broad spectrum of activity, and while some isolates of C. glabrata may be less susceptible, it is not a classic example of intrinsic resistance. 
48.	 A patient who has been taking ampicillin now 
develops diarrhea. Which medication is the 
treatment of choice for this condition? 
(A)	Oral metronidazole 
(B)	 Oral fidaxomicin 
(C)	Oral ciprofloxacin 
(D)	Bezlotoxumab 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Oral metronidazole
Antibiotic-associated diarrhea is a common side effect, often caused by the overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (formerly Clostridium difficile). For an initial, non-severe episode of C. difficile infection (CDI), the traditional drug of choice has been oral metronidazole or oral vancomycin. While recent guidelines often favor oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin for all severities due to better efficacy, oral metronidazole remains a viable and often-used first-line agent for mild-to-moderate initial episodes, especially in resource-limited settings. Fidaxomicin is a narrow-spectrum antibiotic typically reserved for severe CDI or recurrent episodes due to its high cost. Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone and is actually a common cause of CDI, so it would not be used for treatment. Bezlotoxumab is a monoclonal antibody used to prevent recurrence of CDI, not for treating an active infection. 
49.	 A young patient receiving therapy for multidrug-
resistant tuberculosis develops weight gain, cold 
intolerance, and lethargy. Lab results show high 
TSH with low T3 and T4 levels. Which drug 
in the MDR-TB regimen is most likely causing 
these symptoms? 
(A)	Cycloserine 
(B)	 Ethionamide 
(C)	Streptomycin 
(D)	Pyrazinamide 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Ethionamide
The patient's clinical symptoms (weight gain, cold intolerance, lethargy) and laboratory findings (high TSH, low T3/T4) are classic for primary hypothyroidism. Several second-line anti-tuberculosis drugs can cause this side effect. Ethionamide and prothionamide are well-known to cause hypothyroidism by inhibiting thyroid hormone synthesis, similar to the action of thionamide drugs used to treat hyperthyroidism. This adverse effect occurs in a significant number of patients on long-term therapy. Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) is another anti-TB drug that can cause hypothyroidism. Cycloserine is associated with neuropsychiatric side effects. Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside known for ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. Pyrazinamide can cause hyperuricemia and hepatotoxicity. Therefore, ethionamide is the most likely culprit for the patient's hypothyroidism. 
50.	 Which of the following protease inhibitors can 
cause altered mental status, headache, and 
intracranial bleed? 
(A)	Tenofovir 
(B)	 Saquinavir 
(C)	Tipranavir 
(D)	Darunavir 
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Tipranavir
Tipranavir is a non-peptidic protease inhibitor used in antiretroviral therapy for HIV. It carries a specific black box warning from the FDA regarding the risk of both fatal and non-fatal intracranial hemorrhage. Patients taking tipranavir have shown an increased risk of this serious adverse event, and the mechanism is not fully understood but may relate to effects on platelet function or vascular integrity. This risk is a distinguishing feature compared to other protease inhibitors. While other protease inhibitors like saquinavir and darunavir have their own side effect profiles, they are not specifically associated with this high risk of intracranial bleeding. Tenofovir is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor, not a protease inhibitor, and is primarily associated with renal toxicity and bone mineral density loss. 
51.	 Which chelation therapy is used to prevent 
doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity?
(A)	Aprepitant
(B)	 Deferoxamine
(C)	Amifostine
(D)	Dexrazoxane
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) Dexrazoxane
Doxorubicin, a potent anthracycline chemotherapeutic agent, is known for its dose-dependent cardiotoxicity. This toxicity is mediated primarily through the generation of reactive oxygen species via iron-catalyzed reactions. Dexrazoxane is a cardioprotective agent specifically approved to prevent this complication. It is a cyclic derivative of EDTA and acts as an intracellular iron-chelating agent. By binding to free iron within cardiac cells, dexrazoxane prevents the formation of the iron-doxorubicin complex, which is responsible for the production of harmful free radicals that damage myocyte mitochondria and membranes. Deferoxamine (B) is another iron chelator but is used for systemic iron overload, not specifically for doxorubicin toxicity prevention. Aprepitant (A) is an antiemetic used to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea. Amifostine (C) is a cytoprotective agent used to reduce renal toxicity from cisplatin and xerostomia from radiation therapy.
FORENSIC MEDICINE
52.	 Which of the following substances was the East 
India Company smuggling to China in the 18th 
century?
(A)	Opium
(B)	 Cannabis
(C)	Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD)
(D)	Cocaine
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Opium
In the 18th and 19th centuries, the British East India Company engaged in a large-scale trade of opium, which was cultivated in British-controlled India, and smuggled it into China. This trade was established to reverse a significant trade imbalance, as Britain had a high demand for Chinese goods like tea, silk, and porcelain, but China had little demand for British goods. The widespread opium addiction that resulted in China led to social and economic disruption. The Chinese government's attempts to suppress the illegal opium trade, including the seizure and destruction of large quantities of opium, culminated in the First and Second Opium Wars with Great Britain. These conflicts resulted in treaties that were highly unfavorable to China, forcing it to open ports and cede Hong Kong. Cannabis, LSD, and cocaine were not part of this specific historical trade conflict.
53.	 Identify the option that does not correspond to 
grievous hurt according to Section 320 of the 
Indian Penal Code (IPC)?
(A)	Emasculation
(B)	 Fracture of femur
(C)	Permanent privation of hearing
(D)	7 days hospital admission
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) 7 days hospital admission
Section 320 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) defines "grievous hurt" through eight specific categories of injury. These include emasculation (A), permanent privation of the sight of either eye, permanent privation of the hearing of either ear (C), privation of any member or joint, permanent impairment of the powers of any member or joint, permanent disfiguration of the head or face, fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth (B), and any hurt that endangers life or which causes the sufferer to be, during the space of twenty days, in severe bodily pain, or unable to follow their ordinary pursuits. The option of 7 days hospital admission does not meet the eighth criterion, which specifies a period of twenty days of severe pain or inability to perform ordinary activities. Therefore, while it may indicate a significant injury, it does not, by itself, legally constitute grievous hurt under the IPC.
54.	 What causes the blackening around a gunshot 
entry wound?
(A)	Smoke particles
(B)	 Unburned gunpowder
(C)	Muzzle of firearm
(D)	Fire effect
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Smoke particles
The characteristics of a gunshot entry wound vary depending on the range of fire. When a firearm is discharged at close range (but not in direct contact), several elements are expelled from the muzzle along with the bullet. The blackening (also called soiling or smudging) seen around the entry wound is caused by the deposition of fine smoke particles (soot) from the combustion of the gunpowder. This soot can typically be wiped away. In contrast, unburned or partially burned gunpowder particles (B) cause "tattooing" or "stippling," which are small punctate abrasions that cannot be wiped away as they are embedded in the skin. The fire effect (D), or searing from the flame, is only seen in contact or very close-range shots. A muzzle imprint (C) is a patterned abrasion seen only in hard-contact wounds, where the muzzle is pressed firmly against the skin.
55.	 A 13-year-old girl arrives at the OPD with her 
mother, complaining of abdominal pain, and 
her urine pregnancy test comes back positive. 
As the medical officer, what should be your first 
step?
(A)	Start physical examination
(B)	 Inform the police
(C)	Take consent from the patient's mother
(D)	Preserve the patient's clothes
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Inform the police
In India, the age of consent for sexual activity is 18 years. Sexual intercourse with a minor below this age, even if consensual, is considered statutory rape under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012. A positive pregnancy test in a 13-year-old girl is definitive evidence that sexual activity has occurred. The POCSO Act mandates that any person, including a medical officer, who has an apprehension that a child is a victim of a sexual offense must report it to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or the local police. This reporting is a legal and mandatory obligation. Therefore, the first and most critical step is to inform the police. While taking consent (C) and performing a physical examination (A) are parts of medical management, the legal duty to report under POCSO takes precedence and must be initiated immediately.

71.	 Which of the following viruses needs reverse 
transcription for PCR?
(A)	RSV
(B)	 EBV
(C)	CMV
(D)	Adenovirus
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) RSV
Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is a technique used to amplify a segment of DNA. Standard PCR can only work with a DNA template. When the starting genetic material is RNA, an initial step of reverse transcription is required to convert the RNA into complementary DNA (cDNA). This cDNA then serves as the template for the PCR amplification. The combined technique is called Reverse Transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR). The question asks which virus requires this process. We need to identify the RNA virus among the options. Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is a single-stranded RNA virus. Therefore, to detect it using PCR, its RNA genome must first be reverse-transcribed into cDNA. The other viruses listed—Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Adenovirus—are all DNA viruses. Their DNA genomes can be directly amplified by standard PCR without the need for a reverse transcription step.
72.	 A patient has had a fever for 3 days, and CBC 
shows a platelet count below 90,000. Dengue is 
suspected. Which of the following tests cannot 
be performed on day 3 of illness?
(A)	PCR
(B)	 NS1
(C)	IgM ELISA
(D)	Xenodiagnosis using culture in Aedes 
mosquito
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) IgM ELISA
During a primary dengue infection, the virus and viral components are detectable first, followed by the host's immune response. On day 3 of the illness, the patient is typically in the acute viremic phase. During this time, the dengue virus itself can be detected, so methods like PCR (which detects viral RNA) would be positive. The dengue NS1 antigen is a viral non-structural protein that is secreted into the blood during active infection and is detectable from day 1 up to day 9. Xenodiagnosis, though not a routine clinical test, would also be possible as the mosquito could become infected by feeding on the viremic patient. In contrast, the host's antibody response takes time to develop. IgM antibodies, which are detected by ELISA, usually do not appear until day 4-5 of the illness and then rise to detectable levels. Therefore, on day 3, an IgM ELISA is the least likely test to be positive.
73.	 The HIV genome needs which of the following 
to enter the membrane?
(A)	GP120
(B)	 CCR5
(C)	GP41
(D)	CXCR4
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) GP120
The entry of HIV into a host cell is a multi-step process mediated by its envelope glycoproteins. The process is initiated by the binding of the viral surface glycoprotein, gp120, to the primary CD4 receptor on the surface of the target cell (like a T-helper cell). This initial binding induces a conformational change in gp120, which then allows it to bind to a second receptor, a chemokine co-receptor, which is either CCR5 or CXCR4. This co-receptor binding triggers another conformational change, exposing the fusion peptide of the transmembrane glycoprotein, gp41. The gp41 then inserts into the host cell membrane and mediates the fusion of the viral and cellular membranes, allowing the viral capsid to enter the cytoplasm. Therefore, while all listed components are involved, the initial binding step that is essential for entry is the interaction of gp120 with the CD4 receptor.
74.	 A patient who recovered from COVID-19 and 
received steroid therapy now presents, after 3 
weeks, with nasal discharge. The image shows 
a fungal organism. What is the most probable 
diagnosis?
(A)	Mucor
(B)	 Aspergillus
(C)	Candida
(D)	Trichosporon
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Mucor
The clinical scenario of a patient recovering from COVID-19, particularly one treated with corticosteroids, developing invasive sino-orbital or sino-cerebral fungal infection is highly characteristic of mucormycosis. The image likely shows broad, ribbon-like, irregularly branched, and pauciseptate (or non-septate) hyphae, which are the classic microscopic features of fungi belonging to the order Mucorales (e.g., Rhizopus, Mucor). COVID-19 infection, diabetes, and corticosteroid use are major risk factors that create an ideal environment for this opportunistic fungus to invade. In contrast, Aspergillus typically shows thinner, septate hyphae with acute-angle branching. Candida usually presents as yeast cells and pseudohyphae. Trichosporon also forms hyphae and arthroconidia but is a less common cause of such aggressive rhinocerebral infections.
75.	 Which bacterial toxin exerts its effect by 
inhibiting the activity of elongation factor-2 
(EF-2)?
(A)	Diphtheria	
(B)	 Clostridium
(C)	Bacillus	
(D)	Vibrio
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Diphtheria
Diphtheria toxin, produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, and Exotoxin A, produced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, both act by the same mechanism: they inhibit protein synthesis in eukaryotic cells. The A-subunit of these toxins catalyzes the ADP-ribosylation of eukaryotic Elongation Factor 2 (eEF-2). EF-2 is essential for the translocation step of protein synthesis on the ribosome, where it facilitates the movement of the ribosome along the mRNA strand. By attaching an ADP-ribose group to a specific diphthamide residue on EF-2, the toxin inactivates it. This irreversible inactivation halts polypeptide chain elongation, leading to the cessation of all protein synthesis and subsequent cell death. The toxins produced by Clostridium, Bacillus, and Vibrio species have different mechanisms, such as acting as proteases, adenylate cyclase activators, or pore-forming toxins.
76.	 Which of the following is/are an advantage(s) of 
a saline mount compared to an iodine mount?
1	
Motility of trophozoites
2	
Internal structure of cysts
3	
Differentiate bile-stained vs non-bile stained
(A)	1
(B)	 1 and 3
(C)	2 and 3
(D)	1,2 and 3
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) 1 and 3
A saline mount is commonly used in stool microscopy for the detection of intestinal parasites. Compared to an iodine mount, it has certain advantages.
1	
Motility of trophozoites – This is a major advantage of saline mount. It allows observation of the characteristic motility of protozoan trophozoites (e.g., Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia), which is essential for diagnosis. Iodine mount kills the organisms, so motility cannot be appreciated.
2	
Internal structure of cysts – This is better visualized with iodine mount, not saline. Iodine enhances nuclear detail and glycogen mass in cysts.
3	
Differentiation of bile-stained vs non-bile-stained eggs – Saline mount helps identify natural color differences (e.g., bile-stained ova like Ascaris vs non-bile-stained ova like hookworm). Iodine may obscure natural coloration.
Thus, advantages of saline mount over iodine mount are motility of trophozoites and differentiation of bile-stained vs non-bile-stained eggs, making option (B) correct.
77.	 Identify the organism and staining
(A)	Nocardia and acid-fast stain
(B)	 Streptococcus and gram stain
(C)	Cryptococcus and India ink
(D)	Coccidioidomycosis and PAS 
stain
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Nocardia and acid-fast stain
The image displays filamentous, branching rods. This morphology is characteristic of Actinomycetes, which includes both Nocardia and Actinomyces. A key distinguishing feature is their staining property. Nocardia species contain mycolic acids in their cell walls, similar to Mycobacteria, which makes them partially acid-fast. They will stain positive (appearing red/pink) with a modified acid-fast stain (e.g., modified Kinyoun or Ziehl-Neelsen). Streptococcus appears as Gram-positive cocci in chains. Cryptococcus is a yeast that is typically visualized with an India ink stain, which highlights its prominent polysaccharide capsule as a clear halo against a dark background. Coccidioidomycosis is caused by a dimorphic fungus, appearing as large spherules containing endospores in tissue, which stain well with PAS or GMS stains. The image's appearance is most consistent with Nocardia stained to show its acid-fast properties.
78.	 What is the most probable diagnosis in an HIV 
patient who develops a white patch on the 
tongue or buccal mucosa that does not scrape 
off?
(A)	EBV	
(B)	 Candida
(C)	HSV	
(D)	HHV8
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) EBV
The clinical description of a white, corrugated or "hairy" patch, typically on the lateral borders of the tongue, that cannot be scraped off is the classic presentation of Oral Hairy Leukoplakia (OHL). This condition is an opportunistic infection strongly associated with immunosuppression, particularly in HIV-infected individuals. The causative agent of OHL is the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). In contrast, oral candidiasis (thrush), caused by Candida (B), typically presents as creamy white plaques that can be scraped off, often leaving an erythematous base. Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) (C) causes painful vesicles and ulcers. Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) (D) is associated with Kaposi's sarcoma, which appears as purplish vascular nodules. Therefore, the inability to scrape off the lesion is a key feature pointing to OHL caused by EBV.

(A)	Cobalt blue Trypan blue - 
Corneal ulcer

The image shows a common ophthalmological diagnostic procedure. Fluorescein is a dye that stains areas of the cornea where the epithelial layer is absent, such as in an abrasion or an ulcer. The dye pools in the defect and, when illuminated with a cobalt blue light, it fluoresces, appearing as a bright green or yellow-green area. 94.	 1D sph and -2D at 180 is what type of refractive 
error?
(A)	With the rule astigmatism
(B)	 Against the rule astigmatism
(C)	Simple astigmatism
(D)	Mixed astigmatism
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) With the rule astigmatism
The prescription +1.00 D sphere with −2.00 D cylinder at 180° represents with-the-rule (WTR) astigmatism.
Astigmatism occurs when the cornea has unequal curvature in different meridians, causing light rays to focus at different points. In a cylindrical prescription, the axis indicates the meridian that has no cylindrical power, and the cylinder power acts 90° away from that axis.
Here, the cylinder axis is 180°, meaning the cylindrical correction acts at 90° (vertical meridian). Since the cylinder power is negative (−2.00 D), it corrects excess refractive power in the vertical meridian. This implies that the vertical meridian is steeper than the horizontal meridian, which is the defining feature of with-the-rule astigmatism.
In with-the-rule astigmatism, the cornea is more curved vertically and flatter horizontally. It is called “with-the-rule” because this pattern follows the normal corneal curvature seen in younger individuals.
The +1.00 D sphere component indicates underlying hyperopia, but the key determinant of astigmatism type is the cylinder axis at 180°.
Therefore, the correct answer is : (A) With-the-rule astigmatism.
95.	 Iritis is most commonly associated with which 
of the following?
(A)	Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
(B)	 Behcet's Disease
(C)	Psoriatic Arthropathy
(D)	Ulcerative colitis
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Behcet's Disease
Iritis, a form of anterior uveitis, is inflammation of the iris and is often associated with systemic inflammatory conditions. Behçet's disease is a multi-systemic inflammatory vasculitis, and ocular involvement is a major criterion for diagnosis and a common cause of morbidity. It frequently presents as a recurrent, bilateral, non-granulomatous panuveitis or posterior uveitis, but severe anterior uveitis (iritis) with hypopyon is a classic finding. While the other listed conditions—the seronegative spondyloarthropathies like psoriatic arthropathy and ulcerative colitis, and connective tissue diseases like SLE—can also be associated with anterior uveitis, the association is particularly strong and characteristic in Behçet's disease. Among the given options, Behçet's is most renowned for its severe and recurrent iritis, often leading to significant visual impairment.

96.	 Which anticoagulant is contained in the light 
blue vacutainer commonly used for coagulation 
tests?
(A)	Trisodium Citrate
(B)	 Heparin
(C)	Potassium Oxalate
(D)	EDTA
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Trisodium Citrate
Vacutainer tubes are color-coded to indicate the type of additive they contain. The tube with a light blue top is specifically designed for coagulation studies, such as prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT). The anticoagulant used in this tube is 3.2% or 3.8% buffered sodium citrate. Sodium citrate works by chelating calcium ions in the blood sample. Calcium is an essential cofactor for many steps in the coagulation cascade, so its removal prevents the blood from clotting. This action is reversible, which is crucial for testing; calcium can be added back in the laboratory to initiate clotting under controlled conditions. Heparin is typically in green-top tubes, EDTA in lavender-top tubes (for hematology), and potassium oxalate (often with sodium fluoride) in grey-top tubes (for glucose measurement).
97.	 A patient was started on amitriptyline and was 
found unconscious. Which of the following does 
not suggest TCA toxicity?
(A)	Arrhythmia
(B)	 Confusion
(C)	Hypothermia
(D)	Pupillary dilatation
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Hypothermia
Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose, such as with amitriptyline, is a medical emergency with a characteristic toxidrome. The major toxic effects are due to anticholinergic activity, sodium channel blockade in the heart, and alpha-adrenergic blockade. Clinical features include central nervous system effects like sedation, confusion, delirium, seizures, and coma (B). Anticholinergic effects cause pupillary dilatation (mydriasis) (D), dry mouth, urinary retention, and tachycardia. The most life-threatening effect is cardiotoxicity from sodium channel blockade, leading to a widened QRS complex and potentially fatal ventricular arrhythmias (A). A common finding in TCA overdose due to its effect on thermoregulation is hyperthermia (elevated body temperature), not hypothermia. Therefore, hypothermia is the finding that would not suggest TCA toxicity.
98.	 Match the columns:
1.
Autosomal dominant
A. Duchenne 
muscular dys-
trophy
2.

B.
Leber heredi-
tary optic neu-
ropathy
3.

(A)	A-1, B-4, C-2, D-3
(B)	 A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1
(C)	A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4
(D)	A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive disorder. The defective gene is located on the X chromosome, so males are predominantly affected because they have only one X chromosome. Females are usually carriers. Hence, it matches with X-linked recessive (2).
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy shows mitochondrial inheritance. Mitochondrial DNA is transmitted only from the mother to all her children, but only daughters pass it to the next generation. Therefore, it matches with mitochondrial inheritance (4).
Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7. The disease appears only when an individual inherits two defective alleles, one from each parent. Thus, it matches with autosomal recessive (3).
Myotonic dystrophy (myotonia dystrophica) is an autosomal dominant disorder. Only one mutated allele is sufficient to cause the condition, and it often shows anticipation in successive generations. Hence, it matches with autosomal dominant (1).
Therefore, option (D) is correct.
99.	 What method is employed for the detection of 
autoantibodies?
(A)	Direct Immunofluorescence
(B)	 ELISA
(C)	Indirect Immunofluorescence
(D)	FISH
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Indirect Immunofluorescence
Indirect Immunofluorescence (IIF) is the gold standard technique for screening and detecting circulating autoantibodies in a patient's serum, such as antinuclear antibodies (ANA). The procedure is 'indirect' because it involves two main steps. First, the patient's serum (containing the primary autoantibody) is incubated with a substrate (e.g., HEp-2 cells). If autoantibodies are present, they will bind to their specific target antigens within the cells. Second, a fluorescently labeled secondary antibody, which is designed to bind to human immunoglobulins, is added. This secondary antibody binds to the patient's autoantibodies, and the resulting fluorescence can be visualized under a microscope, revealing specific staining patterns. Direct immunofluorescence detects antibodies that are already bound to patient tissues in a biopsy specimen. ELISA can also detect autoantibodies, but IIF is the classic screening method. FISH detects nucleic acid sequences.
100.	 Which of the following will increase in size on 
electrophoresis in Nephrotic syndrome?
(A)	Gamma globulin
(B)	 Alpha 2 globulin
(C)	Beta globulin
(D)	Albumin
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Alpha 2 globulin
Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), primarily due to the loss of smaller proteins like albumin through the damaged glomerular filtration barrier. This leads to significant hypoalbuminemia. On serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP), the albumin peak will be markedly decreased. In response to the low plasma oncotic pressure caused by albumin loss, the liver increases the synthesis of various proteins, particularly lipoproteins and larger proteins. This compensatory mechanism leads to a characteristic increase in the levels of alpha-2 globulins (which include alpha-2 macroglobulin, a large protein that is retained, and haptoglobin) and beta globulins (which include lipoproteins). Gamma globulin levels are typically normal or decreased due to urinary losses. Therefore, a decreased albumin peak and an elevated alpha-2 globulin peak are classic SPEP findings in nephrotic syndrome.

(A) Meniere's Disease
The clinical presentation describes the classic triad of symptoms for Meniere's Disease: episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss (typically low-frequency initially, as shown in the audiogram), and tinnitus. The episodes are often accompanied by a sensation of aural fullness. While endolymphatic hydrops is the pathological finding, Meniere's Disease is the clinical syndrome. 87.	 In a patient with bilateral hearing loss and 
progressive worsening in the right ear due to 
otosclerosis, which set of clinical findings would 
prompt the physician to advise a stapedectomy?
(A)	Rinne's Test - positive; Weber's Test - 
lateralized to left ear
(B)	 Rinne's Test - positive; Weber's Test - 
lateralized to right ear
(C)	Rinne's Test - negative; Weber's Test - 
lateralized to left ear
(D)	Rinne's Test - negative; Weber's Test - 
lateralized to right ear
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) Rinne's Test - negative; Weber's Test - lateralized to right ear
Otosclerosis is a primary cause of conductive hearing loss, resulting from the abnormal fixation of the stapes bone in the oval window. Tuning fork tests are essential for diagnosis. The Rinne's test compares air conduction (AC) to bone conduction (BC). In conductive hearing loss, BC is heard louder or longer than AC, which is a negative Rinne's test. Since the right ear is worse, a negative test would be expected on the right. The Weber's test involves placing a vibrating tuning fork on the midline of the forehead. In unilateral or asymmetrical conductive hearing loss, the sound lateralizes to the more affected ear because the conductive block masks ambient noise, making the bone-conducted sound seem louder on that side. Therefore, in a patient with worse hearing in the right ear due to otosclerosis, the expected findings would be a negative Rinne's test on the right and the Weber's test lateralizing to the right.
88.	 A patient reports difficulty hearing and says 
they can understand speech only when it is 
very loud or amplified. According to the WHO 
classification of speech-understanding ability, 
how should this degree of hearing loss be 
classified?
(A)	Mild hearing loss
(B)	 Moderate hearing loss
(C)	Severe hearing loss
(D)	Profound hearing loss
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Severe hearing loss
The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies the degree of hearing impairment based on the hearing threshold in decibels (dB HL) and the associated functional limitations. A person who can only hear and understand loudly spoken or shouted speech falls into the category of severe hearing loss. According to the WHO grades, this corresponds to an average hearing threshold of 61-80 dB HL in the better ear. Individuals with mild hearing loss (26-40 dB HL) can hear and repeat words spoken at a normal volume. Those with moderate hearing loss (41-60 dB HL) can hear and repeat words spoken in a raised voice. Profound hearing loss (>81 dB HL) means the individual may not be able to hear or understand even shouted speech and often relies on lip-reading or sign language.

91.	 Which of the following is not seen in very severe

AAns

Diabetic retinopathy is classified into Non-proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR) and Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR). The hallmark feature that defines the transition from NPDR to the more advanced PDR is the development of neovascularization (the growth of new, abnormal blood vessels). (C) Temporal lobe
The patient described can perceive basic visual features such as color, texture, and shape, which means primary visual processing is intact. This function is mainly carried out by the occipital lobe, specifically the primary visual cortex. Since basic perception is preserved, the lesion is unlikely to be in the occipital lobe.

110.	 A diabetic man presents to the emergency 
department with chest pain and palpitations. His 
ECG indicates NSTEMI. What is the appropriate 
management?
(A)	Aspirin + Clopidogrel
(B)	 Aspirin + Statin
(C)	Aspirin + Clopidogrel + LMWH
(D)	Aspirin + LMWH
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Aspirin + Clopidogrel + LMWH
The management of Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) focuses on preventing further thrombus formation and reducing myocardial oxygen demand. The standard initial medical management involves a combination of antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy. This includes aspirin (an antiplatelet agent) and a P2Y12 inhibitor like clopidogrel (dual antiplatelet therapy or DAPT), which work synergistically to inhibit platelet aggregation. In addition, an anticoagulant is required to inhibit the coagulation cascade and prevent thrombus growth. Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH), such as enoxaparin, is a commonly used and effective anticoagulant in this setting. While a statin (B) is crucial for long-term management, it is not the immediate priority for acute antithrombotic therapy. Using single antiplatelet therapy (D) or DAPT without anticoagulation (A) would be insufficient for managing an acute NSTEMI.
111.	 What 
is 
the 
most 
common 
cause 
of 
hypercalcemia in a hospitalized patient?
(A)	Malignancy
(B)	 Parathyroid Adenoma
(C)	Parathyroid hyperplasia
(D)	Follicular thyroid CA
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) Malignancy
While primary hyperparathyroidism (caused by a parathyroid adenoma) is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in the outpatient setting, malignancy is the most common cause in hospitalized (inpatient) patients. This is referred to as hypercalcemia of malignancy. It can occur through several mechanisms. The most common is the secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) by tumors (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, renal cell carcinoma), which mimics the action of PTH. Another mechanism is the production of osteolytic lesions from bone metastases (e.g., from breast cancer or multiple myeloma), which directly destroy bone and release calcium. Less commonly, tumors can produce active vitamin D (calcitriol), as seen in some lymphomas. Therefore, in a patient who is sick enough to be hospitalized, malignancy should be the primary suspicion for the cause of hypercalcemia.

113.	 After undergoing an adrenalectomy and during 
the hospital stay, a young patient develops 
hyperpigmentation on the distal parts of the 
fingers. What underlying condition most likely

(A)	Addison's disease
(B)	 Conn's syndrome
(C)	Nelson syndrome
(D)	Cushing syndrome
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Nelson syndrome
Nelson syndrome is a specific clinical condition that can occur after a bilateral adrenalectomy is performed to treat Cushing's disease (a pituitary adenoma secreting ACTH). The removal of the adrenal glands eliminates the production of cortisol. This removes the negative feedback that cortisol normally exerts on the pituitary gland. In the absence of this feedback, the pre-existing pituitary adenoma can grow aggressively and secrete extremely high levels of Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) and its precursor, pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC). POMC is also cleaved to produce melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH). The excessively high levels of ACTH and MSH stimulate melanocytes, leading to the characteristic intense hyperpigmentation of the skin and mucous membranes. The other conditions do not fit this specific post-surgical context.

The diagnosis of infective endocarditis (IE) heavily relies on isolating the causative microorganism from the blood. 103.	 Comment on the diagnosis from the ECG shown 
below.
(A)	First degree heart block
(B)	 Second-degree 
infra-nodal 
heart block
(C)	Complete heart block
(D)	AV dissociation
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Second-degree infra-nodal heart block
On the ECG strip, there are regular P waves occurring at a constant rate, but not every P wave is followed by a QRS complex. Some atrial impulses fail to conduct to the ventricles, resulting in dropped QRS complexes. The PR intervals of the conducted beats appear constant rather than progressively lengthening. This pattern is characteristic of Mobitz type II second-degree AV block, which usually occurs below the AV node, in the His-Purkinje system (infra-nodal level).
In contrast, first-degree heart block shows prolonged PR interval but no dropped beats. Complete heart block demonstrates total AV dissociation, where atrial and ventricular rhythms are independent. AV dissociation can occur in various settings and does not necessarily imply complete block.
Mobitz type II is clinically significant because it can progress to complete heart block and often requires pacemaker insertion. The presence of sudden non-conducted P waves with constant PR intervals in conducted beats supports the diagnosis of second-degree infra-nodal (Mobitz type II) heart block.

105.	 Which is not a risk factor for Ca Gall Bladder?
(A)	Porcelain Gall Bladder
(B)	 Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis
(C)	Polyp <10 mm
(D)	Gallstone >3 cm
AAns

Gallbladder carcinoma has several well-established risk factors. Gallstones (cholelithiasis) are the single most important risk factor, with the risk increasing with the size of the stones; a stone >3 cm significantly elevates the risk. A porcelain gallbladder, characterized by intramural calcification, carries a very high risk of underlying malignancy. Chronic inflammatory conditions of the biliary tree, such as Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis, also increase the risk. Therefore, a small polyp (<10 mm) is not considered a significant risk factor.

Biosafety levels (BSLs) are a series of protection levels designed for laboratory facilities. BSL-3 is applicable to clinical, diagnostic, and research facilities where work is done with indigenous or exotic agents that may cause serious or potentially lethal disease through the inhalation route of exposure. 65.	 Which of the following acts by the mechanism 
illustrated in the given image?
(A)	Vibrio cholerae
(B)	 Streptococcus pyogenes
(C)	Clostridium difficile
(D)	Clostridium botulinum
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Streptococcus pyogenes
The image illustrates the mechanism of action of a superantigen. Unlike conventional antigens that are processed and presented in the peptide-binding groove of an MHC molecule, a superantigen binds externally to the MHC Class II molecule on an antigen-presenting cell and to the Vβ region of the T-cell receptor on a T-cell. This cross-linking bypasses the need for specific antigen recognition and leads to the massive, non-specific activation of a large fraction (up to 20%) of the T-cell population. This results in a "cytokine storm" and can cause systemic inflammation and shock. Streptococcus pyogenes produces several superantigens, such as the streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (e.g., SpeA, SpeC), which are responsible for the clinical manifestations of scarlet fever and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome. Cholera toxin, botulinum toxin, and C. difficile toxins have different mechanisms of action (e.g., ADP-ribosylation, SNARE protein cleavage).

(A) Scrub typhus
The clinical presentation of fever, thrombocytopenia (platelet count of 88,000), and mild renal impairment (creatinine of 1.4) in a farmer is suggestive of several zoonotic infections. However, the presence of an eschar (the necrotic lesion shown in the image) is a pathognomonic finding for scrub typhus. Scrub typhus is caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi and is transmitted by the bite of a chigger (larval mite). The chigger bite often results in an inoculation lesion that develops into a painless, dark-centered necrotic eschar with a surrounding erythematous halo. This finding, combined with the systemic symptoms and patient's occupation (exposure to mites in vegetation), makes scrub typhus the most likely diagnosis. Brucellosis, leptospirosis, and anthrax present differently and do not typically feature this type of eschar.
67.	 In which of the following does the genetic 
material show adenine not equal to thymine?
(A)	Mitochondrial DNA of humans
(B)	 E. coli
(C)	HIV
(D)	Herpes
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) HIV
Chargaff's rules state that in double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), the amount of adenine (A) is equal to the amount of thymine (T), and the amount of guanine (G) is equal to the amount of cytosine (C). This rule applies to any organism with a dsDNA genome. Human mitochondrial DNA (A), E. coli bacteria (B), and Herpesviruses (D) all have dsDNA genomes, so in them, A=T and G=C. The Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) (C) is a retrovirus, and its genome consists of two copies of single-stranded RNA (ssRNA). Because its genetic material is single-stranded, there is no complementary strand to enforce the base-pairing rules. Therefore, the amounts of adenine and uracil (the RNA equivalent of thymine) are not necessarily equal, and the same is true for guanine and cytosine. This makes HIV the correct answer.
68.	 After 3 days of dengue infection, diagnosis can 
be made by all except which of the following?
(A)	ELISA for antigen
(B)	 Viral load
(C)	ELISA for antibody
(D)	RT PCR
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) ELISA for antibody
During a primary dengue infection, the virus and viral components are detectable first, followed by the host's immune response. On day 3 of the illness, the patient is typically in the acute viremic phase. During this time, the dengue virus itself can be detected, so methods like viral load measurement or RT-PCR (which detects viral RNA) would be positive. The dengue NS1 antigen is a viral non-structural protein that is secreted into the blood during active infection and is detectable by ELISA from day 1 up to day 9. In contrast, the host's antibody response takes time to develop. IgM antibodies, which are detected by ELISA, usually do not appear until day 4-5 of the illness and then rise to detectable levels. Therefore, on day 3, an antibody ELISA is the least likely test to be positive and is not the recommended diagnostic method for this early stage.

70.	 Vibrio cholerae disrupts which extracellular cell 
adhesion?
(A)	Integrin
(B)	 Cadherin
(C)	Occludens
(D)	None of the above
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(C) Occludens
Vibrio cholerae causes profuse watery diarrhea primarily through the action of cholera toxin, which leads to massive secretion of chloride ions and water into the intestinal lumen. However, recent research has also highlighted the role of other virulence factors in disrupting the intestinal barrier integrity. The cholera toxin's effect is compounded by proteases and other factors that disrupt the tight junctions between intestinal epithelial cells. Tight junctions, also known as zonula occludens, are multiprotein complexes that seal the paracellular pathway. The main transmembrane proteins forming these junctions are occludins and claudins. Disruption of these junctions by V. cholerae increases the permeability of the intestinal barrier, contributing to the massive fluid loss. Cadherins are components of adherens junctions, while integrins mediate cell-matrix adhesion.

116.	 Which diagnostic investigation should be

(C)	Total T3
(D)	USG Neck
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(A) TSH and free T4
The patient's constellation of symptoms—palpitations, weight loss despite a good appetite, tremors, heat intolerance (sweating), and diarrhea—is classic for hyperthyroidism or thyrotoxicosis. The initial and most crucial step in confirming this diagnosis is to perform thyroid function tests. The best initial screening and diagnostic tests are the measurement of serum Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) and free Thyroxine (free T4). In primary hyperthyroidism (the most common cause, e.g., Graves' disease), the thyroid gland overproduces T4 and/or T3, which suppresses the pituitary's production of TSH. 117.	 What is the recommended medication for 
treating watery diarrhea that occurs in a patient 
who developed this symptom while taking 
ampicillin for a URTI?
(A)	Metronidazole
(B)	 Fidaxomicin
(C)	Ciprofloxacin
(D)	Bezlotoxumab
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Fidaxomicin
A patient who develops watery diarrhea while taking ampicillin most likely has antibiotic-associated diarrhea due to overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile. Broad-spectrum antibiotics like ampicillin disrupt the normal intestinal flora, allowing C. difficile to proliferate and produce toxins (toxin A and toxin B). These toxins cause inflammation of the colon, leading to diarrhea, abdominal pain, and sometimes pseudomembranous colitis.
Current guidelines recommend Fidaxomicin as the preferred first-line treatment for an initial episode of C. difficile infection. Fidaxomicin is a narrow-spectrum, bactericidal antibiotic that specifically targets C. difficile with minimal effect on normal gut flora. This selective action results in lower recurrence rates compared to oral vancomycin. It is administered orally and acts locally within the gastrointestinal tract.
Metronidazole is no longer first-line except when other agents are unavailable. Ciprofloxacin may worsen the condition. Bezlotoxumab is used only to prevent recurrence, not as primary therapy. Thus, fidaxomicin is recommended.

119.	 A 30-year-old HIV-positive man presents with

by a positive India ink stain. In this context,

unchanged.

(C)	Begin treatment with fluconazole taken by

(D)	Brain imaging shows changes $in>80\%$ of

AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(B) Delay antiretroviral therapy by 4-6 weeks after the initiation of antifungal treatment.
The clinical picture describes cryptococcal meningitis, a common opportunistic infection in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS. A major concern in managing this condition is the risk of Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS) if antiretroviral therapy (ART) is started too soon. IRIS can lead to a paradoxical worsening of symptoms and increased intracranial pressure. 122.	 Workup of a 25-year-old hotel worker shows the 
following profile:
•	
HBsAg = Negative
•	
Anti-HBs = Negative
•	
HBeAg Negative
•	
Anti-HBe Negative
•	
Total anti-HBc = Positive
What is the diagnosis?
(A)	Chronic hepatitis B
(B)	 Inactive carrier
(C)	Hepatitis B in remote past
(D)	Window period/Gap period
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2023
(D) Window period/Gap period
In this serological profile:
HBsAg = Negative
Anti-HBs = Negative
HBeAg = Negative
Anti-HBe = Negative
Total anti-HBc = Positive
The key finding is isolated anti-HBc positivity. During the natural course of acute hepatitis B infection, there is a phase called the window period. In this period, HBsAg has disappeared, but anti-HBs has not yet appeared. Therefore, both HBsAg and anti-HBs are negative.
The only detectable marker during this time is anti-HBc, particularly IgM anti-HBc, which indicates recent infection. Total anti-HBc includes both IgM and IgG antibodies, so its positivity supports exposure to hepatitis B virus.
Chronic hepatitis B would show persistent HBsAg positivity. An inactive carrier state also requires HBsAg positivity. Remote past infection would typically show anti-HBs positivity along with anti-HBc.
Since HBsAg and anti-HBs are both negative but anti-HBc is positive, the most appropriate diagnosis is the window (gap) period of acute hepatitis B infection.
