125.	 Hamman sign is seen in which of the following 
conditions?
(A)	Pneumomediastinum
(B)	 Pneumoperitoneum
(C)	Pneumopericardium
(D)	Hydropneumothorax
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(A) Pneumomediastinum
Hamman's sign, also known as Hamman's crunch, is a distinctive and pathognomonic clinical finding for pneumomediastinum (the presence of gas or air in the mediastinum). It is described as a crunching, crackling, or bubbling sound heard over the precordium that is synchronous with the heartbeat. The sound is produced by the heart beating against the air-filled mediastinal tissues. It is often best heard when the patient is in the left lateral decubitus position. Pneumomediastinum can result from various causes, including alveolar rupture (e.g., from severe coughing or Valsalva), esophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndrome), or trauma. While sometimes associated with pneumothorax or pneumopericardium, the sign itself localizes the air to the mediastinum.

147.	 What is the approximate estimated glomerular 
filtration rate (eGFR) for a 4-year-old boy 
weighing 15 kg and 100 cm tall, admitted with 
renal failure and laboratory values showing a 
blood urea of 100 mg/dL and serum creatinine 
of 1 mg/dL?
(A)	33 ml/min/1.73 m² BSA
(B)	 40 ml/min/1.73 m² BSA
(C)	55 ml/min/1.73 m² BSA
(D)	80 ml/min/1.73 m² BSA
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(B) 40 ml/min/1.73 m² BSA
In children, the estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) is commonly calculated using the Bedside Schwartz formula:
eGFR = (k × Height in cm) / Serum Creatinine (mg/dL)
The constant 'k' is age-dependent. For a child aged 2-12 years, the constant k is 0.55. (Note: Older formulas used 0.413, which also yields a similar result).
Using the standard k value of 0.55:
Height = 100 cm
Serum Creatinine = 1 mg/dL
eGFR = (0.55 × 100) / 1 = 55 ml/min/1.73 m²
Using the older constant k of 0.413:
eGFR = (0.413 × 100) / 1 = 41.3 ml/min/1.73 m²
Given the options, 40 ml/min/1.73 m² is a closer approximation to the result from the older, more commonly tested formula. Both calculations indicate significant renal impairment.

This clinical scenario is a classic presentation of Sheehan's syndrome, or postpartum pituitary apoplexy/necrosis. 164.	 Which of the following statements is NOT true

(C) It has an inhibitory effect on the cerebral cortex, thereby preventing seizures and lowering the BP
This statement contains multiple inaccuracies. The exact antiseizure mechanism of magnesium sulfate is not fully understood, but it is not believed to be a primary cortical depressant like a sedative. In pregnancy, both symptomatic UTIs and asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) are treated to prevent complications like pyelonephritis and preterm birth. The diagnosis rests on a quantitative urine culture. 169.	 Which of the following is included in the 
modified biophysical profile (BPP)?
(A)	NST and fetal tone
(B)	 NST and AFI
(C)	NST and breathing movements
(D)	NST and gross fetal movements
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(B) NST and AFI
The full biophysical profile (BPP) is an antenatal test for fetal well-being that assesses five components: fetal breathing, gross body movements, fetal tone, amniotic fluid volume, and a non-stress test (NST). The modified biophysical profile (mBPP) is a simplified, yet effective, screening version of the full test. It combines just two key elements: the Non-Stress Test (NST) and the Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI). The NST is a short-term marker of fetal acid-base status and neurologic integrity, reflecting acute oxygenation. The AFI is considered a long-term marker of placental function, as adequate amniotic fluid depends on fetal urine production, which in turn depends on adequate renal perfusion over time. An abnormal result on either component of the mBPP necessitates further evaluation with a full BPP or other testing.

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(C) Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion
The image demonstrates the testing of a deep tendon reflex (DTR). A DTR is a simple spinal reflex arc involving a sensory neuron and a motor neuron. This reflex arc is under constant inhibitory control from descending pathways originating in the brain. These descending pathways are composed of upper motor neurons (UMNs). When there is a lesion affecting the UMNs (e.g., from a stroke, spinal cord injury, or multiple sclerosis), this inhibitory influence is lost. As a result, the spinal reflex becomes disinhibited and hyperactive, leading to enhanced reflexes (hyperreflexia), clonus, and spasticity. In contrast, any lesion that damages the reflex arc itself—such as a peripheral neuropathy (A), a nerve root compression (radiculopathy, B), or any other lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion (D)—will result in decreased (hyporeflexia) or absent reflexes.

158.	 Which nerve is most likely to be damaged in 
cases of anterior shoulder dislocation?
(A)	Axillary nerve
(B)	 Median nerve
(C)	Radial nerve
(D)	Suprascapular nerve
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(A) Axillary nerve
The axillary nerve is the most frequently injured nerve in an anterior dislocation of the shoulder. The nerve originates from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and has a close anatomical relationship with the inferior aspect of the shoulder joint capsule as it courses around the surgical neck of the humerus. During an anterior-inferior dislocation, the humeral head is displaced, putting the axillary nerve under tension and at high risk for a traction injury or compression. A clinical examination after a shoulder dislocation must include an assessment of the axillary nerve. This is done by testing for motor function of the deltoid muscle (shoulder abduction) and sensory function over the "regimental badge" area on the lateral aspect of the shoulder.

(D) Paucibacillary leprosy
The cardinal sign of leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a skin lesion with a definite loss of sensation. This patient's well-demarcated, hypopigmented patches with anesthesia are highly characteristic. Leprosy is classified on a spectrum based on the patient's immune response and bacterial load. Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy represents the high-immunity end of the spectrum. It is characterized by a small number of lesions (1-5), a robust cell-mediated immune response, and a very low number of bacteria. 108.	 Zellweger syndrome results from an abnormality 
in the formation of:
(A)	Peroxisomes
(B)	 Lysosomes
(C)	Mitochondria
(D)	Nucleus
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(A) Peroxisomes
Zellweger syndrome is the prototypical and most severe of the peroxisomal biogenesis disorders (PBDs). Peroxisomes are essential membrane-bound organelles involved in numerous metabolic pathways, including the breakdown of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) and the synthesis of plasmalogens, which are crucial for brain and nerve myelination. In PBDs, mutations in PEX genes lead to a failure in the assembly of functional peroxisomes. As a result, peroxisomal enzymes are not correctly imported into the organelle and remain in the cytosol, rendering them non-functional. This leads to the toxic accumulation of substances like VLCFAs, causing severe neurological defects, dysmorphic features, and liver dysfunction. The condition is incompatible with long-term survival. It is fundamentally a disease of peroxisome formation, distinct from disorders of lysosomes, mitochondria, or the nucleus.

Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer, especially in elderly individuals and in sun-exposed areas such as the ear, face, and neck. The lesion shown appears ulcerated with crusting and irregular margins, which is typical of an advanced BCC. A classic description of BCC is a “rodent ulcer” — a slowly enlarging lesion with central ulceration and raised rolled borders. It may bleed easily and develop crust formation over time.
BCC is characteristically slow-growing, which fits the history of gradually worsening skin lesions. Although diabetes is not a direct cause, elderly patients with chronic sun exposure are at high risk.
In contrast:
1.	
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) tends to be more hyperkeratotic and indurated and has a higher metastatic potential.
2.	
Melasma presents as flat hyperpigmented patches, not ulcerative lesions.
3.	
Discoid lupus erythematosus causes scaly erythematous plaques with scarring, not destructive ulcerated tumors.
Because of the slow progression, sun-exposed location, and ulcerated appearance with crusting, the most likely diagnosis is Basal Cell Carcinoma (A).
110.	 Which statement in rapid sequence intubation 
is incorrect?
(A)	Preoxygenation with 100% oxygen for 3 min 
is done
(B)	 High-volume, low-pressure cuff is used
(C)	It is the first choice of treatment in cardiac 
arrest patients
(D)	The induction agent and muscle relaxant 
are given simultaneously
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(C) It is the first choice of treatment in cardiac arrest patients
This statement is incorrect. Rapid Sequence Intubation (RSI) is a specific technique for endotracheal intubation in patients who have a full stomach or are otherwise at high risk of aspiration and who still have intact airway reflexes. It involves the near-simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a neuromuscular blocking agent. Patients in cardiac arrest are, by definition, unconscious and flaccid; they have no muscle tone and no protective airway reflexes. Therefore, there is no need to administer anesthetic or paralytic drugs to facilitate intubation. Airway management in cardiac arrest prioritizes chest compressions and involves basic maneuvers followed by intubation without drugs. The other statements are correct components of RSI: preoxygenation (A) is vital, high-volume, low-pressure cuffs (B) are standard for modern endotracheal tubes, and the co-administration of induction and paralytic agents (D) is the defining feature of the technique.
111.	 What is the most distinctive feature of Kallmann 
syndrome among the options provided?
(A)	Anosmia
(B)	 Syndactyly in males
(C)	Precocious puberty in females
(D)	White forelock
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(A) Anosmia
Kallmann syndrome is a genetic disorder that causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, resulting in delayed or absent puberty. The feature that uniquely distinguishes Kallmann syndrome from other forms of isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is the associated anosmia (complete loss of smell) or hyposmia (reduced sense of smell). This specific combination of symptoms occurs due to a developmental defect where the neurons responsible for producing gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) fail to migrate from their embryonic origin in the olfactory placode to their proper location in the hypothalamus. Because the olfactory bulbs also fail to develop properly during this process, the sense of smell is impaired. While other anomalies like syndactyly (B) can occur, anosmia is the most consistent and distinctive feature. The condition causes absent puberty, not precocious puberty (C). A white forelock (D) is seen in Wurttemberg syndrome.
112.	 A 40-year-old man with chronic alcoholism is 
undergoing withdrawal, and his liver function 
tests show elevated AST, ALT, and GGT levels. 
Given his impaired liver function, which 
benzodiazepine is the safest choice for managing 
his withdrawal symptoms?
(A)	Diazepam
(B)	 Alprazolam
(C)	Clonazepam
(D)	Lorazepam
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(D) Lorazepam
Benzodiazepines are the cornerstone of therapy for alcohol withdrawal. However, in a patient with compromised liver function, as suggested by the elevated liver enzymes, the choice of agent is critical. Most benzodiazepines, including diazepam, are metabolized through oxidative pathways in the liver (cytochrome P450 system), which can be significantly impaired in liver disease. This can lead to drug accumulation and prolonged sedation. Lorazepam, however, is metabolized primarily through glucuronidation, a process that is much better preserved in patients with liver dysfunction. For this reason, lorazepam, along with oxazepam and temazepam (mnemonic: "Outside The Liver"), are the preferred benzodiazepines in patients with alcoholic liver disease. They have a shorter half-life and no active metabolites, making them a safer choice to manage withdrawal symptoms in this patient population.
113.	 Which of the options listed below does not assist 
in the identification of spinal cord lesions?
(A)	Contralateral hemiplegia
(B)	 Fasciculation at the level of lesion
(C)	Upper motor neuron lesion and lower motor 
neuron lesion
(D)	Bladder involvement
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(A) Contralateral hemiplegia
Contralateral hemiplegia—paralysis of the arm, leg, and face on the side of the body opposite the lesion—is the hallmark of a lesion in the brain, specifically in the motor pathways above the decussation of the pyramids in the medulla (e.g., motor cortex, internal capsule). Spinal cord lesions produce different patterns. A key feature of a spinal cord lesion is a combination of lower motor neuron (LMN) signs (like flaccid paralysis and fasciculations) at the specific level of the cord that is damaged, and upper motor neuron (UMN) signs (like spasticity and hyperreflexia) in all segments below the level of the lesion (C). Bladder involvement (D), such as urinary retention or incontinence, is also a very common and localizing sign of a significant spinal cord injury. Therefore, contralateral hemiplegia points to an intracranial, not a spinal cord, lesion.
114.	 A woman presents with palpitations and stable 
vital signs, and her ECG shows the pattern 
displayed below. What should be the initial step 
in her management?
(A)	Amiodarone
(B)	 Adenosine
(C)	DC cardioversion
(D)	Primary PCI
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(B) Adenosine
The ECG demonstrates a regular, narrow QRS complex tachycardia, which is characteristic of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). The patient is described as having stable vital signs. According to established treatment algorithms (like ACLS), the initial management for a stable patient with SVT is to attempt vagal maneuvers (e.g., Valsalva, carotid massage) to increase vagal tone and block the AV node. If these maneuvers fail to terminate the rhythm, the first-line pharmacological agent is adenosine. Adenosine is an ultra-short-acting drug that temporarily blocks conduction through the AV node, interrupting the reentrant circuit that is responsible for most SVTs (like AVNRT). DC cardioversion (C) is reserved for hemodynamically unstable patients. Amiodarone (A) may be used if adenosine is ineffective or contraindicated. Primary PCI (D) is a treatment for acute myocardial infarction.
115.	 Which of the following is not characteristic of

(D)	Ipsilateral loss of proprioception
AAns

(A) Complete transection of spinal cord
Brown-Séquard syndrome is, by definition, an incomplete spinal cord injury syndrome resulting from the hemisection of the spinal cord (damage to the right or left half). A complete transection would affect all tracts on both sides. The hemisection in Brown-Séquard syndrome produces a unique and predictable pattern of neurological deficits below the level of the injury:
Ipsilateral spastic paralysis due to damage to the corticospinal tract.
Ipsilateral loss of proprioception, vibration, and fine touch (B, D) due to damage to the dorsal columns.

Therefore, complete transection is contrary to the definition of this syndrome.

171.	 Which of the following statements about

AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022

This statement is incorrect. By convention, the gestational age or period of gestation (POG) is calculated from the FIRST day of the woman's last menstrual period (LMP), not the last day. 172.	 Which 
methods 
are 
used 
to 
evaluate 
contraceptive failure?
(A)	Pharmacological index
(B)	 Pearl index
(C)	Performance index
(D)	Efficacy index
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(B) Pearl index
The Pearl Index is the most common and historically significant statistical method used to measure the effectiveness and failure rate of a contraceptive method. It represents the number of unintended pregnancies that occur per 100 woman-years of use of a particular method. It is calculated with the formula: (Number of unintended pregnancies × 1200) / (Total months of use by all study subjects). A lower Pearl Index signifies a more effective contraceptive method with a lower failure rate. This standardized measure allows for the comparison of efficacy across different birth control options. The other terms listed are not standard epidemiological measures for contraceptive failure.

175.	 Which of the following is NOT a cause of uterine

176.	 Which of the following is NOT a characteristic

178.	 Which of the following is NOT a non-

Combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) offer numerous non-contraceptive health benefits. 180.	 Consider the following steps in the Active 
Management of the Third Stage of Labor 
(AMTSL). Place them in the correct sequence:

3.	 Check for additional fetuses

(C)	2,4,3,1
(D)	2,4,1,3
AAns

Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL) is a crucial intervention to prevent postpartum hemorrhage. The components must be performed in a specific, rapid sequence immediately following the birth of the baby:
1.	
Check for additional fetuses: Immediately palpate the abdomen to rule out the presence of another baby before giving a uterotonic. (Step 3)
2.	
Administer uterotonic: If no other baby is present, administer oxytocin 10 IU IM within one minute of birth. (Step 2)

Perform controlled cord traction (CCT): Once the uterus is well-contracted, apply gentle downward traction on the cord while applying counter-traction on the uterine fundus to deliver the placenta. (Step 4)

Uterine massage: Immediately after the placenta is delivered, massage the uterine fundus to stimulate it to contract firmly and prevent atony. (Step 1)

ANAESTHESIA
186.	 Which local anesthetic among the following 
leads to an increase in blood pressure?
(A)	Cocaine
(B)	 Lignocaine
(C)	Bupivacaine
(D)	Prilocaine
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(A) Cocaine
Cocaine is unique among local anesthetics. In addition to its primary action of blocking voltage-gated sodium channels to produce anesthesia, it also potently inhibits the reuptake of catecholamines, particularly norepinephrine, at sympathetic nerve terminals. This sympathomimetic action leads to an excess of norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft, causing intense vasoconstriction. This is why cocaine is the only local anesthetic that does not require the addition of epinephrine. The systemic effects of this catecholamine excess include hypertension (an increase in blood pressure), tachycardia, and an increased risk of cardiac arrhythmias and myocardial ischemia. In contrast, most other local anesthetics, such as lignocaine (B) and bupivacaine (C), are vasodilators at clinically used concentrations.

(B)	 IVa

(D)	III
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022

On axial CT imaging, liver segments are identified according to Couinaud’s classification, which divides the liver into eight functionally independent segments based on portal vein and hepatic vein anatomy.
In an axial section:
1.	
The right lobe lies on the left side of the image (radiologic convention).
2.	
The left lobe appears on the right side of the image.
3.	
The portal vein divides the liver into superior (segments VII, VIII, IVa) and inferior (segments V, VI, III, IVb) segments.
The highlighted region in the image lies in the right lobe, anterior and inferior to the portal vein level. Segment V is located in the anterior inferior part of the right lobe, below the portal vein plane and medial to segment VI.
Segment VII is posterior superior, segment VIII is anterior superior, and segment III belongs to the left lobe.
Since the indicated region corresponds to the anterior inferior portion of the right lobe, it represents Couinaud segment V.

Sigmoid volvulus is a common cause of large bowel obstruction, particularly in elderly, constipated, or institutionalized patients who often have a long, redundant sigmoid colon. A cecal volvulus (C) has a different appearance and location (more like a kidney bean shape in the left upper quadrant). The image is not suggestive of small bowel obstruction or perforation.

What is the location of Macula densa located?
(A)	
Junction of thick descending limb and DCT
(B)	
Junction of thick descending limb and PCT
(C)	
Junction of thick ascending limb and DCT
(D)	
Junction of DCT and collecting duct
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
18.	 (C) Junction of thick ascending limb and DCT
The macula densa is a specialized plaque of 
modified epithelial cells in the wall of the 
nephron tubule. It is a key component of the 
juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), which is 
critical for regulating blood pressure and 
glomerular filtration rate (GFR). The precise 
anatomical location of the macula densa is 
at the very end of the thick ascending limb 
of the loop of Henle, at the transition point 
where it becomes the distal convoluted tubule 
(DCT). In this location, the tubule comes into 
direct physical contact with the afferent and 
efferent arterioles of its own glomerulus. These 
specialized cells function as chemoreceptors, 
sensing the concentration of sodium chloride 
in the tubular fluid. This information is 
used to provide feedback to the glomerulus 
(tubuloglomerular 
feedback) 
to 
modulate 
GFR. This strategic placement allows for the 
autoregulation of individual nephron function.
Misincorporation of uracil into DNA is seen in deficiency of:
(A)	
Vitamin B12
(B)	
Folate
(C)	
Vitamin B6
(D)	
Vitamin E
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
19.	 (B) Folate
DNA synthesis requires a balanced supply of 
all four deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates 
(dNTPs): dATP, dGTP, dCTP, and dTTP. The 
synthesis of thymidine triphosphate (dTTP) 
involves 
the 
conversion 
of 
deoxyuridine 
monophosphate (dUMP) to deoxythymidine 
monophosphate 
(dTMP) 
by 
the 
enzyme 
thymidylate synthase. This critical methylation 
step requires N5,N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate 
as a methyl group donor. This cofactor is derived 
from folate (vitamin B9). In folate deficiency, 
the pool of this cofactor is depleted, which 
impairs the conversion of dUMP to dTMP. 
This leads to an imbalance in the dNTP pool, 
with an accumulation of dUTP relative to 
dTTP. DNA polymerase can then mistakenly 
incorporate dUTP (uracil) into the growing 
DNA strand instead of dTTP (thymine). This 
uracil misincorporation can lead to DNA strand 
breaks and mutations, contributing to the 
megaloblastic anemia seen in folate deficiency. 
Vitamin B12 deficiency can indirectly affect 
this by trapping folate in an unusable form, but 
folate is the direct cofactor.
Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by:
(A)	
Calcium
(B)	
Glucose-6-phosphate
(C)	
Insulin
(D)	
Protein phosphatase
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
20.	 (A) Calcium
Glycogen phosphorylase is the rate-limiting 
enzyme of glycogenolysis, the process of 
breaking down glycogen into glucose. Its activity 
is regulated through both covalent modification 
(phosphorylation) and allosteric mechanisms. 
The enzyme is converted from its less active 'b' 
form to its highly active 'a' form by the enzyme 
phosphorylase kinase. Phosphorylase kinase 
itself is activated by two principal mechanisms: 
phosphorylation by protein kinase A (cAMP-
dependent pathway, stimulated by glucagon 
and epinephrine) and direct allosteric activation 
by calcium ions (Ca2+). In muscle cells, for 
example, the release of Ca2+ during muscle 
contraction directly binds to the calmodulin 
subunit of phosphorylase kinase, activating it. 
This, in turn, activates glycogen phosphorylase, 
linking the demand for energy (contraction) 
with the supply of glucose from glycogen stores. 
Insulin (C) and glucose-6-phosphate (B) are 
inhibitors of glycogenolysis, while protein 
phosphatase (D) deactivates the enzyme by 
dephosphorylation.
A baby is brought to the outpatient clinic with lethargy and feeding difficulties, and the urine has a characteristic burnt-sugar smell. This condition is linked to a deficiency of which enzyme?

197.	 How should you manage a patient who comes 
to the outpatient department with upward 
eye deviation after taking risperidone for 
schizophrenia?
(A)	Lorazepam
(B)	 Promethazine
(C)	Olanzapine
(D)	Stop antipsychotic
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(B) Promethazine
The patient's symptom of sustained, involuntary upward deviation of the eyes is an oculogyric crisis, a form of acute dystonic reaction. This is a well-known extrapyramidal side effect of antipsychotic medications like risperidone. This is a medical emergency that requires immediate treatment. The first-line treatment is the parenteral administration of an anticholinergic agent (e.g., benztropine, biperiden) or a first-generation antihistamine with strong anticholinergic properties, such as diphenhydramine or promethazine. These drugs rapidly reverse the dystonic reaction. Lorazepam (A) may be used as an adjunctive agent for sedation and muscle relaxation but is not the primary treatment. Simply stopping the antipsychotic (D) or switching to another (C) will not resolve the acute crisis, which requires immediate pharmacological intervention.
198.	 Which of the following diseases is solely 
observed in females?
(A)	Rett syndrome
(B)	 Asperger syndrome
(C)	Selective mutism
(D)	Atypical autism
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(A) Rett syndrome
Rett syndrome is a unique, X-linked dominant neurodevelopmental disorder that is observed almost exclusively in females. It is caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene. Because the gene is located on the X chromosome and the mutation is dominant, it is almost always lethal in utero for male fetuses, who only have one X chromosome. Females survive because of X-inactivation, resulting in cellular mosaicism where some cells express the normal allele. For this reason, it is considered a disease solely observed in females. In contrast, Asperger syndrome (B), selective mutism (C), and atypical autism (D) are all conditions that are diagnosed in both males and females, although there may be differences in prevalence between the sexes.

191.	 Which of the following is NOT included in 
the whole-body CT scan protocol for a trauma 
patient?
(A)	CT Head
(B)	 CT Cervical spine
(C)	CT Limbs
(D)	CT Abdomen
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(C) CT Limbs
A whole-body CT (WBCT) or "pan-scan" for a major trauma patient is a standardized protocol designed to rapidly identify life-threatening injuries in the head, spine, and trunk. A typical WBCT protocol includes a non-contrast CT of the head (A), a CT of the cervical spine (B), and a contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen (D), and pelvis. This approach allows for the quick detection of intracranial bleeding, unstable spinal fractures, and major thoracic or abdominal organ injury and hemorrhage. CT of the limbs (C) is not a routine part of this initial screening protocol. Extremity injuries are generally assessed by physical examination and plain X-rays. A CT of a specific limb would only be performed subsequently if a complex fracture or vascular injury is suspected.
192.	 Which of the following conditions does not 
exhibit egg-shell calcification?
(A)	Silicosis
(B)	 Sarcoidosis
(C)	Post radiation therapy lymph nodes
(D)	Metastatic lymph nodes
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(D) Metastatic lymph nodes
Eggshell calcification refers to a specific pattern seen on imaging where there is a fine, curvilinear rim of calcification at the periphery of a lymph node. This pattern is highly characteristic of two granulomatous diseases: silicosis (A) and sarcoidosis (B), where it is typically seen in hilar and mediastinal nodes. It can also be seen less commonly in lymph nodes after radiation therapy (C). However, this pattern is not typical for metastatic lymph nodes (D). While metastases from certain tumors (e.g., papillary thyroid carcinoma, mucinous adenocarcinoma of the colon) can calcify, the pattern is usually punctate, amorphous, or chunky, rather than a delicate peripheral eggshell rim.
193.	 A 55-year-old man presents with hematuria, and

The provided contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) scan shows a large, solid mass arising from the kidney. 195.	 A 34-year-old woman is brought to the 
emergency department after a road traffic 
accident. Although her vital signs are stable 
and her GCS score is 3, her non-contrast CT 
head scan is normal. What is the most likely 
diagnosis?
(A)	Subdural hemorrhage
(B)	 Extradural hemorrhage
(C)	Diffuse axonal injury
(D)	Cerebral contusion
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
(C) Diffuse axonal injury
The clinical scenario presents a significant discrepancy: a patient in a deep coma (GCS of 3, the lowest possible score) but with a normal initial head CT scan. This pattern is the hallmark of diffuse axonal injury (DAI). DAI is a severe form of traumatic brain injury caused by shearing forces from rapid acceleration, deceleration, or rotation of the head. This causes widespread, microscopic damage to axons in the brain's white matter. Because the injury is microscopic, it is often not visible on an initial non-contrast CT scan. In contrast, major hemorrhages like subdural (A), extradural (B), or cerebral contusions (D) are macroscopic bleeds that are typically readily apparent on an initial CT. Therefore, severe clinical findings with a normal initial CT strongly suggest DAI.
196.	 A breast lump is detected in a female patient.

(B)	 PET scan
(C)	Clinical examination
(D)	Histology and cytology

(B) PET scan
The standard approach for evaluating a breast lump to diagnose or exclude cancer is the "triple assessment." This consists of:
1.	
Clinical examination (C) by a trained professional.
2.	
Radiological investigations (A), which include mammography and/or breast ultrasound.
3.	
Pathological sampling (D), such as fine-needle aspiration for cytology or core needle biopsy for histology.
When all three components are concordantly benign, cancer can be excluded with a very high degree of confidence. A PET (Positron Emission Tomography) scan (B), however, is not a primary tool for diagnosing a breast lump. PET scans measure metabolic activity and are primarily used in oncology for staging known cancers, looking for metastases, or assessing treatment response. They lack the resolution and specificity to be used as a frontline tool to rule out cancer in a newly discovered lump.

Which of the following vessels is not a branch of the facial artery within the facial region?
(A)	
Lateral nasal artery
(B)	
Mental artery
(C)	
Superior labial artery
(D)	
Inferior labial artery
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
1.	
(B) Mental artery
The facial artery, a branch of the external carotid 
artery, supplies the superficial structures of the 
face. Its major branches in the facial region 
include the inferior labial artery, the superior 
labial artery, and the lateral nasal artery. The 
inferior and superior labial arteries supply the 
lower and upper lips, respectively, while the 
lateral nasal artery supplies the skin of the ala 
and dorsum of the nose. The mental artery, 
conversely, is not a direct branch of the facial 
artery. It is the terminal branch of the inferior 
alveolar artery, which itself originates from the 
maxillary artery. The inferior alveolar artery 
travels through the mandibular canal and exits 
onto the face through the mental foramen as 
the mental artery, where it supplies the skin 
of the chin and the lower lip. Therefore, the 
mental artery has a different origin and is not 
considered a branch of the facial artery.
Which of the following structures does not receive innervation from the superior gluteal nerve?
(A)	
Gluteus medius
(B)	
Gluteus minimus
(C)	
Piriformis
(D)	
Tensor fasciae latae
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
2.	
(C) Piriformis
The superior gluteal nerve originates from the 
sacral plexus, with contributions from spinal 
nerve roots L4, L5, and S1. It exits the pelvis 
through the greater sciatic foramen, superior to 
the piriformis muscle. Its primary function is to 
provide motor innervation to three key muscles 
in the gluteal region: the gluteus medius, the 
gluteus minimus, and the tensor fasciae latae. 
These muscles are essential for abduction and 
medial rotation of the thigh and play a crucial 
role in stabilizing the pelvis during walking. 
Damage to this nerve leads to a characteristic 
Trendelenburg gait. The piriformis muscle, 
while located in the same region, receives its 
innervation from the nerve to piriformis, which 
arises directly from the ventral rami of S1 and 
S2. The piriformis functions as a lateral rotator 
of the thigh. Thus, it is the only muscle listed 
that is not supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.
Which foramen in the skull is created by the union of three bones?

The foramen lacerum is a unique, irregularly 
shaped foramen located in the base of the middle 
cranial fossa. It is distinguished by being formed 
at the junction of three different bones: the apex 
of the petrous part of the temporal bone, the 
basilar part of the occipital bone, and the body

located completely within the sphenoid bone. 
The foramen jugulare (D), or jugular foramen, 
is formed at the suture line between just two 
bones: the petrous part of the temporal bone 
and the occipital bone.

In the graph shown, which ions do labels A and B represent with respect to their permeability during the generation of an action potential?
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
14.	 (A) A is Na+, B is K+
The graph illustrates the time course of ion 
permeability changes during a typical neuronal 
action potential. The initial rapid rising phase 
(depolarization) from the threshold potential 
to a positive value is caused by the opening of 
voltage-gated sodium channels, leading to a 
massive and transient influx of sodium ions (
Na+). This corresponds to curve A, which shows 
a sharp, early peak in permeability that drives the 
membrane potential upward. The subsequent 
falling phase (repolarization) and the after-
hyperpolarization are primarily caused by the 
delayed opening of voltage-gated potassium 
channels. This allows potassium ions (K+) to 
flow out of the cell, returning the membrane 
potential to a negative value. This corresponds 
to curve B, which shows a slower and more 
sustained increase in permeability that begins 
as the sodium permeability is decreasing. Thus, 
A represents the permeability to Na+ and B 
represents the permeability to K+.
Which of the following is not a component of innate immunity?
(A)	
Alpha defensins
(B)	
B lymphocytes
(C)	
Gamma Delta T lymphocytes
(D)	
Lectin pathway
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
15.	 (B) B lymphocytes
The immune system consists of two main 
branches: innate and adaptive immunity. Innate 
immunity provides immediate, non-specific 
defense against pathogens. Its components 
include physical barriers, phagocytic cells (like 
macrophages), antimicrobial peptides such 
as alpha defensins (A), and the complement 
system, which can be activated via pathways 
like the lectin pathway (D). Gamma Delta 
T lymphocytes (C) are a type of T cell that 
possesses characteristics of both innate and 
adaptive immunity and are often considered part 
of the innate-like immune response. In stark 
contrast, B lymphocytes (B) are a cornerstone 
of adaptive immunity. Their primary function 
is to differentiate into plasma cells that produce 
highly specific antibodies against a particular 
antigen and to form memory cells that provide 
long-lasting immunity. This specificity and 
memory are the defining features of the adaptive 
immune system, not the innate system.
Please arrange the following steps of ventricular action potential in the correct order.
1.	
Activation of calcium channels regulated by changes in voltage.
2.	
Repolarizing  currents
3.	
Opening of voltage - gated sodium channels
4.	
Transient outward flow of potassium
(A)	
3,4,1,2
(B)	
4,3,2,1
(C)	
3,4,2,1
(D)	
1,2,3,4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
16.	 (A) 3,4,1,2
The cardiac ventricular action potential has five 
distinct phases (0-4). The sequence of events is 
as follows: Phase 0 is the rapid depolarization, 
caused by the rapid opening of voltage-gated 
sodium channels (3), leading to a massive influx 
of Na+. Phase 1 is the initial brief repolarization, 
which occurs due to the inactivation of the 
sodium channels and the opening of transient 
outward potassium channels (4). Phase 2 is the 
characteristic plateau phase, maintained by 
a balance between the inward current of Ca2+ 
through L-type voltage-gated calcium channels 
(1) and an outward potassium current. This 
prolonged depolarization is vital for cardiac 
function. Phase 3 is the final rapid repolarization, 
where the calcium channels close and the 
delayed rectifier potassium channels fully open, 
leading to a large efflux of K+ (2), which returns 
the membrane potential to its resting state. 
Therefore, the correct chronological order of the 
listed events is 3, 4, 1, and 2.

Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) represents 
the pressure gradient that drives blood flow 
to the brain, which is essential for delivering

driving force of blood flow is the Mean Arterial 
Pressure (MAP), which is the average pressure 
in the systemic circulation during a cardiac 
cycle. Therefore, to calculate the net pressure 
perfusing the brain, the opposing intracranial 
pressure must be subtracted from the driving 
mean arterial pressure. The universally accepted 
formula is CPP

Meckel's diverticulum, a remnant of the 
vitelline duct, is the most common congenital 
malformation of the gastrointestinal tract. 
While it is often asymptomatic, it can contain 
ectopic (heterotopic) mucosa in about 50% of 
cases, which can lead to complications. The 
most common type of ectopic tissue found is 
gastric mucosa. The acid secreted by this ectopic 
gastric tissue can cause ulceration, bleeding, or 
perforation of the adjacent ileal mucosa. The 
second most common type of ectopic tissue is 
pancreatic tissue. The presence of these two 
tissues accounts for the vast majority of ectopic 
findings in Meckel's diverticulum. Other tissues, 
such as colonic or duodenal mucosa, can be 
found but are much less frequent. Ectopic 
thyroid or lung tissue is not associated with this 
condition. Therefore, the combination of gastric 
and pancreatic tissue is the most frequently 
encountered, with gastric mucosa being the 
most clinically significant.
When a patient aspirates while lying in the supine position, which lobe of the lung is most likely to be affected?
(A)	
Lingula
(B)	
Upper part of right inferior lobe
(C)	
Right superior lobe
(D)	
Right middle lobe
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
10.	 (B) Upper part of right inferior lobe
The location of aspirated material in the lungs is 
determined by gravity and the patient's position. 
In the supine position (lying on the back), the 
most dependent portions of the tracheobronchial 
tree are the superior segments of the lower lobes 
and the posterior segments of the upper lobes. 
Due to the anatomy of the main bronchi—the 
right being wider and more vertical than the 
left—aspiration occurs more frequently into 
the right lung. When an individual is supine, 
the aspirated contents are most likely to flow 
into the superior (apical) segment of the right 
inferior lobe, as it is the most dependent segment 
in this position. The lingula (A) is part of the left 
upper lobe. The right superior (C) and middle 
(D) lobes are located more anteriorly and are 
therefore less likely to be the primary sites of 
aspiration in a supine patient.
What causes the detachment of myosin from actin filaments?
(A)	
Attachment of ATP to the myosin head
(B)	
Cessation of calcium release from the sarcoplasm
(C)	
Conformational change in Troponin T
(D)	
Dissociation of ADP and Pi
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
11.	 (A) Attachment of ATP to the myosin head
The process of muscle contraction is governed 
by the sliding filament theory, involving a cycle 
of attachment, pivoting, and detachment of 
myosin heads from actin filaments. After the 
"power stroke," during which the myosin head 
pulls the actin filament, the myosin remains 
firmly bound to the actin in a low-energy state, 
known as the rigor state. The detachment of 
the myosin head from the actin binding site 
is an active process that requires the binding 
of a new molecule of adenosine triphosphate 
(ATP) to the myosin head. This binding of ATP 
causes a conformational change in the myosin 
head, reducing its affinity for actin and leading 
to its release. Subsequently, ATP is hydrolyzed 
to ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi), which 
"re-cocks" the myosin head into a high-energy 
position, ready for the next contraction cycle. 
The dissociation of ADP and Pi (D) initiates the 
power stroke, it does not cause detachment.
Which proteins facilitate the transport of iron into enterocytes?
(A)	
Transferrin
(B)	
Ferroportin
(C)	
Hepcidin
(D)	
Divalent metal transporter - 1
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
12.	 (D) Divalent metal transporter - 1
The absorption of dietary non-heme iron from 
the gut lumen into the intestinal epithelial 
cells (enterocytes) is a regulated process. First, 
dietary ferric iron (Fe3+) is reduced to ferrous 
iron (Fe2+) by an enzyme on the brush border 
called duodenal cytochrome B (Dcytb). The 
ferrous iron is then transported across the 
apical membrane of the enterocyte into the cell 
by the Divalent Metal Transporter 1 (DMT1). 
Therefore, DMT1 is the specific protein 
responsible for the initial uptake of iron into 
the enterocyte. Once inside the cell, iron can 
be stored as ferritin or transported out of the 
cell into the bloodstream. This exit across the 
basolateral membrane is mediated by another 
protein called ferroportin (B). Transferrin (A) 
is the protein that binds and transports iron 
within the bloodstream. Hepcidin (C) is a liver-
produced hormone that regulates iron levels by 
downregulating ferroportin, thereby controlling 
iron's exit from the enterocyte.

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022 Answer
G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) transduce 
extracellular signals into intracellular responses 
via heterotrimeric G proteins, which are 
classified based on their α-subunit. The Gα 
subunit determines the downstream effector 
enzyme or ion channel. The Gq family of 
α-subunits (including Gq and G11) couples 
to the effector enzyme phospholipase C-β 
(PLCβ). Upon activation by a ligand-bound 
GPCR, the Gq protein activates PLCβ. PLCβ 
then hydrolyzes the membrane phospholipid 
phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) 
into two important second messengers: inositol 
1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol 
(DAG). IP3 triggers the release of calcium 
from intracellular stores, while DAG activates 
protein kinase C. In contrast, Gs proteins 
activate adenylyl cyclase, and Gi proteins inhibit 
adenylyl cyclase. Therefore, the phospholipase 
C pathway is the canonical signaling cascade for 
Gq-coupled receptors.
What is the source of fructosamine formation through glycation?
(A)	
Fructose
(B)	
Albumin
(C)	
Urea
(D)	
Glycosaminoglycan
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
23.	 (B) Albumin
Fructosamine is a term used to describe glycated 
proteins, primarily glycated serum albumin. 
Glycation is a non-enzymatic reaction where 
a sugar molecule, such as glucose, binds to 
a protein. In the bloodstream, glucose reacts 
with the amino groups of proteins, particularly 
albumin, due to albumin's high concentration in 
the serum. This process forms a stable ketoamine 
product. The concentration of fructosamine 
in the blood reflects the average blood glucose 
levels over the preceding 2 to 3 weeks, which 
corresponds to the half-life of albumin. This 
makes the fructosamine test a useful tool for 
monitoring short- to medium-term glycemic 
control in diabetic patients, especially when 
HbA1c measurements may be unreliable (e.g., 
in hemoglobinopathies). Therefore, albumin 
is the primary protein source for the clinical 
measurement of fructosamine.
Refsum disease is due to:
(A)	
Absence of alpha oxidation in peroxisomes
(B)	
Absence of beta-oxidation in peroxisomes
(C)	
Absence of alpha oxidation in lysosomes
(D)	
Absence of beta-oxidation in lysosomes
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
24.	 (A) Absence of alpha oxidation in peroxisomes
Adult Refsum disease is an autosomal recessive 
disorder of lipid metabolism characterized by 
the accumulation of phytanic acid, a branched-
chain fatty acid obtained from the diet. The 
methyl group on the beta-carbon of phytanic 
acid prevents it from being metabolized by 
the usual beta-oxidation pathway. Instead, 
it must first undergo alpha-oxidation. This 
process occurs exclusively in peroxisomes and 
involves the removal of the carboxyl carbon, 
shortening the chain by one carbon and 
allowing subsequent beta-oxidation to proceed. 
The key enzyme for the initial step is phytanoyl-
CoA hydroxylase (PAHX). In Refsum disease, 
a deficiency in this enzyme (or other proteins 
involved in the pathway) leads to the absence 
of alpha-oxidation in peroxisomes. This causes 
phytanic acid to accumulate to toxic levels in 
plasma and tissues, leading to neurological 
symptoms, retinitis pigmentosa, and anosmia.
An increased anion gap is seen in:
(A)	
Respiratory acidosis
(B)	
Respiratory alkalosis
(C)	
Metabolic acidosis
(D)	
Metabolic alkalosis
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
25.	 (C) Metabolic acidosis
The serum anion gap (AG) is a calculated value 
used to help determine the cause of metabolic 
acidosis. It is calculated as: AG = [Na+] - ([Cl-] + 
[HCO3
-]). This value represents the concentration 
of unmeasured anions (e.g., albumin, phosphate, 
sulfate) in the plasma. Metabolic acidosis can 
be broadly divided into two types based on the 
anion gap. A high anion gap metabolic acidosis 
occurs when there is an increase in unmeasured 
anions due to the accumulation of acids other 
than hydrochloric acid. Examples include 
lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, and ingestion of 
toxins like methanol or ethylene glycol. In 
these conditions, the added acid is buffered by 
bicarbonate (HCO3), which decreases, and the 
unmeasured anion of the acid increases, thus 
widening the anion gap. In contrast, normal 
anion gap metabolic acidosis involves a loss of 
bicarbonate that is compensated by an increase 
in chloride, keeping the gap normal.

"Cell in cell" appearance is seen in which of the following?
(A)	
Necrosis
(B)	
Apoptosis
(C)	
Necroptosis
(D)	
Entosis
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
35.	 (D) Entosis
The 
"cell-in-cell" 
structure 
describes 
the 
presence of one or more cells within the 
cytoplasm of another cell. While this can be 
seen when a phagocyte engulfs an apoptotic 
body 
(emperipolesis), 
the 
term 
is 
most 
specifically associated with entosis. Entosis is 
a distinct biological process where one living 
epithelial cell actively invades and is engulfed 
by a neighboring cell. The internalized "guest" 
cell remains alive for some time within a 
vacuole inside the "host" cell. The fate of the 
internalized cell can vary: it may be degraded, it 
may be released, or it may undergo cell division 
within the host. This phenomenon is distinct 
from phagocytosis of dead cells. Entosis is 
often observed in tumors and is thought to be 
a mechanism of cell competition. Necrosis (A) 
and necroptosis (C) are forms of lytic cell death 
and do not involve cell engulfment.

What is the oncotic pressure value of normal tissue?
(A)	
12 mmHg
(B)	
25 mmHg
(C)	
32 mmHg
(D)	
54 mmHg
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
38.	 (B) 25 mmHg
The question is slightly ambiguous but most 
likely refers to the plasma colloid osmotic 
(oncotic) pressure, which is a major determinant 
of fluid movement between the capillaries and 
the interstitial tissue. This pressure is generated 
by plasma proteins, primarily albumin, which 
are too large to pass freely across the capillary 
wall. This protein concentration creates an 
osmotic force that pulls fluid from the interstitial 
space back into the capillaries. The normal value 
for plasma oncotic pressure is approximately 25 
mmHg. The oncotic pressure of the interstitial 
fluid itself is much lower (around 8 mmHg) 
due to the low protein concentration in the 
tissue space. In the context of the Starling forces 
that govern tissue fluid balance, 25 mmHg is 
the standard value representing the inward-
pulling force of the plasma. The other values are 
outside the normal physiological range for this 
parameter.

Neurosecretory bodies are seen in all the following except:
(A)	
Medullary thyroid carcinoma
(B)	
Pituitary adenoma
(C)	
Paraganglioma
(D)	
Adrenal cortical tumor
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
31.	 (D) Adrenal cortical tumor
Neurosecretory bodies, also known as dense-
core granules, are membrane-bound vesicles 
containing hormones or neurotransmitters. 
They are the characteristic ultrastructural 
feature of neuroendocrine cells. Medullary 
thyroid carcinoma (A) is a neuroendocrine 
neoplasm arising from the calcitonin-producing 
C-cells of the thyroid. Pituitary adenomas 
(B) are tumors of the anterior pituitary gland, 
which is composed of various hormone-
secreting neuroendocrine cells. Paragangliomas 
(C), including pheochromocytomas, are tumors 
arising from chromaffin cells, which are also of 
neuroendocrine origin. All of these tumors are 
expected to contain neurosecretory granules. In 
contrast, adrenal cortical tumors originate from 
the adrenal cortex, which has a mesodermal 
origin, not a neuroectodermal one. The adrenal 
cortex produces steroid hormones (e.g., cortisol, 
aldosterone). Steroids are synthesized and 
released on demand and are not stored in 
secretory granules. Therefore, adrenal cortical 
tumors lack these characteristic neurosecretory 
bodies.

Rett 
syndrome 
is 
a 
progressive

disorder

Immune checkpoint inhibitors are a class 
of cancer immunotherapy drugs that block

Which of the following cytokines is not associated with the Th1 response?
(A)	
IFN-gamma
(B)	
IL-2
(C)	
IL-12
(D)	
IL-4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
41.	 (D) IL-4
CD4+ T helper (Th) cells differentiate into 
distinct subsets characterized by the cytokines 
they produce. The Th1 response is critical for 
cell-mediated immunity against intracellular 
pathogens. This response is driven by the 
cytokine IL-12 (C), which is produced by antigen-
presenting cells. Once differentiated, Th1 
cells produce a signature profile of cytokines, 
including IFN-gamma (A), which activates 
macrophages, and IL-2 (B), which is a T-cell 
growth factor that promotes clonal expansion. 
In contrast, IL-4 is the hallmark cytokine of the 
Th2 response. IL-4 promotes the differentiation 
of naive T cells toward the Th2 lineage and is 
central to humoral immunity, B-cell activation, 
class switching to IgE, and defense against 
extracellular parasites like helminths. Therefore, 
IL-4 is fundamentally associated with the Th2 
pathway, not the Th1 pathway.
A smoker presents with breathlessness and chest pain, and a lung mass that stains positive for chromogranin. What is the most likely diagnosis?

(B)

42.	 (D) Small cell carcinoma
The combination of a strong smoking history and

clue here is the positive chromogranin staining. 
Chromogranin A is an immunohistochemical 
marker for neuroendocrine differentiation. Its 
presence indicates that the tumor originates 
from neuroendocrine cells. Among primary 
lung cancers, the most common type with

and are negative for these neuroendocrine 
markers. Mesothelioma (C) is a tumor of the

and has a different set of markers (e.g., calretinin,

Which of the following is true about phenylketonuria (PKU)?
(A)	
PKU is characterized by a mousy odor in the urine due to a decrease in tyrosine, dopamine, and norepinephrine levels.
(B)	
PKU is characterized by a fruity odor in the urine due to a decrease in tyrosine, dopamine, and norepinephrine levels.
(C)	
PKU is characterized by a mousy odor in the urine due to an increase in tyrosine, dopamine, and norepinephrine levels
(D)	
PKU is characterized by a fruity odor in the urine due to an increase in tyrosine, dopamine, and norepinephrine levels.
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
28.	 (A) PKU is characterized by a mousy odor in the 
urine due to a decrease in tyrosine, dopamine, 
and norepinephrine levels.
Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive 
disorder caused by a deficiency in the enzyme 
phenylalanine 
hydroxylase. 
This 
enzyme 
normally converts phenylalanine into tyrosine. 
In its absence, phenylalanine accumulates and 
is metabolized into phenylketones, including 
phenylacetate, which is excreted in the urine 
and sweat, imparting a characteristic "mousy" 
or "musty" odor. Because the conversion of 
phenylalanine to tyrosine is blocked, there is 
a resultant deficiency of tyrosine. Tyrosine 
is a crucial precursor for the synthesis of 
catecholamine neurotransmitters (dopamine, 
norepinephrine, epinephrine) and melanin. 
Therefore, the biochemical consequences of 
untreated PKU include not only the mousy odor 
but also a decrease in the levels of tyrosine and 
its downstream products, which contributes 
to the severe intellectual disability and hypo 
pigmentation associated with the disease. A 
fruity odor is more typical of ketoacidosis.

For which drug is urinary alkalinization most useful in treating toxicity?
(A)	
Beta-blockers
(B)	
Aspirin
(C)	
Acetaminophen
(D)	
Calcium channel blockers
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
49.	 (B) Aspirin
Urinary alkalinization is a method of enhanced 
elimination used for overdoses of certain drugs, 
particularly weak acids. The principle is "ion 
trapping." Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is a weak 
acid (pKa ≈ 3.5). By administering intravenous 
sodium bicarbonate, the pH of the urine is 
raised (made more alkaline). In an alkaline 
environment, the weak acid ($HA$) is driven to 
dissociate into its ionized form ($H^+ + A^-$). 
This charged, ionized form (salicylate anion) is 
less lipid-soluble and cannot easily diffuse back 
across the renal tubular epithelium into the 
blood. It is thus "trapped" within the tubule and 
excreted in the urine, significantly increasing the 
drug's clearance from the body. This method is 
not effective for beta-blockers, acetaminophen, 
or calcium channel blockers, whose elimination 
pathways are not significantly affected by 
urinary pH. Acetaminophen toxicity is treated 
with N-acetylcysteine.
In the viral life cycle shown in the image, which drug acts at step 5?

50.	 (A) Raltegravir
The image provided illustrates the replication 
cycle of a retrovirus such as HIV. Step 5 in 
this cycle represents the critical process where 
the newly synthesized viral DNA is inserted 
into the host cell's own DNA. This integration 
is carried out by the viral enzyme integrase. 
Raltegravir belongs to a class of antiretroviral 
drugs known as integrase strand transfer 
inhibitors (INSTIs). Its mechanism of action is 
to specifically bind to and inhibit the integrase 
enzyme, thereby preventing the viral DNA 
from being incorporated into the host genome. 
This effectively stops the virus from hijacking 
the cell's machinery and halts the replication 
process. Enfuvirtide (B) is a fusion inhibitor 
that acts on viral entry (step 1). Tenofovir (C) 
and Zidovudine (D) are reverse transcriptase 
inhibitors that block the conversion of viral 
RNA to DNA (step 4), which occurs before 
integration.

The correct matching is A-4, B-1, C-3, D-2 based 
on renal physiology.
Acetazolamide 
is 
a 
carbonic 
anhydrase 
inhibitor. Carbonic anhydrase plays a major 
role in bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal 
convoluted tubule (PCT). By inhibiting this 
enzyme, acetazolamide reduces sodium and 
bicarbonate reabsorption in the PCT. Therefore, 
it acts at site 4 (proximal convoluted tubule).
Torsemide is a loop diuretic. Loop diuretics

the distal convoluted tubule (DCT), increasing 
sodium and water excretion. Therefore, it acts at 
site 3 (distal convoluted tubule).
Vasopressin (ADH) acts on V₂ receptors 
in the collecting duct, increasing water 
reabsorption through insertion of aquaporin-2 
channels. Hence, it acts at site 2 (collecting 
duct).
Thus, the correct matching is A-4, B-1, C-3, D-2.

In a murder trial where Sagar is accused of killing Mohan, Shikhar states in court that he saw Sagar holding a knife in the park. What is the legal term for Shikhar’s statement?
(A)	
Direct evidence
(B)	
Indirect evidence
(C)	
Hostile evidence
(D)	
Hearsay evidence
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
54.	 (A) Direct evidence
Direct evidence is evidence based on a witness’s 
personal knowledge or observation of a fact in 
issue, without requiring inference. If a person 
testifies in court about what they personally 
saw, heard, or experienced, that testimony is 
considered direct evidence.
In this case, Shikhar states that he saw 
Sagar holding a knife in the park. Since Shikhar 
is describing what he personally observed with 
his own senses, his statement qualifies as direct 
(ocular) evidence.
Indirect evidence (also called circumstantial 
evidence) requires the court to draw an inference. 
For example, if Shikhar had testified that he saw 
Sagar running away from the park after hearing 
screams, that would be circumstantial because 
the court would need to infer involvement in the 
crime.
Hostile evidence refers to testimony given 
by a witness who turns against the party that 
called them.
Hearsay evidence is a statement made 
outside court and repeated by someone else in 
court.
Thus, Shikhar’s testimony is direct evidence.
What clinical features are typically seen in cases of chronic arsenic poisoning?
1.	
Raindrop pigmentation
2.	
Peripheral neuritis
3.	
Mees line
4.	
Luminous vomit
(A)	
1,2,3 are correct
(B)	
2,3 are correct
(C)	
1,4 are correct
(D)	
Only 1 is correct
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
55.	 (A) 1,2,3 are correct
Chronic arsenic poisoning (arsenicosis) affects 
multiple organ systems and has several classic 
manifestations.
1.	 Raindrop pigmentation: A characteristic 
skin finding where small, dark spots of 
hyperpigmentation are interspersed with 
areas of normal skin or hypopigmentation, 
particularly on the trunk.
2.	 Peripheral neuritis: A painful, symmetrical, 
sensory-motor peripheral neuropathy is 
a common neurological complication of 
chronic exposure.
3.	 Mees' lines: Transverse white bands that 
appear across the fingernails (and toenails) 
weeks after a significant systemic insult, 
including poisoning by arsenic and other 
heavy metals.
4.	 Luminous vomit: This is a pathognomonic 
sign of acute phosphorus poisoning, where 
the vomitus glows in the dark due to the 
oxidation of elemental phosphorus. It is not 
associated with arsenic poisoning.
Therefore, the first three manifestations are 
correct for chronic arsenic poisoning.

The image shows a bruise with reddish-purple 
discoloration beneath intact skin. There is 
no break in the skin surface, which rules 
out abrasion, laceration, or stab wound. This 
appearance is characteristic of a contusion,

A contusion occurs when small blood 
vessels (capillaries) rupture due to impact, 
leading to extravasation of blood into the 
surrounding tissues. Because the skin remains 
unbroken, the bleeding occurs internally. The

or purple initially, to blue, green, and yellow—
as hemoglobin breaks down into biliverdin and 
bilirubin.
An abrasion involves superficial damage to the 
epidermis.

What type of strangulation method is the Spanish windlass?

Bansdola
(B)	
Garrotting
(C)

(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
58.	 (B) Garrotting
The Spanish windlass is a specific technique 
of garrotting. Garrotting is a form of ligature 
strangulation where a device is used to twist and 
tighten a cord or wire placed around the neck. 
In the Spanish windlass method, a stick or rod 
is inserted into a loop of the ligature and then 
rotated. This mechanical advantage allows for 
immense constricting force to be applied rapidly 
and with little effort, leading to asphyxiation. 
Throttling (D) refers to manual strangulation 
(using hands). Mugging (C) typically involves 
a chokehold from behind with the forearm. 
Bansdola (A) is another form of ligature 
strangulation where the ligature is tightened by 
pulling on its ends while pressing a foot against 
the neck for leverage.
Which technique is used to identify interactions between DNA and proteins?
(A)	
DNA footprinting
(B)	
DNA fingerprinting
(C)	
ELISA
(D)	
Northern blotting
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
59.	 (A) DNA footprinting
DNA footprinting is a technique used to 
determine the exact DNA sequence to which 
a specific protein (like a transcription factor) 
binds. The principle is that a protein bound to 
DNA will protect the DNA sequence it is covering 
from cleavage by a nuclease (like DNase I) or 
a chemical agent. When the DNA fragments 
are then separated by gel electrophoresis, the 
protected region appears as a gap, or "footprint," 
in 
the 
otherwise 
continuous 
ladder 
of 
fragments. This reveals the precise binding site 
of the protein. DNA fingerprinting (B) is used to 
identify individuals based on their unique DNA 
profiles. ELISA (C) is an immunological assay 
used to detect and quantify proteins, antibodies, 
or antigens. Northern blotting (D) is a technique 
used to detect specific RNA sequences.
What is the technique shown in the image that was used to confirm Ewing sarcoma in a patient with an EWSR1 gene mutation?

60.	 (A) Fluorescent in situ hybridisation
The image shown is a classic example of 
Fluorescent In Situ Hybridization (FISH). 
This cytogenetic technique uses fluorescently 
labeled DNA probes that bind to specific target 
DNA sequences on chromosomes within 
intact cells. The diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma is 
often confirmed by detecting a characteristic 
translocation involving the EWSR1 gene on 
chromosome 22. The image likely shows the 
result of a "break-apart" FISH assay. In this test, 
two probes of different colors (e.g., red and green) 
are designed to bind to regions on either side of 
the EWSR1 gene. In normal cells, the probes 
are close together and produce a fused yellow 
signal. In tumor cells with the translocation, 
the EWSR1 gene is broken, separating the probe 
binding sites. This results in distinct, separate 
red and green signals, confirming the gene 
rearrangement.

(B)

(C)	
Serum creatinine - 5.2 mg/dL
(D)

The 
patient's 
presentation 
with 
altered 
sensorium indicates severe malaria caused by P. 
falciparum. The WHO defines severe malaria by 
the presence of complications. Let's analyze the 
options based on these criteria:
(A)	Hypoglycemia (blood glucose <40 mg/
dL) is a defining complication of severe 
malaria.
(C)	Acute kidney injury (serum creatinine >3 
mg/dL) is also a criterion for severe malaria.

(D)	Cerebral malaria, defined by an unarousable

Which of the following agents can be used as a disinfectant rather than a sanitizer?

63.	 (D) Bleaching powder
A disinfectant is a chemical that destroys 
or irreversibly inactivates most pathogenic 
microorganisms on inanimate surfaces. A 
sanitizer reduces microbial contamination to a 
safe level but does not eliminate all pathogens. 
Bleaching powder (calcium hypochlorite) is a 
powerful oxidizing agent that releases chlorine. 
It is a broad-spectrum, high-level disinfectant 
used for surfaces and water treatment, capable 
of killing bacteria, viruses, and fungi. Hydrogen

antibiotic for therapeutic use inside the body.

used to inhibit microbial growth in products 
like cosmetics and foods; it is bacteriostatic/
fungistatic, not a disinfectant. Bleaching 
powder's primary role is disinfection.

Which microscopy method is used to produce high-contrast images of transparent, living bacteria?
(A)	
Phase contrast microscopy
(B)	
Dark field microscopy
(C)	
Electron microscopy
(D)	
Polarized microscopy
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
69.	 (A) Phase contrast microscopy
Unstained living cells, like bacteria, are mostly 
transparent and difficult to see with a standard 
bright-field microscope because they absorb 
very little light. Phase contrast microscopy is 
an optical microscopy technique specifically 
designed to enhance contrast in such transparent 
specimens without the need for staining, thus 
allowing observation of viable cells. It works 
by converting phase shifts in light passing 
through a transparent specimen to brightness 
changes in the image. These phase shifts are 
caused by differences in refractive index and 
thickness within the specimen. This technique 
is invaluable for studying the morphology and 
behavior of living microorganisms. Dark field 
microscopy (B) illuminates the specimen from 
the side, making it appear bright against a dark 
background. Electron microscopy (C) offers 
much higher magnification but requires fixed, 
non-living specimens.

Which of the following tests is not used to assess nasal mucociliary clearance?

89.	 (B) Electron microscopy
Nasal mucociliary clearance is the physiological 
process of cleaning the nasal passages. Several 
tests measure its function:
The Saccharine test (A) and Charcoal 
powder method (C) are functional tests that 
measure the time it takes for a substance placed 
in the nose to be transported to the pharynx.
Scintigraphy (D) is a more objective 
functional test using a radioactive tracer to 
visualize and quantify the movement of mucus.
In contrast, electron microscopy (B) is 
a structural test, not a functional one. It is 
used to examine the ultrastructure of the cilia

defects, such as those seen in Primary Ciliary 
Dyskinesia 
(PCD).

an 
abnormal 
structure can explain poor function, electron 
microscopy does not directly measure the rate 
or effectiveness of clearance.

types of tympanoplasty based on the status

reconstruct sound conduction.

If otoacoustic emissions (OAEs) are absent, which additional tests can be used for hearing screening?
(A)	
Pure tone audiometry
(B)	
Tympanometry
(C)	
Free field audiometry
(D)	
Speech audiometry
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
91.	 (B) Tympanometry
Otoacoustic emissions (OAEs) are sounds 
generated by the outer hair cells of the cochlea, 
used for newborn hearing screening. A "pass" 
result indicates a healthy cochlea. A "refer" 
result (absent OAEs) can mean a problem in 
the cochlea (sensorineural hearing loss) OR a 
problem in the outer or middle ear that prevents 
the sound from getting in or the emission from 
getting out. The most common reason for a 
"refer" in a newborn is fluid in the middle ear 
(otitis media with effusion). Therefore, the 
immediate next step is to assess the middle ear 
status. Tympanometry is an objective test that 
measures the mobility of the eardrum and the 
pressure in the middle ear. It can quickly and 
reliably detect middle ear problems like fluid 
or eustachian tube dysfunction, helping to 
differentiate the cause of the absent OAEs.

(B)	
1 only is correct

1 and 4 are correct

scenario 
illustrates 
several 
key 
epidemiological concepts.
1.	 Index case: The first case to be brought to 
the attention of the health system. Since 
Ram was taken to the PHC, he is the index 
case. (Correct)
2.	 Primary case: The first person to introduce

descriptions of the situation.
While checking a patient’s blood pressure at a primary health centre, the sphygmomanometer fell and broke, spilling mercury on the floor. What steps should be taken to clean up the mercury safely?
(A)	
Use a card to gather the mercury onto a sheet of paper and place it in a sealed jar.
(B)	
Sweep up the mercury with a broom and dispose of it outside.
(C)	
Sweep up the mercury and flush it down the toilet.
(D)	
Pick up the mercury by hand and wash hands with water afterward.
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
76.	 (A) Use a card to gather the mercury onto a 
sheet of paper and place it in a sealed jar.
Elemental mercury is a hazardous substance; 
its vapor is toxic when inhaled, and it can 
be absorbed through the skin. Spills must be 
handled carefully to minimize exposure and 
contamination. The correct procedure for a 
small spill is to consolidate the mercury beads 
without breaking them up further. Using a 
stiff piece of paper or cardboard to gently roll 
the beads together and then onto another sheet 
of paper is the recommended method. The 
collected mercury should then be placed into 
an airtight, unbreakable container (like a sealed 
glass jar), labeled as hazardous waste, and 
disposed of according to local guidelines. Using 
a broom (B) or vacuum cleaner will disperse the 
mercury into smaller, more volatile droplets. 
Flushing it (C) contaminates the water supply, 
and direct hand contact (D) is dangerous.
Which field of statistics is involved in describing the internal data collection?

77.	 (B) Descriptive statistics
The field of statistics is broadly categorized into 
two main branches. Descriptive statistics is the 
branch that deals with methods of summarizing, 
organizing, and presenting data in a meaningful 
way. It aims to describe the basic features of a 
dataset. This includes calculating measures 
like mean, median, and mode, creating 
frequency distributions, and generating visual 
representations such as histograms and bar 
charts. The phrase "describing the internal data 
collection" aligns perfectly with the function 
of descriptive statistics. In contrast, inferential 
statistics (D) involves using data from a sample 
to make conclusions or predictions about a larger 
population from which the sample was drawn. 
It involves hypothesis testing and estimation.

In which of the following conditions is atropine not recommended for use?
(A)	
Acute congestive glaucoma
(B)	
Acute anterior uveitis
(C)	
Malignant glaucoma
(D)	
Corneal ulcer
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
98.	 (A) Acute congestive glaucoma
Atropine is a strong mydriatic (pupil-dilating) 
and cycloplegic (ciliary muscle-paralyzing) 
agent. Its use is absolutely contraindicated in 
acute congestive glaucoma, which is another 
term for acute angle-closure glaucoma. In a 
patient with a narrow anterior chamber angle, 
dilating the pupil with atropine causes the 
peripheral iris to bunch up and physically block 
the trabecular meshwork, which is the eye's 
drainage system. This obstruction prevents 
the outflow of aqueous humor, leading to a 
rapid and dangerous increase in intraocular 
pressure, which can cause blindness. In all the 
other conditions listed, atropine is therapeutic. 
In uveitis (B) and corneal ulcers (D), it relieves 
painful ciliary muscle spasm and prevents the 
iris from sticking to the lens. In malignant 
glaucoma (C), it is used to pull the lens-iris 
diaphragm backward.
During a routine eye check using a Snellen chart, a patient's visual acuity is recorded as 6/6. With this level of vision, what is the minimum angle at which the patient can distinguish two distinct points?
(A)	
15 minutes of arc
(B)	
5 minutes of arc
(C)	
10 minutes of arc
(D)	
20 minutes of arc
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
99.	 (B) 5 minutes of arc
This question is slightly tricky in its wording. 
The standard of normal vision (6/6 or 20/20) 
is defined by the ability to resolve a detail that 
subtends a visual angle of 1 minute of arc. The 
letters on a Snellen chart are designed so that 
the entire letter subtends an angle of 5 minutes 
of arc at the specified distance (e.g., 6 meters 
for the 6/6 line). The individual components 
of the letter, like the strokes and the gaps 
between them, subtend an angle of 1 minute 
of arc. Therefore, to be able to "differentiate 
two separate points or objects" that make up 
the letter (i.e., to identify the letter), the patient 
must be able to see the overall letter. The size 
of this smallest identifiable letter on the 6/6 line 
corresponds to a visual angle of 5 minutes of arc.

to cause disease. It corresponds to the period

A 30-year-old patient presents with hypopigmented skin patches. Examination shows a few well-defined, slightly elevated lesions with sensory loss, and skin smears are negative for acid-fast bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	
Multibacillary leprosy
(B)	
Psoriasis
(C)	
Tinea versicolor
(D)	
Paucibacillary leprosy
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
106.	 (D) Paucibacillary leprosy
The 
cardinal 
sign 
of 
leprosy 
(Hansen's 
disease) is a skin lesion with a definite loss 
of sensation. This patient's well-demarcated, 
hypopigmented patches with anesthesia are 
highly characteristic. Leprosy is classified on 
a spectrum based on the patient's immune 
response and bacterial load. Paucibacillary (PB) 
leprosy represents the high-immunity end of the 
spectrum. It is characterized by a small number 
of lesions (1-5), a robust cell-mediated immune 
response, and a very low number of bacteria.

smears for acid-fast bacilli are typically negative. 
In contrast, multibacillary (MB) leprosy (A) is

mediated immunity, a high bacterial load, and 
positive skin smears. Psoriasis (B) and tinea 
versicolor (C) do not cause sensory loss within 
the lesions. The combination of few lesions, 
sensory loss, and negative smears points directly 
to paucibacillary leprosy.
Zellweger syndrome results from an abnormality in the formation of:
(A)	
Peroxisomes
(B)	
Lysosomes
(C)	
Mitochondria
(D)	
Nucleus
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
107.	 (A) Peroxisomes
Zellweger syndrome is the prototypical and most 
severe of the peroxisomal biogenesis disorders 
(PBDs). Peroxisomes are essential membrane-
bound 
organelles 
involved 
in 
numerous 
metabolic pathways, including the breakdown 
of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) and the 
synthesis of plasmalogens, which are crucial 
for brain and nerve myelination. In PBDs, 
mutations in PEX genes lead to a failure in the 
assembly of functional peroxisomes. As a result, 
peroxisomal enzymes are not correctly imported 
into the organelle and remain in the cytosol, 
rendering them non-functional. This leads to the 
toxic accumulation of substances like VLCFAs, 
causing severe neurological defects, dysmorphic 
features, and liver dysfunction. The condition 
is incompatible with long-term survival. It 
is fundamentally a disease of peroxisome 
formation, distinct from disorders of lysosomes, 
mitochondria, or the nucleus.

In a 2-year-old child with sudden breathing

A known substance addict is hospitalized for intoxication, and an eye examination shows characteristic findings. Which statement about this scenario is correct?
(A)	
This action can be reversed by phenylephrine
(B)	
It cannot be reversed by levallorphan
(C)

93.	 (C) It is caused by activation of the Edinger-

The image shows severe pupillary constriction 
(miosis), often described as "pinpoint pupils." In 
a patient with a history of substance abuse, this is 
the pathognomonic sign of opioid intoxication. 
Opioids cause miosis by stimulating mu and 
kappa receptors in the brainstem, which in turn 
leads to parasympathetic stimulation of the eye. 
This stimulation originates from the Edinger-
Westphal nucleus, the parasympathetic nucleus 
of the oculomotor nerve (CN III). Activation of 
this nucleus causes contraction of the sphincter 
pupillae muscle, resulting in miosis.
(A)	Phenylephrine is a mydriatic (dilator), but 
reversal is done with opioid antagonists.
(B)	Levallorphan is an opioid antagonist, so it 
can reverse the effect.
(D)	Miosis (along with constipation) is a notable 
effect of opioids to which very little or no 
tolerance develops, even with chronic use.
What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient who presents with vertigo and horizontal nystagmus, with the slow phase beating to the left?
(A)	
Posterior canal BPPV
(B)	
Superior canal BPPV
(C)	
Right hypoactive labyrinth
(D)	
Left hypoactive labyrinth
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
94.	 (D) Left hypoactive labyrinth
In peripheral vestibular disorders, nystagmus 
results from an imbalance in vestibular tone 
between the two ears. A hypoactive (weakened) 
labyrinth sends fewer signals to the brainstem. 
The brain interprets this lack of signal as a 
head turn towards the opposite, healthy side. 
The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) then tries to 
compensate by slowly moving the eyes towards 
the side of the hypoactive labyrinth. This 
slow movement is the slow component of the 
nystagmus. In this case, the slow component 
is directed to the left. This indicates that the 
left labyrinth is hypoactive. The fast, corrective 
saccade will be in the opposite direction (to the 
right), so this would be described clinically as 
a right-beating nystagmus. Benign Paroxysmal 
Positional Vertigo (BPPV) in the posterior or 
superior canals (A, B) typically causes torsional-
vertical nystagmus, not purely horizontal 
nystagmus.

Which of the following statements is false regarding rabies immunoglobulin?
(A)	
It is exclusively given only in the deltoid
(B)	
The dose is 20 IU/kg
(C)

(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
79.	 (A) It is exclusively given only in the deltoid
This statement is false. The most critical 
principle of rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) 
administration is to infiltrate as much of the 
dose as is anatomically feasible directly into 
and around the wound(s). This is done to 
neutralize the virus at the site of inoculation. 
Any remaining RIG that cannot be infiltrated 
around the wound should be given as a deep 
intramuscular injection at a site distant from

for human RIG (HRIG) is 20 IU/kg (B), it should 
be given as soon as possible after exposure (C), 
and equine RIG (ERIG) is the alternative if 
HRIG is not available (D).
If a point-of-care test with 98% sensitivity gives a negative result in a patient, what does this imply?
(A)	
The patient would need another point-of-care diagnostic test for the same clinical condition
(B)	
The prevalence of the disease is 2%
(C)	
The patient is less likely to have the disease
(D)	
The patient has been wrongly ruled out due to false negatives
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
80.	 (C) The patient is less likely to have the disease
Sensitivity refers to a test's ability to correctly 
identify individuals who have a specific disease 
(the true positive rate). A test with 98% sensitivity 
will correctly detect the disease in 98 out of 
100 people who are truly infected, with only 
a 2% false-negative rate. Because of this high 
sensitivity, a negative result carries significant 
weight. There is a very high probability that 
a person who tests negative with such a test 
does not have the disease. This concept is 
often summarized by the mnemonic "SnNout" 
(a highly Sensitive test, when Negative, helps 
to rule out the disease). Therefore, a negative 
result from this test indicates that the patient is 
very unlikely to have the condition.
