Which cranial nerves does the oculocephalic reflex evaluate for their integrity?
1.	
III
2.	
IV
3.	
VI
4.	
VIII
5.	
VII
(A)	
1 and 3
(B)	
1 and 5
(C)	
1 and 4
(D)	
1, 3 and 4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
101.	 (D) 1, 3 and 4
The oculocephalic reflex, also known as the 
"doll's eye" reflex, is a test of brainstem integrity 
in a comatose patient. The reflex arc begins with 
the stimulation of the vestibular system when 
the head is turned. The afferent (sensory) limb 
of this reflex is the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN 
VIII) (4), which carries information from the 
semicircular canals to the vestibular nuclei in 
the brainstem. From there, signals are relayed 
via the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) to 
the motor nuclei of the extraocular muscles. The 
efferent (motor) limb involves the oculomotor 
nerve (CN III) (1), the trochlear nerve (CN 
IV) (2), and the abducens nerve (CN VI) (3). 
An intact reflex (eyes move conjugately in the 
opposite direction of the head turn) confirms the 
integrity of this entire pathway. Therefore, the 
reflex assesses CN III, IV, VI, and VIII. Option 
(D) is the most comprehensive choice provided.
What characteristic clinical sign is seen in Klumpke’s paralysis, which results from injury to the lower brachial plexus?

Klumpke's paralysis is a palsy of the lower

A 50-year-old man has a positive Trendelenburg test on the right side. Which nerve is involved?
(A)	
Right inferior gluteal nerve
(B)	
Right superior gluteal nerve
(C)	
Left superior gluteal nerve
(D)	
Left inferior gluteal nerve
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
104.	 (B) Right superior gluteal nerve
The Trendelenburg test assesses the function 
of the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus 
muscles, which are responsible for stabilizing 
the pelvis during walking. These muscles are 
innervated by the superior gluteal nerve.
In a normal person standing on the right leg, 
the right gluteus medius and minimus contract 
to keep the pelvis level. If these muscles are weak 
or paralyzed, the pelvis drops on the opposite 
(left) side. This is a positive Trendelenburg sign.
A positive Trendelenburg test on the right 
side means that when the patient stands on the 
right leg, the pelvis drops on the left side. This 
indicates weakness of the right gluteus medius 
and minimus, and therefore injury to the right 
superior gluteal nerve.
The inferior gluteal nerve supplies the 
gluteus maximus, which is involved in hip 
extension, not pelvic stabilization. Hence, it is 
not responsible for a positive Trendelenburg 
sign.
Therefore, the involved nerve is the right 
superior gluteal nerve.

__________ is the regulation of genes whose expression depends on whether they are maternally or paternally inherited, which is controlled by DNA methylation.
(A)	
Gonadal mosaicism
(B)	
Genomic imprinting
(C)	
Anticipation
(D)	
Incomplete penetrance
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
71.	 (B) Genomic imprinting
Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic process 
where certain genes are expressed in a parent-of-
origin-specific manner. For an imprinted gene, 
only one of the two inherited alleles (either the 
maternal or the paternal) is expressed, while the 
other is silenced. This "imprint" is established in 
the germ cells of the parents and is maintained 
throughout the somatic cells of the offspring. 
The primary mechanism controlling this 
monoallelic expression is DNA methylation 
at specific DNA regions called imprinting 
control centers. This methylation pattern marks 
the allele for silencing. It is a form of gene 
regulation that does not involve changes to the 
DNA sequence itself. Disorders like Prader-
Willi syndrome and Angelman syndrome are 
classic examples of diseases caused by defects in 
genomic imprinting.

A 40-year-old man with chronic alcoholism is undergoing withdrawal, and his liver function tests show elevated AST, ALT, and GGT levels. Given his impaired liver function, which benzodiazepine is the safest choice for managing his withdrawal symptoms?
(A)	
Diazepam
(B)	
Alprazolam
(C)	
Clonazepam
(D)	
Lorazepam
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
111.	 (D) Lorazepam
Benzodiazepines are the cornerstone of therapy 
for alcohol withdrawal. However, in a patient 
with compromised liver function, as suggested 
by the elevated liver enzymes, the choice of agent 
is critical. Most benzodiazepines, including 
diazepam, are metabolized through oxidative 
pathways in the liver (cytochrome P450 system), 
which can be significantly impaired in liver 
disease. This can lead to drug accumulation and 
prolonged sedation. Lorazepam, however, is 
metabolized primarily through glucuronidation, 
a process that is much better preserved in 
patients with liver dysfunction. For this 
reason, lorazepam, along with oxazepam and 
temazepam (mnemonic: "Outside The Liver"), 
are the preferred benzodiazepines in patients 
with alcoholic liver disease. They have a shorter 
half-life and no active metabolites, making them 
a safer choice to manage withdrawal symptoms 
in this patient population.
Which of the options listed below does not assist in the identification of spinal cord lesions?
(A)	
Contralateral hemiplegia
(B)	
Fasciculation at the level of lesion
(C)	
Upper motor neuron lesion and lower motor neuron lesion
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
112.	 (A) Contralateral hemiplegia
Contralateral hemiplegia—paralysis of the arm, 
leg, and face on the side of the body opposite 
the lesion—is the hallmark of a lesion in the 
brain, specifically in the motor pathways above 
the decussation of the pyramids in the medulla 
(e.g., motor cortex, internal capsule). Spinal 
cord lesions produce different patterns. A key 
feature of a spinal cord lesion is a combination 
of lower motor neuron (LMN) signs (like flaccid 
paralysis and fasciculations) at the specific 
level of the cord that is damaged, and upper 
motor neuron (UMN) signs (like spasticity and 
hyperreflexia) in all segments below the level of 
the lesion (C). Bladder involvement (D), such as 
urinary retention or incontinence, is also a very 
common and localizing sign of a significant 
spinal cord injury. Therefore, contralateral 
hemiplegia points to an intracranial, not a spinal 
cord, lesion.

Which of the following factors are associated with a higher likelihood of febrile seizure recurrence?
1.	
Age <1 year
2.	
Temperature of 38-39°C
3.	
Duration of fever <24 h
4.	
Duration of fever >48 h
(A)	
1,2,4
(B)	
1,4
(C)	
1,2,3
(D)	
1,3,4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
149.	 (C) 1,2,3
The risk of recurrence after a first simple febrile 
seizure is approximately 30%. Certain factors are 
known to increase this risk:
1.	 Young age at onset: The risk of recurrence 
is significantly higher if the first seizure 
occurs in an infant less than 12 or 15 
months old.
2.	 Lower degree of fever: A seizure occurring 
with a relatively low-grade fever (e.g., 38-
39°C) suggests a lower seizure threshold for 
that child, increasing the risk of recurrence 
with future febrile illnesses.
3.	 Short duration between fever onset and 
seizure: If the seizure occurs very soon after 
the fever begins (e.g., fever for less than 24 
hours), the risk of recurrence is higher.
4.	 A family history of febrile seizures in a first-
degree relative is another major risk factor.
Therefore, factors 1, 2, and 3 are all established 
predictors for an increased risk of febrile seizure 
recurrence.
For a child with thalassemia who receives regular blood transfusions, what is the most effective method to monitor the development of iron overload?
(A)	
Liver iron concentration
(B)	
MRI T2\ myocardium
(C)	
Serum ferritin
(D)	
NTBI (Non-transferrin-bound iron)
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
150.	 (A) Liver iron concentration
Chronic blood transfusions inevitably lead to 
iron overload (hemosiderosis), as the body has no 
physiological mechanism to excrete excess iron. 
Monitoring this iron burden is crucial to guide 
chelation therapy and prevent organ damage. 
While serum ferritin (C) is the most commonly 
used screening test, it is an acute-phase reactant 
and can be elevated by inflammation, making 
it an unreliable quantitative marker. The gold 
standard for assessing total body iron stores is 
the liver iron concentration (LIC) (A), which 
can be measured directly via biopsy or, more 
commonly now, non-invasively and accurately 
using specialized MRI techniques (R2 or T2\). 
The most life-threatening complication of iron 
overload is cardiac siderosis leading to heart 
failure. MRI T2\ of the myocardium (B) is the 
best method to specifically quantify cardiac iron, 
which is the strongest predictor of mortality. 
However, LIC remains the best overall measure 
of total body iron stores.
What is the probable diagnosis in a child who persistently wears socks even in warm weather because of cold feet, has lower limb pulses weaker than the radial pulse, and shows a clear radio-femoral delay?
(A)	
There is hypertrophy of ductus arteriosus
(B)	
Coarctation distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery
(C)	
Supply is from the posterior to the anterior thoracic artery
(D)	
Collaterals develop to supply the upper limb
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
151.	 (B) Coarctation distal to the origin of the left 
subclavian artery
This clinical presentation is the classic textbook 
description of coarctation of the aorta. This 
congenital heart defect involves a narrowing 
of the aorta, most commonly in the juxtaductal 
position, i.e., just distal to the origin of the left 
subclavian artery (B). This stenosis obstructs 
blood flow to the lower part of the body. 
Consequently, blood pressure is high in the 
vessels proximal to the coarctation (supplying 
the arms), leading to strong or bounding radial 
pulses. Distal to the narrowing, blood flow is 
reduced, causing low blood pressure, weak 
or absent femoral pulses, and symptoms like 
cold feet. The difference in arrival time of the 
pulse wave between the upper and lower limbs 
creates the pathognomonic radio-femoral delay. 
Over time, collateral arteries develop to bypass 
the blockage and supply the lower body, not the 
upper limbs (D).

A male patient who has ingested an unknown substance now exhibits profuse sweating, excessive tearing, diarrhea, muscle weakness, and tachycardia. What is the correct management for this condition?
(A)	
Calcium gluconate
(B)	
Pralidoxime
(C)	
Obidoxime
(D)	
Atropine
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
128.	 (D) Atropine
The 
patient's 
symptoms—diaphoresis 
(sweating), lacrimation (tearing), diarrhea, 
and muscle weakness—are classic features 
of a cholinergic crisis. This is most commonly 
caused by poisoning with acetylcholinesterase 
inhibitors, 
such 
as 
organophosphate 
or 
carbamate insecticides. These toxins cause 
an excess of acetylcholine at both muscarinic 
and nicotinic synapses. The immediate, life-
saving antidote is atropine. Atropine is a 
competitive antagonist of acetylcholine at 
muscarinic receptors. It works by blocking 
the excessive parasympathetic effects, thereby 
drying up secretions (bronchorrhea, salivation), 
increasing the heart rate (if bradycardic), and 
reducing bronchospasm. Large and repeated 
doses are often required. Pralidoxime (B) is an 
oxime used as an adjunct in organophosphate 
(but not carbamate) poisoning to reactivate 
the cholinesterase enzyme and treat nicotinic 
symptoms like muscle weakness, but atropine is 
the first-line and most critical intervention.
What is the probable diagnosis in an elderly woman who suffered a fall and then, after several days, began to develop a headache and neurological deficits?
(A)	
Multi-infarct dementia
(B)	
Frontal lobe meningioma
(C)	
Korsakoff disease
(D)	
Subdural hematoma
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
129.	 (D) Subdural hematoma
The combination of head trauma (even a 
seemingly minor fall) in an elderly person 
followed by the gradual onset of headache and 
neurological symptoms (such as confusion, 
lethargy, or focal deficits) over days to weeks is 
the classic presentation of a chronic subdural 
hematoma (SDH). Elderly individuals are 
predisposed to this condition because age-related 
brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins that 
cross the subdural space. A minor trauma can 
tear these veins, leading to a slow, low-pressure 
venous bleed. The hematoma gradually expands, 
causing symptoms as it exerts mass effect on the 
brain. The other options are not consistent with 
this acute-on-chronic presentation following 
trauma. A chronic SDH is a critical diagnosis to 
consider in any elderly patient with a recent fall 
and new neurological complaints.
Which of the following statements is true regarding shock?
(A)	
Anaerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide
(B)	
Septic shock-most common type
(C)	
Stage of compensatory shock is also called stage 2 of shock
(D)	
Anaphylactic shock-is due to Type 2 hypersensitivity reaction
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
130.	 (C) Stage of compensatory shock is also called 
stage 2 of shock
Shock is commonly divided into stages:
1.	 Initial stage (Stage 1) – Early cellular 
hypoxia begins; anaerobic metabolism 
starts.
2.	 Compensatory stage (Stage 2) – The body 
activates compensatory mechanisms such 
as tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction, 
and activation of the renin–angiotensin–
aldosterone system to maintain blood 
pressure and perfusion.
3.	 Progressive stage (Stage 3) – Worsening 
tissue hypoxia and metabolic acidosis.
4.	 Irreversible stage (Stage 4) – Multi-organ 
failure and death.
Now reviewing other options:
1.	 (A) is false because anaerobic respiration 
produces lactic acid, not carbon dioxide.
2.	 (B) is incorrect in general classification; 
hypovolemic shock is often cited as the 
most common overall, though septic shock 
is the most common distributive type.
3.	 (D) is false because anaphylactic shock is due 
to a Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity 
reaction, not Type II.
Thus, the correct statement is (C).

Which of the following statements is accurate concerning split-thickness and full-thickness skin grafts?
1.	
Primary contractures are more in split-thickness skin grafts
2.	
Secondary contractures are more in split-thickness skin grafts
3.	
Primary contractures are more in full-thickness grafts
4.	
Secondary contractures are more in full-thickness grafts
(A)	
2,3
(B)	
2,4
(C)	
1,3
(D)	
1,4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
133.	 (A) 2,3
Skin grafts undergo two distinct types of 
contraction.
Primary contracture is the immediate elastic 
recoil of the skin graft upon harvesting. This 
is proportional to the amount of dermis in the 
graft. Since full-thickness grafts contain the 
entire dermis, they have significantly more 
primary contracture (3 is correct, 1 is incorrect).
Secondary contracture is the shrinkage of 
the graft after it has been placed on the wound 
bed, driven by myofibroblasts. The dermis 
provides a scaffold that resists this contraction. 
Since split-thickness grafts have less dermis, 
they are less able to resist this force and undergo 
more secondary contracture (2 is correct, 4 is 
incorrect).
The rule of thumb is: the thicker the graft (full-
thickness), the more primary contraction and 
the less secondary contraction.
What is the primary cause of severe malnutrition among the options provided below?
(A)	
Pancreatic fistula
(B)	
Duodenal fistula
(C)	
Distal ileal fistula
(D)	
Colonic fistula
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
134.	 (C) Distal ileal fistula
Severe malnutrition is most likely when there is 
loss of absorptive surface or significant nutrient-
rich intestinal effluent. The distal ileum plays a 
crucial role in:
1.	 Absorption of vitamin B12
2.	 Reabsorption of bile salts
3.	 Absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins 
(A, D, E, K)
4.	 Significant fluid and electrolyte absorption 
: A distal ileal fistula leads to continuous 
loss of bile salts and nutrients, causing fat 
malabsorption, steatorrhea, diarrhea, and 
electrolyte imbalance. Loss of bile salts 
further impairs fat digestion, worsening 
nutritional deficiency. Chronic losses result 
in protein-energy malnutrition and vitamin 
deficiencies.
In comparison:
5.	 Pancreatic fistula mainly causes enzyme 
loss but can often be managed with 
supplementation.
6.	 Duodenal fistula causes fluid and electrolyte 
loss but does not affect the primary site of 
B12 and bile salt absorption.
7.	 Colonic fistula mainly results in water and 
electrolyte loss; the colon is not a major site 
of nutrient absorption.
Because the distal ileum is essential for critical 
nutrient absorption, a fistula at this site most 
significantly predisposes to severe malnutrition.

Which nerve is likely to be affected when a patient develops loss of sensation over the root of the penis following an open hernia surgery?

Iliohypogastric nerve

(C)

135.	 (B) Ilioinguinal nerve
During an open inguinal hernia repair, several 
nerves that traverse the inguinal region are at 
risk of injury or entrapment. The ilioinguinal 
nerve runs along the spermatic cord within the 
inguinal canal. It provides sensory innervation 
to the skin over the pubic symphysis, the

A 25-year-old woman presents with a breast lump showing no skin changes or induration, and histology confirms a fibroadenoma. This lesion would fall under which BI-RADS classification?

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
136.	 (D) BI-RADS 2
The BI-RADS (Breast Imaging Reporting and 
Data System) is a standardized system for 
classifying imaging findings. A fibroadenoma 
is a common benign breast tumor. When a 
breast lesion on mammography or ultrasound 
has classic, unequivocally benign features 
(e.g., circumscribed, oval, wider-than-tall), it 
is categorized as BI-RADS 2: Benign Finding. 
This category indicates there is a 0% probability 
of malignancy and that routine screening is all 
that is required. Since the question states that 
histological analysis has already confirmed 
a benign fibroadenoma, the corresponding 
imaging finding would have been classified as 
BI-RADS 2. BI-RADS 1 is a negative exam. BI-
RADS 3 is "probably benign" and requires short-
term follow-up. BI-RADS 4 is "suspicious" and 
requires biopsy.
A patient develops severe abdominal pain two days after an appendectomy, and an exploratory procedure reveals an intra-abdominal blood collection. Which artery, if inadequately ligated during the original operation, is most likely the source of the bleeding?
(A)	
Ileocolic artery
(B)	
Right colic artery
(C)	
Superior rectal artery
(D)	
Superior mesenteric artery
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
137.	 (A) Ileocolic artery
The appendix receives its blood supply from the 
appendicular artery. This artery is an end-artery 
that arises from the ileocolic artery, which is one 
of the main branches of the superior mesenteric 
artery (D). During an appendectomy, a critical 
step is the ligation of the mesoappendix, 
which contains the appendicular artery and 
vein. Postoperative hemorrhage is a known 
complication that typically results from a 
slipped ligature on the appendicular artery 
stump. Because the appendicular artery is a 
direct branch of the ileocolic artery, a poorly 
placed or insecure ligature could compromise 
the ileocolic artery itself, or the bleeding could 
originate from the stump of the appendicular 
artery where it branches from the ileocolic. 
Among the choices, the ileocolic artery is the 
most proximate and relevant parent vessel to the 
appendix.
What are the accurate characteristics of gall bladder carcinoma?
(A)	
Palpable abdominal lump is the earliest sign
(B)	
Median survival is 6 months
(C)	
Earliest sign is jaundice
(D)	
Clinical presentation of gallstones can be distinguished from gallbladder cancer
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
138.	 (B) Median survival is 6 months
Gallbladder carcinoma is a highly aggressive 
cancer with a dismal prognosis, primarily 
because it is usually diagnosed at a very late 
stage. The early symptoms are vague and non-
specific, often mimicking those of cholelithiasis 
(gallstones), making it nearly impossible to 
distinguish between the two based on clinical 
presentation alone (D is incorrect). By the time 
more specific signs develop, such as a palpable 
abdominal lump (A) or obstructive jaundice 
(C), the cancer is typically advanced, having 
invaded the liver or biliary tree, and is often 
unresectable. Due to this late diagnosis and the 
tumor's aggressive biology, the overall prognosis 
is extremely poor. The median survival from the 
time of diagnosis is widely reported to be only 
around 6 months, with 5-year survival rates 
in the single digits. This grim statistic is a key 
characteristic of the disease.

The patient's clinical presentation with altered

Hamman sign is seen in which of the following conditions?
(A)	
Pneumomediastinum
(B)	
Pneumoperitoneum
(C)	
Pneumopericardium
(D)	
Hydropneumothorax
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
124.	 (A) Pneumomediastinum
Hamman's sign, also known as Hamman's 
crunch, is a distinctive and pathognomonic 
clinical finding for pneumomediastinum (the 
presence of gas or air in the mediastinum). 
It is described as a crunching, crackling, or 
bubbling sound heard over the precordium that 
is synchronous with the heartbeat. The sound 
is produced by the heart beating against the air-
filled mediastinal tissues. It is often best heard 
when the patient is in the left lateral decubitus 
position. Pneumomediastinum can result from 
various causes, including alveolar rupture (e.g., 
from severe coughing or Valsalva), esophageal 
perforation (Boerhaave syndrome), or trauma. 
While sometimes associated with pneumothorax 
or pneumopericardium, the sign itself localizes 
the air to the mediastinum.

What is an appropriate alternative to breast milk for low-birth-weight (LBW) infants?
(A)	
Cow's milk
(B)	
Preterm formula
(C)	
Term formula
(D)	
Human donor milk
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
145.	 (B) Preterm formula
For low-birth-weight (LBW) infants—especially 
those born preterm—nutritional requirements 
are higher than those of term infants. They 
require increased calories, protein, calcium, 
phosphorus, and micronutrients to support 
rapid growth and organ development.
While mother’s own breast milk is the best 
option, if it is unavailable, the preferred 
alternative is preterm formula. Preterm formula 
is specifically designed to meet the higher 
nutritional needs of LBW and preterm infants. 
It contains:
1.	 Higher caloric density
2.	 Increased protein content
3.	 More calcium and phosphorus for bone 
mineralization
4.	 Additional vitamins and minerals
Cow’s milk is not suitable due to high protein 
and renal solute load.
Term formula does not provide adequate 
nutrients for preterm/LBW infants.
Human donor milk is preferred over formula 
when available, but if unavailable, preterm 
formula is the appropriate substitute.
Thus, when breast milk is not available, the 
correct alternative for LBW infants is preterm 
formula.
What is the approximate estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) for a 4-year-old boy weighing 15 kg and 100 cm tall, admitted with renal failure and laboratory values showing a blood urea of 100 mg/dL and serum creatinine of 1 mg/dL?
(A)	
33 ml/min/1.73 m² BSA
(B)	
40 ml/min/1.73 m² BSA
(C)	
55 ml/min/1.73 m² BSA
(D)	
80 ml/min/1.73 m² BSA
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
146.	 (B) 40 ml/min/1.73 m² BSA
In children, the estimated Glomerular Filtration 
Rate (eGFR) is commonly calculated using the 
Bedside Schwartz formula:
eGFR = (k × Height in cm) / Serum Creatinine 
(mg/dL)
The constant 'k' is age-dependent. For a child 
aged 2-12 years, the constant k is 0.55. (Note: 
Older formulas used 0.413, which also yields a 
similar result).
Using the standard k value of 0.55:
Height = 100 cm
Serum Creatinine = 1 mg/dL
eGFR = (0.55 × 100) / 1 = 55 ml/min/1.73 m²
Using the older constant k of 0.413:

Which of the following is not characteristic of Brown-Séquard syndrome?
(A)	
Complete transection of spinal cord
(B)	
Ipsilateral loss of vibration & touch
(C)	
Contralateral loss of pain & temperature
(D)	
Ipsilateral loss of proprioception
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
114.	 (A) Complete transection of spinal cord
Brown-Séquard syndrome is, by definition, 
an incomplete spinal cord injury syndrome 
resulting from the hemisection of the spinal 
cord (damage to the right or left half). A 
complete transection would affect all tracts on 
both sides. The hemisection in Brown-Séquard 
syndrome produces a unique and predictable 
pattern of neurological deficits below the level 
of the injury:
Ipsilateral spastic paralysis due to damage to the 
corticospinal tract.
Ipsilateral loss of proprioception, vibration, 
and fine touch (B, D) due to damage to the 
dorsal columns.
Contralateral loss of pain and temperature 
sensation (C) due to damage to the spinothalamic 
tract, which decussates (crosses over) soon after 
entering the spinal cord.
Therefore, complete transection is contrary to 
the definition of this syndrome.
A 65-year-old woman weighing 60 kg is on mechanical ventilation for ARDS due to urosepsis. Her ventilator settings are: tidal volume 360 mL, respiratory rate 30/min, PEEP 5 cm H₂O, and FiO₂ 90%. Arterial blood gas results show PaO₂ 50 mmHg, PaCO₂ 38 mmHg, and pH 7.38. What should be the next adjustment to her ventilatory management?
(A)	
Increase PEEP
(B)	
Reduce FiO2
(C)	
Increase tidal volume
(D)	
Increase respiratory rate
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
115.	 (A) Increase PEEP
The patient has severe ARDS, evidenced by 
refractory hypoxemia (PaO2 of 50 mmHg on 90% 
FiO2). The goal is to improve oxygenation while 
minimizing ventilator-induced lung injury. 
Her tidal volume is 6 ml/kg (360/60), which is 
appropriate for a lung-protective strategy. Her 
PaCO2 and pH are normal, so her ventilation 
is adequate; there is no need to change the 
respiratory rate (D). Reducing FiO2 (B) would 
worsen 
the 
life-threatening 
hypoxemia. 
Increasing the tidal volume (C) would violate the 
lung-protective strategy. The most appropriate 
intervention is to increase the PEEP. In ARDS, 
the lungs are stiff and prone to alveolar collapse 
(atelectasis). Increasing PEEP helps to recruit 
collapsed alveoli, keep them open at the end 
of expiration, improve ventilation-perfusion 
matching, and thereby enhance oxygenation. 
This allows for a subsequent reduction in the 
FiO2 to less toxic levels (<60%).
Which nerve is most likely injured when alcohol ingestion or other factors impair the cough reflex that normally prevents foreign bodies from entering the laryngeal inlet?
(A)	
Internal laryngeal nerve
(B)	
Glossopharyngeal nerve
(C)	
External laryngeal nerve
(D)	
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
116.	 (A) Internal laryngeal nerve
The cough reflex is a vital protective mechanism. 
The sensory (afferent) limb of this reflex detects 
the presence of foreign material or irritants 
in the airway. The most sensitive area for 
triggering this reflex is the laryngeal mucosa, 
particularly the area around the laryngeal inlet, 
aryepiglottic folds, and the vestibule above the 
vocal cords. The general sensory innervation to 
this entire supraglottic region is provided by the 
internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve 
(a branch of the vagus nerve). Blunting of this 
nerve's function—whether by local anesthesia, 
neurological injury, or CNS depressants like 
alcohol—impairs the ability to detect foreign 
material, thus compromising the airway and 
increasing the risk of aspiration. The recurrent 
laryngeal nerve (D) provides sensory innervation 
below the vocal cords and motor function to 
most laryngeal muscles.

Which type of lesion would lead to an exaggerated reflex on clinical examination?
(A)	
Polyneuropathy
(B)	
Radiculopathy
(C)	
Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion
(D)	
Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
155.	 (C) Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion
The image demonstrates the testing of a deep 
tendon reflex (DTR). A DTR is a simple spinal 
reflex arc involving a sensory neuron and a 
motor neuron. This reflex arc is under constant 
inhibitory control from descending pathways 
originating in the brain. These descending 
pathways are composed of upper motor neurons 
(UMNs). When there is a lesion affecting the 
UMNs (e.g., from a stroke, spinal cord injury, 
or multiple sclerosis), this inhibitory influence 
is lost. As a result, the spinal reflex becomes 
disinhibited 
and 
hyperactive, 
leading 
to 
enhanced reflexes (hyperreflexia), clonus, and 
spasticity. In contrast, any lesion that damages 
the reflex arc itself—such as a peripheral 
neuropathy (A), a nerve root compression 
(radiculopathy, B), or any other lower motor 
neuron (LMN) lesion (D)—will result in 
decreased (hyporeflexia) or absent reflexes.

197.	 (A) Rett syndrome
Rett syndrome is a unique, X-linked dominant 
neurodevelopmental disorder that is observed 
almost exclusively in females. It is caused by 
mutations in the MECP2 gene. Because the 
gene is located on the X chromosome and the 
mutation is dominant, it is almost always lethal 
in utero for male fetuses, who only have one 
X chromosome. Females survive because of 
X-inactivation, resulting in cellular mosaicism 
where some cells express the normal allele. 
For this reason, it is considered a disease solely 
observed in females. In contrast, Asperger 
syndrome (B), selective mutism (C), and atypical 
autism (D) are all conditions that are diagnosed 
in both males and females, although there may 
be differences in prevalence between the sexes.

163.	 (C) It has an inhibitory effect on the cerebral

This statement contains multiple inaccuracies.

185.	 (A) Cocaine
Cocaine is unique among local anesthetics. 
In addition to its primary action of blocking 
voltage-gated sodium channels to produce 
anesthesia, it also potently inhibits the reuptake 
of catecholamines, particularly norepinephrine, 
at 
sympathetic 
nerve 
terminals. 
This 
sympathomimetic action leads to an excess of 
norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft, causing 
intense vasoconstriction. This is why cocaine is 
the only local anesthetic that does not require the 
addition of epinephrine. The systemic effects of 
this catecholamine excess include hypertension 
(an increase in blood pressure), tachycardia, and 
an increased risk of cardiac arrhythmias and 
myocardial ischemia. In contrast, most other 
local anesthetics, such as lignocaine (B) and 
bupivacaine (C), are vasodilators at clinically 
used concentrations.
Please identify the liver segment that is indicated in the image provided.
(A)	
V
(B)	
IVa
(C)	
VII
(D)	
III
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
186.	 (A) V
On axial CT imaging, liver segments are 
identified according to Couinaud’s classification, 
which divides the liver into eight functionally 
independent segments based on portal vein and 
hepatic vein anatomy.
In an axial section:
1.	 The right lobe lies on the left side of the 
image (radiologic convention).
2.	 The left lobe appears on the right side of the 
image.
3.	 The portal vein divides the liver into 
superior (segments VII, VIII, IVa) and 
inferior (segments V, VI, III, IVb) segments.
The highlighted region in the image lies in the 
right lobe, anterior and inferior to the portal 
vein level. Segment V is located in the anterior 
inferior part of the right lobe, below the portal 
vein plane and medial to segment VI.
Segment VII is posterior superior, segment 
VIII is anterior superior, and segment III belongs 
to the left lobe.
Since the indicated region corresponds to 
the anterior inferior portion of the right lobe, it 
represents Couinaud segment V.
Therefore, the correct answer is (A) V.

The cyst fluid contains numerous protoscolices

Which of the following statements about determining the period of gestation (POG) is incorrect?
(A)	
1st-trimester USG is the best assessment
(B)	
Calculated from the last day of the last menstrual period
(C)	
In an IVF pregnancy, day of embryo transfer/day of fertilization is needed to calculate POG
(D)	
Crown-rump length is the best measure of the period of gestation in the first trimester
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
170.	 (B) Calculated from the last day of the last 
menstrual period
This statement is incorrect. By convention, the 
gestational age or period of gestation (POG) is 
calculated from the FIRST day of the woman's 
last menstrual period (LMP), not the last day. 
This is the basis of Naegele's rule for estimating 
the due date. The other statements are correct. 
A first-trimester ultrasound (USG) (A) is the 
most accurate method for dating a pregnancy, 
and the measurement used is the crown-rump 
length (CRL) (D). For pregnancies conceived 
through in-vitro fertilization (IVF) (C), the 
precise date of fertilization or embryo transfer is 
known, providing the most accurate gestational 
age determination, which overrides any LMP or 
ultrasound-based estimation.
Which methods are used to evaluate contraceptive failure?
(A)	
Pharmacological index
(B)	
Pearl index
(C)	
Performance index
(D)	
Efficacy index
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
171.	 (B) Pearl index
The Pearl Index is the most common and 
historically significant statistical method used 
to measure the effectiveness and failure rate of a 
contraceptive method. It represents the number 
of unintended pregnancies that occur per 100 
woman-years of use of a particular method. 
It is calculated with the formula: (Number of 
unintended pregnancies × 1200) / (Total months 
of use by all study subjects). A lower Pearl Index 
signifies a more effective contraceptive method 
with a lower failure rate. This standardized 
measure allows for the comparison of efficacy 
across different birth control options. The other 
terms listed are not standard epidemiological 
measures for contraceptive failure.
Which of the following patients would be categorized as experiencing primary amenorrhea?

(B)

(C)

172.	 (B) 14-year-old girl with Tanner stage 1 breasts
Primary amenorrhea is the failure of menarche to 
occur. A clinical evaluation is warranted if a girl 
meets either of two criteria: 1) no menstruation 
by age 15, regardless of sexual development, OR 
2) no menstruation by age 13 in the complete 
absence of secondary sexual characteristics (like 
breast development). Tanner stage 1 represents 
the prepubertal state with no breast budding. 
Therefore, a 14-year-old girl with Tanner stage 1 
breasts meets the second criterion, as she is past 
the age of 13 and has not yet begun pubertal 
development. The 11-year-old (A) is too young. 
The 12- and 13-year-old girls (D, C) are showing 
appropriate pubertal progression and have not 
yet reached the age of 15, so they do not meet 
the criteria for primary amenorrhea.
The child of a woman who received diethylstilbestrol (DES) during pregnancy is at increased risk for which condition?

(B)	
Clear cell carcinoma
(C)	
Adenocarcinoma
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
173.	 (B) Clear cell carcinoma
Diethylstilbestrol (DES) was a synthetic estrogen 
prescribed to pregnant women to prevent 
miscarriage from the 1940s to 1971. It was later 
found to be a potent teratogen. Female offspring 
exposed to DES in utero have a significantly 
increased risk of developing a rare cancer of 
the lower genital tract, specifically clear cell

Uterine dysfunction, or dystocia, refers to

The question asks for probable signs of 
pregnancy that are present at 8 weeks.

exam from about 6-8 weeks of gestation.

Which of the following is NOT a non-contraceptive use of oral contraceptives?
(A)	
Reduction in the risk of ovarian cancer
(B)	
Improve bone density
(C)	
Protection against sexually transmitted diseases, including HIV
(D)	
Reduction in the risk of endometrial cancer
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
177.	 (C) Protection against sexually transmitted 
diseases, including HIV
Combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) offer 
numerous non-contraceptive health benefits. 
They are well-known to significantly reduce the 
lifetime risk of developing both ovarian cancer 
(A) and endometrial cancer (D). They are also 
widely used to manage menstrual disorders, 
such as dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia, and to 
treat conditions like acne and hirsutism. Some 
evidence suggests they can also help maintain 
or improve bone mineral density (B). However, 
it is a critical point of counseling that OCPs are 
a hormonal method and provide NO protection 
whatsoever against sexually transmitted diseases 
(STDs), including HIV. For STD prevention, 
barrier methods such as condoms must be used.

Consider the following steps in the Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL). Place them in the correct sequence:
1.	
Uterine massage
2.	
Administer uterotonic (oxytocin 10 mg)
3.	
Check for additional fetuses
4.	
Perform controlled cord traction
(A)	
3,1,2,4
(B)	
3,2,4,1
(C)	
2,4,3,1
(D)	
2,4,1,3
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
179.	 (B) 3,2,4,1
Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor 
(AMTSL) is a crucial intervention to prevent 
postpartum hemorrhage. The components 
must be performed in a specific, rapid sequence 
immediately following the birth of the baby:
1.	 Check for additional fetuses: Immediately 
palpate the abdomen to rule out the 
presence of another baby before giving a 
uterotonic. (Step 3)
2.	 Administer uterotonic: If no other baby 
is present, administer oxytocin 10 IU IM 
within one minute of birth. (Step 2)
3.	 Perform controlled cord traction (CCT): 
Once the uterus is well-contracted, apply 
gentle downward traction on the cord while 
applying counter-traction on the uterine 
fundus to deliver the placenta. (Step 4)
4.	 Uterine massage: Immediately after the 
placenta is delivered, massage the uterine 
fundus to stimulate it to contract firmly and 
prevent atony. (Step 1)
The correct sequence is 3 → 2 → 4 → 1.

How would you most appropriately characterize a urinary tract infection (UTI) in a woman who is in her second trimester of pregnancy?
(A)	
Growth of 103 coliform in a suprapubic sample
(B)	
Growth of 105 coliform in a voided urine sample
(C)	
Frequency with dysuria with >3 WBC/HPF
(D)	
Frequency with dysuria with positive nitrite and leukocyte esterase dipstick test
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
166.	 (B) Growth of 105 coliform in a voided urine 
sample
In pregnancy, both symptomatic UTIs and 
asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) are treated 
to prevent complications like pyelonephritis 
and preterm birth. The diagnosis rests on 
a quantitative urine culture. The accepted 
definition of significant bacteriuria in a pregnant 
woman, whether symptomatic or not, is the 
presence of at least 100,000 (105) colony-forming 
units (CFU) per mL of a single uropathogen in 
a clean-catch, midstream voided urine sample. 
While symptoms and dipstick results (C, D) 
are suggestive, they are not diagnostic. A 
suprapubic aspirate (A) is rarely performed, but 
in that sterile sample, any growth is considered 
significant. For routine screening and diagnosis, 
the threshold of 105 CFU/mL from a voided 
specimen is the definitive standard that 
mandates treatment in pregnancy.
Which of the following statements about uterine innervation is incorrect?
(A)	
Sensory level is from T10 to L1
(B)	
Uterine contractility is mediated by innervation from levels T7-T8
(C)	
In the 1st stage of labor, pain is due to fibers at the level of T10-L1
(D)	
In early labor, pain is usually due to uterine contractions
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
167.	 (B) Uterine contractility is mediated by 
innervation from levels T7-T8
This 
statement 
is 
inaccurate. 
Uterine 
contractions during labor are primarily driven 
by hormones, especially oxytocin, and local 
factors like prostaglandins. The autonomic 
nervous system modulates the contractions but 
does not mediate (initiate) them. Furthermore, 
the sympathetic innervation that influences 
the uterus originates from a broader range of 
spinal levels, typically T5 to L2, not specifically 
T7-T8. The other statements are correct. The 
visceral pain from uterine contractions and 
cervical dilation during the first stage of labor 
is transmitted by afferent fibers that accompany 
the sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord 
between T10 and L1 (A and C are both correct). 
This pain is indeed caused by the uterine 
contractions themselves (D).
Which of the following is included in the modified biophysical profile (BPP)?
(A)	
NST and fetal tone
(B)	
NST and AFI
(C)	
NST and breathing movements
(D)	
NST and gross fetal movements
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
168.	 (B) NST and AFI
The full biophysical profile (BPP) is an 
antenatal test for fetal well-being that assesses 
five components: fetal breathing, gross body 
movements, fetal tone, amniotic fluid volume, 
and a non-stress test (NST). The modified 
biophysical profile (mBPP) is a simplified, yet 
effective, screening version of the full test. It 
combines just two key elements: the Non-Stress 
Test (NST) and the Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI). 
The NST is a short-term marker of fetal acid-
base status and neurologic integrity, reflecting 
acute oxygenation. The AFI is considered a 
long-term marker of placental function, as 
adequate amniotic fluid depends on fetal urine 
production, which in turn depends on adequate 
renal perfusion over time. An abnormal result 
on either component of the mBPP necessitates 
further evaluation with a full BPP or other 
testing.

Which of the following is NOT included in the whole-body CT scan protocol for a trauma patient?
(A)	
CT Head
(B)

(C)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2022
190.	 (C) CT Limbs
A whole-body CT (WBCT) or "pan-scan" for a 
major trauma patient is a standardized protocol 
designed to rapidly identify life-threatening 
injuries in the head, spine, and trunk. A typical 
WBCT protocol includes a non-contrast CT 
of the head (A), a CT of the cervical spine 
(B), and a contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, 
abdomen (D), and pelvis. This approach allows 
for the quick detection of intracranial bleeding, 
unstable spinal fractures, and major thoracic 
or abdominal organ injury and hemorrhage. 
CT of the limbs (C) is not a routine part of this 
initial screening protocol. Extremity injuries are 
generally assessed by physical examination and 
plain X-rays. A CT of a specific limb would only 
be performed subsequently if a complex fracture 
or vascular injury is suspected.
Which of the following conditions does not exhibit egg-shell calcification?

(B)	
Sarcoidosis
(C)

(D)

191.	 (D) Metastatic lymph nodes
Eggshell calcification refers to a specific pattern 
seen on imaging where there is a fine, curvilinear 
rim of calcification at the periphery of a lymph 
node. This pattern is highly characteristic of 
two granulomatous diseases: silicosis (A) and 
sarcoidosis (B), where it is typically seen in 
hilar and mediastinal nodes. It can also be seen

therapy (C). However, this pattern is not 
typical for metastatic lymph nodes (D). While 
metastases from certain tumors (e.g., papillary 
thyroid carcinoma, mucinous adenocarcinoma 
of the colon) can calcify, the pattern is usually 
punctate, amorphous, or chunky, rather than a 
delicate peripheral eggshell rim.

1.	
Arrange the following structures in the correct 
order as they participate in the direct pathway of 
the basal ganglia :
1	
Striatum
2	
Globus pallidus
3	
Substantia nigra
4	
Thalamus
5	
Cortex
(A)	1,2,3,4,5
(B)	 5,4,2,3,1
(C)	5,1,2,3,4
(D)	1,3,4,2,5
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(C) 5,1,2,3,4
The direct pathway of the basal ganglia is a crucial circuit that facilitates the initiation of voluntary movement. The sequence begins with excitatory glutamatergic signals from the cerebral cortex (5) to the striatum (1) (caudate and putamen). The striatum then sends inhibitory GABAergic projections directly to the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi) and the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) (2 & 3). This inhibitory signal from the striatum suppresses the tonic inhibitory output of the GPi/SNr complex. The GPi/SNr normally inhibits the thalamus (4). By inhibiting the GPi/SNr, the striatum effectively disinhibits the thalamus, allowing it to send excitatory signals back to the motor cortex, thus promoting movement. Therefore, the correct sequence of information flow in the direct pathway is Cortex → Striatum → Globus Pallidus Internus/Substantia Nigra Pars Reticulata → Thalamus → Cortex. The provided option C reflects this pathway core sequence.
2.	
Which ligament links the medial cuneiform 
bone to the base of the second metatarsal?
(A)	Spring
(B)	 Deltoid
(C)	Chopart
(D)	Lisfranc
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(D) Lisfranc
The Lisfranc ligament is a critical structure for maintaining the stability of the midfoot. It is a strong, short ligament that connects the medial cuneiform bone to the base of the second metatarsal. This ligament forms a key part of the Lisfranc joint complex, which comprises the articulations between the tarsal bones (cuneiforms and cuboid) and the bases of the metatarsals. Injury to this ligament can lead to significant instability and dislocation of the tarsometatarsal joint, an injury known as a Lisfranc fracture-dislocation. The spring ligament (A) supports the head of the talus and the longitudinal arch of the foot. The deltoid ligament (B) is on the medial side of the ankle, connecting the tibia to the tarsal bones. The Chopart joint (C) refers to the transverse tarsal joint, not a specific ligament connecting the described bones.

Which pharyngeal pouch is most likely

The pharyngeal pouches are endodermal outpouchings that give rise to several important structures in the head and neck. The third pharyngeal pouch has two components : a dorsal wing and a ventral wing. The dorsal wing develops into the inferior parathyroid glands, while the ventral wing develops into the thymus. Failure of the third pharyngeal pouch to develop properly leads to DiGeorge syndrome, a condition characterized by thymic aplasia (leading to T-cell deficiency and immunodeficiency) and absence of the inferior parathyroid glands (leading to hypocalcemia). Therefore, the concurrent absence of the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands points directly to a developmental defect of the third pharyngeal pouch.

What is the typical prostate volume in adult 
males with normal health?
(A)	20cc
(B)	 50cc
(C)	75cc
(D)	100cc
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(A) 20cc
The prostate is a gland in the male reproductive system located just below the bladder. In a healthy young adult male, the prostate is roughly the size of a walnut. Its volume is typically measured in cubic centimeters (cc) or milliliters (mL), which are equivalent units. The normal prostate volume is approximately 20 cc (or 20 grams). With age, the prostate often undergoes benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), which causes an increase in its size. Volumes of 50 cc, 75 cc, or 100 cc are indicative of significant prostatic enlargement, commonly seen in older men with BPH, and can lead to lower urinary tract symptoms due to compression of the urethra. Therefore, for an adult male in normal health without pathology, 20 cc represents the typical prostate volume. This standard value is important for diagnosing and staging conditions like BPH and prostate cancer.

Arrange the lung hilar structures in order from

The hilum of the lung is the region on the medial surface where structures enter and exit. The arrangement of these structures from anterior to posterior is a key anatomical relationship. 10.	 At high altitudes, which of the following 
physiological adaptations does not occur?
(A)	Pulmonary vasoconstriction
(B)	 Polycythemia
(C)	Respiratory acidosis
(D)	Hypoxia
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(C) Respiratory acidosis
Acclimatization to high altitudes involves several physiological changes to cope with the lower partial pressure of oxygen (hypobaric hypoxia). Hypoxia (D) is the primary stimulus for these adaptations. In response to hypoxia, the peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies) are stimulated, leading to hyperventilation. This increased breathing rate blows off more carbon dioxide (), leading to a decrease in arterial . A decrease in  causes respiratory alkalosis, not respiratory acidosis. Respiratory acidosis would imply  retention. Hypoxia also causes pulmonary vasoconstriction (A) as a direct effect on the pulmonary arterioles, which can lead to pulmonary hypertension. For long-term adaptation, the kidneys produce more erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates red blood cell production, resulting in polycythemia (B) to increase the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. Therefore, respiratory acidosis is the physiological change that does not occur.
11.	 In which parts of the body is the countercurrent 
mechanism found?
1	
Eye
2	
Testes
3	
Kidney
4	
Gut
5	
Lungs
(A)	1 and 2 are correct
(B)	 1, 2, 3 are correct
(C)	1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are correct
(D)	2, 3, 4, 5 are correct
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(B) 1, 2, 3 are correct
A countercurrent mechanism involves two adjacent fluids flowing in opposite directions to maximize the exchange of heat, ions, or gases. The most well-known example is in the kidney (3), specifically the loop of Henle and vasa recta, which establish a medullary osmotic gradient crucial for concentrating urine. The testes (2) utilize a countercurrent heat exchange mechanism in the pampiniform plexus of veins, which cools arterial blood before it reaches the testes, maintaining a temperature optimal for spermatogenesis. The choroid plexus in the eye (1) is also thought to utilize a countercurrent mechanism to help regulate ion transport and fluid secretion. The gut and lungs do not employ a classical countercurrent exchange system for their primary functions. Therefore, the eye, testes, and kidney are the correct locations among the options provided where this mechanism is found.

13.	 In a pressure-volume curve, what does a reading 
of zero pressure imply?
(A)	Residual volume
(B)	 Tidal volume
(C)	Functional residual capacity
(D)	Inspiratory reserve volume
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(C) Functional residual capacity
The pressure-volume curve of the respiratory system plots lung volume against pressure. The pressure referred to is the transthoracic or trans-respiratory system pressure, which is the pressure difference between the airway opening (mouth) and the body surface. A reading of zero pressure signifies the point where the respiratory system is at rest, with no muscular effort being exerted. At this equilibrium point, the inward elastic recoil of the lungs is perfectly balanced by the outward elastic recoil of the chest wall. The volume of air remaining in the lungs at this specific point is the Functional Residual Capacity (FRC). It is the sum of the expiratory reserve volume (ERV) and the residual volume (RV). Residual volume (A) is the air left after maximal forced expiration. Tidal volume (B) is the air exchanged during normal breathing. Inspiratory reserve volume (D) is the extra air that can be inhaled after a normal inspiration.

14.	 What is indicated by the curve labeled as 'A' in 
the given oxygen dissociation curve graph?
(A)	Myoglobin
(B)	 Carboxyhemoglobinemia
(C)	Methemoglobin
(D)	Fetal hemoglobin
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(A) Myoglobin
In the given oxygen dissociation graph, curve A is shifted markedly to the left and rises steeply at low partial pressures of oxygen. This indicates a very high affinity for oxygen. Such a curve is characteristic of myoglobin, which binds oxygen more avidly than hemoglobin and becomes saturated at relatively low oxygen tensions.
Myoglobin, found in muscle tissue, serves as an oxygen storage protein. Its dissociation curve is hyperbolic, unlike the sigmoid (S-shaped) curve of hemoglobin. The sigmoid shape of hemoglobin’s curve is due to cooperative binding between its subunits, whereas myoglobin, being a monomer, does not exhibit cooperativity.
Carboxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin alter the hemoglobin dissociation curve but do not produce a separate distinct hyperbolic curve like that shown. Fetal hemoglobin causes a leftward shift compared to adult hemoglobin but still maintains a sigmoid shape.
Therefore, the curve labeled A represents myoglobin due to its high oxygen affinity and hyperbolic dissociation pattern.
15.	 Among the given options, which organ exhibits 
the smallest disparity in oxygen levels between 
the arteries and veins?
(A)	Brain
(B)	 Kidney
(C)	Skin
(D)	Liver
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(B) Kidney
The disparity in oxygen levels between arteries and veins is known as the arteriovenous oxygen difference ( diff). It reflects the amount of oxygen extracted and consumed by the organ's tissues. The kidney receives a very high blood flow, approximately 20-25% of the cardiac output, which is far in excess of its metabolic needs. The primary function of this high flow is filtration, not oxygen delivery. Consequently, the kidneys extract a relatively small fraction of the oxygen delivered to them, resulting in the smallest arteriovenous oxygen difference among all major organs. The brain (A) and liver (D) are metabolically active and have significant oxygen extraction. The skin (C) has a variable  difference, as its blood flow is highly regulated for thermoregulation, but it is generally higher than that of the kidney.
16.	 What is the corrected reticulocyte count when 
the hemoglobin (Hb) level is 5 g/dL and the 
absolute reticulocyte count percentage is 9%?
(A)	5
(B)	 4.5
(C)	3
(D)	1.8
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(C) 3
The corrected reticulocyte count (CRC) is calculated to account for the degree of anemia, as a lower red blood cell count can falsely elevate the reticulocyte percentage. The formula for CRC is :
CRC (%) = Reticulocyte count (%) × (Patient's Hemoglobin / Normal Hemoglobin)
Assuming a normal hemoglobin level of 15 g/dL for calculation purposes.
Given :
Reticulocyte count = 9%
Patient's Hb = 5 g/dL
Normal Hb = 15 g/dL
CRC = 9 × (5 / 15) = 9 × (1/3) = 3%
A further correction, the Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI), is often calculated to account for the premature release of reticulocytes (shift cells), but based on the options, only the CRC is required. The corrected count of 3% indicates the bone marrow's response to the anemia. A value greater than 2-3% suggests an adequate marrow response (e.g., hemolysis or hemorrhage), while a value less than 2% suggests an inadequate response (hypoproliferation).

Type II transmembrane proteins are single-pass proteins oriented with their N-terminus in the cytoplasm and their C-terminus in the extracellular space or organelle lumen. Unlike proteins with a cleavable N-terminal signal peptide (Type I proteins), Type II proteins utilize an internal, non-cleavable signal sequence. This sequence serves two functions : it acts as a signal peptide to target the ribosome-nascent chain complex to the endoplasmic reticulum, and it also functions as a transmembrane anchor. This internal signal-anchor sequence is hydrophobic and becomes embedded inside the membrane, establishing the protein's orientation. The flanking positive charges on the N-terminal side of the sequence ensure that the N-terminus remains in the cytoplasm according to the "positive-inside rule." Therefore, the signal sequence is not at the N-terminal (C) or C-terminal (B), but is an internal segment that becomes the transmembrane domain.
18.	 For glucose uptake, which tissues rely on 
insulin?
(A)	Skeletal muscle and adipose tissue
(B)	 Liver
(C)	Brain
(D)	Kidneys
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(A) Skeletal muscle and adipose tissue
The uptake of glucose into cells is mediated by glucose transporter (GLUT) proteins. The expression and activity of these transporters vary among tissues. Skeletal muscle and adipose tissue express the GLUT4 transporter. The translocation of GLUT4 from intracellular vesicles to the plasma membrane is an insulin-dependent process. In the presence of insulin, GLUT4 is inserted into the cell membrane, facilitating the entry of glucose into these cells. This is a primary mechanism by which insulin lowers blood glucose levels. In contrast, the brain (C) primarily uses GLUT1 and GLUT3, the liver (B) uses GLUT2, and the kidneys (D) also use insulin-independent transporters like GLUT1 and GLUT2. These transporters are constitutively present on the cell surface and do not require insulin for glucose uptake, ensuring these vital organs have a constant glucose supply regardless of insulin levels.
19.	 What is the typical amount of water loss through 
insensible means?
(A)	100 mL/hour
(B)	 150 mL/hour
(C)	50 mL/hour
(D)	200 ml./hour
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(C) 50 mL/hour
Insensible water loss refers to the water lost from the body through routes that are not easily perceived or measured, primarily through evaporation from the skin (not sweating) and from the respiratory tract during breathing. In a healthy, afebrile adult at rest in a temperate environment, the total insensible water loss is approximately 700-1000 mL per day. To convert this to an hourly rate :
800 mL / 24 hours ≈ 33 mL/hour.
1000 mL / 24 hours ≈ 42 mL/hour.
The value of 50 mL/hour (which equates to 1200 mL/day) is a commonly used clinical estimate, especially when considering factors that might increase this loss, such as fever, hyperventilation, or low ambient humidity. The other options represent significantly higher rates of water loss : 100 mL/hr (2400 mL/day), 150 mL/hr (3600 mL/day), and 200 mL/hr (4800 mL/day), which are not typical for basal insensible loss.
20.	 What is the correct sequence of events that 
occur during vomiting in a woman who feels 
nauseated after eating spicy food?
1	
LES is open and UES is closed
2	
Strong contractions in the stomach
3	
Inspiration against a closed glottis
4	
Relaxation of the pyloric sphincter
5	
LES opens and UES opens
6	
Reverse peristalsis in the small intestine
(LES : Lower esophageal sphincter; UES : Upper 
esophageal sphincter)
(A)	6,4,2,5,1,3
(B)	 6,4,2,3,1,5
(C)	4,6,2,1,3,5
(D)	4,6,2,5,3,1
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(B) 6,4,2,3,1,5
Vomiting is a coordinated reflex controlled by the vomiting center in the medulla.
First, reverse peristalsis in the small intestine (6) occurs, pushing intestinal contents back toward the stomach.
Next, the pyloric sphincter relaxes (4), allowing duodenal contents to enter the stomach.
Then, strong contractions of the stomach (2) take place along with contraction of abdominal muscles to increase intra-abdominal pressure.
Following this, there is inspiration against a closed glottis (3). This action fixes the diaphragm and increases intra-abdominal pressure, helping propel gastric contents upward.
At this stage, the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) opens while the upper esophageal sphincter (UES) remains closed (1), allowing contents to move into the esophagus but preventing immediate expulsion.
Finally, both LES and UES open (5), permitting expulsion of gastric contents through the mouth.
Thus, the correct physiological sequence is 6 → 4 → 2 → 3 → 1 → 5, corresponding to option (B).
21.	 In the instrument shown for determining 
hemoglobin levels, hemoglobin is converted 
into which of the following forms?
(A)	Alkaline hematin
(B)	 Acid hematin
(C)	Oxyhemoglobin
NODIA

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(D)	Deoxyhemoglobin
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(B) Acid hematin
The instrument shown is Sahli's haemoglobinometer, which is used for the colorimetric estimation of hemoglobin concentration in the blood. This method, also known as the acid hematin method, involves mixing a blood sample with a weak acid, typically 0.1 N hydrochloric acid (HCl), in a graduated tube. The acid lyses the red blood cells, releasing hemoglobin. The globin portion of the hemoglobin is denatured, and the heme is oxidized from ferrous () to ferric () state, forming a brown-colored compound called acid hematin (hematin hydrochloride). Distilled water is then added drop by drop until the color of the solution in the tube matches the color of the standard brown glass comparator rods in the instrument. The hemoglobin concentration is then read directly from the calibrated scale on the tube. This method is simple but less accurate than modern automated methods.

23.	 Iron in tissues is stained by which of the 
following?
(A)	Masson's trichrome
(B)	 Prussian blue
(C)	PAS
(D)	File Faraco
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(B) Prussian blue
Prussian blue, also known as Perls' stain, is the classic and most widely used histochemical stain for detecting the presence of ferric iron () deposits in tissues. This reaction is based on treating the tissue section with an acidic solution of potassium ferrocyanide. The ferrocyanide reacts with any ferric iron present to form an insoluble, bright blue pigment called ferric ferrocyanide, which is visually identifiable under a microscope. This stain is crucial for diagnosing conditions involving iron overload, such as hemochromatosis and hemosiderosis. Masson's trichrome (A) is used to stain collagen blue/green, muscle and keratin red, and cytoplasm pink. 24.	 In a patient with maple syrup urine disease 
(MSUD), the diet should restrict all of the 
following amino acids except which one?
(A)	Methionine
(B)	 Valine
(C)	Leucine
(D)	Isoleucine
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(A) Methionine
Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency in the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKAD) complex. This enzyme is essential for the catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) : leucine (C), isoleucine (D), and valine (B). When this enzyme is deficient, these amino acids and their toxic byproducts (alpha-ketoacids) accumulate in the blood and urine, leading to neurotoxicity and a characteristic maple syrup or burnt sugar odor in the urine. The mainstay of management for MSUD is a lifelong dietary restriction of these three branched-chain amino acids. Methionine (A) is a sulfur-containing amino acid, not a BCAA, and its metabolic pathway is different. Therefore, methionine is not restricted in the diet of a patient with MSUD.
25.	 What is the product of deamination of 
methylated cytosine?
(A)	Uracil	
(B)	 Cytosine
(C)	Guanine	
(D)	Thymine
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(D) Thymine
Deamination is the removal of an amine group from a molecule. In the context of DNA bases, spontaneous deamination is a common form of DNA damage. When an unmethylated cytosine undergoes deamination, it is converted into uracil (A). This is easily recognized by DNA repair enzymes (uracil DNA glycosylase) as an abnormal base in DNA and is efficiently removed. However, in many organisms, cytosine can be methylated at the 5th carbon position to form 5-methylcytosine, an important epigenetic mark. When 5-methylcytosine undergoes spontaneous deamination, it is converted into thymine. Since thymine is a normal DNA base, this C-to-T transition is not as easily recognized by repair systems, making methylated cytosine residues "hotspots" for mutation. This process is a significant source of single nucleotide polymorphisms in the genome.
26.	 What is the cause of elevated H+ ions in the 
intermembrane space of mitochondria?
(A)	Decreased oxidative phosphorylation
(B)	 Increased ATP production
(C)	Reduced chemiosmosis
(D)	Water retention in inner mitochondrial 
space
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(B) Increased ATP production
During cellular respiration, the electron transport chain (ETC) located on the inner mitochondrial membrane actively pumps hydrogen ions (H⁺) from the mitochondrial matrix into the intermembrane space. This process occurs as electrons pass through complexes I, III, and IV. The energy released from electron transfer is used to pump protons against their concentration gradient, resulting in an accumulation of H⁺ ions in the intermembrane space.
This creates a proton gradient and an electrochemical potential difference known as the proton motive force. The elevated concentration of H⁺ ions in the intermembrane space is essential for ATP synthesis. When protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, the energy released drives the conversion of ADP and inorganic phosphate into ATP.
Thus, increased ATP production is associated with active electron transport and proton pumping, which leads to elevated H⁺ concentration in the intermembrane space. Therefore, option (B) is correct.
27.	 In which pathway does Cyclooxygenase have a 
role?
(A)	Kreb's cycle	
(B)	 Prostaglandin
(C)	Leukotriene	
(D)	Vitamin K
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(B) Prostaglandin
Cyclooxygenase (COX), also known as prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase (PTGS), is the key enzyme in the synthesis of prostanoids, which include prostaglandins, prostacyclin, and thromboxanes. The pathway begins with the release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2. COX then catalyzes the conversion of arachidonic acid into prostaglandin H2 (PGH2). PGH2 serves as the precursor for the various specific prostaglandins and thromboxanes, which are potent lipid mediators involved in inflammation, pain, fever, blood clotting, and gastric protection. The Krebs cycle (A) is central to cellular respiration. The leukotriene pathway (C) also uses arachidonic acid as a substrate but is initiated by the enzyme lipoxygenase. The Vitamin K cycle (D) is involved in the post-translational modification of clotting factors.

28.	 How does the mutation of the cystic fibrosis 
gene occur?
(A)	Tryptophan at 708 position, chloride 
channel
(B)	 Phenylalanine at 708 position, calcium 
channel
(C)	Phenylalanine at 508 position, chloride 
channel
(D)	Tryptophan at 508 position, calcium channel
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(C) Phenylalanine at 508 position, chloride channel
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the gene that encodes the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) protein. The CFTR protein functions as a chloride channel on the surface of epithelial cells in the lungs, pancreas, sweat glands, and other organs. The most common mutation, accounting for approximately 70% of CF cases worldwide, is a deletion of three nucleotides that results in the loss of a phenylalanine amino acid at position 508 of the CFTR protein. This mutation is denoted as ΔF508. The ΔF508 mutation causes the CFTR protein to misfold, preventing its proper processing and trafficking to the cell membrane. This leads to a severe reduction in chloride ion transport, resulting in thick, sticky mucus and the characteristic multi-organ pathology of cystic fibrosis.
29.	 What is the likely diagnosis for a baby who 
has 
delayed 
developmental 
milestones, 
hepatosplenomegaly, and the shown bone 
marrow microscopic findings?
Click Here to Buy book on Amazon
page  447  	
INICET Examination Paper
(C)	Cmax
(D)	t-1/2
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(B) Area under the curve
In pharmacokinetics, the absorption of a drug is characterized by two main parameters : the rate of absorption and the extent of absorption. The rate describes how quickly the drug enters the systemic circulation, which is indicated by Tmax (the time to reach maximum concentration) and Cmax (the maximum plasma concentration achieved). The extent of absorption, however, refers to the total amount or fraction of the administered drug that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. This is a measure of the drug's bioavailability. The most reliable measure of the extent of absorption is the Area Under the Plasma Concentration-Time Curve (AUC). A larger AUC indicates that more of the drug has been absorbed into the systemic circulation over a period of time. T-1/2 (D) is the elimination half-life, which relates to drug elimination, not absorption.

This question tests knowledge of common and specific adverse drug reactions.

57.	 What is the advised length of time a woman 
should stop taking tamoxifen before attempting 
pregnancy after undergoing a mastectomy for 
breast cancer?
(A)	1 month
(B)	 3 months
(C)	No need to stop
(D)	Can be stopped and conceived soon after 
stopping
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(B) 3 months
Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) used as adjuvant therapy for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. It is a known teratogen and is contraindicated during pregnancy due to the risk of significant fetal abnormalities. Additionally, it has a long elimination half-life of about 5-7 days, and its active metabolites can persist even longer. To ensure that the drug and its metabolites are completely cleared from the system before conception is attempted, a "washout" period is required. The standard recommendation is to discontinue tamoxifen for at least 2 to 3 months before attempting to conceive. This allows for adequate clearance of the drug, minimizing the teratogenic risk to the fetus. Therefore, stopping and conceiving immediately is unsafe, and a 1-month period is generally considered insufficient.

patient

with

(A) Isoniazid
The image displays the unique, complex cell wall of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a key feature of which is the thick, waxy outer layer of mycolic acids. This layer is crucial for the bacterium's survival and virulence. Isoniazid (INH) is a cornerstone of first-line anti-tubercular therapy, and its primary mechanism of action is the inhibition of mycolic acid synthesis. 59.	 Which sign or symptom likely led clinicians to 
suspect muscarinic poisoning in a male patient 
brought to the emergency department after 
ingesting an unknown toxin?
(A)	Mydriasis
(B)	 Diuresis
(C)	Muscle fasciculations
(D)	Bradycardia
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(D) Bradycardia
Muscarinic poisoning, or cholinergic crisis, results from the overstimulation of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. This can be caused by organophosphate insecticides or certain mushrooms. The symptoms can be remembered by the mnemonics DUMBELS (Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia/Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation) or SLUDGE (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis). Bradycardia (a slow heart rate) is a key cardiovascular sign due to the stimulation of M2 receptors in the heart. Mydriasis (A) or pupil dilation is an anticholinergic sign. Diuresis (B) is part of the syndrome, but bradycardia is a more specific cardiovascular finding. Muscle fasciculations (C) are a sign of nicotinic receptor stimulation, which is seen in organophosphate poisoning but is not a purely muscarinic effect. Therefore, bradycardia is a classic and reliable indicator of muscarinic overstimulation.

62.	 What is the most appropriate management for 
a young man who was stung by a scorpion 2 
hours ago and now presents with hypertension 
(168/100 mm Hg), a heart rate of 72/min, 
respiratory rate of 32/min, and breathlessness?
(A)	Metoprolol
(B)	 Ivabradine
(C)	Prazosin
(D)	Frusemide
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(C) Prazosin
Scorpion envenomation (particularly from the red scorpion, Mesobuthus tamulus) can cause a massive release of catecholamines (adrenergic storm) and acetylcholine (cholinergic storm). The patient's presentation with severe hypertension, tachycardia (which may be masked by reflex bradycardia or cholinergic effects, hence the 72 bpm), and breathlessness (suggesting early pulmonary edema) is characteristic of an adrenergic crisis. The cornerstone of management is to block the effects of the excessive catecholamines. Prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic blocker, is the drug of choice. The image displays the genome of the Human Papillomavirus (HPV). High-risk HPV types (like HPV-16 and HPV-18) are the primary cause of cervical cancer and other anogenital cancers. Their oncogenic potential is primarily attributed to two early viral proteins, E6 and E7. 36.	 Except for which of the following conditions, 
can thrombolysis be considered?
(A)	MRI showing density in less than 1/3rd of 
the area supplied by MCA
(B)	 Blood pressure of more than 185/110 mmHg
(C)	Ischemic stroke within 2 hours
(D)	Onset of symptoms <4 hours
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(B) Blood pressure of more than 185/110 mmHg
Thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) is a critical treatment for acute ischemic stroke, but it has strict inclusion and exclusion criteria to minimize the risk of hemorrhagic transformation. Statements (C) and (D) represent the therapeutic time window; treatment is most effective when given early, typically within 3 to 4.5 hours of symptom onset. Statement (A) is an inclusion criterion; if a large area of the brain supplied by the middle cerebral artery (MCA) is already infarcted (hypodense on CT or evident on MRI), the risk of hemorrhage with thrombolysis is high. Therefore, evidence of infarction in less than one-third of the MCA territory is favorable. Statement (B), a persistently elevated blood pressure of more than 185/110 mmHg, is a major contraindication to thrombolysis. High blood pressure significantly increases the risk of intracranial hemorrhage after tPA administration. The blood pressure must be carefully lowered and maintained below this threshold before thrombolysis can be initiated.

The image displays a cell with characteristic features of a mast cell or its circulating counterpart, the basophil. The key identifying feature is the presence of numerous large, coarse, metachromatic granules in the cytoplasm that stain intensely dark blue or purple with Wright-Giemsa stain. 39.	 Which abdominal site is most commonly 
involved in tuberculosis?
(A)	Rectum	
(B)	 Colon
(C)	Small intestine	
(D)	Ileocecal junction
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(D) Ileocecal junction
Abdominal tuberculosis can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, peritoneum, lymph nodes, or solid organs. However, the most common site of involvement within the gastrointestinal tract is the ileocecal junction. This predilection is attributed to several factors in this region : a relative abundance of lymphoid tissue (Peyer's patches), which are a primary site for mycobacterial invasion; physiological stasis, which allows for prolonged contact time between the bacilli and the mucosa; and a higher rate of fluid and electrolyte absorption. The terminal ileum and cecum are affected in approximately 80-90% of cases of intestinal tuberculosis. Clinically, this can mimic other conditions like Crohn's disease or appendicitis. The colon (B), small intestine (C), and rectum (A) can also be affected, but less frequently than the ileocecal region.

30.	 Identify the distinctive structure in the provided 
slide, which is characteristic of a specific disease.
(A)	Sclerotic body
(B)	 Budding yeast
(C)	Negri body
(D)	Asteroid body
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(A) Sclerotic body
The histological image shows a thick-walled, round, brown-pigmented structure within tissue, characteristic of a sclerotic body (also called a Medlar body or “copper penny” body). These structures are seen in chromoblastomycosis, a chronic fungal infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue caused by dematiaceous (pigmented) fungi such as Fonsecaea or Cladophialophora species.

31.	 Antigen binding to MHC class I activates which 
of the following cells?
(A)	B cells
(B)	 NK cells
(C)	Cytotoxic T cells
(D)	Helper cells
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(C) Cytotoxic T cells
Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) class I molecules are present on the surface of almost all nucleated cells. Their primary function is to present endogenous antigens—peptides derived from proteins synthesized within the cell, such as viral proteins or mutated tumor proteins—to the immune system. The T-cell receptor (TCR) of Cytotoxic T cells (also known as CD8+ T cells) specifically recognizes these peptide antigens when presented by MHC class I molecules. This recognition, along with co-stimulation, activates the cytotoxic T cell to kill the antigen-presenting cell, thereby eliminating infected or malignant cells. Helper T cells (CD4+ T cells) (D) recognize antigens presented by MHC class II molecules on professional antigen-presenting cells. B cells (A) recognize intact antigens via their B-cell receptors. NK cells (B) recognize cells lacking MHC class I expression.
32.	 Which statement regarding anti-CMV IgG 
antibodies is accurate?
(A)	Denotes latent CMV infection
(B)	 Denotes chronic CMV infection with 
immunity to other serotypes
(C)	Indicates acute CMV infection
(D)	IgG avidity assay helps in differentiating 
past and primary infection
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(D) IgG avidity assay helps in differentiating past and primary infection
The presence of anti-CMV (Cytomegalovirus) IgG antibodies indicates that a person has been infected with CMV at some point in their life, but it does not, by itself, distinguish between a recent (primary) infection and a past or latent infection (A, C). After a primary infection, IgG antibodies are produced and typically persist for life. To determine the timing of the infection, an IgG avidity assay is used. This test measures the binding strength between IgG antibodies and the CMV antigen. Low-avidity IgG antibodies are characteristic of a recent primary infection (typically within the last 3-4 months), as the immune response is still maturing. High-avidity IgG antibodies indicate a past infection, as antibody binding strength increases over time. This differentiation is critically important, especially in managing pregnant women and transplant recipients. Statement (B) is incorrect as immunity is serotype-specific.
33.	 In a healthy adult, what is the proportion 
between T cells and B cells?
(A)	1 :1
(B)	 3 :1
(C)	1 :2
(D)	1 :3
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2022
(B) 3 :1
T cells (T lymphocytes) and B cells (B lymphocytes) are the two major types of lymphocytes that constitute the adaptive immune system. They are found in blood, lymph, and lymphoid organs. In the peripheral blood of a healthy adult, T cells are significantly more numerous than B cells. T cells typically constitute about 70-80% of the circulating lymphocyte population, while B cells make up about 10-20%. This results in a T cell to B cell ratio that is approximately 3 :1 to 4 :1. This reflects the central role of T cells in orchestrating and executing adaptive immune responses, including cell-mediated immunity (by cytotoxic T cells) and the regulation of antibody production (by helper T cells). The other ratios are incorrect representations of the normal lymphocyte distribution in peripheral blood.
