During exercise, the body’s oxygen consumption stabilizes at 1500 ml/min. Given that the baseline oxygen consumption is 250 ml/min, what is the resulting MET (Metabolic Equivalent of Task) score?
(A)	
5
(B)	
6
(C)	
1/5
(D)	
1/6
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
88.	 (B) 6
The Metabolic Equivalent of Task (MET) is a 
unit used to express the energy cost of physical 
activities. By definition, 1 MET is equivalent to 
the energy expenditure of sitting quietly, which 
corresponds to a baseline oxygen consumption 
rate of approximately 3.5 mL of oxygen per 
kilogram of body weight per minute. For an 
average 70 kg person, this equates to a total 
resting oxygen consumption of 3.5 × 70 = 245 
mL/min, which is given in the problem as a 
baseline of 250 mL/min. The MET score of an 
activity is calculated by dividing the oxygen 
consumption during the activity by the baseline 
oxygen consumption.
Oxygen consumption during exercise = 1500 
mL/min Baseline oxygen consumption = 250 
mL/min MET score = (1500 mL/min) / (250 
mL/min) = 6.
Therefore, the activity has an energy expenditure 
that is six times the resting metabolic rate.
Several new vaccines are currently under development, and their efficacy results are shown in the provided image. Which of these newly developed vaccines exhibit effectiveness similar to that of the earlier vaccine?
(A)	
D only
(B)	
D and E
(C)	
C, D and E
(D)	
A, B, C and D
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
89.	 (C) C, D and E
The figure represents results from an equivalence 
or non-inferiority trial. The vertical dashed lines 
indicate the predefined equivalence margins (−δ 
and +δ). Any vaccine whose entire confidence 
interval lies completely within these two margins 
is considered to have efficacy comparable to the 
previous (comparator) vaccine. If the confidence 
interval lies entirely to the left of −δ, the vaccine 
is inferior. If it lies entirely to the right of +δ, 
it demonstrates superiority rather than simple 
equivalence.
Vaccine A and B lie clearly on the inferior 
side of the graph, outside the equivalence 
margin, so they are not comparable. Vaccine C 
overlaps the left equivalence boundary; since 
part of its confidence interval lies within the 
equivalence zone and it does not extend beyond 
the predefined limit of inferiority, it can still 
be interpreted as comparable in this graphical 
context. Vaccines D and E lie entirely within 
the equivalence zone, fulfilling the criteria for 
comparable efficacy. Vaccines F and G lie beyond 
the right equivalence boundary, indicating 
superiority rather than equivalence.
Thus, the vaccines showing comparable efficacy 
are C, D, and E, making option (C) correct.
When the surrounding temperature reaches 47°C, which mechanism becomes the main way the body loses heat?
(A)	
Radiation
(B)	
Conduction
(C)	
Convection
(D)	
Sweating
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
90.	 (D) Sweating
The human body dissipates heat through four 
main mechanisms : radiation, conduction, 
convection, and evaporation. Radiation (A), 
conduction (B), and convection (C) are all 
processes that depend on a temperature 
gradient; heat flows from a warmer object to a 
cooler one. When the ambient environmental 
temperature is higher than the body's skin 
temperature (which is typically around 33-
35°C), these three mechanisms no longer work 
to cool the body. In fact, the body will gain heat 
from the environment through these processes. 
In this situation, the only effective mechanism 
for heat dissipation is the evaporation of sweat. 
The process of converting liquid sweat into 
water vapor on the skin's surface requires a 
significant amount of energy (the latent heat 
of vaporization), which is drawn from the 
body, thereby cooling it down. Therefore, at an 
ambient temperature of 47°C, sweating and 
subsequent evaporation is the sole physiological 
means of losing heat.

The combination of vestibular symptoms

In a 12-year-old child with fever and difficulty swallowing who presented with swelling in the shown region, persistent bleeding occurs after surgery. Which blood vessel is most likely injured?
(A)	
Tonsillar branch of facial artery
(B)	
Ascending pharyngeal artery
(C)	
Paratonsillar vein
(D)	
Retromandibular vein
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
102.	 (C) Paratonsillar vein
The child described has fever, difficulty 
swallowing, and swelling in the peritonsillar 
region, suggesting a peritonsillar abscess 
(quinsy). This condition involves infection and 
pus collection in the space between the tonsillar 
capsule and the superior constrictor muscle. 
Surgical drainage is commonly performed to 
relieve symptoms.
Persistent bleeding after the procedure 
most commonly occurs due to injury to the 
paratonsillar vein, also known as the external 
palatine vein. This vein lies in close proximity 
to the lateral aspect of the tonsil, just outside 
the tonsillar capsule. Because of its superficial 
location in the peritonsillar space, it is 
particularly vulnerable during incision and 
drainage or tonsillectomy.
The tonsillar branch of the facial artery 
is deeper and less commonly injured. The 
ascending pharyngeal artery is smaller and 
located more posteriorly. The retromandibular 
vein is situated more laterally and is not directly 
related to the tonsillar bed.
Therefore, in cases of persistent bleeding 
following drainage of a peritonsillar abscess, 
the most likely injured vessel is the paratonsillar 
vein.
Which of the following methods is accurate for measuring the nasogastric tube?
(A)

103.	 (A) Tip of nose to ear lobule to xiphisternum
The correct and universally taught method 
for estimating the proper insertion length of a 
nasogastric (NG) tube is the NEX measurement. 
This acronym stands for the path the tube 
follows from the Tip of the Nose to the Earlobe, 
and then down to the Xiphisternum. This 
method provides an anatomical approximation 
of the distance from the patient's nostril to the 
esophagogastric junction or the body of the 
stomach. Ensuring the tube is inserted to at 
least this length helps to confirm that the tip has 
passed beyond the esophagus and is correctly 
positioned within the stomach, which is crucial 
for safe and effective use. Using incorrect 
landmarks can lead to dangerous complications, 
such as placing the tube too short (coiled in 
the esophagus) or too long (advancing into the 
duodenum), or, most critically, misplacement 
into the trachea and lung. The other options 
describe incorrect measurement techniques that 
should not be used.

While receiving the second dose of a COVID vaccine, a patient developed a flabby, flattened, and asymmetrical shoulder, and the nurse noticed a loss of the normal shoulder contour. Which structure was likely injured, and could this injury have been avoided?
(A)	
Rotator cuff
(B)	
Posterior circumflex artery
(C)

(D)

122.	 (D) Axillary nerve
The described signs—a flabby, flat shoulder with 
loss of the normal rounded contour—are classic 
for deltoid muscle atrophy. The deltoid muscle 
is the main muscle that gives the shoulder its 
shape, and it is responsible for abduction of the 
arm. The deltoid muscle is innervated by the 
axillary nerve. The recommended site for an

would lead to denervation and subsequent 
atrophy of the deltoid muscle, resulting in the 
observed flattening of the shoulder contour and 
weakness in abduction. This is a known, though 
rare, complication of shoulder injections and is 
preventable by using the correct landmarking 
technique for the injection.

Identify the site of the lesion based on the visual field defect shown in the image.
(A)	
Left occipital lobe
(B)	
Right occipital lobe
(C)	
Left geniculate body
(D)	
Optic chiasma
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
109.	 (A) Left occipital lobe
The visual field charts show loss of the right 
half of the visual field in both eyes. This pattern 
represents a right homonymous hemianopia.
In homonymous hemianopia, the same side 
of the visual field is lost in both eyes. This occurs 
due to a lesion posterior to the optic chiasm — 
specifically in the optic tract, lateral geniculate 
body, optic radiation, or occipital cortex on the 
opposite side of the visual field defect.
Since the right visual field is lost, the lesion 
must be on the left side of the visual pathway 
(because visual pathways cross after the chiasm). 
Fibers from the right visual field of both eyes 
project to the left occipital lobe.
An optic chiasm lesion would cause 
bitemporal hemianopia, not homonymous 
hemianopia. A lesion in the left lateral 
geniculate body could also produce a similar 
defect, but cortical lesions are the most common 
cause, especially when the defect is congruous 
and respects the vertical meridian.
Therefore, the most likely site of the lesion is the 
left occipital lobe.
Which device in conventional oxygen therapy will provide the highest ?
(A)	
Venturi mask
(B)	
Hudson mask
(C)	
Non-rebreathing mask
(D)	
Nasal cannula
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
110.	 (C) Non-rebreathing mask
The fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) delivered 
to a patient depends on the oxygen delivery 
device. A nasal cannula (D) is a low-flow device 
that provides an approximate FiO2 of 24-44%. A 
Hudson mask (B), or simple face mask, is also a 
low-flow device delivering an FiO2 of about 40-
60%. A Venturi mask (A) is a high-flow device that 
can deliver a precise, fixed FiO2 (e.g., 24%, 28%, 
35%, 40%, 60%) by entraining a specific amount 
of room air. The device capable of delivering the 
highest possible FiO2 via conventional therapy 
is the non-rebreathing mask (NRB). An NRB has 
a reservoir bag and one-way valves designed to 
minimize the mixing of exhaled air and room air 
with the oxygen supply. When run at a high flow 
rate (10-15 L/min), an NRB can deliver an FiO2
of approximately 80% to over 95%, making it the 
device of choice for treating severe hypoxemia.

The instrument shown in the image is a Veress 
needle. It is a specialized, spring-loaded needle 
specifically designed for the initial insufflation of 
the abdomen (creation of a pneumoperitoneum) 
at the beginning of a laparoscopic procedure. 
Its key safety feature is a blunt, spring-loaded 
inner stylet that protrudes from the sharp outer 
cannula. As the needle is pushed through the 
layers of the abdominal wall, the blunt stylet 
retracts. Once the needle tip enters the peritoneal 
cavity, the loss of resistance allows the blunt 
stylet to spring forward, shielding the sharp tip 
and reducing the risk of inadvertently injuring 
the intra-abdominal organs. Carbon dioxide is 
then infused through the needle to create the 
space needed for the laparoscopic instruments. 
The other names listed are not associated with 
this instrument.

What is the needle placement angle when using the interrupted suturing technique to suture a laceration in the Emergency Room (ER)?
(A)	
60 degrees
(B)	
70 degrees
(C)	
80 degrees
(D)	
90 degrees
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
139.	 (D) 90 degrees
Proper suturing technique is essential for 
achieving good wound apposition and cosmetic 
results while minimizing scarring. When placing 
a simple interrupted suture, the goal is to evert 
the wound edges slightly. This is achieved by 
ensuring the needle enters and exits the skin at 
the correct angle and distance. The needle should 
enter the skin surface at a 90-degree angle. This 
perpendicular entry allows the needle to follow 
a curved path through the dermis, taking a 
wider bite of tissue at the base of the wound 
than at the surface. When the suture is tied, this 
configuration causes the wound edges to roll 
slightly upwards and evert. Entering the skin at 
an oblique angle (A, B, C) is incorrect technique 
and tends to invert the wound edges, which can 
lead to a depressed and more prominent scar 
after healing.

Which congenital heart defect shows equal oxygen saturation in all four cardiac chambers?
(A)	
Tetralogy of Fallot
(B)	
Total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation
(C)	
Tricuspid atresia
(D)	
Transposition of great arteries
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
118.	 (B) 
Total 
anomalous 
pulmonary 
venous 
circulation
In a healthy heart, the oxygen saturation in the 
right-sided chambers (carrying deoxygenated 
systemic venous blood) is much lower than in 
the left-sided chambers (carrying oxygenated 
pulmonary venous blood). A condition where 
saturation levels are equivalent across all four 
chambers indicates a complete mixing of the 
systemic and pulmonary venous returns. This 
occurs in Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous 
Connection/Circulation (TAPVC). In TAPVC, 
all four pulmonary veins, which should drain 
into the left atrium, instead drain anomalously 
into the systemic venous circulation (e.g., into 
the superior vena cava or right atrium). This 
results in the entire pulmonary venous return 
mixing with the systemic venous return in the 
right atrium. For the infant to survive, there 
must be an interatrial communication (an ASD 
or PFO) allowing this mixed blood to pass from 
the right atrium to the left atrium and then to 
the systemic circulation. This complete mixing 
results in nearly identical oxygen saturation in 
all chambers.
Which of the following statements accurately describes Korsakoff syndrome?
(A)	
Triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia
(B)	
Loss of long-term memory but intact personality
(C)	
Anterograde amnesia with loss of recent memory
(D)	
Loss of implicit memory and immediate recall
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
119.	 (C) Anterograde amnesia with loss of recent 
memory
Korsakoff syndrome is a chronic neurological 
disorder that is often a sequela of an untreated 
episode of Wernicke's encephalopathy, both 
caused by severe thiamine (Vitamin B1) 
deficiency, typically in the setting of chronic 
alcoholism. The statement describing the triad 
of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia (A) 
is the classic presentation of acute Wernicke's 
encephalopathy, not Korsakoff syndrome. The 
hallmark of Korsakoff syndrome is a profound 
and disproportionate memory deficit. The 
most prominent feature is severe anterograde 
amnesia, which is the inability to form new 
memories. Patients also have a significant 
retrograde amnesia affecting recent events 
more than distant ones. A characteristic feature 
is confabulation, where the patient invents 
memories to fill in the gaps. Immediate recall 
(digit span) and implicit memory (D) are often 
relatively preserved, as are other cognitive 
functions and personality (B).

The angiography image shows severe, diffuse, 
symmetrical narrowing and "beading" of

This appearance is characteristic of intense

clinical 
history 
provides 
the crucial link. The patient is HIV-positive

(like ritonavir), are potent inhibitors of the

What is the primary mode of dissemination of retinoblastoma?
(A)	
Optic nerve invasion
(B)	
Hematogenous
(C)	
Direct invasion
(D)	
Lymphatic spread
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
105.	 (A) Optic nerve invasion
Retinoblastoma, the most common intraocular 
cancer in children, can spread outside the eye 
through several pathways. While hematogenous 
spread (B) to distant sites like bone marrow 
and direct invasion (C) through the sclera into 
the orbit can occur, the most common and 
prognostically significant route of extraocular 
dissemination is direct invasion along the optic 
nerve. The tumor cells can infiltrate the optic 
nerve head and travel posteriorly, past the 
lamina cribrosa, into the subarachnoid space. 
This provides a direct pathway for the cancer 
to spread to the central nervous system (CNS), 
leading to intracranial and leptomeningeal 
metastases. This is a devastating complication 
that dramatically worsens the prognosis. 
For this reason, assessing the extent of optic 
nerve invasion during the histopathological 
examination of the enucleated eye is a critical 
part of staging the disease and determining the 
need for adjuvant therapy. Lymphatic spread 
(D) is not a typical feature of retinoblastoma.

106.	 (A) Capsulorrhexis
The image shows a critical step in modern 
cataract surgery. An instrument is being used 
to create a continuous, circular tear in the 
anterior capsule of the eye's natural lens. This 
technique is known as Continuous Curvilinear 
Capsulorrhexis (CCC), or simply capsulorrhexis. 
The goal is to create a perfectly round, smooth-
edged opening in the capsular bag that is slightly 
smaller than the optic of the intraocular lens 
that will be implanted later. A well-executed 
capsulorrhexis is essential for the safety and 
success of the subsequent steps of the surgery. 
It allows the surgeon to access and remove the 
cataractous lens nucleus (lens aspiration) while 
preserving the integrity of the capsular bag, 
which will securely hold the new artificial lens 
in place. Hydrodissection (B) is the next step, 
where fluid is injected to separate the lens cortex 
from the capsule.

107.	 (A) Vossius ring
The image shows the anterior surface of the 
crystalline lens, visible through the pupil. The 
arrow is pointing to a circular ring of fine, 
brown pigment deposited on the anterior 
lens capsule. This specific finding is known 
as a Vossius ring. It is a pathognomonic sign 
of previous significant blunt trauma to the 
eye. The ring is formed when the force of the 
impact rapidly and forcefully compresses the 
iris against the anterior lens capsule. Pigment 
from the posterior epithelial layer of the iris is 
imprinted onto the lens in a circular pattern that 
matches the shape of the pupillary margin at the 
moment of impact. A Weiss ring (B) is a circular 
opacity seen in the vitreous humor, representing 
a posterior vitreous detachment. A Fleischer's 
ring (C) is an iron line at the base of the cone 
in keratoconus. A Kayser-Fleischer ring (D) is a 
copper deposit in Descemet's membrane seen in 
Wilson's disease.

What does the yellow-colored tracing on this device in the operating room signify?
(A)

 Pressure in Inhaled Air

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
127.	 (A) Capnography
The image shows a typical screen from an 
anesthesia monitor. The waveform displayed 
in yellow is a capnogram. Capnography is the 
continuous monitoring of the concentration 
or partial pressure of carbon dioxide (CO2
) in the respiratory gases. The waveform 
shows the level of CO2 throughout the 
respiratory cycle. A normal capnogram has a 
characteristic rectangular shape, showing near-
zero CO2 during inspiration and a rapid rise 
to a plateau during expiration, with the peak 
value representing the end-tidal CO2 (CO2). 
Capnography is a standard of care in anesthesia 
and critical care. Its most critical function is 
to immediately confirm correct placement 
of an endotracheal tube in the trachea. It also 
provides vital information about the patient's 
ventilation, perfusion, and metabolism. The 
other waveforms on a monitor are typically 
color-coded differently (e.g., green for ECG, blue 
for SpO2, red for arterial pressure).

128.	 (C) Levopropoxyphene
This drug is specifically classified as a centrally 
acting opioid antitussive. It works by directly 
suppressing the cough reflex center in the 
medulla oblongata of the brainstem. It is the levo-
isomer of propoxyphene and, unlike its dextro-
isomer (an analgesic), it has minimal pain-
relieving effects, making its primary therapeutic 
use the suppression of non-productive coughs.
Why the Other Options are Incorrect
(A)	Ambroxol : This is a mucolytic, not an 
antitussive. It works peripherally by 
thinning mucus in the airways to make it 
easier to expel, rather than suppressing the 
cough reflex centrally.
(B)	Diphenoxylate : This is an opioid agonist 
used primarily as an antidiarrheal. It slows 
intestinal motility and is not classified or 
used as a cough suppressant.
(D)	Levorphanol : This is a potent opioid 
analgesic for severe pain. While most strong 
opioids possess antitussive properties as 
a secondary effect, Levorphanol's main 
classification is as a powerful pain reliever, 
not primarily as an antitussive.

The Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic 
Hormone Secretion (SIADH) is a disorder of 
impaired water excretion caused by the non-
physiological release of ADH. This leads to the 
retention of free water, which dilutes the body's 
sodium, resulting in euvolemic hyponatremia. 
The diagnostic criteria include :
(B)	Hyponatremia with a corresponding low 
serum osmolality, so serum sodium < 135 
mEq/L (B) is correct.
(C)	Inappropriately concentrated urine relative 
to the serum osmolality, so urine osmolality 
> 100 mOsm/kg (C) is correct.
(D)	The patient is typically clinically euvolemic 
(D), without signs of dehydration or 
significant edema.
In response to the water retention, the 
body tries to excrete sodium to maintain 
volume balance. This results in a high urinary 
sodium concentration, typically > 40 mEq/L. 
The statement that urinary sodium is < 20 
mEq/L (A) is therefore incorrect. A low urinary 
sodium would be expected in hypovolemic 
hyponatremia.
What is the treatment of choice for providing symptom relief during an acute cluster headache attack?
(A)	
Oral sumatriptan
(B)	
Subcutaneous sumatriptan
(C)	
100% oxygen at 6 L/minute
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
114.	 (B) Subcutaneous sumatriptan
Cluster headache is an excruciatingly severe, 
unilateral headache with a rapid onset. The 
acute (abortive) treatment needs to be very fast-
acting. Oral sumatriptan (A) has a slow onset 
of action and is generally ineffective for the 
rapid relief required. The two first-line abortive 
treatments are high-flow oxygen and injectable 
sumatriptan. Inhaling 100% oxygen via a non-
rebreather mask is a highly effective treatment, 
but it must be administered at a high flow rate, 
typically 12 to 15 L/minute, not the lower rates 
of 6 or 8 L/minute mentioned in options C and 
D. The other first-line option, which is extremely 
effective and rapid, is subcutaneous sumatriptan 
(usually a 6 mg injection). Its rapid absorption 
provides relief within minutes. Given that the 
oxygen flow rates offered in the options are 
suboptimal, subcutaneous sumatriptan stands 
out as the most effective and correctly described 
first-line choice.

115.	 (B) Mitral stenosis
The image shows a gross pathological specimen 
of a heart valve viewed from the atrial side. 
The valve leaflets are markedly thickened and 
fibrotic, and there is fusion of the commissures 
(the points where the leaflets meet). This process 
has resulted in a severe narrowing of the valve 
orifice, giving it a characteristic slit-like or "fish 
mouth" appearance. This specific pathology is 
the hallmark of chronic rheumatic heart disease 
leading to mitral stenosis. Rheumatic fever 
is the most common cause of mitral stenosis 
worldwide, and the pathological changes of 
commissural fusion, leaflet thickening, and 
chordal shortening are classic. Tricuspid 
stenosis (A) is much rarer and has a similar 
appearance but involves the tricuspid valve. 
The cardiomyopathies (C, D) are diseases of 
the heart muscle itself, not the valves, and have 
different gross appearances.

116.	 (A) Endo-myocardial biopsy
Myocarditis is an inflammatory disease of the 
heart muscle. While clinical presentation, 
ECG changes, elevated cardiac enzymes (like 
troponin), and imaging can all be suggestive, 
the definitive gold standard for the diagnosis of 
myocarditis is an endomyocardial biopsy (EMB). 
The biopsy allows for direct histopathological 
examination of the heart tissue. The diagnosis 
is confirmed by the Dallas criteria, which 
require the presence of an inflammatory 
infiltrate within the myocardium associated 
with myocyte damage or necrosis that is not

A patient presents to the outpatient clinic with a burn on the right thigh featuring a moist, red, blistered lesion and a sharply defined distal margin. What is the most probable cause of this burn?
(A)	
Electric burn
(B)	
Chemical burn
(C)	
Dry heat
(D)	
Moist heat
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
134.	 (D) Moist heat
The description of the burn provides key clues 
to its etiology. The lesion is damp, red, and 
blistered, which is characteristic of a partial-
thickness burn. The crucial finding is the 
clear demarcation line extending distally. This 
pattern is typical of a scald burn caused by a hot 
liquid, or moist heat. When a hot liquid is spilled 
on the body, it runs downwards due to gravity, 
creating a burn with a "trickle-down" pattern 
and a very sharp, clear line of demarcation 
at the point where the liquid stopped or was 
absorbed by clothing. In contrast, a burn from 
dry heat (C) (e.g., a flame or hot object) would 
have a less distinct margin, corresponding to 
the area of contact. An electric burn (A) would 
have distinct entry and exit wounds. A chemical 
burn (B) can have sharp margins but often 
has associated coagulation necrosis or specific 
coloration depending on the agent.
Which of the following observations manifests later in compartment syndrome?
(A)	
Pallor
(B)	
Paralysis
(C)	
Pulselessness
(D)	
Pain on passive stretch
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
135.	 (B) Paralysis
Compartment syndrome occurs when increased 
pressure within a closed fascial compartment 
compromises circulation and tissue perfusion. 
The classic clinical features are remembered as 
the “6 Ps” :
1.	 Pain, 
Paresthesia, 
Pallor, 
Paralysis, 
Pulselessness, and Poikilothermia.
2.	 The earliest and most sensitive sign is pain, 
especially pain out of proportion to injury 
and pain on passive stretch of the muscles 
within the affected compartment.
3.	 As pressure increases, nerve ischemia 
develops, leading to paresthesia (early 
sensory change). With further compromise 
of arterial flow, pallor and diminished 
pulses may occur, although pulselessness is 
typically a late finding.
4.	 Paralysis is a very late manifestation. It 
indicates prolonged nerve and muscle 
ischemia with possible irreversible damage. 
By the time paralysis appears, significant 
tissue necrosis may have already occurred, 
and urgent fasciotomy may not fully reverse 
deficits.
Therefore, among the given options, the 
observation that manifests later in compartment 
syndrome is : (B) Paralysis.

For a patient who had cough and fever due to COVID-19 but recovered without needing hospitalization, how long should elective surgery be deferred?
(A)	
6 weeks
(B)	
8-10 weeks
(C)	
12 weeks
(D)	
4 weeks
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
130.	 (A) 6 weeks
Current perioperative guidelines recommend 
postponing elective surgery after COVID-19 
infection to reduce postoperative pulmonary and 
thrombotic complications. The recommended 
delay depends on severity of illness.
For patients who had symptomatic COVID-19 
(e.g., cough and fever) but did not require 
hospitalization, surgery should generally be 
deferred for at least 6 weeks from the date of 
diagnosis or symptom onset.
Rationale :
1.	 COVID-19 can cause residual pulmonary 
inflammation and endothelial dysfunction.
2.	 Early surgery (within 6 weeks) is associated 
with increased risk of postoperative 
pneumonia, 
respiratory 
failure, 
thromboembolism, and mortality.
3.	 Waiting 6 weeks allows recovery of 
pulmonary function and reduction of 
systemic inflammatory effects.
For more severe cases :
4.	 Hospitalized 
patients 
or 
those 
with 
comorbidities may require 8–10 weeks 
delay.
5.	 ICU admission or severe disease may 
require 12 weeks or more.
Since this patient had mild symptomatic 
infection and recovered without hospitalization, 
the recommended deferral period is 6 weeks.
Therefore, the correct answer is (A) 6 weeks.
What is the likely diagnosis for a 60-year-old male who, during a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, exhibits a sudden drop in end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2) to 8 mmHg, a reduction in oxygen saturation (SpO2) to 90%, a decrease in blood pressure to 80/50 mmHg, and a peak airway pressure of 18 cm H2O?

(C)

131.	 (C) 3 only
This is a classic presentation of a gas embolism, 
specifically a carbon dioxide (CO2) embolism, 
during laparoscopic surgery. The triad of 
sudden, 
profound 
hypotension, 
a 
sharp 
decrease in end-tidal CO2, and hypoxemia 
is pathognomonic. During laparoscopy, the 
abdomen is insufflated with CO2. If a vessel is 
inadvertently injured, a large volume of gas can 
enter the venous circulation and travel to the 
right heart and pulmonary artery, causing an 
air lock that obstructs pulmonary blood flow. 
This catastrophic drop in pulmonary perfusion 
leads to a massive increase in dead space 
ventilation, which is why the EtCO2 plummets. 
The obstruction also causes right heart failure 
and 
circulatory 
collapse 
(hypotension). 
Bronchospasm (4) or single bronchus intubation 
(1) would cause an increase in airway pressure 
and potentially an increase in EtCO2, not a 
sudden drop.

During an appendectomy that begins with a gridiron incision, which anatomical structures does the surgeon cut through?
1.	
External oblique
2.	
Internal oblique
3.	
Transversus abdominis
4.	
Rectus abdominis
(A)	
1,3,4
(B)	
2,3,4
(C)	
1,2,3
(D)	
1,2,4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
142.	 (C) 1,2,3
A gridiron incision (or McBurney's incision) 
is a muscle-splitting incision used for open 
appendectomy. It is centered over McBurney's 
point in the right lower quadrant. The layers are 
opened sequentially :
1.	 The skin and subcutaneous tissue are 
incised.
2.	 The aponeurosis of the external oblique 
muscle is incised in the direction of its 
fibers.
3.	 The fibers of the internal oblique and the 
underlying transversus abdominis muscles 
are then split (not cut) in the direction 
of their fibers, which runs roughly 
perpendicular to the external oblique fibers. 
This creates the "gridiron" pattern.
4.	 The transversalis fascia and peritoneum are 
then incised to enter the abdominal cavity.
The rectus abdominis muscle (4) is located 
medially and is not incised or split during a 
standard gridiron incision.

144.	 (B) Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma
Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft 
tissue sarcoma in children. One of the most 
common primary sites for this tumor is the 
head and neck region, including the orbit. An 
orbital rhabdomyosarcoma typically presents 
with a rapidly developing proptosis (protrusion 
of the eyeball) in a young child. The diagnosis is 
confirmed by biopsy and immunohistochemistry. 
Rhabdomyosarcomas are tumors of primitive 
skeletal muscle cells (rhabdomyoblasts). A key 
immunohistochemical marker that confirms 
skeletal muscle differentiation is desmin, an 
intermediate filament protein found in muscle 
cells. Therefore, a desmin-positive tumor 
causing proptosis in a 5-year-old is the classic 
presentation of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, 
the most common histologic subtype in this age 
group. Ewing's sarcoma (A) is typically a bone 
tumor. Leukemia (C) can present with orbital 
infiltration (chloroma), but would have different 
markers. Retinoblastoma (D) is an intraocular 
tumor.

prior immunity makes transmission to her fetus 
during pregnancy much less likely. The risk

transmission risk associated with a primary 
infection (a mother's first exposure) during 
pregnancy. Therefore, the presence of maternal 
IgG makes congenital infection "unlikely."

A pediatrician attempted to obtain a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample from a 6-month-old boy who presented to the emergency department with seizures. While inserting the needle through the indicated area, which anatomical structures might have been inadvertently pierced?
(A)	
Scalp, dura, arachnoid
(B)	
Scalp, epicranium, endocranium, and dura
(C)	
Scalp synchondrosis membrane, dura, arachnoid
(D)	
Pericranium, dura, arachnoid
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
151.	 (A) Scalp, dura, arachnoid
The image indicates the anterior fontanelle, a 
"soft spot" on an infant's skull. In rare situations 
where a lumbar puncture is not feasible, a 
fontanelle tap can be performed to obtain a 
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample. To reach 
the CSF, which is located in the subarachnoid 
space, the needle must traverse several layers in 
sequence. The needle first passes through the 
scalp, which consists of skin, connective tissue, 
and the galea aponeurotica. Deep to the scalp 
is the pericranium (periosteum of the skull), 
which is also traversed. Since there is no bone at 
the fontanelle, the needle then passes through 
the tough outer meningeal layer, the dura mater, 
and the delicate middle layer, the arachnoid 
mater, to enter the subarachnoid space. An 
accidental puncture or deeper penetration could 
damage the underlying cerebral cortex or, more 
critically, the superior sagittal sinus, a large 
venous sinus that runs in the midline deep to 
the dura. Option A, while simplified (omitting 
the pericranium), lists the essential layers that 
must be passed through in the correct order.
A 3-year-old child is found to have a palpable, movable, kidney-shaped mass on the right side of the abdomen during a bath, with a history of hematuria that resolved on its own two weeks earlier. Which additional investigations should be performed to evaluate this condition?
1.	
CECT
2.	
PET-CT
3.	
24 hour urinary VMA
4.	
FNAC
(A)	
1 and 2
(B)	
2 and 4
(C)	
1, 2 and 3
(D)	
1, 2, 3 and 4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
152.	 (C) 1, 2 and 3
A palpable abdominal mass in a 3-year-old 
child raises immediate suspicion of a pediatric 
malignancy, with the primary differentials 
being Wilms' tumor and neuroblastoma. A 
comprehensive workup is essential. A Contrast-
Enhanced CT (CECT) of the abdomen (1) is 
the cornerstone of imaging to define the origin, 
size, and extent of the tumor. To differentiate 
between the two main possibilities, biochemical 
testing is crucial; a 24-hour urinary collection 
for catecholamine metabolites like VMA (3) is 
mandatory, as elevated levels are diagnostic for 
neuroblastoma. A PET-CT scan (2), specifically 
with MIBG for neuroblastoma or FDG for 
other tumors, is a standard part of the staging 
workup to look for distant metastases. However, 
Fine-Needle Aspiration or Cytology (FNAC) 
(4) is generally contraindicated for a suspected 
Wilms' tumor. Puncturing the tumor capsule 
risks tumor spillage, which would upstage the 
disease and worsen the prognosis. Therefore, 
the appropriate investigations include CECT, 
PET-CT for staging, and urinary VMA, while 
FNAC is avoided.
In a 14-month-old child diagnosed with Haemophilus influenzae meningitis, what reason might lead clinicians to change the initial treatment plan from ampicillin to ceftriaxone?
(A)	
Hemophilus alters penicillin-binding protein sites, hence resistant to ampicillin
(B)	
Easier to administer IV ceftriaxone than IV ampicillin
(C)	
Cotrimoxazole is the drug of choice, but the patient is allergic to sulfa drugs
(D)	
Hemophilus produces beta-lactamase, hence resistant to ampicillin
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
153.	 (D) Haemophilus produces beta-lactamase, 
hence resistant to ampicillin
This is a duplicate of a previous question. The 
most prevalent mechanism of resistance to 
ampicillin in Haemophilus influenzae is the 
production of the enzyme beta-lactamase. This 
enzyme effectively inactivates the ampicillin 
molecule by cleaving its beta-lactam ring, 
rendering the antibiotic useless. Due to the high 
prevalence of beta-lactamase-producing strains, 
ampicillin is no longer considered a reliable 
empirical choice for treating serious infections 
like meningitis caused by H. influenzae. Third-

The management of severe COVID-19 in

A child presents with fever, vesicular lesions on the upper and lower limbs including the palms and soles, oral lesions, neck stiffness, and CSF findings showing normal glucose with elevated lymphocytes and protein. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Bacterial meningitis with sepsis
(B)

(C)

(D)

This patient presents with two distinct clinical

The presence of vesicular lesions on the hands, 
feet (including palms and soles), and in the

Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD). The 
neurological symptoms of neck stiffness, along

What are the factors that can lead to seizures in newborns?
1.	
Hypocalcemia
2.	
Hyponatremia
3.	
Hypomagnesemia
4.	
Hypoglycemia
(A)	
1, 2, 3 only
(B)	
1, 2, 3, and 4
(C)	
1, 3, 4 only
(D)	
2, 4 only
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
148.	 (B) 1, 2, 3, and 4
Neonatal seizures are a sign of significant 
underlying central nervous system dysfunction. 
A major category of causes is acute metabolic 
disturbances, as the neonatal brain is highly 
vulnerable to such imbalances. All four options 
listed are well-established metabolic causes 
of seizures in a newborn. Hypoglycemia 
(4) (low blood sugar) is a very common 
cause, as glucose is the brain's primary fuel. 
Electrolyte abnormalities are also frequent 
triggers. Hypocalcemia (1) (low calcium) and 
hypomagnesemia (3) (low magnesium) both 
increase neuronal excitability and can precipitate 
seizures. Hyponatremia (2) (low sodium) can 
cause cerebral edema and is also a recognized 
cause of neonatal seizures. Therefore, all four 
of these metabolic derangements are important 
factors that can lead to seizures in the neonatal 
period and should be checked for in any seizing 
infant.
At what age does a child reach half of their adult height?
(A)	
12-18 months
(B)	
20-24 months
(C)	
32-36 months
(D)	
40-48 months
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
149.	 (B) 20-24 months
There is a well-known rule of thumb in 
pediatrics for predicting a child's final adult 
height based on their height at an early age. 
The rule states that a child's height at 2 years 
of age (24 months) is approximately half of 
their eventual adult height. Therefore, one can 
estimate the adult height by simply doubling 
the child's height at their second birthday. This 
approximation works reasonably well because 
the rapid growth of infancy has slowed, and 
the child has settled onto their genetic growth 
curve, but the pubertal growth spurt has not yet 
begun. The period of 20-24 months encompasses 
this two-year milestone. This provides a simple, 
though not perfectly precise, method for long-
term height prediction.

Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS/PCOD)

The provided ultrasound image shows a sagittal

but the upper part of the head, including

Arrange the following steps in sequential order for the collection of samples for Pap smear testing:
1.	
Use posterior vaginal wall retractor
2.	
Take the sample
3.	
Make smear on a slide
4.	
Fix the smear
(A)	
1, 2, 4, 3
(B)	
2, 1, 3, 4
(C)	
3, 1, 2, 4
(D)	
1, 2, 3, 4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
160.	 (D) 1, 2, 3, 4
The procedure for obtaining a conventional Pap 
smear follows a logical and critical sequence to 
ensure a high-quality, interpretable sample.
First, a speculum (such as a Cusco's speculum, 
or a Sims' speculum with a posterior vaginal wall 
retractor) is inserted to visualize the cervix. (Step 
1) Once the cervix is fully visualized, a sampling 
device (such as an Ayre's spatula and/or a 
cytobrush) is used to take the sample by scraping 
cells from the ectocervix and endocervical canal. 
(Step 2) The collected cellular material is then 
immediately and evenly smeared onto a glass 
slide. (Step 3) To prevent air-drying artifacts 
which destroy cellular detail, the slide must be 
immediately fixed, either by immersing it in 
95% ethanol or by using a spray fixative. (Step 
4) This sequence ensures proper visualization, 
adequate sampling, correct preparation, and 
optimal preservation of the cells for cytological 
analysis.

Applying skeletal traction through the proximal 
tibia for a femur fracture requires a specific set 
of orthopedic equipment. First, a rigid pin must 
be passed through the bone; a Steinmann pin 
(3) is a smooth, large-diameter pin used for this 
purpose. A Denham's pin (4) is an alternative

and providing a pulley system for the traction 
weights. A Thomas splint (1) is used for first aid 
transport or different traction setups. A K-wire 
(2) is too thin for this application.
A patient suffers a type IIIa compound fracture of the tibia after a road traffic accident. How should the following external fixators be ranked from the most stable to the least stable?
1.	
Ilizarov fixator
2.	
Uniplanar with a single rod
3.	
Uniplanar with double rod
4.	
Biplanar frame/Ring with a cylindrical rod
(A)	
1>2>3>4
(B)	
2>4>3>1
(C)	
1>4>3>2
(D)	
2>3>1>4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
156.	 (C) 1>4>3>2
The stability of an external fixator construct is 
determined by its biomechanical properties, 
particularly its resistance to bending, axial, and 
torsional forces. The stability generally increases 
with the complexity of the frame.
Most Stable : The Ilizarov fixator (1), a true 
circular frame with tensioned wires, provides 
multiplanar stability and is considered the most 
stable construct, offering excellent resistance to 
all deforming forces.
Next is a hybrid frame or a biplanar frame 
(4), which uses pins inserted in two different 
planes, providing significantly more stability 
than a simple unilateral frame.
A uniplanar frame with a double rod (3) is 
stiffer and more stable than one with a single 
rod.
Least Stable : The simplest and least stable 
construct is a uniplanar frame with a single 
connecting rod (2).
Therefore, the correct ranking from most 
stable to least stable is Ilizarov > Biplanar > 
Uniplanar (double rod) > Uniplanar (single 
rod), which corresponds to the sequence 1 > 4 
> 3 > 2.

What is the first-line treatment for a woman who presents with frothy vaginal discharge and a strawberry-appearing cervix?

The clinical findings of a profuse, thin, yellow-

In a semen analysis, what percentage range is considered normal for sperm morphology?
(A)	
10%
(B)	
4%
(C)	
6%
(D)	
8%
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
163.	 (B) 4%
This is a duplicate of a previous question. 
According to the 5th and 6th editions of the 
World Health Organization (WHO) laboratory 
manual for the examination of human semen, 
the lower reference limit for sperm morphology 
is 4%. This means that for a semen sample to 
be considered normal in terms of morphology, 
at least 4% of the sperm must have a normal 
form when assessed using strict criteria (often 
referred to as Kruger's strict criteria). These 
criteria evaluate the precise dimensions and 
appearance of the sperm head, midpiece, and 
tail. A value below this 4% threshold is classified 
as teratozoospermia. Previous editions of the 
WHO manual used higher cutoff values (e.g., 
14% or 30%), but the current, more stringent 
standard is 4%.

Relative to pregnancy, which nutrient must be supplemented in greater amounts during lactation?
(A)	
Vitamin A
(B)	
Calcium
(C)	
Iron
(D)	
Folic acid
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
176.	 (B) Calcium
The nutritional requirements for several key 
nutrients are higher during lactation than 
during pregnancy to support the production 
of nutrient-rich breast milk. While needs for 
nutrients like Vitamin A (A) are increased, the 
most significant difference is for calcium. A 
lactating woman secretes a substantial amount 
of calcium into her breast milk (approximately 
200-300 mg per day) to support the infant's 
bone development. To meet this demand 
without depleting her own bone stores, the 
recommended dietary allowance for calcium 
is higher during lactation. In contrast, the 
requirement for iron (C) is actually lower during 
exclusive lactation than during pregnancy. This 
is because menstruation has not yet returned 
(lactational amenorrhea), so the woman is not 
losing iron through menstrual blood. Similarly, 
the need for folic acid (D) is highest in the 
periconceptional period and first trimester of 
pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects.
Asherman syndrome is most commonly associated with:
(A)	
Oligomenorrhea
(B)	
Hypomenorrhea
(C)	
Dysmenorrhea
(D)	
Menorrhagia
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
177.	 (B) Hypomenorrhea
Asherman's syndrome is an acquired uterine 
condition characterized by the formation of 
intrauterine adhesions or scar tissue. The 
most common cause is trauma to the basal 
layer of the endometrium, typically from a 
vigorous dilatation and curettage (D&C), often 
postpartum or post-abortion. These adhesions 
can obliterate the endometrial cavity to varying 
degrees. The most common clinical presentation 
is a change in the menstrual pattern. Since the 
amount of functional endometrial tissue is 
reduced, the menstrual flow becomes scanty 
or very light. This is known as hypomenorrhea. 
In severe cases, the scarring can completely 
obstruct the cavity, leading to secondary 
amenorrhea (complete absence of periods). 
Dysmenorrhea (C) can also occur. Menorrhagia 
(D), or heavy bleeding, is the opposite of what 
is seen. Oligomenorrhea (A) refers to infrequent 
cycles.

178.	 (A) Cusco's speculum
The instrument depicted is a Cusco's speculum. 
It is a bivalved, self-retaining vaginal speculum. 
It consists of two blades (valves) that are hinged 
together and can be opened and held in place 
by a screw mechanism. This design allows it 
to be inserted into the vagina and then opened

179.	 (A) Pap smear
The instruments shown in the image are used 
for performing a Pap smear (Papanicolaou test), 
which is a screening procedure for detecting 
premalignant and malignant lesions of the 
cervix. The set includes a vaginal speculum, 
Ayre’s spatula, endocervical brush, glass slides, 
and a fixative container.
The vaginal speculum is inserted into the 
vagina to visualize the cervix clearly. Once the 
cervix is exposed, the Ayre’s spatula is used to 
scrape cells from the ectocervix, particularly 
from the transformation zone where cervical 
dysplasia commonly develops. The endocervical 
brush is then inserted gently into the endocervical 
canal to collect columnar epithelial cells.
The collected cellular material is spread 
evenly onto glass slides and immediately 
placed in a fixative solution to preserve cellular 
morphology. These slides are later examined 
under a microscope to detect abnormal epithelial 
changes such as dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, or 
invasive carcinoma.
These instruments are not used for 
hysteroscopy, biopsy, or dilatation and curettage, 
as those procedures require different specialized 
tools. Therefore, the instruments shown are 
specifically used for a Pap smear.

What is the recommended dosage of carbetocin for preventing postpartum hemorrhage?

(B)	
150 mcg

200 mcg

172.	 (D) 100 mcg
Carbetocin is a long-acting synthetic analogue 
of oxytocin. It is a potent uterotonic agent used 
for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage 
(PPH) due to uterine atony, particularly after

requires a continuous infusion, carbetocin is

immediately after the delivery of the baby.

standard PPH prevention protocol.
To which biochemical moiety is beta hCG structurally similar?
(A)	
LH
(B)	
FSH
(C)	
ACTH
(D)	
Oxytocin
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
173.	 (A) LH
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is 
a glycoprotein hormone composed of two 
subunits, an alpha (α) subunit and a beta (β) 
subunit. The alpha subunit of hCG is structurally 
identical to the alpha subunits of three other 
pituitary glycoprotein hormones : luteinizing 
hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone 
(FSH), and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). 
The beta subunit is unique to each hormone 
and confers its biological specificity. However, 
the beta subunit of hCG shares significant 
structural homology (about 80% similarity) with 
the beta subunit of LH. Because of this marked 
similarity, hCG can bind to and activate the LH 
receptor. This is the physiological basis for hCG's 
primary function in early pregnancy, which 
is to "rescue" and maintain the corpus luteum 
to continue progesterone production until the 
placenta takes over this role.
What hinders the production of milk during pregnancy?
(A)	
Low luteinizing hormone
(B)	
High estrogen
(C)	
Human somatomammotropin
(D)	
Low thyroid-stimulating hormone
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
174.	 (B) High estrogen
During pregnancy, the breast tissue undergoes 
significant 
development 
and 
proliferation 
(mammogenesis) under the influence of several 
hormones, including estrogen, progesterone, 
prolactin, and human placental lactogen 
(hPL). The pituitary gland secretes high levels 
of prolactin, the primary hormone responsible 
for stimulating milk synthesis (lactogenesis). 
However, despite these high prolactin levels, 
active milk secretion is held in check throughout 
pregnancy. This inhibition is primarily caused 
by the very high circulating levels of estrogen 
and progesterone, which are produced by 
the placenta. These steroid hormones act 
on the breast tissue to block the binding of 
prolactin to its receptors on the alveolar cells, 
thereby hindering its lactogenic effect. After 
delivery, the abrupt withdrawal of estrogen 
and progesterone following the expulsion of 
the placenta removes this inhibition, allowing 
prolactin to act unopposed and initiate copious 
milk production.

How do local anesthetics exert their mechanism of action?
(A)	
Block sodium channels
(B)	
Block potassium channels
(C)	
Block calcium channels
(D)	
Block chloride channels
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
188.	 (A) Block sodium channels
Local anesthetics are drugs that produce a 
transient and reversible loss of sensation, 
particularly pain, in a localized area of the 
body. Their primary mechanism of action is the 
blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels in 
the nerve cell membrane. A nerve impulse, or 
action potential, is generated and propagated 
by the rapid influx of sodium ions through 
these channels, which causes depolarization 
of the nerve membrane. Local anesthetics bind 
to a specific receptor site within the pore of the 
voltage-gated sodium channel. This binding 
physically obstructs the channel, preventing 
the influx of sodium ions. By blocking this 
crucial step, local anesthetics prevent the nerve 
from reaching the threshold for depolarization, 
thereby blocking the generation and conduction 
of action potentials. This interruption of nerve 
impulse transmission is what produces the 
anesthetic effect.

What are the side effects of pituitary irradiation?
(A)	
Hypopituitarism
(B)	
Increased risk of cerebrovascular accident
(C)	
Optic nerve damage
(D)	
All of the above
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
190.	 (D) All of the above
Radiation therapy to the pituitary region, used 
for tumors like pituitary adenomas, can have 
several significant long-term side effects due to 
radiation damage to the gland and surrounding 
structures.
(A)	Hypopituitarism : Radiation can cause 
delayed damage to the normal hormone-
producing cells of the pituitary gland, 
leading to deficiencies in one or more 
pituitary hormones. This is the most 
common late complication.
(C)	Optic nerve damage : The optic nerves and 
chiasm are located in very close proximity 
to the pituitary gland. They are highly 
sensitive to radiation, and damage can lead 
to a progressive and irreversible loss of 
vision, known as radiation-induced optic 
neuropathy.
(B)	Increased risk of cerebrovascular accident 
: Radiation can induce vasculopathy in 
the large arteries at the base of the brain 
(e.g., the internal carotid arteries), leading 
to stenosis or occlusion and a significantly 
increased long-term risk of stroke.
Since all these are well-documented and serious 
potential side effects, the correct answer is all of 
the above.

The provided axial CT scan of the abdomen

low attenuation is consistent with the density of

192.	 (A) USG
The image displays a real-time, cross-sectional

What is the length of time for which short-term memory lasts?
(A)	
3-6 Hours
(B)	
12-18 Hours
(C)	
30-300 Seconds
(D)	
3-4 Seconds
	
EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2021
196.	 (C) 30-300 Seconds
Short-term memory (STM) refers to the 
temporary storage of information for a brief 
period before it is either forgotten or consolidated 
into long-term memory. It typically lasts from 
about 30 seconds to 5 minutes (300 seconds) in 
the absence of rehearsal.
Short-term memory has a limited capacity, 
often described by Miller’s law as 7 ± 2 items, 
although more recent research suggests it may 
be closer to 4–7 items. Information in short-
term memory can be maintained longer through 
active rehearsal (repeating the information 
mentally).
In contrast :
1.	 Sensory memory lasts only a few seconds 
(about 1–3 seconds).
2.	 Working memory is closely related to 
short-term memory but includes active 
processing.
3.	 Long-term memory can last from hours to a 
lifetime.
Thus, the typical duration of short-term memory 
is 30–300 seconds, making option (C) correct.

The patient's symptoms—recurrent, intrusive

and most effective form of psychotherapy for 
OCD is a specific type of Cognitive-Behavioral

Response Prevention (ERP). In ERP, the patient 
is gradually and systematically exposed to the 
situations, objects, or thoughts that trigger their 
obsessions (e.g., touching a "contaminated" 
object). They are then coached to resist and 
refrain from performing their compulsive ritual 
(the response prevention part, e.g., not washing 
their hands). Through this process, the patient 
learns that their anxiety will decrease over 
time without the need for the ritual, leading 
to the habituation of the fear response and a 
significant reduction in symptoms. While ERP

According to ICD-11, which of the following conditions is not classified under obsessive–compulsive disorders?

Trichotillomania
(B)	
Body dysmorphic disorder
(C)	
Hypochondriac disorder
(D)

198.	 (D) PTSD
The ICD-11 (and DSM-5) created a new 
chapter for "Obsessive-Compulsive and Related 
Disorders." This category groups together a set 
of disorders that share features of repetitive 
thoughts 
and/or 
behaviors. This 
chapter 
includes Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) 
itself, as well as Body Dysmorphic Disorder 
(B) (preoccupation with perceived flaws in 
appearance), Trichotillomania (A) (hair-pulling 
disorder), hoarding disorder, and excoriation 
(skin-picking) 
disorder. 
Hypochondriasis 
(illness anxiety disorder) (C) is also included 
in this chapter. In contrast, Post-Traumatic 
Stress Disorder (PTSD) (D) is classified under a 
completely different chapter called "Disorders 
specifically associated with stress." While it 
involves intrusive thoughts (re-experiencing 
the trauma), its etiology and core features are 
distinct from those of the OCD-related disorders, 
as it is directly linked to a traumatic event.

Which of the following branches originate from

(D)	1,4,5,6

The internal iliac artery bifurcates into an anterior and a posterior division. The posterior division supplies the pelvic wall and gluteal region, giving off the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries (1). All the other arteries listed are branches of the anterior division, which primarily supplies the pelvic viscera, perineum, and medial thigh. These visceral and parietal branches include the umbilical artery (from which the superior vesical artery (3) arises), obturator artery, inferior vesical artery (5) (in males), uterine artery (from which the vaginal artery (6) arises in females), middle rectal artery (4), internal pudendal artery, and the inferior gluteal artery (2). 39.	 Which of the following is not associated with 
massive splenomegaly?
(A)	Chronic myeloid leukemia
(B)	 Aplastic anemia
(C)	Hairy cell leukemia
(D)	Lymphoma
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(B) Aplastic anemia
Massive splenomegaly is defined as a spleen that is palpable more than 8 cm below the left costal margin or weighs more than 1000 grams. It is caused by a limited number of conditions, typically those involving significant infiltration of the spleen or chronic congestion. Classic causes include myeloproliferative neoplasms like Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) (A), which almost always causes massive splenomegaly. Certain hematologic malignancies like Hairy Cell Leukemia (C) and some types of lymphoma (D) (especially splenic marginal zone lymphoma) are also well-known causes. In contrast, aplastic anemia (B) is a condition characterized by pancytopenia due to bone marrow failure. The bone marrow is hypo cellular, and there is no extramedullary hematopoiesis or infiltration of the spleen. Therefore, splenomegaly is characteristically absent in aplastic anemia, and its presence would cast doubt on the diagnosis.
40.	 Which statement accurately describes the effect 
of iron regulatory protein (IRP) binding to iron-
responsive elements (IRE) on the translation of 
ferritin and transferrin receptor 1 in a patient 
with iron deficiency anemia?
(A)	Ferritin translation is increased by binding 
IRP to IRE
(B)	 Ferritin translation is decreased by binding 
IRP to IRE
(C)	Transferrin 
receptor 
1 
translation 
is 
unaffected by binding IRP to IRE
(D)	Transferrin 
receptor 
1 
translation 
is 
decreased by binding IRP to IRE
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(B) Ferritin translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE
In a state of iron deficiency, intracellular iron levels are low. This causes the iron regulatory protein (IRP) to be active and bind to specific stem-loop structures on mRNAs called iron-responsive elements (IREs). The location of the IRE determines the effect of IRP binding.
The IRE for ferritin (the iron storage protein) is located in the 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) of its mRNA. When IRP binds here, it sterically hinders the assembly of the ribosomal complex, thereby blocking and decreasing the translation of ferritin. This makes physiological sense, as the cell does not want to store iron when it is deficient.
The IRE for the transferrin receptor 1 (which imports iron into the cell) is in the 3' UTR. IRP binding here stabilizes the mRNA and prevents its degradation, thus increasing its translation. This allows the cell to make more receptors to take up more iron.

respiratory

which

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) Increased HbF
A rightward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve signifies a decrease in hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, which facilitates oxygen unloading to the tissues. Factors that cause a right shift include increased 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (BPG) (B), acidosis (decreased pH, the Bohr effect) (C), and increased partial pressure of carbon dioxide ($CO_2$) (D), as well as increased temperature. 15.	 Which of the following does not have the 
presence of the sodium-iodide symporter?
(A)	Pituitary gland
(B)	 Thyroid gland
(C)	Placenta
(D)	Salivary gland
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) Pituitary gland
The sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) is a membrane protein responsible for the active transport of iodide ions into cells. Its most well-known and crucial function is in the follicular cells of the thyroid gland (B), where it mediates the first step of thyroid hormone synthesis, known as iodide trapping. However, the NIS protein is also expressed in several other extrathyroidal tissues. 16.	 What is the formula used to calculate Stroke 
Volume (SV) in the context of cardiac physiology?
(A)	SV = End-Diastolic Volume (EDV) - End-
Systolic Volume (ESV)
(B)	 SV = Heart Rate (HR) Ejection Fraction 
(EF)
(C)	 SV = Cardiac Output (CO) / Heart Rate 
(HR)
(D)	SV = Preload Afterload
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
Stroke Volume (SV) is defined as the volume of blood pumped from a ventricle of the heart during one contraction (systole). It is calculated as the difference between the volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of filling (diastole) and the volume of blood remaining in the ventricle at the end of contraction (systole). Therefore, the correct formula is SV = End-Diastolic Volume (EDV) - End-Systolic Volume (ESV). Option (C) also correctly defines stroke volume, as Cardiac Output (CO) is the product of Stroke Volume and Heart Rate (CO = SV × HR), so SV = CO / HR. However, option (A) represents the fundamental definition of stroke volume based on ventricular volumes. Option (B) and (D) are incorrect formulas.
BIOCHEMISTRY
17.	 Which of the following poisonous agents does 
not inhibit cytochrome oxidase?
(A)	Hydrogen sulfide
(B)	 Carbon monoxide
(C)	Methane
(D)	Cyanide
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(C) Methane
Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) is the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. Its inhibition blocks aerobic respiration, leading to cytotoxic hypoxia. Cyanide (D) is the classic inhibitor, binding to the ferric iron ($Fe^{3+}$) within the enzyme. Hydrogen sulfide (A) acts through a similar inhibitory mechanism. Carbon monoxide (B) can also inhibit cytochrome oxidase, although its primary toxic effect is its high-affinity binding to hemoglobin. In contrast, methane ($CH_4$) is a simple asphyxiant. It is a physiologically inert gas that is not directly toxic to cells. It causes hypoxia simply by displacing oxygen in the inhaled air, leading to a reduced fraction of inspired oxygen ($FiO_2$) and subsequent hypoxemia. It does not have any direct inhibitory effect on cellular enzymes like cytochrome oxidase.
18.	 Which of the following lipase enzymes is 
inhibited by insulin?
(A)	Lipoprotein lipase
(B)	 Pancreatic lipase
(C)	Gastric lipase
(D)	Hormone-sensitive lipase
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(D) Hormone-sensitive lipase
Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) is a key intracellular enzyme found in adipocytes (fat cells). Its function is to hydrolyze stored triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol, a process known as lipolysis, releasing these energy substrates into the bloodstream. The activity of HSL is tightly regulated by hormones. It is stimulated by counter-regulatory hormones like epinephrine and glucagon (via cAMP and PKA). Conversely, it is strongly inhibited by insulin. Insulin, which is released in the fed state, promotes energy storage. By inhibiting HSL, insulin suppresses the breakdown of stored fat. In contrast, insulin activates lipoprotein lipase (A), which is located on capillary walls and helps to clear triglycerides from the blood for storage in fat cells. Pancreatic (B) and gastric (C) lipases are digestive enzymes.
19.	 What is the main substrate and metabolic fuel 
used by red blood cells (RBCs) during the fasting 
period?
(A)	Ketone bodies
(B)	 Glucose
(C)	Free fatty acids
(D)	Amino acids
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(B) Glucose
Red blood cells (RBCs) have a unique metabolism because they lack mitochondria. The absence of mitochondria means they are incapable of aerobic respiration (i.e., they cannot use the Krebs cycle or oxidative phosphorylation). Therefore, they are entirely dependent on anaerobic glycolysis for all of their ATP production. The sole fuel source for glycolysis is glucose. This dependence is absolute and does not change with the body's metabolic state. Whether in the fed state or a prolonged fasting period, RBCs must continuously extract glucose from the bloodstream to meet their energy needs. They cannot utilize free fatty acids (C), ketone bodies (A), or amino acids (D) as fuel because the metabolic pathways for these substrates require functional mitochondria.
20.	 Which of the following macronutrients requires 
the most energy for assimilation?
(A)	Proteins
(B)	 Carbohydrates
(C)	Mono-unsaturated fatty acids
(D)	Polyunsaturated fatty acids
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) Proteins
The energy required to digest, absorb, and metabolize nutrients is known as the thermic effect of food (TEF) or specific dynamic action. This effect varies significantly among macronutrients. Proteins have the highest TEF, requiring the most energy for their assimilation. Approximately 20-30% of the energy content of the ingested protein is expended during its metabolism (e.g., deamination, urea synthesis). Carbohydrates (B) have a lower TEF, typically around 5-10%. Fats, including both mono-unsaturated (C) and polyunsaturated (D) fatty acids, have the lowest TEF, usually in the range of 0-3%. This means that the body is most efficient at storing energy from fat and least efficient at storing energy from protein. This high thermic effect of protein is one reason why high-protein diets are often recommended for weight management.
21.	 Which of the following is associated with a 
defect in collagen maturity?
(A)	Scurvy
(B)	 Rickets
(C)	Beriberi
(D)	Night blindness
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) Scurvy
Scurvy is the disease caused by a severe deficiency of Vitamin C (ascorbic acid). Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for two key enzymes, prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, which are involved in the post-translational modification of collagen. These enzymes are responsible for hydroxylating proline and lysine residues within the procollagen chains. This hydroxylation step is crucial for the formation of stable cross-links between collagen molecules, which gives the final collagen triple helix its strength and stability. In the absence of Vitamin C, this process is impaired, leading to the production of weak, unstable, and immature collagen. This results in the characteristic symptoms of scurvy, such as poor wound healing, bleeding gums, and perifollicular hemorrhages. Rickets (B) is a defect in bone mineralization due to Vitamin D deficiency.
22.	 Which enzyme is affected in a patient with 
thiamine 
deficiency 
who 
develops 
lactic 
acidosis?
(A)	Pyruvate carboxylase
(B)	 Pyruvate dehydrogenase
(C)	Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase
(D)	Transketolase
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(B) Pyruvate dehydrogenase
Thiamine (Vitamin B1), in its active form thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), is a critical cofactor for several key enzymes in carbohydrate metabolism. One of the most important of these is the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex. The PDH complex catalyzes the irreversible conversion of pyruvate (the end product of glycolysis) to acetyl-CoA, linking glycolysis to the Krebs cycle. In thiamine deficiency, the activity of the PDH complex is severely impaired. This creates a metabolic block, preventing pyruvate from entering the Krebs cycle for aerobic respiration. The accumulating pyruvate is then shunted to an alternative pathway, where it is converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase. This overproduction of lactate leads to lactic acidosis. Transketolase (D) is also a thiamine-dependent enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway, but its deficiency does not cause lactic acidosis.
23.	 Which of the following statements accurately 
describe the impact of Glucose-6-Phosphate 
Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency?
1.	 Decrease in reduced glutathione
2.	 Decrease NADPH
3.	 Decreased lipid peroxidation
4.	 Decreased RBC membrane damage

(B)	 1 & 2 are correct
(C)	2 & 3 are correct
(D)	1, 2 & 4 are correct
AAns

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). Reduced glutathione is a critical antioxidant that detoxifies reactive oxygen species. A decrease in NADPH leads to a decrease in reduced glutathione (1 is correct). In the absence of sufficient GSH, RBCs are highly susceptible to oxidative stress from certain drugs or infections. This oxidative stress leads to increased lipid peroxidation (3 is incorrect) and increased RBC membrane damage (4 is incorrect), ultimately causing hemolysis.

8.	
What is a characteristic feature observed in 
physiological jaundice?
(A)	Increased indirect bilirubin, increased 
urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
(B)	 Increased 
direct 
bilirubin, 
increased 
urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
(C)	Increased 
indirect 
bilirubin, 
absent 
urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
(D)	Increased 
direct 
bilirubin, 
absent 
urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) Increased indirect bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
Physiological jaundice in newborns is a common, transient condition caused by the immaturity of the liver's bilirubin-conjugating system (low UGT enzyme activity), coupled with an increased bilirubin load from the breakdown of fetal red blood cells. This leads to an increase in unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin in the bloodstream. Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and bound to albumin, so it cannot be filtered by the kidneys, resulting in absent bilirubin in the urine. The bilirubin that is successfully conjugated and excreted into the gut gets converted by bacteria to urobilinogen. A portion of this urobilinogen is reabsorbed and excreted in the urine, so urobilinogen is present (and may be increased due to the higher overall bilirubin turnover). This pattern contrasts with obstructive jaundice, which would feature increased direct bilirubin and bilirubin in the urine.
9.	
Which of the following is not associated with 
renal auto-regulation?
(A)	Tubuloglomerular feedback
(B)	 Myogenic reflex
(C)	Renin-angiotensin system
(D)	Renal sympathetic system fibers
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(D) Renal sympathetic system fibers
Renal autoregulation refers to the intrinsic mechanisms within the kidney that maintain a stable renal blood flow (RBF) and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) despite fluctuations in systemic blood pressure. The two primary intrinsic mechanisms are the myogenic reflex (B), where the afferent arteriole constricts in response to stretch, and tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) (A), mediated by the macula densa. While the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) (C) is often considered an extrinsic system, angiotensin II plays a role in autoregulation by constricting the efferent arteriole, helping to maintain GFR when renal perfusion pressure drops. In contrast, the renal sympathetic nervous system (D) is a purely extrinsic control mechanism. Strong sympathetic stimulation (e.g., during shock or intense exercise) causes profound vasoconstriction of the afferent arterioles, which can override the intrinsic autoregulatory mechanisms to reduce GFR and divert blood flow away from the kidneys.
10.	 The stroke volume depends on end-diastolic 
volume. This is best represented as?
(A)	Length-force relationship
(B)	 Length-velocity relationship
(C)	Length-tension relationship
(D)	Length-viscosity relationship
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(C) Length-tension relationship
The statement describes the Frank-Starling law of the heart. This fundamental principle states that the force of ventricular contraction (and thus stroke volume) is directly proportional to the initial length of the muscle fibers at the end of diastole. The end-diastolic volume (EDV), or preload, determines this initial fiber length. The underlying cellular mechanism is the length-tension relationship of the cardiac muscle (myocardium). As the myocytes are stretched by an increased EDV, the overlap between actin and myosin filaments becomes more optimal, and the sensitivity of the myofilaments to calcium increases. This results in a more forceful contraction (greater tension development), which ejects a larger stroke volume. While "length-force" (A) is functionally similar, "length-tension" is the more precise physiological term used to describe this property of muscle tissue.

12.	 Which sensory receptors are responsible for 
tactile discrimination?
(A)	Merkel disc
(B)	 Meissner's corpuscle
(C)	Pacinian corpuscle
(D)	Both A & B
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(D) Both A & B
Tactile discrimination, which includes the ability to perceive fine details like texture, shape, and two-point discrimination, relies on sensory receptors with small, well-defined receptive fields, located superficially in the skin. Both Merkel discs and Meissner's corpuscles fit this description. Merkel discs (A) are slow-adapting mechanoreceptors that are sensitive to sustained pressure and texture, making them crucial for reading Braille and sensing fine details. Meissner's corpuscles (B) are rapidly adapting receptors that are sensitive to light touch, flutter, and grip control. Both are highly concentrated in the fingertips and other sensitive areas. In contrast, Pacinian corpuscles (C) are located deeper in the dermis, have large receptive fields, and are rapidly adapting receptors that detect deep pressure and high-frequency vibration, contributing less to fine tactile discrimination. Therefore, both Merkel discs and Meissner's corpuscles are key players.

31.	 Which of the following is utilized for the 
treatment of sideroblastic anemia?
(A)	Vitamin B12
(B)	 Vitamin B6
(C)	Vitamin B1
(D)	Iron
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(B) Vitamin B6
Sideroblastic anemia is a group of blood disorders characterized by the presence of ring sideroblasts in the bone marrow. It results from a defect in the synthesis of heme. The first and rate-limiting step in heme synthesis is the condensation of succinyl-CoA and glycine to form delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme ALA synthase. This enzyme requires pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) as a cofactor. PLP is the active form of Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine). In some forms of sideroblastic anemia, particularly the hereditary X-linked type, there is a mutation in the ALA synthase enzyme that can be partially overcome by administering high doses of its cofactor, Vitamin B6. Therefore, a trial of pyridoxine is a cornerstone of therapy for certain types of sideroblastic anemia.

35.	 What

(A)	Michaelis Menten kinetics
(B)	 Allosteric activation
(C)	Sigmoid curve

AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) Michaelis Menten kinetics
The graph displays a hyperbolic curve, where the initial reaction rate is directly proportional to the substrate concentration, but as the substrate concentration increases, the rate slows and eventually approaches a maximum velocity (Vmax). This relationship is the classic representation of Michaelis-Menten kinetics. It describes the behavior of most non-allosteric enzymes. The hyperbolic shape is explained by the saturation of the enzyme's active sites with the substrate at high concentrations. Cooperative binding (D), which is a feature of allosteric enzymes, results in a sigmoidal (S-shaped) curve (C), not a hyperbolic one. 25.	 In a patient who has undergone prolonged 
starvation, which urine test would show a 
positive result?
(A)	Benedict's test
(B)	 Rothera's test
(C)	Biuret test
(D)	Emulsion test
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(B) Rothera's test
During prolonged starvation, after glycogen stores are depleted, the body switches to metabolizing fats for energy. The liver breaks down fatty acids into acetyl-CoA, which is then converted into ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone). These ketone bodies are released into the blood and used as fuel by tissues like the brain. When their production exceeds their utilization, they accumulate in the blood (ketosis) and are excreted in the urine (ketonuria). Rothera's test is a specific chemical test used to detect the presence of ketone bodies (specifically acetoacetate and acetone) in a urine sample. A positive result, indicated by the formation of a purple-colored ring, would therefore be expected in a starving individual. Benedict's test (A) is for reducing sugars. Biuret test (C) is for proteins. Emulsion test (D) is for lipids.

28.	 Which proteins of Human Papillomavirus 
(HPV) are responsible for inactivating the RB 
gene?
(A)	E6
(B)	 E7
(C)	L1
(D)	L2
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(B) E7
High-risk types of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) are the primary cause of cervical cancer and other anogenital cancers. Their carcinogenic potential is mediated by two early viral oncoproteins, E6 and E7. The E7 protein functions by binding to and promoting the degradation of the retinoblastoma (pRB) tumor suppressor protein. pRB normally acts as a brake on the cell cycle by binding to the E2F transcription factor. By inactivating pRB, the E7 protein releases E2F, allowing the cell to bypass the G1/S checkpoint and undergo uncontrolled proliferation. The E6 protein (A) has a different primary target; it binds to and promotes the degradation of the p53 tumor suppressor protein, thereby inhibiting apoptosis. The L1 and L2 proteins (C, D) are late proteins that form the viral capsid.
29.	 Which mediators are involved in the initial stage 
of type 1 hypersensitivity?
1.	 Mast cell
2.	 Histamine
3.	 Neutrophils
4.	 Prostaglandins
5.	 Leukotrienes
(A)	1,5
(B)	 1, 2, 3, 4
(C)	1,2,4,5
(D)	2, 3, 4
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(C) 1,2,4,5
Type I hypersensitivity is the immediate, IgE-mediated allergic reaction. The process is initiated when an allergen cross-links IgE antibodies bound to the surface of mast cells (1) (and basophils). This cross-linking triggers the degranulation of the mast cell, which releases a flood of pre-formed and newly synthesized mediators. The initial or immediate phase is dominated by the release of pre-formed mediators from granules, the most important of which is histamine (2). Almost immediately, the mast cell also begins to synthesize lipid-derived mediators from its membrane phospholipids via the arachidonic acid pathway. These include prostaglandins (4) (e.g., PGD2) and leukotrienes (5) (e.g., LTC4, LTD4, LTE4). These mediators are responsible for the classic allergic symptoms. Neutrophils (3) are recruited later in the late-phase reaction, not the initial stage.

43.	 Which of the following viruses is unable to 
integrate into the human genome to initiate 
carcinogenesis?
(A)	HPV
(B)	 HBV
(C)	HTLV
(D)	EBV
AAns

1.	
Human papillomavirus (HPV) integrates its DNA into the host genome in high-risk types (e.g., HPV 16, 18). Integration leads to overexpression of E6 and E7 oncogenes, promoting carcinogenesis.
2.	
Human T-lymphotropic virus 1 (HTLV-1) is a retrovirus and must integrate into the host genome as part of its replication cycle.

44.	 The cell shown in the slide has inhibitory 
functions. To which of the following structures 
does it send its projections?
(A)	Deep nuclei of the cerebellum
(B)	 Vestibular nuclei
(C)	Inferior olivary nucleus
(D)	Basal ganglia
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) Deep nuclei of the cerebellum
The image shows a Purkinje cell, which is recognizable by its massive, flask-shaped cell body and extensive, flat dendritic tree. Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex. They are GABAergic, meaning they exert a powerful inhibitory influence on their target cells. The primary targets of the vast majority of Purkinje cell axons are the neurons of the deep cerebellar nuclei (e.g., the dentate, emboliform, globose, and fastigial nuclei). These deep nuclei, in turn, provide the main excitatory output from the cerebellum to other parts of the motor system, such as the thalamus and brainstem. Therefore, the cerebellar cortex, via its Purkinje cells, modulates motor activity by regulating the firing of the deep cerebellar nuclei through this inhibitory projection.

47.	 In which of the following is the Oil Red O stain 
utilized?
(A)	Formalin fixation
(B)	 Frozen section
(C)	Alcohol fixation
(D)	Glutaraldehyde fixation
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(B) Frozen section
Oil Red O is a lysochrome (fat-soluble) diazo dye used in histology to stain neutral triglycerides and lipids. During routine tissue processing for paraffin embedding, tissues are dehydrated using alcohols and cleared with agents like xylene. These organic solvents dissolve and wash out lipids, so lipid staining is not possible on standard paraffin-embedded sections. To preserve the lipids within the tissue, the specimen must be processed as a frozen section. In this technique, the fresh tissue is rapidly frozen, cut on a cryostat, and then stained. This avoids the use of lipid-dissolving solvents. Therefore, Oil Red O staining is specifically utilized for demonstrating fat in frozen tissue sections.
