(C) Focal epilepsy
Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD) is an autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the central nervous system, primarily targeting astrocytes. The diagnosis is based on a set of core clinical characteristics. The cardinal features are attacks of optic neuritis (D) (inflammation of the optic nerve causing vision loss) and acute myelitis (B) (inflammation of the spinal cord, typically a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis affecting three or more vertebral segments). Another core characteristic is the area postrema syndrome (A), which presents with intractable nausea, vomiting, and hiccups due to lesions in the brainstem's area postrema. These three are key diagnostic criteria for NMOSD. Focal epilepsy (C), while a neurological symptom, is not a characteristic or core diagnostic feature of NMOSD. The pathology of NMOSD primarily affects the optic nerves, spinal cord, and brainstem, not typically the cerebral cortex in a way that would cause epilepsy.
124.	 Which of the following does not show 
hypokinesia movements?
(A)	Parkinson's disease
(B)	 Apraxia
(C)	Catatonia
(D)	Chorea
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(D) Chorea
Hypokinesia refers to a poverty of movement, characterized by slowness (bradykinesia) and reduced amplitude and frequency of voluntary movements. Parkinson's disease (A) is the archetypal hypokinetic movement disorder. Catatonia (C) can present with profound hypokinesia, immobility, and posturing. Apraxia (B) is a disorder of motor planning, not movement initiation itself, but can result in a significant lack of spontaneous movement, appearing as hypokinesia. In contrast, chorea is a hyperkinetic movement disorder. It is characterized by involuntary, continuous, irregular, and non-repetitive flowing or "dance-like" movements that flit from one body part to another. It represents an excess of movement, the opposite of hypokinesia. Huntington's disease is a classic cause of chorea.
125.	 Which of the following conditions are associated 
with hypertension and hypokalemic metabolic 
alkalosis?
(A)	Bartter syndrome
(B)	 Liddle syndrome
(C)	Gitelman syndrome
(D)	Gordon syndrome
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(B) Liddle syndrome
This clinical picture describes a state of apparent mineralocorticoid excess. Liddle syndrome is a rare, autosomal dominant genetic disorder that perfectly fits this description. It is caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the collecting ducts of the kidneys. This mutation leads to excessive and unregulated reabsorption of sodium and, consequently, water. This volume expansion causes severe hypertension. The increased sodium reabsorption also creates a negative electrical potential in the tubular lumen, which drives the excessive secretion of potassium and hydrogen ions, resulting in hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. A key feature is that aldosterone and renin levels are suppressed. Bartter (A) and Gitelman (C) syndromes are salt-wasting tubulopathies that cause hypokalemia but with normal or low blood pressure. Gordon syndrome (D) causes hypertension but with hyperkalemia.

181.	 In a 17-year-old patient, what is the most 
distinctive and characteristic feature of juvenile 
dermatomyositis?
(A)	Photosensitive skin rash
(B)	 Nail bed capillary changes
(C)	Gottron's papules
(D)	Malar rash
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(C) Gottron's papules
Juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM) is an autoimmune inflammatory disease affecting the skin and muscles. While it presents with a constellation of signs, certain skin findings are considered pathognomonic, meaning they are so characteristic that their presence is virtually diagnostic. The two pathognomonic signs of dermatomyositis are the heliotrope rash (a violaceous rash on the eyelids) and Gottron's papules. Gottron's papules are erythematous to violaceous, scaly papules and plaques located over the extensor surfaces of the joints, most classically the knuckles. While other rashes like a photosensitive rash (A) or a malar rash (D) can occur, they are less specific. Nail bed capillary changes (B), such as dilated and tortuous capillary loops seen on capillaroscopy, are highly characteristic and part of the diagnostic criteria, but Gottron's papules are considered the most distinctive cutaneous sign.
182.	 The 
lesions 
shown 
in 
the

are 
characteristically seen in which type of leprosy?

(B)	 Lepromatous leprosy

AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(C) Borderline leprosy
The image shows multiple well-defined, annular plaques with raised erythematous margins and central clearing. Such lesions are characteristic of borderline leprosy, which lies between the tuberculoid and lepromatous forms on the leprosy spectrum. Borderline leprosy demonstrates immunological instability and presents with numerous asymmetrical lesions that may vary in size and shape. The lesions are often infiltrated plaques with irregular borders and may show partial sensory loss.
In contrast, lepromatous leprosy typically presents with numerous symmetrical lesions such as nodules, papules, or diffuse infiltration without well-defined margins. Borderline lepromatous leprosy tends to show more numerous and less well-defined lesions compared to borderline tuberculoid forms. Histoid leprosy is characterized by shiny, dome-shaped nodules over apparently normal skin.
Thus, the annular, well-demarcated plaques seen in the image are most consistent with borderline leprosy.
183.	 What is the likely diagnosis for a 65-year-old 
man who presents with itchy, tense bullae on his 
limbs that collapse after a few days, as shown in 
the image?
(A)	Bullous pemphigoid
(B)	 Pemphigus vulgaris
(C)	Dermatitis herpetiformis
(D)	Linear IgA dermatosis
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) Bullous pemphigoid
The clinical presentation of an elderly patient with widespread, large, tense bullae (blisters) on an erythematous or urticarial base, accompanied by severe itching (pruritus), is the classic picture of bullous pemphigoid. This is an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease. Autoantibodies are directed against hemidesmosomal proteins (BP180 and BP230), causing the epidermis to separate from the dermis. This deep separation results in the formation of tense, durable bullae that do not rupture easily. This contrasts with pemphigus vulgaris (B), which is an intra epidermal blistering disease that produces fragile, flaccid bullae that rupture very easily, leaving erosions. Dermatitis herpetiformis (C) is characterized by intensely itchy small vesicles, typically grouped on extensor surfaces, and is associated with celiac disease. The large, tense bullae in an elderly patient are the key feature of bullous pemphigpoid.

Which of the following does not cause a rightward shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve?
(A)	
Increased HbF
(B)	
Raised 2,3 BPG
(C)	
Acidosis
(D)	
Increased 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
14.	 (A) Increased HbF
A rightward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin 
dissociation curve signifies a decrease in 
hemoglobin's 
affinity 
for 
oxygen, 
which 
facilitates oxygen unloading to the tissues. 
Factors that cause a right shift include increased 
2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (BPG) (B), acidosis 
(decreased pH, the Bohr effect) (C), and increased 
partial pressure of carbon dioxide (CO2) (D), as 
well as increased temperature. These conditions 
are typically found in metabolically active 
tissues. In contrast, fetal hemoglobin (HbF) 
(A) has a higher intrinsic affinity for oxygen 
than adult hemoglobin (HbA). This is because 
HbF binds 2,3-BPG less avidly. The higher 
oxygen affinity of HbF facilitates the transfer of 
oxygen from the maternal circulation across the 
placenta to the fetus. Therefore, an increased 
proportion of HbF causes a leftward shift of the 
dissociation curve, not a rightward shift.
Which of the following does not have the presence of the sodium-iodide symporter?
(A)	
Pituitary gland
(B)	
Thyroid gland
(C)	
Placenta
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
15.	 (A) Pituitary gland
The sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) is a 
membrane protein responsible for the active 
transport of iodide ions into cells. Its most 
well-known and crucial function is in the 
follicular cells of the thyroid gland (B), where 
it mediates the first step of thyroid hormone 
synthesis, known as iodide trapping. However, 
the NIS protein is also expressed in several 
other extrathyroidal tissues. These include the

mammary glands, and the placenta (C), where 
it plays a role in transporting iodide into saliva, 
milk, and to the fetus, respectively. The pituitary 
gland (A), however, is not known to express 
the sodium-iodide symporter. Its function is to 
regulate the thyroid gland via TSH, but it is not 
directly involved in iodide transport.
What is the formula used to calculate Stroke Volume (SV) in the context of cardiac physiology?
(A)	
 End-Diastolic Volume (EDV) - End-Systolic Volume (ESV)
(B)	
 Heart Rate (HR) Ejection Fraction (EF)
(C)	
 Cardiac Output (CO) / Heart Rate (HR)
(D)	
 Preload Afterload
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
16.	 (A) SV = End-Diastolic Volume (EDV) - End-
Systolic Volume (ESV)
Stroke Volume (SV) is defined as the volume 
of blood pumped from a ventricle of the heart 
during one contraction (systole). It is calculated 
as the difference between the volume of blood in 
the ventricle at the end of filling (diastole) and 
the volume of blood remaining in the ventricle 
at the end of contraction (systole). Therefore, 
the correct formula is SV = End-Diastolic 
Volume (EDV) - End-Systolic Volume (ESV). 
Option (C) also correctly defines stroke volume, 
as Cardiac Output (CO) is the product of Stroke 
Volume and Heart Rate (CO = SV × HR), so SV 
= CO / HR. However, option (A) represents the 
fundamental definition of stroke volume based 
on ventricular volumes. Option (B) and (D) are 
incorrect formulas.
Which of the following poisonous agents does not inhibit cytochrome oxidase?
(A)	
Hydrogen sulfide
(B)	
Carbon monoxide
(C)	
Methane
(D)	
Cyanide
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
17.	 (C) Methane
Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) is the 
terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial electron 
transport chain. Its inhibition blocks aerobic 
respiration, leading to cytotoxic hypoxia. 
Cyanide (D) is the classic inhibitor, binding 
to the ferric iron (Fe3+) within the enzyme. 
Hydrogen sulfide (A) acts through a similar 
inhibitory mechanism. Carbon monoxide (B) 
can also inhibit cytochrome oxidase, although 
its primary toxic effect is its high-affinity binding 
to hemoglobin. In contrast, methane (CH4) is a 
simple asphyxiant. It is a physiologically inert gas 
that is not directly toxic to cells. It causes hypoxia 
simply by displacing oxygen in the inhaled air, 
leading to a reduced fraction of inspired oxygen 
(FiO2) and subsequent hypoxemia. It does not 
have any direct inhibitory effect on cellular 
enzymes like cytochrome oxidase.

194.	 What type of MRI image is shown in the 
provided image?
(A)	Proton density image
(B)	 Susceptibility weighted image
(C)	Gradient echo image
(D)	Inversion recovery image
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(B) Susceptibility weighted image
The provided axial MRI of the brain shows multiple small, punctate, dark (hypointense) foci scattered throughout the white matter. These represent chronic micro hemorrhages. The MRI sequence that is most sensitive for detecting blood products (hemosiderin), calcification, and iron deposition is the Susceptibility Weighted Image (SWI). SWI is a type of high-resolution 3D gradient-echo sequence that is specifically designed to be exquisitely sensitive to substances that distort the local magnetic field, a property known as magnetic susceptibility. Blood breakdown products like hemosiderin are paramagnetic and create significant signal loss on SWI, making them appear as prominent black dots. While a standard gradient echo (GRE) image (C) is also sensitive to blood, SWI incorporates both magnitude and phase information, making it even more sensitive for detecting these microbleeds.

196.	 Which imaging technique is most suitable for 
diagnosing primary hyperparathyroidism in a 
woman presenting with confusion, constipation, 
headache, and elevated serum calcium (13.1 mg/
dL) along with elevated alkaline phosphatase 
(ALP) levels?
(A)	MRI
(B)	 FDG PET
(C)	CT
(D)	Sestamibi Scan
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(D) Sestamibi Scan
The patient's symptoms and laboratory findings (hypercalcemia with elevated ALP) are highly suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism, which is most commonly caused by a single, benign parathyroid adenoma. The goal of preoperative imaging is to localize this adenoma. The most common and effective functional imaging technique for this purpose is a Technetium-99m Sestamibi Parathyroid Scan. Sestamibi is a radiotracer that is taken up by both the thyroid gland and any hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue (like an adenoma). In a dual-phase scan, an early image shows uptake in both tissues. A delayed image (at 2-4 hours) is then taken. The tracer washes out of the normal thyroid tissue much faster than it does from the hyperactive parathyroid adenoma, which retains the tracer and appears as a persistent "hot spot." This allows for the precise localization of the adenoma before surgery.

198.	 Which phase of the cell cycle displays the 
highest resistance to radiation?
(A)	M phase	
(B)	 G1 phase
(C)	S phase	
(D)	G2 phase
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(C) S phase
The sensitivity of a cell to the damaging effects of ionizing radiation varies significantly throughout the cell cycle. Cells are most sensitive to radiation during the M (mitosis) phase and the G2 phase. They are less sensitive during the G1 phase. The phase of the cell cycle where cells are the most resistant to radiation is the late S (synthesis) phase. During the S phase, the cell is actively replicating its DNA. The presence of homologous DNA sister chromatids and the upregulation of DNA repair enzymes (like those involved in homologous recombination) during this phase are thought to confer a higher capacity to repair radiation-induced DNA double-strand breaks, thus making the cell more radioresistant. This principle is important in radiation oncology, as it influences the effectiveness of fractionated radiotherapy schedules.

If a patient has low blood oxygen (hypoxemia) but a normal alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient, what medical condition does this typically point to?
(A)	
Right to left shunt
(B)	
Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch
(C)	
Hypoventilation
(D)	
Alveolar membrane damage
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
7.	
(C) Hypoventilation
The Alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient is 
the difference between the partial pressure of 
oxygen in the alveoli (P O
A
2) and in the arterial 
blood (P O
a
2). It reflects the efficiency of oxygen 
transfer across the lungs. An elevated A-a 
gradient signifies a problem with gas exchange, 
such as a shunt (A), V/Q mismatch (B), or 
diffusion impairment (alveolar membrane 
damage, D). However, if a patient is hypoxemic 
(low P O
a
2) but the A-a gradient is normal, it 
implies that the lungs are transferring oxygen 
efficiently. This situation arises when the 
hypoxemia is caused by a low partial pressure 
of oxygen in the alveoli (P O
A
2) to begin with. 
The two main causes for a low P O
A
2with a 
normal A-a gradient are breathing air with a 
low oxygen concentration (e.g., high altitude) 
or hypoventilation. Hypoventilation (reduced 
breathing) causes an increase in arterial CO2, 
which displaces oxygen in the alveoli, lowering 
P O
A
2 and consequently P O
a
2.
What is a characteristic feature observed in physiological jaundice?
(A)	
Increased indirect bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
(B)	
Increased direct bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
(C)	
Increased indirect bilirubin, absent urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
(D)	
Increased direct bilirubin, absent urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
8.	
(A) Increased indirect bilirubin, increased 
urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
Physiological jaundice in newborns is a 
common, transient condition caused by the 
immaturity of the liver's bilirubin-conjugating 
system (low UGT enzyme activity), coupled 
with an increased bilirubin load from the 
breakdown of fetal red blood cells. This leads to 
an increase in unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin 
in the bloodstream. Unconjugated bilirubin 
is lipid-soluble and bound to albumin, so it 
cannot be filtered by the kidneys, resulting in 
absent bilirubin in the urine. The bilirubin that 
is successfully conjugated and excreted into the 
gut gets converted by bacteria to urobilinogen. 
A portion of this urobilinogen is reabsorbed and 
excreted in the urine, so urobilinogen is present 
(and may be increased due to the higher overall 
bilirubin turnover). This pattern contrasts with 
obstructive jaundice, which would feature 
increased direct bilirubin and bilirubin in the 
urine.

Which of the following branches originate from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery?
1.	
Superior gluteal artery
2.	
Inferior gluteal artery

2,3,4,6

2,3,4,5,6
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
1.	
(C) 2,3,4,5,6
The internal iliac artery bifurcates into an 
anterior and a posterior division. The posterior 
division supplies the pelvic wall and gluteal 
region, giving off the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, 
and superior gluteal arteries (1). All the other 
arteries listed are branches of the anterior 
division, which primarily supplies the pelvic 
viscera, perineum, and medial thigh. These 
visceral and parietal branches include the 
umbilical artery (from which the superior 
vesical artery (3) arises), obturator artery, 
inferior vesical artery (5) (in males), uterine 
artery (from which the vaginal artery (6) arises 
in females), middle rectal artery (4), internal 
pudendal artery, and the inferior gluteal artery 
(2). Therefore, all the arteries listed, with the 
exception of the superior gluteal artery, originate 
from the anterior division of the internal iliac 
artery.

A loss of hand-eye coordination suggests a lesion in which brain lobe?
(A)	
Parietal lobe
(B)	
Frontal lobe
(C)	
Temporal lobe
(D)	
Occipital lobe
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
3.	
(A) Parietal lobe
The parietal lobe, particularly the posterior 
parietal cortex, functions as a critical association 
area that integrates visual and somatosensory 
information. It constructs a spatial map of the 
body in relation to its environment, which is 
essential for guiding movements. This region 
is part of the dorsal ("where") visual stream. A 
lesion in the parietal lobe can lead to optic ataxia, 
a specific deficit in visually guided reaching 
and grasping. This condition impairs the ability 
to accurately use visual information to direct 
hand movements, representing a classic deficit 
in hand-eye coordination. The frontal lobe (B) 
is involved in planning and executing motor 
commands. The occipital lobe (D) is responsible 
for primary visual processing. The temporal lobe 
(C) is involved in object recognition (the "what" 
pathway).

(D) Post kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis
This is a classic case presentation for Post-Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL). The key clues are the geographical location (Bihar, a highly endemic area for kala-azar), a past history of prolonged fever suggestive of treated visceral leishmaniasis, and the current presentation of hypopigmented macules. PKDL is a dermatological sequel that can develop months to years after successful treatment for visceral leishmaniasis. The lesions are typically non-ulcerative, non-anesthetic macules, papules, or nodules. The fact that the lesion is described as anesthetic is a distractor and more typical for leprosy. However, the combination of the endemic location and the specific history of treated kala-azar makes PKDL the most likely diagnosis. Tuberculoid leprosy (A) would present with an anesthetic patch but is not linked to a prior history of kala-azar.
185.	 Identify the given condition based on the 
histopathological image.
(A)	Pemphigus vulgaris
(B)	 Leprosy
(C)	Mycosis fungoides
(D)	Visceral leishmaniasis
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) Pemphigus vulgaris
Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune blistering disorder caused by IgG antibodies directed against desmoglein-3 (and sometimes desmoglein-1), which are components of desmosomes responsible for keratinocyte adhesion. Histopathologically, the hallmark feature is suprabasal acantholysis, resulting in an intraepidermal blister. The basal cells remain attached to the basement membrane, creating the characteristic “row of tombstones” appearance. Within the blister cavity, rounded, detached keratinocytes known as acantholytic (Tzanck) cells are seen.
In contrast, leprosy shows granulomatous inflammation with acid-fast bacilli in macrophages. Mycosis fungoides demonstrates atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei infiltrating the epidermis (Pautrier microabscesses). Visceral leishmaniasis shows Leishman-Donovan bodies within macrophages in tissue samples.
Thus, the presence of suprabasal clefting with acantholytic cells confirms the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris.
ANAESTHESIA
186.	 Which anesthetic agent can be used for 
induction, maintenance of anesthesia, and to 
allow safe endotracheal intubation?
(A)	Sevoflurane	
(B)	 Halothane
(C)	Desflurane	
(D)	Isoflurane
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) Sevoflurane
The agent described needs to be suitable for inhalational induction, a technique where anesthesia is induced by breathing the agent rather than by IV injection. This requires an agent that is non-pungent, non-irritating to the airway, and has a low blood :gas partition coefficient for rapid onset. Sevoflurane is the ideal agent that fits all these criteria. It has a pleasant, non-irritating odor, allowing for a smooth inhalational induction, especially in children. Its low solubility allows for rapid induction and emergence. It is also a potent bronchodilator, which can facilitate intubation. In contrast, desflurane (C) is extremely pungent and causes airway irritation, coughing, and laryngospasm, making it unsuitable for inhalational induction. Isoflurane (D) is also pungent and not typically used for induction. Halothane (B) allows for smooth induction but has been largely replaced due to its association with hepatotoxicity and arrhythmias.
187.	 Which anesthetic agent was most likely given to 
a patient who developed rigidity, tremors, and 
trismus after administration?
(A)	Halothane
(B)	 Nitrous Oxide (NO2)
(C)	Thiopentone sodium
(D)	Etomidate
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(D) Etomidate
Etomidate is an intravenous anesthetic induction agent known for its cardiovascular stability. However, one of its most prominent and characteristic side effects is myoclonus, which can manifest as involuntary muscle movements, tremors, rigidity, and sometimes trismus (lockjaw). This is thought to be caused by disinhibition of subcortical neuronal activity. The incidence of myoclonus with etomidate is quite high, occurring in 30-80% of patients if not premedicated. While other agents can occasionally cause movement, it is a hallmark side effect of etomidate. Thiopentone (C) can cause a "hiccup" or tremor but not typically rigidity. Halothane (A) is an inhalational agent. Nitrous oxide (B) does not typically cause these effects when used as an adjunct.
188.	 What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient 
who received a 20% intralipid injection during 
resuscitation?
(A)	Local anesthesia toxicity
(B)	 Asphyxia due to drowning
(C)	Electrocution
(D)	Pulseless electrical activity
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) Local anesthesia toxicity
The administration of a 20% intravenous lipid emulsion (Intralipid) is the specific and standard antidote for managing Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST). LAST is a rare but life-threatening complication that can occur after the administration of a large dose of a local anesthetic, especially if accidentally injected intravenously. It presents with CNS symptoms (seizures, coma) and severe cardiovascular collapse (arrhythmias, asystole). The lipid emulsion is thought to work as a "lipid sink," effectively sequestering the lipophilic local anesthetic molecules from their sites of action in the heart and brain, thereby reversing the toxicity. Seeing this specific treatment being used during a resuscitation strongly implies that the underlying cause of the cardiac arrest was local anesthetic toxicity.
189.	 Which post-bronchodilator pulmonary function 
test (PFT) finding would indicate that a 50-year-
old male with ASA grade 3 requires further 
evaluation of lung function?
(A)	FEV1 0.85 and FEV1/FVC < 0.8
(B)	 FEV1 0.85 and FEV1/FVC < 0.75
(C)	FEV1 0.85 and FEV1/FVC < 0.7
(D)	FEV1 < 0.8 and FEV1/FVC < 0.75
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(C) FEV1 0.85 and FEV1/FVC < 0.7
The diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and other obstructive lung diseases is based on spirometry. The key diagnostic criterion is the presence of airflow limitation that is not fully reversible. This is defined by the ratio of the forced expiratory volume in the first second (FEV1) to the forced vital capacity (FVC). According to the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) criteria, a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of less than 0.70 confirms the presence of persistent airflow limitation. The severity of the obstruction is then graded based on the post-bronchodilator FEV1 percent predicted. An FEV1 of 0.85 (85% of predicted) would indicate mild obstruction (GOLD stage 1), but the diagnostic ratio is the FEV1/FVC < 0.7. An ASA grade 3 status indicates a patient with severe systemic disease, making pre-operative lung function assessment critical.
190.	 Which agent is most likely responsible when a 
patient under halothane anesthesia develops 
hyperthermia and muscle rigidity during 
surgery?
(A)	D-tubocurarine
(B)	 Suxamethonium
(C)	Cisatracurium
(D)	Rocuronium
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(B) Suxamethonium
The patient's presentation of sudden hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, tachycardia, and hypercapnia during general anesthesia is the classic picture of malignant hyperthermia (MH). MH is a rare, life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle. It is triggered in susceptible individuals by exposure to specific anesthetic agents. The two main classes of triggering agents are all volatile halogenated anesthetics (like halothane) and the depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent suxamethonium (succinylcholine). The combination of a volatile agent and suxamethonium is particularly potent in triggering an MH crisis. The other neuromuscular blockers listed—d-tubocurarine (A), cisatracurium (C), and rocuronium (D)—are non-depolarizing agents and are considered safe to use in MH-susceptible patients as they do not trigger the condition.
191.	 A young male receiving regional anesthesia 
with 0.25% bupivacaine becomes unresponsive, 
and his pulse is no longer detectable. What is the 
best management approach?
(A)	CPCR with 20% Intralipid
(B)	 CPCR with sodium bicarbonate
(C)	CPCR with dobutamine
(D)	CPCR with calcium
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) CPCR with 20% Intralipid
The patient has suffered a cardiac arrest immediately following the administration of bupivacaine, a potent local anesthetic. This is highly suggestive of Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST), specifically cardiotoxicity. Bupivacaine is particularly cardiotoxic and can cause refractory arrhythmias and asystole. The management of cardiac arrest due to LAST requires adherence to standard advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) protocols, including high-quality cardiopulmonary cerebral resuscitation (CPCR). However, a specific and crucial addition to the standard protocol is the immediate administration of a 20% intravenous lipid emulsion (Intralipid). This lipid emulsion therapy acts as a "lipid sink," sequestering the lipophilic bupivacaine molecules from cardiac tissue and helping to reverse the toxicity. It is the cornerstone of treatment for severe LAST and should be initiated as soon as the diagnosis is suspected.

192.	 A female patient presents with abdominal pain 
and is found on ultrasound to have multiple 
gallstones without gallbladder wall thickening, 
and a common bile duct diameter of 12 mm. 
Her labs show serum bilirubin 0.8, alkaline 
phosphatase 380, and a five-fold increase in 
GGT. What is the most appropriate next step in 
management?
(A)	MRCP
(B)	 ERCP
(C)	Endoscopic ultrasound
(D)	Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(A) MRCP
This patient has gallstones (cholelithiasis) and evidence strongly suggestive of a stone that has migrated into the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis). The key findings are a dilated common bile duct (12 mm; normal is <6-8 mm) and a cholestatic pattern of liver enzyme elevation (markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT with normal bilirubin). The absence of gallbladder wall thickening makes acute cholecystitis less likely. The next step is to confirm the presence and location of the suspected CBD stone. Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) is the best non-invasive imaging modality for this purpose. It provides detailed images of the entire biliary tree without the risks associated with an invasive procedure. ERCP (B) is an invasive therapeutic procedure used to remove stones but carries a risk of pancreatitis and should be preceded by a non-invasive confirmation with MRCP.

The stroke volume depends on end-diastolic volume. This is best represented as?
(A)	
Length-force relationship
(B)	
Length-velocity relationship
(C)	
Length-tension relationship
(D)	
Length-viscosity relationship
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
10.	 (C) Length-tension relationship
The statement describes the Frank-Starling law 
of the heart. This fundamental principle states 
that the force of ventricular contraction (and 
thus stroke volume) is directly proportional 
to the initial length of the muscle fibers at 
the end of diastole. The end-diastolic volume 
(EDV), or preload, determines this initial fiber 
length. The underlying cellular mechanism is 
the length-tension relationship of the cardiac 
muscle (myocardium). As the myocytes are 
stretched by an increased EDV, the overlap 
between actin and myosin filaments becomes 
more optimal, and the sensitivity of the 
myofilaments to calcium increases. This results 
in a more forceful contraction (greater tension 
development), which ejects a larger stroke 
volume. While "length-force" (A) is functionally 
similar, "length-tension" is the more precise 
physiological term used to describe this property 
of muscle tissue.
Which ion in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle enables the reabsorption of divalent ions?
(A)	
(B)	
(C)	
(D)	
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
11.	 (C) K+
The thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of 
Henle is a major site for reabsorption of ions, 
including divalent cations like calcium (Ca2+
) and magnesium (Mg2+). This reabsorption 
occurs via the paracellular pathway (between the 
cells). The driving force for this movement is a 
unique lumen-positive transepithelial potential. 
This potential is generated by the apical Na-K-
2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2), which brings these 
ions into the cell, and the subsequent recycling 
of potassium (K+) back into the tubular lumen 
through apical ROMK channels. This back-leak 
of positive potassium ions makes the tubular 
lumen electrically positive relative to the 
interstitium. This lumen-positive potential then 
acts as an electrical force that drives the passive 
paracellular reabsorption of other positive ions, 
including Na+, Ca2+, and Mg2+.
Which sensory receptors are responsible for tactile discrimination?
(A)	
Merkel disc
(B)	
Meissner's corpuscle
(C)	
Pacinian corpuscle
(D)	
Both A & B
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
12.	 (D) Both A & B
Tactile discrimination, which includes the 
ability to perceive fine details like texture, shape, 
and two-point discrimination, relies on sensory 
receptors with small, well-defined receptive 
fields, located superficially in the skin. Both 
Merkel discs and Meissner's corpuscles fit this 
description. Merkel discs (A) are slow-adapting 
mechanoreceptors that are sensitive to sustained 
pressure and texture, making them crucial 
for reading Braille and sensing fine details. 
Meissner's corpuscles (B) are rapidly adapting 
receptors that are sensitive to light touch, flutter, 
and grip control. Both are highly concentrated 
in the fingertips and other sensitive areas. In 
contrast, Pacinian corpuscles (C) are located 
deeper in the dermis, have large receptive fields, 
and are rapidly adapting receptors that detect 
deep pressure and high-frequency vibration, 
contributing less to fine tactile discrimination. 
Therefore, both Merkel discs and Meissner's 
corpuscles are key players.

(A) Arterial puncture
The image points to the clavicle. The placement of a central venous catheter via the subclavian approach involves inserting a needle just inferior to the clavicle to access the subclavian vein. The subclavian artery lies immediately posterior and superior to the subclavian vein. Due to this close proximity, the most common immediate mechanical complication during a subclavian line insertion is the inadvertent puncture of the subclavian artery. This can be recognized by the pulsatile backflow of bright red blood and can lead to significant complications like hematoma, hemothorax, or pseudoaneurysm. While other complications like pneumothorax are also common, arterial puncture is generally cited as the most frequent. Thrombophlebitis (B) is a later complication. Empyema (C) is an infectious complication. Chylothorax (D) is a rare complication caused by injury to the thoracic duct, more common on the left side.
200.	 Which of the following are the primary 
diagnostic modalities for identifying placenta 
accreta?
1.	 Ultrasonography
2.	 MRI
3.	 Angiography
4.	 X-ray
(A)	1 and 3 only
(B)	 1 and 2 only
(C)	2 and 3 only
(D)	1 and 4 only
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(B) 1 and 2 only
Placenta Accreta Spectrum (PAS) disorders are life-threatening conditions where the placenta attaches abnormally deeply into the uterine wall. Antenatal diagnosis is crucial for planning a safe delivery. The primary and most important screening and diagnostic modality is ultrasonography (1), particularly a detailed transvaginal ultrasound performed by an experienced operator. Specific sonographic signs include loss of the normal clear space behind the placenta, placental lacunae, and abnormalities of the uterine-bladder interface. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) (2) is used as an adjunctive imaging modality, especially in cases where the ultrasound is inconclusive, for posterior placentas, or to assess the depth of myometrial invasion and potential involvement of adjacent organs like the bladder. Angiography (3) is an interventional radiology technique that may be used therapeutically at the time of delivery to control bleeding but is not a diagnostic tool. A plain X-ray (4) cannot visualize the placenta.

This question correctly matches mental health conditions and work-related stressors, particularly relevant in high-stress professions like medicine, with their appropriate descriptions.
1.	
Depression (a-3) : This matches with "Difficult to diagnose due to the shell of physician's pride." Physicians often face immense pressure to appear competent and resilient. This culture can create a "shell of pride," making it difficult for them to acknowledge vulnerability or seek help for mental health issues like depression. Fear of stigma, professional repercussions, and a belief that they should be able to "handle it" themselves often lead to delayed diagnosis and treatment.
2.	
Suicide (b-4) : This is linked to "Women physicians, substance abuse, relationship troubles." These are all well-documented risk factors for suicide, especially within the medical community. Female physicians, in particular, have a significantly higher suicide rate than the general female population. The high-stress environment can also contribute to substance abuse as a coping mechanism and strain personal relationships, further elevating suicide risk.
3.	
Burnout (c-2) : This is accurately described as a "State of emotional and physical exhaustion caused by prolonged stress, relieved after relaxation." Burnout is a specific work-related syndrome characterized by emotional exhaustion, depersonalization (cynicism), and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment. While relaxation and time off can provide temporary relief, burnout is a deeper state of exhaustion that often requires significant changes in the work environment or coping strategies to fully resolve.
4.	
Overworking (d-1) : This is matched with "The feeling goes away as soon as you leave the hospital." This describes the direct, situational stress of working excessive hours. Unlike the pervasive nature of burnout or depression, the negative feelings associated with simply overworking are often tied directly to the workplace and tend to dissipate once the individual is away from that environment.

This question matches various psychiatric states and conditions with their correct definitions.
1.	
Twilight state (a-2) : This correctly matches with "Impaired level of consciousness." A twilight state is a transient condition where consciousness is clouded. An individual in this state may appear to be awake but has reduced awareness of their surroundings and may perform complex actions (automatisms) for which they later have no memory (amnesia). It can be associated with conditions like epilepsy, head injury, or dissociative disorders.
2.	
Oneiroid state (b-4) : This is linked to "Oneirophrenia." The term 'oneiroid' is derived from the Greek word for dream (oneiros) and describes a dream-like state of consciousness. It is characterized by a blurring of reality and fantasy, often with vivid hallucinations. Oneirophrenia is a psychiatric syndrome, sometimes considered a form of schizophrenia, where this dream-like state is the primary feature.
3.	
Oligophrenia (c-1) : This matches "Subnormal intelligence." Oligophrenia is an outdated term for what is now referred to as intellectual disability. It describes a condition characterized by significantly below-average intellectual functioning and limitations in adaptive behaviors (e.g., communication, self-care) that originates during the developmental period.
4.	
Paranoid ideation (d-3) : This is accurately matched with "Persecution." Paranoid ideation involves thoughts and beliefs centered on being persecuted, harmed, or conspired against by others. These thoughts range from mild, non-delusional suspiciousness to fixed, irrational paranoid delusions. It is a key symptom of paranoid schizophrenia and delusional disorder.
203.	 Which of the following statements accurately 
describes obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)?

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
(C) Depression is a common comorbidity
This statement is the most accurate description of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) among the choices provided.
OCD is an anxiety disorder characterized by obsessions (intrusive, unwanted thoughts) and compulsions (repetitive behaviors performed to relieve anxiety). Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is the most common co-occurring (comorbid) condition with OCD. Studies indicate that over 50% of individuals with OCD will experience a major depressive episode in their lifetime. The constant distress, anxiety, and functional impairment caused by OCD symptoms can contribute to feelings of hopelessness and sadness, leading to depression. Conversely, the presence of depression can worsen OCD symptoms and make treatment more challenging.
The other options are incorrect for the following reasons :
1.	
(A) The first-line treatments for OCD are Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) and a type of cognitive-behavioral therapy called Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP). Atypical antipsychotics are only considered as an add-on treatment in severe, treatment-resistant cases.
2.	
(B) The lifetime prevalence of OCD in the general population is estimated to be around 2-3%, not 7-10%.
3.	
(D) Fear of contamination is one of the most common obsessions in OCD, often leading to compulsions like excessive hand washing, cleaning, or avoidance of "contaminated" objects.

What is the main substrate and metabolic fuel used by red blood cells (RBCs) during the fasting period?
(A)	
Ketone bodies
(B)	
Glucose
(C)	
Free fatty acids
(D)	
Amino acids
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
19.	 (B) Glucose
Red blood cells (RBCs) have a unique 
metabolism because they lack mitochondria. 
The absence of mitochondria means they 
are incapable of aerobic respiration (i.e., 
they cannot use the Krebs cycle or oxidative 
phosphorylation). Therefore, they are entirely 
dependent on anaerobic glycolysis for all of 
their ATP production. The sole fuel source for 
glycolysis is glucose. This dependence is absolute 
and does not change with the body's metabolic 
state. Whether in the fed state or a prolonged 
fasting period, RBCs must continuously extract 
glucose from the bloodstream to meet their 
energy needs. They cannot utilize free fatty 
acids (C), ketone bodies (A), or amino acids (D) 
as fuel because the metabolic pathways for these 
substrates require functional mitochondria.
Which of the following macronutrients requires the most energy for assimilation?
(A)	
Proteins
(B)	
Carbohydrates
(C)	
Mono-unsaturated fatty acids
(D)	
Polyunsaturated fatty acids
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
20.	 (A) Proteins
The energy required to digest, absorb, and 
metabolize nutrients is known as the thermic 
effect of food (TEF) or specific dynamic 
action. This effect varies significantly among 
macronutrients. Proteins have the highest TEF, 
requiring the most energy for their assimilation. 
Approximately 20-30% of the energy content 
of the ingested protein is expended during its 
metabolism (e.g., deamination, urea synthesis). 
Carbohydrates (B) have a lower TEF, typically 
around 5-10%. Fats, including both mono-
unsaturated (C) and polyunsaturated (D) fatty 
acids, have the lowest TEF, usually in the range 
of 0-3%. This means that the body is most 
efficient at storing energy from fat and least 
efficient at storing energy from protein. This 
high thermic effect of protein is one reason why 
high-protein diets are often recommended for 
weight management.
Which of the following is associated with a defect in collagen maturity?
(A)	
Scurvy
(B)	
Rickets
(C)	
Beriberi
(D)	
Night blindness
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
21.	 (A) Scurvy
Scurvy is the disease caused by a severe deficiency 
of Vitamin C (ascorbic acid). Vitamin C is an 
essential cofactor for two key enzymes, prolyl 
hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, which are 
involved in the post-translational modification 
of collagen. These enzymes are responsible for 
hydroxylating proline and lysine residues within 
the procollagen chains. This hydroxylation step 
is crucial for the formation of stable cross-
links between collagen molecules, which gives 
the final collagen triple helix its strength and 
stability. In the absence of Vitamin C, this 
process is impaired, leading to the production 
of weak, unstable, and immature collagen. This 
results in the characteristic symptoms of scurvy, 
such as poor wound healing, bleeding gums, 
and perifollicular hemorrhages. Rickets (B) is a 
defect in bone mineralization due to Vitamin D 
deficiency.
Which enzyme is affected in a patient with thiamine deficiency who develops lactic acidosis?
(A)	
Pyruvate carboxylase
(B)	
Pyruvate dehydrogenase
(C)	
Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase
(D)	
Transketolase
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
22.	 (B) Pyruvate dehydrogenase
Thiamine (Vitamin B1), in its active form 
thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), is a critical 
cofactor for several key enzymes in carbohydrate 
metabolism. One of the most important of these 
is the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex. 
The PDH complex catalyzes the irreversible 
conversion of pyruvate (the end product of 
glycolysis) to acetyl-CoA, linking glycolysis to the 
Krebs cycle. In thiamine deficiency, the activity 
of the PDH complex is severely impaired. This 
creates a metabolic block, preventing pyruvate 
from entering the Krebs cycle for aerobic 
respiration. The accumulating pyruvate is then 
shunted to an alternative pathway, where it is 
converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase. 
This overproduction of lactate leads to lactic 
acidosis. Transketolase (D) is also a thiamine-
dependent enzyme in the pentose phosphate 
pathway, but its deficiency does not cause lactic 
acidosis.

The graph indicates the enzyme kinetics in a manner that suggests
(A)	
Michaelis Menten kinetics
(B)	
Allosteric activation
(C)	
Sigmoid curve
(D)	
Cooperative binding
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
24.	 (A) Michaelis Menten kinetics
The graph displays a hyperbolic curve, where 
the initial reaction rate is directly proportional 
to the substrate concentration, but as the 
substrate concentration increases, the rate 
slows and eventually approaches a maximum 
velocity (Vmax). This relationship is the classic 
representation of Michaelis-Menten kinetics. It 
describes the behavior of most non-allosteric 
enzymes. The hyperbolic shape is explained 
by the saturation of the enzyme's active sites 
with the substrate at high concentrations. 
Cooperative binding (D), which is a feature 
of allosteric enzymes, results in a sigmoidal 
(S-shaped) curve (C), not a hyperbolic one. 
Allosteric activation (B) would also be depicted 
on a sigmoidal curve, causing a leftward shift. 
The curve shown is definitively characteristic of 
Michaelis-Menten kinetics.
In a patient who has undergone prolonged starvation, which urine test would show a positive result?
(A)	
Benedict's test
(B)	
Rothera's test
(C)	
Biuret test
(D)	
Emulsion test
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
25.	 (B) Rothera's test
During prolonged starvation, after glycogen 
stores are depleted, the body switches to 
metabolizing fats for energy. The liver breaks 
down fatty acids into acetyl-CoA, which is then 
converted into ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-
hydroxybutyrate, and acetone). These ketone 
bodies are released into the blood and used as fuel 
by tissues like the brain. When their production 
exceeds their utilization, they accumulate in 
the blood (ketosis) and are excreted in the urine 
(ketonuria). Rothera's test is a specific chemical 
test used to detect the presence of ketone bodies 
(specifically acetoacetate and acetone) in a 
urine sample. A positive result, indicated by 
the formation of a purple-colored ring, would 
therefore be expected in a starving individual. 
Benedict's test (A) is for reducing sugars. Biuret 
test (C) is for proteins. Emulsion test (D) is for 
lipids.

Which proteins of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) are responsible for inactivating the RB gene?
(A)	
E6
(B)	
E7
(C)	
L1
(D)	
L2
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
28.	 (B) E7
High-risk types of Human Papillomavirus 
(HPV) are the primary cause of cervical 
cancer and other anogenital cancers. Their 
carcinogenic potential is mediated by two 
early viral oncoproteins, E6 and E7. The E7 
protein functions by binding to and promoting 
the degradation of the retinoblastoma (pRB) 
tumor suppressor protein. pRB normally acts as 
a brake on the cell cycle by binding to the E2F 
transcription factor. By inactivating pRB, the E7 
protein releases E2F, allowing the cell to bypass 
the G1/S checkpoint and undergo uncontrolled 
proliferation. The E6 protein (A) has a different 
primary target; it binds to and promotes the 
degradation of the p53 tumor suppressor 
protein, thereby inhibiting apoptosis. The L1 
and L2 proteins (C, D) are late proteins that 
form the viral capsid.
Which mediators are involved in the initial stage of type 1 hypersensitivity?
1.	
Mast cell
2.	
Histamine

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
29.	 (C) 1,2,4,5
Type I hypersensitivity is the immediate, 
IgE-mediated allergic reaction. The process 
is initiated when an allergen cross-links IgE 
antibodies bound to the surface of mast cells (1) 
(and basophils). This cross-linking triggers the 
degranulation of the mast cell, which releases 
a flood of pre-formed and newly synthesized 
mediators. The initial or immediate phase 
is dominated by the release of pre-formed 
mediators from granules, the most important of 
which is histamine (2). Almost immediately, the 
mast cell also begins to synthesize lipid-derived 
mediators from its membrane phospholipids 
via the arachidonic acid pathway. These include 
prostaglandins (4) (e.g., PGD2) and leukotrienes 
(5) (e.g., LTC4, LTD4, LTE4). These mediators 
are responsible for the classic allergic symptoms. 
Neutrophils (3) are recruited later in the late-
phase reaction, not the initial stage.

31.	 (B) Vitamin B6
Sideroblastic anemia is a group of blood 
disorders characterized by the presence of ring 
sideroblasts in the bone marrow. It results 
from a defect in the synthesis of heme. The 
first and rate-limiting step in heme synthesis is 
the condensation of succinyl-CoA and glycine 
to form delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), a 
reaction catalyzed by the enzyme ALA synthase. 
This enzyme requires pyridoxal 5'-phosphate 
(PLP) as a cofactor. PLP is the active form of 
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine). In some forms of 
sideroblastic anemia, particularly the hereditary 
X-linked type, there is a mutation in the ALA 
synthase enzyme that can be partially overcome 
by administering high doses of its cofactor, 
Vitamin B6. Therefore, a trial of pyridoxine is 
a cornerstone of therapy for certain types of 
sideroblastic anemia.

is 
a 
rare

or its pharmacology. The nebulizer solution

blockade. In contrast, hypertonic saline (A) is

It is a separate therapeutic agent (a mucolytic) 
that is known to induce bronchoconstriction 
as a primary effect, but this is not a cause 
of 
paradoxical 
bronchoconstriction 
from 
ipratropium itself.

A patient with cirrhosis and ascites presents to you, and the external appearance of his liver is shown in the image. Which statement about the liver tissue is correct?
(A)	
Dark areas represent necrosis, white areas represent viable liver
(B)	
Dark areas represent viable liver tissue, white areas represent necrosis
(C)	
White areas represent central hepatocytes
(D)	
Dark areas represent periportal hepatocytes
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
38.	 (B) Dark areas represent viable liver tissue, 
white areas represent necrosis
The image shows the characteristic gross 
appearance of a "nutmeg liver," which is seen 
in chronic passive venous congestion, often due 
to right-sided heart failure. This pattern reflects 
the zonal anatomy of the liver lobule. The dark 
reddish areas correspond to the congested and 
sometimes hemorrhagic centrilobular regions 
(around the central vein). The hepatocytes in 
this area are the most vulnerable to hypoxia 
and may be necrotic in severe cases, but they 
are primarily congested with red blood cells. 
The paler, yellowish-white areas represent 
the less-congested and often fatty periportal 
regions (around the portal tracts). Therefore, 
the statement that dark areas represent viable 
(though congested) liver tissue and white/pale 
areas represent fatty or less affected tissue is the 
most accurate description of the gross pathology 
of a nutmeg liver.
Which of the following is not associated with massive splenomegaly?
(A)	
Chronic myeloid leukemia
(B)	
Aplastic anemia
(C)	
Hairy cell leukemia
(D)	
Lymphoma
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
39.	 (B) Aplastic anemia
Massive splenomegaly is defined as a spleen 
that is palpable more than 8 cm below the 
left costal margin or weighs more than 1000 
grams. It is caused by a limited number of 
conditions, typically those involving significant 
infiltration of the spleen or chronic congestion. 
Classic 
causes 
include 
myeloproliferative 
neoplasms like Chronic Myeloid Leukemia 
(CML) (A), which almost always causes 
massive splenomegaly. Certain hematologic 
malignancies like Hairy Cell Leukemia (C) 
and some types of lymphoma (D) (especially 
splenic marginal zone lymphoma) are also well-
known causes. In contrast, aplastic anemia (B) 
is a condition characterized by pancytopenia 
due to bone marrow failure. The bone marrow 
is hypo cellular, and there is no extramedullary 
hematopoiesis or infiltration of the spleen. 
Therefore, splenomegaly is characteristically 
absent in aplastic anemia, and its presence 
would cast doubt on the diagnosis.
Which statement accurately describes the effect of iron regulatory protein (IRP) binding to iron-responsive elements (IRE) on the translation of ferritin and transferrin receptor 1 in a patient with iron deficiency anemia?
(A)	
Ferritin translation is increased by binding IRP to IRE
(B)	
Ferritin translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE
(C)	
Transferrin receptor 1 translation is unaffected by binding IRP to IRE
(D)	
Transferrin receptor 1 translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
40.	 (B) Ferritin translation is decreased by binding 
IRP to IRE
In a state of iron deficiency, intracellular iron 
levels are low. This causes the iron regulatory 
protein (IRP) to be active and bind to specific 
stem-loop structures on mRNAs called iron-
responsive elements (IREs). The location of the 
IRE determines the effect of IRP binding.
The IRE for ferritin (the iron storage protein) 
is located in the 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) 
of its mRNA. When IRP binds here, it sterically 
hinders the assembly of the ribosomal complex, 
thereby blocking and decreasing the translation 
of ferritin. This makes physiological sense, as 
the cell does not want to store iron when it is 
deficient.
The IRE for the transferrin receptor 1 (which 
imports iron into the cell) is in the 3' UTR. IRP 
binding here stabilizes the mRNA and prevents 
its degradation, thus increasing its translation. 
This allows the cell to make more receptors to 
take up more iron.

BK 
INICET Examination Paper
69.	 (B) Knock down
RNA interference (RNAi) is a natural cellular 
process for regulating gene expression. In this 
process, small non-coding RNA molecules, such 
as small interfering RNA (siRNA) or microRNA 
(miRNA), bind to a specific target messenger 
RNA (mRNA) molecule. This binding leads 
to the degradation of the target mRNA or the 
inhibition of its translation into protein. The 
result is a significant reduction in the expression 
of the targeted gene. This process of reducing 
or suppressing gene expression is referred to 
as a "knockdown". This is distinct from a gene 
"knock out" (A), which refers to the complete 
and permanent elimination of a gene from the 
genome itself (at the DNA level). RNAi works 
at the post-transcriptional level to temporarily 
suppress gene expression.
Which of the following is the best method to detect HbA1c?
(A)	
Ion-exchange chromatography
(B)	
Electrophoresis
(C)	
Immunoassay
(D)	
Affinity chromatography
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
70.	 (A) Ion-exchange chromatography
Several methods are used to measure Glycated 
Hemoglobin (HbA1c), but High-Performance 
Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) is considered 
the gold standard reference method. One of 
the principal forms of HPLC used for this 
purpose 
is 
ion-exchange 
chromatography. 
This method separates different hemoglobin 
variants based on their differences in electrical 
charge. Glycation of hemoglobin alters its 
charge, allowing the glycated fraction (HbA1c) 
to be separated from the non-glycated fraction 
(HbA0). This provides a highly accurate and 
precise quantification. While immunoassays 
(C) and affinity chromatography (D) are 
also widely used and certified methods, ion-
exchange HPLC is generally regarded as the 
most robust reference standard for the accurate 
determination of HbA1c levels.
Which of the following is the best test for quantitative analysis of an RNA sample?
(A)	
Real-time PCR
(B)	
Reverse Transcriptase PCR
(C)	
PCR-Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism
(D)	
RT-PCR followed by Real-time PCR
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
71.	 (D) RT-PCR followed by Real-time PCR
To perform a quantitative analysis of RNA, 
two steps are required. First, the RNA must be 
converted into a more stable complementary 
DNA (cDNA) molecule. This is achieved through 
Reverse Transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) (B), 
which uses the enzyme reverse transcriptase. 
Second, this newly synthesized cDNA must be 
quantified. Real-time PCR (A), also known as 
quantitative PCR (qPCR), is the gold standard 
method for quantifying DNA. It monitors 
the amplification of a target DNA sequence 
in real-time by using fluorescent probes. The 
rate at which the fluorescence accumulates 
is proportional to the initial amount of the 
target sequence. Therefore, the most accurate 
and standard method for quantifying an RNA 
sample is to first perform reverse transcription 
and then quantify the resulting cDNA using 
real-time PCR. This two-step process is often 
collectively referred to as qRT-PCR or RT-qPCR.
Which of the following statements accurately describe mitochondrial DNA?
1.	
Higher rate of mutations as compared to the nuclear genome
2.	
Double-stranded circular DNA with about 16,000 base pairs
3.	
A slight change in nucleotide sequence as compared to cellular DNA
4.	
Encodes all electron transport chain proteins
(A)	
1 and 3
(B)	
1 and 2
(C)	
2 and 4
(D)	
2 and 3
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
72.	 (B) 1 and 2
1.	 Correct. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) has 
a higher rate of mutation than nuclear DNA. 
This is attributed to its proximity to reactive 
oxygen species generated during oxidative 
phosphorylation and a less efficient DNA 
repair system.
2.	 Correct. Human mtDNA is a small, double-
stranded circular molecule containing 
approximately 16,569 base pairs.
3.	 Incorrect. While the sequence is different, 
this statement is vague and less precise 
than statements 1 and 2. MtDNA also has a 
slightly different genetic code.
4.	 Incorrect. This is a critical point. While 
mtDNA encodes 13 essential protein 
subunits of the electron transport chain 
(ETC) complexes, the vast majority of ETC 
proteins (around 80-90) are encoded by 
nuclear DNA, synthesized in the cytoplasm, 
and then imported into the mitochondria.
Therefore, the two most accurate and defining 
statements are that mtDNA has a higher 
mutation rate and is a small, circular molecule.

In which of the following is the Oil Red O stain utilized?
(A)	
Formalin fixation
(B)	
Frozen section
(C)	
Alcohol fixation
(D)	
Glutaraldehyde fixation
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
47.	 (B) Frozen section
Oil Red O is a lysochrome (fat-soluble) diazo dye 
used in histology to stain neutral triglycerides 
and lipids. During routine tissue processing 
for paraffin embedding, tissues are dehydrated 
using alcohols and cleared with agents like 
xylene. These organic solvents dissolve and 
wash out lipids, so lipid staining is not possible 
on 
standard 
paraffin-embedded 
sections. 
To preserve the lipids within the tissue, the 
specimen must be processed as a frozen section. 
In this technique, the fresh tissue is rapidly 
frozen, cut on a cryostat, and then stained. 
This avoids the use of lipid-dissolving solvents. 
Therefore, Oil Red O staining is specifically 
utilized for demonstrating fat in frozen tissue 
sections.
Which repair mechanism is linked with CRISPR-Cash?
(A)	
Non-homologous end joining
(B)	
Base excision repair
(C)	
Nucleotide excision repair
(D)	
Mismatch repair
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
48.	 (A) Non-homologous end joining
The CRISPR-Cash system is a genome editing 
tool that works by inducing a targeted double-
strand break (DSB) in the DNA at a specific 
location guided by an RNA molecule. Once 
the DSB is created, the cell's own DNA repair 
machinery takes over. The cell has two main 
pathways to repair DSBs. The most common 
and default pathway is non-homologous end 
joining (NHEJ). This pathway is error-prone and 
often introduces small insertions or deletions 
(indels) at the break site as it ligates the broken 
ends back together. This is the mechanism that 
is typically exploited to create gene "knockouts." 
The other, less frequent pathway is homology-
directed repair (HDR), which can be used to 
"knock in" a specific DNA sequence if a template 
is provided. The other options (B, C, D) are 
repair mechanisms for different types of DNA 
damage, not DSBs.
Which thiazide diuretic should be given to a 34-year-old male with hypertension and stage 4 chronic kidney disease, whose estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is below 30 mL/min?
(A)	
Chlorothiazide
(B)	
Chlorthalidone
(C)	
Metolazone
(D)	
Hydrochlorothiazide
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
49.	 (C) Metolazone
Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics, such as 
hydrochlorothiazide (D), chlorthalidone (B), and 
chlorothiazide (A), exert their antihypertensive 
and diuretic effects by inhibiting the Na-
Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted 
tubule. However, their efficacy is significantly 
diminished when the glomerular filtration rate 
(GFR) falls below 30 mL/min, as insufficient 
drug is filtered to reach its site of action. A major 
exception to this rule is metolazone. Metolazone 
is a thiazide-like diuretic that, unlike others in 
its class, retains its efficacy even in patients 
with advanced chronic kidney disease and a low 
GFR. It is often used in combination with a loop 
diuretic in patients with refractory edema due to 
renal failure or heart failure. Therefore, it is the 
most appropriate choice in this clinical scenario.

At what dosage does dopamine function on beta-1 receptors?
(A)	
2-10 mcg/kg/min
(B)	
<2 mcg/kg/min
(C)	
10-20 mcg/kg/min
(D)	
>20 mcg/kg/min
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
56.	 (A) 2-10 mcg/kg/min
Dopamine is a catecholamine with dose-
dependent receptor effects, which is crucial for 
its clinical use as an inotrope and vasopressor.
1.	 Low dose (renal dose) : At infusion rates of 
approximately <2-5 mcg/kg/min, dopamine 
primarily stimulates D1 receptors, causing 
vasodilation in the renal, mesenteric, and 
coronary circulations.
2.	 Moderate dose (cardiac dose) : At infusion 
rates of approximately 2-10 mcg/kg/min, 
dopamine primarily stimulates beta-1 
adrenergic receptors on the heart. This 
results in increased myocardial contractility 
(positive inotropy) and heart rate (positive 
chronotropy), leading to an increased 
cardiac output.
3.	 High dose (vasopressor dose) : At infusion 
rates >10 mcg/kg/min, the effects on 
alpha-1 adrenergic receptors predominate, 
causing systemic vasoconstriction and an 
increase in blood pressure.
Which of the following medications would increase the bioavailability of saquinavir when given concurrently?
(A)	
Ritonavir
(B)	
Vitamin C
(C)	
Cimetidine
(D)	
Ganciclovir
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
57.	 (A) Ritonavir
Saquinavir is an antiretroviral drug from the 
protease inhibitor class. When used alone, it has 
very poor oral bioavailability due to extensive 
metabolism by the cytochrome P450 3A4 
(CYP3A4) enzyme in the gut wall and liver. 
Ritonavir is another protease inhibitor that 
is also a very potent inhibitor of the CYP3A4 
enzyme. This property is exploited clinically by 
using a low, subtherapeutic dose of ritonavir as 
a pharmacokinetic enhancer or "booster". When 
co-administered with saquinavir, ritonavir 
inhibits its metabolism, leading to a significant 
increase in saquinavir's plasma concentration 
and bioavailability, thereby enhancing its 
antiviral efficacy. This boosting strategy is a 
common principle in HIV therapy. The other 
substances listed do not have this specific and 
potent CYP3A4 inhibitory effect.
How does cyclosporine work in terms of its mechanism of action?
(A)	
Inhibition of calcineurin
(B)	
AMP kinase stimulation
(C)	
IMP dehydrogenase inhibition
(D)	
Dihydro-orotate dehydrogenase inhibition
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
58.	 (A) Inhibition of calcineurin
Cyclosporine is a powerful immunosuppressive 
agent widely used in organ transplantation 
to prevent rejection. Its mechanism of action 
involves the inhibition of calcineurin. Inside 
a T-lymphocyte, cyclosporine first binds to an 
intracellular protein called cyclophilin. This 
cyclosporine-cyclophilin complex then binds 
to and inhibits calcineurin, which is a calcium- 
and 
calmodulin-dependent 
phosphatase 
enzyme. The inhibition of calcineurin prevents 
it from dephosphorylating the Nuclear Factor 
of Activated T-cells (NFAT). As a result, NFAT 
cannot translocate to the nucleus to act as a 
transcription factor. This blocks the transcription 
of genes for several crucial cytokines, most 
importantly Interleukin-2 (IL-2). By preventing 
IL-2 
production, 
cyclosporine 
effectively 
suppresses the proliferation and activation of 
T-cells, a central step in the immune response 
leading to organ rejection.

Neonatal 
Respiratory 
Distress 
Syndrome 
(RDS) is caused by a deficiency of pulmonary 
surfactant. Surfactant is a complex mixture 
of lipids and proteins that is produced and 
secreted by Type II pneumocytes (also called

These cuboidal cells are located within the

Which of the following viruses is unable to integrate into the human genome to initiate carcinogenesis?

HPV
(B)

(C)	
HTLV
(D)

43.	 (B) HBV
1.	 Human papillomavirus (HPV) integrates 
its DNA into the host genome in high-risk 
types (e.g., HPV 16, 18). Integration leads 
to overexpression of E6 and E7 oncogenes, 
promoting carcinogenesis.
2.	 Human T-lymphotropic virus 1 (HTLV-1)

to

The cell shown in the slide has inhibitory functions. To which of the following structures does it send its projections?
(A)	
Deep nuclei of the cerebellum
(B)	
Vestibular nuclei
(C)	
Inferior olivary nucleus
(D)	
Basal ganglia
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
44.	 (A) Deep nuclei of the cerebellum
The image shows a Purkinje cell, which is 
recognizable by its massive, flask-shaped cell 
body and extensive, flat dendritic tree. Purkinje 
cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar 
cortex. They are GABAergic, meaning they exert 
a powerful inhibitory influence on their target 
cells. The primary targets of the vast majority of 
Purkinje cell axons are the neurons of the deep 
cerebellar nuclei (e.g., the dentate, emboliform, 
globose, and fastigial nuclei). These deep nuclei, 
in turn, provide the main excitatory output 
from the cerebellum to other parts of the motor 
system, such as the thalamus and brainstem. 
Therefore, the cerebellar cortex, via its Purkinje 
cells, modulates motor activity by regulating the 
firing of the deep cerebellar nuclei through this 
inhibitory projection.

Which of the following rules are used as tests to determine insanity in a given situation?

(A)	
1,2,3 and 4
(B)	
2,3,4 only
(C)	
1,2 only

3,4 only
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
66.	 (C) 1,2 only
In legal contexts, several different standards 
or "rules" have been developed over time to 
determine criminal insanity.
1.	 Durham's rule (also known as the "product 
test") states that a defendant is not 
criminally responsible if their unlawful act 
was the product of mental disease or defect. 
It was adopted in some U.S. jurisdictions 
but has largely been abandoned due to its 
vagueness.
2.	 Curren's rule is a version of the American 
Law Institute (ALI) test, which states that 
a person is not responsible for criminal 
conduct if at the time of such conduct, as a 
result of mental disease or defect, they lack 
substantial capacity either to appreciate the 
criminality of their conduct or to conform 
their conduct to the requirements of the 
law.
Ashley's rule (3) and Murphy's rule (4) (better 
known as Murphy's Law) are not legal standards 
for determining insanity. Therefore, only 
Durham's rule and Curren's rule are valid legal 
tests for insanity among the choices provided.
By what mechanism did the injuries occur in a man brought to the emergency department after a blast, who presents with multiple small puncture wounds on the right side of the chest below the nipple, along with numerous small abrasions and bruises on the left lower abdomen?

Flying missiles

67.	 (A) Flying missiles
Blast injuries are categorized into primary, 
secondary, tertiary, and quaternary types. 
The 
patient's 
injuries—multiple 
small 
puncture wounds, abrasions, and bruises—
are characteristic of secondary blast injuries. 
These injuries are caused by flying missiles and 
fragments from the explosive device itself or 
from the surrounding environment (e.g., glass, 
wood, metal) that are propelled by the force of 
the explosion. Primary blast injuries are caused 
by the direct effect of the blast overpressure 
wave (B) on gas-containing organs. Tertiary 
injuries are caused by the victim being thrown 
by the blast wind into a solid object. Quaternary 
injuries include all other miscellaneous injuries, 
such as burns (C) and crush injuries from a 
building collapse (D). The pattern described 
is classic for being struck by multiple small 
projectiles.

The image shows a unique, fern-like, branching

What follow-up diagnostic procedure is recommended for a child with bilateral proptosis and a peripheral smear suggesting chloroma?

(C)

35.	 (D) Bone marrow biopsy
A chloroma, also known as a granulocytic 
sarcoma or myeloid sarcoma, is a solid, 
extramedullary tumor composed of leukemic 
myeloblasts. It can occur in various parts of the 
body, including the orbit, leading to proptosis. 
Its presence is a manifestation of acute myeloid 
leukemia (AML). While the peripheral smear 
may have been suggestive of AML (e.g., by 
showing circulating blasts), the definitive 
diagnosis of leukemia requires a bone marrow 
biopsy and aspirate. This procedure is essential 
to confirm the diagnosis, determine the

(flow 
cytometry), and cytogenetics, and to assess 
the overall cellularity and extent of bone 
marrow infiltration by the leukemic cells. Flow 
cytometry (C) is performed on the bone marrow 
sample but is not the primary procedure itself.

Neonatal meningitis (occurring in the first 
month of life) is caused by a specific group 
of pathogens typically acquired from the 
mother's genital tract during birth. The most 
common causative organisms are Group B

"What principle forms the basis of the Paul-Bunnell test performed for a 24-year-old male presenting with cervical lymphadenopathy?"
(A)	
Complement fixation
(B)	
Superantigens
(C)	
Heterophile antibodies
(D)	
Haptens
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
79.	 (C) Heterophile antibodies
The 
clinical 
presentation 
of 
cervical 
lymphadenopathy in a young adult is classic for 
infectious mononucleosis, which is caused by 
the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The Paul-Bunnell 
test is a classic laboratory test used to diagnose 
this condition. The principle of the test is the 
detection of heterophile antibodies. These are 
antibodies (typically IgM) that are produced 
during an EBV infection and have the unusual 
property of cross-reacting with and agglutinating 
red blood cells from other species, such as sheep 
and horses. A positive Paul-Bunnell test (or a 
more modern Monospot test, which works on 
the same principle) demonstrates the presence 
of these heterophile antibodies, providing 
strong evidence for a diagnosis of infectious 
mononucleosis.
Which one of these options is classified as a dematiaceous fungus?
(A)	
Mucor species
(B)	
Aspergillus niger
(C)	
Cladosporium
(D)	
Blastomyces dermatitidis
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
80.	 (C) Cladosporium
Dematiaceous fungi are a group of fungi whose 
cell walls contain melanin. This melanin 
imparts a characteristic dark brown or black 
color to their spores and/or hyphae. They are 
responsible for a range of infections, including 
phaeohyphomycosis and chromoblastomycosis. 
Cladosporium is a classic example of a 
dematiaceous mold; it is a common airborne 
fungus that appears dark green to black. In 
contrast, Mucor species (A) are zygomycetes 
characterized by broad, non-septate, hyaline 
(non-pigmented) hyphae. Aspergillus niger (B), 
despite its name, produces black spores but has 
hyaline hyphae, and is generally not classified as 
dematiaceous. Blastomyces dermatitidis (D) is a 
dimorphic fungus that grows as a hyaline mold 
in the environment and as a yeast in tissues.

Please identify the component that causes endotoxic shock in gram-negative bacteria.
(A)	
2
(B)	
4
(C)	
1
(D)	
3
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
82.	 (C) 1
The image displays the structure of a Gram-
negative bacterial outer membrane. The key 
molecule responsible for endotoxic shock is 
lipopolysaccharide (LPS). LPS is composed 
of three parts : the O-antigen (outermost 
carbohydrate chains), a core polysaccharide, and 
Lipid A. Label 1 points to the Lipid A portion, 
which is the lipid component that anchors LPS 
into the outer membrane. It is Lipid A that is 
the biologically active "endotoxin." When Gram-
negative bacteria are lysed, Lipid A is released 
and recognized by the host's innate immune 
system (e.g., via Toll-like receptor 4), triggering 
a massive inflammatory cascade. This leads to 
the release of cytokines like TNF-alpha and 
IL-1, causing fever, hypotension, disseminated 
intravascular coagulation, and septic shock. 
Label 2 points to the O-antigen, and 3 points to 
the outer membrane.

Which of the following organisms is considered a strict anaerobe?
(A)	
Prevotella
(B)	
Burkholderia cepacia
(C)	
Yersinia enterocolitica
(D)	
Stenotrophomonas maltophilia
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
84.	 (A) Prevotella
A strict (or obligate) anaerobe is a microorganism 
that cannot grow in the presence of oxygen and 
may even be killed by it. They lack the enzymes 
(like catalase and superoxide dismutase) needed 
to detoxify reactive oxygen species produced 
during aerobic respiration. Prevotella is a genus 
of Gram-negative bacteria that are classic 
examples of obligate anaerobes. They are part of 
the normal flora of the human mouth, gut, and 
vagina and are often implicated in anaerobic 
infections like dental abscesses and aspiration 
pneumonia. The other organisms listed are not 
strict anaerobes. Burkholderia cepacia (B) and 
Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (D) are aerobic 
Gram-negative rods. Yersinia enterocolitica (C) 
is a facultative anaerobe, meaning it can grow 
either with or without oxygen.

Which of the statements below is correct?
(A)	
In a population with low prevalence of the disease, a positive result with a highly sensitive test means true positive
(B)	
Sensitivity depends on prevalence of the disease
(C)	
Positive predictive value depends on prevalence of disease
(D)	
Specificity depends on prevalence of the disease
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021
87.	 (C) Positive predictive value depends on 
prevalence of disease
Sensitivity (the ability to correctly identify true 
positives) and specificity (the ability to correctly 
identify true negatives) are intrinsic properties 
of a diagnostic test and do not depend on the 
prevalence of the disease in the population 
being tested (making B and D incorrect). In 
contrast, the predictive values of a test are 
highly dependent on the disease prevalence. The 
Positive Predictive Value (PPV) is the probability 
that a person with a positive test result actually 
has the disease. The PPV will increase as the 
prevalence of the disease increases, and it will 
decrease as the prevalence decreases. In a low-
prevalence population, even a highly accurate 
test will have a lower PPV, meaning a positive 
result is more likely to be a false positive (making 
A incorrect).
