EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Fibrocystic change
The patient's symptoms of cyclical breast swelling and nodularity, along with calcifications on mammogram, are highly suggestive of fibrocystic changes. This is a very common, benign condition of the breast that affects many women of reproductive age. The provided histology image confirms this diagnosis. The image shows several features characteristic of fibrocystic change, including the formation of cysts (dilated ducts), stromal fibrosis (increased fibrous connective tissue), and adenosis (an increase in the number of glandular elements or acini within the lobules). These changes are thought to be related to an exaggerated response of the breast tissue to cyclical hormonal stimulation. While calcifications can be seen, and the condition presents as "lumpiness," it is a benign, non-proliferative condition that does not significantly increase the risk for breast cancer.

38.	 A 21-year-old woman presents with generalized 
weakness, 
blurred 
vision, 
and 
difficulty 
swallowing. Examination reveals bilateral ptosis 
and facial muscle weakness. A chest CT shows 
an anterior mediastinal mass, which is surgically 
removed and shown in the image. What is the

(A)	Carcinoid tumour
(B)	 Thymoma
(C)	Hodgkin's lymphoma
(D)	Lymphocytic lymphoma
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Thymoma
This clinical presentation is a classic example of Myasthenia Gravis (MG), an autoimmune disorder that causes fluctuating, fatigable muscle weakness. The symptoms of ocular weakness (ptosis, blurred vision from diplopia) and bulbar weakness (difficulty swallowing) are highly characteristic. Myasthenia gravis has a very strong association with abnormalities of the thymus gland, which is located in the anterior mediastinum. Approximately 65% of patients have thymic hyperplasia, and a crucial 10-15% have a thymoma, which is a tumor of the thymic epithelial cells. The discovery of an anterior mediastinal mass on CT in a patient with myasthenic symptoms is highly indicative of a thymoma. The image shows a lobulated, encapsulated mass consistent with the gross appearance of a thymoma. Surgical removal (thymectomy) is a key part of the management of MG, especially when a thymoma is present.

39.	 Identify the cells marked by a black arrow in 
the blood smear of a patient suffering from liver 
disease.
(A)	Target cells
(B)	 Elliptocytes
(C)	Codocytes
(D)	A & C
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) A & C
The image shows a peripheral blood smear with several abnormally shaped red blood cells indicated by arrows. These cells have a central area of hemoglobinopathies surrounded by a pale zone and then a peripheral rim of hemoglobin, resembling a shooting target. This morphology has two names. They are commonly known as target cells (A). The more formal hematological term for these cells is codocytes (C). Therefore, both terms are correct. Target cells are formed due to an increase in the surface area-to-volume ratio of the red blood cell. This can be caused by either an increase in the membrane surface area (e.g., in liver disease due to altered lipid composition) or a decrease in intracellular volume (e.g., in thalassemia due to reduced hemoglobin content). They are a characteristic, though not specific, finding in patients with significant liver disease, as well as in thalassemia and other hemoglobinopathies.
40.	 Which of the following is not a distinguishing 
feature between Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma 
(HL) and Nodular Lymphocyte Predominant 
Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL)?
(A)	Nodular lymphocyte predominant has poor 
prognosis
(B)	 Nodular lymphocyte predominant is not 
associated with EBV
(C)	Popcorn cells are positive for CD20 & EMA
(D)	Popcorn cells are negative for CD30 & CD15
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Nodular lymphocyte predominant has poor prognosis
This statement is the exception because it is false. Nodular Lymphocyte-Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL) is an indolent lymphoma with a very favorable prognosis, which is generally better than that of most subtypes of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma (CHL). The other statements correctly describe key differences between the two entities. NLPHL is not associated with the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) (B), whereas many cases of CHL are. The malignant cell in NLPHL is the Lymphocytic and Histiocytic (L&H) cell, or "popcorn cell." These cells have a distinct immuno phenotype : they are characteristically positive for B-cell markers like CD20 and EMA (C), and crucially, they are negative for the classic RS cell markers CD15 and CD30 (D). In contrast, the Reed-Sternberg cells of CHL are positive for CD15 and CD30 but are usually negative for CD20 and EMA.
41.	 Which of the following is found in t(11;14)?
A.	 SOX 11
B.	 Cyclin D1
C.	 CD10
D.	 CD200
(A)	Only A
(B)	 A and C only
(C)	A, B and C only
(D)	B and D only
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) B and D only.
The chromosomal translocation t(11;14) is the genetic signature of Mantle Cell Lymphoma (MCL). This genetic event is pivotal because it leads directly to the over expression of a key protein.
B.	
Cyclin D1 : The t(11;14) translocation places the CCND1 gene (which codes for Cyclin D1) next to a powerful gene enhancer. This results in the massive overexpression of Cyclin D1, a protein that pushes the cell cycle forward. It's the defining molecular feature of MCL.
D.	
CD200 : This is a cell surface glycoprotein. While not as fundamental as Cyclin D1, research shows that CD200 is expressed in a notable subset of MCL cases (around 25-40%).
In contrast, CD10 (C) is a marker typically found in other B-cell lymphomas like Follicular Lymphoma and is characteristically negative in MCL. While SOX11 (A) is also a key diagnostic marker for MCL, option (D) is the best choice as it correctly pairs the essential marker (Cyclin D1) with another valid finding (CD200).
42.	 Which of the following conditions is least 
likely to result in a dry tap during bone marrow 
aspiration?
(A)	Chronic myeloproliferative disorders
(B)	 Follicular Lymphoma
(C)	M7 AML
(D)	Hairy Cell Leukemia
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Follicular Lymphoma
A "dry tap" on bone marrow aspiration occurs when no marrow particles can be aspirated, despite the needle being correctly positioned. This is most commonly due to marrow fibrosis (myelofibrosis) or packing of the marrow space by a dense infiltrate of cells. Conditions notorious for causing significant marrow fibrosis and a dry tap include hairy cell leukemia (D), chronic myeloproliferative disorders like primary myelofibrosis (A), and acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (M7 AML) (C). In these conditions, a bone marrow biopsy is essential for diagnosis. In contrast, while follicular lymphoma (B) can infiltrate the bone marrow, the infiltration is typically interstitial or paratrabecular and not usually associated with the extensive fibrosis that would lead to a dry tap. Therefore, among the choices provided, follicular lymphoma is the least likely to result in an inaspirable bone marrow.
43.	 Which of the following is not true about 
telomerase?
(A)	Reverse transcriptase
(B)	 Maintains chromosome length
(C)	Only in eukaryotes
(D)	DNA repair/synthesis
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) DNA repair/synthesis
This question is a near duplicate of a previous one. Telomerase is a unique ribonucleoprotein enzyme. It acts as a specialized reverse transcriptase (A), using its own internal RNA component as a template to synthesize DNA. Its specific function is to add repetitive DNA sequences (telomeres) to the ends of chromosomes, thereby maintaining chromosome length (B) and compensating for the "end-replication problem." This process is specific to linear chromosomes and is thus a feature of eukaryotes (C). The statement that it is involved in general DNA repair/synthesis (D) is not true. While it does synthesize DNA, its function is highly specialized and restricted to the telomeres. The major enzymes for general DNA synthesis (replication) and repair are the various DNA polymerases, not telomerase.
44.	 Which of the following statements about 
Nodular Lymphocyte Predominant Hodgkin 
Lymphoma (NLPHL) is incorrect?
(A)	EBV Negative
(B)	 CD15/CD30 Negative
(C)	CD20 Positive
(D)	Poor prognosis compared to Classical

AAns

(D) Poor prognosis compared to Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma (CHL)
This is a duplicate of question 27. The incorrect statement is that NLPHL has a poor prognosis. Nodular Lymphocyte-Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL) is an indolent (slow-growing) form of lymphoma that typically has a very favorable prognosis, which is generally considered better than that of most subtypes of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma (CHL). The other statements accurately describe the key features of NLPHL that distinguish it from CHL. It is characteristically negative for Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) (A). The malignant cells, known as "popcorn cells," are diagnostically negative for the classic Hodgkin markers CD15 and CD30 (B). 45.	 Pancytopenia on blood examination is seen in :
(A)	Megaloblastic anemia
(B)	 Hairy cell leukemia
(C)	Acute promyelocytic leukemia
(D)	Myelodysplastic syndrome
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Hairy cell leukemia.
All four options are valid causes of pancytopenia.
Megaloblastic anemia, Acute promyelocytic leukemia, and Myelodysplastic syndrome all disrupt the bone marrow's ability to produce sufficient healthy blood cells, leading to low counts.
However, Hairy cell leukemia is uniquely characterized by this presentation. The disease involves malignant B-lymphocytes (the "hairy cells") infiltrating the bone marrow.  This infiltration, combined with the significant marrow fibrosis (scarring) it causes, physically crowds out and suppresses the normal production of red cells, white cells, and platelets.
Therefore, pancytopenia is a hallmark and nearly universal finding at the time of diagnosis for Hairy cell leukemia, often accompanied by a massively enlarged spleen. This makes it a quintessential example of a disease presenting with pancytopenia.
46.	 Which clotting factor deficiency does not affect 
clotting in vivo?
(A)	Factor V
(B)	 Factor VII
(C)	Factor III (Tissue factor)
(D)	Factor XII
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) Factor XII
Factor XII (Hageman factor) is the protein that initiates the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade in vitro, as measured by the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT). A deficiency in Factor XII will therefore cause a markedly prolonged aPTT. However, extensive clinical observation has shown that individuals with Factor XII deficiency do not have a bleeding disorder and do not experience abnormal bleeding in vivo, even after major surgery or trauma. This indicates that the initiation of the intrinsic pathway via Factor XII is not essential for normal hemostasis in the body. In contrast, deficiencies of all other clotting factors, including Factor V (A), Factor VII (B), and Tissue Factor (Factor III) (C), lead to significant and often severe bleeding disorders, highlighting their crucial roles in the in vivo coagulation process.

1. Ethosuximide

(C)	2 Only

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) 1 & 3 Only
Absence seizures are a type of generalized seizure characterized by brief episodes of staring and unresponsiveness, accompanied by a classic 3-Hz spike-and-wave pattern on EEG. The treatment for absence seizures is specific.
1.	
Ethosuximide : This is the first-line and most specific drug for treating uncomplicated childhood absence seizures. It works by blocking T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons.
3.	
Valproic acid : This is a broad-spectrum antiepileptic drug that is also highly effective for absence seizures and is the drug of choice if the patient also has co-existing generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
2.	
Carbamazepine : This is a narrow-spectrum drug used for focal seizures. It is contraindicated in absence seizures as it can exacerbate them.
4.	
Gabapentin : This is used as an add-on for focal seizures and for neuropathic pain; it is not effective for absence seizures.
Therefore, only ethosuximide and valproic acid are used for the treatment of absence seizures.

48.	 If codeine is being introduced to the market 
in combination with dextromethorphan as an 
antitussive, what steps should be taken next?
(A)	Should not be used as it is irrational
(B)	 Can be used to treat cough effectively
(C)	Can be used as it has different MOA
(D)	Should not be used due to addiction
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Should not be used as it is irrational
This question assesses the principles of rational pharmacotherapy. Codeine is an opioid that suppresses cough by acting on the cough center in the brainstem. Dextromethorphan is a non-opioid, synthetic derivative of morphine that also acts centrally to suppress the cough reflex, likely via sigma-1 receptor agonism and NMDA receptor antagonism. Since both drugs are centrally acting antitussives that work to achieve the same therapeutic goal (cough suppression), combining them in a fixed-dose combination offers no proven synergistic or additive benefit over using an adequate dose of a single agent. Such a combination increases the risk of side effects, potential for confusion, and cost without providing any additional efficacy. This violates the principles of rational drug use, and therefore, the combination should not be used as it is irrational.
49.	 Which of the following antidepressants is linked 
to the fewest sexual side effects?
(A)	Mirtazapine
(B)	 Fluoxetine
(C)	Venlafaxine
(D)	Imipenem
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Mirtazapine
Sexual dysfunction (e.g., decreased libido, anorgasmia) is a very common and distressing side effect of many antidepressant medications, particularly those that work primarily by increasing serotonin levels. Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) like fluoxetine (B) and Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors (SNRIs) like venlafaxine (C) are associated with a high incidence of sexual side effects. In contrast, mirtazapine is an atypical antidepressant with a different mechanism of action (a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antagonist, or NaSSA). It blocks α2-adrenergic autoreceptors and certain serotonin receptors (5-HT2 and 5-HT3). This mechanism is associated with a significantly lower incidence of sexual dysfunction compared to SSRIs and SNRIs, and in some cases, it may even improve sexual function. Imipenem (D) is a carbapenem antibiotic, not an antidepressant.
50.	 Which of the following is a bone-forming drug?
(A)	Raloxifene
(B)	 Teriparatide
(C)	Calcitonin
(D)	Bisphosphonates
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Teriparatide
Osteoporosis medications are broadly classified as either anti-resorptive (slowing bone breakdown) or anabolic (promoting new bone formation). Most treatments fall into the first category. Bisphosphonates (D), raloxifene (A) (a SERM), and calcitonin (C) are all anti-resorptive agents that work by inhibiting the activity of osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. In contrast, teriparatide is an anabolic agent. It is a recombinant form of the first 34 amino acids of human parathyroid hormone (PTH). When administered intermittently as a once-daily subcutaneous injection, PTH paradoxically stimulates the activity of osteoblasts, the cells responsible for forming new bone. This leads to a significant increase in bone mineral density and a substantial reduction in fracture risk. It is the primary anabolic or "bone-forming" drug used for the treatment of severe osteoporosis.
51.	 Which of the following statements about 
disulfiram are correct?
(A)	Disulfiram action still persists for a few days 
after being stopped
(B)	 Should be given in doubtful motivated 
persons
(C)	Anti-craving drug
(D)	A & C Both
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Disulfiram action still persists for a few days after being stopped
Disulfiram is a medication used as a deterrent therapy for alcohol dependence. It works by irreversibly inhibiting the enzyme aldehyde dehydrogenase. If a person taking disulfiram consumes alcohol, acetaldehyde accumulates, causing a highly unpleasant reaction (flushing, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia). This statement (A) is true : because the inhibition of the enzyme is irreversible, its action persists for several days (up to a week) after the last dose, until new enzyme is synthesized. It should only be given to highly motivated patients who are committed to abstinence, not those with doubtful motivation (B is false). Disulfiram is an aversive agent; it does not reduce the underlying desire or craving for alcohol. Naltrexone and acamprosate are anti-craving drugs (C is false). Therefore, only statement A is true.
52.	 What is the preferred treatment for a condition 
characterized by subepidermal blisters and 
neutrophilic infiltration?
(A)	Rituximab
(B)	 Dapsone
(C)	Cyclosporine
(D)	Azathioprine
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Dapsone
The histopathological finding of subepidermal blisters (or microabscesses) filled with neutrophils in the dermal papillae is the classic feature of dermatitis herpetiformis (DH). DH is an intensely pruritic, autoimmune blistering skin disease that is a cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease. The treatment of choice for dermatitis herpetiformis is the drug dapsone. Dapsone provides rapid and dramatic relief from the intense itching and blistering, often within 24-48 hours. Its mechanism of action in DH is thought to be related to its ability to inhibit neutrophil chemotaxis and function. While a strict gluten-free diet is essential for long-term management of the underlying celiac disease, dapsone is the first-line pharmacological agent for controlling the acute skin manifestations. Rituximab, cyclosporine, and azathioprine are other immunosuppressants used for different autoimmune conditions.
53.	 The Nigro regimen is used in the treatment of 
which condition?
(A)	Carcinoma of the anal canal
(B)	 Carcinoma of the colon
(C)	Carcinoma of the bladder
(D)	All of the above
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Carcinoma of the anal canal
The Nigro regimen is the standard, definitive treatment protocol for squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal. It is a combined modality chemoradiation therapy that has transformed the management of this disease, allowing for sphincter preservation and avoiding the need for radical surgery (abdominoperineal resection) in the majority of cases. The original regimen, developed by Dr. Norman Nigro, consists of external beam radiation therapy delivered to the primary tumor and regional lymph nodes, given concurrently with chemotherapy. The classic chemotherapy agents used are mitomycin-C and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU). This combined approach is highly effective, achieving complete remission in over 80% of patients with localized disease. The Nigro regimen is specific to anal cancer and is not used for colon or bladder cancer.
54.	 What is the mechanism through which anti-
migraine 
drugs 
can 
produce 
angina-like 
symptoms?
(A)	Release NO
(B)	 Inactivates Ca2+ channels
(C)	5-HT agonist
(D)	5-HT antagonist
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) 5-HT agonist
The primary classes of drugs used for the acute treatment of migraine are the triptans (e.g., sumatriptan) and the ergot alkaloids (e.g., ergotamine). The mechanism of action of both classes involves agonism at serotonin (5-HT) receptors, specifically the 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D subtypes. Their therapeutic effect is mediated by constricting dilated intracranial blood vessels and inhibiting the release of pro-inflammatory neuropeptides in the trigeminal system. However, these drugs are not entirely selective, and their agonist activity at 5-HT1B receptors located on coronary arteries can cause vasoconstriction of the coronary arteries. In susceptible individuals, particularly those with underlying coronary artery disease, this vasoconstriction can be significant enough to induce myocardial ischemia, leading to angina-like symptoms such as chest pain, tightness, or pressure. This is a well-known and important potential side effect of these drugs.

56.	 Which of the following drugs can aggravate

(C)	Lignocaine

(C) Lignocaine.
Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder where antibodies block or destroy acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. This leads to a decreased "safety factor" for muscle contraction, causing weakness. Drugs that interfere with this already fragile transmission can worsen symptoms or trigger a myasthenic crisis.
(C)	
Lignocaine (Lidocaine) : This drug is a local anesthetic and antiarrhythmic that works by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels. These channels are crucial for generating and propagating action potentials along the muscle fiber membrane. (B)	
Alpha blocker : This class of drugs is not typically associated with worsening MG. Beta-blockers, however, are known to be a risk.
(D)	
Penicillin : Penicillins are widely regarded as safe for use in patients with Myasthenia Gravis.
57.	 The HPV vaccine is based on which viral 
proteins?
(A)	E6 & E7
(B)	 E5
(C)	L1
(D)	E2
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) L1
The currently available Human papillomavirus vaccine is based on the L1 major capsid protein of the human papillomavirus (HPV). The L1 protein has the ability to self-assemble into virus-like particles (VLPs). These VLPs resemble the outer shell of the virus but do not contain viral DNA, making them non-infectious and safe.
When administered, these L1-based VLPs stimulate a strong neutralizing antibody response. The antibodies prevent HPV from attaching to and infecting epithelial cells, thereby providing protection against cervical cancer and other HPV-related cancers.
The early proteins E6 and E7 are oncogenic proteins responsible for malignant transformation (they inactivate tumor suppressor proteins p53 and Rb). However, they are not used in current prophylactic vaccines because they are expressed after infection and are associated with oncogenic activity.
Therefore, HPV vaccines such as Gardasil and Cervarix are based on the L1 capsid protein, not E6 or E7.
58.	 Which of the following methods can be used for 
therapeutic drug monitoring in a patient?
(A)	HPLC
(B)	 Nuclear Magnetic Resonance
(C)	Spectrophotometry
NODIA
page  677  	
INICET Examination Paper
(D)	Flow cytometry
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) HPLC
Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is the clinical practice of measuring the plasma concentration of a specific drug to maintain it within a target therapeutic range. This is essential for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, such as certain antiepileptics (e.g., phenytoin), antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin), and immunosuppressants (e.g., tacrolimus). Several analytical techniques are used for this purpose. High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) is a powerful and widely used technique in clinical laboratories for TDM. It works by separating the components of a mixture (like plasma) based on their physicochemical properties, allowing for the precise and accurate quantification of the specific drug of interest. While immunoassays are also very common, HPLC is a gold-standard reference method for many drugs. Spectrophotometry (C) is less specific, and NMR (B) and flow cytometry (D) are not used for routine TDM.
59.	 A psychotic patient presented with voluntary 
purposeless movements and was observed 
to stand still in the ward with negativism and 
waxy flexibility. What is the appropriate medical 
management?
(A)	Haloperidol
(B)	 Lorazepam
(C)	Clonidine
(D)	Risperidone
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Lorazepam
The patient's symptoms—purposeless movements, immobility (stupor), negativism (resistance to instructions), and waxy flexibility (maintaining an imposed posture)—are the classic motor signs of catatonia. Catatonia is a psychomotor syndrome that can occur in the context of psychotic, mood, or medical disorders. The first-line medical treatment for catatonia is a benzodiazepine. A "lorazepam challenge" is often used both diagnostically and therapeutically. Administration of an intravenous or intramuscular dose of lorazepam (typically 1-2 mg) often produces a rapid and dramatic, albeit temporary, improvement in the catatonic symptoms, confirming the diagnosis and guiding further treatment. High doses of benzodiazepines are the mainstay of therapy. While antipsychotics like haloperidol (A) or risperidone (D) may be needed to treat the underlying psychosis, they can sometimes worsen catatonia and carry a risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
60.	 Which of the following is true regarding the 
treatment of gout?
(A)	Aspirin is used because it is effective & most 
safe.

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Aspirin is not used because it increases uric acid levels.
The management of acute gout focuses on rapidly suppressing the intense inflammation. Aspirin is specifically avoided in the treatment of gout. At the low doses typically used for analgesia (<2 g/day), aspirin paradoxically decreases the renal excretion of uric acid by competing for the tubular secretion mechanism, which can worsen hyperuricemia and precipitate or prolong a gouty attack. Therefore, statement (B) is true, and (A) is false. The first-line treatments for an acute gout flare are NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids. Potent NSAIDs like indomethacin (C) or naproxen are highly effective and were traditionally the drugs of choice. While diclofenac (D) is also an effective NSAID, the reason given is not its primary justification. The most accurate statement regarding the options is the one explaining why aspirin is contraindicated.
61.	 A patient taking antiepileptic medication is 
diagnosed with neurocysticercosis. What should 
be the next steps in this patient’s management?
(A)	Give anti-parasite followed by steroid
(B)	 Steroid followed by antihelminthic drug
(C)	Steroid after stopping antiepileptic
(D)	Antiepileptic followed by antihelminthic 
drug
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Steroid followed by antihelminthic drug
Neurocysticercosis is a parasitic infection of the central nervous system caused by the larval cysts of Taenia solium. When antihelminthic drugs (like albendazole or praziquantel) are administered, they kill the cysticerci within the brain. The death of the parasite triggers a significant host inflammatory response around the degenerating cyst. This inflammation can lead to a dangerous increase in cerebral edema, worsening of neurological symptoms, and an increased risk of seizures. To mitigate this inflammatory response, it is standard practice to administer corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) before or concurrently with the initiation of the antihelminthic drug. The antiepileptic medication should be continued throughout this period to control seizures. Therefore, the correct sequence is to start steroids first to suppress inflammation, and then begin the anti-parasitic treatment.

62.	 You are an assistant surgeon working in a CHC 
and 13 year old rape victim is brought to you by 
her parents with history of sexual assault by 22-
year old male. The police from the concerned 
is not accompanying the victim. The victim 
is refusing to give consent for the medical 
examination and any further tests. What should 
be done in the above given scenario?
1	
Start treatment for STD and pregnancy
2	
Inform the police
3	
Record refusal of consent
4	
Take vaginal samples
5	
Start medical examination
(A)	1,2,3
(B)	 2,3,5
(C)	1,2,5
(D)	2,3
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) 1,2,3
This is a 13-year-old minor and therefore a child under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (POCSO Act). Sexual assault of a minor is a mandatory reportable offence, and healthcare providers are legally obligated to inform the police. Hence, informing the police (2) is compulsory, even if police have not accompanied the victim.
Since the child is refusing medical examination, consent is essential before any examination or sample collection. Under medico-legal and ethical guidelines, no physical examination or evidence collection (such as vaginal sampling) can be done without valid consent. Therefore, recording refusal of consent (3) in detail is mandatory.
However, even if examination is refused, the doctor has a duty to provide necessary emergency medical care, including prophylaxis for sexually transmitted diseases and pregnancy prevention, as these are in the best interest of the child. Thus, starting treatment for STD and pregnancy (1) is appropriate.
Taking vaginal samples (4) and starting examination (5) cannot be done without consent.
Therefore, the correct combination is 1, 2, and 3 (Option A).
63.	 Identify the process shown in the image.
(A)	Marbling
(B)	 Tattooing
(C)	Mummification
(D)	Embalming
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Marbling
The image shows a characteristic branching, greenish-black discoloration pattern over the skin, resembling a marble-like network. This is known as marbling, a postmortem change seen during decomposition.
Marbling occurs due to the breakdown of hemoglobin in blood vessels by bacteria during putrefaction. Hydrogen sulfide produced by bacterial action reacts with hemoglobin to form sulfhemoglobin, which stains the superficial veins. This produces a distinct reticular (branching) pattern along the course of subcutaneous veins.
It is an early sign of putrefaction and commonly appears over the abdomen and chest.
The other options are incorrect:
1.	
Tattooing refers to punctate abrasions caused by unburnt gunpowder.
2.	
Mummification is drying and preservation of the body in arid conditions.
3.	
Embalming is an artificial preservation process.
Since the image clearly shows venous pattern discoloration typical of decomposition, the process is marbling.

66.	 In a firearm injury, the blackening seen around 
the entry wound is due to :
(A)	Flame
(B)	 Smoke
(C)	Unburnt powder
(D)	Hot gases
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Smoke
The characteristics of a firearm entry wound provide crucial information about the range of fire. In a close-range or contact shot, several elements are discharged from the muzzle along with the bullet. The blackening of the skin immediately surrounding the entry wound is specifically caused by the deposition of smoke (soot) from the combustion of the gunpowder. This soot can be wiped away from the skin. Unburnt and partially burnt powder particles (C) are also discharged and can cause "tattooing" or "stippling" of the skin, which are small punctate abrasions that cannot be wiped away. The flame (A) and hot gases (D) discharged from the muzzle can cause burning or searing of the skin at very close range. The distinct black discoloration, however, is attributed to the smoke deposit.
67.	 What is the most common substance of abuse 
in India?
(A)	Cannabis
(B)	 Tobacco
(C)	Alcohol
(D)	Opium
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Tobacco
Tobacco is the most commonly abused substance in India. It is widely used in both smoked and smokeless forms, making it highly prevalent across different age groups and socioeconomic strata.
In India, tobacco is consumed as:
1.	
Cigarettes and bidis (smoked forms)
2.	
Gutka, khaini, paan with tobacco, and snuff (smokeless forms)
National surveys such as the Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS) consistently show that tobacco use is more prevalent than alcohol or illicit drugs. The ease of availability, low cost (especially bidis and smokeless tobacco), cultural acceptance in some regions, and addictive nature of nicotine contribute to its widespread use.
Although alcohol is also commonly consumed and cannabis or opium are used in certain areas, their overall prevalence is lower compared to tobacco.
Tobacco abuse is a major public health concern because it is strongly associated with oral cancer, lung cancer, COPD, cardiovascular disease, and stroke.
Therefore, the most common substance of abuse in India is tobacco.

70.	 A 47-year-old man presents with painful lesions 
on the glans penis. What is the likely cause of 
this condition?
(A)	HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus)
(B)	 Haemophilus
(C)	Chlamydia
(D)	Syphilis
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus)
The image displays multiple small blisters (vesicles) clustered together on a reddened base located on the glans penis. This clinical appearance of "grouped vesicles on an erythematous base" is the pathognomonic sign of a genital herpes infection, caused by the Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-2. The patient's symptom of pain is also a classic feature of a herpetic outbreak, which can be accompanied by burning and itching. The vesicles eventually rupture to form painful, shallow ulcers that then crust over and heal. Haemophilus ducreyi (B) causes chancroid, which presents as a painful ulcer from the start, not vesicles. Chlamydia (C) typically causes urethritis, not external lesions. Primary syphilis (D) classically presents as a single, painless ulcer (chancre). The vesicular nature of the lesions is the key diagnostic clue pointing directly to HSV.
71.	 A 22-year-old sexually active male presents with 
painful ulcers (as shown in the image). What is 
the likely finding?
(A)	HP Bodies
(B)	 Tzanck smear
(C)	Pund cells
(D)	None of these
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Tzanck smear
The presence of painful genital ulcers in a sexually active male has a differential diagnosis that primarily includes genital herpes (caused by Herpes Simplex Virus, HSV) and chancroid (caused by Haemophilus ducreyi). The lesions of HSV classically begin as painful vesicles that then rupture to form ulcers. A useful and rapid bedside diagnostic test for a suspected herpetic lesion is a Tzanck smear. This test involves scraping the base of a fresh ulcer or vesicle, smearing the cells onto a glass slide, and staining them with Giemsa or Wright stain. A positive finding is the presence of multinucleated giant cells with molded nuclei and intranuclear inclusions, known as Tzanck cells. This finding is highly suggestive of a herpesvirus infection. HP bodies (Henderson-Paterson bodies) (A) are found in molluscum contagiosum, which causes papules, not ulcers. The other options are not relevant to this clinical presentation.
72.	 Which disease has an almost 100% fatality rate 
once symptoms develop?
(A)	Rabies
(B)	 Nipah
(C)	Ebola
(D)	Measles
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Rabies
Rabies is an acute progressive viral encephalitis transmitted to humans through the saliva of infected animals, typically via a bite. While the disease is preventable with timely post-exposure prophylaxis, once clinical signs and symptoms develop, the disease is almost invariably fatal. The case fatality rate for symptomatic rabies approaches 100%. There are only a very small number of documented survivors of clinical rabies in the entire history of modern medicine, most of whom were treated with an experimental and not reliably successful protocol. This makes rabies one of the most lethal infectious diseases known. In contrast, while Nipah virus infection (B) and Ebola virus disease (C) are also extremely dangerous and have very high case fatality rates (which can range from 40% to over 90% depending on the strain and outbreak), survival is possible with intensive supportive care. Measles (D) has a much lower mortality rate.

(A)	Hyperkalemia
(B)	 Hyperthyroidism
(C)	Serum creatinine level
(D)	Decrease GFR
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Hyperkalemia
While Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) itself is a progressive condition, patients are at risk for several acute, life-threatening complications. The most common and immediate life-threatening electrolyte abnormality in advanced CKD is hyperkalemia (high serum potassium). The kidneys are the primary route for potassium excretion. As the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) falls, the ability to excrete potassium is impaired, leading to its accumulation in the blood. Severe hyperkalemia is a medical emergency because it alters the resting membrane potential of cardiac myocytes, leading to a high risk of fatal cardiac arrhythmias, such as ventricular fibrillation or asystole. While a decreased GFR (D) and high creatinine (C) define the disease, they are not the direct life-threatening event. Hyperthyroidism (B) is unrelated.
105.	 A 50-year-old alcoholic is brought to the hospital 
with bleeding esophageal varices and dies. At 
autopsy, his distended abdomen contains a large 
amount of serous fluid. What is the correct term 
for this fluid?
(A)	Exudate
(B)	 Ascites
(C)	Hemorrhage
(D)	Lymphedema
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Ascites
The clinical history describes a patient with decompensated liver cirrhosis, evidenced by bleeding esophageal varices. A major complication of cirrhosis is the development of portal hypertension. The high pressure in the portal venous system, combined with low serum albumin levels (due to impaired liver synthesis), causes fluid to shift from the vascular space into the peritoneal cavity. The accumulation of this serous fluid within the peritoneal cavity is specifically termed ascites. This fluid is typically a transudate, characterized by a low protein content, as opposed to an exudate (A), which is protein-rich and associated with inflammation. Hemorrhage (C) refers to bleeding, and lymphedema (D) is the accumulation of lymphatic fluid in the interstitial tissues, usually in the limbs. The correct term for the intra-abdominal fluid in this context is ascites.
106.	 A 20-year-old patient is rapidly gaining weight 
and has elevated TSH levels. What is the most 
likely diagnosis?
(A)	Hashimoto's thyroiditis
(B)	 Graves' disease
(C)	Pituitary tumor
(D)	Hypothyroidism
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) Hypothyroidism
The patient's symptoms of weight gain, combined with an elevated Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) level, point directly to a diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism. In primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid gland itself is failing and cannot produce enough thyroid hormone (T4 and T3). The low levels of circulating thyroid hormone lead to a loss of negative feedback on the pituitary gland. In response, the pituitary secretes an increased amount of TSH in an attempt to stimulate the failing thyroid. The clinical symptoms of hypothyroidism, such as weight gain, fatigue, and cold intolerance, are due to the deficiency of thyroid hormone. Hashimoto's thyroiditis (A) is the most common cause of primary hypothyroidism, but "hypothyroidism" (D) is the overall diagnosis. Graves' disease (B) is a cause of hyperthyroidism with a suppressed TSH. A TSH-secreting pituitary tumor (C) would cause hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism.
107.	 A woman presents with dark knuckles and 
anemia. What type of anemia is most likely?
(A)	Megaloblastic anemia
(B)	 Iron deficiency anemia
(C)	Anemia of chronic disease
(D)	None of these
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Megaloblastic anemia
The combination of anemia and hyperpigmentation, particularly over the knuckles and other sun-exposed areas or in skin creases, is a classic, though not universally present, clinical sign of megaloblastic anemia caused by Vitamin B12 deficiency. This hyperpigmentation is thought to be due to increased melanin synthesis, although the exact mechanism is not fully understood. Vitamin B12 deficiency leads to impaired DNA synthesis, affecting rapidly dividing cells in the bone marrow and resulting in the production of large, immature red blood cells (megaloblasts) and anemia. While iron deficiency anemia (B) and anemia of chronic disease (C) are common, they are not typically associated with knuckle hyperpigmentation. This specific skin finding, when present with anemia, should strongly raise the suspicion of Vitamin B12 deficiency.
108.	 A patient has a gangrenous ulcer on the left 
toe and experiences early fatigue in the right 
lower limb while walking. What is the most 
appropriate investigation?
(A)	CT angiogram
(B)	 MR angiogram
(C)	Duplex scan
(D)	Digital subtraction angiography
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) Digital subtraction angiography
The patient's symptoms are highly indicative of severe, multilevel peripheral arterial disease (PAD). The gangrenous ulcer on the left toe represents critical limb ischemia, while the fatigue (claudication) in the right lower limb indicates significant arterial stenosis on that side as well. While a duplex scan (C) is an excellent initial non-invasive test, and CT or MR angiography (A, B) provide detailed anatomical maps, the gold standard for both diagnosis and guiding intervention is Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA). DSA is an invasive procedure where a catheter is inserted into the arterial system and contrast dye is injected. It provides the highest-resolution images of the vascular lumen, allowing for precise localization of stenoses and occlusions, and detailed assessment of collateral circulation. Crucially, it also allows for percutaneous intervention (like angioplasty or stenting) to be performed during the same procedure.
109.	 A patient has had fever, headache, neck stiffness, 
photophobia, and an erythematous chest rash for 
4 days, with no recent travel or tick bite history. 
Which cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings would 
most likely be seen in this case?
(A)	Elevated protein levels
(B)	 Normal glucose levels
(C)	Lymphocytosis
(D)	All of the above
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) All of the above
The patient's clinical presentation of fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia is a classic meningeal syndrome. The presence of a rash and the likely subacute onset point towards a viral or aseptic cause rather than a typical bacterial cause. The characteristic cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profile for aseptic (viral) meningitis includes several key findings. There is typically a pleocytosis (increased white blood cell count), which is predominantly lymphocytic (C). The protein level is usually mildly to moderately elevated (A) due to inflammation and disruption of the blood-brain barrier. Crucially, the glucose level is typically normal (B), as viruses do not consume glucose in the CSF. This is a key feature that distinguishes viral from bacterial meningitis, where the glucose is usually low. Since all three of these CSF findings are characteristic of viral meningitis, the correct answer is all of the above.
110.	 A 68-year-old man with a recent syncopal 
episode, congestive heart failure, and a grade 
III/IV harsh systolic murmur is found on 
echocardiography to have marked ventricular 
septal thickening and systolic anterior motion of 
the mitral valve. Which of the following findings 
is most likely to be present in this patient?
(A)	Radiation of the murmur to the neck
(B)	 Decrease of the murmur with handgrip
(C)	Delayed carotid upstroke
(D)	Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Decrease of the murmur with handgrip
The patient's presentation and echocardiographic findings are diagnostic of Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM). The harsh systolic murmur in HOCM is caused by the dynamic outflow tract obstruction created by the thickened septum and the systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve. The intensity of this murmur is unique in that it changes with maneuvers that alter preload and afterload. Maneuvers that decrease preload or afterload (like standing or Valsalva) make the obstruction worse and increase the murmur's intensity. Conversely, maneuvers that increase preload (squatting) or increase afterload (like a sustained handgrip) will decrease the outflow gradient and therefore decrease the intensity of the murmur. Delayed carotid upstroke (C) and radiation to the neck (A) are characteristic of aortic stenosis. The ejection fraction in HOCM is typically preserved or hyperdynamic, not reduced (D).
111.	 What are the admission criteria for COVID-19?
(A)	Multiple comorbidities
(B)	 Chest discomfort
(C)	Dyspnea
(D)	All the above
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) All the above
The decision to admit a patient with COVID-19 to the hospital is based on an assessment of the severity of their illness and their risk for deterioration. While mild cases can be managed at home, certain signs and symptoms warrant hospital admission for monitoring and treatment. The most important indication is evidence of respiratory compromise, such as dyspnea (shortness of breath) (C) or a low oxygen saturation. The presence of chest discomfort or pain (B) is also a significant symptom that requires evaluation and admission. Additionally, patients with multiple comorbidities (A) (such as diabetes, heart disease, chronic lung disease, or immunosuppression) are at a much higher risk for developing severe disease, and a lower threshold for admission is often applied to this group, even with seemingly mild symptoms. Therefore, all of the factors listed are valid criteria that would contribute to the decision to admit a patient with COVID-19.
112.	 Which of the following is not a part of high-
quality CPR?
(A)	Chest compressions 100-120/min
(B)	 Allow chest recoil
(C)	Chest wall depression of 5-6 cm
(D)	Respiratory rate of 20-25/min
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) Respiratory rate of 20-25/min
High-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is critical for improving outcomes in cardiac arrest. The key components, as defined by international guidelines (e.g., American Heart Association), include :
Pushing hard and fast : Compressing the chest at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute (A) to an adequate depth of at least 2 inches (5-6 cm) in adults (C).
Allowing for full chest recoil between compressions (B) to permit the heart to fill with blood.
 Minimizing interruptions in chest compressions.
When providing rescue breaths with an unprotected airway, the correct compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30 :2. If an advanced airway is in place, breaths are given at a rate of 1 breath every 6 seconds, which equates to a respiratory rate of 10 breaths per minute. A respiratory rate of 20-25/min (D) is too high and would constitute hyperventilation, which is detrimental as it increases intrathoracic pressure and decreases venous return.
113.	 A female develops pallor and cyanosis when 
exposed to cold water. All of the following 
conditions can cause this except which one?
(A)	Hyperthyroidism
(B)	 Migraine
(C)	Sumatriptan use
(D)	Smoking
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Hyperthyroidism
The patient's symptoms of episodic, cold-induced digital color changes (pallor followed by cyanosis) describe Raynaud's phenomenon. This is a condition of exaggerated vasospasm of the digital arteries. It can be primary (Raynaud's disease) or secondary to various conditions. Many factors are known to precipitate or are associated with Raynaud's. Smoking (D) is a major vasoconstrictor and a well-known exacerbating factor. Certain medications, such as sumatriptan (C), which is a serotonin agonist used for migraines, can cause vasospasm and are associated with Raynaud's. There is also a known association between migraine headaches (B) and Raynaud's phenomenon, likely due to a shared underlying predisposition to vasospasm. In contrast, hyperthyroidism (A) is a state of hypermetabolism characterized by heat intolerance and peripheral vasodilation, not vasospasm. Hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism, can sometimes be associated with secondary Raynaud's phenomenon.

due to a diarrheagenic strain of Escherichia coli

type of virulent E. coli best fits this presentation?
(A)	Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC)
(B)	 Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC)
(C)	Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC)
(D)	Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC)

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC)
Escherichia coli has several diarrheagenic strains, each producing distinct clinical syndromes.
Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) invades and destroys colonic epithelial cells, producing an illness similar to shigellosis. It causes fever, malaise, prostration, abdominal cramps, and dysentery (blood and mucus in stool). Because it invades the intestinal mucosa, it produces inflammatory diarrhea with systemic symptoms and dehydration — matching this clinical presentation.
In contrast:
1.	
EAEC causes persistent watery diarrhea, mainly in children and travelers, without prominent dysentery.
2.	
EHEC (e.g., O157:H7) causes bloody diarrhea but typically has little or no fever and may lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). Antibiotics are avoided due to HUS risk.
3.	
EPEC causes watery diarrhea, mainly in infants, without invasive dysentery.
Since this patient has fever, systemic toxicity, dysentery, and dehydration, the presentation is most consistent with Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC).
81.	 A patient presents with pneumonia, and culture

(A) Actinomyces
This question describes the key laboratory features of the genus Actinomyces. Actinomyces species are Gram-positive, filamentous, branching rods that are part of the normal oral flora. They are fastidious and grow best under strict anaerobic conditions. When cultured, they characteristically form colonies that are rough, white, and raised, resembling the surface of a molar tooth. The patient's presentation with pneumonia suggests an aspiration event, which is the typical route for pulmonary actinomycosis. While the question states the organism is catalase and oxidase positive, this is variable among species and may be an error in the question stem, as A. israelii is typically catalase-negative. However, the combination of Gram-positive branching rods, anaerobic growth, and molar tooth colonies is highly specific for Actinomyces. H. influenzae (B), Pseudomonas (C), and E. coli (D) are all Gram-negative organisms.
82.	 A chest X-ray shows cavitary lesions. The

(A) Nocardia asteroides
This question provides a classic constellation of findings for pulmonary nocardiosis. The chest radiograph showing cavitary lesions indicates a necrotizing pneumonia. 83.	 The Gram-stained smear of urethral exudate 
from a male (shown in the photo) is diagnostic 
for which disease?
(A)	Chancroid
(B)	 Gonorrhea
(C)	Lymphogranuloma venereum
(D)	Nongonococcal urethritis
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Gonorrhea
The image provided is a Gram stain of a urethral smear. It shows multiple polymorphonuclear leukocytes (neutrophils), and critically, within the cytoplasm of these neutrophils, there are numerous small, kidney-bean-shaped, Gram-negative (pink) cocci arranged in pairs (diplococci). The presence of these intracellular Gram-negative diplococci is the pathognomonic and diagnostic microscopic finding for gonorrhea, an infection caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae. 85.	 What is the most appropriate method for 
reviewing previous research studies?
(A)	Meta analysis
(B)	 Chi-Square test
(C)	Cross-sectional study
(D)	Case control study
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Meta analysis
To synthesize and study the findings from a collection of previously conducted research studies on a specific topic, the most rigorous and powerful method is a meta-analysis. A meta-analysis is a quantitative, formal, epidemiological study design used to systematically assess the results of previous research to derive conclusions about that body of research. It goes beyond a simple literature review by using statistical methods to combine the effect estimates from individual studies, resulting in a single, more precise, and powerful summary estimate. This allows for a comprehensive and objective evaluation of the existing evidence. A chi-square test (B) is a statistical test used within a single study. Cross-sectional (C) and case-control (D) studies are designs for conducting primary research, not for synthesizing the results of previous studies.
86.	 What is the most suitable option for mass 
chemoprophylaxis 
against 
anemia 
in 
a 
population?
(A)	Ferrous Sulphate
(B)	 Ferrous Fumarate + B12 + Folic Acid + 
Vitamin C
(C)	Intravenous Iron
(D)	Ferrous Ascorbate
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Ferrous Sulphate
For mass chemoprophylaxis of anemia in a population, the ideal preparation should be effective, safe, inexpensive, widely available, and suitable for large-scale public health distribution. Ferrous sulphate fulfills these criteria and is the most commonly recommended iron preparation in national anemia control programs.
Ferrous sulphate contains a high proportion of elemental iron, is cost-effective, and has well-established efficacy in preventing and treating iron deficiency anemia. It is included in government initiatives such as the Anemia Mukt Bharat strategy under the National Health Mission in India. The tablet form allows easy distribution in schools, antenatal clinics, and community health programs.
Combination preparations containing vitamin B12, folic acid, and vitamin C are more expensive and unnecessary for routine mass prophylaxis unless specific deficiencies are documented. Intravenous iron is reserved for severe anemia or malabsorption and is not practical for community-level prophylaxis.
Therefore, for large-scale public health prevention of anemia, ferrous sulphate is the most suitable option.

(A)	Mass is mobile only in plane perpendicular 
to mesentery
(B)	 Mass is brilliantly transilluminating
(C)	Mass felt in the peri-umbilical region
(D)	Fluctuation positive

(A) Mass is mobile only in plane perpendicular to mesentery
A mesenteric cyst is a rare, benign, fluid-filled sac located within the mesentery of the small intestine. A key clinical feature that helps in its diagnosis is its characteristic mobility on physical examination. This is known as Tillaux's sign (or Tillaux's triad, which also includes a dull percussion note and a location in the umbilical region). The sign describes that the mass is mobile in the direction perpendicular to the line of attachment of the mesentery, but its mobility is restricted in the direction parallel to the mesenteric root. The root of the small bowel mesentery runs obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure in the left upper quadrant down to the ileocecal junction in the right lower quadrant. Therefore, the cyst can be moved from side-to-side (perpendicular to this line) but not up-and-down (parallel to this line). This specific pattern of mobility is highly suggestive of a mesenteric origin.

138.	 Persistent dribbling of urine in a child who 
otherwise urinates normally is most likely due 
to which condition?
(A)	Ectopic ureter since birth
(B)	 Ureterocele
(C)	ARPKD
(D)	Cystocele
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Ectopic ureter since birth
The clinical history of continuous, day-and-night urinary dribbling in a female child who also has a normal pattern of voiding (i.e., she can hold urine and void voluntarily) is the classic and pathognomonic presentation of an ectopic ureter. In this congenital anomaly, the ureter from the upper pole of a duplicated renal system or a single system does not insert correctly into the bladder trigone. Instead, it inserts distally to the urethral sphincter mechanism, typically into the urethra, vagina, or vestibule. Because the opening is outside the control of the sphincter, urine from the kidney it drains will leak continuously, causing constant wetness, while the normally draining kidney and bladder function correctly, allowing for normal voiding patterns. A ureterocele (B) may cause obstruction or reflux but not this specific pattern of incontinence.
139.	 A patient with nephrotic syndrome is currently 
taking steroids. Which statement regarding the 
vaccines that can be administered is true?
(A)	Vaccination as per schedule
(B)	 Pneumococcal vaccine has to be given prior 
to treatment
(C)	Only killed vaccines can be given
(D)	OPV should not be given to siblings
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Only killed vaccines can be given
A patient with nephrotic syndrome who is receiving high-dose steroids is considered immunocompromised. Corticosteroids suppress cell-mediated immunity, increasing the risk of infection and reducing the body’s ability to handle live attenuated vaccines safely.
In such patients, live vaccines are contraindicated during immunosuppressive therapy because they may cause vaccine-derived infection. Live vaccines include OPV, MMR, varicella, and BCG. These should be deferred until steroid therapy is stopped and immune function has recovered (usually after at least 1 month of stopping high-dose steroids).
However, inactivated (killed) vaccines are safe and can be administered, although their immune response may be slightly reduced. Vaccines such as inactivated influenza vaccine and pneumococcal vaccine are recommended because nephrotic patients are at increased risk of infections.
Vaccination strictly “as per schedule” is not correct during active immunosuppression. Pneumococcal vaccine ideally should be given before steroid therapy but can still be given later if missed.
Thus, during steroid therapy in nephrotic syndrome, only killed vaccines should be given.

The image shows a radiant warmer, also known as an infant warmer. This is a key piece of equipment found in delivery rooms and neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). 141.	 Congenital pyloric stenosis presents with which 
of the following?
(A)	Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic 
alkalosis
(B)	 Abdominal mass
(C)	Bilious vomiting
(D)	A & B Both
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) A & B Both
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is a condition seen typically in infants between 2–8 weeks of age. It occurs due to hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle, leading to gastric outlet obstruction.
Projectile, non-bilious vomiting is the hallmark feature because the obstruction is proximal to the duodenum; therefore, bile does not mix with gastric contents. Hence, option (C) bilious vomiting is incorrect.
Due to repeated vomiting of gastric contents (which contain hydrochloric acid), there is loss of hydrogen and chloride ions. This results in hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, making option (A) correct. Persistent vomiting also leads to dehydration.
On abdominal examination, a firm, olive-shaped mass may be palpated in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. This palpable “pyloric olive” represents the hypertrophied pylorus, making option (B) correct.
Thus, congenital pyloric stenosis presents with metabolic alkalosis and an abdominal mass, so the correct answer is A and B (Option D).
142.	 A child has a bed-wetting habit, and organic 
causes have been excluded. What is the 
appropriate management?
(A)	Pharmacotherapy
(B)	 Psychotherapy
(C)	Bed alarm
(D)	Acupuncture
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Bed alarm
The condition described is primary nocturnal enuresis, which is bed-wetting in a child older than 5 years who has never achieved a consistent period of nighttime dryness, and in whom organic causes have been excluded. The first-line management involves conservative measures and behavioral therapy. The most effective and recommended behavioral therapy with the highest long-term success rate is the enuresis alarm, or bed alarm. This device consists of a moisture sensor placed in the child's underwear that is connected to an alarm. When the child begins to urinate, the sensor triggers the alarm, which wakes the child. Over time, this conditions the child to recognize the sensation of a full bladder and to wake up to void before the alarm goes off. Pharmacotherapy (A), such as with desmopressin or imipramine, is considered a second-line option for short-term control but has a high relapse rate when stopped.

143.	 If a doctor is inserting screws into the vertebrae, 
where will these screws be placed?
(A)	Pedicle	
(B)	 Lamina
(C)	Spine	
(D)	Facet joints
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Pedicle
In modern spinal fusion and instrumentation surgery, the most common and biomechanically robust method for achieving fixation to the vertebrae is through the use of pedicle screws. The pedicle is a strong, cylindrical pillar of bone that connects the posterior elements (lamina, facets) of a vertebra to the vertebral body. Placing a screw down the central axis of the pedicle and into the vertebral body allows for a rigid, three-column purchase on the vertebra. This provides a very strong anchor point to which rods can be attached to stabilize the spine, correct deformities, or facilitate fusion. While other fixation methods exist (e.g., laminar hooks or screws, facet screws), pedicle screw instrumentation is the workhorse of contemporary spinal surgery due to its superior strength and versatility. "Spine" (C) is too general.

Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic, progressive optic neuropathy characterized by a specific pattern of optic nerve head damage and corresponding visual field loss. A hallmark feature of glaucoma is that it typically affects the peripheral visual field first, while central visual acuity remains preserved until the late stages of the disease. 98.	 In which of the following conditions is iritis 
commonly observed?
(A)	Bechet's disease
(B)	 SLE
(C)	Rheumatoid Arthritis
(D)	Psoriatic Arthritis
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Behçet's disease.
Iritis, which is inflammation of the iris (the colored part of the eye), is a form of anterior uveitis. While it can be associated with several systemic inflammatory conditions, it is a hallmark feature of Behçet's disease.
1.	
Behçet's Disease : This is a rare autoimmune disorder that causes inflammation in blood vessels throughout the body. Ocular involvement is very common, affecting up to 70% of patients. Iritis (anterior uveitis) is one of the most frequent eye problems seen in this condition, often being recurrent and severe.

Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) : In adults with RA, the most common inflammatory eye condition is scleritis (inflammation of the white part of the eye), not iritis. Dry eye syndrome is also very common. Iritis is more typically associated with the juvenile form of arthritis (JIA).
4.	
Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) : Iritis does occur in patients with psoriatic arthritis, with a prevalence of about 7-25%. However, the association and frequency are considered strongest and most characteristic in Behçet's disease.
99.	 Which of the following drugs are used to 
distinguish a fixed, dilated pupil?
(A)	4% Cocaine
(B)	 Pilocarpine
(C)	Phenylephrine
(D)	Adrenaline
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Pilocarpine
A fixed dilated pupil can be caused by several conditions, including a third nerve palsy, pharmacological blockade (mydriasis), or Adie's tonic pupil. A pharmacological test using dilute pilocarpine is used to help differentiate the cause. Pilocarpine is a direct-acting cholinergic agonist that constricts the pupil.
1.	
Adie's tonic pupil : This is caused by denervation of the postganglionic parasympathetic supply to the iris sphincter. The denervated muscle becomes supersensitive to acetylcholine. A very dilute (e.g., 0.125%) pilocarpine solution, which would have no effect on a normal pupil, will cause marked constriction in an Adie's pupil, confirming the diagnosis.
2.	
Pharmacological blockade : If the pupil is dilated by an anticholinergic drug (like atropine), it will not constrict even to a standard strength (1%) pilocarpine solution.
3.	
Third nerve palsy : A pupil dilated due to a third nerve palsy will constrict in response to a standard strength (1%) pilocarpine solution.

101.	 Identify the nerve from the list provided that

(B)	 Oculomotor Nerve
(C)	Trochlear Nerve
(D)	Abducent Nerve
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Optic Nerve
The movements of the eyeball are controlled by the six extraocular muscles, which are innervated by three specific cranial nerves, known as the oculomotor nerves.
1.	
The oculomotor nerve (CN III) (B) innervates the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique muscles.
2.	
The trochlear nerve (CN IV) (C) innervates the superior oblique muscle.
3.	
The abducens nerve (CN VI) (D) innervates the lateral rectus muscle.

103.	 All of the following are true about Gout, except :
(A)	Occurs due to accumulation of urate crystals

(C)	Birefringent crystals are present in joint
(D)	Occurs more in females
AAns

(D) Occurs more in females
This statement is the exception because it is false. Gout has a strong predilection for males, who are affected much more commonly than females, especially before the age of menopause. The incidence in women increases after menopause as the uricosuric effect of estrogen is lost. The other statements are all true. 87.	 What does the difference between the maximum 
and minimum values in a dataset represent?
(A)	Mean	
(B)	 Median
(C)	Range	
(D)	Mode
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Range
In descriptive statistics, several measures are used to summarize a dataset. The range is the simplest measure of dispersion or variability. It is defined as the difference between the maximum (highest) and minimum (lowest) observed values in a dataset. It provides a quick and easy-to-calculate indication of the spread of the data. For example, if the test scores in a class are from 65 to 95, the range is 95 - 65 = 30. While it is simple, it is highly sensitive to outliers and does not provide information about the distribution of values between the two extremes. The mean (A) is the average, the median (B) is the middle value, and the mode (D) is the most frequent value; these are all measures of central tendency, not dispersion.
88.	 All of the following clinical features are seen in 
Zika fever except :
(A)	Guillain-Barre syndrome
(B)	 Petechial rash
(C)	Fever with arthralgia
(D)	Conjunctivitis
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Petechial rash
Zika virus infection is typically a mild febrile illness. The most common clinical features are a low-grade fever with arthralgia (joint pain) (C), a diffuse maculopapular rash, and non-purulent conjunctivitis (D). While the acute illness is usually mild, Zika is known for its severe neurological complications. It is a recognized trigger for the development of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) (A), an acute autoimmune demyelinating polyneuropathy, in adults. The most devastating complication is congenital Zika syndrome in infants born to mothers infected during pregnancy. The rash associated with Zika is typically maculopapular (composed of flat red spots and small raised bumps). A petechial rash (B), which consists of small, non-blanching spots caused by intradermal hemorrhage, is not a characteristic feature of Zika fever. Petechiae are more commonly associated with other viral infections like dengue fever or with meningococcemia.

(D)	C & A
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) A, B & D
The World Health Organization's "5 Moments for Hand Hygiene" outline the critical points during patient care when hand hygiene is required to prevent the transmission of healthcare-associated infections. Alcohol-based hand sanitizer is the preferred method for hand hygiene when hands are not visibly soiled. These moments include :
1.	
Moment : Before touching a patient (A), to protect the patient from harmful germs carried on your hands.
2.	
Moment : Before a clean or aseptic procedure.
3.	
Moment : After a body fluid exposure risk.
4.	
Moment : After touching a patient (B), to protect yourself and the healthcare environment from the patient's germs.
5.	
Moment : After touching the patient's surroundings (D), even if you haven't touched the patient directly.
Crucially, hand sanitizer is not effective when hands are visibly dirty or soiled (C). In that situation, hands must be washed with soap and water.
90.	 Which 
discrete 
probability 
distribution 
describes the likelihood of a certain number of 
events occurring within a fixed interval of time 
or space?
(A)	Gaussian
(B)	 Binomial
(C)	Poisson
(D)	Erlang
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Poisson
The Poisson distribution is a discrete probability distribution that is used to model the number of events occurring within a specified, fixed interval of time or space. It is applicable when these events occur with a known constant mean rate and independently of the time since the last event. Classic examples include the number of phone calls received by a call center in one hour, the number of mutations in a given stretch of DNA, or the number of radioactive decay events in a second. The Binomial distribution (B) describes the number of successes in a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials. The Gaussian (Normal) distribution (A) is a continuous probability distribution, not a discrete one. The Erlang distribution (D) is a continuous distribution related to waiting times.
91.	 Which device is used to indicate heat exposure 
in vaccines?
(A)	VVM
(B)	 VMV
(C)	MMV
(D)	VMM
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) VVM
A Vaccine Vial Monitor (VVM) is a small, heat-sensitive label that is placed on a vaccine vial to provide a visual indication of its cumulative heat exposure over time. The VVM consists of a dark outer circle and a lighter inner square. The inner square is made of a heat-sensitive material that darkens gradually and irreversibly when exposed to heat. The rule for interpreting a VVM is : "If the inner square is the same color as or darker than the outer circle, do not use the vaccine." This simple tool allows healthcare workers to determine if a vaccine has been exposed to potentially damaging temperatures and should be discarded, ensuring that only potent vaccines are administered. It is a critical component of the cold chain management system for many vaccines.

92.	 All of the following are complications of Otitis

(B)	 Griesinger Sign
(C)	Battle Sign
(D)	Bezold's Sign
AAns

(C) Battle Sign
Otitis media can lead to several serious intracranial and extracranial complications. Griesinger's sign (B) is edema and tenderness over the mastoid process due to thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein, a sign of sigmoid sinus thrombosis. Bezold's abscess (D) is a deep neck abscess that forms when pus from mastoiditis erodes through the mastoid tip and tracks down the sternocleidomastoid muscle. 94.	 Sequence of Auditory Pathway?
1.	 Cochlear nucleus
2.	 Spiral ganglion
3.	 Auditary cortex
4.	 Inferior colliculus
5.	 Superior olivary nucleus
6.	 Lateral lemniscus
7.	 Medial geniculate body
(A)	1234567
(B)	 2156473
(C)	2134567
(D)	2176543
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) 2156473
The central auditory pathway follows a specific sequence from the ear to the brain.
1.	
The first-order neurons are in the spiral ganglion (2) in the cochlea. Their axons form the auditory nerve.
2.	
The auditory nerve synapses on the cochlear nucleus (1) in the brainstem.
3.	
From the cochlear nucleus, fibers ascend bilaterally, with many crossing over and synapsing in the superior olivary nucleus (5), which is crucial for sound localization.
4.	
Axons from these nuclei then ascend in a tract called the lateral lemniscus (6).
5.	
The fibers of the lateral lemniscus synapse in the inferior colliculus (4) of the midbrain.
6.	
From the inferior colliculus, neurons project to the medial geniculate body (7) of the thalamus, the main auditory relay station.
7.	
Finally, fibers from the medial geniculate body project to the primary auditory cortex (3) in the temporal lobe.
The correct sequence is 2 → 1 → 5 → 6 → 4 → 7 → 3.
95.	 Which of the following is not an objective test?
(A)	Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry 
(BERA)
(B)	 Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)
(C)	Impedance Audiometry
(D)	Pure Tone Audiometry
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) Pure Tone Audiometry
Audiological tests can be classified as objective or subjective (behavioral). Objective tests do not require a behavioral response from the patient; they measure a physiological response. Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA) or ABR (A), Impedance Audiometry (including tympanometry and acoustic reflex testing) (C), and otoacoustic emissions are all objective tests. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) (B) is an objective imaging test used in ophthalmology, not audiology. In contrast, Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA) is a subjective or behavioral test. It requires the patient to listen to tones of specific frequencies and intensities and provide a conscious response (e.g., by raising a hand or pressing a button) when they hear the tone. The results depend entirely on the patient's perception and cooperation, making it a subjective measure of hearing thresholds.

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D)	Pulmonary TB
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Bronchiectasis
The patient's long-standing history of a chronic productive cough with mucopurulent sputum is the classic symptom of bronchiectasis. Bronchiectasis is a chronic respiratory disease characterized by the permanent and abnormal dilation of the bronchi and bronchioles. This structural damage impairs the mucociliary clearance mechanism, leading to the pooling of secretions, chronic bacterial infection, and a persistent inflammatory cycle. Radiologically, the hallmark of bronchiectasis is bronchial wall thickening ("tram tracking") and airway dilation. On a CT scan, this can appear as dilated, thick-walled airways, a "signet ring" sign, or, in severe cases, the formation of clusters of cystic-like spaces, which is consistent with the finding described in the question. While cystic fibrosis (C) and post-infectious causes like TB (D) are major causes of bronchiectasis, the diagnosis describing the final pathological state is bronchiectasis itself.
115.	 What is the size of a pink IV cannula?

(B)	 18 G
(C)	22 G
(D)	16 G

Intravenous (IV) cannulas are universally color-coded to allow for rapid identification of their gauge size. The gauge number indicates the internal diameter of the cannula, with a smaller number corresponding to a larger diameter and a higher potential flow rate. The standard color code for a 20-gauge IV cannula is pink. 116.	 A farmer develops a painless foot lesion with 
multiple discharging sinuses. What is the most 
likely diagnosis?
(A)	Mycetoma
(B)	 Squamous Cell Carcinoma
(C)	Sporotrichosis
(D)	None of these
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Mycetoma
The clinical triad of a painless, tumefied (swollen) subcutaneous lesion, the formation of multiple draining sinuses, and the discharge of grains (macroscopic colonies of the causative agent) is pathognomonic for mycetoma, also known as Madura foot. This is a chronic, progressive, granulomatous infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissues that can extend to involve the underlying fascia and bone. It is typically caused by the traumatic inoculation of soil-dwelling organisms into the foot, making farmers a high-risk group. The infection can be caused by either fungi (eumycetoma) or filamentous bacteria (actinomycetoma). Sporotrichosis (C) classically presents with lymphocutaneous spread. Squamous cell carcinoma (B) would present as a non-healing ulcer or fungating mass, but not typically with multiple sinuses discharging grains.
117.	 What is the first and specific marker for 
myocardial infarction (MI)?
(A)	LDH
(B)	 Troponin
(C)	CK (Creatine Kinase)
(D)	None of the above
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Troponin
Cardiac troponins (specifically troponin T and troponin I) are regulatory proteins that are components of the contractile apparatus of cardiac muscle. They are highly specific to the myocardium. When myocardial cells are damaged and undergo necrosis during a myocardial infarction (MI), these proteins are released into the bloodstream. The measurement of serum cardiac troponin levels is the current gold standard and the most sensitive and specific biochemical marker for the diagnosis of MI. Troponins begin to rise in the blood within 2-4 hours of the onset of injury, peak at 12-24 hours, and can remain elevated for 7-14 days. While Creatine Kinase (CK), especially the CK-MB isoenzyme, was previously used, it is less specific than troponin as it is also found in skeletal muscle. LDH (A) is even less specific and is no longer used for diagnosing MI.

This is a duplicate of a previous question. The patient has suffered a severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) from an RTA, resulting in a deep coma with a GCS score of 3 (E1, V1, M1). 120.	 A 45-year-old female reports breast pain, edema, 
redness, warmth, and rapid enlargement over 15 
days. What is the likely diagnosis?
(A)	IBC (Inflammatory Breast 
Cancer)
(B)	 Giant fibroadenoma
(C)	Atypical duct hypertrophy
(D)	Galactocele
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) IBC (Inflammatory Breast Cancer)
The patient's presentation with a rapidly progressive, painful, red, warm, and swollen breast is a classic and highly concerning picture for Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC). IBC is a rare but extremely aggressive form of breast cancer. It is characterized by the diffuse infiltration and blockage of the dermal lymphatics by cancer cells. This lymphatic obstruction is what causes the characteristic signs of inflammation : erythema (redness), edema (swelling), and a "peau d'orange" (orange peel) appearance of the skin. A key feature is the rapid onset and progression of these symptoms, often over a period of days to weeks, frequently without a distinct palpable lump. While mastitis is a differential, in a non-lactating woman, IBC must be ruled out first.
121.	 Which of the following statements about a 
pilonidal sinus is incorrect?
(A)	It is more common in men.
(B)	 Hair follicles are seen in the wall of sinus.
(C)	Mostly congenital.
(D)	Treatment of choice is surgical excision of 
sinus tract.
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Mostly congenital.
This statement is incorrect. For many years, pilonidal sinus disease was thought to be a congenital condition arising from a remnant of the neural tube. However, the modern and widely accepted understanding is that it is an acquired condition. The process is believed to begin with the stretching and blockage of hair follicles in the natal cleft. Loose hairs are then driven into these dilated follicles by friction and pressure, creating a foreign body reaction that leads to the formation of a sinus tract and recurrent inflammation or abscess. The other statements are correct. Pilonidal sinus is significantly more common in men (A), particularly in hirsute individuals. The sinus tracts characteristically contain nests of hair, but hair follicles are not seen in the wall of the sinus (B), which supports the acquired theory (hair is driven in from the outside). The definitive treatment is surgical excision of the sinus tract (D).

123.	 What is the most common retroperitoneal 
tumor?
(A)	Liposarcoma
(B)	 Rhabdomyosarcoma
(C)	Synovial sarcoma
(D)	Neurofibrosarcoma
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Liposarcoma
Primary retroperitoneal tumors are rare, and the vast majority are malignant soft tissue sarcomas. The single most common histological type of primary retroperitoneal sarcoma in adults is liposarcoma. These tumors arise from adipose tissue within the retroperitoneum and can grow to an enormous size before they cause symptoms. They account for approximately one-third of all retroperitoneal sarcomas. The second most common type is leiomyosarcoma, which arises from smooth muscle. 125.	 What is the most likely diagnosis for the ulcer

The image shows a deep, "punched-out" ulcer located on a pressure-bearing point on the sole of the foot, specifically over a metatarsal head. The surrounding skin is often callused.
