129.	 Which of the following is not a component of 
the qSOFA score?
(A)	BP
(B)	 RR
(C)	Heart rate
(D)	Mental status
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Heart rate
The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score is a simple bedside tool used to identify patients with suspected infection who are at a high risk of poor outcomes (i.e., sepsis). It consists of three clinical criteria, with one point awarded for each :
1.	
Respiratory Rate (RR) : A high respiratory rate of ≥ 22 breaths per minute.
2.	
Mental Status : An altered mental status, typically assessed with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of < 15.
3.	
Blood Pressure (BP) : A low systolic blood pressure of ≤ 100 mmHg.
A score of 2 or more suggests a high risk of sepsis and warrants further investigation and management. Heart rate is not a component of the qSOFA score, although tachycardia is a common sign of sepsis and is included in the more comprehensive SIRS criteria and the full SOFA score.
130.	 A 13-year-old girl presents with a left-sided neck 
swelling that has grown slowly since childhood 
and feels hard on examination. What is the most 
likely diagnosis?
(A)	Neural tumor
(B)	 Chemodectoma
(C)	Lipoma
(D)	Cystic hygroma
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Neural tumor
In a young patient presenting with a slow-growing, hard, deep-seated neck mass, a benign neural tumor should be a primary consideration. Specifically, a schwannoma or a neurofibroma, which are tumors arising from the nerve sheaths of peripheral nerves, fit this description well. These tumors can originate from various nerves in the neck, such as the vagus nerve or branches of the cervical plexus. They are typically firm, mobile, and grow very slowly over many years. A cystic hygroma (D), a lymphatic malformation, is typically soft, cystic, and present in infancy. A lipoma (C) is a benign tumor of fat cells and is characteristically soft and doughy, not hard. A chemodectoma (B), or carotid body tumor, is a paraganglioma that is typically found in middle-aged adults, is pulsatile, and is classically mobile side-to-side but not vertically (Fontaine's sign). Therefore, a neural tumor is the most likely diagnosis for a hard, slow-growing mass in this age group.
131.	 Regarding the boundaries of the laparoscopic 
anatomy of an inguinal hernia, which of the 
following statements is false?
(A)	Medial boundary of triangle of Doom is vas 
deferens
(B)	 Lateral boundary of triangle of pain is 
Iliopubic tract
(C)	Myopectineal orifice is bounded by internal 
oblique & transverse abdominis superiorly
(D)	Myopectineal orifice is bounded by Iliopubic 
tract inferiorly
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) Myopectineal orifice is bounded by Iliopubic tract inferiorly
In laparoscopic inguinal anatomy, understanding the Myopectineal Orifice of Fruchaud is vital for successful hernia repair. The statement in (D) is false because the inferior boundary of this orifice is the pectineal ligament (Cooper’s ligament) and the superior pubic ramus, not the iliopubic tract.
The iliopubic tract actually serves as a key landmark for the Triangle of Pain, forming its lateral and superior border. This triangle is clinically significant because it contains the lateral femoral cutaneous and genitofemoral nerves; placing surgical tacks here can lead to chronic nerve entrapment.
Conversely, the Triangle of Doom is defined medially by the vas deferens and laterally by the spermatic vessels. Surgeons must avoid this zone to prevent life-threatening injury to the external iliac artery and vein. Finally, the superior boundary of the Myopectineal Orifice consists of the arching fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. Mastering these boundaries allows surgeons to safely navigate the "Circle of Death" and ensure mesh coverage over all potential hernia sites.
132.	 A patient has had severe abdominal pain for 2 
hours, blood pressure 90/60, pulse 112/min with 
an irregular rhythm, repeated vomiting, a soft 
abdomen, and absent bowel sounds. What is the 
most likely diagnosis?
(A)	Peptic perforation
(B)	 Ruptured aortic aneurysm
(C)	Acute mesenteric ischemia
(D)	Severe acute pancreatitis
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Acute mesenteric ischemia
This clinical presentation is a classic picture of acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI). The most pathognomonic feature described is the significant disparity between the patient's severe, excruciating abdominal pain and the relatively benign findings on physical examination (a soft, often non-tender abdomen). This "pain out of proportion to physical findings" is the hallmark of AMI. The patient is also in shock (hypotension and tachycardia) due to bowel ischemia and third-spacing of fluid. The presence of an irregular pulse strongly suggests atrial fibrillation, which is the most common cause of superior mesenteric artery embolism, the leading cause of AMI. The absent bowel sounds indicate an adynamic ileus secondary to the bowel infarction. A peptic perforation (A) would cause peritonitis and a rigid abdomen. Severe pancreatitis (D) and a ruptured aneurysm (B) would typically be associated with significant abdominal tenderness and guarding on examination.

134.	 A 45-year-old female has a 4.5 × 3 cm irregular

(D) a, c & d
The patient has a clinically suspicious breast mass and a palpable axillary lymph node, which is highly concerning for locally advanced breast cancer. 135.	 In the Strasberg classification of biliary injury, a 
posterior sectoral duct injury falls under which 
class?
(A)	Type B	
(B)	 Type C
(C)	Type D	
(D)	Type E
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Type C
The Strasberg classification is a widely used system to categorize iatrogenic bile duct injuries that occur during cholecystectomy.
1.	
Type A : Leak from the cystic duct stump or a small duct in the gallbladder fossa.
2.	
Type B : Occlusion of a part of the biliary tree, most commonly an aberrant right hepatic duct.
3.	
Type C : A transected (but not ligated) duct that is leaking bile. This most commonly involves a transected aberrant right hepatic duct or a posterior sectoral duct.
4.	
Type D : A lateral or partial injury to a major bile duct, such as the common bile duct, with bile leakage.
5.	
Type E : A circumferential injury or transection of the main bile duct, further subdivided based on the level of the injury.
Therefore, an injury involving the transection and subsequent leak from a posterior sectoral duct is classified as a Strasberg Type C injury.
136.	 A 40-year-old female undergoes cholecystectomy 
and later develops postoperative abdominal 
pain. Which test is used to detect a bile leak?
(A)	ERCP
(B)	 MRCP
(C)	HIDA
(D)	CECT
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) HIDA
When a post-cholecystectomy bile leak is suspected, the most sensitive and specific functional imaging study to identify the leak is a HIDA scan (Hepatobiliary Iminodiacetic Acid scan), also known as cholescintigraphy. This is a nuclear medicine test where a radioactive tracer (e.g., technetium-99m labeled mebrofenin) is injected intravenously. The tracer is taken up by the hepatocytes and excreted into the biliary system, mimicking the flow of bile. The flow of the tracer is imaged over time with a gamma camera. In a patient with a bile leak, the scan will show the tracer flowing normally through the bile ducts but will also demonstrate the abnormal extravasation of the tracer from the biliary tree into the peritoneal cavity, confirming the presence, and often the location, of the leak. While MRCP (B) shows anatomy and ERCP (A) is therapeutic, HIDA is the best test to functionally demonstrate an active leak.

74.	 Which structure is disrupted by Vibrio cholerae?
(A)	Hemidesmosome
(B)	 Gap junctions
(C)	Zona occludens
(D)	Zona adherens
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Zona occludens
The massive, watery diarrhea characteristic of cholera is caused primarily by the action of the cholera toxin, which leads to a profound secretory state in the intestinal epithelial cells. However, the integrity of the intestinal barrier is also compromised. The zona occludens, also known as the tight junction, is the most apical intercellular junction that seals the space between adjacent epithelial cells, regulating the paracellular pathway. Vibrio cholerae produces several toxins in addition to the main cholera toxin. One of these is the zonula occludens toxin (Zot), which directly acts on and disrupts the structure of the tight junctions. This disruption increases the permeability of the paracellular pathway, leading to the leakage of fluid and electrolytes from the tissues into the intestinal lumen, which contributes significantly to the voluminous diarrhea. Hemidesmosomes (A) and zona adherens (D) are anchoring junctions, while gap junctions (B) are for cell-to-cell communication.
75.	 Galactomannan in the serum is found in which 
of the following conditions?
(A)	Invasive aspergillosis
(B)	 Candidiasis
(C)	Mucormycosis
(D)	Candida
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Invasive aspergillosis
Galactomannan is a polysaccharide that is a major component of the cell wall of fungi in the genus Aspergillus. During invasive growth, the fungus releases this antigen into the host's circulation. Therefore, the detection of galactomannan antigen in the serum or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid is a highly specific and widely used biomarker for the diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis. This is particularly useful in high-risk, immunocompromised patients, such as those with neutropenia or who have undergone hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, as it allows for an early diagnosis before the disease becomes clinically apparent. The cell walls of Candida species (B, D) are primarily composed of beta-glucan and mannan, not galactomannan. The cell walls of the fungi causing mucormycosis (C) also do not contain galactomannan.

145.	 Which of the following investigations can be 
used in osteoporosis?
1.	 DEXA
2.	 Bone Scan
3.	 Quantitative CT
4.	 Chemical Analysis
Select the answer using the following key-
(A)	1,2	
(B)	 1,2,3
(C)	1,3,4	
(D)	1,2,3,4
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) 1,3,4
Osteoporosis is characterized by reduced bone mineral density (BMD) and increased fracture risk. The investigations used aim to measure bone density and evaluate metabolic causes.
1.	
DEXA (Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) is the gold standard for diagnosing osteoporosis. It measures bone mineral density at the hip and spine and provides a T-score for assessment.
2.	
Quantitative CT (QCT) is another method that measures volumetric bone density and can assess trabecular bone separately. Though less commonly used due to higher radiation exposure and cost, it is a valid diagnostic tool.
3.	
Chemical analysis refers to biochemical investigations such as serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D, and parathyroid hormone levels. These tests help identify secondary causes of osteoporosis.
4.	
Bone scan (nuclear medicine scan) is not used to diagnose osteoporosis. It detects areas of increased bone turnover, such as metastasis, infection, or fractures, but does not measure bone density.
Thus, the correct combination is 1, 3, and 4 (Option C).

147.	 The middle radioulnar joint is which type of 
joint?
(A)	Primary cartilaginous
(B)	 Secondary cartilaginous
(C)	Fibrous joint
(D)	Plain synovial
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Fibrous joint
The forearm contains three joints between the radius and the ulna. The superior (proximal) and inferior (distal) radioulnar joints are both pivot-type synovial joints that allow for pronation and supination. The middle radioulnar joint, however, is not a true articulating joint. It is the connection between the shafts of the radius and ulna, which are joined together by a strong, broad, flat ligamentous sheet called the interosseous membrane. This type of articulation, where two bones are held together by a ligament or a sheet of fibrous tissue, is classified as a syndesmosis, which is a type of fibrous joint. This joint allows for very limited movement but is crucial for transferring forces from the radius to the ulna and for providing a surface for muscle attachment. A primary cartilaginous joint (A) is a synchondrosis, and a secondary cartilaginous joint (B) is a symphysis.
148.	 If all parts of the sternum and the medial end 
of the clavicle are ossified, what is the estimated 
age?
(A)	18-25 years	
(B)	 >25 years
(C)	14-15 years	
(D)	< 15 years
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) >25 years
This question uses key skeletal maturation milestones for age estimation. The sternum ossifies from several centers. The fusion of the manubrium with the body (manubriosternal joint) occurs late in life, but the fusion of the four sternebrae of the body is typically complete by 25 years of age. The xiphoid process also fuses with the body later. The most critical landmark provided is the medial clavicular epiphysis. This is one of the last epiphyses in the entire body to fuse. The fusion process begins around age 18-22 and is generally complete by 25 to 31 years of age. Therefore, if both the sternum and the medial clavicle are observed to be fully ossified and fused, it is a strong indicator that the individual is older than 25 years. This milestone is particularly useful in forensic anthropology for determining if an individual has reached adulthood.

What happens when a person moves from a lying (supine) position to standing?
(A)	
Increase firing in baroreceptor afferents
(B)	
Decrease firing in baroreceptor afferents
(C)	
Vagal output to cardiac fibers increase
(D)	
B and C Both
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
14.	 (B) Decrease firing in baroreceptor afferents
When a person stands up from a supine 
position, gravity causes blood to pool in the 
veins of the lower extremities. This leads to a 
transient decrease in venous return to the heart, 
a decrease in cardiac output, and consequently, 
a drop in arterial blood pressure. This fall in 
blood pressure is sensed by the high-pressure 
baroreceptors located in the carotid sinus and 
the aortic arch. These receptors are stretch 
receptors, and the reduced stretch due to the 
lower blood pressure causes a decrease in the 
firing rate of the baroreceptor afferent nerves 
that travel to the brainstem. This decreased 
afferent signal triggers a compensatory reflex 
: 
sympathetic 
output 
increases 
(causing 
vasoconstriction and increased heart rate), and 
vagal (parasympathetic) output to the heart 
decreases (C is incorrect), all aimed at restoring 
the blood pressure to its normal level.

What is the sequence of events after the "P" wave?
A.	
"a" wave
B.	
1st heart sound
C.	
Rapid filling of ventricles
D.	
"t" wave
(A)	
A > C > B > D
(B)	
C > A > D > B
(C)	
B > D > A > C
(D)	
A > C > D > B
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
16.	 (A) A > C > B > D.
Cardiac Cycle Sequence
To understand the correct order, let's trace the 
events that follow the P wave, which represents 
the electrical depolarization of the atria. 
1.	 P wave (Atrial Depolarization) → Atrial 
Contraction
i.	
A. "a" wave : The contraction of the 
atria increases atrial pressure, causing 
a corresponding pressure wave in the 
jugular veins known as the "a" wave. This 
happens immediately after the P wave.
ii.	 C. Rapid filling of ventricles : The 
contracting atria push the final volume 
of blood into the ventricles. This phase is 
more accurately called "late ventricular 
filling" or the "atrial kick," but it follows 
the "a" wave as the pressure from the 
contraction drives the blood flow.
2.	 QRS Complex (Ventricular Depolarization) 
→ Ventricular Contraction B. 1st heart 
sound (S1) : As the ventricles begin to 
contract (systole), the pressure inside them 
quickly rises above the pressure in the atria. 
This forces the atrioventricular (mitral and 
tricuspid) valves to snap shut, producing the 
first heart sound ("lub"). This event occurs 
after the QRS complex, which follows the P 
wave.
3.	 T wave (Ventricular Repolarization) D. "t" 
wave : This wave on the ECG represents 
the repolarization (electrical reset) of the 
ventricles. It occurs during the latter part of 
ventricular contraction, after the first heart 
sound but before the second heart sound.
Therefore, the correct chronological sequence 
of these events after the P wave is : "a" wave

The patient has severe, extensive plaque psoriasis. Systemic therapies are required for this extent of disease. Methotrexate (A), cyclosporine (D), and phototherapy with Narrowband UVB (C) are all standard and effective treatments for severe psoriasis. Systemic steroids (e.g., oral prednisone), however, should not be used for the chronic management of plaque psoriasis. While they can produce a rapid initial improvement, their withdrawal is notoriously associated with a severe, and sometimes life-threatening, rebound flare of the psoriasis. The clinical presentation of multiple, very painful, soft genital ulcers with ragged, undermined edges is highly characteristic of chancroid, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Haemophilus ducreyi. 162.	 What is the type of lesion seen in the following

In dermatology, lesion shape and configuration are key to diagnosis. The image shows a single skin lesion that is ring-shaped, with a raised or active border and central clearing. This specific shape is described by the term annular. 163.	 What is the investigation of choice for diagnosing 
allergic contact dermatitis?
(A)	IgE
(B)	 Radioallergosorbent test (RAST)
(C)	Patch Test
(D)	ROAT Test
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Patch Test
Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a classic example of a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction. It is T-cell mediated and does not involve IgE antibodies. Therefore, tests for Type I hypersensitivity, such as measuring total or specific IgE (A) or the Radioallergosorbent test (RAST) (B), are not relevant for diagnosing ACD. The gold standard and investigation of choice for identifying the causative allergen in ACD is the patch test. This test involves applying small amounts of suspected allergens onto the skin, usually on the back, under occlusive patches. The patches are left in place for 48 hours and then removed. The skin is then read at 48 hours and again at 72 or 96 hours. A positive reaction, which appears as a localized area of eczema (erythema, papules, vesicles), indicates that the patient is allergic to that specific substance.

164.	 You see an unconscious man, what will you do?
(A)	Check carotid pulse, start CPR, call for help
(B)	 Call for help, check carotid pulse, give CPR
(C)	Go to a hospital emergency
(D)	Observe the patient
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Call for help, check carotid pulse, give CPR
This question assesses the basic life support (BLS) algorithm for an unresponsive adult. The correct sequence of actions for a single rescuer is :
1.	
Check for safety of the scene.
2.	
Check for responsiveness (tap and shout).
3.	
If unresponsive, immediately shout for nearby help and activate the emergency response system (e.g., call the local emergency number). If you are alone, you can do this with a mobile phone on speaker.
4.	
Simultaneously, check for breathing and a carotid pulse for no more than 10 seconds.
5.	
If there is no pulse or no normal breathing, immediately begin high-quality CPR, starting with chest compressions.
Option (B) follows this correct sequence : activating help first, then assessing the patient, and then initiating CPR. Option (A) incorrectly prioritizes starting CPR before calling for help, which would delay the arrival of advanced medical care and a defibrillator.

Different dilutions of adrenaline (epinephrine) are used for specific clinical applications and routes of administration to ensure safety and efficacy.

170.	 What is the most common drawback of the 
instrument shown in the image?
(A)	Portability
(B)	 Does not provide instant 
relief
(C)	Drug deposited in oropharynx
(D)	Must be administered in 
hospital settings
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Drug deposited in oropharynx
The image shows a metered-dose inhaler (MDI), a common device for delivering inhaled medications for asthma and COPD. One of the major drawbacks of using an MDI is that it requires a precise coordination between actuating (pressing) the canister and inhaling slowly and deeply. Many patients have difficulty with this technique. Poor coordination leads to the high-velocity aerosolized drug particles impacting on and being deposited in the oropharynx (the back of the mouth and throat) instead of being inhaled deeply into the lungs. This oropharyngeal deposition reduces the amount of drug reaching the target site in the airways, decreasing its efficacy, and can increase local side effects, such as oral candidiasis with inhaled corticosteroids. Using a spacer device can significantly reduce this problem by slowing the aerosol and allowing more time for inhalation. Portability (A) is an advantage, not a drawback.
171.	 What is the gauge size of the orange cannula?
(A)	14G
(B)	 20G
(C)	22G
(D)	18G
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) 14G
Peripheral intravenous (IV) cannulas are color-coded to provide a quick and reliable way to identify their size (gauge). The gauge number is inversely proportional to the cannula's diameter, so a smaller gauge number indicates a larger bore and a higher potential fluid flow rate. The standard color code for a 14-gauge IV cannula is orange. This is a very large-bore cannula that allows for extremely rapid infusion of fluids or blood products. It is typically reserved for major trauma situations, rapid sequence induction in anesthesia, or major surgeries where massive and rapid fluid resuscitation is anticipated. For reference, a 20G cannula is pink (B), a 22G cannula is blue (C), and an 18G cannula is green (D).

The FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma) exam is a rapid point-of-care ultrasound protocol to detect free fluid (hemoperitoneum) or pericardial effusion in trauma patients. The eFAST (Extended FAST) exam incorporates additional views to assess for intrathoracic injuries. The eFAST exam includes the four standard abdominal views of the FAST exam (hepatorenal, splenorenal, suprapubic/pelvic, and subxiphoid), plus views of the thorax to look for pneumothorax and hemothorax. 173.	 Which X-ray view is used for the frontal sinus?
(A)	Water's view
(B)	 Caldwell Luc view
(C)	Granger's view
(D)	Campwell view
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Caldwell Luc view
The Caldwell view is a specific radiographic projection used to visualize the paranasal sinuses. It is an occipito-frontal view taken with the patient's forehead and nose against the image receptor and the X-ray beam angled approximately 15 degrees caudally. This specific angulation projects the dense petrous ridges of the temporal bone downwards, below the orbits, providing a clear, unobstructed view of the frontal sinuses. It also provides a good view of the ethmoid sinuses. In contrast, the Water's view (A) (occipito-mental view) is angled to provide the best view of the maxillary sinuses. The term "Caldwell-Luc view" is slightly confused; the Caldwell view is the X-ray, while the Caldwell-Luc operation is a surgical procedure on the maxillary sinus. Granger's and Campwell views are not standard sinus views.

The patient's clinical presentation of hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and multiple lytic "punched-out" bone lesions in the skull is the classic picture of the multisystem, multifocal form of Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LCH). LCH is a rare disorder involving the abnormal proliferation of Langerhans cells. The treatment for multisystem LCH involves systemic chemotherapy. Which of the following muscles does not take part in abducting the arm overhead?

Serratus anterior

Deltoid

(D) Pectoralis major
Abduction of the arm to an overhead position 
(180 degrees) is a coordinated movement 
involving both the glenohumeral joint and the 
scapulothoracic articulation, a process known 
as scapulohumeral rhythm. The deltoid muscle 
(B) is the prime mover of abduction at the 
glenohumeral joint up to 90 degrees. To achieve 
abduction beyond 90 degrees, the scapula 
must upwardly rotate on the thoracic wall. 
This crucial upward rotation is accomplished 
by a force couple created by the upper and 
lower fibers of the trapezius muscle (C) and 
the powerful serratus anterior muscle (A). The 
serratus anterior protracts the scapula and is 
essential for its upward rotation. In contrast, the 
primary actions of the pectoralis major muscle 
(D) are adduction and medial rotation of the 
humerus. It acts as an antagonist to abduction 
and therefore is not involved in, and in fact 
opposes, the action of overhead abduction.

(A)Reticular fibers are absent in :
(A)	
Bone marrow
(B)	
Spleen
(C)	
Thymus
(D)	
Lymph node
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
1.	
(C) Thymus
Reticular fibers, which are composed of 
type III collagen, form a delicate, intricate 
meshwork that provides structural support to 
the parenchymal cells of most lymphoid and 
hematopoietic organs. This reticular stroma 
is a characteristic feature of the bone marrow 
(A), the spleen (B) (in the white and red pulp), 
and the lymph nodes (D), creating a scaffold for 
lymphocytes, macrophages, and other immune 
cells. The thymus (C) is the distinct exception 
among these organs. The structural framework 
of the thymus is not made of reticular fibers but 
is instead formed by a unique cytoreticulum 
composed of specialized cells called thymic 
epithelial cells (also known as epithelioreticular 
cells). These cells provide the necessary support 
and create the microenvironment essential for 
the maturation and selection of T-lymphocytes 
(thymocytes). This cellular, rather than fibrous, 
stroma is a key histological feature that 
distinguishes the thymus from other lymphoid 
tissues.

A patient is unable to abduct the upper limb. Which nerve root is affected?
(A)	
C4
(B)	
C5
(C)	
C6
(D)

3.	
(B) C5
The abduction of the upper limb is a complex 
movement primarily performed by the deltoid 
and supraspinatus muscles. The initiation 
of abduction (the first 0-15 degrees) is by the 
supraspinatus muscle, which is innervated by 
the suprascapular nerve (with root values C5 
and C6). The main power for abduction from 
15 to 90 degrees comes from the deltoid muscle, 
which is innervated by the axillary nerve. The

a profound inability to abduct the arm. The C6 
root also contributes but is more associated with 
elbow flexion.

151.	 A pregnant woman experiences nighttime 
cramps. What should the nurse advise her to do?
(A)	Plantar flexion with knee flexion
(B)	 Plantar flexion with knee extension
(C)	Dorsiflexion with knee flexion
(D)	Dorsiflexion with knee extension
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) Dorsiflexion with knee extension
Leg cramps, particularly in the calf muscles (gastrocnemius), are a common and painful complaint during pregnancy. The cramp is a sustained, involuntary contraction of the muscle. To relieve the cramp, the muscle must be passively stretched. The gastrocnemius muscle crosses both the knee and the ankle joint; it acts to flex the knee and plantarflex the foot. Therefore, to achieve the maximum stretch of this muscle, one must perform the opposite actions. This involves keeping the knee in full extension and forcefully dorsiflexing the foot (pulling the toes up towards the head). This maneuver elongates the gastrocnemius muscle, which helps to break the muscle spasm and relieve the cramp. Plantar flexion (A, B) would shorten the muscle and worsen the cramp.

The position of the fetus is described by the relationship of a chosen landmark on the fetal presenting part (in a vertex presentation, this is the occiput) to the mother's pelvis (anterior, posterior, right, or left). In the diagram labeled 'B', the fetal occiput is pointing towards the right side (R) and the anterior quadrant (A) of the maternal pelvis. Therefore, this position is correctly described as Right Occipito-Anterior (ROA). This, along with Left Occipito-Anterior (LOA), is one of the most common and favorable positions for a normal vaginal delivery. An ROT position would have the occiput pointing directly to the right (transverse).
153.	 Identify the procedure in the image shown 
below.

(B)	 Fundal Grip

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Lateral Grip
The image clearly depicts and labels the Second Leopold's Maneuver. This is one of the four standard obstetric maneuvers used to determine the position of the fetus in the uterus. This specific maneuver is also known as the "Lateral Grip" or "Umbilical Grip." It is performed by the examiner placing the palms of their hands on either side of the maternal abdomen. Gentle but deep pressure is then applied to palpate the sides of the uterus. The purpose of this maneuver is to determine on which side the firm, smooth fetal back is located and on which side the irregular, nodular small parts (limbs) are located. This information helps to determine the fetal lie and position. The Fundal Grip is the first maneuver, Pawlik's Grip is the third, and the Pelvic Grip is the fourth.
154.	 A midwife is examining a pregnant woman and 
notices an umbilical cord prolapse. What should 
be the next step in management?
(A)	Gently push the cord back inside the uterus.
(B)	 Immediately 
transfer 
the 
patient 
for

(C)	Perform a per vaginal (PV) examination to 
assess the situation.
(D)	Place the patient in the Trendelenburg 
position.
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) Place the patient in the Trendelenburg position.
Overt umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency where the umbilical cord descends ahead of the fetal presenting part after the membranes have ruptured. The immediate and critical risk is compression of the cord between the fetus and the maternal pelvis, which can cut off the fetal blood supply, leading to severe hypoxia and death. The first-line management is to immediately relieve the pressure on the cord. This is done by placing the mother in a position that uses gravity to move the fetus away from the pelvis, such as the steep Trendelenburg position (head down) or the knee-chest position. Simultaneously, the person who diagnosed the prolapse should insert two fingers into the vagina to manually elevate the fetal presenting part off the cord. Pushing the cord back in (A) is contraindicated. While immediate delivery (B) is the definitive treatment (usually by emergency C-section), relieving the pressure is the first step.
155.	 What is the minimum cervical dilation at which 
a partograph should be initiated?
(A)	2cm
(B)	 4cm
(C)	6cm
(D)	8cm
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) 4cm
A partograph is a graphical tool used to monitor the progress of labor and identify any abnormalities in a timely manner. Plotting on the partograph should begin when the woman enters the active phase of the first stage of labor. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), which developed the most widely used partograph, the active phase of labor is considered to begin when the cervix is dilated to 4 cm and there are regular, painful uterine contractions. Once the woman reaches 4 cm dilation, the cervical dilation is plotted on the partograph against time, with an alert line and an action line to help identify prolonged labor. Starting the partograph before the active phase (e.g., at 2 cm) is not recommended as the rate of cervical dilation during the latent phase is slow and unpredictable. (Note : More recent definitions define active labor as starting at 6 cm, but the 4 cm rule for initiating the partograph is still the standard teaching).
156.	 A woman is advised to undergo a Pap smear and 
asks what it is. How would you explain it to her?

(C)	It's diagnostic for cervical cancer

(A) It's screening for cervical cancer
The Papanicolaou test, or Pap smear, is a cornerstone of public health and preventive medicine. Its primary purpose is to screen for cervical cancer and its precancerous lesions. The test involves collecting a sample of cells from the cervix, which are then examined under a microscope to detect any cytological abnormalities (dysplasia or carcinoma in situ) that could, if left untreated, progress to invasive cervical cancer. It is a screening test, not a diagnostic test. If the Pap smear is abnormal, a diagnostic procedure such as a colposcopy and biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis (C is incorrect). 157.	 HPV causes cervical carcinoma due to which of 
the following?
(A)	E1, E2
(B)	 E2, E6
(C)	L1, E6
(D)	E2,E4
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) E2, E6
Cervical carcinoma caused by high-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is primarily driven by the viral oncoproteins E6 and E7. However, their activity is linked to the function of the E2 protein.
Here's the mechanism :
1.	
E6 and E7 are the main culprits : The E6 protein targets and promotes the degradation of the host's p53 tumor suppressor protein (the "guardian of the genome"). The E7 protein inactivates the retinoblastoma (Rb) tumor suppressor protein. The loss of these two key proteins leads to uncontrolled cell proliferation and prevents damaged cells from undergoing apoptosis (programmed cell death).
2.	
E2 is the regulator : In a normal, non-cancerous HPV infection, the E2 protein acts as a repressor, keeping the expression of E6 and E7 in check.
3.	
The cancerous switch : For cancer to develop, the circular HPV DNA usually integrates into the host cell's chromosome. This integration process often breaks the viral genome within the E2 gene, disrupting its function.  With E2 inactivated, there are no "brakes," leading to massive over expression of E6 and E7, which drives the cell towards malignancy.
Therefore, the interplay between the disruption of E2 and the oncogenic action of E6 is central to HPV-induced cancer.

The slow waves (basic electrical rhythm or BER frequency) are lowest in which of the following?
(A)	
Stomach
(B)	
Duodenum
(C)	
Jejunum
(D)	
Ileum
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
11.	 (A) Stomach
Slow waves, also known as the basic electrical 
rhythm (BER), are spontaneous, rhythmic 
fluctuations in the membrane potential of 
gastrointestinal smooth muscle cells. They are 
generated by specialized pacemaker cells called 
the interstitial cells of Cajal. While these waves 
do not cause contractions themselves, they 
determine the maximum frequency at which 
contractions can occur. The frequency of the 
BER follows a gradient along the GI tract. It is 
highest in the proximal small intestine, with 
the duodenum (B) having a rate of about 12 
cycles per minute. The frequency then decreases 
distally through the jejunum (C) and ileum (D) 
(to about 8-9 cycles per minute). The stomach 
(A), however, has a much lower intrinsic BER 
frequency, with only about 3 slow waves per 
minute. Therefore, among the options provided, 
the frequency of slow waves is least in the 
stomach.

176.	 What is the most common CT scan lung image 
finding in a COVID-19 patient?
(A)	Consolidation
(B)	 Opacities
(C)	Effusion
(D)	Cystic Lesions
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(B) Opacities
The most common and characteristic finding of COVID-19 pneumonia on a chest CT scan is the presence of ground-glass opacities (GGOs). "Opacities" is a general term that encompasses GGOs. GGOs are areas of hazy, increased lung density that do not obscure the underlying bronchial and vascular markings. In COVID-19, these opacities are typically bilateral, have a peripheral and subpleural distribution, and are most prominent in the lower lobes. They often have a rounded or geographic shape. While consolidation (A) (denser opacification that obscures vessels) can also be seen, often in combination with GGOs (a "mixed" pattern), pure GGOs are the earliest and most frequent finding. Pleural effusion (C) and cystic lesions (D) are considered atypical or uncommon findings in COVID-19 pneumonia.
177.	 What is the most common lung finding on chest 
X-ray (CXR) of COVID-19?
(A)	Diffuse alveolar damage
(B)	 Pulmonary infarction
(C)	Fibrin thrombi
(D)	Endothelial injury
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Diffuse alveolar damage (DAD).
The most common findings on a chest X-ray of a patient with COVID-19 pneumonia are bilateral ground-glass opacities and consolidation, often located in the periphery of the lungs. 
These radiological signs are the direct macroscopic result of an underlying microscopic injury : Diffuse Alveolar Damage. DAD is the pathological process where the lung's tiny air sacs (alveoli) and blood vessels are injured, leading to inflammation and fluid leakage. This damage is what creates the hazy, opaque appearance on the X-ray film.
The other options are not primary radiological findings. Endothelial injury (D) and fibrin thrombi (C) are microscopic processes that are invisible on an X-ray. Pulmonary infarction (B) is a possible complication from blood clots, but it is not the most common, characteristic pattern seen in COVID-19 pneumonia.

178.	 A 5-year-old child presents with selective 
mutism. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	Childhood anxiety
(B)	 Childhood fear
(C)	Childhood Depression
(D)	Childhood Psychosis
AAns

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Childhood anxiety
Selective mutism is an anxiety disorder characterized by a child's consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where there is an expectation for speaking (e.g., at school), despite speaking normally in other situations (e.g., at home). The child's inability to speak is not due to a language disorder or physical inability but is driven by severe anxiety. Selective mutism is considered to be a manifestation of social anxiety or social phobia in children. Therefore, the most probable underlying or associated diagnosis is a childhood anxiety disorder. The mutism is a behavioral response to the overwhelming anxiety experienced in certain social settings. It is not typically a feature of childhood depression (C) or psychosis (D). While fear (B) is related, anxiety is the broader and more accurate diagnostic category for the underlying psychopathology.
179.	 Subcortical dementia seen in?
A. Parkinson's disease
B. Wilson's disease
C. Huntington's disease
D. Pick's disease
(A)	ABC only
(B)	 A & B only
(C)	A & C only
(D)	ACD only
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) ABC only
Dementias can be broadly classified as cortical or subcortical, based on the primary site of pathology. Subcortical dementias are characterized by prominent deficits in executive function, psychomotor slowing, and mood changes, with memory impairment being less severe initially. The pathology primarily involves structures deep within the brain, such as the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem nuclei.
Parkinson's disease (A), Wilson's disease (B), and Huntington's disease (C) are all classic examples of conditions that primarily affect subcortical structures and can lead to a subcortical dementia syndrome.
In contrast, Pick's disease (D) (a type of frontotemporal dementia) and Alzheimer's disease are classic examples of cortical dementias, where the pathology predominantly affects the cerebral cortex, leading to prominent early memory loss (amnesia), language deficits (aphasia), and visuospatial problems (agnosia).

181.	 A 40-year-old man says he feels his feet are 
dirty even though he knows this isn’t true. This

aspect of thought?
(A)	Possession
(B)	 Flow
(C)	Form
(D)	Content
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(D) Content
The patient is describing an obsession, which is a key feature of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD). An obsession is a recurrent and persistent thought, urge, or image that is experienced as intrusive and unwanted and causes marked anxiety or distress. The patient's thought that his feet are dirty is the obsession. The key aspect here is what the patient is thinking about. This relates to the content of thought. Disorders of thought content include delusions, overvalued ideas, and obsessions. 182.	 How will you differentiate delirium from 
dementia in Alzheimer's disease?
(A)	Disorientation and agitation
(B)	 Visual hallucinations and impairment of 
memory
(C)	Acute onset and level of consciousness
(D)	Agitation and irritation
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Acute onset and level of consciousness
Delirium and dementia can present with overlapping symptoms like confusion and memory impairment, and delirium is often superimposed on a baseline dementia. However, there are key features that help to differentiate them. The most crucial distinguishing feature is the onset and course. Dementia, like Alzheimer's disease, has an insidious onset and a progressive, chronic course. Delirium, on the other hand, is characterized by an acute onset (developing over hours to days) and a fluctuating course. The second cardinal feature that distinguishes delirium is a disturbance in the level of consciousness, awareness, and attention. Patients with delirium have a clouded sensorium and are inattentive, whereas in dementia, the level of consciousness is typically preserved until the very late stages. While symptoms like agitation (A, D) and hallucinations (B) are common in delirium, they can also occur in dementia, making them less reliable differentiating factors than the acute onset and altered level of consciousness.
183.	 A patient with severe depression was treated 
with a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) and 
showed improvement after 4 weeks. At the 
time of discharge, what is the most important 
concern?
(A)	Suicidal tendencies related to TCA overdose
(B)	 Therapeutic drug monitoring of TCA
(C)	ECG monitoring for arrhythmias
(D)	To prescribe modafinil to counteract 
sedation due to TCA
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(A) Suicidal tendencies related to TCA overdose
A critical period in the treatment of severe depression is when the patient begins to respond to medication. As their energy and motivation start to return, but before their mood and suicidal ideation have fully resolved, the risk of a suicide attempt can paradoxically increase. Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are highly lethal in overdose, primarily due to their cardiotoxic effects (arrhythmias). An overdose of as little as a one-week supply of TCAs can be fatal. Therefore, the most important concern when discharging a patient who is improving from severe depression on a TCA is the risk that they might use their prescribed medication to attempt suicide. This necessitates careful assessment of suicidal ideation and often involves dispensing only a limited supply of the medication at a time. While ECG monitoring (C) and therapeutic drug monitoring (B) are important aspects of TCA management, the immediate risk of intentional overdose is the paramount safety concern at discharge.
184.	 All of the following are good prognostic factors 
in schizophrenia except?
(A)	Late age of onset
(B)	 Associated with depression
(C)	Insidious onset of symptoms
(D)	Positive symptoms
AAns 
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
(C) Insidious onset of symptoms
Certain clinical features at the time of diagnosis of schizophrenia are associated with a better or worse long-term prognosis. Good prognostic factors include a late age of onset (A), an acute or abrupt onset of symptoms, the presence of obvious precipitating factors, good premorbid functioning, a family history of mood disorders, and a clinical picture dominated by positive symptoms (D) (like hallucinations and delusions) rather than negative symptoms. The presence of significant mood symptoms, such as depression (B), during the psychotic episode is also associated with a better outcome. In contrast, an insidious onset (C), where symptoms develop gradually and subtly over a long period, is a well-established poor prognostic factor. It is often associated with a clinical picture dominated by negative symptoms, poor premorbid adjustment, and a more chronic, deteriorating course.

In the following diagram, the areas marked with A and D indicate which of the following conditions?
(A)	
Chronic Respiratory Acidosis & Metabolic Acidosis
(B)	
Metabolic Alkalosis & Metabolic Acidosis
(C)	
Acute Respiratory Acidosis & Chronic Respiratory Acidosis
(D)	
Acute Respiratory Acidosis & Metabolic Acidosis
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
18.	 (A) Chronic Respiratory Acidosis & Metabolic 
Acidosis
The diagram shown is a Davenport diagram, 
which is used to interpret acid–base disorders. 
It plots arterial pH on the X-axis and plasma 
bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) concentration on the 
Y-axis, with curved lines representing different 
levels of PCO₂. The central “normal” zone 
represents normal pH (~7.4), bicarbonate (~24 
mEq/L), and PCO₂ (~40 mmHg).
Area A is located in the upper left region of 
the graph. Here, the pH is low (acidemia), but 
bicarbonate is elevated. This pattern indicates 
chronic respiratory acidosis. In this condition, 
there is prolonged CO₂ retention (elevated 
PCO₂), and the kidneys compensate over time 
by increasing bicarbonate reabsorption, leading 
to a higher HCO₃⁻ level.
Area D is located in the lower left region. 
Both pH and bicarbonate are low, indicating 
metabolic acidosis. In metabolic acidosis, 
there is a primary decrease in bicarbonate 
due to acid accumulation or bicarbonate loss. 
Respiratory compensation may reduce PCO₂, 
but bicarbonate remains low.
Thus, region A represents chronic respiratory 
acidosis, and region D represents metabolic 
acidosis. 
In membrane receptors, the transmembrane region is made up of which type of amino acids?
(A)	
Hydrophobic
(B)	
Hydrophilic
(C)	
Charged
(D)	
None
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
19.	 (A) Hydrophobic
Transmembrane proteins, including membrane 
receptors, must span the lipid bilayer of the 
cell membrane. The core of the lipid bilayer is 
composed of the fatty acid tails of phospholipids, 
creating a highly nonpolar, oily environment. To 
be stably embedded within this environment, 
the segment of the protein that passes through 
the membrane must be composed of amino 
acids with nonpolar, hydrophobic side chains. 
These amino acids (such as leucine, isoleucine, 
valine, and phenylalanine) interact favorably 
with the lipid tails, anchoring the protein in 
the membrane. Typically, this transmembrane 
domain is arranged in an alpha-helical structure. 
In contrast, the extracellular and intracellular 
domains of the receptor, which are exposed to 
the aqueous environments outside and inside 
the cell, are primarily composed of hydrophilic 
(B) and charged (C) amino acids.
High anion gap acidosis is seen in all except :
(A)	
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
(B)	
Lactic acidosis
(C)	
Renal aciduria
(D)	
Respiratory disorders
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
20.	 (D) Respiratory disorders
A high anion gap metabolic acidosis is caused by 
the accumulation of unmeasured organic acids 
in the blood. In diabetic ketoacidosis (A), the 
acids are acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate. 
In lactic acidosis (B), the acid is lactate. Certain 
types of renal failure (uremia) can also lead 
to the accumulation of acids like sulfates and 
phosphates, causing a high anion gap. The term 
"renal aciduria" (C) is ambiguous but likely 
refers to this or a renal tubular acidosis that 
can sometimes be associated with a high anion 
gap. In contrast, respiratory disorders (D) cause 
respiratory acidosis or alkalosis, not metabolic 
acidosis. Respiratory acidosis is caused by the 
retention of CO2. While this lowers the pH, it 
does not involve the addition of an unmeasured 
anion and therefore does not cause a high anion 
gap. It is a distinct acid-base disturbance with a 
different underlying pathophysiology.

a classic 3-Hz spike-and-wave pattern on EEG. 
The treatment for absence seizures is specific.
1.	 Ethosuximide : This is the first-line and most 
specific drug for treating uncomplicated 
childhood absence seizures. It works 
by blocking T-type calcium channels in 
thalamic neurons.
3.	 Valproic acid : This is a broad-spectrum 
antiepileptic drug that is also highly 
effective for absence seizures and is the 
drug of choice if the patient also has co-
existing generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
2.	 Carbamazepine : This is a narrow-
spectrum drug used for focal seizures. It 
is contraindicated in absence seizures as it 
can exacerbate them.
4.	 Gabapentin : This is used as an add-on for 
focal seizures and for neuropathic pain; it is 
not effective for absence seizures.
Therefore, only ethosuximide and valproic acid 
are used for the treatment of absence seizures.
If codeine is being introduced to the market in combination with dextromethorphan as an antitussive, what steps should be taken next?
(A)	
Should not be used as it is irrational
(B)	
Can be used to treat cough effectively
(C)	
Can be used as it has different MOA
(D)	
Should not be used due to addiction
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
48.	 (A) Should not be used as it is irrational
This question assesses the principles of rational 
pharmacotherapy. Codeine is an opioid that 
suppresses cough by acting on the cough 
center in the brainstem. Dextromethorphan is 
a non-opioid, synthetic derivative of morphine 
that also acts centrally to suppress the cough 
reflex, likely via sigma-1 receptor agonism and 
NMDA receptor antagonism. Since both drugs 
are centrally acting antitussives that work 
to achieve the same therapeutic goal (cough 
suppression), combining them in a fixed-dose 
combination offers no proven synergistic or 
additive benefit over using an adequate dose of 
a single agent. Such a combination increases the 
risk of side effects, potential for confusion, and 
cost without providing any additional efficacy. 
This violates the principles of rational drug use, 
and therefore, the combination should not be 
used as it is irrational.
Which of the following antidepressants is linked to the fewest sexual side effects?
(A)	
Mirtazapine
(B)	
Fluoxetine
(C)	
Venlafaxine
(D)	
Imipenem
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
49.	 (A) Mirtazapine
Sexual dysfunction (e.g., decreased libido, 
anorgasmia) is a very common and distressing 
side effect of many antidepressant medications, 
particularly those that work primarily by 
increasing serotonin levels. Selective Serotonin 
Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) like fluoxetine 
(B) and Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake 
Inhibitors (SNRIs) like venlafaxine (C) are 
associated with a high incidence of sexual side 
effects. In contrast, mirtazapine is an atypical 
antidepressant with a different mechanism of 
action (a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic 
antagonist, or NaSSA). It blocks α2-adrenergic 
autoreceptors and certain serotonin receptors 
(5-HT2 and 5-HT3). This mechanism is 
associated with a significantly lower incidence 
of sexual dysfunction compared to SSRIs and 
SNRIs, and in some cases, it may even improve 
sexual function. Imipenem (D) is a carbapenem 
antibiotic, not an antidepressant.
Which of the following is a bone-forming drug?
(A)

(B)	
Teriparatide
(C)

(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
50.	 (B) Teriparatide
Osteoporosis medications are broadly classified 
as 
either 
anti-resorptive 
(slowing 
bone 
breakdown) or anabolic (promoting new bone 
formation). Most treatments fall into the first 
category. Bisphosphonates (D), raloxifene (A) (a 
SERM), and calcitonin (C) are all anti-resorptive 
agents that work by inhibiting the activity of 
osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. In 
contrast, teriparatide is an anabolic agent. It is 
a recombinant form of the first 34 amino acids 
of human parathyroid hormone (PTH). When 
administered intermittently as a once-daily 
subcutaneous injection, PTH paradoxically 
stimulates the activity of osteoblasts, the cells 
responsible for forming new bone. This leads to 
a significant increase in bone mineral density 
and a substantial reduction in fracture risk. It 
is the primary anabolic or "bone-forming" drug 
used for the treatment of severe osteoporosis.

Which of the following statements about telomerase is incorrect?
(A)	
It has reverse transcriptase activity
(B)	
It is only found in eukaryotes
(C)	
It maintains high fidelity during DNA replication
(D)	
It maintains the length of chromosomes
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
27.	 (C) It maintains high fidelity during DNA 
replication
Telomerase is a unique enzyme responsible for 
maintaining the length of chromosomes (D) by 
adding repetitive nucleotide sequences to the 
ends, or telomeres. It is a ribonucleoprotein that 
contains its own RNA template and synthesizes 
DNA from this RNA template. This enzymatic 
activity makes it a specialized type of reverse 
transcriptase (A). Telomerase is a feature of 
eukaryotic chromosomes; prokaryotes have 
circular chromosomes and do not require it (B). 
The statement that telomerase maintains high 
fidelity during DNA replication (C) is incorrect. 
The primary enzyme responsible for the high-
fidelity replication of the main chromosomal 
DNA 
is 
DNA 
polymerase, 
which 
has 
proofreading capabilities. Telomerase's function 
is specifically to solve the "end-replication 
problem" by adding telomeric repeats, a process 
that is separate from the high-fidelity replication 
of the coding regions of the genome.

A.	
Km of an enzyme = 10 µM; kcat = 20s⁻¹

The highest catalytic efficiency is seen in :
(A)	
A
(B)	
B
(C)	
C
(D)	
D
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
28.	 (B) B
Catalytic efficiency is a measure of how 
efficiently an enzyme converts a substrate into 
a product. It is represented by the ratio of two 
kinetic parameters : kcat / Km. A higher kcat 
(turnover number) or a lower Km (substrate 
affinity) will result in a higher catalytic 
efficiency. We need to calculate this ratio for 
each option, ensuring the units are consistent. 
Let's convert all Km values to µM.
A	 : Efficiency = 20 / 10 = 2
B	 : Km = 200 nM = 0.2 µM. Efficiency = 50 / 
0.2 = 250
C	 : Efficiency = 200 / 2 = 100
D	 : Efficiency = 200 / 4 = 50
Comparing the calculated efficiency values 
(A=2, B=250, C=100, D=50), enzyme B clearly 
has the highest catalytic efficiency. This is 
because it has both a very high affinity for its 
substrate (very low Km) and a reasonably high 
turnover rate (kcat).

The image shows a peripheral blood smear 
with several abnormally shaped red blood 
cells indicated by arrows. These cells have a 
central area of hemoglobinopathies surrounded 
by a pale zone and then a peripheral rim of 
hemoglobin, resembling a shooting target. 
This morphology has two names. They are 
commonly known as target cells (A). The more 
formal hematological term for these cells is 
codocytes (C). Therefore, both terms are correct. 
Target cells are formed due to an increase in the

the membrane surface area (e.g., in liver disease 
due to altered lipid composition) or a decrease 
in intracellular volume (e.g., in thalassemia 
due to reduced hemoglobin content). They are 
a characteristic, though not specific, finding in 
patients with significant liver disease, as well as 
in thalassemia and other hemoglobinopathies.

Which of the following increases in COPD?
1	
FRC (Functional Residual Capacity)
2	
TLC (Total Lung Capacity)
3	
VC (Vital Capacity)
4	
FEV1/FVC (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second / Forced Vital Capacity)
(A)	
1 & 2
(B)	
2 & 3
(C)	
3 & 4
(D)	
4 & 1
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
35.	 (A) 1 & 2
Chronic 
Obstructive 
Pulmonary 
Disease 
(COPD) is characterized by persistent airflow 
limitation. This obstruction leads to air 
trapping, where air gets trapped in the lungs at 
the end of expiration. This has several effects 
on lung volumes measured by spirometry and 
plethysmography. The trapped air leads to an 
increase in the volume of air remaining in the 
lungs after a normal expiration, which is the 
Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) (1). It 
also leads to an increase in the volume of air 
remaining after a maximal expiration (Residual 
Volume, RV). As a consequence of the increased 
RV, the Total Lung Capacity (TLC) (2), which 
is the sum of RV and Vital Capacity, is also 
typically increased or normal. In contrast, the 
Vital Capacity (VC) (3) (the maximum volume 
of air that can be exhaled) is often decreased. 
The hallmark of COPD is a reduced FEV1/FVC 
ratio (4), which is decreased, not increased.

The macula densa is a specialized plaque of 
densely packed epithelial cells that is a key 
component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus 
(JGA). The JGA is a structure that regulates 
renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate. 
Anatomically, the macula densa is located at 
the very beginning of the distal convoluted 
tubule (DCT), at the precise point where the 
tubule passes between the afferent and efferent 
arterioles of its own glomerulus. Some texts 
describe its location as the terminal part of the 
thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, right 
at the transition to the DCT. These cells function 
as chemoreceptors, sensing the concentration 
of sodium chloride in the tubular fluid. This 
information is then used to signal the afferent 
arteriole to constrict or dilate, a process known 
as tubuloglomerular feedback, which helps to 
autoregulate the filtration rate of the individual 
nephron.

Which of the following statements about skeletal muscle contraction are correct?
(A)	
Extracellular Ca++ not important for contraction
(B)	
Ca++ released from mitochondria
(C)	
Ca++ released from Sarcoplasmic Reticulum
(D)	
A & C both
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
23.	 (D) A & C both
The process of excitation-contraction coupling 
in skeletal muscle has specific characteristics. 
The action potential travels down the T-tubules, 
where 
it 
activates 
voltage-sensitive 
DHP 
receptors. These receptors are mechanically 
linked to ryanodine receptors on the membrane 
of the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). This 
mechanical coupling triggers the opening of 
the ryanodine receptors, causing a massive 
release of stored calcium ions (Ca++) from the 
SR into the cytoplasm (C is true). This rise in 
intracellular calcium initiates the cross-bridge 
cycle. Unlike cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle 
contraction is not directly dependent on the 
influx of extracellular calcium for triggering 
this release; the process is purely mechanical. 
Therefore, extracellular Ca++ is not important 
for initiating the contraction (A is true). Calcium 
is released from the SR, not the mitochondria (B 
is incorrect). Since both statements A and C are 
true regarding skeletal muscle, option D is the 
correct answer.
DNA methylation is not associated with :
(A)	
Chromatin remodeling
(B)	
RNA splicing
(C)	
Gene silencing
(D)	
Methyl-directed Mismatch Repair
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
24.	 (B) RNA splicing
DNA methylation is a fundamental epigenetic 
mechanism that plays a role in several key 
cellular processes. It is a primary mechanism 
of gene silencing (C), as the methylation 
of CpG islands in a gene's promoter region 
typically prevents the binding of transcription 
factors and recruits repressive proteins. This 
process is intimately linked with chromatin 
remodeling (A), as methylated DNA promotes 
the formation of condensed, transcriptionally 
silent heterochromatin. In prokaryotes, it is also 
crucial for methyl-directed mismatch repair 
(D), a system that uses the methylation status 
of the parental DNA strand to identify and 
correct errors made during DNA replication on 
the newly synthesized strand. However, RNA 
splicing (B) is a post-transcriptional process. 
It involves the removal of introns from a pre-
mRNA molecule to form mature mRNA. This 
process is carried out by the spliceosome and is 
regulated by splicing factors, but it is not directly 
controlled by the methylation status of the DNA 
from which the RNA was transcribed.

A "dry tap" on bone marrow aspiration occurs 
when no marrow particles can be aspirated, 
despite the needle being correctly positioned. 
This is most commonly due to marrow fibrosis 
(myelofibrosis) or packing of the marrow space 
by a dense infiltrate of cells. Conditions notorious 
for causing significant marrow fibrosis and a 
dry tap include hairy cell leukemia (D), chronic 
myeloproliferative 
disorders 
like 
primary 
myelofibrosis (A), and acute megakaryoblastic 
leukemia (M7 AML) (C). In these conditions, a 
bone marrow biopsy is essential for diagnosis. 
In contrast, while follicular lymphoma (B) can 
infiltrate the bone marrow, the infiltration is 
typically interstitial or paratrabecular and not 
usually associated with the extensive fibrosis 
that would lead to a dry tap. Therefore, among 
the choices provided, follicular lymphoma is 
the least likely to result in an inaspirable bone 
marrow.
Which of the following is not true about telomerase?
(A)

(B)	
Maintains chromosome length

Only in eukaryotes

DNA repair/synthesis

43.	 (D) DNA repair/synthesis
This question is a near duplicate of a previous 
one. Telomerase is a unique ribonucleoprotein 
enzyme. It acts as a specialized reverse 
transcriptase (A), using its own internal 
RNA component as a template to synthesize 
DNA. Its specific function is to add repetitive 
DNA sequences (telomeres) to the ends 
of 
chromosomes, 
thereby 
maintaining 
chromosome length (B) and compensating for

feature of eukaryotes (C). The statement that 
it is involved in general DNA repair/synthesis 
(D) is not true. While it does synthesize DNA, 
its function is highly specialized and restricted 
to the telomeres. The major enzymes for general 
DNA synthesis (replication) and repair are the 
various DNA polymerases, not telomerase.

Pancytopenia on blood examination is seen in :

Hairy cell leukemia
(C)

45.	 (B) Hairy cell leukemia.
All four options are valid causes of pancytopenia.
Megaloblastic anemia, Acute promyelocytic 
leukemia, and Myelodysplastic syndrome all

and 
suppresses 
the 
normal 
production of red cells, white cells, and platelets.
Therefore, pancytopenia is a hallmark and 
nearly universal finding at the time of diagnosis 
for Hairy cell leukemia, often accompanied by 
a massively enlarged spleen. This makes it a 
quintessential example of a disease presenting 
with pancytopenia.

Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is an autoimmune

The HPV vaccine is based on which viral proteins?
(A)	
E6 & E7
(B)	
E5
(C)	
L1
(D)	
E2
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
57.	 (C) L1
The currently available Human papillomavirus 
vaccine is based on the L1 major capsid protein 
of the human papillomavirus (HPV). The L1 
protein has the ability to self-assemble into virus-
like particles (VLPs). These VLPs resemble the 
outer shell of the virus but do not contain viral 
DNA, making them non-infectious and safe.
When administered, these L1-based VLPs 
stimulate 
a 
strong 
neutralizing 
antibody 
response. The antibodies prevent HPV from

(they 
inactivate 
tumor

and Cervarix are based on the L1 capsid protein,

Which of the following methods can be used for therapeutic drug monitoring in a patient?
(A)	
HPLC
(B)	
Nuclear Magnetic Resonance
(C)	
Spectrophotometry
(D)	
Flow cytometry
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
58.	 (A) HPLC
Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is the 
clinical practice of measuring the plasma 
concentration of a specific drug to maintain 
it within a target therapeutic range. This is 
essential for drugs with a narrow therapeutic 
index, such as certain antiepileptics (e.g., 
phenytoin), antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin), and 
immunosuppressants (e.g., tacrolimus). Several 
analytical techniques are used for this purpose. 
High-Performance 
Liquid 
Chromatography 
(HPLC) is a powerful and widely used technique 
in clinical laboratories for TDM. It works 
by separating the components of a mixture 
(like plasma) based on their physicochemical 
properties, allowing for the precise and accurate 
quantification of the specific drug of interest. 
While immunoassays are also very common, 
HPLC is a gold-standard reference method 
for many drugs. Spectrophotometry (C) is less 
specific, and NMR (B) and flow cytometry (D) 
are not used for routine TDM.

The Nigro regimen is used in the treatment of which condition?
(A)	
Carcinoma of the anal canal
(B)	
Carcinoma of the colon
(C)	
Carcinoma of the bladder
(D)	
All of the above
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
53.	 (A) Carcinoma of the anal canal
The Nigro regimen is the standard, definitive 
treatment protocol for squamous cell carcinoma 
of the anal canal. It is a combined modality 
chemoradiation therapy that has transformed 
the management of this disease, allowing for 
sphincter preservation and avoiding the need for 
radical surgery (abdominoperineal resection) 
in the majority of cases. The original regimen, 
developed by Dr. Norman Nigro, consists of 
external beam radiation therapy delivered to the 
primary tumor and regional lymph nodes, given 
concurrently with chemotherapy. The classic 
chemotherapy agents used are mitomycin-C and 
5-fluorouracil (5-FU). This combined approach 
is highly effective, achieving complete remission 
in over 80% of patients with localized disease. 
The Nigro regimen is specific to anal cancer and 
is not used for colon or bladder cancer.
What is the mechanism through which anti-migraine drugs can produce angina-like symptoms?

54.	 (C) 5-HT agonist
The primary classes of drugs used for the 
acute treatment of migraine are the triptans 
(e.g., sumatriptan) and the ergot alkaloids 
(e.g., ergotamine). The mechanism of action 
of both classes involves agonism at serotonin 
(5-HT) receptors, specifically the 5-HT1B and 
5-HT1D subtypes. Their therapeutic effect is

with underlying coronary artery disease, this 
vasoconstriction can be significant enough to 
induce myocardial ischemia, leading to angina-
like symptoms such as chest pain, tightness, or 
pressure. This is a well-known and important 
potential side effect of these drugs.

The steps of PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) are :
(A)	
Hybridization → Denaturation → Annealing → Elongation
(B)	
Denaturation → Annealing → Elongation
(C)	
Denaturation → Elongation → Annealing→ Hybridization
(D)	
Hybridization → Annealing → Elongation→-> Denaturation
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
30.	 (B) Denaturation → Annealing → Elongation
The Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is a 
technique used to amplify a specific segment 
of DNA exponentially. It consists of a series 
of repeated cycles, with each cycle comprising 
three distinct temperature-controlled steps :
1.	 Denaturation : The reaction mixture is 
heated to a high temperature (typically 
94-98°C). This breaks the hydrogen bonds 
holding the double-stranded DNA template 
together, separating it into two single 
strands.
2.	 Annealing : The temperature is lowered 
(typically 50-65°C). This allows short, 
single-stranded DNA primers, which are 
complementary to the sequences flanking 
the target region, to bind (anneal) to their 
respective sites on the single-stranded DNA 
templates.
3.	 Elongation 
(or 
Extension) 
: 
The 
temperature is raised again (typically to 
72°C), which is the optimal temperature 
for the thermostable DNA polymerase 
(like Taq polymerase). The polymerase 
then synthesizes a new complementary 
DNA strand, starting from the primers and 
extending along the template strand.
This three-step cycle is repeated 25-35 times, 
leading to an exponential amplification of the 
target DNA sequence.
Compare the normality of 2 mM HCl and 1 mM H2SO4.
(A)	
Same
(B)	
Double
(C)	
Half
(D)	
Four times
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
31.	 (A) Same
Normality (N) is a measure of concentration 
defined as the molarity (M) of a solution 
multiplied by its equivalence factor (or n-factor). 
For an acid, the n-factor is the number of moles 
of hydrogen ions (H+) that one mole of the acid 
can donate.
For hydrochloric acid (HCl), it is a monoprotic 
acid, meaning it donates one H+ ion per 
molecule. Therefore, its n-factor is 1.
1.	 Normality of 2 mM HCl = 2 mM × 1 = 2 
mN (millinormal).
2.	 For sulfuric acid (H2SO4), it is a diprotic 
acid, meaning it can donate two H+ ions per 
molecule. Therefore, its n-factor is 2.
3.	 Normality of 1 mM H2SO4 = 1 mM × 2 = 2 
mN.
Since both solutions have a normality of 2 mN, 
their normalities are the same.
The thermogenic effect of food is highest for :
(A)	
Lipid
(B)	
Carbohydrates
(C)	
Proteins
(D)	
Mixed
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
32.	 (C) Proteins
This is a duplicate of a previous question. The 
thermic effect of food (TEF), also called specific 
dynamic action, is the energy expenditure 
required for the digestion, absorption, and 
metabolism of nutrients after a meal. This 
value varies significantly between the different 
macronutrients. Proteins have the highest TEF, 
with about 20-30% of their ingested energy 
being used for their processing and assimilation. 
This is due to the energy-intensive processes of 
deamination and urea synthesis. Carbohydrates 
(B) have an intermediate TEF, typically in the 
range of 5-10%. Lipids (A), or fats, have the lowest 
TEF, at only about 0-3%, meaning they are the 
most metabolically efficient macronutrient to 
store. Therefore, protein consumption leads to 
the greatest increase in metabolic rate compared 
to the other macronutrients, a principle often 
utilized in diets for weight management.

Which of the following is true regarding the treatment of gout?
(A)	
Aspirin is used because it is effective & most safe.
(B)	
Aspirin is not used because it increases uric acid levels.
(C)	
Indomethacin is used.
(D)	
Diclofenac can be used because it accumulates in the joint.
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
60.	 (B) Aspirin is not used because it increases uric 
acid levels.
The management of acute gout focuses on 
rapidly suppressing the intense inflammation. 
Aspirin is specifically avoided in the treatment 
of gout. At the low doses typically used for

NSAID, the reason given is not its primary 
justification. The most accurate statement 
regarding the options is the one explaining why 
aspirin is contraindicated.
A patient taking antiepileptic medication is diagnosed with neurocysticercosis. What should be the next steps in this patient’s management?
(A)	
Give anti-parasite followed by steroid
(B)	
Steroid followed by antihelminthic drug
(C)	
Steroid after stopping antiepileptic
(D)	
Antiepileptic followed by antihelminthic drug
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
61.	 (B) Steroid followed by antihelminthic drug
Neurocysticercosis is a parasitic infection of 
the central nervous system caused by the larval 
cysts of Taenia solium. When antihelminthic 
drugs (like albendazole or praziquantel) are 
administered, they kill the cysticerci within 
the brain. The death of the parasite triggers a 
significant host inflammatory response around 
the degenerating cyst. This inflammation can 
lead to a dangerous increase in cerebral edema, 
worsening of neurological symptoms, and 
an increased risk of seizures. To mitigate this 
inflammatory response, it is standard practice to 
administer corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) 
before or concurrently with the initiation of 
the antihelminthic drug. The antiepileptic 
medication should be continued throughout this 
period to control seizures. Therefore, the correct 
sequence is to start steroids first to suppress 
inflammation, and then begin the anti-parasitic 
treatment.

When to use hand sanitizer?
A.	
Before touching the patient
B.	
After touching the patient
C.	
When hands are soiled.
D.	
After touching patient's surrounding.
(A)	
A & B
(B)	
B & C
(C)	
A, B & D

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
89.	 (C) A, B & D
The World Health Organization's "5 Moments 
for Hand Hygiene" outline the critical points 
during patient care when hand hygiene 
is required to prevent the transmission of 
healthcare-associated infections. Alcohol-based 
hand sanitizer is the preferred method for hand 
hygiene when hands are not visibly soiled. These 
moments include :
1.	 Moment : Before touching a patient (A), 
to protect the patient from harmful germs 
carried on your hands.
2.	 Moment : Before a clean or aseptic

3.	 Moment : After a body fluid exposure risk.
4.	 Moment : After touching a patient (B), 
to protect yourself and the healthcare 
environment from the patient's germs.
5.	 Moment : After touching the patient's 
surroundings (D), even if you haven't 
touched the patient directly.

hands are visibly dirty or soiled (C). In that 
situation, hands must be washed with soap and 
water.
Which discrete probability distribution describes the likelihood of a certain number of events occurring within a fixed interval of time or space?
(A)	
Gaussian
(B)	
Binomial
(C)	
Poisson
(D)	
Erlang
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
90.	 (C) Poisson
The Poisson distribution is a discrete probability 
distribution that is used to model the number 
of events occurring within a specified, fixed 
interval of time or space. It is applicable when 
these events occur with a known constant mean 
rate and independently of the time since the 
last event. Classic examples include the number 
of phone calls received by a call center in one 
hour, the number of mutations in a given stretch 
of DNA, or the number of radioactive decay 
events in a second. The Binomial distribution 
(B) describes the number of successes in a 
fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials. 
The Gaussian (Normal) distribution (A) is 
a continuous probability distribution, not a 
discrete one. The Erlang distribution (D) is a 
continuous distribution related to waiting times.
Which device is used to indicate heat exposure in vaccines?
(A)	
VVM
(B)	
VMV
(C)	
MMV
(D)	
VMM
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
91.	 (A) VVM
A Vaccine Vial Monitor (VVM) is a small, heat-
sensitive label that is placed on a vaccine vial 
to provide a visual indication of its cumulative 
heat exposure over time. The VVM consists of 
a dark outer circle and a lighter inner square. 
The inner square is made of a heat-sensitive 
material that darkens gradually and irreversibly 
when exposed to heat. The rule for interpreting 
a VVM is : "If the inner square is the same color 
as or darker than the outer circle, do not use 
the vaccine." This simple tool allows healthcare 
workers to determine if a vaccine has been 
exposed to potentially damaging temperatures 
and should be discarded, ensuring that only 
potent vaccines are administered. It is a critical 
component of the cold chain management 
system for many vaccines.

In which of the following conditions is iritis commonly observed?

98.	 (A) Behçet's disease.
Iritis, which is inflammation of the iris (the 
colored part of the eye), is a form of anterior 
uveitis. While it can be associated with several 
systemic inflammatory conditions, it is a 
hallmark feature of Behçet's disease.
1.	 Behçet's Disease : This is a rare autoimmune 
disorder that causes inflammation in 
blood vessels throughout the body. Ocular 
involvement is very common, affecting up 
to 70% of patients. Iritis (anterior uveitis) is 
one of the most frequent eye problems seen 
in this condition, often being recurrent and 
severe. 
2.	 SLE (Systemic Lupus Erythematosus) : 
While SLE can affect almost any part of the 
body, including the eyes, severe iritis is not 
a common manifestation. More frequent 
ocular problems in SLE include dry eye 
syndrome (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and 
retinal disease.
3.	 Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) : In adults with 
RA, the most common inflammatory eye 
condition is scleritis (inflammation of the 
white part of the eye), not iritis. Dry eye 
syndrome is also very common. Iritis is 
more typically associated with the juvenile 
form of arthritis (JIA).
4.	 Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) : Iritis does occur 
in patients with psoriatic arthritis, with a 
prevalence of about 7-25%. However, the 
association and frequency are considered 
strongest 
and 
most 
characteristic 
in 
Behçet's disease.
Which of the following drugs are used to distinguish a fixed, dilated pupil?
(A)	
4% Cocaine
(B)	
Pilocarpine
(C)	
Phenylephrine
(D)	
Adrenaline
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
99.	 (B) Pilocarpine
A fixed dilated pupil can be caused by several 
conditions, including a third nerve palsy, 
pharmacological blockade (mydriasis), or Adie's 
tonic pupil. A pharmacological test using dilute 
pilocarpine is used to help differentiate the 
cause. Pilocarpine is a direct-acting cholinergic 
agonist that constricts the pupil.
1.	 Adie's tonic pupil : This is caused by 
denervation 
of 
the 
postganglionic 
parasympathetic 
supply 
to 
the 
iris 
sphincter. The denervated muscle becomes 
supersensitive to acetylcholine. A very 
dilute (e.g., 0.125%) pilocarpine solution, 
which would have no effect on a normal 
pupil, will cause marked constriction in an 
Adie's pupil, confirming the diagnosis.
2.	 Pharmacological blockade : If the pupil is 
dilated by an anticholinergic drug (like 
atropine), it will not constrict even to a 
standard strength (1%) pilocarpine solution.
3.	 Third nerve palsy : A pupil dilated due to a 
third nerve palsy will constrict in response 
to a standard strength (1%) pilocarpine 
solution.

75.	 (A) Invasive aspergillosis
Galactomannan is a polysaccharide that is a major 
component of the cell wall of fungi in the genus 
Aspergillus. During invasive growth, the fungus 
releases this antigen into the host's circulation.

The presence of painful genital ulcers in a

Which disease has an almost 100% fatality rate once symptoms develop?
(A)	
Rabies
(B)	
Nipah
(C)	
Ebola
(D)	
Measles
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
72.	 (A) Rabies
Rabies is an acute progressive viral encephalitis 
transmitted to humans through the saliva of 
infected animals, typically via a bite. While the 
disease is preventable with timely post-exposure 
prophylaxis, once clinical signs and symptoms 
develop, the disease is almost invariably fatal. 
The case fatality rate for symptomatic rabies 
approaches 100%. There are only a very small 
number of documented survivors of clinical 
rabies in the entire history of modern medicine, 
most of whom were treated with an experimental 
and not reliably successful protocol. This 
makes rabies one of the most lethal infectious 
diseases known. In contrast, while Nipah virus 
infection (B) and Ebola virus disease (C) are 
also extremely dangerous and have very high 
case fatality rates (which can range from 40% to 
over 90% depending on the strain and outbreak), 
survival is possible with intensive supportive 
care. Measles (D) has a much lower mortality 
rate.

Which structure is disrupted by Vibrio cholerae?
(A)

(B)

(C)	
Zona occludens
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
74.	 (C) Zona occludens
The massive, watery diarrhea characteristic 
of cholera is caused primarily by the action of 
the cholera toxin, which leads to a profound 
secretory state in the intestinal epithelial cells. 
However, the integrity of the intestinal barrier 
is also compromised. The zona occludens, also 
known as the tight junction, is the most apical 
intercellular junction that seals the space 
between adjacent epithelial cells, regulating the 
paracellular pathway. Vibrio cholerae produces 
several toxins in addition to the main cholera 
toxin. One of these is the zonula occludens toxin 
(Zot), which directly acts on and disrupts the 
structure of the tight junctions. This disruption 
increases the permeability of the paracellular 
pathway, leading to the leakage of fluid and 
electrolytes from the tissues into the intestinal 
lumen, which contributes significantly to the 
voluminous diarrhea. Hemidesmosomes (A) 
and zona adherens (D) are anchoring junctions, 
while gap junctions (B) are for cell-to-cell 
communication.
