What is the most appropriate method for reviewing previous research studies?
(A)	
Meta analysis
(B)	
Chi-Square test
(C)	
Cross-sectional study
(D)	
Case control study
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
85.	 (A) Meta analysis
To synthesize and study the findings from a 
collection of previously conducted research 
studies on a specific topic, the most rigorous 
and powerful method is a meta-analysis. 
A meta-analysis is a quantitative, formal, 
epidemiological 
study 
design 
used 
to 
systematically assess the results of previous 
research to derive conclusions about that 
body of research. It goes beyond a simple 
literature review by using statistical methods 
to combine the effect estimates from individual 
studies, resulting in a single, more precise, and 
powerful summary estimate. This allows for 
a comprehensive and objective evaluation of 
the existing evidence. A chi-square test (B) is a 
statistical test used within a single study. Cross-
sectional (C) and case-control (D) studies are 
designs for conducting primary research, not for 
synthesizing the results of previous studies.
What is the most suitable option for mass chemoprophylaxis against anemia in a population?
(A)	
Ferrous Sulphate
(B)	
Ferrous Fumarate + B12 + Folic Acid + Vitamin C
(C)	
Intravenous Iron
(D)	
Ferrous Ascorbate
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
86.	 (A) Ferrous Sulphate
For mass chemoprophylaxis of anemia in a 
population, the ideal preparation should be 
effective, safe, inexpensive, widely available, and 
suitable for large-scale public health distribution. 
Ferrous sulphate fulfills these criteria and is the 
most commonly recommended iron preparation 
in national anemia control programs.
Ferrous sulphate contains a high proportion 
of elemental iron, is cost-effective, and has 
well-established efficacy in preventing and 
treating iron deficiency anemia. It is included 
in government initiatives such as the Anemia 
Mukt Bharat strategy under the National Health 
Mission in India. The tablet form allows easy 
distribution in schools, antenatal clinics, and 
community health programs.
Combination 
preparations 
containing 
vitamin B12, folic acid, and vitamin C are 
more expensive and unnecessary for routine 
mass prophylaxis unless specific deficiencies 
are documented. Intravenous iron is reserved 
for severe anemia or malabsorption and is not 
practical for community-level prophylaxis.
Therefore, for large-scale public health 
prevention of anemia, ferrous sulphate is the 
most suitable option.
What does the difference between the maximum and minimum values in a dataset represent?
(A)	
Mean
(B)	
Median
(C)	
Range
(D)	
Mode
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
87.	 (C) Range
In descriptive statistics, several measures are 
used to summarize a dataset. The range is the 
simplest measure of dispersion or variability. It is 
defined as the difference between the maximum 
(highest) and minimum (lowest) observed 
values in a dataset. It provides a quick and easy-
to-calculate indication of the spread of the data. 
For example, if the test scores in a class are from 
65 to 95, the range is 95 - 65 = 30. While it is 
simple, it is highly sensitive to outliers and does 
not provide information about the distribution 
of values between the two extremes. The mean 
(A) is the average, the median (B) is the middle 
value, and the mode (D) is the most frequent 
value; these are all measures of central tendency, 
not dispersion.

In a firearm injury, the blackening seen around the entry wound is due to :
(A)	
Flame
(B)	
Smoke
(C)	
Unburnt powder
(D)	
Hot gases
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
66.	 (B) Smoke
The characteristics of a firearm entry wound 
provide crucial information about the range of 
fire. In a close-range or contact shot, several 
elements are discharged from the muzzle along 
with the bullet. The blackening of the skin 
immediately surrounding the entry wound is 
specifically caused by the deposition of smoke 
(soot) from the combustion of the gunpowder. 
This soot can be wiped away from the skin. 
Unburnt and partially burnt powder particles 
(C) are also discharged and can cause "tattooing" 
or "stippling" of the skin, which are small 
punctate abrasions that cannot be wiped away. 
The flame (A) and hot gases (D) discharged 
from the muzzle can cause burning or searing 
of the skin at very close range. The distinct 
black discoloration, however, is attributed to the 
smoke deposit.

Sequence of Auditory Pathway?

1234567

2134567

2176543
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
94.	 (B) 2156473
The central auditory pathway follows a specific 
sequence from the ear to the brain.
1.	 The first-order neurons are in the spiral 
ganglion (2) in the cochlea. Their axons 
form the auditory nerve.
2.	 The auditory nerve synapses on the cochlear 
nucleus (1) in the brainstem.
3.	 From the cochlear nucleus, fibers ascend 
bilaterally, with many crossing over and 
synapsing in the superior olivary nucleus 
(5), which is crucial for sound localization.
4.	 Axons from these nuclei then ascend in a 
tract called the lateral lemniscus (6).
5.	 The fibers of the lateral lemniscus synapse 
in the inferior colliculus (4) of the midbrain.
6.	 From the inferior colliculus, neurons 
project to the medial geniculate body (7) 
of the thalamus, the main auditory relay 
station.
7.	 Finally, fibers from the medial geniculate 
body project to the primary auditory cortex 
(3) in the temporal lobe.
The correct sequence is 2 → 1 → 5 → 6 → 4 → 
7 → 3.
Which of the following is not an objective test?
(A)	
Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA)
(B)	
Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)
(C)	
Impedance Audiometry
(D)	
Pure Tone Audiometry
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
95.	 (D) Pure Tone Audiometry
Audiological tests can be classified as objective 
or subjective (behavioral). Objective tests do 
not require a behavioral response from the 
patient; they measure a physiological response. 
Brainstem 
Evoked 
Response 
Audiometry 
(BERA) or ABR (A), Impedance Audiometry 
(including tympanometry and acoustic reflex 
testing) (C), and otoacoustic emissions are all 
objective tests. Optical Coherence Tomography 
(OCT) (B) is an objective imaging test used in 
ophthalmology, not audiology. In contrast, 
Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA) is a subjective or 
behavioral test. It requires the patient to listen 
to tones of specific frequencies and intensities 
and provide a conscious response (e.g., by 
raising a hand or pressing a button) when they 
hear the tone. The results depend entirely on the 
patient's perception and cooperation, making it 
a subjective measure of hearing thresholds.
Which of the following statements is true regarding patients with primary open-angle glaucoma?
(A)	
Relatives have 1% chance of developing the same condition
(B)	
Relatives are more likely to develop steroid-induced glaucoma
(C)	
When a pupil is dilated, IOP increases
(D)	
Visual loss can be seen in the peripheral field with normal vision in the central field
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
96.	 (D) Visual loss can be seen in the peripheral 
field with normal vision in the central field
Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is 
a 
chronic, 
progressive 
optic 
neuropathy 
characterized by a specific pattern of optic 
nerve head damage and corresponding visual 
field loss. A hallmark feature of glaucoma is 
that it typically affects the peripheral visual 
field first, while central visual acuity remains 
preserved until the late stages of the disease. The 
characteristic visual field defects include nasal 
steps, arcuate scotomas, and eventually tunnel 
vision. This insidious loss of peripheral vision 
is why glaucoma is often called the "silent thief 
of sight." Statement (A) is incorrect; first-degree 
relatives have a significantly higher risk (up 
to 10-fold) than 1%. A family history of POAG 
is a risk factor for steroid-induced glaucoma 
(B), but this is a more complex association. An 
increase in IOP upon pupillary dilation (C) is 
the mechanism for angle-closure glaucoma, not 
open-angle glaucoma.

A patient develops fever, prostration, malaise, dysentery, and dehydration. The illness is likely due to a diarrheagenic strain of Escherichia coli (E. coli), and no antibiotics were given. Which type of virulent E. coli best fits this presentation?
(A)	
Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC)
(B)	
Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC)
(C)	
Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC)
(D)	
Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC)
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
80.	 (C) Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC)
Escherichia coli has several diarrheagenic 
strains, 
each 
producing 
distinct 
clinical 
syndromes.
Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) invades and 
destroys colonic epithelial cells, producing an 
illness similar to shigellosis. It causes fever, 
malaise, prostration, abdominal cramps, and 
dysentery (blood and mucus in stool). Because 
it invades the intestinal mucosa, it produces 
inflammatory diarrhea with systemic symptoms 
and dehydration — matching this clinical 
presentation.
In contrast:
1.	 EAEC causes persistent watery diarrhea, 
mainly in children and travelers, without 
prominent dysentery.
2.	 EHEC (e.g., O157 :H7) causes bloody 
diarrhea but typically has little or no 
fever and may lead to hemolytic uremic 
syndrome (HUS). Antibiotics are avoided 
due to HUS risk.
3.	 EPEC causes watery diarrhea, mainly in 
infants, without invasive dysentery.
Since this patient has fever, systemic toxicity, 
dysentery, and dehydration, the presentation 
is most consistent with Enteroinvasive E. coli 
(EIEC).

This question describes the key laboratory 
features of the genus Actinomyces. Actinomyces 
species 
are 
Gram-positive, 
filamentous, 
branching rods that are part of the normal oral 
flora. They are fastidious and grow best under 
strict anaerobic conditions. When cultured,

Identify the nerve from the list provided that does not play a role in moving the eyeball.
(A)	
Optic Nerve
(B)	
Oculomotor Nerve
(C)	
Trochlear Nerve
(D)	
Abducent Nerve
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
101.	 (A) Optic Nerve
The movements of the eyeball are controlled 
by the six extraocular muscles, which are 
innervated by three specific cranial nerves, 
known as the oculomotor nerves.
1.	 The oculomotor nerve (CN III) (B) 
innervates the superior rectus, inferior 
rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique 
muscles.
2.	 The trochlear nerve (CN IV) (C) innervates 
the superior oblique muscle.
3.	 The abducens nerve (CN VI) (D) innervates 
the lateral rectus muscle.
These three nerves are purely motor (or mixed 
motor/parasympathetic in the case of CN III) 
and are responsible for all voluntary and reflex 
eye movements. In contrast, the optic nerve (CN 
II) (A) is a purely sensory nerve. It is responsible 
for transmitting visual information from the 
retina to the brain. It has no motor function and 
therefore does not cause any movement of the 
eyeball.
From the options listed below, which one is not considered a standard treatment for COVID-19?
1.

3.

102.	 (D) None
This question asks which of the listed 
interventions are not included in the treatment 
of COVID-19.
1.	 Remdesivir : An antiviral medication that 
has been authorized and used for the 
treatment of hospitalized patients with 
COVID-19 to shorten recovery time.
2.	 Dexamethasone : A corticosteroid that 
has been proven to reduce mortality in 
hospitalized patients with COVID-19 who 
require supplemental oxygen or mechanical 
ventilation.
3.	 Fluids : Intravenous or oral fluids are a 
cornerstone of supportive care for any 
critically ill patient, including those with 
COVID-19, to maintain hydration and 
organ perfusion.
4.	 Antibiotics : While antibiotics have no effect 
on the SARS-CoV-2 virus itself, they are 
frequently used in hospitalized COVID-19 
patients to treat or prevent secondary 
bacterial pneumonia, which is a common 
complication.

comprehensive management of patients with 
moderate to severe COVID-19, the correct 
answer is that none of them are excluded from 
the potential treatment plan.
All of the following are true about Gout, except :
(A)	
Occurs due to accumulation of urate crystals in joint
(B)	
Can be precipitated by pyrazinamide
(C)	
Birefringent crystals are present in joint
(D)	
Occurs more in females
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
103.	 (D) Occurs more in females
This statement is the exception because it is 
false. Gout has a strong predilection for males, 
who are affected much more commonly than 
females, especially before the age of menopause. 
The incidence in women increases after 
menopause as the uricosuric effect of estrogen is 
lost. The other statements are all true. Gout is an 
inflammatory arthritis caused by the deposition 
of monosodium urate crystals in and around 
the joints (A), which occurs in the setting of 
hyperuricemia. Examination of synovial fluid 
from an affected joint under polarized light 
reveals needle-shaped, negatively birefringent 
crystals (C), which is the gold standard for 
diagnosis. Gouty attacks can be precipitated 
by certain medications that increase uric acid 
levels by decreasing its renal excretion, a classic 
example of which is the anti-tuberculosis drug 
pyrazinamide (B).

This clinical presentation is a classic picture

excruciating abdominal pain and the relatively

A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with hyper-resonance, hypotension, and absent breath sounds on the right side. What is the next step in the investigation?
(A)	
Needle in 5th ICS
(B)	
Wide bore needle followed by intercostal tube drainage in 5th ICS
(C)	
Aspirate the collection
(D)	
No intervention needed
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
133.	 (B) Wide bore needle followed by intercostal 
tube drainage in 5th ICS
The clinical triad of unilateral absent breath 
sounds, hyper-resonance to percussion, and 
hypotension in a trauma patient is diagnostic of a 
tension pneumothorax. This is a life-threatening 
emergency that causes obstructive shock and 
requires 
immediate 
intervention 
without 
waiting for radiological confirmation. The first 
and most critical step is to decompress the chest 
by inserting a wide-bore needle into the pleural 
space to release the trapped air, converting the 
tension pneumothorax into a simple one. The 
current ATLS guidelines recommend the 5th 
intercostal space (ICS) at the anterior axillary 
line as the preferred site. This emergency needle 
decompression is a temporizing measure and 
must be immediately followed by the definitive 
treatment, which is the insertion of an intercostal 
drain (chest tube), also typically in the 5th 
ICS. Option (B) correctly includes both the 
immediate life-saving decompression and the 
necessary subsequent definitive management.
A 45-year-old female has a 4.5 × 3 cm irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, not fixed to the pectoralis major, with no skin changes, and a 2 × 1.5 cm palpable lymph node in the right axilla. The opposite breast is normal. What is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
a.	
Mammography
b.	
PET scan
c.	
Biopsy of breast mass
d.	
Ultrasound-guided biopsy of the enlarged axillary lymph node
(A)	
a, b, c & d
(B)	
a & c
(C)	
a, b & c
(D)	
a, c & d
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
134.	 (D) a, c & d
The patient has a clinically suspicious breast 
mass and a palpable axillary lymph node, which 
is highly concerning for locally advanced breast 
cancer. The "triple test" or "triple assessment" is 
the standard of care to confirm the diagnosis. 
This includes clinical examination, imaging, 
and tissue sampling. Mammography (a) (and 
often an ultrasound) is the essential initial 
imaging modality to characterize the mass and 
look for other lesions. A core needle biopsy of 
the breast mass (c) is absolutely mandatory to 
obtain a definitive histological diagnosis, which 
will also provide information on the tumor type, 
grade, and receptor status (ER, PR, HER2). 
Additionally, because there is a clinically 
suspicious axillary lymph node, an ultrasound-
guided biopsy (d) (either FNA or core biopsy) 
of that node is crucial to confirm the presence 
of metastasis. This accurately stages the axilla 
(N-stage) and is critical for planning treatment. 
A PET scan (b) is a staging tool used to look for 
distant metastases after the primary diagnosis is 
confirmed; it is not part of the initial diagnostic 
confirmation process.

A 68-year-old man with a recent syncopal episode, congestive heart failure, and a grade III/IV harsh systolic murmur is found on echocardiography to have marked ventricular septal thickening and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. Which of the following findings is most likely to be present in this patient?
(A)	
Radiation of the murmur to the neck
(B)	
Decrease of the murmur with handgrip
(C)	
Delayed carotid upstroke
(D)	
Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
110.	 (B) Decrease of the murmur with handgrip
The patient's presentation and echocardiographic 
findings 
are 
diagnostic 
of 
Hypertrophic 
Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM). The 
harsh systolic murmur in HOCM is caused by 
the dynamic outflow tract obstruction created 
by the thickened septum and the systolic 
anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve. The 
intensity of this murmur is unique in that it 
changes with maneuvers that alter preload and 
afterload. Maneuvers that decrease preload or 
afterload (like standing or Valsalva) make the 
obstruction worse and increase the murmur's 
intensity. Conversely, maneuvers that increase 
preload (squatting) or increase afterload (like a 
sustained handgrip) will decrease the outflow 
gradient and therefore decrease the intensity of 
the murmur. Delayed carotid upstroke (C) and 
radiation to the neck (A) are characteristic of 
aortic stenosis. The ejection fraction in HOCM 
is typically preserved or hyperdynamic, not 
reduced (D).
What are the admission criteria for COVID-19?
(A)	
Multiple comorbidities
(B)	
Chest discomfort
(C)	
Dyspnea
(D)	
All the above
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
111.	 (D) All the above
The decision to admit a patient with COVID-19 
to the hospital is based on an assessment 
of the severity of their illness and their risk 
for deterioration. While mild cases can be 
managed at home, certain signs and symptoms 
warrant hospital admission for monitoring and 
treatment. The most important indication is 
evidence of respiratory compromise, such as 
dyspnea (shortness of breath) (C) or a low oxygen 
saturation. The presence of chest discomfort 
or pain (B) is also a significant symptom that 
requires evaluation and admission. Additionally, 
patients with multiple comorbidities (A) (such 
as diabetes, heart disease, chronic lung disease, 
or immunosuppression) are at a much higher 
risk for developing severe disease, and a lower 
threshold for admission is often applied to this 
group, even with seemingly mild symptoms. 
Therefore, all of the factors listed are valid 
criteria that would contribute to the decision to 
admit a patient with COVID-19.
Which of the following is not a part of high-quality CPR?
(A)	
Chest compressions 100-120/min
(B)	
Allow chest recoil
(C)	
Chest wall depression of 5-6 cm
(D)	
Respiratory rate of 20-25/min
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
112.	 (D) Respiratory rate of 20-25/min
High-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation 
(CPR) is critical for improving outcomes in 
cardiac arrest. The key components, as defined 
by international guidelines (e.g., American 
Heart Association), include :
1.	 Pushing hard and fast : Compressing the 
chest at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions 
per minute (A) to an adequate depth of at 
least 2 inches (5-6 cm) in adults (C).
2.	 Allowing for full chest recoil between 
compressions (B) to permit the heart to fill 
with blood.
3.	 Minimizing 
interruptions 
in 
chest 
compressions. When providing rescue 
breaths with an unprotected airway, the 
correct compression-to-ventilation ratio 
is 30 :2. If an advanced airway is in place, 
breaths are given at a rate of 1 breath every 
6 seconds, which equates to a respiratory 
rate of 10 breaths per minute. A respiratory 
rate of 20-25/min (D) is too high and 
would constitute hyperventilation, which 
is detrimental as it increases intrathoracic 
pressure and decreases venous return.

Congenital pyloric stenosis presents with which of the following?
(A)	
Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
(B)	
Abdominal mass
(C)	
Bilious vomiting
(D)	
A & B Both
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
141.	 (D) A & B Both
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is a condition seen 
typically in infants between 2–8 weeks of age. It 
occurs due to hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle, 
leading to gastric outlet obstruction.
Projectile, non-bilious vomiting is the 
hallmark feature because the obstruction is 
proximal to the duodenum; therefore, bile does 
not mix with gastric contents. Hence, option (C) 
bilious vomiting is incorrect.
Due to repeated vomiting of gastric contents 
(which contain hydrochloric acid), there is loss 
of hydrogen and chloride ions. This results 
in hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic 
alkalosis, making option (A) correct. Persistent 
vomiting also leads to dehydration.
On abdominal examination, a firm, olive-
shaped mass may be palpated in the right upper 
quadrant or epigastrium. This palpable “pyloric 
olive” represents the hypertrophied pylorus, 
making option (B) correct.
Thus, congenital pyloric stenosis presents 
with metabolic alkalosis and an abdominal 
mass, so the correct answer is A and B (Option 
D).
A child has a bed-wetting habit, and organic causes have been excluded. What is the appropriate management?
(A)	
Pharmacotherapy
(B)	
Psychotherapy
(C)	
Bed alarm
(D)	
Acupuncture
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
142.	 (C) Bed alarm
The condition described is primary nocturnal 
enuresis, which is bed-wetting in a child 
older than 5 years who has never achieved a 
consistent period of nighttime dryness, and in 
whom organic causes have been excluded. The 
first-line management involves conservative 
measures and behavioral therapy. The most 
effective and recommended behavioral therapy 
with the highest long-term success rate is 
the enuresis alarm, or bed alarm. This device 
consists of a moisture sensor placed in the 
child's underwear that is connected to an alarm. 
When the child begins to urinate, the sensor 
triggers the alarm, which wakes the child. Over 
time, this conditions the child to recognize the 
sensation of a full bladder and to wake up to 
void before the alarm goes off. Pharmacotherapy 
(A), such as with desmopressin or imipramine, 
is considered a second-line option for short-
term control but has a high relapse rate when 
stopped.

A road-traffic-accident (RTA) patient with polytrauma has unstable vitals, is intubated due to a low Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), shows no eye opening, no verbal response, no motor response to pain, and CT scan reveals brain edema. What is the most likely cause?
(A)	
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome
(B)	
Diffuse axonal injury
(C)	
Post-concussion syndrome
(D)	
CO2 retention due to respiratory depression by morphine
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
119.	 (B) Diffuse axonal injury
This is a duplicate of a previous question. The 
patient has suffered a severe traumatic brain 
injury (TBI) from an RTA, resulting in a deep 
coma with a GCS score of 3 (E1, V1, M1). 
The CT scan finding of brain edema without 
a focal mass lesion like a hematoma, in the 
context of a high-impact trauma and severe 
neurological deficit, is highly suggestive of 
diffuse axonal injury (DAI). DAI is caused by 
shearing forces from acceleration-deceleration,

to axons throughout the brain. This widespread 
disruption of neuronal pathways results in 
immediate and profound coma. The subsequent 
development of cytotoxic and vasogenic brain 
edema is a common consequence of this severe 
primary injury. Post-concussion syndrome (C) 
follows a mild TBI. PRES (A) has a different 
etiology and imaging appearance.
A 45-year-old female reports breast pain, edema, redness, warmth, and rapid enlargement over 15 days. What is the likely diagnosis?
(A)	
IBC (Inflammatory Breast Cancer)
(B)	
Giant fibroadenoma
(C)	
Atypical duct hypertrophy
(D)	
Galactocele
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
120.	 (A) IBC (Inflammatory Breast Cancer)
The patient's presentation with a rapidly 
progressive, painful, red, warm, and swollen 
breast is a classic and highly concerning 
picture for Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC). 
IBC is a rare but extremely aggressive form 
of breast cancer. It is characterized by the 
diffuse infiltration and blockage of the dermal 
lymphatics by cancer cells. This lymphatic 
obstruction is what causes the characteristic 
signs of inflammation : erythema (redness), 
edema (swelling), and a "peau d'orange" (orange 
peel) appearance of the skin. A key feature is the 
rapid onset and progression of these symptoms, 
often over a period of days to weeks, frequently 
without a distinct palpable lump. This clinical 
diagnosis must be considered an emergency, 
and an urgent skin punch biopsy is required for 
confirmation. While mastitis is a differential, in 
a non-lactating woman, IBC must be ruled out 
first.
Which of the following statements about a pilonidal sinus is incorrect?
(A)	
It is more common in men.
(B)	
Hair follicles are seen in the wall of sinus.
(C)	
Mostly congenital.
(D)	
Treatment of choice is surgical excision of sinus tract.
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
121.	 (C) Mostly congenital.
This statement is incorrect. For many years, 
pilonidal sinus disease was thought to be a 
congenital condition arising from a remnant of 
the neural tube. However, the modern and widely 
accepted understanding is that it is an acquired 
condition. The process is believed to begin with 
the stretching and blockage of hair follicles in 
the natal cleft. Loose hairs are then driven into 
these dilated follicles by friction and pressure, 
creating a foreign body reaction that leads to 
the formation of a sinus tract and recurrent 
inflammation or abscess. The other statements 
are correct. Pilonidal sinus is significantly more 
common in men (A), particularly in hirsute 
individuals. The sinus tracts characteristically 
contain nests of hair, but hair follicles are not 
seen in the wall of the sinus (B), which supports 
the acquired theory (hair is driven in from the 
outside). The definitive treatment is surgical 
excision of the sinus tract (D).

A 42-year-old male has had a cough with mucopurulent discharge for 2 years, and a coronal lung section shows cyst-like spaces in the right middle zone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	
Bronchiectasis
(B)	
Hydatid cyst
(C)	
Cystic Fibrosis
(D)	
Pulmonary TB
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
114.	 (A) Bronchiectasis
The patient's long-standing history of a chronic 
productive cough with mucopurulent sputum 
is the classic symptom of bronchiectasis. 
Bronchiectasis is a chronic respiratory disease 
characterized by the permanent and abnormal 
dilation of the bronchi and bronchioles. This 
structural damage impairs the mucociliary 
clearance mechanism, leading to the pooling 
of secretions, chronic bacterial infection, and a 
persistent inflammatory cycle. Radiologically, 
the hallmark of bronchiectasis is bronchial 
wall thickening ("tram tracking") and airway 
dilation. On a CT scan, this can appear as 
dilated, thick-walled airways, a "signet ring" 
sign, or, in severe cases, the formation of clusters 
of cystic-like spaces, which is consistent with 
the finding described in the question. While 
cystic fibrosis (C) and post-infectious causes like 
TB (D) are major causes of bronchiectasis, the 
diagnosis describing the final pathological state 
is bronchiectasis itself.
What is the size of a pink IV cannula?
(A)	
20 G
(B)	
18 G
(C)	
22 G
(D)	
16 G
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
115.	 (A) 20 G
Intravenous (IV) cannulas are universally color-
coded to allow for rapid identification of their 
gauge size. The gauge number indicates the 
internal diameter of the cannula, with a smaller 
number corresponding to a larger diameter and 
a higher potential flow rate. The standard color 
code for a 20-gauge IV cannula is pink. This is 
a very common, general-purpose size used in 
adults for routine IV fluid administration, giving 
IV medications, and for blood transfusions when 
a larger gauge is not necessary. For reference, 
an 18-gauge cannula is green (B), a 22-gauge 
cannula is blue (C), and a 16-gauge cannula is 
gray (D). Remembering these color codes is an 
essential practical skill in clinical settings.
A farmer develops a painless foot lesion with multiple discharging sinuses. What is the most likely diagnosis?

(B)

(C)

116.	 (A) Mycetoma
The clinical triad of a painless, tumefied 
(swollen) subcutaneous lesion, the formation 
of multiple draining sinuses, and the discharge 
of grains (macroscopic colonies of the causative 
agent) is pathognomonic for mycetoma, also 
known as Madura foot. This is a chronic, 
progressive, granulomatous infection of the 
skin and subcutaneous tissues that can extend 
to involve the underlying fascia and bone. It is 
typically caused by the traumatic inoculation of

farmers a high-risk group. The infection can

lymphocutaneous 
spread.

cell

What is the first and specific marker for myocardial infarction (MI)?
(A)	
LDH
(B)	
Troponin
(C)	
CK (Creatine Kinase)
(D)	
None of the above
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
117.	 (B) Troponin
Cardiac troponins (specifically troponin T 
and troponin I) are regulatory proteins that 
are components of the contractile apparatus 
of cardiac muscle. They are highly specific 
to the myocardium. When myocardial cells 
are damaged and undergo necrosis during a 
myocardial infarction (MI), these proteins are 
released into the bloodstream. The measurement 
of serum cardiac troponin levels is the current 
gold standard and the most sensitive and 
specific biochemical marker for the diagnosis 
of MI. Troponins begin to rise in the blood 
within 2-4 hours of the onset of injury, peak at 
12-24 hours, and can remain elevated for 7-14 
days. While Creatine Kinase (CK), especially 
the CK-MB isoenzyme, was previously used, it 
is less specific than troponin as it is also found 
in skeletal muscle. LDH (A) is even less specific 
and is no longer used for diagnosing MI.

A 40-year-old male with varicose veins presents with eczema and lipodermatosclerosis. According to the CEAP classification, this falls under which category?
(A)	
C3
(B)	
C4
(C)	
C5
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
128.	 (B) C4
The CEAP (Clinical, Etiological, Anatomical, 
Pathophysiological) classification is the standard 
system for describing chronic venous disorders. 
The "C" component describes the clinical signs 
on a scale from 0 to 6.
1.	 C0 : No visible or palpable signs of venous 
disease.
2.	 C1 : Telangiectasias or reticular veins.
3.	 C2 : Varicose veins.
4.	 C3 : Edema.
5.	 C4 : Changes in the skin and subcutaneous

i.

ii.	 C4b : Lipodermatosclerosis or atrophie 
blanche.
iii.	 C4c : Corona phlebectatica.
6.	 C5 : Healed venous ulcer.
7.	 C6 : Active venous ulcer.
Since the patient has both eczema and 
lipodermatosclerosis, he falls under the C4 
clinical category.
Which of the following is not a component of the qSOFA score?
(A)	
BP
(B)	
RR
(C)	
Heart rate
(D)	
Mental status
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
129.	 (C) Heart rate
The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment 
(qSOFA) score is a simple bedside tool used to 
identify patients with suspected infection who 
are at a high risk of poor outcomes (i.e., sepsis). 
It consists of three clinical criteria, with one 
point awarded for each :
1.	 Respiratory Rate (RR) : A high respiratory 
rate of ≥ 22 breaths per minute.
2.	 Mental Status : An altered mental status, 
typically assessed with a Glasgow Coma 
Scale (GCS) score of < 15.
3.	 Blood Pressure (BP) : A low systolic blood 
pressure of ≤ 100 mmHg.
A score of 2 or more suggests a high risk of 
sepsis and warrants further investigation and 
management. Heart rate is not a component 
of the qSOFA score, although tachycardia is a 
common sign of sepsis and is included in the 
more comprehensive SIRS criteria and the full 
SOFA score.
A 13-year-old girl presents with a left-sided neck swelling that has grown slowly since childhood and feels hard on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	
Neural tumor
(B)	
Chemodectoma
(C)	
Lipoma
(D)	
Cystic hygroma
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
130.	 (A) Neural tumor
In a young patient presenting with a slow-
growing, hard, deep-seated neck mass, a benign 
neural tumor should be a primary consideration. 
Specifically, a schwannoma or a neurofibroma, 
which are tumors arising from the nerve sheaths 
of peripheral nerves, fit this description well. 
These tumors can originate from various nerves 
in the neck, such as the vagus nerve or branches 
of the cervical plexus. They are typically firm, 
mobile, and grow very slowly over many years. A 
cystic hygroma (D), a lymphatic malformation, 
is typically soft, cystic, and present in infancy. A 
lipoma (C) is a benign tumor of fat cells and is 
characteristically soft and doughy, not hard. A 
chemodectoma (B), or carotid body tumor, is a 
paraganglioma that is typically found in middle-
aged adults, is pulsatile, and is classically mobile 
side-to-side but not vertically (Fontaine's sign). 
Therefore, a neural tumor is the most likely 
diagnosis for a hard, slow-growing mass in this 
age group.

A 50-year-old alcoholic is brought to the hospital with bleeding esophageal varices and dies. At autopsy, his distended abdomen contains a large amount of serous fluid. What is the correct term for this fluid?
(A)	
Exudate
(B)	
Ascites
(C)	
Hemorrhage
(D)	
Lymphedema
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
105.	 (B) Ascites
The clinical history describes a patient with 
decompensated 
liver 
cirrhosis, 
evidenced 
by bleeding esophageal varices. A major 
complication of cirrhosis is the development of 
portal hypertension. The high pressure in the 
portal venous system, combined with low serum 
albumin levels (due to impaired liver synthesis), 
causes fluid to shift from the vascular space 
into the peritoneal cavity. The accumulation of 
this serous fluid within the peritoneal cavity is 
specifically termed ascites. This fluid is typically 
a transudate, characterized by a low protein 
content, as opposed to an exudate (A), which is 
protein-rich and associated with inflammation. 
Hemorrhage (C) refers to bleeding, and 
lymphedema (D) is the accumulation of 
lymphatic fluid in the interstitial tissues, usually 
in the limbs. The correct term for the intra-
abdominal fluid in this context is ascites.
A 20-year-old patient is rapidly gaining weight and has elevated TSH levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
(A)	
Hashimoto's thyroiditis
(B)	
Graves' disease
(C)	
Pituitary tumor
(D)	
Hypothyroidism
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
106.	 (D) Hypothyroidism
The patient's symptoms of weight gain, 
combined with an elevated Thyroid-Stimulating 
Hormone (TSH) level, point directly to a 
diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism. In 
primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid gland 
itself is failing and cannot produce enough 
thyroid hormone (T4 and T3). The low levels 
of circulating thyroid hormone lead to a loss 
of negative feedback on the pituitary gland. In 
response, the pituitary secretes an increased 
amount of TSH in an attempt to stimulate 
the failing thyroid. The clinical symptoms of 
hypothyroidism, such as weight gain, fatigue, 
and cold intolerance, are due to the deficiency 
of thyroid hormone. Hashimoto's thyroiditis 
(A) is the most common cause of primary 
hypothyroidism, but "hypothyroidism" (D) is the 
overall diagnosis. Graves' disease (B) is a cause 
of hyperthyroidism with a suppressed TSH. A 
TSH-secreting pituitary tumor (C) would cause 
hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism.
A woman presents with dark knuckles and anemia. What type of anemia is most likely?
(A)	
Megaloblastic anemia
(B)

The Strasberg classification is a widely used 
system to categorize iatrogenic bile duct injuries 
that occur during cholecystectomy.
A	 Type : Leak from the cystic duct stump or a 
small duct in the gallbladder fossa.
B	 Type : Occlusion of a part of the biliary tree, 
most commonly an aberrant right hepatic 
duct.
C	 Type : A transected (but not ligated) duct 
that is leaking bile. This most commonly 
involves a transected aberrant right hepatic 
duct or a posterior sectoral duct.
D	 Type : A lateral or partial injury to a major 
bile duct, such as the common bile duct, 
with bile leakage.
E	 Type 
: 
A 
circumferential 
injury 
or 
transection of the main bile duct, further 
subdivided based on the level of the injury.
Therefore, an injury involving the transection 
and subsequent leak from a posterior sectoral 
duct is classified as a Strasberg Type C injury.
A 40-year-old female undergoes cholecystectomy and later develops postoperative abdominal pain. Which test is used to detect a bile leak?
(A)	
ERCP
(B)	
MRCP
(C)	
HIDA
(D)	
CECT
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
136.	 (C) HIDA
When a post-cholecystectomy bile leak is 
suspected, the most sensitive and specific 
functional imaging study to identify the leak is 
a HIDA scan (Hepatobiliary Iminodiacetic Acid 
scan), also known as cholescintigraphy. This is a 
nuclear medicine test where a radioactive tracer 
(e.g., technetium-99m labeled mebrofenin) is 
injected intravenously. The tracer is taken up 
by the hepatocytes and excreted into the biliary 
system, mimicking the flow of bile. The flow of 
the tracer is imaged over time with a gamma 
camera. In a patient with a bile leak, the scan 
will show the tracer flowing normally through 
the bile ducts but will also demonstrate the 
abnormal extravasation of the tracer from the 
biliary tree into the peritoneal cavity, confirming 
the presence, and often the location, of the leak. 
While MRCP (B) shows anatomy and ERCP 
(A) is therapeutic, HIDA is the best test to 
functionally demonstrate an active leak.
What is the Tillaux sign in mesenteric cysts?
(A)	
Mass is mobile only in plane perpendicular to mesentery
(B)

(C)

(D)

137.	 (A) Mass is mobile only in plane perpendicular 
to mesentery
A mesenteric cyst is a rare, benign, fluid-filled 
sac located within the mesentery of the small 
intestine. A key clinical feature that helps in 
its diagnosis is its characteristic mobility on 
physical examination. This is known as Tillaux's 
sign (or Tillaux's triad, which also includes 
a dull percussion note and a location in the 
umbilical region). The sign describes that the 
mass is mobile in the direction perpendicular 
to the line of attachment of the mesentery, 
but its mobility is restricted in the direction 
parallel to the mesenteric root. The root of the 
small bowel mesentery runs obliquely from 
the duodenojejunal flexure in the left upper 
quadrant down to the ileocecal junction in the 
right lower quadrant. Therefore, the cyst can 
be moved from side-to-side (perpendicular to 
this line) but not up-and-down (parallel to this 
line). This specific pattern of mobility is highly 
suggestive of a mesenteric origin.

Primary retroperitoneal tumors are rare, and 
the vast majority are malignant soft tissue 
sarcomas. The single most common histological 
type of primary retroperitoneal sarcoma in 
adults is liposarcoma. These tumors arise from 
adipose tissue within the retroperitoneum and 
can grow to an enormous size before they cause

retroperitoneum, they are all significantly less 
common than liposarcoma.

The image shows a deep, "punched-out" ulcer

All four instruments shown are used in the

The sagittal CT scan of the spine shows extensive

Which of the following investigations can be used in osteoporosis?
1.	
DEXA
2.	
Bone Scan
3.	
Quantitative CT
4.	
Chemical Analysis
Select the answer using the following key-
(A)	
1,2
(B)	
1,2,3
(C)	
1,3,4
(D)	
1,2,3,4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
145.	 (C) 1,3,4
Osteoporosis is characterized by reduced bone 
mineral density (BMD) and increased fracture 
risk. The investigations used aim to measure 
bone density and evaluate metabolic causes.
1.	 DEXA (Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) 
is the gold standard for diagnosing 
osteoporosis. It measures bone mineral 
density at the hip and spine and provides a 
T-score for assessment.
2.	 Quantitative CT (QCT) is another method 
that measures volumetric bone density 
and can assess trabecular bone separately. 
Though less commonly used due to higher 
radiation exposure and cost, it is a valid 
diagnostic tool.
3.	 Chemical analysis refers to biochemical 
investigations such as serum calcium, 
phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, vitamin 
D, and parathyroid hormone levels. These 
tests help identify secondary causes of 
osteoporosis.
4.	 Bone scan (nuclear medicine scan) is not 
used to diagnose osteoporosis. It detects 
areas of increased bone turnover, such as 
metastasis, infection, or fractures, but does 
not measure bone density.
Thus, the correct combination is 1, 3, and 4 
(Option C).

Identify the procedure in the image shown below.
(A)	
Lateral Grip
(B)	
Fundal Grip
(C)	
Pawlik Grip
(D)	
2nd Pelvic Grip
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
153.	 (A) Lateral Grip
The image clearly depicts and labels the Second 
Leopold's Maneuver. This is one of the four 
standard obstetric maneuvers used to determine 
the position of the fetus in the uterus. This 
specific maneuver is also known as the "Lateral 
Grip" or "Umbilical Grip." It is performed by the 
examiner placing the palms of their hands on 
either side of the maternal abdomen. Gentle but 
deep pressure is then applied to palpate the sides 
of the uterus. The purpose of this maneuver is to 
determine on which side the firm, smooth fetal 
back is located and on which side the irregular, 
nodular small parts (limbs) are located. This 
information helps to determine the fetal lie and 
position. The Fundal Grip is the first maneuver, 
Pawlik's Grip is the third, and the Pelvic Grip is 
the fourth.
A midwife is examining a pregnant woman and notices an umbilical cord prolapse. What should be the next step in management?
(A)	
Gently push the cord back inside the uterus.
(B)	
Immediately transfer the patient for delivery.
(C)	
Perform a per vaginal (PV) examination to assess the situation.
(D)	
Place the patient in the Trendelenburg position.
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
154.	 (D) Place the patient in the Trendelenburg 
position.
Overt umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric 
emergency where the umbilical cord descends 
ahead of the fetal presenting part after the 
membranes have ruptured. The immediate and 
critical risk is compression of the cord between 
the fetus and the maternal pelvis, which can 
cut off the fetal blood supply, leading to severe 
hypoxia and death. The first-line management 
is to immediately relieve the pressure on the 
cord. This is done by placing the mother in a 
position that uses gravity to move the fetus away 
from the pelvis, such as the steep Trendelenburg 
position (head down) or the knee-chest position. 
Simultaneously, the person who diagnosed 
the prolapse should insert two fingers into the 
vagina to manually elevate the fetal presenting 
part off the cord. Pushing the cord back in (A) is 
contraindicated. While immediate delivery (B) is 
the definitive treatment (usually by emergency 
C-section), relieving the pressure is the first step.
What is the minimum cervical dilation at which a partograph should be initiated?
(A)	
2cm
(B)	
4cm
(C)	
6cm
(D)	
8cm
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
155.	 (B) 4cm
A partograph is a graphical tool used to 
monitor the progress of labor and identify any 
abnormalities in a timely manner. Plotting on 
the partograph should begin when the woman 
enters the active phase of the first stage of labor. 
According to the World Health Organization 
(WHO), which developed the most widely 
used partograph, the active phase of labor is 
considered to begin when the cervix is dilated 
to 4 cm and there are regular, painful uterine 
contractions. Once the woman reaches 4 cm 
dilation, the cervical dilation is plotted on the 
partograph against time, with an alert line and 
an action line to help identify prolonged labor. 
Starting the partograph before the active phase 
(e.g., at 2 cm) is not recommended as the rate 
of cervical dilation during the latent phase is 
slow and unpredictable. (Note : More recent 
definitions define active labor as starting at 6 cm, 
but the 4 cm rule for initiating the partograph is 
still the standard teaching).

A 25-year-old female has progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, and a barium swallow has been performed. Which investigations are needed to confirm the diagnosis?
(A)	
UGIE +24hr pH monitoring
(B)	
UGIE + Esophageal manometry
(C)	
UGIE CT chest
(D)	
UGIE + biopsy
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
175.	 (B) UGIE + Esophageal manometry
Progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids 
is characteristic of an esophageal motility 
disorder, such as achalasia cardia. The barium 
swallow finding (not shown, but implied to 
be suggestive) would likely show a dilated 
esophagus with a "bird's beak" narrowing at 
the gastroesophageal junction. The essential 
workup to confirm the diagnosis includes 
two key investigations. First, an Upper GI 
Endoscopy (UGIE) is mandatory to visualize

What is the most common CT scan lung image finding in a COVID-19 patient?
(A)	
Consolidation
(B)	
Opacities
(C)	
Effusion
(D)	
Cystic Lesions
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
176.	 (B) Opacities
The most common and characteristic finding 
of COVID-19 pneumonia on a chest CT scan is 
the presence of ground-glass opacities (GGOs). 
"Opacities" is a general term that encompasses 
GGOs. GGOs are areas of hazy, increased lung 
density that do not obscure the underlying 
bronchial and vascular markings. In COVID-19, 
these opacities are typically bilateral, have a 
peripheral and subpleural distribution, and 
are most prominent in the lower lobes. They 
often have a rounded or geographic shape. 
While consolidation (A) (denser opacification 
that obscures vessels) can also be seen, often 
in combination with GGOs (a "mixed" pattern), 
pure GGOs are the earliest and most frequent

Allergic 
contact 
dermatitis 
(ACD) 
is 
a 
classic example of a Type IV (delayed-type) 
hypersensitivity reaction. It is T-cell mediated 
and does not involve IgE antibodies. Therefore, 
tests for Type I hypersensitivity, such as 
measuring total or specific IgE (A) or the 
Radioallergosorbent test (RAST) (B), are not

a localized area of eczema (erythema, papules,

that specific substance.

This question assesses the basic life support 
(BLS) algorithm for an unresponsive adult. The 
correct sequence of actions for a single rescuer 
is :
1.	 Check for safety of the scene.
2.	 Check for responsiveness (tap and shout).
3.	 If unresponsive, immediately shout for 
nearby help and activate the emergency 
response system (e.g., call the local 
emergency number). If you are alone, you 
can do this with a mobile phone on speaker.
4.	 Simultaneously, check for breathing and a 
carotid pulse for no more than 10 seconds.
5.	 If there is no pulse or no normal breathing, 
immediately 
begin 
high-quality 
CPR, 
starting with chest compressions.
Option (B) follows this correct sequence : 
activating help first, then assessing the patient, 
and then initiating CPR. Option (A) incorrectly 
prioritizes starting CPR before calling for help, 
which would delay the arrival of advanced 
medical care and a defibrillator.

If all parts of the sternum and the medial end of the clavicle are ossified, what is the estimated age?
(A)

(B)	
>25 years
(C)	
14-15 years
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
148.	 (B) >25 years
This question uses key skeletal maturation 
milestones for age estimation. The sternum 
ossifies from several centers. The fusion of the 
manubrium with the body (manubriosternal 
joint) occurs late in life, but the fusion of the 
four sternebrae of the body is typically complete 
by 25 years of age. The xiphoid process also fuses 
with the body later. The most critical landmark 
provided is the medial clavicular epiphysis. This 
is one of the last epiphyses in the entire body to 
fuse. The fusion process begins around age 18-
22 and is generally complete by 25 to 31 years 
of age. Therefore, if both the sternum and the 
medial clavicle are observed to be fully ossified 
and fused, it is a strong indicator that the 
individual is older than 25 years. This milestone 
is particularly useful in forensic anthropology 
for determining if an individual has reached 
adulthood.

The image shows a metered-dose inhaler 
(MDI), a common device for delivering inhaled 
medications for asthma and COPD. One of 
the major drawbacks of using an MDI is that 
it requires a precise coordination between 
actuating (pressing) the canister and inhaling 
slowly and deeply. Many patients have difficulty 
with this technique. Poor coordination leads 
to the high-velocity aerosolized drug particles 
impacting on and being deposited in the 
oropharynx (the back of the mouth and throat) 
instead of being inhaled deeply into the lungs. 
This oropharyngeal deposition reduces the 
amount of drug reaching the target site in the 
airways, decreasing its efficacy, and can increase 
local side effects, such as oral candidiasis 
with inhaled corticosteroids. Using a spacer 
device can significantly reduce this problem by 
slowing the aerosol and allowing more time for 
inhalation. Portability (A) is an advantage, not a 
drawback.

Peripheral intravenous (IV) cannulas are color-
coded to provide a quick and reliable way to 
identify their size (gauge). The gauge number is 
inversely proportional to the cannula's diameter, 
so a smaller gauge number indicates a larger

cannula is blue (C), and an 18G cannula is green 
(D).

173.	 (B) Caldwell Luc view
The Caldwell view is a specific radiographic 
projection used to visualize the paranasal 
sinuses. It is an occipito-frontal view taken 
with the patient's forehead and nose against 
the image receptor and the X-ray beam angled 
approximately 15 degrees caudally. This specific 
angulation projects the dense petrous ridges of 
the temporal bone downwards, below the orbits, 
providing a clear, unobstructed view of the 
frontal sinuses. It also provides a good view of the 
ethmoid sinuses. In contrast, the Water's view 
(A) (occipito-mental view) is angled to provide 
the best view of the maxillary sinuses. The term 
"Caldwell-Luc view" is slightly confused; the 
Caldwell view is the X-ray, while the Caldwell-
Luc operation is a surgical procedure on the 
maxillary sinus. Granger's and Campwell views 
are not standard sinus views.

HPV causes cervical carcinoma due to which of the following?
(A)	
E1, E2
(B)	
E2, E6
(C)	
L1, E6
(D)	
E2,E4
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
157.	 (B) E2, E6
Cervical carcinoma caused by high-risk Human 
Papillomavirus (HPV) is primarily driven by 
the viral oncoproteins E6 and E7. However, 
their activity is linked to the function of the E2 
protein.
Here's the mechanism :
1.	 E6 and E7 are the main culprits : The 
E6 protein targets and promotes the 
degradation of the host's p53 tumor 
suppressor protein (the "guardian of the 
genome"). The E7 protein inactivates the 
retinoblastoma (Rb) tumor suppressor 
protein. The loss of these two key proteins 
leads to uncontrolled cell proliferation and 
prevents damaged cells from undergoing 
apoptosis (programmed cell death).
2.	 E2 is the regulator : In a normal, non-
cancerous HPV infection, the E2 protein 
acts as a repressor, keeping the expression 
of E6 and E7 in check.
3.	 The cancerous switch : For cancer to 
develop, the circular HPV DNA usually 
integrates into the host cell's chromosome. 
This integration process often breaks the 
viral genome within the E2 gene, disrupting 
its function. With E2 inactivated, there 
are no "brakes," leading to massive over 
expression of E6 and E7, which drives the 
cell towards malignancy.
Therefore, the interplay between the disruption 
of E2 and the oncogenic action of E6 is central 
to HPV-induced cancer.
In an elderly man with psoriasis involving 50% of his body surface area, which of the following treatments cannot be used?
(A)	
Methotrexate
(B)	
Steroids
(C)	
Narrow band UVB
(D)

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
158.	 (B) Steroids
The patient has severe, extensive plaque 
psoriasis. Systemic therapies are required for this 
extent of disease. Methotrexate (A), cyclosporine 
(D), and phototherapy with Narrowband UVB 
(C) are all standard and effective treatments 
for severe psoriasis. Systemic steroids (e.g., oral 
prednisone), however, should not be used for the 
chronic management of plaque psoriasis. While 
they can produce a rapid initial improvement, 
their withdrawal is notoriously associated with a 
severe, and sometimes life-threatening, rebound 
flare of the psoriasis. This can manifest as a severe 
pustular or erythrodermic psoriasis. Due to this 
high risk of rebound and the significant long-
term side effects, systemic steroids are relatively 
contraindicated for treating plaque psoriasis, 
although they may be used in very specific, 
acute situations under expert supervision.

A 40-year-old man says he feels his feet are dirty even though he knows this isn’t true. This causes him distress, leading him to wash them repeatedly. This represents a disorder of which aspect of thought?
(A)	
Possession
(B)	
Flow
(C)	
Form
(D)	
Content
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
181.	 (D) Content
The patient is describing an obsession, which is 
a key feature of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder 
(OCD). An obsession is a recurrent and persistent 
thought, urge, or image that is experienced as 
intrusive and unwanted and causes marked 
anxiety or distress. The patient's thought that 
his feet are dirty is the obsession. The key aspect 
here is what the patient is thinking about. This 
relates to the content of thought. Disorders of 
thought content include delusions, overvalued 
ideas, and obsessions. The patient recognizes 
that the thought is his own (not a disorder of 
possession, A) and that it is irrational ("knows 
that it's not true"), which is characteristic of an 
obsession. Disorders of thought flow (B) relate 
to the speed of thoughts (e.g., flight of ideas), 
and disorders of thought form (C) relate to 
the logical connection between thoughts (e.g., 
loosening of associations).
How will you differentiate delirium from dementia in Alzheimer's disease?
(A)	
Disorientation and agitation
(B)	
Visual hallucinations and impairment of memory
(C)	
Acute onset and level of consciousness
(D)	
Agitation and irritation
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
182.	 (C) Acute onset and level of consciousness
Delirium and dementia can present with 
overlapping symptoms like confusion and 
memory impairment, and delirium is often 
superimposed on a baseline dementia. However, 
there are key features that help to differentiate 
them. The most crucial distinguishing feature 
is the onset and course. Dementia, like 
Alzheimer's disease, has an insidious onset 
and a progressive, chronic course. Delirium, 
on the other hand, is characterized by an acute 
onset (developing over hours to days) and a 
fluctuating course. The second cardinal feature 
that distinguishes delirium is a disturbance 
in the level of consciousness, awareness, 
and attention. Patients with delirium have a 
clouded sensorium and are inattentive, whereas 
in dementia, the level of consciousness is 
typically preserved until the very late stages. 
While symptoms like agitation (A, D) and 
hallucinations (B) are common in delirium, 
they can also occur in dementia, making them 
less reliable differentiating factors than the 
acute onset and altered level of consciousness.
A patient with severe depression was treated with a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) and showed improvement after 4 weeks. At the time of discharge, what is the most important concern?
(A)	
Suicidal tendencies related to TCA overdose
(B)	
Therapeutic drug monitoring of TCA
(C)	
ECG monitoring for arrhythmias
(D)	
To prescribe modafinil to counteract sedation due to TCA
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
183.	 (A) Suicidal tendencies related to TCA overdose
A critical period in the treatment of severe 
depression is when the patient begins to 
respond to medication. As their energy and 
motivation start to return, but before their 
mood and suicidal ideation have fully resolved, 
the risk of a suicide attempt can paradoxically 
increase. Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are 
highly lethal in overdose, primarily due to their 
cardiotoxic effects (arrhythmias). An overdose 
of as little as a one-week supply of TCAs can 
be fatal. Therefore, the most important concern 
when discharging a patient who is improving 
from severe depression on a TCA is the risk 
that they might use their prescribed medication 
to attempt suicide. This necessitates careful 
assessment of suicidal ideation and often 
involves dispensing only a limited supply of the 
medication at a time. While ECG monitoring

166.	 (B) High flow nasal cannula
The image displays the complete setup for High-
Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) therapy. The key 
components that identify this system are the 
wide-bore nasal cannula prongs, the heated and 
humidified breathing circuit, and the air-oxygen 
blender that allows for the delivery of a very 
high gas flow rate (up to 60-80 L/min) with a 
precisely controlled fraction of inspired oxygen 
(FiO2​). This system provides respiratory support 
by washing out the nasopharyngeal dead space, 
provid ing a small amount of positive airway 
pressu re, and delivering a consistent, high 
FiO2​ to treat hypoxemia. It is distinct from 
conventional CPAP (A) or BiPAP (part of NIV, 
D), w h ich use a tight-fitting mask to deliver 
press u re, and from a mechanical ventilator 
(C), w hich provides invasive support via an 
endotracheal tube.
The blue pipeline in the operating theatre (OT) is for which anesthetic gas?
(A)	
Oxygen
(B)	
Nitrous oxide
(C)	
Air
(D)	
Vacuum
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
167.	 (B) Nitrous oxide
Medical gas pipeline systems in hospitals are 
universally color-coded to prevent accidental 
administration of the wrong gas, which could be 
catastrophic. The standard color coding varies 
slightly by country, but under the widely used 
International Organization for Standardization 
(ISO) system, the colors are :
Oxygen (A) : White
Nitrous Oxide : Blue
Medical Air (C) : Black and White
Vacuum/Suction (D) : Yellow
The image shows a medical gas supply system 
on a wall. According to the standard color code, 
the blue pipeline and outlet are designated for 
nitrous oxide (N2O), an inhalational anesthetic 
and analgesic agent. This consistent color-coding 
is a critical safety feature in any healthcare 
facility where medical gases are used.
Match the dilution of adrenaline with the correct route of administration (ROA) :
(A)	
1-B, 2-A, 3-C
(B)	
2-B, 3-C, 1-A
(C)	
1-C, 2-A, 3-B
(D)	
None of these
	
EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
168.	 (A) 1-B, 2-A, 3-C
Different dilutions of adrenaline (epinephrine) 
are used for specific clinical applications and 
routes of administration to ensure safety and 
efficacy.
1.	 1 : 1,000 (1 mg/mL) is the standard 
concentration for intramuscular (IM) or 
subcutaneous injection, most commonly 
used for treating anaphylaxis. (1-B)
2.	 1 : 10,000 (0.1 mg/mL) is the more dilute 
preparation used for intravenous (IV) or 
intracardiac (IC) administration, primarily 
during cardiac arrest resuscitation (ACLS 
protocol). (2-A)
3.	 1 : 100,000 or 1 : 200,000 (0.01 mg/mL) is a 
very dilute concentration that is combined 
with local anesthetics (e.g., lidocaine). The 
adrenaline acts as a vasoconstrictor, which 
prolongs the duration of the anesthetic 
block and reduces systemic absorption and 
bleeding. (3-C)
The correct matching sequence is therefore 1-B, 
2-A, and 3-C.

EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020
169.	 (B) Reverse Trendelenburg
The image displays a patient lying supine on 
an operating table that is tilted so that the head 
is elevated higher than the feet. This specific 
position is known as the Reverse Trendelenburg 
position. It is commonly used in surgery to 
improve surgical exposure for procedures in 
the upper abdomen and head and neck, as 
gravity causes the abdominal viscera to move 
downwards. It is also used in patient care to 
help reduce intracranial pressure and improve 
respiration in some cases. The standard 
Trendelenburg position (A) is the opposite, 
with the patient's head positioned lower than 
their feet. The lithotomy position (C) involves 
placing the patient's legs in stirrups for pelvic or 
perineal procedures. The jack-knife position (D) 
is a prone position with the hips flexed, used for 
anorectal surgery.
